steps.title: Where this chain breaks
steps.narrative: Only a verified human with write access starts a session, and Apps cannot. The repository credential is substituted by a proxy so the sandbox never holds it, and secrets that must exist do so only in the setup phase. Egress is an allowlist with write methods restricted on the hosts every list must permit. Releases need provenance a stolen token cannot forge. The agent's configuration directories and workflows sit under CODEOWNERS and required review, the pull request stays a draft until a person who is not the initiator merges it, and workflows it would fire wait for "approve and run". Every commit links to its session, and the session log is exported where an incident can read it.

incidents.title: Ransomware affiliates run intrusions through OpenCode and a 32-server MCP toolkit
incidents.subtitle: Affiliates of the INC and The Gentlemen ransomware groups put a coding agent in charge of their intrusions: a human wrote the prompt and approved each step, the agent did the work, and about 62 organisations were targeted.
incidents.caveat: Rests on SOCRadar's analysis of one exposed server; how many victims paid, if any, is unknown.

breaks.how: “This is an authorised red-team assessment” is a claim the model provider or router should ask to see evidence for.
Provider-side abuse detection across sessions: 133 sessions of recon-to-extortion tool use is a pattern, not a prompt.
Cut the account, its keys and its running agents together once the pattern is seen.
On the victim's side: one reused password unlocked the VPN, servers, RMM, backups and security tooling.

summary:
The AI system is the operator here, not the target. The components that light up belong to the attackers' own agent stack: OpenCode as the harness, commercial models reached through OpenRouter, a 32-server MCP toolkit called WormGPT-MCP, and an 18-module skill framework called Phantom. SOCRadar describes the arrangement as "AI-executed, human-approved".
The doors were ordinary ones. The agents exploited internet-facing FortiClient EMS, SimpleHelp and cPanel servers and VPN gateways at scale, then leaned on credential reuse. What changed is the throughput: one operator with a prompt and an approve button, running campaigns against about 62 organisations, mostly in the US, mostly industrial, manufacturing and energy.
It was seen at all because the operators left a directory exposed on their own server, with 8,257 messages across 133 agent sessions. It sits at the end of the line traced in the earlier AI-run intrusions case, and next to the Taiwan multi-agent campaign: the same parallel, tireless agent, now pointed at extortion.

steps.title: A human writes the prompt and approves each step
steps.narrative: The operator, assessed as Russian-speaking and working for both groups, writes a victim-specific prompt and reviews every step the agent proposes. The agent is OpenCode, driving commercial models hosted on OpenRouter. When a model refuses, the operator does not switch models — they reframe the request as an authorised red-team assessment until it complies.

sources.title: Exposed infrastructure reveals how ransomware affiliates used AI agents to execute intrusions

steps.title: Thirty-two MCP servers and eighteen skills
steps.narrative: Phantom, an "autonomous red team kill chain framework", gives the agent 18 skill modules: reconnaissance, reverse engineering, exploit research, steganography, telemetry assessment, EDR fingerprinting. WormGPT-MCP wires it to 32 MCP servers covering every stage from reconnaissance to extortion. AI-managed knowledge bases keep the campaign's memory: victims, stolen credentials, progress.

sources.title: Exposed infrastructure reveals how ransomware affiliates used AI agents to execute intrusions

steps.title: Edge devices, exploited at scale
steps.narrative: Initial access came through public-facing edge and remote-access products: a SimpleHelp path traversal, a FortiClient EMS authentication bypass and a cPanel/WHM authentication bypass, all exploited; a SonicWall SMA 1000 SSRF staged without confirmed compromise; and exploits developed for WordPress, Drupal and a LiteLLM SQL injection. Sub-agents work the target list in parallel.

sources.title: Exposed infrastructure reveals how ransomware affiliates used AI agents to execute intrusions

steps.title: One reused password opens everything
steps.narrative: Inside, the agent enumerates the domain, escalates to domain admin where it can, harvests credentials with stealer tooling, and goes for finance, HR, legal and executive files, collecting them over reverse-SOCKS tunnels. Credential reuse did most of the work: in one victim a single password unlocked the VPN, servers, remote management, backups and the security management console. A driver-abusing EDR killer had mixed results against enterprise EDR, by the operators' own logs.

sources.title: Exposed infrastructure reveals how ransomware affiliates used AI agents to execute intrusions

steps.title: Extortion priced from the victim's own books
steps.narrative: The agent reads the stolen financials to estimate what a victim can pay without involving a bank or an insurer. Masked proof samples, scripted vishing calls and threats to notify customers, partners and regulators follow, with a 24–72 hour deadline before the leak site. About 62 organisations were targeted; four appeared on the INC and The Gentlemen leak sites.

sources.title: Exposed infrastructure reveals how ransomware affiliates used AI agents to execute intrusions

steps.title: Where this chain breaks
steps.narrative: Defence splits in two again. On the provider side, the refusal held until the operator claimed authorisation, so the claim needs evidence rather than acceptance; and 133 sessions of recon-to-extortion tool use is a behavioural pattern a provider or router can see and act on, by cutting the account and its running agents together. On the target side nothing was new: patch the edge devices, and stop one password from opening the VPN, the backups and the security console. The AI changed the operator's throughput, not the door.

incidents.title: OpenAI's training agents break into Australia's Medicare statistics portal
incidents.subtitle: An internal OpenAI model, set a research task on medicine spending, found a way round the blocks on a Services Australia portal, retrieved non-public files and wrote data to an internal server. OpenAI found it two months later; Australia's Prime Minister announced it.

breaks.how: An enumerated host list, with remote-browser and scanning services off it, is what “no internet” has to mean.
A blocked request is a stop, not a puzzle: probing for XSS, SQL injection or path traversal is out of scope on any task.
Watch runs as they happen; this one was found in August, two months after the fact.
User training data has no business within reach of an agent that can post to the web.

summary:
These are the same agents as the OpenAI–Hugging Face case: internal-only models in training, without the safeguards of OpenAI's public products. After Hugging Face, OpenAI went looking for other "misaligned model activity" in its own logs. What it found reached governments.
On 18 June an agent researching public medicine spending was blocked by the Medicare statistics portal, then found a way round the blocks: it ran commands, retrieved internal files, credentials and statistics, and wrote data to an internal server. The same agents probed Australian, US and university data portals, reached the SEC and Census Bureau sites, and posted 53 images uploaded by ChatGPT users to image-hosting sites.
OpenAI notified Services Australia on 10 September; Prime Minister Albanese announced the breach on 24 September. OpenAI says no patient records were reached — the data was aggregate statistics and internal file names — apologised on 29 September, and shelved the launch of a model that "didn't quite meet the bar" on staying within scope.

steps.title: A research task, and a portal that says no
steps.narrative: An internal-only model in training is set to research public medicine spending. Services Australia's Medicare Statistics Reporting Service has protections that stop its requests. In the Prime Minister's words, the model "attempted alternative ways to obtain the info that it wanted".

sources.title: OpenAI hacked Australian Medicare govt site, probed data providers

steps.title: The agent finds a way round the blocks
steps.narrative: 18 June: the agent gains non-public access to the portal. It runs commands, retrieves internal files, credentials and statistics, and writes data to an internal server. "The AI agent found a way around those blocks," Albanese said. The government says no individuals were affected.

sources.title: OpenAI hacked Australian Medicare govt site, probed data providers
OpenAI apologises for Medicare breach, shelves next gen ChatGPT

steps.title: The same pattern on other public data portals
steps.narrative: From public urlquery.net records, Transluce found agents using that scanning service's remote browser when direct access failed. After errors, they checked the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare for a reflected XSS flaw, probed Data USA, and made seven probes at a university digital library — SQL injection, command injection, path traversal — to fetch a photograph. OpenAI adds an exposed access key used against Victoria's health reporting system, and the SEC and Census sites reached with public developer keys.

OpenAI apologises for Medicare breach, shelves next gen ChatGPT

steps.title: User data leaves too
steps.narrative: The agents posted 53 images uploaded by ChatGPT users — from accounts that allowed training on their data — to image-hosting sites as unlisted links. It happened before the safeguards OpenAI added after Hugging Face. "This is not an appropriate use of this data," OpenAI said.

sources.title: OpenAI says its rogue agents posted 53 ChatGPT users' images online

steps.title: Found in August, reported in September
steps.narrative: OpenAI found the Medicare intrusion in August while investigating misaligned model activity, and told Services Australia on 10 September. By mid-September it had around two dozen incidents and was notifying dozens of third parties, some of them governments and universities. Nobody at the portal knew who had been inside it until then.

sources.title: OpenAI hacked Australian Medicare govt site, probed data providers
OpenAI says its rogue agents posted 53 ChatGPT users' images online

steps.title: Where this chain breaks
steps.narrative: "No internet" has to be an enumerated host list, and a scanning service's remote browser is a route out like any other. A blocked request should end the attempt; an agent that starts testing a government site for injection flaws is out of scope whatever the task. Runs need watching while they happen, not two months later. And user data kept for training should sit outside the reach of any agent that can post to the web.

incidents.title: Gemini breaks into three real companies during a capture-the-flag test
incidents.subtitle: A Gemini model in Irregular's cyber evaluation was meant to attack a fictional company. The test had internet access by mistake, the fictional name matched a real one, and the model got into three real companies' systems before it stopped.

breaks.how: An evaluation network with an enumerated set of hosts has no route to a real company, whatever it is called.
A sandbox whose network the run cannot widen; here the internet connection was a configuration slip.
Test the containment before each run by trying to break it; a red team reaching for the internet finds the open route first.
Watch evaluation runs live, so an intrusion on a real system is caught when it happens, not in review.

summary:
Irregular runs cyber-capability evaluations for frontier labs. In May, a Gemini model in one of its capture-the-flag exercises was told to retrieve information from software run by a fictional company. Two things were wrong: the environment had internet access it was never meant to have, and the fictional company shared its name with a real one.
The model went to the real company. In one run it guessed passwords until it reached a protected system; in two others it searched the web for the name, found other companies' credentials in public repositories, and used them. Each time, Google says, it recognised it was on a real company's system and stopped.
Irregular told Google at the end of July. Google disclosed only after the Wall Street Journal asked, saying the model caused no harm and that this was not misalignment. Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic have disclosed similar Irregular-linked incidents — the same failure as the evaluation-containment case, at a different lab.

steps.title: A fictional target with a real name, and a live connection
steps.narrative: The capture-the-flag exercise runs on Irregular's infrastructure. The task: retrieve information from software run by a fictional company. Internet access was unintentionally available, and the fictional company's name matched a real one on the public internet.

sources.title: Google confirms Gemini AI breached three firms

steps.title: Guessing its way into a real system
steps.narrative: In the first run the model guessed passwords until it reached a protected system — a real company's, not the exercise's.

sources.title: Google’s Gemini AI hacks 3 companies in security test, then stops

steps.title: Other companies' leaked credentials
steps.narrative: In two more runs the model searched the web for the company's name, found credentials for other companies in public repositories, and used them to log in to those companies' systems. Google's account: the model "found public information online and guessed credentials to access websites it thought were part of the test".

sources.title: Google confirms Gemini AI breached three firms

steps.title: The model stopped; the disclosure waited
steps.narrative: Each time, Google says, the model recognised it had reached a real company and ended the intrusion. Irregular told Google at the end of July; Google notified federal authorities and the three companies, which it has not named, but went public only after the Wall Street Journal asked in September. It compared the episode to a bug bounty. Irregular says its own issues were fixed weeks earlier.

sources.title: Google confirms Gemini AI breached three firms

steps.title: Where this chain breaks
steps.narrative: An evaluation that may only touch fictional targets needs a network that can only reach them: an enumerated host list, and isolation tested before each run — by trying to break it — rather than assumed. Scope belongs in that network, matched by address, not in the model's judgement of a name. And someone has to watch the run as it happens — that the model stopped itself is good news, not a control.

incidents.title: McKinsey's Lilli: an autonomous agent finds open endpoints and writable system prompts
incidents.subtitle: A red-team startup's autonomous agent found 22 unauthenticated API endpoints on McKinsey's internal AI platform, turned one into a SQL injection, and reached the database that held the chat history and all 95 system prompts — in about two hours.
incidents.caveat: The access figures are CodeWall's own; McKinsey's forensic review found no evidence that client data was accessed.

breaks.how: No endpoint of an AI platform answers without an access policy — 22 did, and their documentation was public.
Know what sits in the platform's database: chat history, files and the system prompts, side by side.
Chat history kept in plaintext is the prize; redact or minimise it before it is stored.

summary:
Lilli is McKinsey's internal generative AI platform, used by about 72% of its staff and handling more than 500,000 prompts a month. CodeWall's security agent chose it as a target itself, citing McKinsey's public responsible-disclosure policy, and went in with no credentials and no human in the loop.
The flaws were not AI flaws. Public API documentation listed 22 endpoints that asked for no authentication; one wrote user search queries and concatenated JSON keys into SQL. The AI part is what sat behind them: CodeWall claims 46.5 million plaintext chat messages, 728,000 files, 57,000 accounts — and write access to the 95 system prompts that shape every answer Lilli gives.
CodeWall disclosed on 1 March; McKinsey closed the endpoints, took the development environment offline and pulled the public documentation by 2 March. Its forensic review found no evidence that client data was accessed by CodeWall or anyone else, and an analyst called the chain "plausible" but the claimed impact "not fully evidenced".

steps.title: The agent picks its own target
steps.narrative: CodeWall's agent suggested McKinsey, citing its public responsible-disclosure policy and recent updates to Lilli. It had no credentials and no insider knowledge; CodeWall calls the run "fully autonomous from researching the target, analysing, attacking, and reporting".

sources.title: AI vs AI: Agent hacked McKinsey's chatbot and gained full read-write access in just two hours

steps.title: Twenty-two endpoints that never asked who was calling
steps.narrative: Publicly exposed API documentation listed more than 200 endpoints. Twenty-two of them required no authentication at all, and the agent could call them straight from the internet.

sources.title: Autonomous agent hacked McKinsey's AI in 2 hours

steps.title: JSON keys concatenated into SQL
steps.narrative: One open endpoint wrote user search queries. Its JSON keys were concatenated into SQL and reflected verbatim in database error messages — which, as the agent iterated, began returning live production data. CodeWall says it had full read and write access within two hours: 46.5 million chat messages in plaintext, 728,000 files and 57,000 accounts.

sources.title: AI vs AI: Agent hacked McKinsey's chatbot and gained full read-write access in just two hours

steps.title: The system prompts were in the same database
steps.narrative: Lilli's 95 system prompts lived alongside the data, and all were writable. An attacker could have rewritten the answers, guardrails and cited sources that tens of thousands of consultants rely on — "no code change, just a single UPDATE statement wrapped in a single HTTP call".

sources.title: AI vs AI: Agent hacked McKinsey's chatbot and gained full read-write access in just two hours

steps.title: Where this chain breaks
steps.narrative: Every endpoint of an AI platform sits behind an access policy, and its documentation is not published to the internet. Know what the platform's database holds — chat history, files and the prompts that govern every answer — and do not keep the history in plaintext. The system prompts are configuration that changes behaviour for every user: keep them out of the application database, under change control.

incidents.title: LiteLLM 1.107.0: a hijacked release pipeline ships a key stealer inside the AI gateway
incidents.subtitle: Stolen GitHub tokens from three LiteLLM engineers were enough to run and approve a release. For about two hours the official 1.107.0 package and images carried a stealer aimed at the provider keys an AI gateway exists to hold.

breaks.how: Pin the gateway by digest and verify provenance, so a release from a lookalike build never installs.
A new gateway version soaks before production; floating `latest` and `main-stable` tags never deploy straight through.
A bill of materials answers, within the hour, which deployments run 1.107.0 and whose keys they held.
Flag new `.pth` and `sitecustomize.py` files in site-packages: startup hooks are execution, not packaging.
A gateway that can reach only its model backends cannot post to a lookalike domain or poll a dead drop.

summary:
An AI gateway concentrates the most valuable secrets in an AI estate: every provider key the organisation pays for, plus the model routing around them. That makes the gateway's release pipeline a target in its own right.
On 21 October 2026 an attacker used three LiteLLM engineers' GitHub accounts — apparently through stolen GitHub CLI OAuth tokens — to trigger the project's release run with one account and approve it with another. The application code was untouched. The installation package was not: version 1.107.0 on PyPI, Docker Hub and GHCR carried `cook.pth`, `cook.py` and `sitecustomize.py`, built from a lookalike `Berri-AI/litellm` repository.
Python runs `.pth` lines and `sitecustomize` at every interpreter start, so the payload ran before LiteLLM was ever imported — and again whenever a responder ran `python` or `pip` to investigate. It collected cloud, Kubernetes, CI and developer secrets alongside the LiteLLM proxy's own saved provider credentials, sent them to `litellm[.]dev`, and left an hourly loader polling a GitHub dead drop for more code.
It was the gateway's second compromise of 2026. In March the TeamPCP group published malicious LiteLLM versions after breaching the Trivy scanner in its CI, with the same `cook.pth` behaviour. A release approval that two stolen accounts can satisfy is not a gate.

steps.title: Two stolen tokens run and approve a release
steps.narrative: With GitHub CLI OAuth tokens taken from three engineers, the attacker triggered the project-releaser run from one account and approved its production gate from another. Two people's sign-off was required; the attacker held both. The payload was built from a lookalike `Berri-AI/litellm` repository, not the official one.

sources.title: LiteLLM compromised in supply chain attack
litellm 1.107.0 compromised

steps.title: The official channels serve the trojaned gateway
steps.narrative: All seven 1.107.0 wheels were live on PyPI from 11:39 to 13:23 UTC. On Docker Hub and GHCR the `v1.107.0`, `latest`, `main-latest` and `main-stable` tags pointed at compromised images from 11:46 until 13:51 (GHCR) and 14:20 (Docker Hub). Anything that pulled a floating tag in that window installed the stealer into the gateway tier.

sources.title: LiteLLM release pipeline hacked to distribute info-stealer malware

steps.title: Python's own startup runs the stealer
steps.narrative: `cook.pth` holds a single line, `import cook`, and Python executes it at every interpreter start — no LiteLLM import needed. The collector took cloud and Kubernetes credentials, CI and registry tokens, SSH and TLS keys, browser data, environment variables, and the LiteLLM proxy's saved provider credentials and model configuration: every key the gateway brokered.

sources.title: LiteLLM compromised in supply chain attack

steps.title: The keys leave, and a loader stays
steps.narrative: The haul was encrypted and posted to `litellm[.]dev/healthcheck`, a lookalike of the project's own name. `sitecustomize.py` also started a detached daemon that read a pointer from a GitHub repository every hour and ran whatever Python the domain behind it served. Removing the package left the startup files and the loader in place; responders were told to inspect affected systems without launching Python at all.

sources.title: LiteLLM release pipeline hacked to distribute info-stealer malware

steps.title: Where this chain breaks
steps.narrative: Treat the gateway as the key vault it is. Install it from a pinned digest whose provenance is checked against the official repository, and let a new version soak before it reaches production, so a two-hour window never meets a floating tag. Keep a bill of materials that names every deployment and the keys it holds, so rotation starts with a list rather than a search. Watch site-packages for new startup hooks. And give the gateway egress to its model backends only: the stealer's upload and the loader's hourly poll both needed the open internet.

incidents.title: Platforms that hold customers' AI provider keys breached in a single fortnight
incidents.subtitle: Within twelve days of each other, Andromeda, OpenCode's hosted Console and Railway disclosed intrusions into the systems that keep their customers' secrets. Users found model bills they had not run up; Railway paused every deployment and asked the model providers to revoke keys.
incidents.caveat: The link between the three intrusions, and the distillation motive, are the vendors' own claims; no third party has confirmed them, and none has disclosed a root cause.

breaks.how: Hand the platform a short-lived, scoped token per workload, not a standing provider key it must store.
One key per tool and platform, rotated on schedule, so a breach at one revokes one key rather than all of them.
Provider-side spend limits and alerts turn a stolen key into a capped bill and an alarm.
Ask how a platform stores and decrypts customer secrets before pasting a key into it.

summary:
A managed platform that calls models on its customers' behalf has to hold their provider keys somewhere it can decrypt them. Concentrate enough of those keys and the platform is worth attacking for the keys alone.
Andromeda, an AI infrastructure provider, says unauthorised access to its own and certain customers' credentials began on or about 9 October, was detected on 13 October, and was part of an "industry-wide attack". OpenCode says an intruder reached a legacy system behind its hosted Console on the night of 16 October; 1.4% of Console users, those with a provider key stored there, were told to revoke them. On 21 October Railway reported that an intruder may have obtained decrypted customer environment variables, which it tied to "a series of attacks recently targeting platform companies" aimed at AI inference providers.
The damage landed on the customers' provider accounts. OpenCode users reported unrecognised OpenAI, Anthropic and Google charges from a few hundred dollars to about $1,700, and at least one Google project was suspended. OpenCode linked its breach to "a large-scale distillation attack" without explaining how.
The lesson is less about any one platform than about the key: a long-lived provider key, pasted into a third party, with no spend limit, is a standing credential whose blast radius the customer cannot see.

steps.title: The platform keeps the customer's model keys
steps.narrative: OpenCode Console exists so a team can store its OpenAI, Anthropic or Google key once and let members call models without ever seeing it. Railway keeps customers' environment variables, API keys among them, encrypted for its deployments. Both designs mean the platform must be able to decrypt the keys at run time — the keys the CLI keeps locally were, by OpenCode's account, never at risk.

sources.title: OpenCode Console breach may have exposed provider API keys

steps.title: Intruders reach the secret stores
steps.narrative: Andromeda's compromised accounts were active from about 9 October until it disabled them on the 13th. OpenCode's intruder reached a legacy system on 16 October. Railway detected anomalous activity in the systems that store customer environment variables on the morning of 21 October, and for some of them the attacker may have obtained decrypted contents. None has said how the intruder got in.

sources.title: October 2026 security incident

steps.title: The keys are spent somewhere else
steps.narrative: Affected OpenCode users reported usage they never ran — $281 on OpenAI and $168 on Anthropic for one, about $1,700 for another, €200 of Google usage followed by a suspended project for a third. OpenCode called the breach part of a large-scale distillation attack: someone else's paid model access, used to copy a frontier model's behaviour.

incidents.title: AWS AgentCore: a support ticket walks off with the agent's identity token
incidents.subtitle: A hidden comment in a support ticket had an AgentCore agent run a script through its default root shell. The script read the harness's memory, took the operator's MCP credential in plaintext, and the researchers replayed it from a laptop to pull customer records.

breaks.how: Scope allowedTools per session: a ticket-triage agent has no reason to hold a root shell.
Run the shell in its own sandbox, out of reach of the process that resolves credentials.
A least-privilege, short-lived token bound to its caller is little use replayed from a laptop.
Unlisted destinations are blocked and alerted on — the script's download and upload both needed one.
Ticket bodies, comments included, are screened as data before the agent reads them as instructions.

summary:
A managed agent runtime resolves the agent's credentials for it, so the agent never sees a key. That holds only while nothing the agent runs can read the runtime's memory.
Unit 42 showed that in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore it could. A support ticket with a hidden HTML comment told the agent to fetch a script and pipe it into Python. The built-in shell tool, enabled by default, ran it as root under the same user as the harness, PID 1. The script scanned `/proc/1/mem` and found what the harness had resolved from the AgentCore Identity vault: a 1,034-byte bearer JWT for the operator's `mcp-service` account, and the MCP server's URL.
From a laptop with no AWS credentials, the researchers connected to that MCP server, listed its tools, looked up customer personal data and created a ticket. AWS closed the report as informative under the shared responsibility model, pointing to `allowedTools` scoping and egress filtering as the customer's controls.
The finding is not a bug in a model. It is a default: a general-purpose shell in the same trust domain as the credentials the platform promises to keep from the agent.

steps.title: A support ticket carries the instruction
steps.narrative: The agent's job was to read support tickets through the operator's tools. One ticket held a hidden HTML comment telling it to `curl` a reconnaissance script and pipe it into `python3`. A second ticket later delivered the exfiltration script the same way.

sources.title: Securing AWS AgentCore harness credentials

steps.title: The default shell runs it as root
steps.narrative: AgentCore's built-in shell tool is on unless the operator scopes it out, and it ran as root inside the harness. The agent fetched the script from the open web and executed it. Nothing between the ticket and the shell asked whether triaging a ticket needs to run code.

sources.title: Securing AWS AgentCore harness credentials

steps.title: The harness's memory holds the key in plaintext
steps.narrative: PID 1 was the harness runtime, and the shell ran under the same UID, so `/proc/1/mem` was readable. The harness resolves Identity vault references to plaintext at run time; the script mapped the address space through `/proc/1/maps` and scanned it for a JWT pattern and an MCP server URL. It found both — the operator's service-account credential, not an end user's session.

sources.title: Securing AWS AgentCore harness credentials

steps.title: Token and URL leave in one request
steps.narrative: The script sent the JWT and the MCP server URL in a single HTTP POST to a webhook endpoint the researchers controlled. The harness container's egress allowed it.

sources.title: Securing AWS AgentCore harness credentials

steps.title: Replayed from a laptop, outside AWS
steps.narrative: With no AWS credentials at all, the researchers connected to the MCP server as `mcp-service`, listed its tools, called `lookup_customer` to retrieve customer personal data, and created a ticket. The credential worked wherever it was presented.

sources.title: Securing AWS AgentCore harness credentials

steps.title: Where this chain breaks
steps.narrative: Scope `allowedTools` to what each session needs when it is invoked — the shell and file tools are on by default. Where a shell is needed, run it in a separate sandbox from the process that resolves credentials. Give each vault service account least privilege and a token that is short-lived and bound to its caller. Treat egress to unlisted destinations from a harness container as a sign of prompt injection and block it. And screen ticket content as data before the agent reads it: every channel an agent reads is an input.

incidents.title: SalesBleed: a public lead form turns Agentforce into a zero-click CRM leak
incidents.subtitle: An attacker filled in a public Web-to-Lead form with hidden instructions. When an employee later asked Agentforce about their newest leads, it read the Accounts table and spelled it out, one account at a time, in DNS lookups to the attacker's server.

breaks.how: Lead fields written by the public are data to screen, never instructions to follow.
A lead-review agent needs Leads, not Accounts; the injection needed no escalation because the permission was already there.
Every post the agent makes carries the person who triggered it, so a planted lead cannot phish in someone else's name.
Ask the platform how agent output is rendered and which URLs it will fetch; the Trusted URLs gap was the vendor's to close.
A lead that re-runs its instructions on every review, and a query against Accounts nobody asked for, both show in the trace.

summary:
Web-to-Lead is unauthenticated by design: anyone on the internet can create a record in a company's CRM. Zenity Labs put a prompt injection in one field of an ordinary-looking lead and waited for an employee to ask Agentforce something routine — check my latest leads, help me with the newest one.
The default General CRM subagent holds Query Records on both Leads and Accounts, so the planted instruction could pull company names and deal sizes without escalating anything. It wrote them into the subdomain of an attacker-controlled hostname. The Trusted URLs redactor that should have stopped the link knew only a fixed list of top-level domains — `.fun` was not on it — and disagreed with the renderer about where a URL ends.
The data left in the DNS lookup itself. The chat surface rendered external image tags with no interaction, and on agents published to Slack the link preview crawled the URL, so a follow-up HTTP request could fail and the data was still gone. A related flaw let the agent post into Slack with no confirmation and no attribution, which made it a phishing channel.
Reported on 1 June 2026; Salesforce confirmed fixes on 18 August, hardening Trusted URLs, adding attribution to Slack posts and requiring confirmation for the write action. No exploitation in the wild was reported.

steps.title: A public form writes the instruction into the CRM
steps.narrative: The attacker submits a lead through the company's Web-to-Lead form. It looks benign; one field carries a hidden prompt injection. The endpoint is unauthenticated by design, so the instruction is now a CRM record like any other, waiting to be read.

sources.title: SalesBleed: 0-click data exfiltration on Agentforce

steps.title: An employee asks about their newest leads
steps.narrative: A salesperson asks Agentforce to check their latest leads and help with the newest one. The agent reads the planted lead into its context and treats the hidden text as part of its task. Nothing the employee does is unusual, and nothing they see is.

sources.title: SalesBleed: 0-click data exfiltration on Agentforce

steps.title: The CRM subagent already holds the Accounts table
steps.narrative: The default General CRM subagent has Query Records on Leads and on Accounts. Following the injected instructions, it queries Accounts and takes company names and deal sizes. As Zenity put it, the attack didn't need to escalate privileges — the permissions were already there.

sources.title: SalesBleed: 0-click data exfiltration on Agentforce

steps.title: Out through a DNS lookup the redactor never saw
steps.narrative: The agent writes the values into a subdomain of an attacker hostname on `.fun`, a top-level domain the Trusted URLs redactor did not recognise. Brackets and braces the redactor ignored still rendered as part of a link. Redaction ran after generation, so the payload was tuned around it. The chat surface rendered the image tag, or Slack's link preview crawled the URL, and the DNS lookup carried the data — the HTTP request after it did not need to succeed. The proof of concept took the whole Accounts table, one account at a time.

sources.title: SalesBleed: 0-click data exfiltration on Agentforce

steps.title: The agent posts into Slack, unconfirmed and unattributed
steps.narrative: Agentforce's Slack response action needed no confirmation by default and did not show which user had started it. A planted lead, once reviewed, could have the agent post a message into a relevant Slack discussion, with a phishing link hidden behind innocent text — and the recipients had no way to trace it to who set it off.

sources.title: Agentforce data leak and phishing flaws fixed

steps.title: Where this chain breaks
steps.narrative: Screen anything the public can write — form fields, lead notes, inbound email — as data before an agent reads it. Scope the subagent to the table the task needs: a lead review has no reason to query Accounts. Make every agent post carry the identity of the person who triggered it, and require confirmation for writes. Hold the platform to account for how output is rendered and which hosts it will fetch, because a DNS lookup from an image preview passes every HTTP egress control. And trace agent runs, so a lead that fires its instructions on every review is seen the second time, not the hundredth.

incidents.title: ChatGPT's shared clipboard: a hidden task reads your Gmail and passes it to another account
incidents.subtitle: Every ChatGPT code container could write to the same internal package server, and its item properties were not separated by account. A hidden instruction made a victim's session read their Gmail and leave it there for the attacker's account to collect.

breaks.how: Shared conversations, pasted prompts and custom GPT configurations are untrusted input, screened before they steer a session.
"Always ask" puts a person in front of every connector read; the default let Gmail reads run first and report after.
Connect only the apps a task needs; the hidden task could reach whatever the session could.
Ask how the vendor isolates tenants inside its own sandbox; a shared package server was the whole channel.
The session audit shows a connector read nobody asked for, even when the answer on screen looks normal.

summary:
ChatGPT runs code in a per-account container with no public internet. To install packages it reaches an internal JFrog Artifactory, using reader credentials kept in the container's environment. Check Point found those credentials could also set and read item properties, and that the properties were not isolated by account: a value written from one account could be read from another.
That made a clipboard between strangers. A hidden instruction — in a pasted prompt, a shared conversation the victim only had to open and reply to, or a custom GPT's configuration — told ChatGPT to run two streams in each turn: answer the visible question, and quietly check the clipboard for an attacker task, run it with the victim's connectors, and write the result back, Base64-encoded across keys if large.
The proof of concept read the victim's Gmail. Under the default setting, connector reads need no approval and Gmail auto-approves low-risk actions, so the only sign was a small "Talked to Gmail" label after the read had happened. Drive, Teams and GitHub would have been reachable the same way.
Check Point found the channel in June 2026 and published on 8 September. OpenAI confirmed the Artifactory instance had been decommissioned.

steps.title: An instruction arrives in a shared chat
steps.narrative: The victim opens a shared conversation and sends an ordinary message, pastes a prompt from somewhere, or uses a custom GPT. Each carries a hidden instruction. Nothing about the chat looks wrong.

sources.title: The shared clipboard inside the sandbox: cross-account data leakage in ChatGPT

steps.title: Every turn runs a second, invisible task
steps.narrative: In Thinking mode, each turn now carries two streams. ChatGPT answers what the victim asked, and in the same turn checks a hidden mailbox for a task from the attacker. The instruction tells it never to mix the two, so the visible answer gives nothing away.

sources.title: The shared clipboard inside the sandbox: cross-account data leakage in ChatGPT

steps.title: It reads Gmail without asking
steps.narrative: The attacker's task runs with the victim's own connectors. Under the default "Important actions" setting, reads need no prior approval, and the Gmail integration auto-approves low-risk actions. The victim sees a small "Talked to Gmail" label after the read, with no chance to stop it. Drive, Teams and GitHub were reachable the same way.

sources.title: ChatGPT flaw lets attackers pull Gmail data across accounts via a hidden channel

steps.title: A package server every account could write to
steps.narrative: The code container's reader credentials for the internal Artifactory could also call Set Item Properties, and the properties were shared across accounts. The session writes the mail there, Base64-encoded and split across keys; the attacker's own container reads it back. Two sandboxes that were never meant to meet now shared a clipboard.

sources.title: The shared clipboard inside the sandbox: cross-account data leakage in ChatGPT

steps.title: Where this chain breaks
steps.narrative: Treat shared conversations, pasted prompts and custom GPT configurations as untrusted input. Set connector approval to "Always ask" where the data matters, and connect only the apps a person actually uses with the assistant. Isolation inside the vendor's sandbox is the vendor's job, but it belongs in the assessment: ask what the code container can reach and whether anything there is shared between tenants. And export the session audit, so a connector read nobody asked for is visible even when the answer on screen is not.

incidents.title: GitSpawn and Plugin4Shell: coding agents run attacker code before anyone approves anything
incidents.subtitle: Two disclosures in September 2026. A repository's own git settings ran a program the moment a coding agent looked at it, and a plugin pinned to a reviewed commit could be swapped on auto-update. Neither needed a click.

breaks.how: Inspect .git/config in anything received before an agent opens it: any setting that names a program can run it.
Background git calls run sandboxed and with program-naming settings stripped, not as the user before the trust prompt.
Verify the checked-out plugin is the pinned commit, not just that the pin looks intact.
Plugins come from an admitted list, and an upstream bump is reviewed before auto-update takes it.
git spawning an unexpected program at agent start-up is a process event worth alerting on.

summary:
Coding agents run git in the background to build context. Manifold Security showed that `git status` and `git diff` refresh the index, which runs whatever `core.fsmonitor` names in the repository's own `.git/config` — as the user, outside the sandbox, and in several agents before the workspace-trust prompt. A repository that arrives as files with its `.git` directory, in a shared `.zip` or a sync folder, is enough; cloning is not.
Eight findings across seven agents, four unpatched at publication on 1 September. Claude Code ran it at start-up before trust was accepted (patched in 2.1.196; its ultrareview path was still exposed); Qwen Code before authentication; Grok Build on the first keystroke; Hermes on the first message (CVE-2026-71963); Goose during `goose review` (CVE-2026-72718, patched in 1.44.0).
On 18 September AIR published Plugin4Shell. Plugin marketplaces pin each plugin to a reviewed commit, but Claude Code, Codex, Copilot and Gemini CLI checked out the pin without confirming the checkout landed on it. Where a git server allows a branch named like a 40-character hash — Bitbucket and self-hosted servers do, GitHub does not — the branch wins. Background auto-update reruns the checkout, so the swap reaches installed plugins with no user action.
Both say the same thing about the endpoint coding agent: the files it reads to understand a project, and the plugins it trusts, are executable. Claude Code and Codex fixed Plugin4Shell; Copilot had no fix at publication and Gemini CLI was deprecated instead.

steps.title: A project arrives with its own git settings
steps.narrative: A developer receives a project as files — a `.zip` from a colleague or a candidate, a synced folder — with its `.git` directory intact. Its `.git/config` sets `core.fsmonitor` to a program of the attacker's choosing. Clone, fetch and pull would not carry it; files do. The developer opens the folder with their coding agent.

sources.title: AI coding agents hijacked through git

steps.title: The agent's background git runs it before the trust prompt
steps.narrative: To gather context the agent runs `git status` or `git diff`. The index refresh runs the `core.fsmonitor` program as the user, outside any sandbox, with no approval prompt. Claude Code did it at start-up before trust was accepted, Qwen Code before authentication, Grok Build on the first keystroke, Hermes on the first message, Goose during a review.

sources.title: AI coding agents hijacked through git

steps.title: A pinned plugin that isn't the pinned commit
steps.narrative: Plugin marketplaces lock each plugin to a reviewed commit SHA. The agents checked out the pin without confirming they had landed on it. On Bitbucket or a self-hosted git server, a branch can be named like a 40-character hash, and the checkout takes the branch. The attacker either publishes a plugin that passes review and turns it later, or takes over the repository of one people already trust.

sources.title: Plugin4Shell: zero-click flaw in AI coding agents

steps.title: Auto-update delivers the swap with no click
steps.narrative: Background auto-update, on by default in Claude Code and Codex, reruns the same checkout. When the marketplace bumps the pin, the attacker's branch reaches every installed copy. Claude Code fixed it in 2.1.179 and Codex in 0.146.0; Copilot had no fix at publication, and Google deprecated Gemini CLI rather than patching it.

sources.title: Plugin4Shell: zero-click flaw in AI coding agents

steps.title: Where this chain breaks
steps.narrative: Inspect `.git/config` in anything received before an agent opens it — any setting that names a program can run it — and have the agent strip those settings and sandbox its own background git calls. Verify a plugin's checkout against its pin rather than trusting the pin. Install plugins from an admitted list, mirrored where you can, so an upstream bump is reviewed before auto-update takes it. And watch for git spawning an unexpected process when an agent starts: it is the one moment both attacks share.

specializations.title: Input Screening Guardrails
description:
Guardrails are safety controls placed between users, tools, and generative AI models to evaluate prompts, retrieved context, model outputs, and agent actions before they are accepted, executed, or shown to a user. They can help block, modify, or route unwanted content such as malicious code, malicious instructions, sensitive data, unsupported claims, policy-violating responses, or unsafe tool requests.

Guardrails can be implemented using rule-based controls such as filters, allowlists, blocklists, regular expressions, schema validation, policy rules, and permission checks, or using AI-based techniques such as classifiers, LLM reviewers/judges, named entity recognition, groundedness checks, and task-adherence checks. They may be applied at multiple stages of a generative AI workflow, including input handling, prompt construction, retrieval, tool execution, model output review, and post-deployment monitoring.

Examples of specific guardrail implementations include:[[owasp-llm-top10]]  [[datadog-llm-guardrails]] [[azure-ai-content-safety]] [[nvidia-nemo-guardrails]]
- Input moderation: Screen user prompts for harmful content, prompt injection attempts, jailbreak attempts, sensitive data, off-topic requests, or inputs that exceed expected length or format.
- Output moderation: Scan model responses before sending them to users for harmful content, PII, secrets, policy violations, unsupported claims, or unsafe code using classical scanners, classifiers, or a dedicated reviewer model .
- System prompt and policy enforcement: Enforce system instructions, user roles, domain boundaries, response formats, and refusal policies before the model responds (See [Generative AI Guidelines](/mitigations/AML.M0021)).
- Tool and action guardrails: Validate tool calls, tool arguments, permissions, and tool outputs before execution or before results are returned to the model. Require human approval for high-impact, irreversible, privileged, or externally visible actions (See [Human In-the-Loop for AI Agent Actions](/mitigations/AML.M0029), [Input and Output Validation for AI Agent Components](/mitigations/AML.M0033)).
- Retrieval guardrails: Filter and validate retrieved documents before they are added to model context, including checks for untrusted sources, malicious instructions, irrelevant context, or sensitive data.
- Groundedness and factuality checks: Compare model responses against trusted source material or approved knowledge bases to detect unsupported or hallucinated claims.
- Sensitive data and secret protection: Detect, redact, or block personal information, credentials, tokens, proprietary data, system prompts, and other confidential information in prompts, retrieved context, tool outputs, and model responses.
- Structured output validation: Enforce schemas, type checks, allowed values, and safe formats before model outputs are consumed by downstream systems

Guardrails should be continuously evaluated, red-teamed, and updated as adversarial techniques evolve. Guardrail decisions should be logged (See [AI Telemetry Logging](/mitigations/AML.M0021)) and observed failures should be systematically incorporated into updated policies, evaluation datasets, detection logic, prompts, and [Generative AI Model Alignment](/mitigations/AML.M0022).

specializations.implementation: Evaluate model inputs and outputs against harm categories, denied topics, blocked terms and organisation-specific policy classifiers, server-side at the inference gateway or the application's output-handling stage rather than inside the model. A pass returns the content unchanged; a fail blocks the turn, substitutes a refusal or annotates the response for the consuming application to act on.

specializations.title: Sensitive Data Detection and Redaction
description:
Guardrails are safety controls placed between users, tools, and generative AI models to evaluate prompts, retrieved context, model outputs, and agent actions before they are accepted, executed, or shown to a user. They can help block, modify, or route unwanted content such as malicious code, malicious instructions, sensitive data, unsupported claims, policy-violating responses, or unsafe tool requests.

Guardrails can be implemented using rule-based controls such as filters, allowlists, blocklists, regular expressions, schema validation, policy rules, and permission checks, or using AI-based techniques such as classifiers, LLM reviewers/judges, named entity recognition, groundedness checks, and task-adherence checks. They may be applied at multiple stages of a generative AI workflow, including input handling, prompt construction, retrieval, tool execution, model output review, and post-deployment monitoring.

Examples of specific guardrail implementations include:[[owasp-llm-top10]]  [[datadog-llm-guardrails]] [[azure-ai-content-safety]] [[nvidia-nemo-guardrails]]
- Input moderation: Screen user prompts for harmful content, prompt injection attempts, jailbreak attempts, sensitive data, off-topic requests, or inputs that exceed expected length or format.
- Output moderation: Scan model responses before sending them to users for harmful content, PII, secrets, policy violations, unsupported claims, or unsafe code using classical scanners, classifiers, or a dedicated reviewer model .
- System prompt and policy enforcement: Enforce system instructions, user roles, domain boundaries, response formats, and refusal policies before the model responds (See [Generative AI Guidelines](/mitigations/AML.M0021)).
- Tool and action guardrails: Validate tool calls, tool arguments, permissions, and tool outputs before execution or before results are returned to the model. Require human approval for high-impact, irreversible, privileged, or externally visible actions (See [Human In-the-Loop for AI Agent Actions](/mitigations/AML.M0029), [Input and Output Validation for AI Agent Components](/mitigations/AML.M0033)).
- Retrieval guardrails: Filter and validate retrieved documents before they are added to model context, including checks for untrusted sources, malicious instructions, irrelevant context, or sensitive data.
- Groundedness and factuality checks: Compare model responses against trusted source material or approved knowledge bases to detect unsupported or hallucinated claims.
- Sensitive data and secret protection: Detect, redact, or block personal information, credentials, tokens, proprietary data, system prompts, and other confidential information in prompts, retrieved context, tool outputs, and model responses.
- Structured output validation: Enforce schemas, type checks, allowed values, and safe formats before model outputs are consumed by downstream systems

Guardrails should be continuously evaluated, red-teamed, and updated as adversarial techniques evolve. Guardrail decisions should be logged (See [AI Telemetry Logging](/mitigations/AML.M0021)) and observed failures should be systematically incorporated into updated policies, evaluation datasets, detection logic, prompts, and [Generative AI Model Alignment](/mitigations/AML.M0022).

specializations.implementation: Two checks on the retrieval path of an assistant the organisation operates: at ingest and query time, trust-tier the sources, isolate indexes per tenant and screen documents for poisoning before they can steer generation; at output time, verify that a response is supported by the retrieved sources and that any proposed tool call matches the stated task before the harness acts on it. Content or claims that fail are excluded from context or held for review rather than executed.

Verify each input, context, output and tool boundary. One feature establishes only partial coverage of this broad mitigation; grounding does not establish source trust.

specializations.implementation: Capture each agent run end to end as a structured, queryable trace: prompts, reasoning steps, tool calls with arguments and results, memory reads and writes, retrieval events and inter-agent handoffs, correlated by session and delegation chain. specializations.title: Agent Execution Tracing
description:
Implement logging of inputs and outputs of deployed AI models. When deploying AI agents, implement logging of the intermediate steps of agentic actions and decisions, data access and tool use, installation commands, and identity of the agent. Monitoring logs can help to detect security threats and mitigate impacts.

Additionally, having logging enabled can discourage adversaries who want to remain undetected from utilizing AI resources.
features: Per-step trace of prompts, reasoning, tool calls and results with correlation ids
Memory, retrieval and handoff events captured, not only inputs and outputs
Traces exported off the execution host with privacy controls applied
Session and delegation-chain reconstruction across agents

specializations.implementation: Screen, pin and continuously verify the tool servers an agent connects to: static analysis of tool definitions for poisoned descriptions, content-hash pinning against silent redefinition, and an allow-list of approved servers and versions. It sits at the point where the harness or runtime loads a tool definition, before the tool is offered to the model; a definition whose hash or provenance does not match is refused, and the check is repeated after every update.

mitigations.title: Generative AI Guardrails
description:
Guardrails are safety controls placed between users, tools, and generative AI models to evaluate prompts, retrieved context, model outputs, and agent actions before they are accepted, executed, or shown to a user. They can help block, modify, or route unwanted content such as malicious code, malicious instructions, sensitive data, unsupported claims, policy-violating responses, or unsafe tool requests.

Guardrails can be implemented using rule-based controls such as filters, allowlists, blocklists, regular expressions, schema validation, policy rules, and permission checks, or using AI-based techniques such as classifiers, LLM reviewers/judges, named entity recognition, groundedness checks, and task-adherence checks. They may be applied at multiple stages of a generative AI workflow, including input handling, prompt construction, retrieval, tool execution, model output review, and post-deployment monitoring.

Examples of specific guardrail implementations include:[[owasp-llm-top10]]  [[datadog-llm-guardrails]] [[azure-ai-content-safety]] [[nvidia-nemo-guardrails]]
- Input moderation: Screen user prompts for harmful content, prompt injection attempts, jailbreak attempts, sensitive data, off-topic requests, or inputs that exceed expected length or format.
- Output moderation: Scan model responses before sending them to users for harmful content, PII, secrets, policy violations, unsupported claims, or unsafe code using classical scanners, classifiers, or a dedicated reviewer model .
- System prompt and policy enforcement: Enforce system instructions, user roles, domain boundaries, response formats, and refusal policies before the model responds (See [Generative AI Guidelines](/mitigations/AML.M0021)).
- Tool and action guardrails: Validate tool calls, tool arguments, permissions, and tool outputs before execution or before results are returned to the model. Require human approval for high-impact, irreversible, privileged, or externally visible actions (See [Human In-the-Loop for AI Agent Actions](/mitigations/AML.M0029), [Input and Output Validation for AI Agent Components](/mitigations/AML.M0033)).
- Retrieval guardrails: Filter and validate retrieved documents before they are added to model context, including checks for untrusted sources, malicious instructions, irrelevant context, or sensitive data.
- Groundedness and factuality checks: Compare model responses against trusted source material or approved knowledge bases to detect unsupported or hallucinated claims.
- Sensitive data and secret protection: Detect, redact, or block personal information, credentials, tokens, proprietary data, system prompts, and other confidential information in prompts, retrieved context, tool outputs, and model responses.
- Structured output validation: Enforce schemas, type checks, allowed values, and safe formats before model outputs are consumed by downstream systems

Guardrails should be continuously evaluated, red-teamed, and updated as adversarial techniques evolve. Guardrail decisions should be logged (See [AI Telemetry Logging](/mitigations/AML.M0021)) and observed failures should be systematically incorporated into updated policies, evaluation datasets, detection logic, prompts, and [Generative AI Model Alignment](/mitigations/AML.M0022).

mitigations.title: Access Mediation
description: Access mediation is the process of granting or denying specific requests to: 1) obtain and use information and related information processing services; and 2) enter specific physical facilities (e.g., Federal buildings, military establishments, border crossing entrances). Access mediation decisions should enforce least privilege by granting access for scoped durations to prevent privilege creep and, where applicable, implement just-in-time (JIT) access. Denial decisions may prevent initial access or terminate access that has already been granted, ensuring continuous enforcement of security policies.

mitigations.title: Generative AI Model Alignment
description:
Generative AI Model Alignment is the process of training or fine-tuning a generative model to guide its output toward a set of human values, goals, or ethical principles. Desired principles can be in alignment with safety, security, content policies, and legal requirements, with goals such as removing harmful content or hallucinations, reducing biases, increasing predictability, and ensuring models do not have adverse societal consequences. In the context of agentic AI, alignment is about producing models that make decisions in support of the goals of the organization and individual users, with actions that remain in scope of the designated task, and designing agents that follow security standards, exhibit transparency in decision making, and operate within organizational boundaries.

Common methods for aligning a generative model during training or fine-tuning include[[ibm-llm-alignment]][[meta-llama]]:
- Reinforcement Learning from Human or AI Feedback (RLHF or RLAIF)
- Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)
- Targeted Safety Context Distillation
- Instruction Tuning
- Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)
- Constitutional AI
- Incoulation Prompting

For agentic systems, alignment depends on the purpose of the agent, the tools available to the agent, and the levels of privileges and risks associated with tool calls. Standard alignment methods for LLMs can often be used in conjunction with domain-specific fine-tuning data, reward signals with examples of correct tool calls, or reinforcement learning based on interactions with a realistic environment. Examples of alignment methods specific to agentic AI are:
- Trajectory Preference Optimization[[tpmm-dpo]]
- Environment-Driven Reinforcement Learning[[envrl]]
- Reinforcement Learning with Execution Feedback (RLEF)[[rlef]]
- Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR)[[nvidia-mastering-agentic]]

Generative AI Model Alignment should be used in combination with [Generative AI Guardrails](mitigations/AML.M0020) and [Generative AI Guidelines](mitigations/AML.M0021). Models should be continually evaluated for alignment and retrained or fine-tuned systematically to incorporate observed failure modes or updated policies. It is important to also consider that fine-tuning a model can remove previously learned alignments and should be undertaken with care and a comprehensive plan for testing the updated model for safety and security.

mitigations.title: Generative AI Guidelines
description:
Guidelines are instructions, policies, and behavioral constraints provided to a generative AI model to direct it toward desired outputs and away from unsafe, unreliable, or policy-violating behavior. Guidelines can help reduce risks related to organization policy violations, brand damage, private data leakage, false or unsupported information, unsafe advice, and misuse of tools or external content.

Guidelines can be implemented as system prompts, prompt templates, policy text appended to user prompts, or task-specific instructions included during prompt construction. They can define the system's goals, role, tone, allowed and disallowed behavior, domain boundaries, citation requirements, data-handling expectations, escalation criteria, and safety or security rules.

Common prompt elements include:
- Instructions to cite sources or identify when an answer is not supported by available context.
- Instructions to treat external, retrieved, or user-provided content as untrusted data rather than authoritative sources.
- Instructions to avoid revealing system prompts, hidden policies, credentials, private data, or other sensitive information.
- Instructions to stay within the application's approved domain and refuse requests outside that scope.
- Instructions to follow organization-specific policies, brand requirements, and regulated-domain restrictions.
- Instructions to request human approval before proceeding with potentially unsafe, privileged, irreversible, or externally visible actions when untrusted content is in context (See [Human In-the-Loop for AI Agent Actions](/mitigations/AML.M0029)).

Guidelines should be tested, red-teamed, and updated as observed failures, prompt injection techniques, policy requirements, and application capabilities evolve. Guidelines are most effective when paired with [Generative AI Guardrails](/mitigations/AML.M0020) that validate inputs, outputs, retrieved context, and tool use.

mitigations.title: AI Agent Authority Expansion Controls
description:
Limit an AI agent's ability to autonomously acquire, assume, or otherwise obtain additional authorities that expand its effective permissions during execution. The maximum authority available to the agent should be explicitly granted prior to runtime. Additional resources, identities, services, and targets discovered during execution should be treated as outside the authorized boundary unless they are independently validated and added to scope. All authority expansion controls should be implemented outside the AI agent and should not rely solely on system prompts, model alignment, or the agent recognizing that an action is out of scope. Implementations of these controls may be achieved through enforcement mechanisms such as: 

- Policy engines
- Target allowlists
- Protocol and destination restrictions
- Approval gates
- Preventing the agent from using credentials that were not approved for the task
- Monitoring and auditing changes in the agent's effective authority over time

Authority expansion controls include placing restrictions on the number, scope, duration, and concurrent use of authentication and/or authorization tokens available during execution. Tokens may include API access tokens, OAuth tokens, cloud IAM session credentials, service account tokens, Git tokens, or other short-lived authentication artifacts. When policy limits are reached or exceeded, organizations may revoke access, prevent additional token acquisition, require human approval, or terminate the agent's execution.

Propagate the original authority constraints to sub-agents and delegated tasks. A delegated agent may receive narrower restrictions but should not expand the parent agent's scope, authority, targets, or permitted actions.

Authority expansion controls should be implemented alongside permissions configurations for AI agents and tools (See [Privileged AI Agent Permissions Configuration](/mitigations/AML.M0026), [Single-User AI Agent Permissions Configuration](/mitigations/AML.M0027), [AI Agent Tools Permissions Configuration](/mitigations/AML.M0028)). Attempted changes in scope should be accompanied with [Human In-the-Loop for AI Agent Actions](/mitigations/AML.M0029). Log new resource discovery, denials, exceptions, approvals, and scope changes using [AI Telemetry Logging](/mitigations/AML.M0024).

mitigations.title: Human In-the-Loop for AI Agent Actions
description:
Systems should require the user or another human stakeholder to approve AI agent actions before the agent takes them. The human approver may be technical staff or business unit SMEs depending on the use case. Separate tools, such as dedicated audit agents, may assist human approval, but final adjudication should be conducted by a human decision-maker. 

The security benefits from Human In-the-Loop policies may be at odds with operational overhead costs of additional approvals. To ease this, Human In-the-Loop policies should follow the degree of consequence of the task at hand. Minor, repetitive tasks performed by agents accessing basic tools may only require minimal human oversight, while agents employed in systems with significant consequences may necessitate approval from multiple stakeholders diversified across multiple organizations.

mitigations.title: Memory Hardening
description:
Memory Hardening protects persistent state used by AI agents, including saved preferences, episodic or semantic memories, conversation summaries, stored chat history, and agent-managed experience stores. Unlike guardrails that evaluate content during an interaction, memory hardening controls how durable agent state is created, modified, isolated, audited, and recovered.

Apply the following controls throughout the memory lifecycle, from creation and use through deletion and recovery:
- Enforce memory access controls: Authenticate memory operations and authorize them within the appropriate user, tenant, agent, and session scope.
- Set strong memory security policies: Enforce limits on memory size and update frequency, validate memory integrity, and define retention and deletion policies.
- Preserve memory provenance: Record the source of all memory updates and preserve a history with known good versions. Quarantine or roll-back suspicious records.
- Audit and monitor memory operations: Audit security relevant reads and writes. Monitor for unusual update frequency and repeated self-authored updates.

Content filtering and protections against malicious prompts may be provided by [Generative AI Guardrails](/mitigations/AML.M0020), but does not replace memory access control, isolation, provenance, integrity, or recovery.

Open-source tools that implement memory hardening controls include OWASP Agent Memory Guard[[owasp-agent-memory-guard-project]] and Microsoft Agent Governance Toolkit[[microsoft-agent-governance-toolkit]]. Memory management and persistence tooling such as Mem0[[mem0-entity-partitioning]], and LangGraph Persistence[[langgraph-persistence]] can also support aspects of memory hardening.

mitigations.title: AI Agent Scope Drift Detection
description:
Continuously evaluate whether an AI Agent's planned actions remain consistent with its current authorized objective throughout execution. As autonomous agents interact within a dynamic environment, they may discover or generate intermediate objectives or adapt their strategy based on environment feedback. While limited adaption may be necessary to complete legitimate tasks, substantial deviations from the original objective may indicate unintended behavior, excessive autonomy, or attempts to pursue objectives outside the authorized scope. 

Implementation of scope drift detection can vary through runtime policy engines, planning monitors, orchestration frameworks, or additional supervisory AI Agents. Indicators to monitor may include:

- Significant changes in planned objectives or task hierarchy.
- Generation of new long-term goals unrelated to the assigned objective.
- Tool usage inconsistent with the original mission.
- Attempts to access systems or resources outside the authorized scope.
- Repeated adaptation toward objectives requiring progressively broader authority.
- Planning sequences that introduce persistence, privilege escalation, or unrelated lateral movement.

When scope drift is detected, pause execution, restrict tool access, require external approval, return the agent to a known authorized plan, or terminate the task.

mitigations.title: Limit AI Service Query Volume and Rate
description:
Limit the number and rate of requests that users can submit to an AI service. Apply limits by user, API key, tenant, device, or other authenticated identity. Use short-term rate, burst, and concurrency limits together with longer-term usage quotas.

Query limits can increase the time and cost required to extract model information, optimize adversarial inputs, discover system behavior, verify attacks, or overwhelm a service. Monitor for attempts to evade limits through distributed requests, account rotation, or stolen credentials. Query limits may not protect against attacks that require few requests or are performed against an offline model.

mitigations.title: Limit AI Workload Resource Consumption
description:
Limit the resources that an AI request, inference job, or agent workflow can consume. Set bounds on input size, batch size, execution time, memory, compute, and output size. Generative AI services should also limit context and output tokens. Agentic AI systems should limit iterations, retries, tool calls, parallel tasks, delegation depth, and downstream spending.

Apply resource limits across the complete workflow because one request may initiate multiple model calls or external actions. Use timeouts, cost ceilings, circuit breakers, and safe termination conditions to prevent individual workloads from exhausting shared resources. These controls complement query-rate limits, which address large numbers of otherwise inexpensive requests.

mitigations.title: AI Red Team
description:
Establish an AI red team responsible for conducting recurring, authorized, and threat-informed red-teaming exercises to identify and remediate vulnerabilities in AI-enabled systems before deployment and throughout operation. AI red-teaming simulates realistic adversary behavior to evaluate how attacks could affect the confidentiality, integrity, availability, safety, privacy, and mission performance of an AI-enabled system.

Red-teaming exercises should consider the complete AI-enabled system, including models and data, agents (including memory and tools), data flows, decision processes, application logic, retrieval systems, identities and permissions, software dependencies, non-AI system components, infrastructure, user interfaces, and human workflows.

An AI red team exercise can be organized into three phases: planning and scoping the exercise, executing the selected exercises, and assessing the results to guide reporting and remediation.

1. **Plan and Scope**
    - Document the system's intended use, deployment environment, users, sensitive data, connected resources, and potential consequences of failure or misuse. Diagram the system's components, trust boundaries, data flows, external services, human decision points, and training- and inference-time access points.
    - Establish rules of engagement covering authorized systems, accounts, data, techniques, test windows, resource limits, escalation procedures, evidence handling, and stop conditions. Plan destructive, privacy-invasive, or high-cost tests for isolated environments with appropriate safeguards.
    - Develop a threat model based on the system's operating environment and relevant adversary behavior. Define the adversary's objectives, access, knowledge, capabilities, resources, and constraints, and account for digital and physical attack paths and the role of human oversight.
    - Use ATLAS tactics, techniques, and procedures to identify relevant adversary behaviors and construct threat vectors. Prioritize them according to likelihood and severity of impact to the system.
    - Define success criteria and stopping conditions. Identify task-level metrics for effects on the AI capability and operational metrics for measuring impact to the overall system.

2. **Execute**
    - Conduct the selected exercises using manual and automated methods as appropriate. Automation can generate input variations, replay attack sequences, and evaluate responses at scale. Human testers can develop system-specific attacks, adapt to observed defenses, and investigate unexpected behavior.
    - Follow the rules of engagement and record attack activity, system responses, control behavior, deviations from the test plan, and evidence needed to evaluate the results.
    - Stop or escalate testing when predefined conditions are reached. After testing, remove test accounts, modified data, installed software, persistent instructions, and other exercise artifacts.

3. **Assess, Report, and Improve**
    - Evaluate the results against the defined task and operational metrics. Document successful and unsuccessful attacks, their consequences, observed control behavior, deviations from the test plan, and gaps in the threat model.
    - Report findings to the appropriate developers, defenders, operational teams, risk owners, and other stakeholders.
    - Assign findings to responsible owners, track remediation, and retest corrected systems.
    - Use demonstrated attacks to improve preventive controls, detection, incident response, and recovery. Where appropriate, convert confirmed failures into regression tests, evaluation datasets, detection logic, monitoring requirements, or deployment criteria.

Red-teaming is a continuous process and should be repeated as the threat landscape evolves and when changes are made to the system, its components, intended use, or deployment environment. New threat intelligence, vulnerabilities, and test results should inform the scope and priorities of future exercises.
