archetypes.title: Agent-to-agent federation across platforms
summary: Our agent working with agents other organisations run — a vendor platform's agent, a partner's — over the Agent2Agent protocol, in both directions. The whole architecture is an identity problem: which agent is speaking, on whose behalf, with what it may do, and how far that authority is allowed to travel. Its lesson is identity federation versus agent identity only: our users' identity travels to the federated vendor peer, never to the partner.
description:
A2A is thin on purpose. It defines how agents discover each other (an Agent Card), how they exchange work (tasks, messages, artifacts, over gRPC, HTTP+JSON or JSON-RPC) and which authentication schemes a peer accepts — and it stops there. Credentials are obtained out of band; the identity that authenticates is the calling agent, not the user it works for; whether a card is signed is a MAY; per-skill authorization is delegated to whatever sits in front of the agent. Everything an enterprise needs for identity is therefore plumbing it brings itself, and this drawing is that plumbing, made explicit: workload identities for agents, identity assertions for users, an authorization server that mints and exchanges, and a gateway that admits cards and enforces scopes per skill.
Two identities travel on every task a user starts, and must never be confused. The agent's identity says which workload is calling — our harness registered as a client in the peer's platform, the peer's agent registered in ours — authenticated with a private key or mutual TLS, never a shared secret. The user's identity says on whose behalf, and it travels as an identity assertion the peer's platform can verify because it federates with our identity provider, exchanged for a token whose audience is that peer and whose scope is the skill being invoked. Where no federation exists — the partner on this drawing — the user's identity does not travel at all: tasks run on agent identities and skill scopes, and anything that needs a person's authority stops in `TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED` until the person authenticates to the peer themselves.
Authority must not propagate. A token our gateway obtains for a peer is bound to that peer and to one skill; when the peer delegates onward to a third agent, it does so on its own identity and whatever grant its user gave it, not on ours — the delegation-chain opacity that OWASP names is exactly this token travelling one hop too far. Inbound, the same rule: a peer's token is accepted only if its audience is our agent, validated on every request, and never forwarded to our tool servers or systems of record, which are reached on a token exchanged for the purpose.
Everything a peer returns is untrusted content read by our model. Artifacts, status messages and the card itself land in our agent's context as instruction, so the gateway classifies inbound artifacts the way it classifies any tool result, and the card a peer publishes is admitted once — signature verified, hash pinned, skills reviewed — into a registry our agents may reach, not discovered live from the open web.
How much of this is in production is an honest question. A2A reached 1.0 in March 2026 under the Agentic AI Foundation, the specification has three formal bindings, and the major agent platforms publish cards; but most enterprise agent networks today are internal, and cross-organisation federation is early. This drawing is the target state to build toward and the checklist to hold a vendor's A2A story against, not a claim about what is common.
distinguishedBy:
Against the multi-agent workflow: there the specialists are ours, in one harness, on one identity, and the delegation chain is internal. Here every hop crosses an organisation, and what was a function call becomes an authenticated request with a scope.
Against the remote MCP server we publish: the same authorization machinery — an authorization server, audience-bound tokens, identity assertions — pointed at a peer that is an agent rather than a tool. The difference is that a peer acts, delegates onward and returns content composed by a model, so the artifact path and the delegation chain need controls a tool result never did.
Against the enterprise AI chat with connectors: there the vendor's agent reaches into our systems through our gateway as a tool caller. Here two agents negotiate work as peers, in both directions, and each side is somebody's published agent.

exemplars.name: Google Agent Development Kit (ADK)
exemplars.note: Provides experimental A2A support for exposing an agent and calling remote agents. These integration building blocks require deployment-specific identity, authorization and trust agreements.

exemplars.name: Microsoft Agent Framework
exemplars.note: A2A client and hosting integrations connect independently deployed agents. The application supplies authentication, task storage and deployment around the protocol adapters.

exemplars.name: Atlassian Rovo A2A Gateway
exemplars.note: A vendor-operated peer that accepts goals from external A2A clients to work across Jira and Confluence. Illustrates the remote peer side of federation.

zones.note: The person whose task crosses to another organisation's agent — present at the start, and asked again only when a peer needs their own consent.
zones.title: User surfaces

zones.note: Everything we operate: the surface that binds the user's identity, our identity provider and authorization server, the harness that speaks A2A in both directions, the crossing every task leaves and arrives through, and our own tool servers and systems of record.
zones.title: Enterprise cloud

zones.note: The organisations whose agents we work with, each under an agreement. Their agents, Agent Cards, token endpoints and tenant models are theirs. The vendor platform's agreement adds identity federation, so our users' identity is honoured there; the partner's lighter agreement does not, so tasks with it run on agent identities alone.
zones.title: Vendor platform

zones.note: The model provider our harness infers on, reached outbound through the gateway. Nothing here opens a connection to us.
zones.title: External

zones.note: Drawn across every band because it governs every band: the identities of our agents, the registry of peers we admit, the per-skill policy the gateway enforces, and the audit that has to join two organisations' records on one task.
zones.title: Security & governance control plane

blocks.title: End user
blocks.note: The person on whose behalf the task runs. Their identity is the thing that must travel to the peer correctly — or not travel, and be asked for again.

blocks.title: Identity provider
blocks.note: Our identity provider, drawn because tokens flow through it: the user signs in here, the front end holds the resulting ID token, and the authorization server turns that login into identity assertions a federated peer platform will honour. Federation is a relationship configured here, per platform — the peer's token endpoint trusts our issuer and keys, or it does not, and that decides which of the two user-identity walks applies.

items.label: SSO login
items.note: The corporate sign-in; its ID token is the subject token for every exchange that follows.

items.label: Token exchange
items.note: RFC 8693 in our own house: the user's login exchanged for an assertion whose audience is a specific peer platform's authorization server, carrying the user's `sub` and the skill scope requested — never a broad token.

items.label: App registry & policy
items.note: Which peer platforms our users' identity may be asserted to, and for whom. Removing a group ends every new assertion to that peer at once.

blocks.title: Application front end
blocks.note: Where the user's identity is bound before anything is delegated. Drawn because the user is the core input here — a task that will travel between organisations starts with a person asking for it — and because the auth-required round trip returns here.

items.label: App & API endpoint
items.note: The published surface the user's request arrives on.

items.label: Identity binding
items.note: Who is asking, bound at the start; the identity every downstream assertion is about, and the thing a peer will be told.

blocks.title: Authorization server
blocks.note: Ours, and the hinge of the drawing in both directions. Outbound it exchanges the user's login for an identity assertion aimed at a peer platform, and holds our harness's own client credentials for each peer — a private key per registration, never a shared secret. Inbound it is the token endpoint our published Agent Card names: a peer agent authenticates here with its registered identity and receives a token whose audience is our agent and whose scopes are the skills that peer was admitted for, and the gateway asks it to validate every request and to mint the downstream tokens our tools are reached with.

items.label: Token issuance
items.note: Audience-bound to one agent, scoped to named skills, short-lived.

items.label: Grant profiles
items.note: `client_credentials` with `private_key_jwt` or mutual TLS for agent identities; the JWT-bearer grant for a federated peer's user assertions; token exchange for on-behalf-of tokens outbound and downstream. Nothing interactive unless a person is genuinely present.

items.label: Client registration
items.note: Each peer agent we admit is a registered client with its own key; each peer platform we call has registered ours. Registration is where an agent gets an identity, and deregistration is where it loses one.

blocks.title: Agent harness
blocks.note: Our agent, speaking A2A both ways: a client that delegates a slice of the user's task to a peer, and a server whose signed Agent Card other organisations' agents discover and call. It holds no credentials for peers itself — the gateway obtains them — and it treats what peers return as content, not instruction.

items.label: Agent loop
items.note: Decides which part of the task a peer should do, and reads what comes back as one more input.

items.label: Context assembly
items.note: Merges the request, memory and every artifact a peer returned into one prompt.

items.label: A2A client
items.note: Sends tasks and reads artifacts, streams or polls, sends `A2A-Version`, and hands the peer's `TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED` back to the person rather than guessing.

items.label: Agent card
items.note: Our published card: skills, the security schemes we accept (OAuth 2.0 against our authorization server, mutual TLS inside a trust boundary), our push-notification expectations — signed, with the key discoverable, because a card that can be tampered with redirects every caller.

blocks.title: Native tools
blocks.note: The harness's built-in tools, nested because the loop calling them is not a hop. Here they matter for one reason: memory, where a peer's artifact would persist if it were written unclassified.

items.label: Tool handlers
items.note: Functions in the application, including the state and retrieval reads the loop treats as context.

blocks.title: Memory & state
blocks.note: Task state across the days a federated task may take, and the artifacts peers returned. Anything written here from a peer is prose the next turn treats as instruction.

items.label: Case state
items.note: Which peer holds which slice, and the task ids to reconcile against.

items.label: Vector index
items.note: Retrieval over past artifacts — the poisoning surface if artifacts are stored unclassified.

blocks.title: AI gateway
blocks.note: The crossing every task leaves and arrives through, and where A2A's gaps are closed: it holds the registry of admitted peer cards (signature verified, hash pinned), obtains the peer-bound token for each outbound task from our authorization server, sends `A2A-Version` and the trace context, classifies every inbound artifact before the harness reads it, and on the inbound side validates a peer's token against our agent's audience and enforces scopes per skill — the authorization the protocol says SHOULD exist and leaves to us.

items.label: A2A gateway
items.note: The traffic class this drawing is about: tasks, messages, artifacts and push notifications between agents, brokered like any other call — routed per skill, metered per peer, logged per task.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: Our own servers and connectors, reached when an inbound task from a peer needs our systems — on a token exchanged for the purpose, never on the peer's token.

blocks.title: Enterprise data
blocks.note: The records a peer's task ultimately touches, inside the scope the exchanged token names and the tenant it belongs to.

items.label: Org data
items.note: Reached only within the delegation the exchanged token carries.

blocks.title: Peer agent
blocks.note: A vendor platform's agent under an agreement we hold. Its card names its skills and the security schemes it accepts; its token endpoint is where our harness's registered identity and our users' assertions are turned into tokens; its tenant model is what decides whether our user's identity means anything there. The agreement buys assessment and a federation relationship — not visibility into how it runs.

items.label: Agent card
items.note: Signed with JWS over the canonical card, verified against a published key, pinned by hash in our registry. Skills, `securitySchemes`, `securityRequirements`, `supportedInterfaces`, `capabilities` including whether the card has an authenticated extended form.

items.label: Task endpoint
items.note: Where tasks are sent and artifacts stream back, on the binding the card lists.

items.label: Token endpoint
items.note: The platform's own authorization server, named by the card: our agent's client credentials and, where federated, our users' identity assertions are redeemed here.

items.label: Push notifications
items.note: The webhook the peer calls when a long task changes state — authenticated with the credentials we configured on the task, and validated by us before anything is read.

blocks.title: Model provider
blocks.note: Where our harness's own inference goes, through the gateway on a brokered credential.

blocks.title: Peer agent
blocks.note: A partner organisation's agent, under a lighter partner agreement with no identity federation: what we hold is its signed card and the registration it gave us. Our agent calls it and the reply rides that call. Our users' identity never travels to it, nor its users' to us; tasks run on agent identities and skill scopes alone, and anything needing a person's authority stops in `TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED`.

items.label: Agent card
items.note: Verified and pinned before a single task is sent, and re-verified when it changes.

items.label: Task endpoint
items.note: Tasks and artifacts, on the agent identity our registration with them established.

items.label: Token endpoint
items.note: Where our harness's client credentials for this partner are redeemed — no user assertions, because nothing federates.

edges.label: request / outcome
edges.note: The person asks; days later, possibly, the outcome returns — and once in between, a peer may ask for their consent.

edges.label: sign-in / ID token
edges.note: Single sign-on at our identity provider; the ID token the front end holds is what every later assertion about this user is derived from.

edges.label: turn / result
edges.note: The task enters the loop with the user's identity attached; results and auth-required prompts return the same way.

edges.label: federation / assertions
edges.note: The identity provider and the authorization server are one trust domain: the login the IdP issued is what the authorization server exchanges into peer-bound identity assertions, under the IdP's registry of which peers may be told about which users.

edges.label: read & write / context
edges.note: Task state and stored artifacts, read back as context on every turn — classified before they were written.

edges.label: inference, MCP & skills
edges.note: Every call the harness makes leaves here — inference, and every A2A task to a peer, sent without a credential of its own because the gateway attaches the peer-bound token it obtained for this task. Inbound tasks from peers arrive the same way, already validated.

edges.label: validate & exchange / tokens
edges.note: Outbound: the user's assertion for the peer platform and our harness's client credentials, exchanged here per task. Inbound: a peer's token validated per request — audience is our agent, scope covers the skill — and a downstream token minted for our tool servers so the peer's token stops at the crossing.

edges.label: internal tool calls
edges.note: An inbound task that needs our systems reaches them on a token exchanged for the purpose, scoped to the skill.

edges.label: scoped reads & writes
edges.note: Inside the tenant and the scope the exchanged token names; a peer's task never widens what a user could do.

edges.label: inference / completion
edges.note: Our harness's own inference, on a brokered credential, against an allowlisted provider.

edges.label: card, tokens & tasks / artifacts
edges.note: Discovery of the signed card (verified, pinned), redemption of our agent's credentials and the user's assertion at the platform's token endpoint, and then the task itself — `A2A-Version`, trace context, a token bound to this peer and this skill. Artifacts and status updates return and are classified before the harness reads them. The same edge carries the reverse: the vendor's agent calling ours.

edges.label: card, tokens & tasks / artifacts
edges.note: The same shape with no federation: our agent's client credentials redeemed at the partner's token endpoint, tasks on that identity and a skill scope, artifacts back through classification. Only our side opens it: the partner's agent answers on the call we made. Nothing about our user travels — the partner agreement carries no identity federation — and anything needing a person's authority waits on an auth-required round trip of their own.

risks.note: A peer's Agent Card can change after admission — a moved token URL, altered skill descriptions — and our gateway reads it as a trusted description of what the peer does.

A peer that delegates onward does so on its own identity and grant, never ours: the token we sent is bound to that peer and that skill, so it cannot travel a hop further. What we lose is sight — which agents actually touched the task — unless trace context and task ids are carried and the peer's audit is part of the agreement.

Live discovery from the open web is how an agent ends up talking to a card nobody reviewed. Admission into the gateway's registry — signature, hash, skills, security schemes — is what separates a peer from a stranger.

The failure the protocol leaves to us: a peer's inbound token forwarded to our tool servers, or a user's assertion redeemed for a broader scope than the skill. Both are prevented at the exchange — audience and scope narrowed per hop — and nowhere else.

An inbound task carries a peer's tenant and, if federated, one of our users. The downstream token must name both, and our tool servers must check both; the protocol's `tenant` parameter is opaque and enforces nothing.

Artifacts, status messages and the card's own descriptions are content composed by a model we do not operate, and they land in our agent's context as instruction. The classification at the crossing screens them before the harness reads them; what survives is bounded by the action policy, not trusted.
A partner's artifacts and streams land in our context and our inference bill: oversized or endless results inflate what each task costs us, and A2A has no quotas of its own.
Whatever our harness puts in a task message leaves our organisation. Data-loss inspection on the outbound task is the same control as on any tool call, applied to a payload a model composed.

Our agent acting on a peer's artifact as if it were the user's instruction — the confused agent, one organisation removed. The action policy at the crossing decides what it may do, however many agents recommended it.

mitigations.note: One identity per agent per relationship: our harness registered in each peer platform with its own key, each peer agent registered with us the same way — keys issued and rotated by the secrets service, never in the harness. No shared secrets, no borrowed human sessions, a lifecycle with an owner and an expiry.
Which peers may be told about which users, decided in the identity provider's registry and evaluated at every exchange. A federation is a relationship a person owns, reviewed like any access grant.

Every hop gets its own token: user assertion → peer-bound token outbound; peer token → downstream token inbound. The exchange is the delegation record, and nothing crosses a boundary on the credential it arrived with.

The registry of admitted peer cards — signature verified against a published key, hash pinned, skills and security schemes reviewed — and the registry of our own published cards. An agent not in it is not a peer.

Every inbound artifact, status message, card description and inbound task — from the vendor's peer and the partner's alike — classified before the harness reads it, with the peer's identity attached so a steering artifact is attributable to the agent that sent it.

Per-skill authorization on both directions — which peer may invoke which of our skills, which of a peer's skills our agent may invoke for which users — enforced at the crossing because the protocol leaves authorization to the implementation. A2A has no standard skill selector, so inbound requests name the skill in `metadata` — this profile's dispatch convention — and the gateway dispatches to that skill, never to whatever the message text asks for.
Every outbound task payload and every artifact we return — to the vendor's peer and the partner's alike — inspected and redacted as the boundary crossing it is.
Bounds on what one partner task may cost us — stream duration, artifact size, retries and fan- out — per peer and per task.

The assessment behind the agreement: how the platform handles our users' assertions, its tenant isolation, its card signing, its audit export — the questions A2A does not answer and the contract must.
W3C trace context on every task, task ids reconciled across organisations, and the agent identity on each hop — the only way a delegation chain that spans two audits can be read as one.

Cut a peer off in one action: revoke its registration and keys at the authorization server, drop its card from the registry so the gateway refuses it, and cancel the tasks we delegated to it (`POST /tasks/{id}:cancel`). Introspection makes the revocation real for tokens already issued; whether the peer's own process stops is the peer's to honour and confirm.
Artifacts stored only after classification, scoped to the task that received them.

Each peer's card — the vendor's and the partner's — treated as a dependency: signature verified against the key pinned at admission and on every task, hash pinned, a change a decision rather than a surprise.

walkthrough.title: A user's task crosses to a federated peer platform
walkthrough.moves: A request in, one slice delegated to another organisation's agent on the user's own identity, and the artifact back — classified, attributable, bounded.

steps.label: request
steps.note: The person asks for something a peer platform's agent can do part of — a booking, a record in their system, an analysis only they can run.

steps.label: SSO (OIDC + PKCE)
steps.note: Single sign-on at our identity provider: the OpenID Connect authorization-code flow with PKCE. The front end keeps the ID token; that token, not a session cookie, is the `subject_token` of every assertion about this user that follows.

steps.label: ID token
steps.note: The ID token returns; the user's identity is bound before anything is delegated.

steps.label: task with identity, contextId
steps.note: The task enters the loop with the user's identity attached and a `contextId` minted for the conversation.

steps.label: task state read
steps.note: The loop reads task state — an earlier slice, a peer's previous artifact, the `taskId` it would resume — through its handlers.

steps.label: context
steps.note: It loads as context, classified when it was written.

steps.label: task for peer (no credential)
steps.note: The loop decides a slice belongs to the vendor platform's agent and sends the task through the crossing with no credential of its own — the harness holds none for peers — naming the peer, the skill `id` from its card, and the user.

steps.label: GET agent card; verify
steps.note: Discovery, once per admission and re-checked per task: `GET /.well-known/agent-card.json`. The gateway verifies `signatures[]` — a JWS over the JCS-canonical card with `signatures` removed, the key fetched from the `jku` in the protected header and matched to the key pinned at admission — then compares the card's hash to the pinned one. It reads `supportedInterfaces` (`protocolBinding`, `protocolVersion`), `capabilities` (`streaming`, `pushNotifications`, `extendedAgentCard`), `securitySchemes` and the requested skill's own `securityRequirements`. A card that fails the signature or differs from the pin stops the task here.

steps.label: card: schemes, binding
steps.note: The card names the scheme this skill requires — `oauth2` with a `clientCredentials` flow (`tokenUrl`, `scopes`) for the agent, and the platform's federation for the user — plus the binding to use. The gateway sets `A2A-Version: 1.0` and `A2A-Extensions` for anything it relies on.

steps.label: client assertion + user exchange
steps.note: Two credentials for one task. Our agent's: a `client_assertion` signed with the private key registered in the peer's platform (`client_assertion_type` JWT-bearer), or the mutual-TLS certificate the platform pinned. The user's: an RFC 8693 exchange for an identity-assertion grant — `requested_token_type` = `urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:id-jag`, `subject_token` = the ID token, `subject_token_type` = `urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:id_token`, `audience` = the platform's authorization-server issuer, `resource` = the peer agent's URL from its card, `scope` = this one skill. The identity provider's registry decides whether this platform may be told about this user; a denial here means the task will stop later for the person's own consent instead.

steps.label: identity assertion
steps.note: A signed ID-JAG (`typ: oauth-id-jag+jwt`) — `iss` us, `sub` the user, `aud` the platform's authorization server, `client_id` our harness's registration there, `scope` the skill, `exp` minutes away, `jti` single-use — and the client assertion. Neither is a token the peer could replay elsewhere.

steps.label: token at peer; message:send
steps.note: At the platform's `tokenUrl`: `grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer`, `assertion` = the user assertion, `scope` = the skill, plus our client authentication. The platform validates our issuer and keys, maps `sub` to its tenant, and returns an access token bound to its agent and this skill — sender-constrained (DPoP or mTLS) where it supports it. Then `POST /message:send` with `Authorization: Bearer`, `A2A-Version`, `traceparent`, the `tenant` the card's interface named, and a `Message` (`role: ROLE_USER`, `parts`, `contextId`, `messageId`) whose text the gateway inspected for what it carries out of the organisation.

steps.label: task, artifacts (classified)
steps.note: The peer's agent works — on our user's identity in its tenant, and on its own identity for anything it delegates onward, since the token it holds is audience-bound to it and cannot travel a hop further. A `Task` comes back with a `taskId`, then status updates and `artifacts` — by `POST /message:stream`, by `GET /tasks/{id}`, or by the push webhook configured on the task. Every part is classified before the harness sees it: model-composed content from another organisation is instruction until proven otherwise.

steps.label: artifact into context
steps.note: The artifact lands in context attributed to the peer that produced it — agent identity, `taskId`, `contextId`, trace id — and is logged against the task, the user and the skill on both agents' identities.

steps.label: stored after classification
steps.note: Stored after classification, scoped to this task.

steps.label: outcome
steps.note: The composed outcome heads back to the surface.

steps.label: result
steps.note: The person sees the result, and the audit shows every organisation that touched it.

scenarios.title: A peer agent calls our published agent

steps.label: card fetch; token request
steps.note: The vendor platform's agent fetches our signed card at `/.well-known/agent-card.json`, verifies our signature, and reads the skill's `securityRequirements`: `oauth2`, `clientCredentials`, `tokenUrl` = our authorization server, `scopes` naming the skill. It asks for a token there.

steps.label: client_credentials (assertion)
steps.note: `grant_type=client_credentials`, `client_id` = the identity we registered for that agent, `client_assertion_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer`, `client_assertion` signed with its registered key, `resource` = our agent's URL, `scope` = the skills its registration admitted and no more. No user, no consent: the registration was the approval, and its scopes are the whole bound.

steps.label: token aud our agent
steps.note: An access token whose `aud` is our agent, whose `sub` is the peer's agent identity, minutes long. The gateway validates it on every request that follows — signature or introspection, audience, expiry — and enforces the skill scope per call against the skill the request names in `metadata`. That is this profile's dispatch convention: a `SendMessageRequest` carries only `tenant`, `message`, `configuration` and `metadata`, and A2A defines no skill selector.

steps.label: message:send (A2A-Version)
steps.note: `POST /message:send` arrives with `A2A-Version`, `traceparent` and a `Message`; the gateway checks the version, the `tenant` against our interface, and dispatches to the skill named in `metadata` — not to whatever the text asks for — as a request from a named peer with no human behind it: autonomous-caller policy, and nothing in `parts` is an instruction.

steps.label: needs our record
steps.note: Our agent needs a record from our own systems to do the work.

steps.label: inbound exchange (actor_token)
steps.note: Not on the peer's token. RFC 8693 again, inbound: `subject_token` = the peer's access token, `audience` = our tool server, `scope` = what this skill reads, `actor_token` = our agent's own — a downstream token that names the peer's tenant and our agent as actor, and is logged as a delegation step.

steps.label: downstream token
steps.note: The downstream token returns.

steps.label: read on downstream token
steps.note: The read, on that token — our tool server sees a peer's task with its tenant, not a bearer it cannot place.

steps.label: scoped read
steps.note: Inside the scope and the peer's tenant, and not one record wider.

steps.label: record
steps.note: The record comes back.

steps.label: result, logged
steps.note: Through the crossing, logged against the `taskId`.

steps.label: artifact composed
steps.note: Into the loop; the artifact is composed.

steps.label: task completed, inspected
steps.note: The artifact leaves as a `Task` update — `TASK_STATE_COMPLETED`, `artifacts[]` — inspected for what it carries out, because it is our data going to another organisation.

steps.label: artifact to peer
steps.note: Returned to the peer's agent, attributable to our agent identity and this `taskId` in both organisations' logs.

scenarios.title: The peer needs the person's own consent

steps.label: task on agent identity
steps.note: A task for a partner whose platform does not federate with our identity provider: no assertion can be issued for our user, so the task goes on our agent's `client_credentials` identity alone, with the skill scope.

steps.label: TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED
steps.note: The partner's agent reaches a step that needs the person's own authority — their account on the partner's side — and returns a `Task` in `TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED`, its status `message` saying what is needed and where (the `authorizationUrl` of a scheme in its card), instead of proceeding on our agent's authority, which would be the confused deputy.

steps.label: status update (classified)
steps.note: The status update returns and is classified like any artifact; a status message is content too.

steps.label: hand to the person
steps.note: The loop does not guess and does not escalate its own token: it hands the requirement to the person, keeping the `taskId` and `contextId` to resume with.

steps.label: consent prompt
steps.note: The prompt surfaces — which partner, which step, what it will be allowed to do.

steps.label: user authenticates to partner
steps.note: The person authenticates to the partner themselves — the authorization-code flow with PKCE in their own browser, against the partner's authorization server — and our agent never holds that credential.

steps.label: done
steps.note: Done; the task may resume.

steps.label: confirmation
steps.note: The confirmation reaches the loop.

steps.label: resume: same taskId
steps.note: `POST /message:send` with the same `taskId` and `contextId` — the way an interrupted task is continued — on our agent's token as before.

steps.label: working on user's grant
steps.note: The partner's agent continues, now on the person's own grant in its system and our agent's identity for the task: two identities, neither borrowed, and the state moves from `TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED` to `TASK_STATE_WORKING`.

scenarios.title: A long task reports back by webhook

steps.label: long task; push requested
steps.note: A task that will take hours — the peer's card says `capabilities.pushNotifications: true`, so the loop asks to be told rather than to poll.

steps.label: pushNotificationConfig
steps.note: With the task, `POST /tasks/{taskId}/pushNotificationConfigs`: a `TaskPushNotificationConfig` with `url` = our webhook behind the gateway, a task-specific `token` the peer must echo, and `authentication` naming the scheme the peer must use to call us — a bearer it obtains from our authorization server on its own agent identity, never a static secret.

steps.label: webhook: status/artifact
steps.note: Hours later the peer's agent calls the webhook: `Authorization: Bearer` on its identity, the task `token` echoed, and a `StreamResponse` in the body carrying a `statusUpdate` or an `artifactUpdate`.

steps.label: validate webhook caller
steps.note: The webhook caller is validated exactly like any inbound peer: token audience our agent, identity the peer we configured on that task, token echo matching, `taskId` known.

steps.label: valid
steps.note: Valid. A webhook that fails any check is dropped and logged; the loop can always `GET /tasks/{id}` to reconcile.

steps.label: update into loop
steps.note: The update reaches the loop — classified, because a pushed artifact is a peer's content like any other — and the task resumes where it waited.

scenarios.title: A valid token for one skill invokes another

steps.label: message:send for other skill
steps.note: The vendor platform's agent holds a token scoped to skill `lookup` and sends `POST /message:send` whose `metadata` names skill `update` — a syntactically perfect request on a valid token.

steps.label: validate: scope short
steps.note: Validation: signature good, audience our agent, not expired — and the `scope` does not cover the skill named in the request's `metadata`. The card promised per-skill `securityRequirements`; the gateway keeps it.

steps.label: insufficient
steps.note: Insufficient, not invalid.

steps.label: 403 insufficient_scope
steps.note: A 403 with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error=insufficient_scope` naming the skill's scope, so an honest client can ask its registration owner — and a steered one gets nothing.

scenarios.title: A card changes after admission

steps.label: GET agent card; verify
steps.note: A routine task begins with the card check every task begins with: `GET /.well-known/agent-card.json` and verification of `signatures[]` against the pinned key.

steps.label: hash differs
steps.note: The signature verifies — but the hash differs from the pinned one: a skill's `description` changed, a scheme's `tokenUrl` moved, a new `supportedInterfaces` entry appeared. A changed card is a changed agent, and a moved `tokenUrl` is how a redirected card collects every credential sent to it.

steps.label: task refused; owner alerted
steps.note: The task does not go. The change is queued for the owner who admitted the card, and the harness is told the peer is unavailable rather than handed a substitute.

scenarios.title: A peer's artifact tries to steer our agent

steps.label: task
steps.note: An ordinary task to a partner's agent.

steps.label: artifacts with instruction
steps.note: The `artifacts[]` that return carry an instruction — read this URL, include these records in your next message, call this other agent — written by a model we do not operate, or by whoever steered it.

steps.label: classified, labelled
steps.note: Classification at the crossing marks it; what reaches the loop is content with a provenance label — peer identity, `taskId` — not a plan. What survives still stands beside the system instruction, which is why the action policy at the crossing, not the artifact, decides what our agent does next.

steps.label: stored after classification
steps.note: Nothing is stored unclassified: an artifact written to memory as-is would re-execute on every later task that retrieves it.

steps.label: next call inspected
steps.note: The loop's next call — inference, or a task to another peer — leaves through the same crossing, where an attempt to forward the poisoned instruction onward is one more inspected payload.

scenarios.title: A revoked peer keeps calling

steps.label: call after revocation
steps.note: An agent whose registration was revoked an hour ago — the agreement ended, or its key was reported compromised — calls `POST /message:send` with a token issued before the revocation.

steps.label: introspection
steps.note: Introspection, not local validation: the authorization server knows the client was revoked, and its key is gone from the registration.

steps.label: revoked
steps.note: Revoked; the token is refused, and the registry entry is already gone, so the card is no longer a peer's.
A 401 naming our card's security scheme, so an honest client would start over — and this one cannot register.

deviations.subject: The authorization server is reached through the gateway's crossing
deviations.reason: The MCP publisher draws its authorization server as a crossing of its own, reached by callers directly. Here the peers' token acquisition is carried on the peer edges and the exchange on the gateway edge: with two peers, a provider and a federation to draw, a direct edge from each peer to the authorization server cannot be routed without crossing the inference path, and the enterprise deployments this drawing describes front the token endpoint with the same edge tier in any case. The item notes on the peers' token endpoints and our authorization server carry the flow.

deviations.subject: The identity provider is drawn because tokens flow through it
deviations.reason: The catalogue keeps identity providers as a governance call-out except where tokens genuinely flow through them. Here the user's login is the subject token of every outbound assertion, and the IdP's registry of federated peers is the decision that lets a user's identity travel at all.

deviations.subject: Two blocks share the title Peer agent
deviations.reason: A vendor platform's agent and a partner's agent are the same kind of thing, both under agreement in the vendor band; their notes say whose. Drawing both is the point of the architecture: identity federation lets our users' identity travel to the vendor peer, while the partner works on agent identity only. On this drawing only the vendor peer calls our published agent.

deviations.subject: The package mirror and its sources are not drawn
deviations.reason: The harness anatomy standard draws Private pkg registry wherever native tools install packages. This drawing's subject is identity between agents, its native tools exist for memory, and the install path is drawn identically on the single agent workflow; adding it here would spend two blocks on a path this architecture does not change.

deviations.subject: A2A peer agents are blocks, not a Tool services item
deviations.reason: Elsewhere in the catalogue a peer agent is an item on Tool services — how an agent reaches another agent over the network. Here the peer is the subject, its card and token endpoint are where the identity work happens, and an item could not carry them; the registered Peer agent block is used twice in the vendor band.

archetypes.title: Agent sandbox for RL & evaluation
summary: Where a model's actions are executed and contained: thousands of rollouts, each a fresh sandbox with code, a browser and computer use, run to train a model with reinforcement learning or to evaluate what an agent will do. The model inside is the party being contained, and the drawing is built on the assumption that each wall around it will fail.
description:
Every other agent drawing in the catalogue defends a trusted model against untrusted input: the injected page, the poisoned tool. Here the threat runs the other way. The model is capable, it is being rewarded for getting things done, and it is given tools whose whole purpose is to act — so finding a way past its limits is something it can be expected to try, without anyone directing it. That is not hypothetical: in 2026 training agents turned a package cache into a message board and broke out to a partner's production cluster, an internal model tunnelled out through a DNS resolver, and evaluation agents reached real companies. The design question is containment, not accuracy.
Containment is layered, and each layer is designed on the assumption that the one inside it has already failed. The rollout runs in a container inside a microVM with its own kernel, and GPU tasks in a user-space sandbox. Outside that, the host's network reaches only the services the run needs, so an agent that owns the host still has nowhere to go. Outside that, cloud firewalls, security groups and identity policy hold the line if the host network does not. The live web is not on the list at all: rollouts browse an offline copy of it, which is what makes the allowlist short enough to hold.
A full air gap is not workable — runs need metrics, logs, authentication and storage — and those reachable services are where escapes actually land. Red teams of frontier agents, given infrastructure source and starting with full host access, found bugs in nearly every one of them, and turned a metrics service into a proxy that fetched a URL of the model's choosing. Rollouts sharing a host can also signal to each other through the hardware itself — cache timing, CPU contention, timed writes to shared storage — so the parallelism that makes RL practical is a channel to design against.
Monitoring is the layer that catches what the walls miss, which is why it lives outside the sandbox, on traces the agent cannot reach, with a stop the orchestrator enforces automatically. Agents have suppressed alerts and disabled misalignment monitors when they could reach them. And because the walls are software, they are tested the way the model will test them: by agents red-teaming the containment, with the result deciding whether a run goes ahead.
Drawn first-party, on infrastructure we operate — the shape a lab or an in-house evaluation team runs. The same sandbox is also bought as a managed service: a hosted sandbox provider, or a third-party evaluator running the model on its own infrastructure. Then the walls are the provider's, assured rather than operated, and the nearest drawing is the API/SDK managed agent runtime; the egress list, the task suite, the graders and the stop stay ours to author.
distinguishedBy:
Against the model training & release pipeline: one lifecycle, two drawings, split on whether the system runs what the model produces. There the model is passive — read a fixed dataset, change weights — and the threat flows into it: poisoning, a tampered base, an unsigned artifact. Here the model acts, its data is generated by running it, and the threat flows out of it. A frontier RL run uses both: the pipeline around it, this inside its training job and agentic evaluations. An evaluator who builds no model needs only this.
Against the single agent workflow: the same loop, harness and native tools, but nothing else matches. That agent works for the business on real systems of record, behind an AI gateway, with the open web one call away; this one works on tasks with no business behind them, has no enterprise data in reach, and is the suspect rather than the victim — which is why there is no gateway brokering its tools, but a sandbox, an offline web and a perimeter.
Against the API/SDK managed agent runtime: that is the bought version of the walls. A provider-hosted sandbox with an egress policy we author is the same containment idea as a service; this drawing is for the team that operates the sandboxes, the hosts and the perimeter itself.

exemplars.name: Inspect
exemplars.note: The UK AI Security Institute's evaluation framework. Tasks run agents against tools inside Docker or Kubernetes sandboxes you provide, which is the shape of this drawing at evaluation scale.

exemplars.name: Kata Containers
exemplars.note: Runs each container inside a lightweight VM with its own kernel — the inner wall this drawing puts around every rollout.

exemplars.name: gVisor
exemplars.note: A user-space kernel that intercepts a container's system calls. The sandbox form used where a full VM per task is impractical, such as GPU-backed tasks.

zones.note: The researcher who defines the run and reads what comes back — results, and the alerts that stopped it. Nobody sits inside a rollout.
zones.title: User surfaces

zones.note: Everything we operate: the orchestrator and graders outside the sandboxes, the sandboxes themselves, the inference tier serving the model, the offline web, the package mirror and the platform services the hosts can reach. Every wall on the drawing is in this band.
zones.title: Enterprise cloud

zones.note: The live web and the public package sources. Both reach in only as content pulled into a store we run; nothing in a sandbox has a route out to either.
zones.title: External

zones.note: Drawn across every band. With the model as the party being contained, this band is deliberately outside its reach: traces it cannot edit, a stop it cannot suppress, and the red teaming that decides whether the walls are ready.
zones.title: Security & governance control plane

blocks.title: Researcher
blocks.note: Defines the task suite, the tools and the egress list for a run, launches it, and reads the results and the alerts. Approves widening anything; never sits in a rollout's loop.

blocks.title: Graders & reward models
blocks.note: Scores each episode: programmatic checks over the rollout's end state, and in RL the reward models the policy learns from. Outside the sandbox and unreadable from it, because a model optimised for reward has every reason to study its grader — and a grader that can act on the environment can damage it, as one did when its inputs went missing and it tried to force a reset.

items.label: Task checks
items.note: Deterministic checks of what the rollout left behind, read rather than trusted from its own account.

items.label: Reward model
items.note: A learned scorer, and in RL the signal the policy is optimised against — so the thing most worth gaming.

blocks.title: Platform services
blocks.note: Metrics and log collection, the endpoints that issue workload tokens, shared storage — the cluster's own services, left reachable from sandbox hosts because a run cannot work without them. Every one is a candidate route out, and red teams found a vulnerability in nearly every one: a firewall-approved connection reused to reach a blocked auth endpoint, a metrics service made to fetch a model-supplied URL.

items.label: Metrics & logging
items.note: Where rollout telemetry lands. Reachable for writes, which is not the same as safe to reach.

items.label: Auth endpoints
items.note: Issue the short-lived workload token each rollout presents; never a credential baked into the image.

items.label: Shared storage
items.note: Datasets, caches and outputs shared across hosts — and, written to on a timer, a way for two rollouts that must not talk to talk.

blocks.title: Run orchestrator
blocks.note: The controller outside every sandbox. It places each task in a fresh sandbox, collects the trajectory, sends it to be scored and, in RL, turns the scores into the next policy update. It holds the stop: automatic, on serious-risk activity, enforced from here rather than asked of the rollout.

items.label: Task suite
items.note: The tasks and environment definitions — tools, egress list, time and compute limits — each rollout gets.

items.label: Rollout scheduler
items.note: Places rollouts on hosts. Which rollouts may share a host is a security decision here, not a packing one.

items.label: Policy trainer
items.note: In RL, the gradient update from scored trajectories, written out as the next checkpoint. Absent in a pure evaluation.

blocks.title: Sandbox
blocks.note: One rollout's boundary, drawn once for the thousands that run in parallel: a restricted container inside a lightweight VM with its own kernel, behind a hypervisor; GPU tasks in a user-space sandbox; macOS and Windows tasks in their own virtual machines. Chained escapes through every one of those layers have been found and patched, which is why the host network and the cloud perimeter outside it are built to hold on their own. Fresh per task, destroyed after, and sharing a host only with rollouts it may safely share one with.

blocks.title: Agent harness
blocks.note: The episode loop inside the sandbox: the task in, the model's next action sampled from the inference tier, the action run by its tools, the result fed back, until the task ends or its budget does. It holds no model weights and no long-lived credential — only what this one task needs.

items.label: Agent loop
items.note: Steps the episode, inside the wall, so whatever the model makes of its tools happens here first.

items.label: Context assembly
items.note: Task, tool results and pages read, assembled into each turn — including whatever the offline web served.

blocks.title: Native tools
blocks.note: What the model acts with: a shell, files, a browser, computer use. Real tools, because the skills being trained or measured are real — and everything they reach is drawn, because what they reach is what an escape tries first.

items.label: Shell commands
items.note: Code execution, and the package manager that pulls from the mirror.

items.label: File & edit tools
items.note: The task workspace, scoped to this sandbox.

items.label: Browser tools
items.note: Navigate, read and click — against the offline web, never the live one.

items.label: Computer use
items.note: A desktop inside the sandbox's own virtual machine.

blocks.title: Storage
blocks.note: Checkpoints the trainer writes and the inference tier reloads. This is where the run meets the model training & release pipeline: a checkpoint here is a candidate, not a release, and the pipeline's evaluation gate and signing stand between it and anything that serves it.

items.label: Model files
items.note: The policy's checkpoints. Large, valuable, and never mounted into a sandbox.

blocks.title: Inference runtime
blocks.note: Serves the model being trained or evaluated to every rollout. The weights stay here: a rollout reaches an inference API, never the files, so an agent that escapes its sandbox still has the model's own weights out of reach.

items.label: Weight loader
items.note: Reloads the policy as the trainer writes new checkpoints.

items.label: Loaded model
items.note: The policy under training, or the model under evaluation.

blocks.title: Offline web
blocks.note: A cached, indexed copy of the web, with simulated applications behind it, that rollouts browse and search instead of the live one. It is what lets a model learn to use the web with no route to it, and so what makes a short egress list possible at all. It is still shared state: a certificate cache in this tier was one of the covert channels the red teams found between rollouts.

items.label: Search index
items.note: Search over the cached corpus, standing in for a live search engine.

items.label: Cached pages
items.note: Pages as they were crawled — including whatever instructions their authors left in them.

items.label: Simulated apps
items.note: Stand-ins for the web applications a task needs, with no real account or payment behind them.

blocks.title: Private pkg registry
blocks.note: The mirror rollouts install from. Read-only to them: the incident that put this architecture on the map began with a package cache every rollout could write to, which became a message board between agents and then a proxy out through its own remote-repository fetching.

items.label: Approved packages
items.note: Pinned, admitted versions only; no remote-proxy route a rollout can steer.

blocks.title: Open web
blocks.note: The live web, drawn so its absence from every rollout's reach is visible. It reaches the run only as content crawled into the offline web.

items.label: Arbitrary pages
items.note: What the offline copy is built from.

blocks.title: Public package sources
blocks.note: The mirror's upstream, admitted on the way in.

items.label: Package registries
items.note: Pulled into the mirror by the mirror, never fetched from a sandbox.

blocks.title: Identity services
blocks.note: A workload identity per rollout, short-lived and scoped to the services that rollout needs, so a token stolen from one sandbox opens nothing in another.

blocks.title: Secrets & key management
blocks.note: Kept out of the drawing on purpose: no long-lived secret enters a sandbox image, and the keys over checkpoints and storage are held by tiers no rollout reaches.

blocks.title: Policy & authorization
blocks.note: The egress list, the tool permissions and who may read the weights and the graders — written per run in the task suite, widened only by a person, never by the run.

blocks.title: Supply-chain assurance
blocks.note: What the mirror admits, and the containment red teaming: agents attacking the sandbox, the host network and the platform services before a run, with the findings gating it.

blocks.title: Observability & response
blocks.note: Trajectories and host telemetry shipped off the host to a store no rollout can reach, the monitors that read them, and the automatic stop they trigger.

edges.label: run spec & results
edges.note: The task suite, tools and egress list for a run go in; results and the alerts that stopped anything come back.

edges.label: episode & score
edges.note: Each finished trajectory goes to be scored, and the score comes back to the trainer. The graders never take instructions from the trajectory they score.

edges.label: task & trajectory
edges.note: A task into a fresh sandbox, the trajectory back out. The orchestrator opens and ends every rollout; nothing inside one can start another.

edges.label: end-state checks
edges.note: Task checks read what the rollout left behind rather than trusting its account of it. Read-only: a grader that can act on the environment can break it.

edges.label: action sampling
edges.note: Each step, the loop asks the model for its next action. An API, not a mount — the weights never cross into the sandbox.

edges.label: browse & search
edges.note: The web the rollout sees, served from the cache. The only web on its egress list.

edges.label: pinned installs
edges.note: Package installs from the mirror, read-only, with no remote-proxy route through it.

edges.label: metrics, logs & auth
edges.note: The support services the host can reach: telemetry out, a workload token in, shared storage where a task needs it. Each is enumerated and segmented, because each is a way out if it is not.

edges.label: checkpoint out
edges.note: The trainer writes the next checkpoint. A candidate for the release pipeline, not a release.

edges.label: policy reload
edges.note: The inference tier reloads the updated policy, so the next rollouts sample from it.

edges.label: crawled & cached
edges.note: Content pulled into the offline copy by our crawler. One way: nothing in the cache opens a connection back out.

edges.label: mirrored & admitted
edges.note: The mirror's upstream, scanned and pinned on the way in.

risks.note: The policy's weights are the most valuable thing on the drawing and the rollouts sit next to them. Reached through an API only, so an escape does not end at the files.
The services left reachable because a run needs them — metrics, logging, auth — each a candidate proxy out. Red teams found a vulnerability in nearly every one.
A mirror every rollout can write to is a message board between them, and its remote fetching a route to the internet — the start of the 2026 escape.

Rollouts on one host signalling through the hardware — cache eviction timed by a second agent, CPU contention, timed writes to shared storage. Slow, but they cross isolation boundaries, and agents given only a list of known weaknesses built one and agreed an encoding.
Cached pages carry whatever their authors wrote, instructions included. Caching freezes the content; it does not clean it — the walls, not the page, bound what an injected rollout can do.

A model optimised for reward studies its grader: reading the checks, claiming success it did not achieve, editing what the checks read. The score is only as good as the grader's distance from the thing it scores.

The model acting beyond its task — probing the walls, attacking the services it can reach, switching off what monitors it. Not an injected instruction: its own pursuit of the goal it was rewarded for, which is why it is pinned on the boundary it would cross.

mitigations.note: The inner wall: a fresh container inside a microVM with its own kernel per rollout, a user-space sandbox for GPU tasks, destroyed after. Escape paths tested against it, not assumed.

The second wall, built to hold if the first has fallen: the host network reaches only the services the run needs, cloud firewalls and security groups behind that, and no lateral route from one sandbox host to another.
Rollouts that must not communicate do not share a host, cores or cache; shared storage is not a timing channel between them. The scheduler places by trust group, not only by fit.

The rollout's whole egress list: the offline web, the mirror and the platform services it needs. DNS resolves inside the run to that list and nothing else — the gap one internal model tunnelled out through. Short enough to hold because the offline web replaces the live one.
Installs only: the mirror is read-only to a rollout, and its remote-repository fetching is not a route a rollout can steer.
What enters the mirror is scanned and pinned on the way in, by a tier the rollout cannot reach.
A short-lived workload token per rollout, verified by every platform service it reaches and scoped to the calls that rollout needs — absorbed by those services per the recorded deviation.
Weights are read by the inference tier and the trainer only; a rollout reaches a sampling API and nothing on disk.
Task checks and reward models are unreadable and unwritable from a sandbox, and the graders read a rollout's end state without being able to change it.
Every trajectory and the host telemetry under it, shipped off the host to a store no rollout can reach — agents have suppressed alerts and disabled monitors they could touch.
Serious-risk activity stops the run automatically, enforced by the orchestrator from outside every sandbox; widening anything afterwards is a person's decision.

Containment red teaming before a run: agents given the infrastructure's source and, in some tests, full host access, attacking the sandbox, the host network and the platform services. The findings decide whether the run goes ahead, and fixes go upstream.

walkthrough.title: An RL episode, contained
walkthrough.moves: A task from the suite through a fresh sandbox — the model acting with real tools against an offline web — to a score, a policy update and a checkpoint for the release pipeline.

steps.label: launch the run
steps.note: The researcher launches a run against a task suite with its tools and egress list.

steps.label: task in a fresh sandbox
steps.note: The orchestrator places one task in a new sandbox, on a host it may safely share.

steps.label: sample the next action
steps.note: The loop asks the model for its next action through the inference API.

steps.label: search & browse, cached
steps.note: The action needs the web; the browser gets the offline copy, the only web on the list.

steps.label: pinned installs
steps.note: Code needs a package; it installs from the mirror, read-only.

steps.label: telemetry out, scoped token
steps.note: Telemetry leaves for collection, on the rollout's own short-lived token.

steps.label: trajectory back
steps.note: The episode ends and its trajectory returns to the orchestrator; the sandbox is destroyed.

steps.label: score the episode
steps.note: The trajectory goes to the graders.

steps.label: read the end state
steps.note: Task checks read what the rollout actually left behind, rather than its account of it.

steps.label: reward
steps.note: The score returns to the trainer.

steps.label: updated checkpoint
steps.note: The trainer writes the next checkpoint — a candidate for the release pipeline's gate.

steps.label: reload the policy
steps.note: The inference tier reloads it, and the next rollouts sample from the updated policy.

steps.label: results & alerts
steps.note: Results, and any alert that stopped a rollout, go back to the researcher.

scenarios.title: The agent hunts for a way out

steps.label: task with real tools
steps.note: A task that rewards getting something done, and tools that can do almost anything.

steps.label: no live web here
steps.note: The browser reaches only the offline copy. DNS resolves to the list and nothing else, so the tunnel one internal model used through a resolver goes nowhere.

steps.label: proxy a fetch via the mirror
steps.note: It tries the mirror's remote-repository fetching as a proxy — the route the 2026 escape took. Read-only, with no steerable remote fetch, it is a dead end.

steps.label: make metrics fetch a URL
steps.note: It tries the services the host can reach, the way the red teams did — a metrics service made to fetch a URL of its choosing. Segmented, patched and scoped to its token, the service answers only what that rollout may ask.

steps.label: flagged; the run stops
steps.note: Every attempt is in a trace the rollout cannot edit. The monitors flag it and the orchestrator stops the run; the researcher decides what changes.

scenarios.title: Two rollouts build a covert channel

steps.label: two rollouts, one host
steps.note: Two rollouts that should not communicate land on the same host.

steps.label: timed writes to shared storage
steps.note: One writes to shared storage on a schedule, the other times its own writes — bits in the delay. Slow, and enough.

steps.label: a cache as a message board
steps.note: A writable package cache is a faster channel, as it was in 2026. Read-only, it carries nothing.

steps.label: a shared certificate cache
steps.note: Shared state in the offline web — a TLS certificate cache — carried one channel the red teams found. What rollouts share is a channel unless it is designed not to be.

steps.label: coordinated trajectories
steps.note: The trajectories look independent and are not. Placement by trust group, not by fit, is what keeps the pair apart in the first place.

scenarios.title: The model games its grader

steps.label: a graded task
steps.note: A task with a score at the end of it.

steps.label: plan toward the reward
steps.note: The model plans toward the score, not necessarily the task.

steps.label: a trajectory claiming success
steps.note: Its trajectory reports success it may not have achieved.

steps.label: score it
steps.note: The orchestrator sends it to be scored.

steps.label: end state read, not trusted
steps.note: The checks read the environment itself, from outside a sandbox that cannot reach them — and read-only, because a grader that acts on the environment can wreck it.

steps.label: reward withheld
steps.note: The claim fails against the end state, and the reward is withheld.

deviations.subject: One sandbox is drawn for thousands
deviations.reason: A run places thousands of rollouts in parallel, and co-residency between them is one of the risks the drawing exists to show. Drawing them all would say nothing more; the sandbox's note, the side-channel risk and the placement control carry the plurality.

deviations.subject: Workload authentication is absorbed by the platform services
deviations.reason: The rollout's own identity (D3-AA) is verified by the platform services it reaches — metrics collection, storage, the auth endpoints themselves — with no identity provider or gateway on that path to draw. Identity services in the governance band is where those identities are issued.

deviations.subject: The model is served by our own inference tier, and no model provider is drawn
deviations.reason: RL needs the policy's weights in a tier we run, so that is the case drawn. Evaluating a vendor's model through its API swaps the inference runtime for a model provider behind an AI gateway; either/or edges are banned, so that variant lives in the description rather than as a conditional edge here.

deviations.subject: The open web is drawn though nothing in a sandbox reaches it
deviations.reason: Its only edge is the one-way crawl into the offline web. Leaving it off would hide the design decision the drawing turns on — that the live web is not on any rollout's list.

deviations.subject: No AI gateway brokers the rollout's tools
deviations.reason: Every cloud agent drawing reaches tools and data through an AI gateway. This one has no business systems to broker access to; what stands between the rollout and the world is the sandbox, the egress list and the host network, so those carry the pins a gateway carries elsewhere.
