archetypes.title: Multi-agent workflow
summary: A hosted agent system doing real work over business records: requests, schedules and events start it, a durable orchestration layer plans and delegates across subagents, and every network tool call leaves through one governed gateway. The shape agent deployments converge on once the work outlives a single request.
description:
The spine is a trigger path: requests, schedules and events start the process, and it runs through supervisor agent, subagents, AI gateway, tool services and the systems of record behind them — there is no user interface, because nobody is conversing with it. The architecture's security posture lives almost entirely in one decision — that agents do not hold credentials for, or reach, network tools directly. Every network tool call, model call and connector call leaves through the gateway, which brokers short-lived credentials, enforces policy per call, applies rate and budget limits, and writes the audit trail as a tap rather than a favour asked of the agent.
Orchestration is durable: a supervisor decomposes work for subagents and an engine journals every step so the process survives crashes. Durability has two consequences nobody expects from reliability machinery. Everything a step returns is written down, so a step that returns a credential has persisted it. And the engine replays steps to recover, so a side effect that is not idempotent can execute more than once — including a payment.
Delegation is the other axis. Each subagent is, structurally, the single agent workflow nested one level down — the same loop, the same gateway crossing, a narrower grant. A subagent should inherit a narrowed slice of the supervisor's authority, not all of it; delegation that does not narrow is privilege distribution. And inter-agent messages are model output becoming model input — one confused agent propagates through the graph, which is what distinguishes multi-agent failure from a single agent with more tools.
The governance plane is drawn as its own plane beneath the drawing because it is what the personal-agent archetype lacks: a logical principal for every agent — short-lived tokens minted and constrained at the gateway, revocable per specialist even though the specialists share one process — a registry deciding what may run and which tools are admitted, evaluation gates in front of change, an append-only audit sink, and a stop that works while a process is mid-flight.
distinguishedBy:
Against the endpoint personal agent: the loop is nearly identical; the governance is not. Hosting buys an identity per agent, a policy boundary on every tool call, an audit trail and an administrator — none of which the endpoint pattern supplies.
Against the single agent workflow: each subagent here is that architecture nested one level down. What this page adds is everything the nesting brings — a supervisor whose routing is itself steerable, durable state that outlives any single request, replay that can re-execute side effects, and delegation chains that must narrow at every hop.

exemplars.name: LangGraph
exemplars.note: A stateful orchestration runtime for coordinating agents and deterministic steps, with persistence and durable execution. Used here in an application the organization hosts.

exemplars.name: Microsoft Agent Framework
exemplars.note: Graph workflows coordinate multiple agents and functions with explicit execution order. Illustrates the orchestration layer of a customer-operated multi-agent application.

exemplars.name: OpenAI Agents SDK
exemplars.note: Agents-as-tools and handoffs support coordination between specialist agents. The application chooses its delegation pattern, hosts the workers and supplies durable workflow infrastructure where needed.

zones.note: Nobody, most of the time: the operator appears only when a step escalates, reached through a work queue and answering with a signal. The approval they gave at the start is the only human decision until something escalates.
zones.title: User surfaces

zones.note: Everything we operate: the triggers that start the workflow — requests, schedules, events and resumptions — the supervisor and its specialists, the durable state they journal to, the crossing every brokered call leaves through, and our own tool servers and data.
zones.title: Enterprise cloud

zones.note: Outside the company — the model provider, the open web the agents search, and the public sources the package mirror admits from. Nothing here connects in; every call is ours.
zones.title: External

zones.note: Drawn across every band because it governs every band. A workflow that runs for days with nobody watching has no in-flight human gate, so this band carries the whole of the oversight.
zones.title: Security & governance control plane

blocks.title: Triggers & schedules
blocks.note: Requests, timers, webhooks and queue messages that start work with no human in the room — and the resumptions that wake a workflow which has been suspended for hours or days, including an operator's approval. There is no front end: this is the only way in, and whose authority the workflow carries for its whole life is bound here.

items.label: Schedules & events
items.note: The request, timer or queue message that starts a run, and the signal that resumes a suspended one. Each carries the grant the run acts on — a service principal with its own named scope, or an on-behalf-of grant that must outlive the session, because the work does.

blocks.title: Operator
blocks.note: The approver for consequential steps — an operator work queue, reached by a tool call and answering with a signal that resumes the suspended step, possibly days later. Present only when a step escalates; the workflow runs without them the rest of the time.

blocks.title: Agent harness

items.label: MCP client
items.note: The harness's own MCP client — the party that connects out, through the gateway's MCP brokerage, to remote servers.

blocks.note: One runtime, not a fleet of services. A supervisor and its specialists are objects in the same process, dispatched by the graph's own scheduler — no service boundary and no network hop. Each agent is a logical principal the scheduler assigns, with its own gateway-minted grant; the process is one trust boundary, so a compromise of it is a compromise of all of them. Drawing them nested says that, where drawing them side by side implied a deployment that does not exist.

blocks.title: Native tools
blocks.note: The tools compiled into the application itself, nested because the loop calling them is not a hop: decorated functions running in the loop's own process, under its identity, with its egress and its secrets, and the sandbox the loop's generated code runs in. This is the default way a tool gets attached, and the reason it is drawn: the in-process tool set is invisible to any gateway. What these tools reach is drawn — memory and retrieval through their handlers, and the package mirror through the sandbox's package manager.

items.label: Tool handlers
items.note: Functions in the application, holding whatever the application holds — including the outbound calls it makes itself, with no broker in front, and the retrieval and state reads the loop treats as context.

items.label: Sandboxed tools
items.note: Code execution in an isolated runtime inside the harness's own tool surface — the loop writes code, only the sandbox runs it, and what it installs comes from the mirror and nowhere else. Bash is where the package manager lives.

blocks.title: Supervisor agent
blocks.note: Decomposes the goal, routes work to the subagents and owns the process; the durable engine journals every step and replays to recover. Delegation should narrow authority at every hop.

items.label: Agent loop
items.note: Decomposes the goal and routes work to specialists.

items.label: Durable engine
items.note: Journals results and replays to recover. Replay without re-authorisation re-executes side effects.

blocks.title: Subagents
blocks.note: The specialists the supervisor drives, each with its own context and tool set. Structurally each one is the single agent workflow nested one level down — the supervisor above it is the only real difference.

items.label: Specialist agents
items.note: Each runs the same loop as the single agent workflow, as its own logical principal.

items.label: Inter-agent messages
items.note: Model output becoming model input — one confused agent propagates through the graph.

blocks.title: Memory & state
blocks.note: What the workflow knows and what it has done. The journal is a reliability feature and a secrets sink in the same breath.

items.label: Step journal
items.note: Everything a step returns is persisted here. A returned credential is a stored one — and when the engine is a hosted service, the journal lives with the vendor, payloads included, unless a payload codec encrypts them under our keys.

items.label: Vector index
items.note: Retrieval context for the agents.

items.label: Shared memory
items.note: Cross-step working state the agents read back as context.

blocks.title: AI gateway
blocks.note: The one door for every brokered call that leaves over the network. Agents hold no credentials for those calls and reach no remote tool directly; every network model and tool call is brokered, policy-checked, rate-limited and logged here — the in-process tool set is the drawn exception. Its items are the traffic classes it brokers — the checks it runs are the numbered pins on this block and its edges, and the call-outs beneath.

blocks.title: Model provider
blocks.note: The published inference interface, called many times across the process. Everything behind it is the provider's, and is not drawn.

items.label: Inference API
items.note: Reached only through the gateway, on brokered credentials.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: Our own action surface, admitted by the registry and reached only through the gateway.

blocks.title: Enterprise data
blocks.note: The systems of record the agents write to — where a wrong action becomes a real one, and where a workflow that ran for two days did most of its damage before anyone looked.

items.label: Org data
items.note: The authoritative state the workflow changes.

items.label: File storage
items.note: Artifacts a step produced and a later step reads back as context.

blocks.title: Open web
blocks.note: Search results and fetched pages, reached only through the gateway's web search and fetch tool. Every page is authored by someone else, and its text enters a graph in which one confused agent propagates to all the others.

items.label: Web search
items.note: The search tool's results — ranked by somebody else, and read as context.

items.label: Arbitrary pages
items.note: Visible and hidden text alike, served by whoever owns the page.

blocks.title: Public package sources
blocks.note: Where the mirror gets what it serves: the public package registries and the skill and extension hubs it proxies and admits from. Nothing here is ours, which is why admission happens at the mirror and not at the tool that asked.

items.label: Package registries
items.note: PyPI, npm and their kind — mirrored, never reached by a tool directly in the target state.

items.label: Skill & extension hubs
items.note: Community catalogues of skills, extensions and images, admitted through the same door.

blocks.title: Identity services
blocks.note: One logical principal per agent, so a supervisor and its specialists are distinguishable in the audit and revocable separately, though they share one process. A graph of agents sharing one identity is a graph with no accountability in it.

blocks.title: Secrets & key management
blocks.note: Short-lived credentials fetched at step time rather than held for the process's life — which matters more here than anywhere, because the process's life may be days.

blocks.title: Policy & authorization
blocks.note: A per-call decision about this agent, this tool, this argument — never a standing grant, and the brake on a loop that would otherwise be metered only by the invoice.

blocks.title: Supply-chain assurance
blocks.note: Which agents and tools exist at all. In a multi-agent graph the registry is also the inventory: an agent nobody registered is an agent nobody can revoke.

blocks.title: Observability & response
blocks.note: The trail is assembled from the gateway's record and the engine's own traces, not volunteered by the agents — and the stop has to reach a workflow that is suspended mid-flight, not just one that is currently running.

blocks.title: Private pkg registry
blocks.note: The organisation's package registry: public packages mirrored and admitted, and the organisation's own builds published by its CI pipelines. It serves whatever the sandbox installs — a dependency the agent's generated code needs, a tool package a step pulls in — pinned by digest. Pulling and publishing are separate grants: agents pull, build pipelines publish, and the registry's own proxying of upstream sources is bounded to what admission allows.

edges.label: trigger
edges.note: Timers, webhooks and queue messages that start work with no human in the room — and the signals that resume a workflow suspended for hours or days.

edges.label: escalation
edges.note: The reach-back: a proposal above the threshold is written to an approval channel — a work queue, a ticket, a chat — as an ordinary tool call, bound to the exact action, arguments and case, with an expiry. Nobody is on a socket waiting for it.

edges.label: approval / instruction
edges.note: The human's answer arrives the way everything arrives here: as an event. It is validated against the parked proposal before anything executes — a blanket "yes" approves nothing in particular.

edges.label: read & write / context
edges.note: The shared memory and the retrieval context, read and written through the tool handlers every specialist runs. Durable by design, which is why everything a step returns persists.

edges.label: checkpoint / journal
edges.note: The durable engine's own path: every step checkpointed to the journal as machinery, not as a tool call, and the journal read back to rebuild a run after a crash or a sleep of days. Replay re-executes side effects unless the fencing on the tool path stops it.

edges.label: delegate / results
edges.note: Work handed down and results handed back. A specialist's output becomes the supervisor's input, which is how one confused agent propagates through the graph.

edges.label: inference, MCP & skills
edges.note: Every brokered call the agents make — inference, MCP, skills and APIs — crosses here on a brokered, step-scoped credential. The in-process handlers' own calls do not.

edges.label: pinned installs
edges.note: What the harness's sandbox installs — a package manager running as a shell command — is pulled straight from the mirror, pinned by digest, never from a public registry. The gateway is the other doorway into the harness, for inference, MCP, skills and APIs; it is not on this path.

edges.label: inference / completion
edges.note: Inference on the brokered credential, for every agent in the graph.

edges.label: internal tool calls
edges.note: Admitted against the registry and narrowed to a scoped grant before anything executes.

edges.label: scoped reads & writes
edges.note: Where the workflow's effects land on systems of record, and where artifacts a later step reads back as context are stored.

edges.label: web search & fetch
edges.note: A specialist's search or page fetch, opened by the gateway on its behalf. What returns rides back on it, untrusted, into a graph where it can become several agents' input at once.

edges.label: mirrored & admitted
edges.note: The mirror's own supply chain: public packages proxied in, scanned, pinned and admitted before anything inside can pull them. Build pipelines publish the organisation's own artifacts beside them.

risks.note: Skill and tool packages reach the harness from the community hubs through this mirror, and their manifests and descriptions become tool metadata every agent selects from. Admitted without verifying the publisher and the signature, a deceptive description or a shadowed tool name enters here.

Handlers compiled into the harness's process hold whatever the process holds and cross no chokepoint — the gateway never sees a vulnerable or malicious in-process tool, and the workload's network policy is the drawn bound on where it can reach.
The admission list is the tool supply chain; whoever writes it programs the agents.
Three hops in, nobody can say which agent decided what on whose behalf — the chain the shared subagents block exists to carry, legible only if delegation is traced as it happens.
A subagent that inherits its parent's full authority is privilege distribution, not delegation.
Records, documents and API responses read over the process's lifetime are chances to steer an agent whose output another agent will trust.
Search results and fetched pages enter a graph in which one confused agent propagates to all the others — classified at the crossing or trusted by every specialist at once.
The request that starts a process is model input like any other — it reaches the same context window as the system instruction, and the workflow acts on it for days.
Shared memory is cross-step instruction: an injection journaled on day one re-enters every agent's context for the rest of the process — memory poisoning by its OWASP name.
Inference called many times across days of process is a spend surface worth a brake.
The loop materializes here — agents re-planning against each other can run for as long as nobody notices; the gateway's ceilings brake only what crosses it.

The journal records everything a step returns — a returned secret is a persisted one, and every writer is in scope: the specialists journal to the same store, so the secrets-sink risk multiplies with the agent count.
Inter-agent messages are model output landing in another agent's context as instruction.
The completion decides the next delegation and the next tool call, and it is untrusted output — the provider return is where it enters the graph.
Consequential writes with no human present — and replay can execute a non-idempotent one twice.
Steer the supervisor's routing — through injected content or a tampered route definition — and every specialist downstream works from the attacker's plan without any individual agent misbehaving.
The vector index is written by steps and read by every later one; a poisoned entry is retrieved into the context of an agent that never saw it arrive.

mitigations.note: Shared memory is what lets one branch of the graph steer another. Scoping it per run, and treating what a step wrote as untrusted when a later step reads it, is the control.
Behavioural checks in front of every model, prompt or agent change — the last point at which a change can be caught before it runs unattended for days.

The delegation graph has to be legible after the fact and while it runs: which agent decided what, on whose behalf, and what it passed to the next one — an append-only trail assembled here from the traces the gateway and the engine record, and read while the process is still running, because coordinated fan-out and autonomous persistence are visible only if something is reading.

The grant a run carries, bound at ingress: a service principal with its own named scope, or an on-behalf-of grant scoped to this request — not a standing power, and governed in the directory for as long as the work lives.

A logical principal per agent — the supervisor and each specialist, never one shared identity — with short-lived tokens minted and constrained at the gateway, so every step in the chain is attributable and separately revocable. The specialists share one process; a compromise of the harness is a compromise of all of them, which is why the grants and not the process boundary carry the separation.
Credentials brokered at step time, short-lived and scoped; agents hold none for network calls — the in-process tool set is the drawn exception.
A policy decision on every tool call — agent, tool, arguments — outside the loop.
Each tool runs on the calling specialist's own task-scoped grant: only the actions and records its step needs, never the workflow's whole reach.
Authority narrows where it is handed down: a specialist receives tokens scoped to its task, never the supervisor's credentials — delegation that does not narrow is privilege distribution.

Rate and budget ceilings on the crossing: every model and remote tool call any agent makes counts against the run's budget, so a loop that keeps re-planning hits the ceiling. Work that never crosses — in the sandbox or in process — is not metered here.

Returned record and web content is classified at the crossing before it reaches any agent's context, and the initiator's request text on its first crossing, before the model reads it. Inter-agent messages and shared-memory reads never cross here.
Redaction on what steps may journal, because the journal outlives the process — and every writer is in scope, the specialists included.
Per-run index scoping and ingest trust on what enters the corpus — the answer to a poisoned index, distinct from scoping what a step may read.

An approval gate on consequential writes, sized to the blast radius. The engine suspends the step and resumes only on an approval bound to the exact action and workflow state — see the escalation scenario.
Reads scoped to the workflow's grant rather than the service's reach — the same entitlement filter the siblings enforce on this edge.
Generated code runs only in the sandbox — an isolated runtime with its own filesystem and network, torn down per task — never in the harness's own process beside the agents.

Admission for agents and tools — nothing runs or is offered by default, and in a multi-agent graph the registry is also the inventory: an agent nobody registered is an agent nobody can revoke. The gateway enforces the resulting list per call.
A stop that works mid-flight, because these processes run for days.

Tool definitions reach the harness's MCP client through the gateway's brokerage, and each is checked against the content hash pinned at admission before any agent's model is offered it — a definition changed after admission, the rug-pull, is refused, and the check repeats after every update.

Network policy on the whole harness workload, not just the sandbox: the sandbox reaches only the AI gateway and the package mirror, and the in-process handlers' own calls reach a named allowlist. Shell commands, fetches and handler calls are bounded here — not at the gateway, which brokers model, MCP and API calls and sees nothing else.

Admission scanning at the mirror: malware and typosquat checks on everything proxied in from a public source, before anything inside can pull it. The registered embodiment of artifact scanning, on the one edge where it applies.

walkthrough.title: A request starts a days-long process
walkthrough.moves: A long-running process: work delegated to specialists, journalled at every step.

steps.label: request with delegated grant
steps.note: The request arrives as an API call or a queue message, and a delegated grant scoped to this workflow is bound to it — a binding that must outlive the session, because the work does. Nobody stays connected for what follows.

steps.label: first checkpoint
steps.note: The run is journaled from its first step by the durable engine — everything a step returns will persist here, which is the durability the drawing exists to show.

steps.label: durable identity
steps.note: The journal acknowledges; the run now has a durable identity.

steps.label: plan request
steps.note: The supervisor's first call is for a plan — nothing is delegated before the goal is decomposed — and every brokered call any agent makes funnels through this one door.

steps.label: inference
steps.note: Inference on brokered credentials, limits applied.

steps.label: decomposition
steps.note: The decomposition comes back across the crossing.

steps.label: plan into supervisor
steps.note: Into the supervisor as a plan — untrusted output, now the work breakdown.

steps.label: delegate narrowed task
steps.note: The supervisor delegates; each specialist takes its task with a narrowed grant, not the supervisor's authority.

steps.label: shared memory read
steps.note: The specialist reads shared memory and the retrieval context through the tool handlers — state this run's other steps wrote.

steps.label: context, attributed
steps.note: It comes back as context labelled with the step that wrote it, and is read as untrusted input.

steps.label: specialist's calls
steps.note: A specialist's model and tool calls leave through the same door, on its own grant.

steps.label: scoped tool call
steps.note: Tool calls carry the narrowed per-step grant.

steps.label: write behind gate
steps.note: The write lands — behind the approval gate when it is consequential; the escalation scenario walks that suspension.

steps.label: record confirmed
steps.note: The record confirms the write.

steps.label: result
steps.note: The result crosses back through the same door.

steps.label: result to specialist
steps.note: It lands with the specialist that asked, which decides its next call.

steps.label: next call, web search
steps.note: The specialist's next call is a web search, through the same door.

steps.label: search & fetch
steps.note: The gateway opens the call to the open web.

steps.label: classified return
steps.note: What returns is classified before any agent reads it, because one confused agent propagates.

steps.label: classified result to specialist
steps.note: The classified result lands with the specialist that asked.

steps.label: slice reported
steps.note: Each specialist reports its slice back to the supervisor, which checkpoints the step to the journal. Days may pass before an event wakes the run — the journal is what it wakes into.

steps.label: final checkpoint
steps.note: The final checkpoint: the run is complete and durable, possibly days after the request.

scenarios.title: A step replays after a crash

steps.label: rebuild from journal
steps.note: The engine rebuilds state from the journal — including anything a step persisted.

steps.label: replayed steps
steps.note: Replayed steps land on their specialists again.

steps.label: fresh credentials
steps.note: Replayed steps re-request credentials; nothing survives from the first run.

steps.label: fencing check
steps.note: Idempotency fencing decides whether the side effect may run again.

steps.label: write, once or twice
steps.note: Without fencing, the payment executes twice. The journal replays; the world does not.

scenarios.title: A consequential write escalates for approval

steps.label: write above threshold
steps.note: A step proposes a write above the threshold.

steps.label: threshold trips; suspend
steps.note: The per-call policy trips the threshold; the engine suspends the workflow rather than executing.

steps.label: suspension
steps.note: The suspension comes back as the step's result.

steps.label: step parked in journal
steps.note: The supervisor parks the step in the journal.

steps.label: approval-channel call
steps.note: The workflow reaches back — a call to the approval channel, admitted like any tool.

steps.label: approval channel (tool)
steps.note: The approval channel is a tool: a work queue, a ticket, a chat.

steps.label: queue item for operator
steps.note: An operator finds the proposal in the queue, bound to the exact action, arguments and workflow state, with an expiry. Nothing is waiting on a socket for them.

steps.label: approval signal
steps.note: The approval returns as a signal, possibly days later, and is validated against the suspended step — a blanket "resume" approves nothing in particular.

steps.label: step resumes
steps.note: The suspended step resumes, on credentials fetched now.

steps.label: action leaves
steps.note: Only then does the action leave.

steps.label: admitted with approval
steps.note: Under the same per-call policy as before.

steps.label: write lands
steps.note: The write lands, attributable to both the workflow and the approver.

scenarios.title: An event fires days into the process

steps.label: timer or webhook resumes
steps.note: A timer or webhook resumes work with nobody watching — the waiting step wakes days after the request that started the process.

steps.label: re-plan on fresh grant
steps.note: The supervisor re-plans from the journal, on credentials fetched now — the ones from day one would be stale authority.

steps.label: inference
steps.note: Inference on the fresh grant.

steps.label: plan for waking step
steps.note: The plan for the waking step comes back.

steps.label: into supervisor
steps.note: Into the supervisor.

steps.label: re-narrowed delegation
steps.note: Delegation re-narrows — the waking specialist gets its slice, not the run's whole grant.

steps.label: specialist's call
steps.note: The specialist's call leaves through the same door.

steps.label: action under per-call policy
steps.note: The action proceeds under the same per-call policy as an attended run.

scenarios.title: A dependency arrives with the task

steps.label: package install (pinned)
steps.note: A sandboxed step needs a package its generated code imports; the package manager runs as a shell command inside the harness's own tool surface and pulls from the mirror — the one destination the sandbox's network policy allows.

steps.label: admitted build
steps.note: The admitted build comes back, pinned by digest — the hop a poisoned package actually arrives on, which is why admission and pinning are the controls that live here.

deviations.subject: Subagents are drawn as one block
deviations.reason: There are several, with different contexts and tools. They share one block because the risks — inherited authority, message propagation, chain opacity — are properties of the delegation pattern rather than of any particular specialist; each specialist individually is the single agent workflow, one level down.

deviations.subject: Two of this architecture's risks have no CoSAI equivalent
deviations.reason: OWASP's agentic taxonomy names memory poisoning and cascading hallucination as distinct threats; CoSAI's risk set has neither. They are pinned here as prompt injection and insecure model output, the nearest true statements, which lose the compounding that makes both dangerous in a multi-agent system. Recorded rather than papered over.

archetypes.title: Chat agent with tools
summary: A hosted conversational agent where a human is in the loop for every turn: chat is the core input, tools execute mid-conversation on the user's behalf, and consequential actions are proposed in the thread before they run. The human-present counterpart of the single agent workflow, and the shape most domain copilots take.
description:
The defining property is that consequential actions must be proposed and approved in the thread before they execute. That is a target-state requirement, not a fact about tool-calling chat: real loops run many read-only tools mid-turn before anything renders, so the control set splits actions into two classes — automatic read-only tools, and mutating actions that wait for the human. In-thread approval is the primary gate for the second class, where the single agent workflow, acting with nobody present, has to lean on compensating transactions instead. The gate is only as good as the proposal text: an approval rendered as "OK to proceed?" approves nothing in particular.
Authority is on-behalf-of. The tools act as the conversing user, on a grant scoped to the session, not as a workload identity with standing powers — the reachable set is what this user may touch, decided per call. Sessions end and the grant ends with them; an agent tier that accumulates authority across conversations has quietly become the single agent workflow without its controls.
The conversation itself is the persistence surface. Context accumulates across turns — retrievals, tool results, uploaded files — and everything in it stands beside the system instruction on the next model call. One poisoned tool result steers every later action in the session, which is why memory is scoped to the conversation and why returned content is classified on the way back in.
Every network model and tool call leaves through the AI gateway on brokered credentials, the same crossing every agent architecture in this catalogue draws — the in-process tool set is the drawn exception. The chat surface changes who is watching, not how the calls leave.
distinguishedBy:
Against the durable multi-agent workflow: the horizon is one conversation, not a days-long process. No supervisor, no journal, no replay — the thread is the state, and the human in it is the gate that durability machinery replaces there.
Against the single agent workflow: the same loop with the human kept in the turns. In-thread approval replaces the compensating transaction as the primary control; remove the human from the turns and you are in that architecture, and should be reading its page.
Against the enterprise AI chat with connectors: the same conversational surface, bought rather than built. There the vendor operates the loop and the controls are tenant configuration and assurance; here the whole workload is ours, which is what makes every pin on this page enforceable.

exemplars.name: Vercel AI SDK
exemplars.note: Build a streaming chat interface with server-side tool execution and tool approval. The application connects the conversation to its own authenticated business APIs.

exemplars.name: OpenAI Agents SDK
exemplars.note: Use sessions, tools, streaming and human approval to implement a conversational agent. The chat interface and customer-operated application wrap the SDK’s agent loop.

zones.note: The person in the conversation — present for every turn, and the approval gate for the actions that matter.
zones.title: User surfaces

zones.note: Everything we operate: the chat surface that establishes identity, the loop, its state, the crossing every brokered call leaves through, and our own tool servers and systems of record. The whole workload is ours, which is what distinguishes this from the endpoint agents.
zones.title: Enterprise cloud

zones.note: Outside the company: the model provider, the open web the agent searches, and the public sources the package mirror admits from. Nothing here connects in; every call is ours.
zones.title: External

zones.note: Drawn across every band because it governs every band. The in-thread approval is a control the user operates; this band is the set the operator does.
zones.title: Security & governance control plane

blocks.title: End user
blocks.note: Present for every turn, and the approval gate for the actions that matter. Also the author of untrusted input — the conversation is model input written by the party the actions will benefit.

blocks.title: Triggers & schedules
blocks.note: Chat agents run unattended too now — scheduled digests, triggered follow-ups, jobs a conversation set up and walked away from. Drawn because a run nobody started has no human in the thread to approve it: its read-only tools run, and a mutating action suspends at the gateway until the user approves it in the thread. A scheduler that carries its own approval would make it the single-agent workflow wearing a chat interface.

items.label: Schedules & events
items.note: A timer or trigger the conversation configured, firing with the thread closed.

blocks.title: Application front end
blocks.note: The chat surface and its session machinery. The identity established here is the authority every tool call downstream acts on.

items.label: App & API endpoint
items.note: The published chat surface — web, app or embedded widget.

items.label: Identity binding
items.note: Who is conversing, bound to the session before the loop runs — the identity the tools act as.

items.label: File upload
items.note: Documents dropped into the thread — content authored anywhere, entering the same context window as the user's words.

blocks.title: Native tools
blocks.note: The tools compiled into the application itself, nested because the loop calling them is not a hop: decorated functions running in the loop's own process, under its identity, with its egress and its secrets, and the sandbox the loop's generated code runs in. This is the default way a tool gets attached, and the reason it is drawn: the in-process tool set is invisible to any gateway, so nothing on the crossing authorizes or meters it — the handlers' own checks and the workload's network policy are its bounds. What these tools reach is drawn — memory and retrieval through their handlers, and the package mirror through the sandbox's package manager.

items.label: Tool handlers
items.note: Functions in the application, holding whatever the application holds — including the outbound calls it makes itself, with no broker in front, and the retrieval and state reads the loop treats as context.

items.label: Sandboxed tools
items.note: Code execution in an isolated runtime inside the harness's own tool surface — the loop writes code, only the sandbox runs it, and what it installs comes from the mirror and nowhere else. Bash is where the package manager lives.

blocks.title: Agent harness
blocks.note: Plans within a turn, proposes actions in the thread, and carries the conversation's accumulated context into every model call. Runs under its own workload identity but acts on the user's grant.

items.label: Agent loop
items.note: Reads the turn and the history, calls the model, proposes the next reply or action.

items.label: Context assembly
items.note: Merges the turn, the conversation memory and the tool results into one prompt. Everything merged stands beside the system instruction.

items.label: MCP client
items.note: The harness's own MCP client — the party that connects out, through the gateway's MCP brokerage, to remote servers.

blocks.title: Memory & state
blocks.note: The conversation's accumulated context and the retrieval index behind it. Scoped to the session and the user — cross-conversation memory would let one user's text steer another's actions.

items.label: Conversation state
items.note: Every turn, retrieval and tool result so far — read back on each call as context.

items.label: Vector index
items.note: Grounding content retrieved into the thread, with the permissions of the asking user.

blocks.title: AI gateway
blocks.note: The one crossing every network-brokered model and tool call leaves through — the in-process tool set is the drawn exception. The agent tier holds no standing credentials for these calls; the gateway brokers them per call, meters spend and writes the audit trail as a tap on the crossing. Its items are the traffic classes it brokers — the checks it runs are the numbered pins on this block and its edges, and the call-outs beneath.

blocks.title: Model provider
blocks.note: The published inference interface. What runs behind it is the provider's and is not drawn.

items.label: Inference API
items.note: Returns the reply and the proposed tool calls — content the thread renders and the human reads.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: Our own tool servers and service APIs. Every call carries the conversing user's grant rather than the service's own authority, which is what makes the identity established at the front end load-bearing all the way down here.

blocks.title: Enterprise data
blocks.note: The systems of record a conversation actually changes, and the grounding content it reads back. Reached through our own tool surface rather than straight from the gateway, so the scoping and the record happen somewhere.

items.label: Org data
items.note: The systems of record the approved actions land on.

items.label: File storage
items.note: Documents retrieved into the thread as grounding — written by many hands, read back as context.

blocks.title: Open web
blocks.note: Search results and fetched pages, reached only through the gateway's web search and fetch tool. Every page is authored by someone else, and its text stands beside the user's words on the next call.

items.label: Web search
items.note: The search tool's results — ranked by somebody else, and read as context.

items.label: Arbitrary pages
items.note: Visible and hidden text alike, served by whoever owns the page.

blocks.title: Public package sources
blocks.note: Where the mirror gets what it serves: the public package registries and the skill and extension hubs it proxies and admits from. Nothing here is ours, which is why admission happens at the mirror and not at the tool that asked.

items.label: Package registries
items.note: PyPI, npm and their kind — mirrored, never reached by a tool directly in the target state.

items.label: Skill & extension hubs
items.note: Community catalogues of skills, extensions and images, admitted through the same door.

blocks.title: Identity services
blocks.note: The user's identity and the agent's workload identity, issued and kept distinct. In this archetype the two are deliberately not the same thing: the loop runs as itself and acts on the user's grant.

blocks.title: Secrets & key management
blocks.note: Short-lived, user-scoped credentials minted per call, so the agent tier holds no standing keys for brokered calls.

blocks.title: Policy & authorization
blocks.note: What the conversation may reach and what it may spend, decided outside the loop that would otherwise be arguing for itself.

blocks.title: Supply-chain assurance
blocks.note: Which tools may be offered to a conversation at all — admission, not discovery — and the behavioural checks in front of every model, prompt or tool change.

blocks.title: Observability & response
blocks.note: Append-only and off the agent's write path, because the thread is not the audit trail — plus the stop that ends the sessions and revokes the identity without a deploy.

blocks.title: Private pkg registry
blocks.note: The organisation's package registry: public packages mirrored and admitted, and the organisation's own builds published by its CI pipelines. It serves whatever the sandbox installs — a dependency the agent's generated code needs, a tool package a step pulls in — pinned by digest. Pulling and publishing are separate grants: agents pull, build pipelines publish, and the registry's own proxying of upstream sources is bounded to what admission allows.

edges.label: conversation
edges.note: Turn in, reply back — and the in-thread approval prompt when an action is consequential. Read-only tools run mid-turn without ceremony; mutating actions wait for the human.

edges.label: scheduled run
edges.note: The same loop, with nobody reading the reply: reads proceed, and a mutating action waits for the in-thread approval this path cannot supply.

edges.label: turn / reply & proposal
edges.note: The turn arrives with the user's identity attached; the reply and any action proposal return on the same path.

edges.label: read & write / context
edges.note: The conversation so far reads back as context on every call through the state and retrieval handlers, and each turn's results are written forward by them — the persistence that lets one turn's injection reach the next.

edges.label: inference, MCP & skills
edges.note: Every brokered call out of the loop — inference, MCP, skills and APIs — crosses here on a credential scoped to the conversing user. The in-process handlers' own calls do not.

edges.label: pinned installs
edges.note: What the harness's sandbox installs — a package manager running as a shell command — is pulled straight from the mirror, pinned by digest, never from a public registry. The gateway is the other doorway into the harness, for inference, MCP, skills and APIs; it is not on this path.

edges.label: inference / completion
edges.note: Inference on the brokered credential. The completion proposes the reply and the tool calls — content the human will read, and untrusted output all the same.

edges.label: internal tool calls
edges.note: Approved actions leave with the user's narrowed grant; tool results return into the thread as context.

edges.label: scoped reads & writes
edges.note: Where an approved action becomes a real one on a system of record — and where the grounding content a later turn will treat as instruction is read from.

edges.label: web search & fetch
edges.note: A search or page fetch mid-turn, opened by the gateway on the conversation's behalf. What returns rides back on it — untrusted content entering the conversation.

edges.label: mirrored & admitted
edges.note: The mirror's own supply chain: public packages proxied in, scanned, pinned and admitted before anything inside can pull them. Build pipelines publish the organisation's own artifacts beside them.

risks.note: Skill and tool packages reach the harness from the community hubs through this mirror, and their manifests and descriptions become tool metadata the agent selects from. Admitted without verifying the publisher and the signature, a deceptive description or a shadowed tool name enters here.

Handlers compiled into the loop's process hold whatever the process holds and cross no chokepoint — the gateway never sees a vulnerable or malicious in-process tool, and the workload's network policy is the drawn bound on where it can reach.
The admission list is the tool supply chain; whoever writes it programs the agent.
The agent acts for the user with the service's reach. Keeping every tool call on the user's grant, not the workload's, is what closes the gap.

The conversation is model input authored by the party the actions benefit, and it reaches the same context window as the system instruction — and uploaded documents, authored by anyone, arrive on the same edge.
Search results and fetched pages return into the thread — content somebody else authored, standing beside the user's words on the next call.

Conversation memory carries a poisoned turn forward: one bad retrieval steers every later action in the session — memory poisoning by its OWASP name, pinned as prompt injection per the recorded deviation.
Grounding content read back from records and files was written by many hands — the scenario beside this drawing walks exactly this path.
Per-token inference behind a public chat surface makes unbounded conversation a spend problem.
An agentic turn runs many tool calls before anything renders, and the scheduled path runs with nobody watching — rate limits at the entry never see a mid-turn loop.
The session accumulates everything retrieved on earlier turns; a late question can surface records the current topic never needed.
The completion proposes the tool calls, and it is untrusted output.
An action the human approved without reading is not an overseen action, and a scheduled run has nobody in the thread to approve at all. Approval fatigue is this architecture's version of no gate.
The vector index grounds the thread; content planted in the indexed sources returns as trusted context with the asking user's permissions.

mitigations.note: Tools exist in a conversation only because the registry admitted them — admission, not discovery. Admission is a change-time decision made here; the gateway enforces the resulting list per call.
Behavioural checks in front of every model, prompt or tool change, because the thing being changed is what decides the next action the human is asked to approve.

In-thread approval before consequential writes, with the proposal specific enough to be worth reading — the architecture's primary control. Scheduled runs have no thread, so their writes stop at the action policy.
A delegated grant scoped to the session and the user, not a standing power the service holds.
Every tool call bounded by what the conversing user may touch, decided per call.
A distinct workload identity for the agent tier, verified at the gateway and kept separate from the user grants it carries.
Brokered, per-call, user-scoped credentials; the loop holds no standing keys for brokered calls.
Conversation-scoped memory with hard boundaries — no cross-session reads, ever.
Retrieval scoped to the user's own grant, not the service's reach — what a read may return is decided at the store, per session.

Ingest trust on what enters the indexed sources and per-tenant isolation inside the index — the answer to a poisoned index, distinct from scoping what a read may return: an entitled document can still be a malicious one.

The user's turns, uploaded documents and returned record and web content are classified on the crossing before the model reads them — classification here, permission containment at the tool scoping pin.
The front end renders model output — sanitise markup and links before display, because a rendered image URL can carry the conversation to an attacker without a single click.
Redaction on what a session may accumulate, because the thread outlives the turn that needed it.
Session and per-user rate ceilings at the edge, before token spend and action volume are committed.
Every proposal, approval and action recorded off the agent's write path — the thread is not the audit trail.
A stop that ends live sessions and revokes the agent's identity without a deploy.

Mutating actions are refused unless the call carries an approval bound to this action, its arguments and this session — a scheduled run's included; read-only actions pass on the user's grant. This is the decision the in-thread approval exists to feed.
Per-turn tool-call and token ceilings on the crossing — the brake a mid-turn loop actually meets, which the session ceiling at the entry never sees.
User grant, agent workload identity and session scope intersect on every call; the gateway exchanges the user's token for a narrowed one and never forwards it.

Tool definitions reach the harness's MCP client through the gateway's brokerage, and each is checked against the content hash pinned at admission before the model is offered it — a definition changed after admission, the rug-pull, is refused, and the check repeats after every update.

Network policy on the whole harness workload, not just the sandbox: the sandbox reaches only the AI gateway and the package mirror, and the in-process handlers' own calls reach a named allowlist. Shell commands, fetches and handler calls are bounded here — not at the gateway, which brokers model, MCP and API calls and sees nothing else.

Admission scanning at the mirror: malware and typosquat checks on everything proxied in from a public source, before anything inside can pull it. The registered embodiment of artifact scanning, on the one edge where it applies.
Generated code runs only in the sandbox — an isolated runtime with its own filesystem and network, torn down per task — never in the harness's own process.

walkthrough.title: A turn that ends in an action
walkthrough.moves: A question, a reply, and the approved action the conversation decided on.

steps.label: consequential request
steps.note: The user asks for something consequential, in their own words.

steps.label: turn with identity
steps.note: The turn enters the loop with the user's identity attached.

steps.label: conversation state read
steps.note: The conversation so far is requested.

steps.label: context loads
steps.note: And loads as context.

steps.label: context, user-scoped
steps.note: The context leaves the loop on a brokered, user-scoped credential.

steps.label: inference
steps.note: The model proposes a reply and a tool call.

steps.label: reply & tool proposal
steps.note: The completion comes back across the crossing.

steps.label: pending proposal
steps.note: And into the loop — untrusted output, now a pending proposal.

steps.label: proposal to render
steps.note: The proposal travels to the surface to be rendered, nothing yet executed.

steps.label: proposal in thread
steps.note: It renders in the thread — specific enough to be worth reading: the action, the target, the amount, the expiry.

steps.label: approval (bound)
steps.note: The user approves. The approval is bound to that exact action and its arguments — an "OK" with nothing attached approves nothing in particular.

steps.label: confirmation validated
steps.note: The confirmation is validated against the pending proposal before anything executes.

steps.label: approved action
steps.note: Only now does the approved action leave the loop.

steps.label: user's narrowed grant
steps.note: It crosses with the user's narrowed grant, not the service's.

steps.label: action on record
steps.note: The action lands on the system of record, attributable to the session that approved it.

steps.label: record confirmed
steps.note: The record confirms the change.

steps.label: result
steps.note: The result crosses back through the same door.

steps.label: outcome
steps.note: The outcome lands in the loop.

steps.label: reply to render
steps.note: And heads for the surface.

steps.label: rendered, attributable
steps.note: It renders in the thread, attributable to the approval that allowed it.

scenarios.title: A tool result steers the next turn

steps.label: routine lookup
steps.note: A routine lookup runs mid-conversation.

steps.label: admitted on user's grant
steps.note: Admitted against the catalogue on the user's grant.

steps.label: fetch record
steps.note: The fetch reaches a record somebody else authored.

steps.label: embedded instruction
steps.note: An embedded instruction returns with the content.

steps.label: poisoned tool result
steps.note: The poisoned content crosses back through the gateway like any tool result.

steps.label: re-enters as context
steps.note: And re-enters the loop as context.

steps.label: persists to state
steps.note: It persists into conversation state like any other result.

steps.label: read back each turn
steps.note: Every later turn this session reads it back.

steps.label: carried in next call
steps.note: And carries it out with the next call.

steps.label: inference beside instruction
steps.note: The model reads it beside the system instruction — the approval gate is now the control.

scenarios.title: A scheduled run fires with the thread closed

steps.label: scheduled job wakes
steps.note: The job a conversation configured wakes with the thread closed — nobody is there to approve anything it proposes.

steps.label: unattended context
steps.note: The run crosses on the same brokered credential an attended turn would.

steps.label: inference, unread
steps.note: The model proposes a write no one is reading.

steps.label: proposed write
steps.note: The proposal comes back across the crossing.

steps.label: proposal into the loop
steps.note: Into the loop, which dispatches it like any action.

steps.label: write, no approval bound
steps.note: The write leaves the loop carrying no approval — there was nobody to give one.

steps.label: refused; run suspends
steps.note: The action policy refuses a mutating call with no approval bound to this action, its arguments and a session. The run suspends and the proposal waits in the thread for the user's return: the reads ran, nothing was written.

scenarios.title: The session outlives the topic

steps.label: late question
steps.note: An innocuous late question, many turns into the conversation.

steps.label: turn enters
steps.note: It enters the loop like any other turn.

steps.label: thread requested
steps.note: Context assembly asks for the thread.

steps.label: everything retrieved
steps.note: Everything earlier turns retrieved comes back with it.

steps.label: records travel along
steps.note: Records the current question never needed travel with it.

steps.label: inference over all of it
steps.note: The model reads all of it.

steps.label: reply
steps.note: The reply can draw on any of it.

steps.label: into the loop
steps.note: Back into the loop.

steps.label: toward surface
steps.note: And toward the surface.

steps.label: reply may surface any of it
steps.note: The reply can surface any of it — session-scoped memory and DLP on accumulation are what bound the answer.

scenarios.title: A web page enters the thread

steps.label: web search mid-turn
steps.note: A read-only web search runs mid-turn, without ceremony.

steps.label: search & fetch
steps.note: The gateway opens the call to the open web.

steps.label: somebody else's page
steps.note: What returns was authored by somebody else.

steps.label: classified, re-enters thread
steps.note: It is classified at the crossing before it re-enters the thread — which is how one poisoned page would otherwise steer every later turn in the session.

scenarios.title: A dependency arrives with the task

steps.label: package install (pinned)
steps.note: A sandboxed step needs a package its generated code imports; the package manager runs as a shell command inside the harness's own tool surface and pulls from the mirror — the one destination the sandbox's network policy allows.

steps.label: admitted build
steps.note: The admitted build comes back, pinned by digest — the hop a poisoned package actually arrives on, which is why admission and pinning are the controls that live here.

deviations.subject: Memory poisoning is pinned as prompt injection
deviations.reason: OWASP's agentic taxonomy names memory poisoning as a distinct threat; CoSAI's risk set has no equivalent, so the conversation-state risk is pinned as prompt injection — the nearest true statement, recorded rather than papered over, matching the multi-agent sibling.

deviations.subject: The application front end absorbs the service edge
deviations.reason: Rate limiting and abuse controls for the public chat surface are drawn as the chip on the entry block rather than a separate Service edge — the front end absorbs the duty in this simple deployment shape, and a high-traffic deployment fronting the same surface with a dedicated edge tier should read the remote MCP server's drawing for that block.
