archetypes.title: Remote MCP server you publish
summary: A tool server operated as a service for other people's agents: an OAuth resource server whose clients are language models. The scopes, the tenancy and the tool descriptions are all your design decisions — and the descriptions execute as instruction inside somebody else's model.
description:
The inversion is what makes this its own architecture. Every other cloud archetype here calls tools; this one is the tool. The caller is an autonomous agent acting for a user, the arguments were produced by a model, and the tool descriptions this server publishes become instructions inside that model's context. A poorly worded description causes misuse; a deliberately worded one is an attack on the caller. Publishing a server means treating changes to descriptions and error messages with the seriousness of an API contract change.
Authorization is the second inversion. Standard OAuth answers "may this client act for this user", and here that is necessary and not sufficient: the client is an agent that may have been steered by content it read elsewhere. Scopes therefore need to be narrow enough that a hijacked agent's blast radius is bounded, and consequential operations need confirmation semantics the protocol can express, rather than relying on the client to prompt its user. In an enterprise deployment the identity work is federated rather than invented: the user signs in at the IdP the organisation already governs, an identity assertion is exchanged for an audience-bound token, and admin policy and revocation stay where the organisation already enforces them. Client registration is pre-arranged or metadata-document based — the self-service dynamic registration of the early protocol is deprecated.
The deployment shape is deliberately conventional: a gateway tier in front terminating hostile machine traffic, one stateless application behind it, data and upstream systems behind that. The protocol is stateless by design — there are no sessions to bind, only server-minted state handles whose possession proves nothing — so the service scales horizontally like any web tier, and every request re-verifies authorization from the token. The ordinary multi-tenant disciplines apply with unusual force: every read and write checks both that the scope permits the operation and that the tenant on the token matches the tenant on the record; rate limits are sized for machine callers that retry, loop and parallelise; and results are bounded in size, because an oversized result is both a cost problem for the caller and a way to crowd their context window. There is no model anywhere in this service — every distinctive control follows from the client being one.
The one rule with no exceptions is at the back: the caller's token never travels upstream. A handler that reaches another system does so as its own OAuth client, on a credential a secrets manager issued to this service — passing the inbound token onward is the confused deputy the protocol documents by name, and it turns one compromised agent into a multi-service problem.
distinguishedBy:
Against a third-party MCP server you consume: opposite side of the same boundary. There the scopes are someone else's design and the work is admission and observation; here the scopes, the tenancy and the descriptions are all design decisions.
Against an AI-augmented API backend: that one has AI inside it and a conventional client. This one has no AI inside it at all and a model as the client. The security work is entirely about the caller's nature.

exemplars.name: GitHub MCP server
exemplars.note: GitHub’s official remote server exposes repository and collaboration tools to agent clients. Illustrates a product vendor publishing tools for its own service.

exemplars.name: Atlassian Rovo MCP server
exemplars.note: A remote MCP service connecting agent clients to Jira, Confluence and other Atlassian capabilities under the signed-in user’s permissions. Illustrates the service-publisher role.

exemplars.name: Cloudflare Workers and Agents SDK
exemplars.note: Build and host a remote MCP server with Streamable HTTP and OAuth integration. A hosting implementation for your published tools, with application-specific permissions supplied by you.

zones.note: Everything we build and run. This architecture is drawn from the publisher's chair, so almost all of it is ours — which is unusual in this catalogue and is the reason it earns a page: the controls that matter when you *publish* an MCP server have nowhere else to live.
zones.title: Enterprise cloud

zones.note: Deliberately light. For a published server the governed questions are what the catalogue admits and what the tool descriptions say — because both execute inside somebody else's model.
zones.title: Security & governance control plane

blocks.title: MCP clients
blocks.note: Deliberately unnamed. Agents, chat products and other services all reach a published server the same way, and naming any one of them would make the drawing about that integration rather than about the server we are building. Three kinds of caller matter for identity: a public client nobody pre-registered (a developer's tool, identified by a client-ID metadata document), an enterprise client the IdP knows (single sign-on, no per-server consent), and an autonomous workload with no user behind it (its own workload identity).

blocks.title: Identity provider
blocks.note: The enterprise identity provider, drawn because tokens flow through it: under enterprise-managed authorization the caller signs in here once, and trades that login for an identity-assertion grant (ID-JAG) naming this server — after the IdP has checked its own registry of approved MCP servers, the user's groups and roles, and any conditional-access rule. Nobody consents per server; the administrator decided once. For a customer organisation's callers this is their IdP, federated to our authorization server by trusting its issuer and keys — the same mechanism, somebody else's policy.

items.label: SSO login
items.note: The corporate sign-in the client already does. The ID token it yields is the subject token for everything that follows.

items.label: Token exchange
items.note: RFC 8693 at the IdP: `grant_type=token-exchange`, `subject_token` = the ID token, `requested_token_type` = `id-jag`, `audience` = our authorization server's issuer, `resource` = this server's canonical URI, `scope` as requested. The answer is a signed JWT (`typ: oauth-id-jag+jwt`) with `iss`, `sub`, `aud`, `client_id`, `resource`, `scope`, `jti`, `exp` — or a policy denial.

items.label: App registry & policy
items.note: Which MCP servers exist for this organisation, who may reach each, with which scopes, under which conditions. Evaluated at every exchange, so removing a user from a group is revocation for every new token from that moment.

blocks.title: AI gateway
blocks.note: The entry point, and for the first time genuinely useful on MCP traffic. The 2026-07 revision requires every request to mirror its method and tool name into `Mcp-Method` and `Mcp-Name` headers, so this tier can route, meter and authorize **per tool** without parsing bodies. That only holds if it enforces the matching rule: a server that processes the body must reject any request whose headers disagree with it, because a gateway routing on the header while the server executes the body is a policy-bypass primitive. One operating concern survives the stateless revision: a subscription is a long-lived POST stream, so this tier's idle timeouts and response buffering are configuration, not defaults.

items.label: MCP & API gateway
items.note: The one traffic class this gateway carries — MCP calls, routed and metered per tool.

blocks.title: Authorization server
blocks.note: Token issuance for the server we publish, and the one place every identity flow converges. It speaks three grant profiles: the authorization-code grant with PKCE and `resource` for a public client through a consent screen; the JWT-bearer grant that accepts an ID-JAG from a trusted identity provider and issues an access token without any redirect (enterprise-managed authorization); and `client_credentials` with `private_key_jwt` for an autonomous workload. It also performs the token exchange a handler needs to call an upstream system on the caller's behalf — a downstream-audience token, never the inbound one. Every token it mints is audience-bound to this server by canonical URI and short-lived; refresh tokens rotate.

items.label: Token issuance
items.note: Audience-bound to this server by name, so a token minted for another is refused.

items.label: Grant profiles
items.note: Advertised in the authorization-server metadata: `code_challenge_methods_supported` (S256, or the client must refuse to proceed), `client_id_metadata_document_supported`, `authorization_grant_profiles_supported` including `id-jag`, and the token-exchange grant for on-behalf-of calls upstream. Dynamic client registration is deprecated and absent.

items.label: Consent records
items.note: What each client was granted, by whom — the record a per-client review reads, and the thing the enterprise profile replaces with the consuming organisation's policy.

items.label: Client registration
items.note: Dynamic registration is deprecated in favour of client metadata documents, where the client's identifier is a URL we fetch — which quietly makes this component an outbound HTTP client, and a new SSRF surface.

blocks.title: MCP service
blocks.note: A stateless HTTP application — an ASGI app, for example, mounted on its own or inside an existing API. Stateless is not a style choice: sticky sessions do not work reliably with MCP clients, so horizontal scale requires it. The 2026-07 revision removed protocol sessions entirely, which moved a security property with it: there is nothing to validate once and trust afterwards, so every request carries a bearer token and every request is validated — signature or introspection, audience equals this server's canonical URI, expiry, scope against the tool being called, and the subject the handler will act as. What it does with the token stops there: never forwarded, never accepted for another audience.

items.label: Protocol endpoint
items.note: One POST endpoint. GET and DELETE are gone, along with the session header and stream resumability.

items.label: State handles
items.note: Server-minted, opaque, expiring, and bound to the authenticated principal. Possession is not authentication — the protocol will not enforce that for us.

items.label: Tool handlers
items.note: Ordinary application code behind the protocol, and ordinary attack surface. A consequential handler returns `input_required` and executes only on the retry that carries the caller's confirmation — tool annotations are hints the client must treat as untrusted, so this is the confirmation lever the server actually holds. The confirmation proves the client answered, not that a person reviewed the action.

items.label: Resource metadata
items.note: The Protected Resource Metadata document every client reads first, naming which authorization server this resource trusts. Unauthenticated and public by design, and a security artifact: a tampered one points every caller at somebody else's server.

blocks.title: Tool definitions
blocks.note: Names, descriptions and schemas. Versioned content that executes as instruction inside a caller's model, which makes a wording change a release rather than a copy edit. The spec gives no integrity mechanism and no tool-level version field, so pinning by hash where the service loads them is something we build rather than something we get.

items.label: Tool descriptions
items.note: Text that lands in somebody else's context window and steers their agent.

items.label: Input schemas
items.note: What the server will accept — and, where a parameter is header-mirrored, what a gateway can route on.

blocks.title: Enterprise data
blocks.note: The records the service reaches on the caller's behalf, and the internal systems its handlers wrap — each with authorization of its own, reached on a downstream-audience token or our own service credential, never the caller's token. Per-tenant scoping is entirely ours to build: the protocol has no notion of a tenant, so nothing is isolated by default.

items.label: Org data
items.note: Reached only within the delegation the presented token carries.

blocks.title: Identity services
blocks.note: Scope design and the delegation model. The scopes we publish should be the minimal set for basic function, with more granted by step-up — a wildcard or omnibus scope is the named anti-pattern, and claimed scopes in a token are never sufficient without our own authorization logic behind them.

blocks.title: Secrets & key management
blocks.note: The upstream credentials this service's handlers call on — issued, scoped and rotated by a secrets manager, one per upstream, never the caller's token forwarded.

blocks.title: Policy & authorization
blocks.note: Per-tenant limits sized for callers that retry, loop and parallelise — limits tuned for human clients are not limits here — plus origin validation against DNS rebinding and the egress policy that keeps the authorization server's discovery fetches off internal addresses.

blocks.title: Supply-chain assurance
blocks.note: Description review and definition pinning. Our tool text is a security property of somebody else's system, so it is reviewed like code; and behind the protocol this is a published application that deserves ordinary application testing.

blocks.title: Observability & response
blocks.note: Per-call audit attributable to a tenant and a delegation, and revocation that reaches tokens already minted rather than only future ones.

edges.label: SSO & exchange / ID-JAG
edges.note: The enterprise path. The client signs the user in at the IdP once and keeps the ID token; when a server requires enterprise-managed authorization it comes back here to exchange that ID token for an identity-assertion grant naming this server — and the IdP's policy says yes or no before our authorization server ever sees a request. Repeat exchanges happen at token expiry and at every scope step-up, so a policy change bites within one token lifetime.

edges.label: authorization / tokens
edges.note: Where every grant is redeemed. A public client arrives through the browser: the PKCE authorization-code flow with `resource` naming this server, a client-ID metadata document as its identity, a consent screen showing the client's name and redirect host, and an `iss` in the response the client checks before it will redeem the code. An enterprise client arrives with an ID-JAG and no browser at all. An autonomous workload arrives with a signed client assertion. All three leave with the same thing: a short-lived access token whose audience is this server and nothing else.

edges.label: tool calls / results
edges.note: Whoever they are. Machine traffic at machine rates, arriving with the method and tool name mirrored into headers so this tier can act on them without reading bodies.

edges.label: routed call
edges.note: The admitted request reaches the application, and the result — including our tool descriptions — returns.

edges.label: validate & exchange / verdict
edges.note: Audience, scope, expiry and subject are verified per request, because there is no session left to verify them once. Drawn as introspection — the deliberate choice here, because it is also how revocation reaches a token that has not yet expired; the common alternative is local JWT validation against the issuer's keys, which is faster and blind to revocation. The same edge carries the on-behalf-of exchange: a handler that must call an upstream system swaps the inbound token for one whose audience is the upstream, scoped down, so the caller's token never leaves this service.

edges.label: published schemas
edges.note: Versioned content loaded by the service and served to callers as instruction. The list a caller sees is filtered by its scopes, so the hash consumers pin is computed per scope-set — or the description-edit scenario false-alarms on every scope change.

edges.label: scoped read & write / records
edges.note: Bounded by the delegation the token carries. One tenant's agent reaching another tenant's records is this architecture's defining failure, and nothing in the protocol prevents it. A handler that wraps an internal system with authorization of its own calls it on a downstream-audience token — or as the service, where no delegation exists — and the forbidden shape is forwarding the caller's token, which breaks audit, rate limits and the trust boundary in one move.

risks.note: The service is built on the official SDK, and the SDK's CVE stream is ours to ship — the 2026 request-handling flaws reached every server built on it, up to 200,000 instances by the disclosed count.
A LiteLLM-class tier with its own CVE stream and its own release channel — the backdoored gateway release is this component, fronting everything we publish.
A changed description changes somebody else's agent behaviour. The protocol offers no integrity mechanism and no version field, so an unnoticed edit is a silent change to a system we do not run.

Interception, replay and DNS rebinding on the inbound leg: a bearer lifted from a plain-HTTP or downgraded connection is replayed, or a browser page rebinds DNS to reach the endpoint. HTTPS throughout and `Origin` validated on every request are the defence; a state handle's binding to its principal is a separate check in the service.

A static client identifier with no per-user record of which clients a user already approved is the classic confused deputy at the registration surface. Consent must be per client and recorded before the flow proceeds.
Token passthrough — forwarding the caller's token upstream — is the confused deputy the protocol documents by name: one compromised agent becomes a multi-service problem wearing our audit identity.

A retired server still answering at an address callers discovered — a stale DNS name, registry entry or load-balancer route — keeps receiving tool calls, and whoever claims that address receives them; one that outlives its team keeps its live grants too. Decommissioning removes all of them.
Records written by third parties — issue text, comments, documents — come back through our tools as results, and a model we do not operate reads them as instruction.
A looping agent calling a tool whose handler does billed work — a paid upstream API, a heavy query — runs up our bill with every retry, and the spec has no quotas or back-pressure to slow it.

Where a handler falls back to our own service credential, whatever it reaches upstream it reaches with our authority regardless of who asked, and the upstream's audit shows us rather than them; where it exchanges on the caller's behalf, a scope wider than the tool needs exports more than the caller asked for.

mitigations.note: Tokens audience-bound to this server by name, and refused if minted for anything else; the `resource` audience is asserted at issuance and checked on every request.

The inbound token stops at the service. A handler that needs an upstream system exchanges it for a downstream-audience token scoped to the tool, or calls as the service on its own credential — and the exchange is logged as a delegation step, so the chain stays legible.
Per-client and per-tenant, sized for callers that retry and parallelise. This is ours to build entirely — the protocol provides no quota mechanism at all.

Minimal scopes with step-up rather than an omnibus grant, and the whole set needed for an operation emitted in one challenge instead of drip-fed. The tool list is filtered by the presenting token's scopes on every request — a tool the caller cannot invoke is never shown to its model.

The service loads only the reviewed release of its definitions: each is checked against the hash recorded at review and refused on mismatch, so an edit that skipped the pipeline never serves. The spec gives no integrity mechanism, so this is built here or it does not exist. Consuming clients pin what they receive on their side — their check, not one this server can enforce.
Behind the protocol this is a published application, and its handlers are ordinary attack surface.
Per-tenant scoping enforced in our own code, because the protocol has no tenants.
A separate, vaulted credential for each upstream we call, short-lived and rotated, scoped to that upstream alone.
Every invocation with its parameters, its tenant and its delegation, retained where an incident can query it.

Revocation that reaches tokens already issued, not merely future ones — introspection, short lifetimes and refresh tokens revoked with the grant — with the delay until they stop working measured, not assumed. A call already executing completes.

The SDK, the gateway and the handlers' dependencies enumerated against vulnerability feeds and prioritised by exposure — a published server ages like any other application; the fix itself ships through the release gate.

Identity governance where it already lives: the IdP's registry of approved MCP servers, the groups and roles that may reach each, and the conditional-access rules — evaluated at every ID-JAG exchange. Joiners get access by group; leavers lose every new token at once.

Client metadata documents make this component an outbound HTTP client: its discovery fetches are blocked from private and metadata addresses — the SSRF surface the move away from dynamic registration newly created, answered where the fetch happens.

An autonomous workload is a client with no user: it authenticates with `private_key_jwt` under `client_credentials`, its key registered against its own identity, and receives narrower scopes than a delegated user would — no consent, no step-up, no borrowed authority.

walkthrough.title: A public client authorizes and invokes a tool
walkthrough.moves: Discovery, consent and a bounded token — then one tool call inside that bound.

steps.label: unauthenticated call
steps.note: An unauthenticated first call. The answer is a 401 whose `WWW-Authenticate` header carries `resource_metadata` — the URL of this server's Protected Resource Metadata — and the `scope` this operation needs, so the client asks for no more than that.

steps.label: 401 + resource metadata
steps.note: The 401 goes back. The client now knows where to read the metadata and which scopes to request.

steps.label: GET protected resource metadata
steps.note: The client fetches the Protected Resource Metadata: `resource` (this server's canonical URI), `authorization_servers`, `scopes_supported`, `bearer_methods_supported`. Fetched over HTTPS, private address ranges refused — the metadata URL came from a stranger.

steps.label: metadata: servers, scopes
steps.note: The document returns; the client picks an authorization server from the list and keeps separate client state for it — credentials for one issuer are never reused at another.

steps.label: AS metadata discovery
steps.note: Authorization-server metadata discovery: RFC 8414 well-known first, OpenID discovery second, path components handled in the specified order. The client verifies `issuer` in the document equals the URL it built, refuses to proceed unless `code_challenge_methods_supported` is present, and notes `client_id_metadata_document_supported`.

steps.label: metadata, issuer recorded
steps.note: The metadata returns and the client records the issuer it will hold every later response to.

steps.label: authorization request (PKCE)
steps.note: The authorization request through the user's browser: `client_id` is the HTTPS URL of the client's metadata document, `redirect_uri` one of those it lists, PKCE `S256`, `resource` naming this server, `state`, and the challenged scopes. The authorization server fetches the metadata document (private ranges blocked), checks `client_id` matches the URL and the redirect URI matches exactly, applies its domain trust policy, and shows a consent screen naming the client and the redirect host — with a warning if that host is `localhost`.

steps.label: code + iss
steps.note: The user approves; the code returns with `iss`. The client compares `iss` to the issuer it recorded before redirecting and abandons the code on any mismatch — the mix-up defence.

steps.label: token request (code_verifier)
steps.note: The token request: code, `code_verifier`, `resource`. For a public client the `state` was single-use and the code is bound to the verifier, so an intercepted code is worthless.

steps.label: access token (aud, scopes)
steps.note: An access token audience-bound to this server's canonical URI, short-lived, with the granted scopes — possibly fewer than asked — and a refresh token that rotates on every use.

steps.label: tool call (bearer + headers)
steps.note: The tool call, `Authorization: Bearer`, never in the query string, with `Mcp-Method` and `Mcp-Name` mirrored into headers so the gateway can route, meter and authorize per tool.

steps.label: routed per tool
steps.note: Routed and metered per tool without the body being parsed — and the service checks the headers against the body, refusing a mismatch outright.

steps.label: validate token
steps.note: Per-request validation: signature or introspection, `aud` equals this server, not expired, scope covers this tool, and the subject the handler will act as.

steps.label: valid; delegation bounds
steps.note: Valid. The delegation the token carries is now the bound on the call — and the tenant on the token is what the handler must match against the record.

steps.label: scoped read
steps.note: The read happens inside that delegation, and not one record wider.

steps.label: record
steps.note: The record comes back inside the same delegation.

steps.label: result
steps.note: The result — bounded in size, because it lands in somebody else's context window.

steps.label: logged & returned
steps.note: Logged per call against client, user, tenant and tool, and returned.

scenarios.title: Enterprise-managed authorization — sign in once, no per-server consent

steps.label: SSO (kept ID token)
steps.note: The client already signed the user in at the corporate IdP and kept the ID token. It declares support for the `enterprise-managed-authorization` extension in its request capabilities.

steps.label: ID token
steps.note: The ID token is the subject token for what follows; nothing else from the login is reused.

steps.label: unauthenticated call
steps.note: The first tool call, unauthenticated, is answered with a 401 and the resource metadata URL.

steps.label: 401 + metadata
steps.note: The client reads the Protected Resource Metadata and finds this server's authorization server.

steps.label: AS metadata (id-jag)
steps.note: Authorization-server metadata: `authorization_grant_profiles_supported` includes `id-jag`, so the client knows to use the enterprise flow and does not open a browser.

steps.label: issuer recorded
steps.note: The client records the issuer — it becomes the `audience` of the exchange it is about to ask for.

steps.label: token exchange (ID-JAG)
steps.note: Token exchange at the IdP: `grant_type=token-exchange`, `subject_token` = the ID token, `requested_token_type` = `id-jag`, `audience` = our authorization server's issuer, `resource` = this server's canonical URI, `scope` = what the challenge asked for. The IdP evaluates its policy — is this server approved for this organisation, is this user in a group that may reach it with these scopes, do conditional-access rules pass.

steps.label: ID-JAG
steps.note: An ID-JAG: a signed JWT, `typ: oauth-id-jag+jwt`, with `iss` (the IdP), `sub` (the user), `aud` (our authorization server), `client_id`, `resource` (this server), `scope`, `jti`, `exp`. Or a policy denial the client surfaces as such — no token, no consent screen, nothing to retry.

steps.label: JWT-bearer grant
steps.note: The JWT-bearer grant: `grant_type=jwt-bearer`, `assertion` = the ID-JAG, `client_id`, and `private_key_jwt` client authentication where the client has a key. Our server validates the assertion against the IdP's published keys, checks `iss` is a trusted IdP, `aud` is itself, `exp` and `jti` unused, and links the account by `sub` — `email` only as a fallback for accounts that predate the federation.

steps.label: access token
steps.note: An access token audience-bound to the `resource` in the assertion, scopes no wider than the ID-JAG carried. The user never saw a consent screen for this server; their administrator decided once, in the IdP.

steps.label: tool call
steps.note: The tool call, bearer token in the header, method and tool name mirrored into headers.

steps.label: routed per tool
steps.note: Routed and metered per tool.

steps.label: validate token
steps.note: Validated per request — audience, scope, expiry, subject — exactly as for any other token.

steps.label: valid
steps.note: Valid; the delegation bounds the call.

steps.label: scoped read
steps.note: The read, inside the tenant and the scope the token names.

steps.label: record
steps.note: The record comes back.

steps.label: result
steps.note: The result, bounded and logged against client, user, tenant and tool.

steps.label: returned
steps.note: Returned. Onboarding was a group membership; offboarding will be its removal.

scenarios.title: Step-up — a consequential tool needs a scope the token lacks

steps.label: write with read-only token
steps.note: A call to a write tool with a token that carries only the read scopes it started with — least privilege at first grant, by design.

steps.label: routed
steps.note: Routed and metered like any call.

steps.label: validate: scope short
steps.note: The token is valid — audience, expiry, subject all good — but its scopes do not cover this tool.

steps.label: insufficient scope
steps.note: Insufficient, not invalid.

steps.label: 403 insufficient_scope
steps.note: A 403 with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="insufficient_scope"`, `scope` listing every scope this operation needs in one challenge, and `resource_metadata`. One round trip, not one scope per retry.

steps.label: scope union computed
steps.note: The client computes the union of what it already holds and what was challenged, so nothing previously granted is lost.

steps.label: exchange with wider scope
steps.note: For an enterprise client the step-up is another token exchange, with the wider scope — and the IdP's policy decides again. A user who may read but not write is told so here, by the organisation, not by a consent screen.

steps.label: new ID-JAG
steps.note: A new ID-JAG with the widened scope, or a denial the client treats as final after a few tries.

steps.label: JWT-bearer grant
steps.note: The JWT-bearer grant again (a public client would re-run the authorization-code flow and see a consent screen listing exactly the added scope).

steps.label: token with union
steps.note: A new token with the union of scopes.

steps.label: retry
steps.note: The original request, retried once.

steps.label: routed
steps.note: Routed and metered.

steps.label: write (confirmed)
steps.note: The write, inside the widened delegation — and, for a consequential action, only on the retry that carries the confirmation the tool asked for through `input_required`.

steps.label: record confirmed
steps.note: The record confirms the change.

steps.label: logged with elevation
steps.note: Logged with the scope elevation that preceded it, so the audit shows why this token could write.

steps.label: result
steps.note: The write's result returns to the caller, on a token whose scopes now say why it could.

scenarios.title: A handler calls an upstream system on the caller's behalf

steps.label: tool call
steps.note: An ordinary call to a tool whose handler wraps an existing internal API.

steps.label: handler needs upstream
steps.note: The handler has the caller's token in hand, and the upstream wants a credential.

steps.label: token exchange (OBO)
steps.note: Not that one. The service exchanges the inbound token: `grant_type=token-exchange`, `subject_token` = the caller's access token, `audience` = the upstream API, `scope` narrowed to what this tool needs — an on-behalf-of token that still names the user.

steps.label: downstream-audience token
steps.note: A downstream-audience token. The exchange is logged as a delegation step: who asked, through which tool, for which upstream, with which scope.

steps.label: upstream call (OBO token)
steps.note: The upstream call carries that token, so the upstream sees who is really asking and applies its own authorization — instead of a service account that can see everything, or the caller's token forwarded, which the spec forbids outright.

steps.label: upstream result
steps.note: The upstream result returns.

steps.label: tool result
steps.note: Composed into the tool result, bounded in size.

steps.label: returned; two audits
steps.note: Returned, with two audit lines that join on the same delegation: ours and the upstream's.

scenarios.title: An autonomous workload calls with no user behind it

steps.label: client_credentials (private_key_jwt)
steps.note: A scheduled agent, not a person. `grant_type=client_credentials`, authenticated with `private_key_jwt` under its own registered identity, `resource` naming this server, and the scopes its registration allows — narrower than any user's, because nobody will be asked to approve a step-up.

steps.label: workload token
steps.note: An access token whose subject is the workload itself. No consent, because there is no resource owner; the registration of that identity was the approval.

steps.label: tool call
steps.note: The tool call, on the workload's token and its own rate limits.

steps.label: routed as machine identity
steps.note: Routed and metered against a machine identity.

steps.label: validate; autonomous policy
steps.note: Validated per request. The handler notes the subject is a workload and applies the policy for autonomous callers: no delegation chain to honour, so the scopes are the whole bound.

steps.label: valid
steps.note: Valid.

steps.label: read within registration
steps.note: The read, inside what the workload's registration permits — and nothing a human's membership would have added.

steps.label: record
steps.note: The record comes back, logged against a non-human identity with its own lifecycle.

steps.label: result
steps.note: The result, bounded and logged against the workload.

steps.label: returned
steps.note: Returned to the workload, on its own rate limits.

scenarios.title: A token minted for another server is refused

steps.label: call with wrong-audience token
steps.note: A call carrying a perfectly valid token — issued by the same authorization server, for a different MCP server, or for an upstream API the client also uses.

steps.label: routed
steps.note: Routed like any call; the gateway may pre-check the audience but the service must not rely on it.

steps.label: validate: aud mismatch
steps.note: Validation: signature good, not expired — and `aud` is not this server's canonical URI.

steps.label: refused
steps.note: Refused. A server that accepts a token issued for any other audience is the passthrough failure in its first form, and everything downstream of it inherits the confusion.

steps.label: 401 + metadata
steps.note: A 401 with the resource metadata, so an honest client can start the right flow.

steps.label: returned
steps.note: Returned. The client that keeps per-issuer, per-resource token state never sends this.

scenarios.title: Revocation reaches an agent mid-task

steps.label: call after revocation
steps.note: An agent mid-task calls again with a token issued a minute ago — and in that minute an administrator revoked the client's grant at the authorization server, and the user left the group that grants this server.

steps.label: routed
steps.note: Routed like any call.

steps.label: introspection
steps.note: Introspection, not local validation: the authorization server revoked the grant itself, so it knows at once. The group change at the IdP reaches it only through a revocation signal, where one is wired, or at the next exchange.

steps.label: revoked
steps.note: Revoked.
A 401. The refresh token was revoked with the grant, so it fails too.

steps.label: recovery attempt
steps.note: The agent tries to recover the way an honest client would.

steps.label: fresh exchange
steps.note: A fresh token exchange — and the IdP's policy, the source of truth for membership, says no.

steps.label: denied
steps.note: Denied. Each grain stopped where it lives: the grant at the authorization server at once, the membership at the IdP on the next exchange — within one token lifetime, which is the argument for lifetimes measured in minutes.

scenarios.title: A description edit ships

steps.label: reviewed wording change loads
steps.note: A reviewed wording change ships as a release: the loader accepts its new hash. An edit that skipped review would be refused here.

steps.label: tools/list carries it
steps.note: The next tools/list response carries it outward.

steps.label: lands as instruction
steps.note: And it lands in every consuming agent's context as instruction. Nothing in the protocol versions this: a client that pinned the old hash notices and re-admits it — their check, which a release of ours cannot make for them.

scenarios.title: One tenant's agent asks for another tenant's record

steps.label: request for other tenant's id
steps.note: A syntactically perfect request — the object id just belongs to somebody else.

steps.label: routed
steps.note: Routed and metered like any call; nothing at this tier knows what the id means.

steps.label: validate token
steps.note: The token is checked — audience, scope and subject.

steps.label: valid
steps.note: All valid. The protocol is satisfied.

steps.label: tenant check
steps.note: The tenant check in our own application code is the only thing left standing, because the protocol has no notion of a tenant at all. This architecture's defining failure happens on this hop or nowhere.

steps.label: refused
steps.note: Refused by the tenant check — the one control the protocol did not supply.
A 403, and an audit line naming the tenant that asked and the tenant it asked for.

scenarios.title: A handler forwards the caller's token

steps.label: tool call
steps.note: An ordinary call to a tool whose handler reaches an upstream system.

steps.label: handler holds token
steps.note: The handler has the caller's token in hand, and the upstream wants a credential.

steps.label: token forwarded (forbidden)
steps.note: Forwarding it is the confused deputy the spec forbids outright: audit, rate limits and the trust boundary all break in one move. The handler calls as itself, on a credential the secrets manager issued to this service, or the design is wrong.

scenarios.title: The header lies about the body

steps.label: header read_ticket, body delete
steps.note: `Mcp-Name: read_ticket` in the headers; `delete_ticket` in the body. The gateway routes and meters on the header, because that is what the header is for.

steps.label: metered as read; mismatch
steps.note: Routed and metered as a read. The service parses the body — and must refuse the mismatch outright, or the meter, the per-tool policy and the audit line all describe a call that never happened.

steps.label: refused outright
steps.note: Refused outright: a header that disagrees with the body is a malformed request, not a read.
A 400, logged as the mismatch it was.

deviations.subject: The AI gateway carries MCP traffic only
deviations.reason: There is no model anywhere in this service, so a Model proxy item would be false, and nothing fetches skills through this crossing either. The gateway is drawn with its one real traffic class rather than the registered aiGatewayTraffic pack, following the low-code builder's precedent: the honest signal that a gateway is not on the model path is its own contents.

deviations.subject: The service is drawn as one application block, not protocol stages
deviations.reason: Transport, router and handlers deploy as one stateless service, so they are one block with items — the thing a team ships and scales. Tool definitions stay separate because they are a different artifact class: versioned content with a review pipeline, whose distinctive edge runs into the caller's context rather than through the service.

deviations.subject: The identity provider is drawn because tokens flow through it
deviations.reason: The catalogue keeps identity providers as a governance call-out, drawn as a block only where tokens genuinely flow through them. Here they do: under enterprise-managed authorization the client's ID token is exchanged at the IdP for an identity-assertion grant, and the IdP's policy is the authorization decision. For a customer organisation's callers the block stands for their IdP, federated by trusting its issuer and keys; the mechanism is identical and the policy is theirs. The authorization server's trust in the IdP — issuer allowlist and key fetch — is configuration rather than a data path, and is carried on the Grant profiles item rather than drawn as an edge (2026-09-03).

deviations.subject: The callers origin sits in our cloud band as a layout necessity
deviations.reason: Whoever calls a published server — internal agents, chat products, other services — the drawing deliberately claims no ownership over them: the origin is unnamed and its band placement is geometry, not custody. Moving it to an external band would put that band left of ours, against the band order; the origin kind exists precisely so an edge can arrive from an unclaimed source.

deviations.subject: Upstream secrets and egress are absorbed by the service and the authorization server
deviations.reason: Credential hardening (D3-CH) and egress control are embodied by the AI gateway, which sits on the inbound side only. On the upstream hop the service itself holds the credential the secrets manager issued, and the authorization server's discovery fetches are bounded where they happen — recorded here rather than drawing an egress tier that nobody runs.

deviations.subject: Definition pinning is enforced on the data path
deviations.reason: Tool and MCP server integrity is a management capability, and the supply-chain call-out cites it — but the hash pin is checked where definitions load and serve, so the chip sits on the toolDefs edge. The locus departure is deliberate: the service's loader is where a definition that skipped review can be refused.

deviations.subject: The authorization server's metadata fetch path is not drawn
deviations.reason: Fetching a client metadata document is a single outbound HTTP request to a URL the client chose; drawing a standing edge for it would overstate it. The surface is carried on the clientReg item and answered by the egress pin on the block.

deviations.subject: Sessions are gone because the protocol removed them
deviations.reason: The current protocol revision deleted sessions and the initialize handshake; cross-call state is explicit server-minted handles carried as arguments. Transport hijacking stays on the inbound leg; a handle's binding to its principal is an ordinary authorization check in the service.

archetypes.title: Self-hosted model inference
summary: An open-weights model served on infrastructure the organisation operates — the same inference runtime as the endpoint local model runtime, with an AI gateway in front of it and a governance plane behind it. Weights land in storage from a public hub or the organisation's own training & release pipeline, and the whole model-provider role moves inside the boundary.
description:
The trade is explicit: the provider-boundary disclosure risk goes away and a supply-chain, availability and safety risk arrives — while logs, caches, storage and co-tenancy keep their own disclosure paths in-house. There is no provider applying content policy, no provider absorbing a traffic spike, and no provider patching the serving stack. Every control a managed API supplies by default is now a component this organisation runs or does without — which is why the gateway and the governance plane are the blocks that separate this architecture from the same software installed by one person on a workstation.
The supply chain is the distinctive risk. Weights are large artifacts that arrive in storage from a public hub or from the organisation's own training & release pipeline, and several distribution formats execute code on load. The control is scanning and format policy in the promotion gate, before an artifact reaches the runtime — a blocking gate, not a report — and digest verification at load, so the gate cannot be bypassed by writing to storage directly.
Multi-tenancy inside the runtime has no equivalent elsewhere in this catalogue. Continuous batching mixes tenants' requests in one forward pass on shared accelerators, the KV cache holds their context, and prefix caching across tenants is a performance feature that is also a disclosure path. Whether cache entries are shared across tenants is a serving setting with data-protection consequences — in vLLM, a secret salt the gateway must set on every request — and it rarely reaches a review.
Availability is a security property here in a way it is not with a managed API. Capacity is finite and expensive, admission control at the gateway is what stops one caller becoming everyone else's outage, and quotas are a control rather than a billing feature.
distinguishedBy:
Against the endpoint local model runtime: identical software, entirely different operational position. There it was installed by one person and has no inventory entry; here it has a gateway in front, a promotion pipeline, an identity and someone on call.
Against consuming a managed model API: this architecture replaces one boundary crossing with a whole subsystem. The guardrails, abuse monitoring, capacity management and patching the provider was doing are now blocks on this diagram.

exemplars.name: vLLM
exemplars.note: An inference engine with an OpenAI-compatible serving API, deployed on infrastructure you operate. It fills the model-serving tier behind the organization’s access and traffic controls.

exemplars.name: NVIDIA NIM
exemplars.note: Containerized model-serving software deployed on your own GPU infrastructure. This example uses the self-hosted container mode, with model storage and service exposure managed by your organization.

exemplars.name: KServe
exemplars.note: A Kubernetes platform for deploying predictive and generative inference services, including vLLM-backed serving. Illustrates the cluster-managed deployment of the runtime and model-loading path.

zones.note: Everything we operate. This architecture is almost entirely one band, which is the point: the organisation took the model in-house and inherited every control the provider was applying on the way in and out.
zones.title: Enterprise cloud

zones.note: Outside the company — the public hubs and pipelines the weights arrive from.
zones.title: External

zones.note: Drawn across every band because it governs every band. With no vendor and no human in the request path, admission of the artifact and inventory of the runtime are most of what governance can do here.
zones.title: Security & governance control plane

blocks.title: Consuming applications
blocks.note: Internal applications and agents sharing one cluster. Their isolation from each other is a property of the serving configuration, not of the network between them.

blocks.title: AI gateway
blocks.note: The governed front door in front of finite capacity — the same gateway block every hosted architecture in this catalogue routes through. With no provider applying content policy, the guardrail checks enforced here are a service the organisation runs itself or does without. Its items are the traffic classes it brokers — the checks it runs are the numbered pins on this block and its edges, and the call-outs beneath.

items.label: Model proxy
items.note: The one traffic class this gateway carries — inference, brokered per tenant.

blocks.title: Inference API
blocks.note: The OpenAI-compatible endpoint the serving stack publishes — the same component the local runtime draws, at a different scale. Authentication here is opt-in too: vLLM's `--api-key` is a flag, not a default, and a serving tier reachable without one is the same failure as an unauthenticated laptop, with a much larger blast radius.

items.label: Completion endpoint
items.note: The published interface every internal caller shares.

items.label: Interface binding
items.note: Which network the tier is reachable from, and the whole of the trust boundary if auth is off.

blocks.title: Inference runtime
blocks.note: The same runtime the endpoint architecture draws — loading weights, batching requests, serving completions — operated here as a shared service across tenants on shared accelerators. The serving stack is third-party code with its own CVE stream, and its distributed control plane assumes a trusted network: job APIs and inter-node channels ship unauthenticated by design, so network isolation is a control, not a hardening step.

items.label: Weight loader
items.note: Where a pickle-based format turns file opening into code execution — and where the registry digest is verified.

items.label: Loaded model
items.note: Open weights with no provider-side guardrail, abuse monitoring or content policy.

items.label: Continuous batching
items.note: Mixes tenants' requests in one forward pass on shared accelerators. Efficiency and co-tenancy are the same mechanism.

items.label: KV & prefix cache
items.note: Tenants' live context, held to avoid recomputing it. Sharing prefixes across tenants is a performance feature and a disclosure path in the same setting.

blocks.title: Storage
blocks.note: Versioned weight artifacts — expensive to reproduce, trivial to copy. Promotion binds a release to an immutable approved digest recorded outside this store's write path, so replacing a file and the digest beside it does not make it loadable.

items.label: Model files
items.note: Multi-gigabyte artifacts whose format determines whether loading them is deserialization or execution.

blocks.title: Model sources
blocks.note: Where hub weights come from: a public catalogue, where publisher identity says nothing about what the artifact does on load. The organisation's own fine-tuned models do not enter here — they arrive from the model registry, inside our custody.

items.label: Open-weights catalogue
items.note: Declared behaviour and actual behaviour are separate facts.

blocks.title: Identity services
blocks.note: Workload identity per calling tenant — the thing every quota, cache-isolation and attribution decision on this page keys off, issued by the platform rather than a shared key in a config map.

blocks.title: Supply-chain assurance
blocks.note: Format and content inspection as a blocking gate in the promotion pipeline, and the record of which artifact is actually serving. The control a managed provider would have supplied, now operated in-house.

blocks.title: Policy & authorization
blocks.note: Per-tenant ceilings on finite capacity — what stops one caller becoming everyone's outage — and the content policy no provider is applying any more.

blocks.title: Secrets & key management
blocks.note: The internal credentials this system runs on — storage pulls, registry reads, control-plane tokens — and the weights themselves treated as an asset worth protecting rather than a file on a disk.

blocks.title: Observability & response
blocks.note: Which versions serve where and at what configuration — including whether cross-tenant cache sharing is on — plus per-version red teaming, because a new checkpoint from the same publisher is a new model nobody else has tested.

blocks.title: Model registry
blocks.note: The training & release pipeline's output, and the block the two drawings share literally: a promoted release arrives here signed by an identity the training job never held, with lineage back to its data, base and run. What it publishes needs no second gate — its signature and lineage are verified, not re-evaluated.

items.label: Signed releases
items.note: Signature and lineage are the admission evidence. Withdrawal stops future loads only where the loader checks current release status; instances already serving keep running until stopped.

edges.label: inference request
edges.note: The tenant on the token is what quotas and cache-isolation decisions key off. A request that arrives without one gets whatever the default tenant can do.

edges.label: brokered inference
edges.note: Every caller crosses the gateway, which is where the tenant identity, the per-tenant quota and the spend attribution live — the things the endpoint drawing has nowhere to put.

edges.label: request / completion
edges.note: Admitted requests scheduled into the batch; completions back through the guardrail checks. Output-side policy is the half most often omitted when self-hosting.

edges.label: promoted release
edges.note: A signed release lands in the store with its promotion record; the load path verifies the signature against it. This is where this drawing meets the training pipeline.

edges.label: weights in
edges.note: Hub artifacts arrive in storage, fetched by the ingest tooling. The serving runtime holds no source-fetch credentials; provenance establishes who made the artifact and nothing about what it does on load.

edges.label: load
edges.note: Only promoted artifacts load, digest-verified against the promotion record. Without that verification the gate can be bypassed by writing to storage directly.

risks.note: Publisher identity is the only assurance the hub offers, and it says nothing about the artifact's behaviour.
Several weight formats execute code on load, and the loader is where the file is opened. Format policy at promotion is what keeps this leg deserialization rather than execution.

The compile and torch caches are loaded without integrity verification, in formats that can execute; a writable cache directory is a write-to-execute path the serving stack's own guide says never to share.
The stored artifact is expensive to reproduce and trivial to copy, which makes storage access control an asset-protection question.
A load path that skips digest verification turns the promotion gate into a suggestion.
Weight-update, pause and abort endpoints outside the versioned API are not covered by the API key on the common serving stacks; reachable from a tenant, they swap the model under every other tenant.

Sustained query access is all extraction needs, and every internal caller — or whatever compromises one — has it. A proprietary fine-tune distilled out through its own completion endpoint is theft that looks like traffic; rate ceilings and anomaly review on the crossing are the answer.
The serving stack is third-party code with its own CVE stream, and no provider is patching it on anyone's behalf.

The gateway is third-party code that sees every tenant's prompts and completions and sets the cache salts and quotas — a compromised release of the gateway itself is all of it, a supply- chain incident class with recent precedent.

Shared accelerators are a physical substrate common to every tenant, below every namespace boundary. Process isolation does not close this channel; dedicated accelerators per sensitivity tier are the deployment choice where the residual is unacceptable.
Dynamic adapter-loading endpoints load LoRA weights at runtime by path — a second load path that skips storage, the digest and the promotion gate, and one the serving stack ships behind a flag.
Capacity is finite and there is no provider to absorb a spike. Admission control here is an availability control, not a billing feature.
A caller that reaches the inference API without the gateway gets unfiltered completions from models fine-tuned on internal data — authentication is opt-in on this class of server.

The sharpest risk that exists here and not on the endpoint. Continuous batching mixes several tenants' requests into one forward pass, and prefix caching makes time-to-first-token a side channel — a crafted prefix plus response timing is enough to reconstruct prompts and secrets cached from another tenant's request. Efficiency and isolation are the same settings; partition the cache by tenant, and note the risk compounds under disaggregated serving, where the cache crosses the network onto SSD and object storage.
With no provider applying output policy, an unguarded return leg hands raw completions to every caller.

mitigations.note: Verify at load, not at download. For a promoted release that is the OpenSSF Model Signing signature with its Sigstore bundle — a detached signature, so nothing has to be repackaged; for a hub artifact, which mostly carries none, it is the promotion record's digest. This is the gate between the store and the loader.
The record of which artifact is actually serving — publisher, version, format and the scan that cleared it. Without it the question "what is running" has no answer.

Every request and completion recorded from the tap at the crossing every caller shares, kept privacy-consciously: the log of an inference service is itself a corpus of everything the organisation asked.
Format and content scanning as a blocking gate on ingest, before any artifact can be promoted — absorbed by the promotion gate over Storage, per the recorded deviation.

Safety and adversarial evaluation of each model version gates its promotion; then the new version serves a slice before it serves everyone, and the previous promoted artifact stays loadable — rollback is a registry operation, not a re-download.
Workload identity per calling tenant, issued by the platform rather than a shared key in a config map.
Per-tenant quotas on finite capacity, enforced at admission rather than discovered at saturation.
Content-policy classification of request and response, because no provider is applying policy for you.

Hardware-enforced isolation per sensitivity tier — dedicated accelerators, or confidential- computing modes with attestation — so one tier's process cannot read another's memory, on the host or the accelerator.
Enumerate the known vulnerabilities in the serving stack and the gateway against the versions actually running, so every advisory maps to the instances it affects. Patching them is the owner's job.
Access control on weights at rest: only the promotion pipeline writes, and only the serving identity reads.

Runtime weight and adapter updating disabled, the control endpoints outside the versioned API unreachable from any tenant, and the serving configuration reviewed as security settings rather than tuning knobs. Cache isolation is part of it: the gateway sets a secret per-tenant cache salt on every request, overwriting any the caller sent, or prefix sharing is off; and the compile and kernel cache directory is private to the serving identity, never shared or tenant-writable.
The distributed serving plane talks between nodes with no authentication by design; network isolation of that plane is the control, absorbed by platform network policy per the recorded deviation.

walkthrough.moves: Prompts from our own services into weights we host, and completions back.

steps.label: hub artifact with provenance
steps.note: A hub artifact arrives with provenance recorded. Scanning and per-version evaluation gate its promotion here — blocking, or it is not a gate.

steps.label: or a signed release
steps.note: The other input, separately: a release from our own pipeline arrives already gated — its signature and lineage are verified, and nothing is evaluated twice.

steps.label: spike
steps.note: Admission control decides who waits. There is no provider to absorb the spike.

steps.label: within-quota scheduled
steps.note: Within-quota traffic is scheduled; everything else is shed at the front door rather than at the accelerator.

scenarios.title: A tenant probes another's prefix

steps.label: crafted prompt
steps.note: A crafted prompt sharing a suspected prefix with another tenant's traffic, well within quota.

steps.label: admitted
steps.note: Admitted like any call; nothing at the crossing knows what the prefix is for.

steps.label: timing reveals cache
steps.note: Time to first token says whether the prefix was already cached by someone else. A secret per-tenant salt, set by the gateway on every request, keeps other tenants' entries out of reach; the common serving stack leaves the salt opt-in, so without it the channel is open.

deviations.subject: No separate GPU or cache blocks are drawn
deviations.reason: The accelerators, the batch and the KV cache are internals of the inference runtime — the same block the endpoint architecture draws — so they appear as items inside it rather than as blocks, and the multi-tenancy risks pin to the runtime and its serving path.

deviations.subject: Admission scanning and per-version evaluation are absorbed by the promotion gate
deviations.reason: Hub artifacts have no scanning or evaluation block of their own here; both duties run in the promotion gate over Storage — scanning (D3-FA) pinned on the store, evaluation as the first step of the rollout gate on the load path. Releases from the model registry arrive already evaluated and signed. Evaluation inline on an artifact path is the ontology's own canonical exception.

deviations.subject: The AI gateway carries inference only
deviations.reason: No MCP, tool or skills traffic exists on this drawing, so the gateway lists its one real traffic class rather than the registered aiGatewayTraffic pack — the same honesty rule the SaaS drawings and the MCP publisher apply in the other direction.

deviations.subject: Network isolation of the serving plane is absorbed by platform policy
deviations.reason: The nodes of a distributed serving plane talk to each other unauthenticated by design. The control (D3-NI) is an isolated network for that plane, delivered by the cluster's network policy rather than by any block on the drawing; the pin sits on the runtime because that is what it protects.
