archetypes.title: Model training & release pipeline
summary:
A build system whose artifact is a model. Curated data goes in, a trained or tuned checkpoint comes out, is evaluated, signed and released to a registry, and everything that is true of a compiler and its supply chain is true here — except that the output cannot be diffed and the defects cannot be found by reading it.
The model is passive on this drawing: it is the thing being built, never the thing acting. Where a run executes what the model generates — RL with tools, agentic evaluation — that stage happens in the agent sandbox for RL & evaluation, and this pipeline is its outer shell.
description:
Treating this as a build pipeline is the whole of the correct framing. It has source inputs, a build environment, dependencies, an artifact, a registry and a promotion path, and it deserves the controls a software pipeline gets: reproducibility, provenance, signed artifacts, and a promotion gate nothing bypasses. Where the analogy breaks is inspection: a compiled binary can be decompiled and diffed; a tuned checkpoint cannot be read for backdoors in any practical sense. Input control and evaluation are the substitutes for code review — what went into the training set and how the result behaves are the only two things anyone can actually examine.
Poisoning is therefore the primary risk and it is durable: what a poisoned example taught is in the weights, ships with every deployment of the artifact, and cannot be deleted from it the way a bad row is deleted from a table. The dose can be small: published results found a near-constant few hundred poisoned documents implanted a trigger backdoor across the model sizes tested, so poisoning needs a foothold, not a percentage. A targeted poisoning that only activates on a trigger phrase is invisible to accuracy metrics and to any evaluation that does not know what to look for — which is why curation is the last place a bad example can be removed rather than baked in, and why lineage from every promoted model back to its exact dataset is what makes a discovered poisoning scopeable at all.
Training data is also a disclosure surface in a way inference data is not. Memorised examples can be extracted from the model afterwards, so restricted-access content in the corpus becomes part of an artifact served far more widely than the dataset ever was. The two access questions to settle early: who may promote a checkpoint to production, and who may read the corpus. Both default to a broad platform-team role, and both are higher-privilege than they look — which is why promotion is a separated human decision and the signing key lives outside the training environment, so a compromised job cannot sign its own output.
distinguishedBy:
Against the agent sandbox for RL & evaluation: one lifecycle, two drawings, split on whether the system runs what the model produces. Here the threat flows into the model — poisoned data, a tampered base, an unsigned artifact — and the controls are provenance, signing and promotion. There, the model's actions are executed, the threat flows out of it — escape, egress, covert channels — and the controls are isolation, egress and monitoring. A frontier RL run uses both: this pipeline around it, the sandbox inside the training job and the agentic evaluations; a fine-tuning team needs only this one, an evaluator only that one.
Against an ordinary data or software build pipeline: same trust properties, different artifact. A dataset or binary can be corrected in place and diffed; a model cannot — which is why the evaluation gate and the promotion decision carry the weight code review carries elsewhere.
Against self-hosted inference: that consumes artifacts, this produces them. They meet at the model registry this drawing now shows, and the promotion gate in front of it is where both archetypes' supply-chain controls concentrate.

exemplars.name: Hugging Face Transformers
exemplars.note: Trainer and model libraries provide the fine-tuning job in a pipeline you operate. Your deployment supplies curated datasets, compute, evaluation gates and artifact promotion.

exemplars.name: Hugging Face PEFT
exemplars.note: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning creates adapters alongside a base model. A training building block for the same data, artifact and promotion pipeline, using customer-operated compute.

exemplars.name: MLflow Model Registry
exemplars.note: Tracks registered model versions, lineage and aliases for promotion between environments. Illustrates the registry tier alongside training and evaluation jobs run by your organization.

zones.note: Where the two inputs come from — the corpora we did not author and the base checkpoint we did not train. Drawn on the left because this is an ingest architecture: the outside world is its source, not its destination.
zones.title: External

zones.note: The build system end to end: the mirror that admits upstream artifacts, the curation stage, the assembled dataset, the GPU pool, the candidate store, and the evaluation and registry tiers that stand between a new checkpoint and anything that serves it.
zones.title: Enterprise cloud

zones.note: Sparse, and deliberately. The dataset's provenance and the output's signature are the two things that make a run auditable six months later; the rest of an MLOps platform is a different architecture.
zones.title: Security & governance control plane

blocks.title: Base model & deps
blocks.note: The starting checkpoint and the frameworks around it, pulled from a public hub or an internal mirror. One of the run's two inputs, and the one whose format decides whether loading it is deserialization or execution.

items.label: Base checkpoint
items.note: The weights the run starts from — open, or one of our own earlier outputs.

items.label: Frameworks & dependencies
items.note: The training stack itself, and an ordinary software supply chain with model-shaped consequences.

blocks.title: Training content origins
blocks.note: Scraped, purchased, internal and human-labelled content. The other input, and the one that carries the most sensitivity: it is usually proprietary, it is read by every worker in the job, and it is the point where poisoning enters.

items.label: Scraped & purchased sets
items.note: Content authored by people who did not know it would train a model.

items.label: Internal records
items.note: Our own data, and the reason the dataset store is the most sensitive thing on this page.

items.label: Human labels & preferences
items.note: Labels and preference judgements steer behaviour directly, and the workforce that writes them typically gets no scrutiny relative to that influence.

blocks.title: Private pkg registry
blocks.note: The organisation-maintained mirror where base checkpoints and training frameworks are admitted before any job may pull them — format policy and scanning run here, by a tier the job cannot bypass, which is what makes the intake control independent of the thing it protects.

items.label: Approved packages
items.note: The base weights and dependencies a run may use — admitted, scanned, and pinned by digest.

blocks.title: Curation & filtering
blocks.note: The processing tier between raw origins and the versioned corpus — the last point at which a poisoned or improperly sourced example is a deletion rather than a retraining decision.

items.label: Quality & safety filters
items.note: What a pipeline calls "curation" — filtering jobs somebody runs and tunes.

items.label: Sensitive-content removal
items.note: Restricted-access content removed before it can be memorised into a wider-served artifact.

items.label: Provenance capture
items.note: Per-example source and licence, recorded at ingest because it cannot be reconstructed later.

blocks.title: Training corpus
blocks.note: The assembled, versioned dataset the run actually reads — an object-storage bucket or a shared filesystem, mounted by every worker. Access control and provenance here matter more than anything else in the drawing.

items.label: Dataset versions
items.note: The exact bytes a given run consumed, addressable after the fact or the run is unreproducible.

blocks.title: Training job
blocks.note: The GPU pool and the framework running on it. The technique decides the shape more than anything else does: a quantized low-rank run fits on a single node, while a full fine-tune needs sharded optimizer state across nodes and a high-bandwidth interconnect. Everything the job holds — the dataset, the base weights, the credentials it was handed — is in one blast radius for the hours it runs.

items.label: GPU compute
items.note: One node or many, gang-scheduled; the interconnect is what decides whether multi-node is viable.

items.label: Tuning run
items.note: Full fine-tune, or the low-rank techniques that collapse the same job onto far less hardware. RL and agentic recipes execute model-generated actions, so the job hands its rollouts to the agent sandbox for RL & evaluation — a drawing of its own.

items.label: Reproducibility record
items.note: Which data, which base, which code, which seed — recorded during the run, not reconstructed later.

blocks.title: Storage
blocks.note: Where the candidate lands, unsigned. For a low-rank run that is an adapter directory of megabytes rather than a model; for a full fine-tune it is a complete checkpoint. Nothing serves from here: a candidate becomes loadable only by passing the gate and being signed at promotion. Encryption over these bytes is our keys, managed from the governance band.

items.label: Model files
items.note: The new weights, or the adapter that layers over the base — candidates until promoted.

blocks.title: Evaluation & red teaming
blocks.note: The blocking gate in front of promotion — candidates flow through it, which is why it is a block here and a governance item on the agent drawings. With an artifact that cannot be read, how the result behaves is one of only two things anyone can examine; the benchmarks themselves are custody-controlled, because a gate whose answer key the candidate's authors can edit gates nothing. It loads untrusted candidates, so it runs isolated, reads the store with a read-only identity, and holds no signing or registry-write credential.

items.label: Capability & safety evals
items.note: Task performance and the safety regressions benign fine-tuning measurably causes.

items.label: Backdoor probing
items.note: Trigger-phrase hunting — the only chance to catch a poisoning accuracy metrics cannot see.

items.label: Memorisation testing
items.note: Whether restricted corpus content can be extracted back out of the artifact.

blocks.title: Model registry
blocks.note: Version, lineage, stage, approval, signature and rollback — the promotion semantics the title promises, operated as its own tier. The artifact bytes stay in the store behind it; what lives here is the decision record that makes one of them loadable. This is where this drawing meets self-hosted inference.

items.label: Candidate checkpoints
items.note: Every artifact the pipeline produced, promoted or not.

items.label: Lineage metadata
items.note: Which data, which base, which run — the record that scopes a discovered poisoning.

items.label: Signed releases
items.note: Signed at promotion, by an identity the training job never holds, so the serving tier's load-time verification proves the gate was passed.

blocks.title: Supply-chain assurance
blocks.note: What went in and what came out: the provenance of every example, the format check on the base checkpoint before a loader opens it, and the record tying an artifact to the run that produced it.

blocks.title: Policy & authorization
blocks.note: Who may read the dataset and who may authorise a run against it. The dataset is the sensitive asset here, not the model.

blocks.title: Secrets & key management
blocks.note: Signing keys for the output, and the credentials the job holds for its whole run.

blocks.title: Observability & response
blocks.note: The lineage record and the documentation that travel with an artifact — the only reason a question asked long after the run has an answer.

blocks.title: Identity services
blocks.note: A workload identity per run, minted for the dataset version it was approved against and structurally unable to sign — the identity is what makes the promotion gate independent of the thing it gates.

edges.label: content in
edges.note: Raw material from outside, entering the one stage where a bad example is still a deletion. Everything after this hop is versioned and, eventually, learned.

edges.label: filtered set
edges.note: What survives filtering, with provenance stamped per example, assembled into the named, versioned set the run will read.

edges.label: base weights & deps in
edges.note: The starting checkpoint and its frameworks arrive at the mirror, where format policy and scanning gate admission. For several formats opening the file is itself the execution event, which is why this check runs at a tier the job cannot skip.

edges.label: approved artifacts
edges.note: The job pulls only what the mirror admitted, pinned by digest.

edges.label: dataset read
edges.note: Every worker in the job reads the same set, which is what makes its access control load-bearing.

edges.label: candidate out
edges.note: The output artifact — a full checkpoint, or an adapter of a few megabytes — lands unsigned. The job holds no signing identity; what it writes is a candidate, not a release.

edges.label: candidate under test
edges.note: The gate loads the candidate the way a serving tier would, and probes what cannot be read.

edges.label: artifact digest
edges.note: The registry records the digest of the bytes the store holds; the signed release points at exactly that artifact and nothing else. Candidates are immutable once written, and promotion signs only the digest the evaluator tested, so a candidate replaced after evaluation fails the match.

edges.label: promotion
edges.note: A passing candidate is promoted: a separated human decision, a signature from an identity the job never held, and a registry entry tying artifact to data, base and run.

risks.note: A poisoned example entering the pipeline. The injection point of the whole architecture, and the reason curation and provenance stand between origins and the corpus rather than being assumed.
Content that was never licensed, consented to, or cleared for this use, learned irreversibly.

A backdoored or tampered base checkpoint, or a compromised framework package, arriving from upstream. Publisher identity says nothing about what was changed — which is what admission at the mirror exists to decide.
More collected and kept than the run needs — whole tables where a field would do, and dataset versions retained past the deletion and retention terms that bind the source records.
Format policy at the mirror is what makes this leg a deserialization: a digest-pinned pickle is still pickle, and the loader opens it as the job.
The output is the expensive thing and it is small — an adapter is megabytes. Egress from the artifact store deserves the attention a model-sized file would not attract.
The job holds the dataset, the base weights and its own credentials at once, for hours. Whatever compromises the training container gets all three.
An adapter layers over a clean, verified base at serve time — a trojaned one rides the base's reputation. Who may register an adapter, and which base it is approved against, is decided here.

Memorised examples can be extracted from the artifact afterwards, so restricted corpus content becomes part of something served far more widely than the dataset ever was. Memorisation testing here is where that surfaces before promotion does.

A gate whose benchmarks the candidate's authors can read or edit gates nothing — and a targeted poisoning is invisible to any evaluation that does not know what to look for. Benchmark custody is the control the gate itself depends on.

mitigations.note: Quality, safety and sensitive-content filtering at the drawn stage — the last point at which a bad example is removable rather than learned.
Where every example came from, recorded at ingest, because it cannot be reconstructed after training.
Who may read the set, enforced at the store rather than trusted to the job.
Reads from the candidate store are scoped like corpus reads — the answering control for exfiltration of an artifact small enough to walk out unnoticed.
Format and content inspection gating admission to the mirror — before any loader in the job opens the file, and independent of the job it protects.

Sign at promotion, with the OpenSSF Model Signing spec and a Sigstore bundle, using an identity the training job never possesses and only on a separated human decision — so a signature proves the gate was passed, not merely that a job finished.
The behavioural half of what substitutes for code review: capability, safety, backdoor and memorisation checks, blocking promotion rather than advising it.
Our keys over the candidate store and the checkpoints the run wrote on the way — managed here, enforced as storage encryption from this service.
The record tying this artifact to this data, this base and this run.
Approval state and the model card gate promotion: what the artifact is and what it was trained on travel with it in the registry, kept distinct from the bill of materials.
Deny-by-default egress from the job: the mirror, the corpus store and the artifact store are the whole allowlist. Absorbed by the compute platform's network policy per the recorded deviation.

Each run has its own workload identity, verified wherever it reads or writes — the dataset version its approved specification names, its own experiment and candidate — and denied the promotion identity, the separation the whole drawing rests on.

Rollouts in an RL or agentic recipe execute what the model generates; that execution is contained in the agent sandbox for RL & evaluation, drawn separately — absorbed here per the recorded deviation.

walkthrough.title: A tuning run produces a promoted adapter
walkthrough.moves: Curated data and an admitted base checkpoint through GPU compute, evaluation and promotion, into a signed registry entry.

steps.label: raw content
steps.note: Raw content enters the filtering stage — the last point a bad example is a deletion.

steps.label: versioned set
steps.note: What survives is assembled into a named, versioned set with provenance per example.

steps.label: same set, checked grant
steps.note: Every worker reads the same set, on a grant that is checked at the store.

steps.label: pinned base & frameworks
steps.note: The job pulls the base checkpoint and frameworks from the mirror, pinned by digest — only what was scanned and admitted when it arrived from upstream, which the base-checkpoint scenario walks.

steps.label: unsigned candidate
steps.note: The candidate lands, unsigned — the job holds no signing identity.

steps.label: evaluation gate
steps.note: The gate loads the candidate and probes what cannot be read.

steps.label: promotion, signed
steps.note: A human promotes; the artifact is signed by an identity the job never held, and the registry entry ties it to its data, base and run.

scenarios.title: A poisoning is discovered months later

steps.label: provenance to batch
steps.note: The provenance record maps the poisoned examples back to the batch they arrived in.

steps.label: to dataset version
steps.note: And to the dataset version they were assembled into.

steps.label: to every run
steps.note: And forward to every run that read that version — which is why versioning is not bookkeeping.

steps.label: every candidate suspect
steps.note: Every candidate those runs wrote is now suspect.

steps.label: passed gate, still suspect
steps.note: Including the ones that passed the gate — a behavioural backdoor is what the probes may have missed.

steps.label: promoted artifacts withdrawn
steps.note: The lineage metadata identifies every artifact those runs promoted, and they are withdrawn — which stops future loads where the serving tier checks release status. Instances already serving them are stopped by the serving tier.

scenarios.title: The base checkpoint is the attack

steps.label: tampered checkpoint
steps.note: A tampered checkpoint arrives — a format that executes on load, or weights carrying a trained-in backdoor. Format policy and scanning refuse the first class here.

steps.label: admitted bytes
steps.note: A behavioural backdoor survives scanning — the mirror admits bytes, not behaviour.

steps.label: backdoor carried forward
steps.note: The candidate carries the backdoor forward; tuning does not remove it.

steps.label: backdoor probing
steps.note: Backdoor probing is the last control with a chance — and only if the probes do not come from a benchmark set the attacker could study.

scenarios.title: A compromised job tries to promote its own output

steps.label: unsigned candidate
steps.note: The job writes a candidate it would like the world to serve. It cannot sign it.

steps.label: gate it cannot pass
steps.note: The only road to promotion runs through a gate the job has no credentials for.

steps.label: signed on human approval
steps.note: Signature and registry entry happen here, on a human approval — a candidate that skipped the gate has no signature, and the serving tier's load-time verification refuses it.

deviations.subject: The external band is drawn on the left
deviations.reason: Band order is left-to-right by convention; this drawing reverses it because it is an ingest architecture — the outside world is its source, not its destination, and the read order should follow the data.

deviations.subject: Evaluation is drawn inline
deviations.reason: Everywhere else in the catalogue evaluation is a governance item, because it gates change rather than data. Here candidates flow through the gate, so it is a block — the ontology's own canonical example of a locus that legitimately differs by architecture.

deviations.subject: Mixed-custody origins are drawn as one external block
deviations.reason: Internal records reach the corpus beside scraped and purchased sets, and a self-trained base checkpoint can arrive beside an open one. Both are drawn entering from the external band because the ingest treatment — curation, provenance, admission — is identical regardless of custody; splitting the origins by owner would double the ingest chain to say nothing new. The custody difference is carried in the item notes.

deviations.subject: Job egress and rollout containment are absorbed, and the rollouts drawn elsewhere
deviations.reason: Deny-by-default egress from the training job (D3-NI) is delivered by the compute platform's network policy rather than by any block the drawing could name. Containment of the actions an RL or agentic recipe executes (D3-EI) is a whole architecture — rollout sandboxes, an offline web, graders, the services the hosts can reach — and is drawn as the agent sandbox for RL & evaluation rather than squeezed into this block. The pins sit on the job because that is what they bound.

deviations.subject: Workload authentication is absorbed by the stores the run touches
deviations.reason: The run's own identity (D3-AA) is verified by the corpus store, the experiment tracker and storage themselves; no identity provider or gateway sits on this path to draw. Identity services in the governance band is where those identities are issued.

archetypes.title: Browser AI agents & extensions
summary: AI operating inside the user's web browser, in two shapes that share one drawing: a browser with the agent built in, whose side panel reads the open tabs and navigates, clicks and types for the user; and an extension from a model vendor that connects an assistant to the browser the user already runs. Either way the agent works inside sessions that are already signed in — every rendered page is untrusted input, and the profile's cookie jar is the credential.
description:
Every other endpoint archetype keeps some separation between the content it reads and the authority it holds. Here there is none. The agent acts inside a profile that is already authenticated to the user's mail, calendar, workspace, bank and internal applications, and the instruction it follows arrives as text on a page served by whoever owns that page. The same-origin policy is the boundary the web is built on, and this archetype's job is to cross it: an agent that reads one origin and acts on another has done exactly what two decades of browser security exist to prevent, with the user's cookies attached. From the application's side the click is the user's — no grant was ever issued to an agent, so nothing downstream can tell them apart.
The two product shapes differ in packaging, not architecture. A built-in agent ships inside a browser the vendor controls end to end; an extension arrives from a public store into a browser somebody else builds, with host permissions on every site and an automatic update channel nobody enrolled. Both are the same harness: a loop, a context assembled from the page, and a tool surface that is the browser's own APIs — navigate, read the DOM and the screenshot, click, type. The extension is the broader exposure in practice, because it sees the pages the user would never point an agent at, and its store is a supply chain with a one-click admission decision.
The controls that work constrain what the session can reach rather than what the model may say. A dedicated, managed browser profile with a narrow set of signed-in origins and no saved passwords converts an unbounded blast radius into a bounded one — the vendors' own safety pages now recommend exactly this, and it is a configuration choice rather than a product feature. Site-level permissions — act, read only, no access — enforced from the vendor's admin console and the browser's policy tier decide where the agent may act before any page is read; confirmation before consequential actions is what remains for the pages the allowlist admits. On the network, the managed browser sends every session through our edge and trusts the enterprise root, so the secure service edge can inspect what leaves for the vendor and classify what comes back from the web, wherever it can parse the payload. The coding agents' drawings leave their vendor sessions uninspected by choice; here inspection is the baseline.
What the vendor supplies is a managed-settings tier — an organisation toggle, site allow and block lists that override user permissions, an audit export — and, inside the product, injection classifiers and action screening that are assured rather than drawn. What the organisation supplies is everything else: the managed profile, browser policy over which extensions may install at all, the edge that sees the traffic, and in-browser telemetry of what the agent read and clicked, which is the only vantage point that sees either.
distinguishedBy:
Against the coding and desktop agents: those read a repository the developer chose and act on a filesystem, with a working directory to scope them to. This one reads pages an attacker can serve and acts through credentials the user already holds, and the nearest thing to a scope is the profile's list of signed-in origins.
Against computer use on a desktop agent: that tool drives the whole machine through the GUI and its blast radius is the OS session. This one lives inside the browser, speaks its APIs — DOM, tabs, navigation — and its blast radius is the set of websites the profile is signed in to. Overlapping products exist; the authority, the permission model and the store's update channel are different problems.
Against enterprise AI chat: the same vendor's chat client in a tab reads what the user pastes or uploads. This archetype reads every tab the user opens and clicks on their behalf — the chat surface with the browser's authority behind it.

exemplars.name: Claude in Chrome
exemplars.note: A browser extension that reads pages and performs browser actions through the user’s sessions. Organization settings govern access and permitted sites.

exemplars.name: Gemini in Chrome
exemplars.note: A browser-integrated assistant using page and tab context. Its auto browse feature adds task automation and is documented as a preview with plan and regional availability limits.

exemplars.name: Microsoft Copilot in Edge
exemplars.note: A browser-integrated assistant that uses page and multi-tab context. Illustrates the authenticated browser-context surface; available actions and organizational controls depend on the selected product mode.

zones.note: The person at the keyboard, stating goals and answering confirmations in the side panel.
zones.title: User surfaces

zones.note: The managed device, running the browser: the profile whose sessions the agent acts with, the agent itself, and the memory it keeps between sessions. Ours to manage, theirs to build — and ours to see, because the managed browser trusts our root and leaves through our edge.
zones.title: Managed endpoint

zones.note: Infrastructure we operate — the secure service edge every browser session leaves through, which is where the organisation inspects, allowlists and records.
zones.title: Enterprise cloud

zones.note: The vendor's own environment under an enterprise agreement: their backend and their admin console — and, each under its own agreement, the SaaS tenants the profile is signed in to. Configured through what they publish; everything inside is assured, not drawn.
zones.title: Vendor platform

zones.note: Reached across the open network — the model provider behind the vendor's service (a disclosed subprocessor of theirs), the open web the agent reads, and the stores the extension updates from.
zones.title: External

zones.note: Drawn across every band because it governs every band — including which origins the profile may hold sessions to, and which pages the agent may be pointed at.
zones.title: Security & governance control plane

blocks.title: User
blocks.note: Sets the goal and answers confirmations, and is usually not reading the pages the agent reads on the way to the outcome — which is why the confirmation prompt is the last human decision on most of these walks.

blocks.title: Browser profile
blocks.note: The container the agent runs inside: a profile is a self-contained browser instance with its own tabs, its own extensions and its own cookie jar, and everything drawn inside acts with the sessions it holds. The frame is the scope decision — the highest-value control in the archetype: a dedicated, managed profile signed into the few origins the agent needs and holding no saved passwords, which the vendors' own safety guidance now recommends. The common state is the user's everyday profile, signed into everything.

blocks.title: Agent harness
blocks.note: The built-in agent or the vendor's extension — the same loop either way: reads the extracted page, decides the next navigation or click, and repeats. Once page text is in context it is indistinguishable from the user's goal. Inference goes to the vendor's own service on the signed-in account, through the browser's network stack — which is what lets our edge see it.

items.label: Agent loop
items.note: Plans the next action from the goal and everything the browser has shown it.

items.label: Context assembly
items.note: Merges the goal, the memories and the extracted pages into one prompt.

items.label: Page extraction
items.note: Turns a rendered page into context — the only point where hidden and off-screen content can be stripped before it becomes instruction, and where the vendor's injection classifiers run.

blocks.title: Native tools
blocks.note: The browser's own APIs offered to the loop as tools, nested because the loop calling them is not a hop. Their authority is the profile's cookie jar; from the browser's perspective the agent's click is the user's. What they reach is drawn: the tabs, and the memory the agent keeps.

items.label: Browser tools
items.note: Navigate, read the DOM and the screenshot, click and type — the per-site permission (act, read only, no access) is enforced here, before any request leaves.

blocks.title: Browser
blocks.note: The tabs the agent reads and drives, the extension host that loads the code doing the reading, and the profile's cookie jar. Every page rendered here — visible text, hidden text, alt attributes, comments — becomes model input with the same standing as the user's goal. The user signs into the profile's origins here, which is how the sessions the agent inherits came to exist.

items.label: Tabs & rendered pages
items.note: Pages fetched with the profile's cookies, rendered, and handed to page extraction.

items.label: Extension host
items.note: Where the extension variant lives: host permissions on every site, and an automatic update channel from the store into the code that reads every page. Which extensions may install at all is browser policy, enforced here.

items.label: Session cookies
items.note: Standing authentication to every signed-in origin in the profile, attached to every request the agent causes — the credential on this drawing.

items.label: Saved passwords & autofill
items.note: Credentials the browser will type into a form the agent navigated to — absent from the dedicated profile in the target state.

blocks.title: Memory & state
blocks.note: What the agent keeps between sessions and reads back as context: the conversation, and the browser memories several products build from the pages the user visited. Outside the profile because it outlives the session — and, for most products, synced to the vendor's side as well.

items.label: Conversation state
items.note: Side-panel sessions saved to history and synced across the user's devices.

items.label: Search index
items.note: Browser memories: pages visited, summarised and retrievable — a page the attacker served once, kept as context for every later task.

blocks.title: AI gateway
blocks.note: The organisation's secure service edge, which every session from the managed profile leaves through: the agent's inference calls to the vendor, and the browsing it causes. Because the browser trusts the enterprise root, this tier can inspect what leaves for the vendor and classify what comes back from the web, wherever it can parse the payload. Its item is the traffic class it carries; the checks it runs — inspection, allowlisting, the record — are the numbered pins on this block and its edges. It brokers no model or MCP traffic here: the vendor's agent calls its own model.

items.label: Secure web gateway
items.note: The forward-proxy tier for the browser's sessions — inspected where policy allows, allowlisted where it does not.

blocks.title: Vendor service
blocks.note: The vendor's backend and the published surfaces of its control plane. What is listed is only what the organisation can configure or receive; the injection classifiers and action screening the vendor runs inside are assured, not drawn.

items.label: Managed settings
items.note: The organisation toggle, site allow and block lists that override user permissions, per-role enablement, and the policy that binds the extension to our tenant. Off, or on by default, depending on the plan — worth checking rather than assuming.

items.label: Session audit export
items.note: Exported sessions and actions — in an unmanaged install, no record at all.

blocks.title: Model provider
blocks.note: The inference API behind the vendor's service. For a vendor that is also the model provider this leg collapses into their own backend; otherwise it is a disclosed subprocessor under the same agreement.

items.label: Inference API
items.note: Receives page content from authenticated sessions; the completion selects the next click.

blocks.title: Open web
blocks.note: Every page is authored by someone else, and the agent reads all of them with the same standing. A hostile page needs no vulnerability — its text is already model input. The extension stores live here too: the update channel pulls from them directly, and nothing of ours admits what arrives.

items.label: Arbitrary pages
items.note: Visible and hidden text alike, served by whoever owns the page — and the form an exfiltration is typed into.

items.label: Skill & extension hubs
items.note: The public extension stores: reviewed by the store, installed in one click, updated automatically.

blocks.title: Downstream services
blocks.note: The signed-in origins the profile holds — our SaaS tenants for mail, calendar and workspace, and the applications that hold our records, each under its own agreement and reached through their web front ends. The agent acts on these as the user, and the applications cannot tell the difference: no grant was ever issued to an agent.

items.label: SaaS
items.note: Mail, calendar, workspace and payment tenants — readable and actionable as the user on every turn.

items.label: Org data
items.note: Our records in the applications that hold them, reached the way the browser reaches any site — through their web front ends on the SSO session, with no connector, no gateway grant and no record of ours beyond the edge.

blocks.title: Identity services
blocks.note: The IdP behind the vendor account, and the managed profile's binding to the workforce identity — the two logins that decide whether the enterprise agreement applies to this traffic at all.

blocks.title: Secrets & key management
blocks.note: Keeping the user's standing sessions and saved credentials out of the agent's profile — the cookie jar is the secret on this drawing.

blocks.title: Policy & authorization
blocks.note: The site-level decisions — act, read only, no access — authored in the vendor console and the browser policy tier, the destinations the edge admits, and what may leave for inference.

blocks.title: Supply-chain assurance
blocks.note: Which browsers and extensions may install at all, pinned to which versions, and the vendor assessment behind the allowlist entry.

blocks.title: Observability & response
blocks.note: The edge's record fused with the vendor's export, in-browser telemetry of what the agent read and clicked, discovery of the extensions nobody enrolled, and the policy push that removes one everywhere at once.

edges.label: local session
edges.note: The user states an outcome in the side panel and answers confirmations. The pages that determine how the outcome is reached are not theirs.

edges.label: navigate, read & click
edges.note: Actions out as navigation, clicks and keystrokes indistinguishable from the user's own; rendered pages back as extracted context. The per-site permission is enforced on the way out, the stripping of hidden content on the way back.

edges.label: read & write / context
edges.note: Conversation and browser memories written as the agent works and read back as context on the next task — the persistence that lets one hostile page outlive the session it was read in.

edges.label: inference & session
edges.note: Page content — including content from authenticated pages — leaves for inference on the signed-in vendor account, through the browser's network stack and therefore through our edge; the completion that returns selects the next click and is not authenticated content.

edges.label: browser egress
edges.note: Every request the agent causes, with the profile's cookies attached, leaves through the edge; every page comes back through it. The one hop on this drawing where the organisation sees the agent's browsing.

edges.label: to the approved vendor
edges.note: Admitted by the allowlist an assessment put it on, and inspected, because the browser trusts the enterprise root and the edge can parse the inference payload. What crosses is the user's pages and the plan that comes back.

edges.label: inference / completion
edges.note: The vendor's service calls the model provider; everything behind that interface is theirs.

edges.label: browsing / page content
edges.note: Browsing out; page text back in. The primary injection path — any page the agent reads can steer what it does on every origin the profile reaches — and the exfiltration path, when the agent is steered into typing what it read into a form the attacker owns.

edges.label: authenticated requests
edges.note: Requests out with the user's cookies; authenticated content — mail, records, internal pages — back in as model input. Where a purchase, a send or a permission change lands.

edges.label: extension install & update
edges.note: The extension variant's supply chain: installed from the store in one click, updated silently on the store's schedule, straight into the host that reads every page. Physically this traverses the edge like everything else; nothing there admits it — the admission decision is browser policy, enforced at the host.

risks.note: The store's review is the only review, and the update channel is automatic: one silent update changes the code that reads every page, with no further decision by anyone.

The extension variant is third-party code with host permissions on all sites, reading every page the user opens — including the ones they would never point an agent at — and replaced silently by whatever the store's update channel delivers next.
An extension is one click to install and appears in no inventory; assistant panels ship enabled to an installed base nobody enrolled, and the default flips from plan to plan.
Instructions from one origin act on another with the user's cookies attached. The application receives a request it cannot distinguish from the user's, because no grant was ever issued to an agent.
Page text is instruction once extracted — visible or hidden — and the author is whoever owns the page the agent happened to read.
Browser memories are prose a later task treats as context; a page the attacker served once is kept, summarised, and re-read on the next task the user asks for.
An agent that retries a click, reloads and retries again, with no meter but the vendor's and a human who has switched tabs — each iteration a real request on a real session.

Whole pages, screenshots and every tab the agent opened on the way go to the vendor and into its retention — usually more than the user pictured sharing, and synced to the vendor's side as memory for most products.
The exfiltration path: an agent steered by one page types what it read on another — mail, records, a one-time code — into a form on a page the attacker owns, on a request that looks like browsing.
The completion selects a click on a real, signed-in application, and nothing authenticates its intent.
A purchase, a send or a permission change is one click, and the set of actions the confirmation gate covers is narrower than users assume.

mitigations.note: Confirmation before consequential clicks — payments, sends, publishing, credential entry. The approval mode is the user's choice and no admin setting removes "skip all approvals", so the covered set is policy and training, not enforcement.
Site-level permissions enforced where the tools run: which origins the agent may act on, which it may only read, which it may not touch — set in the vendor console over the user's own grants.

A dedicated managed profile with a narrow set of signed-in origins and no saved passwords — the control that converts an unbounded blast radius into a bounded one, and the one the vendors' own safety guidance asks for.

The vendor's classifiers scan untrusted page content before it becomes context — not admin- configurable, credited through the assessment. Where the product supports inference hooks, our own screening server returns an allow or deny verdict on requests and tool results. No hidden- content stripping is documented.

Scope which origins may be remembered at all and keep the sensitive ones out; record the page each memory came from, so memories can be deleted or rolled back by origin; and treat what is read back as untrusted input.

In-browser telemetry of what the agent read and clicked — the only vantage point that sees either — compared against the agent's normal pattern per origin, so a read on one site followed by a form submission to another raises an alert.

The browser policy allowlist of extensions and agentic browsers permitted to install — by identifier, blocked by requested permission, pinned to reviewed versions — enforced at the host, not at the store. Admission of an extension is a supply-chain decision, and an update is a decision rather than an event.
Inventory the extensions and assistant panels that never enrolled, from the device and from the edge — this archetype spreads one click at a time.
The edge's session record fused with the vendor's audit export — only the combination shows what was read, what left, and what was clicked.

Classify and redact what page content may leave for inference, on the hop where the browser's trust in our root lets the secure web gateway decrypt and parse the agent's payload — because the pages are authenticated ones. A payload the gateway cannot parse is blocked, not passed.

An allowlist on where the agent may browse, enforced at the secure service edge — with TLS inspection where policy allows — and by managed browser policy on the agent's profile, which is what lets the rule apply to the agent's browsing and not the user's.

MFA enforced at our IdP on the federated sign-in to the agent's vendor account — SSO alone is not MFA — so the agent's vendor session inherits a multi-factor login. Zone-2 configuration, because the account layer is the only lever on this path; the tenant binding that keeps the extension from signing into a personal account is separate configuration in the same tier.

Organisation allow and block lists, set in the vendor's admin tier and enforced by the extension whatever the user chooses. The blocked action classes are the vendor's and the approval mode is the user's — neither can be pinned by an administrator.
The assessment behind the allowlist entry, pinned on the vendor itself: their classifiers, retention terms and memory sync are the substance of the review.
Force-remove the extension by browser policy, disable the agent in the vendor console, and revoke the profile's sessions — each reachable without waiting for the user to notice.

walkthrough.title: The user asks for something on a signed-in site
walkthrough.moves: A goal stated in the side panel, the signed-in page it needs, inference through the vendor, and the confirmed click that lands as the user.

steps.label: goal stated in the side panel
steps.note: The user states an outcome — reschedule the meeting, pay the invoice — and stays for the session.

steps.label: memory & history read
steps.note: The loop assembles context — the conversation so far and the browser memories.

steps.label: context loads
steps.note: All of it loads as context — including whatever an earlier task persisted.

steps.label: open the tab, read the page
steps.note: The browser tools open the signed-in application and read what is rendered.

steps.label: authenticated request
steps.note: The request leaves with the profile's cookies attached, through the edge.

steps.label: on the signed-in session
steps.note: The application answers the user's own session; it has no idea an agent is driving.

steps.label: page / record back
steps.note: Records, mail, a calendar — authored by many hands, none of them the user.

steps.label: page rendered
steps.note: Back through the edge, where returned content can be classified, and rendered.

steps.label: page extracted into context
steps.note: Page extraction strips hidden content and hands the rest to the loop as context.

steps.label: context leaves for inference
steps.note: The goal and the extracted pages leave for the vendor on the signed-in account — and through our edge, which is where classification of what leaves is real.

steps.label: inspected, to the approved vendor
steps.note: Admitted by the allowlist, inspected because the browser trusts our root.

steps.label: vendor's model call
steps.note: The vendor's service calls the model provider; everything past that interface is theirs.

steps.label: completion
steps.note: The completion comes back to the vendor's service.

steps.label: plan
steps.note: And back across the edge — unauthenticated content, about to become the plan.

steps.label: plan into loop
steps.note: The loop treats the completion as its next action.

steps.label: approval prompt
steps.note: The consequential action surfaces for confirmation before it runs — rare enough, in the target state, that the prompt is read.

steps.label: approved (this action)
steps.note: Approved — this action, on this site, not a blanket yes.

steps.label: the consequential click
steps.note: The click, on an origin the site permissions allow the agent to act on.

steps.label: request with cookies attached
steps.note: Out through the edge with the user's session.

steps.label: action lands as the user
steps.note: The application applies it as the user's own action, and records it as such.

steps.label: confirmation
steps.note: The confirmation page returns.

steps.label: rendered
steps.note: And renders in the tab.

steps.label: result extracted
steps.note: Extracted into context, so the loop knows the action landed.

steps.label: outcome reported
steps.note: The outcome, reported in the side panel — and written to memory for the next task.

scenarios.title: A hostile page steers the agent

steps.label: routine goal (compare prices)
steps.note: The user asks for something routine — compare prices, find a venue.

steps.label: navigate to results
steps.note: The agent navigates; the browser fetches whatever the task surfaces.

steps.label: fetch
steps.note: Out through the edge, as ordinary browsing.

steps.label: browsing
steps.note: To a page the attacker owns, or one they were able to write on.

steps.label: page with hidden instruction
steps.note: A page comes back carrying text addressed to the agent — off-screen, white on white, or in a comment — which the edge can classify and rarely does.

steps.label: rendered, hidden text included
steps.note: Rendered in the tab, hidden text and all.

steps.label: extracted into context
steps.note: Page extraction is the last point the hidden text could be stripped; past it, the text is context.

steps.label: poisoned context leaves
steps.note: The poisoned context goes to the vendor for inference, indistinguishable from the user's goal.

steps.label: inference
steps.note: The vendor's classifiers are the last defence on this hop, and they are the vendor's.

steps.label: attacker's plan as completion
steps.note: The completion carries the attacker's instruction as the next step.

steps.label: next click
steps.note: The loop treats it as the next click.

steps.label: click on a signed-in origin
steps.note: The next click lands on a signed-in origin — the mail tab, the internal application — if the site permissions let the agent act there.

steps.label: request with the user's cookies
steps.note: With the user's cookies attached.

steps.label: acts on the signed-in app
steps.note: The application receives a request it cannot distinguish from the user's.

steps.label: records read
steps.note: What the attacker wanted read — mail, a record, a one-time code — comes back.

steps.label: rendered
steps.note: Rendered in the tab.

steps.label: extracted
steps.note: And extracted into context, where the plan already says what to do with it.

steps.label: typed into the attacker's form
steps.note: The agent types it into a form on the page it was steered from.

steps.label: exfil request
steps.note: A request that looks like browsing.

steps.label: content leaves to the attacker's page
steps.note: The content leaves to the attacker's page — the edge's classification of what leaves is the last control standing, and the destination allowlist the one before it.

scenarios.title: Summarise my inbox

steps.label: summarise my inbox
steps.note: A legitimate request against the user's own mail.

steps.label: open the mail tab
steps.note: The agent opens the mail tab in the profile.

steps.label: authenticated request
steps.note: Out with the standing session.

steps.label: inbox on the standing session
steps.note: The browser fetches the inbox on the standing session.

steps.label: mail, incl. strangers' messages
steps.note: Mail content returns — including messages written by strangers, which are now model input.

steps.label: rendered
steps.note: Rendered in the tab.

steps.label: inbox extracted into context
steps.note: The whole inbox view is extracted into context.

steps.label: the inbox leaves for inference
steps.note: The inbox leaves for inference, which is more than the user pictured sharing.

steps.label: DLP-inspected, to the vendor
steps.note: Classified at the edge on the way out — the one place a mail transcript can be redacted before it becomes the vendor's to retain.

steps.label: summary
steps.note: The summary comes back.

steps.label: into the loop
steps.note: Into the loop.

steps.label: summary in the side panel
steps.note: And to the user — with the inbox now in the vendor's retention and, likely, its memory.

scenarios.title: The extension updates itself

steps.label: silent update from the store
steps.note: A new version arrives over the store's channel into the extension host — the code that reads every page has changed, with no decision by the user and no admission by us.

steps.label: every open page, read by new code
steps.note: The updated code reads every tab the profile has open, on the permissions it already held.

steps.label: requests on every session's cookies
steps.note: Whatever it now does, it does with the profile's cookies attached.

steps.label: on every signed-in origin
steps.note: On every signed-in origin the profile holds — which is why the profile's scope, and the policy allowlist that pins the version, are the controls this walk pins.

scenarios.title: A memory carries the injection forward

steps.label: poisoned page kept as a memory
steps.note: A page read on one task is summarised into browser memories — hidden instruction included, because the summariser read it too.

steps.label: read back on the next task
steps.note: The next task, unrelated, loads the memory as context.

steps.label: into inference, on a clean goal
steps.note: The injection re-enters inference under a goal the user never associated with the page — memory scoping and treating memories as untrusted on read are what bound it.

deviations.subject: The AI gateway is the secure service edge, and carries no model proxy
deviations.reason: Every product in this class calls its own vendor's model on the signed-in account, so the organisation's tier brokers no inference and no MCP traffic; the aiGatewayTraffic pack is not used and the block lists the one traffic class it carries — the secure web gateway the managed browser's sessions leave through. It is drawn as the AI gateway because it is the customer-operated tier every session crosses, and because it is the registered embodiment of egress control; what it does here is admission, inspection and the record, which are the pins on it and on its two edges. A reader comparing this to the coding agents should see the same block doing a narrower job.

deviations.subject: The vendor's path is inspected here, unlike the coding agents' vendor sessions
deviations.reason: The sibling coding drawings admit the vendor session by allowlist and leave it uninspected — a policy choice, not an impossibility, since enterprise TLS-inspection proxies work for CLIs that trust the enterprise root. Here inspection is the baseline: extensions and built-in agents use the browser's network stack, which trusts the root and already leaves through the secure service edge, so AI DLP is pinned on the vendor hop. It holds only where the edge can parse the agent's payload; where it cannot, the hop is blocked rather than passed uninspected.

deviations.subject: Injection defence is absorbed by the harness's page extraction
deviations.reason: The registered embodiment of input screening (cap-input-guardrails) is the AI gateway, but page content becomes context inside the agent, and the vendor's injection classifiers and the inference hooks act there. The pin sits on the harness and the control is absorbed by it; the edge can classify returned pages on the browsing leg and that is recorded on the edge's own notes, not as a second embodiment.

deviations.subject: The profile is drawn as a boundary around the browser and the agent
deviations.reason: A reader expects a profile inside a browser. The drawing inverts that on purpose: a profile is a self-contained browser instance — its own tabs, extensions and cookie jar — and it is the boundary this archetype actually has, so it is drawn as the frame around everything that acts with its sessions, the way the personal agent draws its sandbox. The Browser block inside it holds the tabs, the extension host and the cookie jar the frame scopes; credential isolation pins on the frame because the frame is the decision.

deviations.subject: The extension supply path is drawn direct from the store to the host
deviations.reason: Physically the update traverses the secure service edge like every other request; drawing it that way would suggest the edge admits it, and nothing there does. The admission decision — which extensions may install, at which versions — is browser policy enforced at the extension host, and the edge from the store to the host is where that decision and the provenance risk are pinned.
