archetypes.title: Local model runtime
summary: An open-weights model served on the user's own machine, listening on a local port so other local processes can call it. Chosen to keep data off a vendor's infrastructure, which succeeds once the runtime's own cloud features are switched off — and moves every control the vendor was providing onto the device.
description:
The reason people run this is sound: prompts and documents can stay on the machine — provided the runtime's own cloud models and web search are switched off — there is no per-token cost, and it works offline. The architectural consequence is that the guardrails, rate limiting, abuse monitoring and content policy a hosted API applies on the way in and out are simply absent, and nothing replaces them by default. Guardrails here are a control the device owner deploys on the request path, not a component the runtime ships — in the common install nothing sits on that path, and raw model output goes straight back to the caller.
The runtime is a local network service. It binds a port, speaks an HTTP API, and historically ships without authentication because the assumed caller is a process on the same machine. That assumption fails in two directions: any local process — including a browser tab, through a permissive CORS policy — can call it, and a runtime bound to a routable interface rather than loopback is reachable from the network. Who may bind the port and who may call it are the admission decisions of this architecture, and by default nobody makes them.
The supply chain is the axis specific to this archetype. Weights are large binaries fetched from public hubs, and several serialization formats execute code on load — on that load-time-execution axis alone, a safe-by-construction tensor format from an unknown publisher beats a pickle-based one from a known publisher. It is one gate among several, not a ranking: format policy, publisher provenance, scanner results and behavioural evaluation are independent checks, and passing one buys nothing at the others. Safe-by-construction has limits of its own: the formats that cannot execute on load are still opened by fast-moving native parsers whose memory bugs are a code-execution class of their own, and one popular format embeds chat templates that execute at inference time, past every static scan. The target sequencing is fetch-to-quarantine: the artifact is acquired without being loaded, verified and scanned at rest, then promoted to approved local storage the runtime loads from — never fetched and opened in one step.
The common install has no governance at all: no model inventory, no weight scanning pipeline, no policy on binding or sources. The target state adds exactly what this page's governance band draws — artifact assurance, inventory, evaluation and response — and every control named here presumes someone first learns the runtime exists, because it is installed by one person in an afternoon and appears in no inventory.
distinguishedBy:
Against self-hosted inference in a datacentre: identical software, entirely different operational reality. There the runtime has a network policy, an identity, a scanner in the pipeline and someone on call. Here its port is protected by the assumption that nothing else on the machine is hostile.
Against the other endpoint archetypes: this one is not an agent. It has no loop, no tools and no autonomy — it is a dependency the others consume. It earns its own architecture because its risks are supply chain and local exposure rather than agency.

exemplars.name: Ollama
exemplars.note: Runs model inference behind a local API. This example uses local models with cloud features disabled, keeping the serving process and model artifacts on the managed device.

exemplars.name: LM Studio
exemplars.note: A desktop application that can serve downloaded models through a local API. Illustrates the GUI-managed local inference service consumed by other applications on the device.

exemplars.name: llama.cpp server
exemplars.note: A native HTTP inference server over local model artifacts. Illustrates the directly operated runtime and loader beneath applications that call an OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

zones.note: The machine and everything the runtime puts on it: the local API, the process that loads the weights, and the artifacts on disk. The whole architecture lives here, which is why the one band that matters is the boundary around it.
zones.title: Managed endpoint

zones.note: The person at the machine — the only caller a local runtime is for. Editors, agents and tools call the port on their behalf; nothing off the machine is meant to.
zones.title: User surfaces

zones.note: Outside the company: the public hubs the weights come from. Nothing else reaches in — a routable bind is the failure this drawing's pins describe, not a path it draws.
zones.title: External

zones.note: Sparse here by comparison with the agent architectures, and deliberately so — there is no gateway, no vendor and no identity on the data path, so what governance can do is decide which artifacts are allowed and notice the runtimes nobody registered.
zones.title: Security & governance control plane

blocks.title: Developer
blocks.note: The person the runtime was installed for. They drive it through local applications — an editor, an agent, a chat window — and never through the port directly, which is why the applications are the drawn caller and the person is the only principal.

blocks.title: Local applications
blocks.note: Everything on the machine that can open a socket to the port. The consumers the runtime was installed for — editors, agents and tools calling the local API instead of a hosted one, usually built expecting a hosted API's safety floor — and the browser, which is local software too, and which a visited web page can drive through a permissive cross-origin policy. Nothing on the path tells the two apart.

blocks.title: Inference API
blocks.note: In the target state this is an authenticated policy wrapper: the raw runtime endpoint — unauthenticated by design in the flagship runtimes, whose vendors point at VPNs and reverse proxies rather than shipping auth — sits behind it on a socket or port only the wrapper's service account can reach, and caller identity, per-caller ceilings and origin policy are enforced here. Which interface it binds and who may call it are this architecture's admission decisions, and exposure scans keep finding the installs that made neither.

items.label: Completion endpoint
items.note: The published local interface every consumer on the machine shares.

items.label: Interface binding
items.note: Loopback is an assumption, not a policy. Bound to a routable interface, the runtime is reachable from the network.

items.label: Cross-origin policy
items.note: Origin policy decides who may read a reply; a simple cross-origin POST is acted on regardless, and a DNS-rebinding page reads as well. The control is Host and Origin validation plus caller authentication, not CORS alone.

blocks.title: Inference runtime
blocks.note: Loads weights, batches requests, serves completions — from approved local storage only, never straight from a fetch. Whatever safety behaviour exists is whatever the weights carry.

items.label: Weight loader
items.note: Where a pickle-based format turns file opening into code execution — and where a malformed file in a "safe" format exercises the native parser, a different bug class with the same outcome.

items.label: Loaded model
items.note: Open weights with no provider-side guardrail, abuse monitoring or content policy.

blocks.title: Storage
blocks.note: Quarantine and approved storage in one tier: artifacts land here on fetch, are scanned and verified at rest, and only promoted files are loadable. Format determines whether loading is deserialization or execution — a more useful question than who published them. Public base weights are not secret; the confidentiality case is the organisation's own fine-tunes and adapters stored beside them.

items.label: Model files
items.note: Readable by any process with the user's privileges, and swappable by the same — including any org-tuned adapters, which are the part worth stealing.

blocks.title: Supply-chain assurance
blocks.note: The whole governance story of this archetype, and the reason the scan sits after the fetch and before the load: the artifact lands in quarantine unopened, because for several formats opening the file is the execution event.

blocks.title: Observability & response
blocks.note: Every control named on this page presumes someone first learns the runtime exists. It is installed by one person in an afternoon and appears in no inventory, so discovery is not a supporting control here — it is the precondition for all the others.

blocks.title: Public model hub
blocks.note: Distribution for open weights. Publisher identity ranges from verified to arbitrary, and neither transport security nor a signature says anything about what the artifact does when the runtime opens it.

items.label: Open-weights catalogue
items.note: Declared behaviour and actual behaviour are separate facts.

edges.label: local session / replies
edges.note: The person at the machine, authorised by holding it. Every call the port sees is made on their behalf by software they run, which is the whole admission model of a local runtime.

edges.label: completion request
edges.note: Local software calls the local API the way it would a hosted one. In the target state each application presents its own token and the wrapper refuses disallowed origins and unknown Host names; in the common install it is the same unauthenticated request on the same port, whether it came from the editor the runtime was installed for or from a web page driving the browser — locality standing in for authorization.

edges.label: request / completion
edges.note: Prompts in, raw completions back. Input and output classification is a control deployed on this path — in the common install it is a straight pipe.

edges.label: load
edges.note: Only promoted, integrity-checked artifacts load, and never in the same step as a fetch. For several formats the load is an execution event, which makes this the supply chain's last gate.

edges.label: weight fetch
edges.note: The artifact is pulled to quarantine without being opened — by the management tooling in the target state, by the runtime's own downloader in the common install, where fetch and load collapse into one step and the whole promotion story disappears. Transport is authenticated and the publisher may be verifiable; neither says anything about what the artifact does when the loader opens it.

risks.note: Publisher identity at publish time, nothing at load time — and a hub account is a takeover target.
Pickle-class formats execute code on load. The risk is a property of the artifact format, not of the publisher.
The chat template embedded in the weights runs on every request — past the load gate and every static scan.
The artifacts sit on disk with the user's file permissions — readable by anything running as the user.
What the runtime serves is whatever sits in its model directory; a swap there — by a stranger on an exposed port or by any local process — is served on the next request with nothing to notice.
The serving stack itself is fast-moving native code with its own CVE history, running unsandboxed — and patched over an auto-update channel that is part of the attack surface.
Any local process can saturate the runtime; a browser tab can do it from a web page.

Loopback is an assumption, not a policy: bound to a routable interface with the authentication it shipped — usually none — the port serves free inference to whoever finds it, and on some runtimes the management surface too. The headline exposure class the scans keep documenting, and the reason the bind is a pinned control rather than a default.

With no provider-side safety layer, a crafted prompt the weights misread — an adversarial suffix, an obfuscated or encoded request — meets only the refusal behaviour the weights carry, unless the wrapper's classification catches it first.

A model-name suffix or a search flag routes the prompt to the vendor's cloud through the same local API — unless the runtime's local-only switch is on and the device firewall denies the runtime process outbound traffic, as the target state requires.
Where no classifier sits on this path — the common case — raw model output goes straight to callers built expecting a hosted API's floor.

mitigations.note: Format and content inspection at quarantine, before promotion — a scan that runs after the runtime opens the file has documented an incident, not prevented one.

Caller identity at the wrapper rather than locality as authorization: each local application presents its own token, because a browser tab is local too. The raw runtime is reachable only by the wrapper's service account, and the wrapper's bind (loopback only) and Host and Origin validation are set by device management rather than hoped from defaults. Absorbed by the API wrapper per the recorded deviation.
Deploy the input and output classification a hosted API would have applied — nothing supplies it here by default.
Bound what any single caller can consume, because the callers share one unmetered port.

Restrictive permissions on the model store: only the promotion step writes approved files and only the runtime's service account reads them, so no other process running as the user can swap a model or copy the organisation's adapters.

The risk assessment behind the posture: whether local inference may run at all, on which runtimes, from which sources and on which machines — weighed against the exposure, supply-chain and data-handling risks on this page, recorded, and re-run when a runtime CVE or a new source changes them.
Endpoint telemetry over the serving process: what it executes, which ports it listens on and which interfaces it binds.

A bill of materials for every promoted artifact — model file and digest, format, publisher and source, version, base model and adapters — the record every response to a bad release or a parser CVE starts from.
Find the runtimes nobody registered, derived from the machine rather than self-reported.
Evaluate what the weights actually do before promoting them for other software to call — a gate on change, run from the governance band; there is no provider evaluation to inherit.
Weights load only after their digest matches the approved artifact, so a swapped model file is refused rather than served.

walkthrough.title: An application asks for a completion
walkthrough.moves: A prompt from local software into weights on the same machine, and the completion back.

steps.label: task at the machine
steps.note: The person asks their editor, agent or chat window for something that needs a model.

steps.label: completion request
steps.note: A local tool calls the OpenAI-compatible endpoint as if it were hosted, presenting its own token.

steps.label: to runtime
steps.note: The wrapper has authenticated the caller, checked its origin and its quota, and classified the prompt; the runtime serves the completion with whatever behaviour the weights carry.

steps.label: completion to the wrapper
steps.note: The raw completion returns to the wrapper, where output classification runs before anything reaches the caller.

steps.label: screened response
steps.note: The response returns to the authenticated caller, screened — the floor a hosted API would have supplied, deployed here.

steps.label: answer
steps.note: The answer reaches the person through the application that asked.

scenarios.title: A poisoned checkpoint

steps.label: download
steps.note: A well-reviewed model name, a compromised artifact — the download verifies transport, not behaviour. It lands in quarantine unopened, which is the step the common install skips.

steps.label: load after scan
steps.note: Only after scan and promotion does the runtime open the file. In a pickle-class format the load is the execution event; in a safe format, a malformed header exercises the parser instead — either way, with the user's privileges.

scenarios.title: A browser tab finds the port

steps.label: cross-origin POST
steps.note: A failure scenario: the wrapper is missing or misconfigured — no caller token, a permissive origin policy, no Host check against DNS rebinding — and the port is reachable. A visited web page fires a simple-request POST at the local endpoint through the browser, the unauthenticated server acts on it, and a rebinding page reads the answer too. The caller is local software; nobody chose to serve it.

steps.label: local inference for a page
steps.note: With those checks off, nothing distinguishes this caller from the intended ones. The page now drives local inference — for free, and invisibly to the user.

deviations.subject: Quarantine, scanning and rate limiting are absorbed rather than drawn
deviations.reason: The scanning embodiment (the private package registry) and a separate quarantine tier are not drawn: the storage block carries quarantine and promotion state, the management tooling runs the scan (D3-FA), and the API wrapper absorbs caller identity (D3-AA) and per-caller ceilings (AML.M0004). Recorded here because each is an inline duty a simple endpoint drawing folds into the nearest real tier.

deviations.subject: The runtime's own distribution channel is not drawn
deviations.reason: The serving binary updates itself over its vendor's channel — attack surface the insecure-component risk note names, but a single outbound updater hop that a standing edge would overstate. The same process's cloud-model offload and web-search calls ride the same undrawn egress. An organisation that mirrors the runtime binary through its package registry closes the first at the mirror. In the target state the runtime's local-only switch disables its cloud models and web search and the device firewall denies the runtime process any outbound destination, so local means local; model acquisition stays the separate fetch to quarantine.

deviations.subject: Guardrails are a control on the request path, not a block
deviations.reason: Input and output classification (cap-output-guardrails) is something the device owner deploys, not a component of the runtime — so it is pinned as a numbered control on the API-to-runtime path rather than drawn as a service that does not exist in the common install.

archetypes.title: Personal autonomous agent
summary: An always-on daemon on a personal device that takes ambient messages from anyone who can reach its channels, runs an unattended agent loop with the user's own credentials, and keeps what it learns in files it will read back as instruction. Assembled by the user from a harness, wired-up tools and pasted-in keys — there is no vendor application wrapping it.
description:
The harness is a long-lived process, not an invocation. It owns the channel bridges, the agent loop, a heartbeat that fires with nobody watching, and a memory directory the next turn treats as context. Nothing about it is scoped to a task: it starts when the machine starts and ends when the user kills it.
Three default postures make this a distinct architecture rather than a variation on a coding assistant — each now exists as an opt-in feature over there, and is the resting state here. It listens — whoever can reach a bridge can address the agent, and the bridge is the authorization decision. It runs unattended — the heartbeat starts the loop with no human seeing the plan before the tools execute. And it remembers in a medium it re-reads as instruction — one successful injection written into memory survives restarts and re-executes on the schedule.
The target state wraps the harness whole. A microVM-class sandbox contains the daemon, its memory and a deliberately local tool surface — files, shell and skills, with their own kernel, filesystem, packages and network — and remote reach is pushed outside the boundary. The AI gateway brokers what leaves for a model, an MCP server or an API — credentials injected at the crossing so the sandbox itself holds no secrets, and the audit tap — while the sandbox's own network policy makes the gateway, the mirror and the web tools' search and fetch the only routes out. Our own remote MCP servers and APIs sit behind the gateway as the cloud tool surface; nothing outside an agreement is wired in as a tool. Two other openings exist: a read-only pull from a private, organisation-maintained package registry, and the owner's workspace folders, shared into the sandbox explicitly and nothing else. The boundary is also what the approval prompts traded away — shipped sandboxes run the agent approval-free inside, on the position that isolation, egress policy and credential injection replace per-command consent. Products now ship exactly this wrap for the popular harnesses; the drawing is that pattern, vendor-neutral.
The governance band this drawing carries is entirely the organisation's addition — the assembled-by-user common state has none of it: no agent identity distinct from the user, no policy engine consulted per tool call, no audit sink beyond the gateway's tap, no kill switch beyond killing the process. The sandbox bounds the blast radius; the governance services drawn beneath are what it takes to actually govern the agent.
distinguishedBy:
Against the coding and desktop agents: the capabilities have converged — those now take remote steering, scheduled runs and agent-written memory too — so what separates the archetypes is defaults, identity and custody. There, each of those is opt-in, reaches the machine as an outbound relay only the owner's vendor account can address, and can be switched off from an admin console. Here, listening is the resting state, the sender set is whoever the messaging platform admits, the keys are long-lived and pasted in, and the whole thing is pieced together by the user with no console anyone can switch anything off from. The exposure scans still tell the story: personal gateways bind ports and get found by the tens of thousands; a vendor agent's remote channel opens no inbound port at all.
Against a cloud agent service: the same loop hosted by a provider gets an identity, a policy boundary, an audit trail and an administrator by default. Moving this architecture off the endpoint changes almost nothing about the loop and almost everything about the governance.

exemplars.name: OpenClaw
exemplars.note: A self-hosted personal assistant with a persistent gateway, messaging channels, tools and memory. This example places its runtime on a managed endpoint with the reference containment controls added.

zones.note: The owner and the surfaces they instruct the agent from — messaging apps, the gateway's control UI, the local terminal.
zones.title: User surfaces

zones.note: The managed device and the sandbox on it: the loop, its local tools and its state. Nothing here reaches our systems or the outside except through a crossing.
zones.title: Managed endpoint

zones.note: Infrastructure we operate — the messaging relay, the bundled AI gateway, and the internal servers and data the agent is meant to reach. The crossings live here alongside what they protect.
zones.title: Enterprise cloud

zones.note: The contracted messaging tenant — the one vendor relationship this architecture has. A consumer channel with no agreement is a different posture, recorded as a deviation rather than drawn.
zones.title: Vendor platform

zones.note: Outside the company: model providers, the open web, and the public sources the mirror admits from. Whoever else the messaging platform admits is bounded at the bridge's allowlist, not drawn as a caller.
zones.title: External

zones.note: Drawn across every band because it governs every band: identity and secrets the crossing consumes, the policy it enforces, the registry it serves from, the audit it writes, and the kill switch that ends all of it — including what may be reached externally.
zones.title: Security & governance control plane

blocks.title: Owner
blocks.note: The person the agent acts for — and, from the agent's side, indistinguishable from anyone else the platform admits.

blocks.title: Remote device
blocks.note: The surfaces the owner instructs from: messaging apps, the gateway's control UI, and the local terminal. Identity here is whatever the platform asserts.

items.label: Messaging apps
items.note: The owner's chat clients — the same platforms an unbounded sender set can reach.

blocks.title: Sandbox
blocks.note: A microVM-class boundary around the loop, its state and its local tools — the core recommendation for this archetype, and the control that bounds every other failure on this page. Its own kernel, filesystem and network, and no approval prompts inside, because the boundary replaces them. Three openings are deliberate and each is a control decision. The workspace is mounted directly at the same path and propagates both ways, so a read-only clone is the safer default. Skills persist across sandboxes and are therefore a contamination channel between them. Egress leaves through a host-side proxy whose allowlist ships with broad wildcards worth pruning. The target state runs local MCP servers inside this boundary with the rest of the tool surface; the common state runs them on the host with host privileges — the gap common implementations share, carried as the risk pinned on the native tools. What earns the boundary its keep: the model credential is injected into request headers by that host-side proxy, so the key never enters the sandbox and an agent that can exfiltrate cannot steal it.

blocks.title: Channel bridges
blocks.note: One adapter per platform, each implementing its own sender check. The count of channels is the count of independent admission surfaces.

items.label: Channel adapters
items.note: Per-platform inbound and outbound handling, bound to loopback.

items.label: Pairing records
items.note: Which platform identity is bound to this agent — the artifact the admission decision reads, and as strong as the platform that issued it.

blocks.title: Agent harness
blocks.note: The long-lived loop that plans, calls tools and reads results back as context, with the heartbeat that starts it when nobody is watching.

items.label: Agent loop
items.note: Plans, calls tools, reads results back as context. Nobody reviews the plan.

items.label: Heartbeat
items.note: The tick that converts a one-time injection into a recurring one.

items.label: Context assembly
items.note: Merges the message, the memory and the tool results into one prompt.

items.label: MCP client
items.note: The harness's own MCP client — the party that connects out: to the local servers in its native tools, and through the gateway's MCP brokerage to remote ones.

items.label: Local API server
items.note: The daemon's control WebSocket and dashboard on loopback — the surface the exposure scans keep finding on routable interfaces, and a documented token-exfiltration surface even when the bind is right.

blocks.title: Memory & state
blocks.note: Cross-session files the agent writes and reads back as instruction — the persistence primitive, and the reason an injection outlives the message that carried it.

items.label: Memory files
items.note: Prose the next turn treats as instruction.

items.label: Rules & instructions
items.note: The bootstrap files the agent reads as its own standing instruction — and, on the harnesses that write their own skills, edits.

items.label: Search index
items.note: Retrieval over everything the agent has ever kept.

blocks.title: Native tools
blocks.note: The harness's built-in tools, nested because the loop calling them is not a hop: files, shell, the local MCP servers it spawns, skills and computer use — all inside the sandbox in the target state, none of it on the host. Remote transports are not here: they live behind the enterprise crossing by construction. What these tools reach is drawn — memory, the mounted workspace, the package mirror and the open web.

items.label: File & edit tools
items.note: Read and write on the sandbox filesystem and the mounted workspace.

items.label: Shell commands
items.note: Command execution inside the sandbox, never on the host.

items.label: Local MCP servers
items.note: Local child processes, run inside the boundary in the target state so they hold the sandbox's authority rather than the user's. The common state runs them on the host — the containment gap the risk pin records.

items.label: Installed skills
items.note: Prose that instructs the loop to run installers, plus code loaded into the daemon's own process — the "prerequisites" step is where a stealer ran.

items.label: Computer use
items.note: Drives the host browser over the debugging protocol and inherits every signed-in session in it — outside the boundary by construction. Disabled in the target state, or pointed at a browser that lives inside the sandbox.

blocks.title: Owner workspace
blocks.note: The host folders shared into the sandbox — mounted read-only with a private clone in the enterprise posture, so an agent edit is a reviewable diff rather than a host write.

items.label: Shared folders
items.note: Explicitly listed paths only; the home directory and its credentials are simply absent.

blocks.title: Messaging relay
blocks.note: The outbound-only connector between the endpoint and the messaging platform, so platform credentials never sit on the device and no inbound port is ever opened.

items.label: Outbound connector
items.note: The endpoint dials out; nothing dials in.

items.label: Platform credentials
items.note: The messaging tenant's credentials, held here so they never sit on the device.

blocks.title: AI gateway
blocks.note: The single bundled crossing this organisation operates: model proxying, MCP and tool brokerage, and skills admission in one tier. Model, MCP and API calls leave through here; everything else a tool emits is bounded by the sandbox's network policy, not by this tier.

items.label: Model proxy
items.note: The only provider endpoint the harness knows — allowlisted models, routed by data class.

items.label: MCP & API gateway
items.note: The approved server catalogue, tool-level scoping and token exchange to the owner's scope.

items.label: Skills catalogue
items.note: Admission for skills: which skills and images are permitted at all, and the pins the mirror serves against. The bytes do not pass through here — the sandbox pulls them from the mirror directly.

blocks.title: Private pkg registry
blocks.note: The organisation-maintained mirror the sandbox pulls skills and images from — reviewed, signed and pinned before anything is installable. The registry moves the review earlier; it does not remove the risk.

items.label: Approved packages
items.note: Skills, plugins and sandbox base images — the only sources the gateway will serve.

blocks.title: Public package sources
blocks.note: Where the mirror gets what it serves: the public package registries and the skill and extension hubs it proxies and admits from. Nothing here is ours, which is why admission happens at the mirror and not at the tool that asked.

items.label: Package registries
items.note: PyPI, npm and their kind — mirrored, never reached by a tool directly in the target state.

items.label: Skill & extension hubs
items.note: Community catalogues of skills, extensions and images, admitted through the same door.

blocks.title: Identity services
blocks.note: The IdP and the non-human identity plane: one workload identity per agent, bound to its owner and device, the pairing admission the bridges enforce, and the revocation that ends every brokered path at once.

blocks.title: Secrets & key management
blocks.note: The vault and the just-in-time credential path — short-lived, scoped tokens issued from outside whatever is asking for them.

blocks.title: Policy & authorization
blocks.note: The policy engine the crossings consult per call, and the egress and rate decisions it carries — authored where the workload cannot reach them.

blocks.title: Supply-chain assurance
blocks.note: The registry, signing and scanning that decide which agents, tools, servers and images are admitted at all, and the vendor assessments behind them.

blocks.title: Observability & response
blocks.note: Telemetry, the audit trail the workload cannot amend, discovery of what nobody registered, the baseline that notices drift, and the containment path when something goes wrong.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: The organisation's own tool servers and service APIs — the connectors we publish for our own agents. This is what the agent is actually meant to reach, and the gateway in front of it is what decides which of them it may.

items.label: Remote MCP servers
items.note: Our own servers, listed in the catalogue the gateway enforces.

items.label: APIs & connectors
items.note: Service APIs reached on grants the gateway issues, scoped to the owner.

blocks.title: Enterprise data
blocks.note: The systems of record behind our own tool servers — the data the agent reads and the records it changes. Ours to classify, ours to log, and the reason the crossing exists.

items.label: Org data
items.note: Documents, tickets and records the internal servers read and write.

items.label: File storage
items.note: Governed content stores reached through our own connectors, not the device's mounts.

blocks.title: Messaging platform
blocks.note: The messaging vendor's cloud, holding the corporate tenant under an agreement we signed. It authenticates senders to its own satisfaction, which is the only sender assurance this architecture inherits.

items.label: Platform tenant
items.note: Where the corporate bot lives, and where message retention actually happens.

blocks.title: Model provider
blocks.note: The inference API, reached only through the gateway on a brokered credential.

items.label: Inference API
items.note: The completion it returns is unauthenticated content that drives tool calls.

blocks.title: Open web
blocks.note: What the agent's web tools search and fetch, through the sandbox's egress proxy. Every page is authored by someone else, and on an unattended loop its text is the instruction nobody reviews.

items.label: Web search
items.note: Results and snippets written by strangers, read straight into context.

items.label: Arbitrary pages
items.note: Attacker-writable content that re-enters the loop as context.

edges.label: instruction / reply
edges.note: The owner writes on their own surfaces; everything after this rides platform identity.

edges.label: local session
edges.note: The other way in, and the one most owners actually use day to day: a terminal or TUI on the machine attaching straight to the loop. No bridge, no pairing record, no channel admission — proximity to the device is the whole of the authorisation, which is why the device's own posture carries this path.

edges.label: messaging apps
edges.note: The owner's chat client talks to the messaging platform, exactly like anybody else's. It does not reach the laptop directly and has no privileged route to it — which is why the owner's instruction and a stranger's arrive by the same path and are told apart, if at all, by whatever the platform asserts about the sender.

edges.label: outbound only
edges.note: The endpoint dials the relay; the relay holds the platform credentials. No inbound port is opened on the device, which is what the exposure scans keep finding elsewhere.

edges.label: send / receive
edges.note: The relay speaks to the messaging tenant on credentials that never touch the endpoint.

edges.label: message / reply
edges.note: Normalised messages in; rendered replies out, to wherever the agent addresses them.

edges.label: read & write / context
edges.note: The file tools are how the loop writes what it learns and reads it back as instruction on every later turn; context assembly loads the bootstrap files at start through the same filesystem.

edges.label: workspace mount
edges.note: The shared folders, mounted read-only with a private clone so an agent edit returns as a reviewable diff rather than a host write.

edges.label: inference, MCP & skills
edges.note: The one general-purpose crossing: every model call, every remote tool call and every skill fetch leaves the endpoint here, on a credential the gateway injects.

edges.label: inference / completion
edges.note: Inference on a brokered credential, against an allowlisted model, logged at the crossing.

edges.label: internal tool calls
edges.note: The path the organisation actually wants the agent to use: our own MCP servers and APIs, admitted by the catalogue and reached on grants the crossing issues.

edges.label: scoped reads & writes
edges.note: Our systems of record, reached under the owner's scope rather than a standing service account — and logged on our side of the boundary.

edges.label: web search & fetch
edges.note: The web tools search and fetch from inside the sandbox, out through the host-side proxy's allowlist — no gateway and no broker on the hop. What comes back re-enters the loop as context.

edges.label: pinned installs
edges.note: Skills, images and packages pulled straight from the mirror, pinned by digest — never from a community hub. The sandbox's egress policy is what makes the mirror the only place it can fetch from; the AI gateway brokers model and tool calls and is not on this path.

edges.label: mirrored & admitted
edges.note: The mirror's own supply chain: public packages proxied in, scanned, pinned and admitted before anything inside can pull them. Build pipelines publish the organisation's own artifacts beside them.

risks.note: Skills are prose plus executable code; the registry moves the review earlier, it does not remove it.

The target draws MCP servers inside the boundary; common implementations run them on the host with host privileges, and browser control drives the host browser outright. Until an implementation closes that gap, third-party code in this surface has the user's full authority, and the containment the drawing shows is the requirement, not the shipped state.

The listening surface itself: the daemon's control WebSocket bound to a routable interface instead of loopback is the exposure the scans keep finding, and the loopback dashboard is a documented token-exfiltration surface even when the bind is right — the owner's own browser defeats "localhost is not reachable" from inside.
The catalogue decides what the agent can be made to do; whoever edits it programs the agent.
Installed by one person in an afternoon, in no inventory until something looks for it.
The agent acts on the owner's accounts with whatever the token exchange granted — delegation that does not narrow to the task is the owner's whole reach on a loop nobody is watching.

Anyone the platform admits can address the bot, and the message body is model input from a set the organisation does not bound. The bridge's pairing records decide who reaches the loop; screening at the relay limits what their messages can say.
Memory is prose the next turn treats as instruction; an injection written here survives restarts and re-executes on the heartbeat.
Fetched pages and search results re-enter the loop indistinguishable from the owner's own words.
Org documents and records are unrelated instruction entering context — many hands wrote them, none of them authenticated as the owner.
The heartbeat restarts the loop unattended, and nothing bounds what a bad turn spends.
Everything the loop has assembled — memory, workspace content, tool results — crosses here. The gateway's inspection is the only place it can be seen.
The reply is addressed by the loop, not the owner: whatever the turn read — memory, workspace content, tool results — leaves here to whichever chat the message named, and never touches the gateway.
The completion is unauthenticated content, and it chooses the next tool call.
Unattended triggering and owner-scoped authority compound on writes to systems of record.

mitigations.note: Classify inbound content at the first tier we operate — every message is untrusted, the owner's included; the platform before this hop is somebody else's cloud.
Outbound classification on the reply leg — the only inspection the messaging path gets, because the gateway never sees it.

One pairing policy for every channel — directory-bound, re-checked, and administered centrally rather than reimplemented per platform; each adapter enforces it on every inbound message. Identity is the whole of the admission on this surface.

Proposed actions evaluated per call at the crossing before they leave — this action, this scope, now — rather than a session-time grant the loop argues with itself about. Unattended turns are tagged at ingress and bound to a read-only or draft class on every brokered leg.

The daemon's control socket accepts only messages from an authenticated client — a per-client token checked on every WebSocket message, replays refused, origin checked at the handshake — so a page in the owner's browser can neither drive the loop nor read the token. Loopback binding and the outbound-only relay are configuration around it, not the authentication.

Scope writes to the agent's own memory files, with the bootstrap rules read-only to it; record which message or tool result each write came from; snapshot memory so a poisoned entry can be rolled back; and treat what is read back as untrusted input.

The boundary itself, with its own kernel, filesystem and network — the operator owns the spec and the agent cannot edit it. Note what this buys beyond containment: with the model credential injected at the host-side proxy, the key never enters the boundary, so an agent that can exfiltrate cannot take it — though memory, workspace content and tool results can still leave through the allowed routes.
Per-tool grants on the native tools instead of the daemon's full authority — enforced where the tools run, inside the harness.

On-behalf-of exchange at the crossing: each remote call carries a token whose audience is that one tool server and whose scope is the task — never the owner's standing grants, never a token passed through — and the server refuses a token minted for anyone else. That bounds the delegation; whether the instruction came from the owner is still the pairing and approval pins' question.
Credentials brokered per call at the crossing and injected into request headers by the host-side proxy, so nothing is at rest inside the boundary and the loop never holds a key it could leak.
Completions are classified at the gateway before they reach the loop — the inspection a hosted product would have applied, run by the organisation because the completion becomes the next tool call.
Provenance, signing and version pinning on the supply path — an update is a decision, and drift between what was reviewed and what installs is an alert.
Approval on consequential writes to systems of record, mirroring the coding-agent siblings — rare enough that each prompt is read.
Spend and iteration ceilings on the crossing, sized for a loop that wakes itself.

One correlated trace per brokered call — prompt, tool calls, effects — captured at the crossing and written where the agent cannot amend it. Chat replies and local tool work never cross here, so the relay's log and the endpoint telemetry are joined to it.

Revoking the agent's identity cuts off every model and tool call at the crossing within seconds, without a deploy. The rest of the stop is enforced from outside the sandbox — the daemon and its children ended, the heartbeat and queued turns cancelled, the relay pairing expired — because the relay path, the mirror and local tools never cross the gateway.
Find the installs nobody registered, derived from the device rather than self-reported.
A long-lived daemon with shell access is exactly the workload endpoint telemetry exists for — incident 06's payload was a commodity stealer, and the device tooling is what would have seen it.
Every daemon that reaches the crossing is inventoried there — the one archetype whose incident says owners were found by scanning, not by inventory.

The microVM's network policy: the only routes out of the boundary are the AI gateway, the package mirror, the relay the bridges dial, and web search and fetch on the proxy's allowlist. Shell commands, fetches and browser traffic are bounded here — not at the gateway, which brokers model, MCP and API calls and sees nothing else.

Admission scanning at the mirror: malware and typosquat checks on everything proxied in from a public source, before anything inside can pull it. The registered embodiment of artifact scanning, on the one edge where it applies.

walkthrough.title: The owner asks the agent to do something
walkthrough.moves: An instruction from the owner, the inference it drives, and the action that lands on their accounts.

steps.label: owner at the machine
steps.note: The owner is at the machine and talks to the loop directly — authorised by nothing but holding the device, which is the assumption the whole drawing rests on.

steps.label: memory & instructions read
steps.note: The loop assembles context through its file tools: the system instruction, long-term memory files, and the transcript of everything said before.

steps.label: context loads
steps.note: All of it loads as context — including whatever an earlier turn persisted.

steps.label: model call
steps.note: The one exit the harness knows; direct provider domains are refused at this tier.

steps.label: inference
steps.note: Inference on a brokered credential, against an allowlisted provider.

steps.label: completion
steps.note: The completion comes back across the crossing.

steps.label: plan into loop
steps.note: And into the loop as a plan, not a decision — what happens next is the loop's to act on and ours to bound.

steps.label: work on mounted workspace
steps.note: Local work runs in the native tools inside the sandbox, on the workspace mounted read-only.

steps.label: diff on private clone
steps.note: Edits land in the sandbox's private clone of the read-only mount and come back as a reviewable diff, not a host write; the result lands in the loop.

steps.label: action on brokered crossing
steps.note: The action leaves on the same brokered crossing, which is where scope, spend and the record are decided rather than at the tool.

steps.label: admitted internal tool
steps.note: The flow the deployment exists for: our own servers and APIs, admitted by the catalogue on grants the crossing issues.

steps.label: read/write on record
steps.note: Reads and writes on our systems of record, under the owner's scope and behind the approval gate — logged on our side of the boundary.

steps.label: record
steps.note: The record comes back.

steps.label: result, logged
steps.note: Through the crossing again, where it is logged against the call that caused it.

steps.label: result into loop
steps.note: The result returns to the loop, which decides the next call — the gateway does not.

steps.label: web search & fetch
steps.note: The loop's next step searches the web and fetches a page, through the sandbox's egress proxy — the gateway is not on this hop.

steps.label: page into context
steps.note: What the page says — authored by somebody else — lands in the loop as context.

steps.label: reply
steps.note: The reply, to the owner at the machine — and into memory, where the next turn will read it.

scenarios.title: The owner steers the agent from their phone

steps.label: message from chat client
steps.note: The owner types into a chat client, away from the machine. Everything after this rides platform identity — there is no privileged owner channel.

steps.label: to messaging platform
steps.note: The chat client reaches the messaging platform, exactly as anybody else's would.

steps.label: relay collects
steps.note: Our relay collects from the platform; it is outbound-only and opens no inbound port.

steps.label: to channel adapter
steps.note: Down to the per-platform adapter, where the pairing record is the whole admission decision.

steps.label: into the loop
steps.note: Into the loop — indistinguishable at this point from any other message the platform admits, because the owner's instruction arrived by the identical hops and nothing on this path asserts anything about the sender. Consequential approvals deserve a surface with better assurance than either.

scenarios.title: The heartbeat fires with nobody watching

steps.label: memory read on heartbeat
steps.note: The heartbeat has no arrow of its own because it fires inside the harness rather than calling it from outside — so what it actually carries into the loop is whatever memory holds, read through the same file tools, and that is the injection's second life.

steps.label: unattended turn
steps.note: The unattended turn crosses like any other, but it belongs to a read-only or draft action class enforced here at the crossing — not to the same authority an attended turn carries.

steps.label: read-only action class
steps.note: A one-time injection has become a recurring one, bounded now by the action class.

scenarios.title: A page in the owner's browser reaches the dashboard

steps.label: loopback call from a page
steps.note: A malicious page in the owner's own browser makes the same loopback calls the dashboard makes — localhost is not a boundary against software already on the right side of it. An admitted call enters the loop, or walks off with the dashboard token: the documented exfiltration surface, defeated only by authenticated transport and origin checks on the bind.

steps.label: pivot leaves via crossing
steps.note: Whatever the pivot achieved leaves through the crossing — which is where the record, and the revocation, live.

scenarios.title: A skill is installed

steps.label: install from mirror
steps.note: The install runs as a shell command in the native tools inside the sandbox — served from the mirror, scanned, signed, pinned, and from nowhere else; the egress policy allows no other source.

steps.label: signed skill
steps.note: The signed skill comes back into the sandbox and its prerequisites run as shell — inside the boundary, where a stealer finds no keychain and no key. Signing and pinning admit exactly this step; containment bounds what it can do.

deviations.subject: The messaging tenant is contracted; consumer channels are a variant
deviations.reason: The drawn posture is an enterprise tenant under an agreement, which is why the platform sits in the vendor band. A consumer channel with no agreement — the common state for personal installs — moves the platform to the external band and removes the tenant controls with it; that posture is recorded here rather than drawn as a second topology.

deviations.subject: The local session is drawn as its own path
deviations.reason: A terminal on the machine and a phone across town are not the same admission problem: the phone's message is checked by a bridge against a pairing record, while the local session is authorised by nothing but being on the device. Drawing one edge for both hid that difference, so the direct path is drawn and the device posture is what governs it.

deviations.subject: Pairing admission and inbound injection defense are absorbed by the bridges and the relay
deviations.reason: Two inline pins sit on components that are not their registered embodiment. Identity governance on the channel bridges is the directory-bound pairing check inside each adapter; injection defense on the relay is a content classifier on the collected messages. Nothing else on the messaging path can hold either, and both are named so the assessment can ask for them by product.

deviations.subject: The remote dashboard is reached over a tunnel that is not drawn
deviations.reason: The daemon's dashboard is served on the same loopback port as its control socket. Away from the machine it is reached over an identity-bound tunnel service — the coding agents' Remote relay — never over the messaging relay, which carries chat and nothing else. The tunnel is not drawn here because the messaging path is this drawing's remote surface; the local API server item and its pins carry the exposure either way.

archetypes.title: Enterprise AI chat with connectors
summary: A workforce assistant under an enterprise tenant, with user-authorized or administrator-managed connections to business data. Tenant policy, source permissions and upload controls determine which information the assistant can access and disclose.
description:
Connector grants can belong to an individual or be configured centrally. Inventory both, preserve the requesting user's source permissions, and review the aggregate reach of the tenant. Administrative installation does not authorize every user to retrieve every document.
Pasted text and uploaded files provide another data path. Apply the available tenant, browser and network controls to those transfers; connector policy alone cannot govern them. Audit coverage and retention differ by product and plan.
Enterprise and personal accounts can expose different data terms and controls. Restrict organizational use to the approved tenant and verify the selected workspace's retention, training, connector and export settings.
distinguishedBy:
Against the UI/low-code managed agent runtime: the primary service is a workforce assistant. Custom agent creation can be an additional feature; use the builder reference when authoring, publication and a population of independently configured agents become the main concern.
Against the API/SDK managed agent runtime: the vendor supplies the application and agent loop. The customer administers the tenant and connected systems rather than integrating the loop into a customer-built application.

exemplars.name: ChatGPT Enterprise
exemplars.note: Workforce chat with enterprise workspace administration and connected apps. This example covers the chat experience; Dots and Work Cloud have separate execution profiles.

exemplars.name: Claude Enterprise
exemplars.note: Enterprise assistant with organization administration and connected business context. Verify connector permissions and retention for the selected plan; Cowork cloud is a separate mode.

exemplars.name: Microsoft 365 Copilot
exemplars.note: Workforce assistant grounded in Microsoft 365 and connected business data. Retrieval must preserve user permissions; central connector installation is not universal document access.

exemplars.name: Gemini Enterprise app
exemplars.note: Employee chat and search across connected business data. This example covers the assistant experience; Workflow Builder and custom agent hosting have different authoring and execution contracts.

zones.note: The employee, and the prompt and attachment they are about to send somewhere else.
zones.title: User surfaces

zones.note: The managed device. There is one thing on it and it is a browser — the vendor's client, running where we can at least see it.
zones.title: Managed endpoint

zones.note: The vendor's assistant backend under an enterprise agreement, and the SaaS we hold under agreement that its connectors reach. The employee reaches the vendor first, and the vendor reaches back into us second. The service is one block, deliberately — how they build their harness is assured, not drawn.
zones.title: Vendor platform

zones.note: What we still run, and the reason this is not simply a picture of a SaaS product: our own gateway and tool services, which the vendor's product can be pointed at so an employee's chat can reach our internal MCP servers.
zones.title: Enterprise cloud

zones.note: What other providers operate outside any agreement of ours: the same vendor's unmanaged offering, one login away and carrying none of the enterprise terms, and the open web the assistant searches.
zones.title: External

zones.note: On a bought product this band and the tenant configuration are the entire control set. Everything else is assurance.
zones.title: Security & governance control plane

blocks.title: Employee
blocks.note: The person, and the party who decides how much context to paste in. Every control on this page is downstream of a judgement they already made.

blocks.title: Browser
blocks.note: The vendor's client on a device we manage — a browser tab, or their desktop app. It is not a surface we built and it does nothing we control; it is drawn because it is the last place the material is still on our equipment.

items.label: Browser / client
items.note: Where the prompt is typed.

items.label: File upload
items.note: The parallel path and often the larger one: a document pasted or attached crosses the boundary with no connector and no grant. Endpoint or browser DLP is the control at submission; the vendor's audit export may record it afterwards.

blocks.title: Vendor chat service
blocks.note: Their backend and the published surfaces of its control plane. One block on purpose: what they run inside it is assured through assessment, never drawn — the rule that stops this page becoming a guess about somebody else's architecture.

items.label: Tenant configuration
items.note: Retention, training use, connector policy — including the admin-granted corpus-wide connectors — and the admin toggles that are the zone-2 surface.

items.label: Agent modes
items.note: The vendor's agentic features — scheduled tasks, code execution, autonomous research — each a tenant toggle that changes the risk profile of every session.

items.label: Tenant corpus
items.note: The admin-granted corpus — the mailbox, drive and site indexes the assistant grounds on inside the vendor's own tenant. No connector, no tunnel and no gateway are on this path; it is where the zero-click exfiltration incidents actually ran, and the primary control on it is what the tenant admin granted.

items.label: Session audit export
items.note: Their record of what was asked, which is not ours until it is exported.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: The SaaS we hold under agreement — our own Microsoft 365, Google Workspace or CRM tenant — reached through the vendor's connectors on a grant an employee or an administrator issued. A service outside any agreement is not connected: the target tenant's admin consent and the vendor's connector policy decide what counts as approved.

blocks.title: Tunnel connector
blocks.note: Vendor-supplied software we run inside our own network so their cloud can reach an MCP server that is not publicly exposed. The topology is inverted and outbound-only: this client long-polls the vendor for work and posts results back, so no inbound firewall rule is opened and the MCP server stays on a private address. Two things it does not do, both from the vendor's own architecture notes. It does not make the data path local — requests, responses and auth artifacts still traverse their cloud — and it does not authenticate to our MCP server, which we still do ourselves. The runtime credential on this host is the load-bearing secret. Both first-party vendors now ship one for their chat product — one generally, the other as an Enterprise research preview — and the public-endpoint form is a recorded deviation.

items.label: Outbound connector
items.note: Long-polls the vendor for work; opens nothing inbound.

blocks.title: AI gateway
blocks.note: Where a vendor-hosted chat is admitted into our systems, and the only component on that path we operate. Everything about what the product may reach — which servers, on whose grant, recorded by whom — is decided here rather than in their console.

items.label: MCP & API gateway
items.note: Which of our servers the vendor's assistant may reach, and on whose grants.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: Our own MCP servers and connectors, offered to a product we did not build. This is the thing the tunnel exists for.

blocks.title: Enterprise data
blocks.note: The systems of record behind those servers, reached on grants we scope and record.

blocks.title: Consumer product
blocks.note: The same client, a personal login, and none of the enterprise terms — different retention, different training use, a tenant we cannot enumerate or export. The sharpest control on this page is simply telling the two apart.

items.label: Personal accounts
items.note: Indistinguishable from sanctioned use at the keyboard, and entirely different in contract.

blocks.title: Open web
blocks.note: Search results and fetched pages, reached only through the vendor's web search. Every page is authored by someone else, and its text enters the conversation as model input.

items.label: Web search
items.note: The search tool's results — ranked by somebody else, and read as context.

items.label: Arbitrary pages
items.note: Visible and hidden text alike, served by whoever owns the page.

blocks.title: Identity services
blocks.note: Which tenant an employee lands in, enforced by domain capture and forced account consolidation. The single most consequential control here — and one that governs only accounts on domains we own. A personal address on a corporate device is a proxy problem, not a tenant one.

blocks.title: Secrets & key management
blocks.note: The tunnel host's runtime credential — the load-bearing secret on the one path we run — issued, rotated and revoked from here.

blocks.title: Policy & authorization
blocks.note: What may leave, inspected on the one path we can see, plus the tenant policy that decides retention and training use — authored here, enforced at the browser and the vendor's configuration surface.

blocks.title: Supply-chain assurance
blocks.note: The vendor assessment, and the connector inventory. Their internals are assured here rather than drawn anywhere, which is the whole of what a bought product allows.

blocks.title: Observability & response
blocks.note: Their export fused with our own record, and the discovery of the personal accounts nobody enrolled. The second is usually the larger number.

edges.label: prompt & attachment
edges.note: The question, the pasted excerpt and the uploaded file — the moment the material leaves the person.

edges.label: to the corporate tenant
edges.note: Straight out to the vendor, crossing our cloud band without touching it. Allowlisted because an assessment cleared it, and governed by the agreement once it arrives.

edges.label: blocked or logged
edges.note: The same client with a personal login. Retention, training use and tenancy all differ, and distinguishing the two at this point is the control the archetype turns on.

edges.label: outbound-only tunnel
edges.note: Their cloud reaching our internal MCP servers through software they publish and we run. Note the direction: our side dials out and polls, so nothing is opened inbound and the server stays private.

edges.label: tool call / result
edges.note: The tunnel hands to our gateway rather than reaching past it into the tool surface directly.

edges.label: brokered tool calls
edges.note: Which of our servers a vendor product may call, on grants we issue and record.

edges.label: scoped reads & writes
edges.note: The systems of record behind our own MCP servers.

edges.label: approved SaaS connectors
edges.note: The vendor's backend reaching the SaaS we hold under agreement, on grants an employee or an administrator issued. This path never touches our network, so no component of ours can sit on it — the limitation is recorded rather than papered over.

edges.label: web search
edges.note: The vendor's web search, opened from their side. What returns rides back on it — content nobody vouches for, entering the conversation.

risks.note: Same software, personal login, no enterprise terms. Domain capture governs accounts on our domains and nothing else, so a personal address on a managed device is invisible to every tenant-side control.
A vendor-hosted assistant exercising our authority against our own MCP servers. The grant is what bounds it, and our gateway is what issues the grant.

A document planted in any connected source returns into the conversation as model input — the zero-click exfiltration class published against exactly this archetype, arriving on a path nothing of ours can inspect.
Search results and fetched pages return into the conversation — content somebody else authored, read with the same standing as the employee's question.
Our own records ground the vendor's answers, and many hands wrote them — the internal return is untrusted input to a loop we cannot see.
A document anyone could write into the admin-granted corpus is retrieved as grounding and read as instruction — the transient half of the injection story, on a path nothing of ours touches.
More context leaves than the task needed — whole documents pasted for one answer — and it is retained and processed under whatever terms the tenant was configured with.
A chat product with connector access reads far more than any single question warranted.
Writes into systems of record from a conversation nobody else read.

The assistant indexes connected mailboxes and drives; a planted document persists in their retrieval and fires on later queries — the persistence half of the injection story, distinct from the transient return.

mitigations.note: The corporate tenant reachable and personal tenants blocked. A hostname allowlist cannot tell the two apart at the same host: that needs the vendor's tenant-restriction header, injected by a proxy that inspects TLS for the client in use, or a managed browser that enforces the tenant.
Endpoint or managed-browser DLP inspects the paste or upload at submission and blocks or masks a hit before it is sent, because after this hop it is somebody else's.

Their controls, retention terms and tenancy assured through assessment rather than drawn — the only representation a vendor-internal control gets — and the tenant configuration re-assessed on a clock: agent modes, connector policy, retention and training use drift as the vendor ships.

Write-capable connectors gated on approval, bound to the exact action — surfaced through the protocol's elicitation, relayed through the vendor's client (support per client is unverified), and enforced by our gateway refusing the write without it. A chat that can read is a disclosure question; a chat that can write is an action question.
Know what is behind the connectors before attaching them: which systems, which data and where it lives, so attaching a connector is a decision rather than a discovery.
The tunnel carries traffic but does not authenticate to our server — we still do that ourselves — and the runtime credential sitting on the tunnel host is the load-bearing secret on this path.
Which of our MCP servers the product may reach, and on whose grant, decided at our tier.
The connector inventory — which sources users attached on their own authority, and which corpora administrators granted. We cannot sit on those paths, so knowing what is on them is the control.
The vendor's audit or compliance export — prompts, agent and tool calls, and the resources each one accessed — fused with our gateway's record; a trail only in their console is one we cannot query.
Finding the personal accounts and unsanctioned connectors nobody enrolled.
The scope of the admin-granted corpus — which sites, drives and mailboxes the assistant may index, per user's own permissions — is the primary control on a vendor assistant grounding on our tenant.

Admin consent on the target tenant — our own workspace, code-hosting or CRM tenant decides whether the chat vendor's app may be granted at all. The only customer enforcement point on a SaaS-to-SaaS grant.

Disable the assistant or the offending agent mode in the tenant and revoke every connector grant — the SaaS form of the stop. Personal-account use is stopped by blocking the consumer product, not here.
Records read through our gateway are classified before they go back to the vendor's cloud as grounding — the one return leg we can inspect.

walkthrough.title: An employee asks the assistant a work question
walkthrough.moves: A question from a managed browser to a vendor's assistant, answered from our own systems.

steps.label: question (enterprise tenant)
steps.note: Typed into the managed browser, signed in with the enterprise tenant — the one control that separates this from the walk below it.

steps.label: to vendor service
steps.note: Out to the vendor's service. Nothing of ours sits on this hop; what governs it is the agreement and the tenant configuration, not a tier we run.

steps.label: approved SaaS connectors
steps.note: Their connectors reach the SaaS we hold under agreement, on grants an employee or an administrator issued — a path that never touches our network, so the levers are the target tenant's admin consent, the connector policy in their tenant configuration and the inventory we keep ourselves.

steps.label: connector content
steps.note: What those services return enters the assistant's context.

steps.label: web search
steps.note: Where the question needs it, the vendor searches the web from their side.

steps.label: search results
steps.note: Results and fetched pages enter the context too, written by whoever owns the page.

steps.label: tunnel request
steps.note: To answer, their cloud reaches back through software they publish and we run — outbound-only, so nothing is opened inbound. The data path is not local, and the tunnel does not authenticate for us.

steps.label: across our edge
steps.note: Across our edge, which is the first and only control of ours on the whole journey.

steps.label: admitted, scoped grant
steps.note: Admitted against the catalogue and narrowed to a grant scoped to this employee.

steps.label: grounding records
steps.note: The records that ground the answer, read on our terms and recorded on our side.

steps.label: records
steps.note: The records come back.

steps.label: recorded read
steps.note: Through our gateway, which is where the read is recorded.

steps.label: into connector
steps.note: And into the connector, bound for their cloud.

steps.label: grounded result
steps.note: The grounded result travels back the way the request came, through the tunnel we run.

steps.label: assembled answer
steps.note: Their service assembles the answer and returns it to the client.

steps.label: answer
steps.note: And to the person who asked — the whole round trip crossing ours exactly once.

scenarios.title: An employee pastes a contract into the assistant

steps.label: contract pasted
steps.note: The material leaves the person — and this hop is where endpoint or browser DLP can still block or mask it. Whatever that inspection misses is sent.

steps.label: into the corporate tenant
steps.note: Out to the corporate tenant. Whether the network edge can read it depends on the client and on TLS inspection; afterwards, the vendor's audit export is the record, with coverage and retention set by plan.

scenarios.title: The same person, signed in personally

steps.label: same client, personal login
steps.note: Identical software, identical interface, one different login. Telling the two walks apart is most of what governing a bought product means.

steps.label: no enterprise terms
steps.note: A personal login, and none of the enterprise terms follow. If the address is not on a domain we verified, no tenant-side control sees this at all.

scenarios.title: The assistant queries an internal system

steps.label: request through tunnel
steps.note: Their cloud asks for work through the connector we run inside our network.

steps.label: to our gateway
steps.note: Handed to our gateway rather than reaching past it.

steps.label: admitted, scoped
steps.note: Admitted to a named server on a scoped grant, and recorded.

steps.label: read on our side
steps.note: The read happens on our side of the boundary, which is the only reason it is bounded at all.

deviations.subject: The tunnel absorbs secrets consumption
deviations.reason: Credential hardening (D3-CH) is embodied by the AI gateway, but the load-bearing secret on this path is the runtime credential on the tunnel host — the pin sits where the credential lives, the management story in the governance call-out. Consumption here, issuance and rotation there.

deviations.subject: The AI gateway carries tool and data traffic only
deviations.reason: The vendor calls its own model inside its own cloud — no Model provider block exists on this drawing — and nothing fetches skills through our crossing. The gateway is drawn with its one real traffic class rather than the registered aiGatewayTraffic pack, following the low-code builder's precedent: the honest signal that a gateway is not on the model path is its own contents.

deviations.subject: Inline inspection and egress control are pinned on the browser with no secure-edge component drawn
deviations.reason: On a bought product there is no tier of ours between the client and the vendor, and drawing one would assert a control nobody operates. What actually exists is inspection at the network or in the managed browser, so outbound traffic filtering sits on the browser block and the absorption is recorded here. A previous version of this drawing invented an "Identity & secure edge" component to satisfy the same pin; that component was a control wearing a component's name and has been removed.

deviations.subject: The tunnel is drawn; the public-endpoint form is recorded
deviations.reason: OpenAI's Secure MCP Tunnel serves ChatGPT; Anthropic's MCP tunnels serve claude.ai custom connectors as an Enterprise research preview, by request and without continuity commitments. Where a tunnel is unavailable or not adopted, the same crossing exists in weaker form — a custom connector calling an internet-facing endpoint of ours, admitted by allowlisting the vendor's published IP ranges — and it lands on the same AI gateway. The tunnel is the target state and is drawn; the public-endpoint form is this deviation, with its compensating controls (audience-bound tokens, per-user OAuth, rate limiting on a public listener) carried by the gateway pins. Re-check per vendor on a clock; the asymmetry is a product decision, not an architecture.

deviations.subject: No customer component sits on the native connector path
deviations.reason: The dominant connector class is SaaS-to-SaaS — the vendor's broker calling the API of a provider we hold under agreement, on a grant a user or an administrator issued — and no customer component can sit on that path; the target tenant's admin consent and our connector inventory are the levers. A service outside any agreement is not connected. Custom connectors into our own systems take the drawn tunnel, AI gateway and Tool services chain.
