archetypes.title: Coding & desktop session managed agent runtime
summary: A vendor-operated agent performs bounded coding or desktop work in a hosted task environment. Vendor interfaces, repository events or schedules initiate the session. The coding profile shown here produces a reviewed change; desktop work requires authorization before application or file effects, with an explicit lifetime for retained sessions and artifacts.
description:
The provider operates the loop and task environment. Verify the selected product's isolation unit, credentials, retained state and cleanup behavior; ending compute does not necessarily delete conversation history, files or grants. Persistent personal and shared teammates belong to the persistent managed agent reference even when they delegate bounded coding sessions here.
For coding tasks, repository content, issue text and review comments enter as untrusted material. Authorize triggers separately from the content they carry. Limit branch and repository permissions, require human review before merge, and gate privileged workflows. A merge gate does not authorize earlier network requests or connector effects.
For general desktop tasks, the completion gate is the permitted application or file action, not a pull request. Apply the supported tool, destination and approval controls before that effect. Saved files, browser sessions and connector grants need their own retention and revocation rules. Local-computer access — the agent acting on the user's own machine — is an endpoint execution path, drawn on the third-party coding & desktop agents reference, not here.
In the provider-hosted mode represented here, inference stays with the provider. A customer gateway governs only traffic actually routed through it. Shell network policy, repository access, backend connectors and browser access may have separate enforcement paths; verify each enabled path rather than assuming one allowlist covers the service.
Record the initiator, workload identity and downstream credential separately. Products may use user grants, a repository App, or a shared automation account. These choices determine who can start a task, what it can change, and which grants must be revoked when it stops.
The critical boundary is the way back in. To be useful the agent needs our code bases and data, and it reaches them through exactly two controlled crossings: a GitHub App installed on named repositories of our GitHub Enterprise Cloud, admitted only from the vendor's published IPs, for code; and an outbound-only tunnel we run to our AI gateway, for tool calls to our tool servers and the data behind them. Source control is never behind the gateway, and nothing else of the vendor's crosses into our systems.
distinguishedBy:
Against endpoint coding and desktop agents: the loop and selected task environment are hosted. Optional local access or customer-operated workers require their own execution controls; endpoint policy does not automatically follow the hosted session.
Against the API/SDK managed agent runtime: vendor product surfaces normally initiate and present the task. In the API reference, a customer-built application integrates the loop, binds callers to sessions, and handles custom tools and approval events.
Against persistent managed agents: this is a bounded task service. Durable artifacts alone do not make it a continuing teammate with ongoing cross-task authority. That drawing lists the differences: retained state, channel and scheduled triggers, standing grants, approval at dispatch, and a stop that must also clear what the agent kept.

exemplars.name: OpenAI Codex cloud
exemplars.note: Hosted coding tasks in configured environments, producing changes for review. Cloud environment and network settings govern this mode; local Codex settings are a separate surface.

exemplars.name: Cursor Cloud Agents
exemplars.note: Hosted coding agents started from Cursor and supported integrations. Review repository grants, environment network policy and whether the initiator is a person or shared automation.

exemplars.name: GitHub Copilot cloud agent
exemplars.note: Coding work through GitHub's hosted agent workflow and pull requests. Repository permissions, workflow approval and human review define the promotion boundary.

exemplars.name: Claude Code in the cloud
exemplars.note: Claude Code sessions on managed task environments, with repository and network configuration. Self-hosted execution changes the worker boundary while provider orchestration remains separate.

exemplars.name: Claude Cowork in the cloud
exemplars.note: General work in temporary hosted session environments with retained sessions and files. App actions need their own authorization; availability and cloud defaults vary by plan and rollout.

exemplars.name: ChatGPT Work Cloud
exemplars.note: General tasks in a selected cloud environment. Check local-access and execution-location settings; application effects require authorization independently of any coding review workflow.

zones.note: The developer who starts and reviews the session in the browser, and the same person — or, on a chat surface, not necessarily the same person — steering from a phone or a channel while the session runs.
zones.title: User surfaces

zones.note: The browser on a device we manage — the vendor's web app, where a session is started, steered and reviewed. The vendor's desktop and mobile apps show the same synced sessions and add nothing on this path. A hand-off from a local CLI or desktop session, and anything the local application executes itself, is the third-party coding & desktop agents drawing.
zones.title: Managed endpoint

zones.note: Our GitHub Enterprise Cloud tenant, reached by the vendor's GitHub App; the tunnel the vendor's connector calls arrive through; our gateway, and the tool servers and systems behind it.
zones.title: Enterprise cloud

zones.note: Two blocks for the agent vendor, because a session is admitted by one and executed by the other: the control plane — settings, environments, the relay and the scheduler — and the runtime that holds the loop, the model and the sandbox. Beneath the runtime, the vendor's connectors to the SaaS we approved. What they operate inside each is assured, not drawn.
zones.title: Vendor platform

zones.note: What the session reaches out to under its egress policy: package registries in the setup phase, public repositories and the open web in the agent phase. Every edge here is opened from the vendor's side; nothing in this band connects back in.
zones.title: External

zones.note: On a runtime we do not operate, this band is where the vendor's exports are fused with our record — and where "stop this agent" has to be defined with its delay, because revoking an App or a seat does not stop a running session.
zones.title: Security & governance control plane

blocks.title: Developer
blocks.note: Present at the start and at the end — the hand-off and, on the coding profile, the merge — and absent for the run in between. General desktop work has no merge: its approval comes before each consequential application or file effect.

blocks.title: Remote device
blocks.note: The doors that start and steer a session away from the managed device: the vendor's mobile apps, and an @-mention in a chat channel. Admission is the vendor's account binding for the first and whoever the channel admits for the second — the widest admission decision on the drawing.

items.label: Vendor apps
items.note: The vendor's phone app on the owner's device, signed into the vendor account the session is bound to.

items.label: Chat channels
items.note: A session raised from Slack, Teams or Linear runs on the vendor's cloud under a shared channel identity on most products — not as the person who typed.

blocks.title: Browser
blocks.note: The vendor's web app on a device we manage — claude.ai/code, chatgpt.com/codex, cursor.com/agents, GitHub's agents panel — where a task is written, a session is watched and its result is reviewed. The desktop app shows the same synced session and is no different here; the loop runs in the managed runtime whichever client the person uses.

items.label: Browser / client
items.note: Where the task is typed and the session is steered.

blocks.title: Source control
blocks.note: The one tier that is ingress, egress, definition and gate at once on the coding profile. Issue text, comments and review threads enter the session as instruction; a branch and a draft pull request come back out; the instruction files, setup scripts and environment configuration committed beside the code are the session's definition; review, merge and "approve and run workflows" are the gate. It is our GitHub Enterprise Cloud tenant, so it sits in our band, and the vendor reaches it only through a GitHub App installed on named repositories, admitted by the enterprise IP allow list from the vendor's published IPs — under branch protection, CODEOWNERS on the agent's own configuration and a rule for who may trigger a run.

items.label: Repositories & instruction files
items.note: The code, and CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, setup scripts, hooks and MCP configuration — content that executes as instruction and is versioned like code because it is code.

items.label: Issues & PR threads
items.note: Writable by anyone the repository admits, read by the session as instruction. Hidden characters and HTML comments carry payloads the human reviewer never sees.

items.label: Pull requests & CI
items.note: The draft the session opens, the review a person gives, the workflows the pull request would fire — and the single branch the session may write.

blocks.title: Managed runtime
blocks.note: The vendor's own agent, hosted: the loop, context assembly and compaction, the model, session state and one sandbox per session, on compute the vendor operates. What we configure about it — the environment, the network policy, the credentials it may draw — is drawn as pins on this block and on the sandbox nested inside it; the execution behind them is assured, not inspected. Product-specific caveats — retention, session sharing, snapshot lifetimes, which plans get proxied credentials — belong on the exemplars and the tool records, not here.

items.label: Agent harness
items.note: Their harness running the repository's instructions — the loop, context assembly, compaction and retries, theirs to operate — with the built-in tools nested beneath.

items.label: Model inference
items.note: Their model, called inside their boundary. It does not cross our AI gateway in the hosted mode drawn here; verify per product, including the worker variants.

items.label: Memory store
items.note: Agent-written memory and session transcripts the vendor holds: persisted after the browser closes, shareable on some plans, and merged into later sessions on the products that ship auto-memory.

items.label: Credential vault
items.note: The git proxy that substitutes a scoped credential so the sandbox never holds the repository token, the environment secrets that exist only in the setup phase, and the runtime secrets redacted from transcripts — each a different product's answer to the same requirement, and the plan-gated gaps recorded per product.

items.label: MCP client
items.note: The harness's own MCP client. On most products its calls leave through the vendor's connector proxy, outside the sandbox's network policy — which is why the path to our servers is drawn from the runtime rather than from Native tools, and why the connector allowlist is a control-plane setting rather than a sandbox one.

blocks.title: Native tools
blocks.note: The sandbox: a microVM or container created for the session and reclaimed after it, holding the file tools, the shell, the skills the repository names and the hosted browser where the product offers one. Two phases where the product has them — setup with network for dependencies, then the agent phase under the environment's allowlist. Drawn because what it may reach is ours to author; where a product moves execution to a worker we run, this block is what moves.

items.label: File & edit tools
items.note: Read, write, edit, glob and grep across the cloned repository.

items.label: Shell commands
items.note: Command execution inside the session sandbox — and the place a hook, a task file or a virtual-environment interpreter written now is executed later by a tool nobody sandboxed.

items.label: Installed skills
items.note: Packaged instructions the repository or the environment names, downloaded at session start — content that executes as instruction.

items.label: Computer use
items.note: The hosted browser and remote desktop, where offered: the widest reach a session can be given, and the one whose content returns unclassified.

blocks.title: Vendor service
blocks.note: The published surfaces of the vendor's control plane: the settings that reach a hosted session (server-managed, never the device's), the shared environments an owner defines, the org-level switch for the hosted mode, the relay behind the phone and the channel, the scheduler behind routines and automations, and where connectors and the GitHub App are configured and approved. This is the tier a hosted session is admitted by and steered through; it runs nothing and opens no connection of its own — every data path leaves the runtime beside it, the tier the session executes in.

items.label: Managed settings
items.note: Server-managed settings and organisation-shared environments — network access level, environment variables, setup script — plus the toggles that enable hosted mode at all.

items.label: Session audit export
items.note: Session logs, agentic audit events and compliance exports — whose coverage of the hosted surface differs by product and plan, and is verified rather than assumed.

items.label: Remote & scheduled sessions
items.note: The relay that admits a phone or a channel to a running session, and the scheduler that starts one with nobody present at all.

blocks.title: Tunnel connector
blocks.note: Vendor-supplied software we run inside our own network so the hosted runtime's MCP calls can reach our gateway without an inbound rule: it dials out, holds the connection open and carries the vendor's MCP requests in. Transport only — it does not authenticate to the upstream, and the payloads still traverse the vendor's cloud — so tool calls go to the AI gateway, never straight to a tool server or the data. Git uses neither the tunnel nor the gateway: it reaches our GitHub Enterprise Cloud through the vendor's GitHub App. The tunnel token and the TLS key on this host are the load-bearing secrets. Both first-party vendors ship one for their connectors (OpenAI's Secure MCP Tunnel for ChatGPT and Codex; Anthropic's MCP tunnels, an Enterprise research preview, for claude.ai connectors); where a product has none, the reach-back is an internet-facing gateway endpoint, recorded as a deviation.

items.label: Outbound connector
items.note: Dials out to the vendor's edge; opens nothing inbound.

blocks.title: AI gateway
blocks.note: The customer-operated crossing where the hosted runtime's MCP calls are admitted to our MCP servers: the one component on the reach-back path where the grant is ours to scope and revoke and the call is recorded on our terms. Not on the inference path: the hosted loop's model calls stay with the vendor.

items.label: MCP & API gateway
items.note: Which of our servers a hosted session may reach, and on whose grants.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: Our own MCP servers and connectors — ticketing, documentation, systems of record — that a hosted session is adopted in order to reach beyond the repository.

blocks.title: Enterprise data
blocks.note: The systems of record behind those servers, reached on grants we scope per session.

blocks.title: Public package sources
blocks.note: What the setup phase installs from under the environment's allowlist. The reviewed setup script installs only pinned versions verified against lockfile hashes or signatures, and fails on a mismatch. A registry is also a write-capable host every allowlist permits.

items.label: Package registries
items.note: PyPI, npm and the rest — pinned versions, verified against lockfile hashes at install.

items.label: Skill & extension hubs
items.note: Skills and plugins the repository or the environment names, pinned to reviewed versions.

blocks.title: Open web
blocks.note: What the sandbox searches and fetches in the agent phase, where the environment allows it. Every page is someone else's text, and it enters a loop nobody is watching as instruction.

items.label: Web search
items.note: Results ranked by someone else, read as context.

items.label: Arbitrary pages
items.note: Visible and hidden text alike, served by whoever owns the page.

blocks.title: Source control
blocks.note: Public source control: open repositories a session clones read-only — an upstream dependency, an example, a project to patch. Untrusted like any page: the instruction files and issue text in someone else's repository are someone else's instructions.

items.label: Public repositories
items.note: Cloned read-only, never with the session's write credential.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: The vendor's connectors to the SaaS we approved — ticketing, chat, documents — called from the runtime under our agreement, on tokens the vendor holds, outside both the sandbox's egress policy and our gateway. A service outside any agreement is not connected.

blocks.title: Identity services
blocks.note: Who may start a session and as whom it runs: federated login and trusted devices at the vendor's account layer, and approved initiators at the repository host. The App installations, service identities and user-bound sessions a product acts through are inventoried in the registry, each with an owner and an expiry.

blocks.title: Secrets & key management
blocks.note: The repository credential the proxy substitutes, the environment secrets that exist only in the setup phase, and the tunnel token and TLS key on the host we run for the reach-back — with the plan-gated gaps recorded per product rather than assumed of the class.

blocks.title: Policy & authorization
blocks.note: One branch, no merge, a human reviewer who is not the initiator, workflows that wait for approval, a network allowlist an administrator locks, a connector allowlist the session cannot widen — and a session budget, because an unattended loop bills by the minute.

blocks.title: Supply-chain assurance
blocks.note: Routines, automations, environments and connector registrations inventoried like agents, each with an owner; the platform assessed on a clock because its defaults move.

blocks.title: Observability & response
blocks.note: The vendor's session logs and agentic audit events exported and fused with the repository host's record and our gateway's — one trail per session, from trigger to merge — and a stop whose delay is known: disabling the App or the seat prevents the next session, not the one that is running.

edges.label: web session
edges.note: The person at the managed device, in the vendor's web app — or its desktop app, which shows the same session.

edges.label: away from the machine
edges.note: The same person on a phone or in a browser — or, on a chat surface, whoever the channel admits.

edges.label: start, steer & review
edges.note: The browser talks to the vendor's control plane: the task, the chosen environment and repository, steering while the session runs, and the result. Allowlisted because an assessment cleared it; admission is the vendor's account binding behind our SSO.

edges.label: start & steer session
edges.note: The phone, the browser or the channel talks to the vendor's relay directly. Nothing we operate is on this path — a personal device on a cell network has no reason to traverse our egress — so admission is the vendor's account binding and whatever the managed settings allow, and on a channel it is whoever the channel admits.

edges.label: admission & settings
edges.note: The control plane admitting a session to the runtime: which environment it runs in, what the server-managed settings permit, which connectors it may call, and — from the scheduler — sessions that start with nobody present at all. Status and results come back the same way for the person steering.

edges.label: GitHub App · IP allowlist
edges.note: Both directions of our GitHub Enterprise Cloud tenant, on a GitHub App installed on named repositories and admitted by the enterprise IP allow list only from the vendor's published IPs; the vendor's git proxy holds the credential outside the sandbox. Inward: the code, instruction files and threads, and the events that start or steer work. Outward: the push to the session's own branch and the draft pull request — the only writes the installation allows. It never rides the tunnel or the AI gateway.

edges.label: review & merge
edges.note: The gate. A person reviews the draft, approves the workflows it would fire, and merges — or does not. Require that the initiator's approval does not count and that the agent cannot approve, mark ready or merge; verify that each product enforces both.

edges.label: approved connectors
edges.note: The runtime's connectors calling the SaaS we approved from the vendor's side, on grants the vault holds. Its allowlist is a control-plane setting the session cannot widen; what these connectors return reaches the loop without crossing anything we run.

edges.label: outbound-only tunnel
edges.note: The reach-back path, and the crossing this drawing exists to govern: compute we do not operate calling back into our systems for data connectors, down a connection our side opened, so nothing is exposed inbound. Git does not use it: it reaches our GitHub Enterprise Cloud through the vendor's GitHub App. The public-endpoint form — the runtime calling an internet-facing gateway URL, admitted at our edge by the vendor's IP ranges — is recorded as a deviation rather than drawn as a second path.

edges.label: tool call / result
edges.note: Tool calls the tunnel hands to our gateway's aggregate MCP endpoint, never straight to a tool server or the data; git never comes this way — it reaches our GitHub Enterprise Cloud through the vendor's GitHub App: admitted on audience-bound tokens and per-user grants our own authorization server issued, per-call policy evaluated at the gateway, the servers and tools scoped to a named list, and every call recorded against the grant. The vendor's identity and IP ranges admit the caller; they authorise nothing.

edges.label: brokered tool calls
edges.note: Which of our servers a hosted session may call, on short-lived grants we issue.

edges.label: scoped reads & writes
edges.note: The records and systems the session was adopted to reach beyond the repository.

edges.label: setup installs
edges.note: The setup phase installing the reviewed setup script's pinned, hash-verified dependencies under the environment's allowlist; a changed or unpinned package fails the install before the agent phase. That phase has network before the agent does and caches its result for the next user of the environment. The registry is also a write-capable host every allowlist permits, which is what makes it an exfiltration channel.

edges.label: web fetch under egress policy
edges.note: The sandbox's own reach to the web in the agent phase, where the environment allows it — closed by default on some products, open by default on others — and the content that comes back as instruction.

edges.label: clone public repos
edges.note: A read-only clone of a public repository — through the sandbox's egress or the vendor's git proxy, depending on the product — under the same allowlist. The session's scoped write credential belongs to the rented host alone.

risks.note: A malicious or compromised package or skill runs as root in the setup phase, with network, before the agent starts. Pinning and hash verification stop a changed artifact; they do not make a reviewed version benign.

A channel raises sessions for whoever it admits, a schedule runs them for an owner who may have left — on a grant nobody revoked — and none of it appears in any inventory we keep unless the vendor's export is queried.

The session exercises the user's grant, an App installation's, or a shared service identity's — whichever the product uses — and the repository host cannot tell an injected instruction from an intended one. What bounds it is the token's scope: one repository, one branch, no merge.

Their infrastructure exercising our authority, steered by whatever the session read. The grant is the only thing bounding it, and the grant is issued at our gateway — which is the entire argument for drawing one and for never letting the vendor's tunnel or allowlisted IP range reach past it.

Issue text, comments, review threads and instruction files enter the session as instruction, and most are writable by people with no commit access. The dominant ingress of the archetype, and the one every 2026 incident used.
A fetched page enters a loop nobody is watching. On the products where the agent phase has internet by default this is the unclassified ingress the environment policy exists to close.
Ticket text, chat messages and documents the vendor's connectors return enter the loop as model input, on a path nothing of ours inspects.

Automations that re-run on CI failure and review comments, and sessions that reply to their own threads, make a loop with no natural end — billed by the minute and bounded only by the budget the tenant sets.

The package registries every setup allowlist permits are write-capable: a package publish carries whatever the sandbox holds to a public index, the route stolen tokens took in the vendor's own 2026 evaluation incidents.

The repository, the transcript, tool output and environment variables all live on their side under their retention terms; sessions persist after the browser closes, snapshots outlive the run, and on some plans a session can be shared publicly with private-repository content inside it.

A push, a pull request, a reply on the thread — from a loop that reads its own thread. An agent's reply can fire comment-triggered automation, and an automation configured to approve low-risk pull requests removes the gate this drawing rests on.

mitigations.note: Hosted mode is an organisation decision: enabled per role or group behind federated login and trusted-device enrolment, the relay bound to the owner's account, and the switches that widen it — personal-token setup, self-hosted runners, remote control — off until someone owns them. Zone-2 configuration, because nothing we operate is on the remote path.

The repository host's trigger policy admits only approved initiators — people with write access, and registered automations or schedules with a named owner and a bounded identity — to start or steer a session; non-collaborators and unregistered Apps or bots are refused. The setting that decides whether a public issue is an attack surface.

The environment an administrator owns and locks: the connector and MCP allowlist the session cannot widen, the built-in tools enabled and the permission mode, with bypass modes removed. Unattended runs have no prompt to answer, so these settings are the whole of the in-session control.

A token that reaches one repository and one branch, cannot push the default branch, mark ready, approve or merge; protected scopes and repository blocklists on the products that have them; a session that can reach only repositories its trigger could already reach.

Which servers and tools a hosted session may reach, on whose grant — a per-user, audience-bound grant our authorization server issued, never the vendor's service identity: one aggregate endpoint fronting a named list per vendor, read-mostly unless a write has a named owner. A marketplace that admits every server to every caller is the failure this pin exists to name.
Session budgets, usage ceilings and automation caps in the tenant, because an unattended loop that re-triggers itself bills by the minute and nobody is watching the meter.

The repository credential and the secrets stay out of the sandbox: the vendor's git proxy substitutes a scoped credential for a placeholder, and setup-phase secrets are removed before the agent runs. Environment variables are treated as visible to the model and to everyone who shares the environment. Where a product does not proxy, the credential is in the sandbox and the finding says so.

What persists and who can read it: agent-written memory merged into later sessions, transcripts that can be shared, snapshots that outlive the run — each a setting whose default is wider than most adopters assume, set deliberately.

Their isolation, retention and tenancy assured by assessment rather than drawn — the only representation a vendor-internal control gets — and re-assessed on a clock, because the defaults move: egress on or off, self-approving automations, which plan gets proxied credentials, whether the audit export covers this surface.

One microVM or container per session around the built-in tools, created for the run and reclaimed after it, with no shared filesystem between sessions. The vendor provides it, so it is verified per product — whether follow-up runs reuse the same machine, what survives between them — and the choices the product exposes, such as which runner a session uses, are ours to set.

The environment's network policy, authored by us and enforced by the vendor around the sandbox: an allowlist, locked by an administrator, with the setup phase separated from the agent phase and write methods restricted on the hosts the list must permit. Paths outside the sandbox's network — the git proxy, the connector proxy, inference — are verified per product and bounded elsewhere.

The gate: a draft pull request a person reviews and merges, an initiator whose approval does not count, workflows that wait for "approve and run", and the agent's own configuration — instruction files, hooks, setup scripts, MCP config — under CODEOWNERS. It approves the output, not the actions taken to produce it: a session's tool calls and network effects have already happened when the reviewer arrives, which is why the sandbox and egress pins exist.

The tunnel token and TLS private key on this host are the load-bearing secrets on the path — issued scoped, rotated like a service credential, and revocable without redeploying the host. The tunnel carries traffic on them but never authenticates to our server; that is the gateway's job.

Tool and connector content returned through this gateway is classified here before it goes back to a loop we cannot see. Connectors the vendor calls directly never cross it, so this pin covers none of their content.
Routines, automations, scheduled tasks, shared environments and App installations inventoried like agents, with an owner each — the population a hosted runtime makes cheap enough to sprawl.

The vendor's session logs — every commit linking to the session that made it — exported to our side and fused with the repository host's audit events and our gateway's record, so one session has one trail from trigger to merge. The export's coverage of the hosted surface is a per-product fact to verify.

Disable hosted mode in the tenant, uninstall the App, revoke the seat — and know the delay: none of it stops a session that is already running, so the stop for that is the vendor's cancel, and the finding names how long it takes.

walkthrough.title: A task handed to the cloud comes back as a pull request
walkthrough.moves: A developer's conversation becomes a hosted session, the session works on the repository and reaches our systems through our gateway, and a person merges what it made. This is the coding profile; general desktop work ends at an authorized application or file action instead.

steps.label: task in the web app
steps.note: The task starts in the vendor's web app, naming the repository and the environment.

steps.label: session requested
steps.note: The control plane takes the task; a session starts from it on the vendor's compute.

steps.label: environment applied
steps.note: The control plane admits the session to a shared environment: network access level, setup script, connectors, permission mode — the settings that reach a hosted session, none of which came from the device.

steps.label: clone via git proxy
steps.note: The sandbox clones through the proxy on a scoped credential it never sees.

steps.label: instructions & threads in context
steps.note: The instruction files, the issue and the review thread enter the session as instruction — classified on the way in, because most of them were not written by us.

steps.label: pinned, verified installs
steps.note: The reviewed setup script installs pinned dependencies verified against lockfile hashes — a mismatch fails the setup — and caches the result; then the network closes and the agent phase begins.

steps.label: tool call down the tunnel
steps.note: The runtime's MCP client calls back into us — the one crossing on the drawing where external compute reaches our systems — down the outbound-only connection our tunnel holds open.

steps.label: to our gateway
steps.note: The tunnel hands the request to our gateway's aggregate MCP endpoint: admitted on a per-user grant we issued, evaluated per call, scoped to a named server list, recorded against the grant.

steps.label: per-session grant
steps.note: Admitted to a named server on a short-lived grant scoped to this session.

steps.label: read on our side
steps.note: The read happens on our side, which is the only reason it is bounded.

steps.label: record
steps.note: The record comes back.

steps.label: recorded
steps.note: Through the crossing, where the call is recorded against the grant.

steps.label: into the tunnel
steps.note: Classified at the gateway, then back into the connector.

steps.label: tool result
steps.note: And back to the session.

steps.label: push branch, open draft PR
steps.note: The session pushes to its own branch and opens a draft — the only write the token allows. Commits are signed and link back to the session.

steps.label: review & merge
steps.note: A person reviews the draft, approves the workflows it would fire, and merges. The gate approves the output; everything the session did to produce it already happened.

scenarios.title: A comment becomes a command

steps.label: hostile issue in context
steps.note: Someone with no commit access files an issue whose hidden text is an instruction. A session starts on it — or reads it while working on something else.

steps.label: attacker page fetched
steps.note: The instruction sends the sandbox to a page the attacker controls, where the second stage waits — on a product where the agent phase has internet, or an environment where someone opened it.

steps.label: exfiltration via an allowed host
steps.note: What the sandbox holds — environment variables, the clone, whatever the setup phase left behind — leaves through a host the allowlist permits: a package publish. The list said where the sandbox may talk, not what it may say.

steps.label: hook committed, PR opened
steps.note: The session commits a hook, a task file or a workflow change into its branch and opens the draft. The payload is now in the repository, waiting for a tool nobody sandboxed to execute it.

steps.label: the gate holds — or not
steps.note: A person is the last check: CODEOWNERS on the agent's configuration directories, required review, and workflows that wait for approval are what stand between the branch and the default branch.

scenarios.title: Nobody at the machine: a channel and a schedule

steps.label: from a phone or a channel
steps.note: The owner on a phone — or, in a shared channel, anyone the channel admits.

steps.label: session raised on the relay
steps.note: The relay admits whoever the account binding or the channel allows; a session raised from a channel runs under a shared identity on most products.

steps.label: scheduled & re-triggered runs
steps.note: A routine fires on a schedule; an automation re-runs the session on every CI failure and review comment. The loop has no natural end and no person in it.

steps.label: the ticket, through a connector
steps.note: The run reads the ticket or thread it was raised from through the vendor's connector.

steps.label: its author's text, as input
steps.note: Whatever the ticket's author wrote enters the loop as model input, on a path nothing of ours inspects.

steps.label: replies that trigger automation
steps.note: The session's own replies on the thread fire comment-triggered automation — and an automation configured to approve low-risk pull requests approves its own.

scenarios.title: Variant: execution moves to a worker we run

steps.label: placed on our runner
steps.note: In this variant the environment names a self-hosted runner. Orchestration and inference stay with the vendor; the sandbox, drawn here in the Vendor band, would run in our cloud.

steps.label: clone on our credentials
steps.note: The git proxy leaves the path: our deployment supplies the git credential, our firewall becomes the egress policy, and isolation becomes our responsibility.

steps.label: installs through our firewall
steps.note: Setup still installs pinned, verified packages from the public index, now through our firewall. Tool inputs and outputs still cross to the vendor's loop, and inference stays with the vendor.

deviations.subject: Desktop and mobile apps are clients of the same session, not endpoint applications
deviations.reason: A third-party SaaS drawing shows the browser-based interface and nothing that runs on the machine. The vendor's desktop and mobile apps show the same synced sessions as the web app, so they add no path here. What a local application does itself — run the loop, read local files, hand a local conversation up to the cloud or teleport a cloud branch back down — is the third-party coding & desktop agents drawing, where the local harness is drawn in full.

deviations.subject: Our source control is reached through a scoped GitHub App
deviations.reason: Our GitHub Enterprise Cloud tenant sits in our band: the policy on the data path — App installation scope, the enterprise IP allow list, branch protection, CODEOWNERS on agent configuration, who may trigger a run, "approve and run workflows" — is ours. Every major provider connects the same way: a GitHub App on named repositories, its credential held in the vendor's git proxy, admitted from the vendor's published IPs. A self-hosted GitHub Enterprise Server changes only the network path: the vendor's IPs allowlisted at our firewall, private connectivity where a vendor offers it (AWS PrivateLink or Cloudflare Tunnel), or execution moved inside on self-hosted runners — recorded here rather than drawn. The endpoint drawings reach the same block from the local agent's git, on the developer's own credentials; public repositories a session only clones are a second Source control block, in the External band.

deviations.subject: Two vendor blocks for one vendor
deviations.reason: The three-zone rule draws a vendor as one block. This drawing has two for the agent vendor because a session is admitted by one tier and executed by another, and the controls sit on different ones: the control plane carries the settings, the connector and App approvals, the relay and the scheduler, all of which we configure; the runtime carries the loop, the model, the sandbox and every connection out — git, tool calls and connectors — of which we configure only the reach. The endpoint drawing has the first, the API/SDK drawing the second; this one needs both.

deviations.subject: The tunnel is drawn; the public-endpoint reach-back is recorded
deviations.reason: The target state is the API/SDK sibling's: the vendor reaches our gateway through an outbound-only tunnel, so no MCP endpoint of ours faces the internet. Where a product has no tunnel, the runtime calls an internet-facing gateway URL instead, admitted at our edge by the vendor's published IP ranges — the same crossing with a weaker admission, because an inbound listener now exists. Either way the gateway, not the transport, is the control. Products whose tool calls leave from compute we run — a self-hosted runner or a privately networked one — reach the gateway from inside our network and need neither. Source control is not on this path: a rented code host is reached by the vendor over the internet, and a self-hosted one over the vendor's private connectivity where it offers any.

deviations.subject: The self-hosted execution variant is recorded as a scenario, not drawn
deviations.reason: Several products offer execution on workers we run — self-hosted environments, team pools, self-hosted runners — with orchestration and inference staying with the vendor. It would move the nested Native tools block into our cloud band and remove the git proxy from the path. It is a variant scenario here until an organisation adopts it, because a drawing that shows both at once implies a choice nobody has made; the scenario names the two facts to carry into that drawing when it comes — the credential proxy is gone, and inference stays with the vendor.

deviations.subject: Identity binding is absorbed into the vendor's account layer
deviations.reason: Access policy (D3-APA) is embodied by an identity provider, an authorization server or an Identity binding item elsewhere in the catalogue. On this drawing the binding is the vendor's account layer for the remote path and the repository host's write-access check for the event path; neither is a tier we run, so the capability is pinned on the control plane and on the event edge and the embodiment is absorbed into them.

deviations.subject: The AI gateway carries tool traffic only
deviations.reason: The vendor calls its own model inside its own runtime — drawn as the Model inference item on the Managed runtime block, with no Model provider block on this drawing — and the hosted mode drawn here does not route the loop's inference through us. The gateway is drawn with its one real traffic class rather than the registered aiGatewayTraffic pack, following the SaaS siblings: the honest signal that a gateway is not on the model path is its own contents.

deviations.subject: Native tools nest inside the Managed runtime, the fused-runtime exception
deviations.reason: The same exception the API/SDK sibling records (2026-09-09): the built-in tools are the vendor's coding-agent tool surface, bounded by an environment egress policy we author, and in the self-hosted variant they execute on a worker we run. What we configure, we draw. Unlike the sibling, edges do leave the nested block here — setup installs and web fetch — because the setup phase needs package registries and the agent phase may be given the web; the reference requires pinned, verified installs and an administrator-locked allowlist on both. Public clones leave from the runtime, because depending on the product they take the sandbox's egress or the vendor's git proxy.

archetypes.title: UI/low-code managed agent runtime
summary: A vendor platform where business and technical teams assemble agents from instructions, connectors and triggers. The reference governs who can build, publish and invoke them, which credentials they exercise, and how changes reach production.
description:
A builder UI lowers the effort needed to publish an agent, but review and staged rollout remain necessary. Use the platform's inventory, environments and supported publication controls to assign an owner and approved scope to each deployed agent. Reconcile connector grants and triggers when ownership changes.
Credential inheritance depends on the connector and execution mode. An agent may use a maker's connection, a service identity or the invoking user's authorization. Shared maker credentials can give callers access they do not otherwise have. Select the intended model explicitly and check permissions at the destination for each consequential operation.
Instructions, knowledge sources and tool descriptions are untrusted-input paths regardless of the builder's technical background. Configure the vendor's supported runtime controls and publication gates, and enforce authorization at customer-operated tool services. Treat supplier safeguards and customer-enforced checks as separate evidence.
distinguishedBy:
Against the API/SDK managed agent runtime: authoring and publication primarily use the vendor's builder UI. Both modes can support engineering review and deployment pipelines; this reference emphasizes governance across many makers and published agents.
Against an internal AI platform you operate: the vendor operates the authoring and agent runtime services. Customers configure supported policies and govern their own connections, identities and destination systems.

exemplars.name: Microsoft Copilot Studio
exemplars.note: Graphical agent and workflow authoring with connectors, publishing and organization administration. Select the harness and credential mode explicitly; capabilities differ across them.

exemplars.name: Salesforce Agentforce
exemplars.note: Salesforce's agent platform for business workflows and CRM actions. This example covers builder-authored agents; scope their actions and data access to the intended execution identity.

exemplars.name: Gemini Enterprise Workflow Builder
exemplars.note: Google's no-code workflow authoring within Gemini Enterprise. Govern published workflows, connected apps and user permissions separately from the employee chat experience.

exemplars.name: Amazon Quick Automate
exemplars.note: AWS visual authoring for agentic business automation. This example covers managed workflow execution and integrations, with publication, connection ownership and action permissions configured explicitly.

zones.note: Two populations, and the distinction is the archetype: the colleagues who build agents without being engineers, and the colleagues who then use what they published.
zones.title: User surfaces

zones.note: The platform, and effectively the whole system. Authoring, the orchestrator, the model calls, the sandbox and the connector runtime all execute here — there is no customer-hosted agent runtime on offer — and, beneath it, the SaaS we hold under agreement that its connectors reach. A maker reaches the platform first, and the platform reaches back into us second.
zones.title: Vendor platform

zones.note: The narrow strip that is still ours: the tunnel the platform reaches us through, the gateway a published agent is admitted at, and our own tool servers and data behind it.
zones.title: Enterprise cloud

zones.note: The model the vendor calls on our behalf, and the open web its search reads.
zones.title: External

zones.note: Governance covers the agent population and its changes. Where the platform offers deployment pipelines, publication review and environment policy, use them to keep maker access separate from production use; they are optional, so population controls remain the baseline.
zones.title: Security & governance control plane

blocks.title: Citizen builder
blocks.note: A business or technical maker configuring an agent. Require the review and publication controls appropriate to the data and actions the deployed agent can reach.

blocks.title: Agent consumers
blocks.note: Colleagues who run what a maker published, usually without knowing who built it or whose access it acts on.

blocks.title: Agent builder platform
blocks.note: One block, because from our side it is one thing: the authoring surface, the orchestrator, the harness, the sandbox and the connector runtime all run in the vendor's cloud. The only part of it we operate is policy configuration, and that is the whole of our leverage.

items.label: Authoring surface
items.note: Where an agent is built and published, by someone who does not think of it as shipping.

items.label: Agent runtime
items.note: Their harness executing the maker's agent, with the model calls theirs to make.

items.label: Connector framework
items.note: Hundreds of prebuilt connectors, executing in their cloud on credentials that are the crux of this page.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: The SaaS we hold under agreement — our own Microsoft 365, Google Workspace or Salesforce tenant — reached through the platform's connectors on whichever credential the maker chose. A service outside any agreement is not connected: connector policy and the target tenant's admin consent decide what counts as approved.

blocks.title: AI gateway
blocks.note: Where a published agent is admitted into our systems, and the policy point on that path. It carries no inference here — the vendor calls its own model — so this is purely about tools and data, which is the useful distinction from every other gateway in the catalogue.

items.label: MCP & API gateway
items.note: Which of our servers a published agent may reach, and on whose grants.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: Our own APIs and MCP servers, reached only through our gateway and never exposed to the platform directly. The platform's data policies regulate its MCP tools the same way they regulate its connectors.

blocks.title: Tunnel connector
blocks.note: The platform's on-premises data gateway, or its private-network equivalent: vendor-supplied software on a host we run that dials out, so nothing is opened inbound, and relays the platform's connector calls to our gateway — the same chain as on every SaaS sibling. It does not run agents, and its payload limits make it a query path rather than a bulk one. It connects with the credentials stored for each connection, whoever invoked the agent, so the invoker's identity does not reach the far side — the confused-deputy path this archetype turns on. Those stored credentials sit on this host, which is why the secrets pin lands here.

items.label: Outbound connector
items.note: Polls outward; no inbound firewall rule, and a small ceiling on what any one call may carry.

blocks.title: Enterprise data
blocks.note: The systems of record a maker attached as grounding or as an action target — often without anyone asking whether the agent's audience should reach them.

blocks.title: Model provider
blocks.note: The model service the platform calls each turn, on the vendor's agreement with its provider rather than ours. We neither broker the call nor hold the key, which is why our own gateway carries no inference on this page.

blocks.title: Open web
blocks.note: Search results and fetched pages, reached only through the platform's web search. Every page is authored by someone else, and its text enters the agent's turn as model input.

items.label: Web search
items.note: The search tool's results — ranked by somebody else, and read as context.

items.label: Arbitrary pages
items.note: Visible and hidden text alike, served by whoever owns the page.

blocks.title: Identity services
blocks.note: Whose credentials a published agent runs on, which on these platforms is a configuration choice. Require end-user credentials; which mode is the default differs by platform and connector. Maker credentials are the ambient-authority case: every consumer of that agent transitively inherits the maker's access to the backend. Where the platform's inventory records which mode each connector uses, that field is the most useful thing an administrator can query here.

blocks.title: Secrets & key management
blocks.note: The tunnel host's cached connection credentials — issued, rotated and revoked from here, because they sit on a host we run and nowhere our gateway can see.

blocks.title: Policy & authorization
blocks.note: Data policies that classify every connector, forbid mixing groups across the boundary and block publication of a violating agent. Whether a platform enforces them by default, and which agents they exempt, differs by platform.

blocks.title: Supply-chain assurance
blocks.note: The inventory and the publication gate. On a platform where anyone can build, an agent nobody registered is an agent nobody can revoke — and that is the normal case rather than the exception.

blocks.title: Observability & response
blocks.note: Run history, and the population view: which agents exist, who built them, which have outlived their author. The unit of observation here is the population, not a deployment.

edges.label: authors & publishes
edges.note: Built and shipped inside the vendor's surface. The platform's environments and deployment pipelines can put a review here, but they are optional and many makers publish straight from the builder.

edges.label: uses a published agent
edges.note: Colleagues run what a maker published, on whichever credential the maker configured.

edges.label: their model
edges.note: The vendor calls its own model provider. We are not on this path and hold no key for it, which is why our gateway carries tools and data only.

edges.label: brokered tool calls
edges.note: Which of our servers a published agent may call, on grants we scope rather than the maker's standing access.

edges.label: scoped reads & writes
edges.note: Grounding content and action targets, reached on our terms.

edges.label: outbound-only tunnel
edges.note: Their cloud reaching back into us through software we run. Outbound-only, so nothing is opened inbound; the public-endpoint form most platforms default to is recorded as a deviation.

edges.label: tool call / result
edges.note: The tunnel hands to our gateway rather than to a server or the data. A vendor-hosted agent reaching our data crosses here or it does not reach it at all.

edges.label: approved SaaS connectors
edges.note: Connectors reaching the SaaS we hold under agreement. This path never touches our network, so the connector policy in their tenant is the only control on it.

edges.label: web search
edges.note: The platform's web search, opened from their side. What returns rides back on it — content nobody vouches for, entering the agent's turn.

risks.note: An agent is a form away, and the unregistered population accumulates in the platform — not in any one builder. Without the inventory queried, the population is unbounded, and agents outlive the people who built them.

The defining risk of the archetype, and it materializes in the platform's connection store: a maker attaches a connector on their own credentials and publishes to a team; every consumer then transitively holds the maker's access to that backend. Nobody granted it, nobody sees it in an access review — and most of it plays out on paths our gateway never touches.
The relay reads with each connection's stored credential whoever is asking, so an agent can answer with records the person invoking it could never open.
Grounding content and connector results re-enter the agent as instruction. A document dropped in a shared folder is an instruction channel on this platform.
Search results and fetched pages return into the agent's turn — content somebody else authored, read with the same standing as the maker's instructions.
A document in a grounding folder anyone can write to comes back as a tool result and enters their runtime as instruction — the path the shared-drive scenario walks.
Grounding content sent to a model we do not broker — more than the turn needs, or kept and used outside the terms the vendor agreed with its provider.
Publish to a public channel with authentication off and the audience is the internet: the agent's grounding and connectors answer anyone with the URL — found by the thousands by recon tooling.
Knowledge a maker uploads is answered to everyone who can use the agent, whatever the source file's permissions — the agent discloses what its audience could never open.
Writes into systems of record from an agent nobody reviewed.

A maker attaches a folder as grounding and the platform indexes it. Whoever can write to that folder can write to the index, and every agent grounded on it reads what they left — the poisoning is of the retrieval source, not of the model.

mitigations.note: Whose credentials a published agent runs on, and who may run it at all: end-user credentials required, maker credentials as a deliberate, reviewed exception, and authentication on for every channel an agent is published to — an agent published with authentication off answers anyone with the URL.
Each published agent signs in as its own directory principal; the identity provider verifies that credential and conditional access can refuse it, per agent rather than for the whole population.
The platform's own inventory, queried rather than assumed — including which connectors use maker credentials, which is the field that finds the ambient-authority agents.

Versioned agents promoted through the platform's environments or pipelines with a named approver, a limited first audience where offered, and rollback by re-activating or redeploying the previous version. Optional on these platforms and often unused by makers; unpublish alone is the weaker response.

Their runtime, their sandbox, their model — assured by assessment rather than drawn, because none of it is ours to inspect, and re-assessed on a clock: connector defaults, publication channels and authentication toggles drift as the vendor ships.

Connector policy authored centrally in the tenant: every connector classified, a confidential source never paired with a path that sends data out, unclassified connectors blocked — enforced at publication where the platform supports it. The only control on a path that never touches our network.
Which of our servers a published agent may reach, decided at our tier rather than by the maker.

The cached connection credentials on the tunnel host — issued scoped and short-lived, rotated, and revocable without redeploying the host. Absorbed here per the recorded deviation, because this is where the secret actually sits.
Grounding read through our gateway is classified before it goes back to their runtime — the one return leg we can inspect.

What a maker may attach as grounding: sources with governed write access only, classified before they are attachable, and every read scoped to the invoker's entitlement and refused when no invoker comes with it. The default connector set is the real policy, and a permissive default is a decision nobody remembers making.

Each run's steps — tool and connector calls, retrieval and hand-offs — correlated by session and exported where we can query them. Platforms differ: some capture steps org-wide, others leave step-level capture to a per-agent maker setting.

Unpublish or quarantine the one agent and revoke its connection grants — the SaaS form of the stop, and the response the departed-author and public-link scenarios actually invoke. Disabling the platform for the tenant is the last resort, not the routine stop.

walkthrough.title: An agent is built, published, and used
walkthrough.moves: A colleague assembles an agent from prompts and connectors; another colleague runs it, and the answer comes back.

steps.label: build & publish
steps.note: Built and published inside the vendor's surface, often straight from the builder: deployment pipelines exist but are optional and commonly unused, so population management rather than change review is the baseline.

steps.label: colleague runs it
steps.note: A colleague runs what was published — on their own credentials if the maker chose end-user auth, and on the maker's if they did not.

steps.label: vendor's model call
steps.note: Now the model is called — on the vendor's key, for the running turn. We are not on this path, which is why our gateway carries tools and data only.

steps.label: completion
steps.note: The completion comes back into their runtime as the turn's plan.

steps.label: web search
steps.note: Where the plan calls for it, the platform searches the web from their side.

steps.label: search results
steps.note: Results and fetched pages enter the turn, written by whoever owns the page.

steps.label: down the tunnel
steps.note: Their cloud reaches back into us through the connection our tunnel holds open.

steps.label: reach into our data
steps.note: Handed to our gateway. A published agent reaching our data crosses here or not at all.

steps.label: scoped grant
steps.note: Scoped to grants we decided, rather than to the maker's standing access.

steps.label: records
steps.note: The records the agent was built to reach.

steps.label: records
steps.note: The records come back.

steps.label: recorded
steps.note: Through our crossing, where the call is recorded.

steps.label: into the tunnel
steps.note: Classified at the gateway, then back into the connector.

steps.label: tool result
steps.note: And up the tunnel to their runtime as a tool result.

steps.label: grounded model call
steps.note: The records go to the model with the turn, on the vendor's key.

steps.label: grounded completion
steps.note: The answer is composed from what the records said.

steps.label: reply
steps.note: The reply returns to the colleague who ran it, grounded on everything the walk touched.

scenarios.title: A maker attaches a connector on their own credentials

steps.label: publish with connectors
steps.note: Prompt written, connectors attached, agent published to a team.

steps.label: run; inherit maker's access
steps.note: Colleagues run it — and inherit the maker's access to whatever it was attached to. The gap between who built an agent and whose access it uses is where this archetype's incidents live.

steps.label: back into us
steps.note: The agent reaches back into our systems through the tunnel.

steps.label: reach bounded at our tier
steps.note: Which is only bounded at all because the reach into our systems crosses a tier we run.

scenarios.title: A shared drive becomes an instruction channel

steps.label: folder as grounding
steps.note: A running agent asks for a folder somebody uses as grounding.

steps.label: to our gateway
steps.note: The request comes up the tunnel to our gateway.

steps.label: admitted read
steps.note: Admitted like any other read.

steps.label: folder read
steps.note: The folder is read.

steps.label: document with instruction
steps.note: A document written by anyone with access to that folder comes back with the rest.

steps.label: tool result
steps.note: It crosses back as an ordinary tool result.

steps.label: into the tunnel
steps.note: Classified at the gateway, which cannot tell it apart from any other record.

steps.label: model input
steps.note: And enters their runtime as model input.

steps.label: acts with maker's authority
steps.note: The agent acts on it with the maker's authority — on connectors that never touch our network, so nothing of ours can intervene past this point.

scenarios.title: The author leaves

steps.label: agent outlives maker
steps.note: An agent outlives the person who built it, still holding their connector grants.

steps.label: SaaS grants keep flowing
steps.note: The maker's connector grants to our SaaS tenants keep flowing — these never touch our network, so only the platform's connection-ownership transfer or revocation can cut them. That inventory operation is the primary response.

steps.label: grants into us
steps.note: The departed maker's grants into our systems still arrive through the tunnel.

steps.label: our slice cut
steps.note: Our gateway cuts the slice it issued — the grants into our own systems — which is real, and is not most of what the departed maker left behind.

scenarios.title: Published to anyone with the link

steps.label: stranger's question
steps.note: A failure variant: a maker publishes to a public channel and leaves authentication off. The "consumer" is now anyone who finds the URL, and recon tooling finds them by the thousands.

steps.label: down the tunnel
steps.note: The stranger's question comes back into us through the tunnel.

steps.label: agent's own grants
steps.note: It reaches our crossing on the agent's stored credential, with no invoker identity behind it.

steps.label: admitted like any run
steps.note: Admitted like any run of this agent. With no invoker to check, the invoker-scoped read is bypassed rather than enforced.

steps.label: grounding for a stranger
steps.note: The grounding answers a stranger. Authentication on every channel, and refusing reads that carry no invoker, are what would have stopped it.

deviations.subject: The tunnel absorbs secrets
deviations.reason: Credential hardening (D3-CH) is embodied by the AI gateway, but the load-bearing secrets on this path are the connection credentials cached on the tunnel host — the pin sits where they live, and the issuance story in the governance call-out.

deviations.subject: The tunnel is drawn; the public endpoint and the direct data path are recorded
deviations.reason: The target state is the SaaS siblings': the platform reaches our gateway through an outbound-only tunnel on a host we run, so none of our endpoints faces the internet. Most platforms in this class default instead to calling an internet-facing endpoint of ours, admitted at our edge by their published IP ranges — the same crossing with a weaker admission — and some offer private networking in place of a relay. The on-premises data gateway can also carry the platform's standard data connectors straight to an on-premises source, bypassing our gateway; where that path is used, the connector's data-policy classification and the relay's scoped credentials are the only controls on it, and it is recorded here rather than drawn as a second chain.

deviations.subject: The AI gateway does not reach a model provider
deviations.reason: Everywhere else in the catalogue the gateway is the model path, and the registered pattern says so. Here it is not: the vendor calls its own model, on its own key, and our gateway exists only to admit a published agent to our tools and data. Drawing an inference leg out of our gateway would assert a broker we do not operate. The model edge is therefore vendor to provider; the SaaS siblings absorb the model into the vendor block instead, with the same gateway-without-inference result. The gateway is drawn with its own items rather than the registered aiGatewayTraffic pack for the same reason: no model proxy, because there is no model traffic to proxy.

deviations.subject: The vendor platform is a single block despite containing an orchestrator, a harness and a sandbox
deviations.reason: The three-zone responsibility rule forbids drawing vendor internals we cannot inspect. On a platform with no customer-hosted runtime option, everything but policy configuration is theirs, so the honest drawing is one block assured by assessment rather than four boxes implying visibility we do not have.
