archetypes.title: API/SDK managed agent runtime
summary: A customer application invokes a provider-operated agent loop through an API or SDK. The customer defines permitted tools and environments, binds users to sessions, handles supported approval events and custom tools, and exports evidence. Provider features and enforcement coverage must be verified for the selected mode.
description:
The provider operates orchestration; model routing depends on the selected service. The diagram exposes the configuration and native-tool surfaces customers can govern. A customer AI gateway sees only traffic routed through it, such as calls back into enterprise tools. It does not automatically inspect provider-internal inference, direct calls to external model providers, or native browser traffic. Configure and verify model routing independently of the tool gateway.
The hosted baseline keeps tool execution with the provider. A self-hosted executor moves selected shell, filesystem and local-tool operations to customer-controlled compute while tool inputs and results still reach the provider loop. A platform hosting customer-written agent code is a different contract: the customer owns that loop and its enforcement logic.
Private tool connectivity is product-specific. Where an outbound tunnel is supported, it supplies transport rather than upstream authorization. Authenticate the caller and enforce permitted operations at the gateway and destination. Other modes use approved public MCP endpoints or application-handled function tools; a tunnel is not universal.
The sandbox reaches the open web, public source control and public package sources under the environment definition's allowlist, which we author and the provider enforces; anything else is refused. Browser-enabled sessions add a wider route. Bind origin and sign-in decisions to the authenticated caller, session and pending request. Those decisions do not approve every subsequent send, purchase or deletion. Custom-tool authorization remains the customer's responsibility even when the provider exposes approval events.
Define memory scope, retention and deletion independently of compute lifetime. Record the application's workload identity, any executor credential, and each downstream user or service grant. A saved agent identifier is not necessarily a separately revocable principal. Verify which identity and policy features the chosen provider exposes.
The critical boundary is the way back in. To be useful the agent needs our code bases and data, and it reaches them through exactly two controlled crossings: a GitHub App installed on named repositories of our GitHub Enterprise Cloud, admitted only from the vendor's published IPs, for code; and an outbound-only tunnel we run to our AI gateway, for tool calls to our tool servers and the data behind them. Source control is never behind the gateway, and nothing else of the vendor's crosses into our systems.
distinguishedBy:
Against building the agent tier: the provider owns the loop. Customers configure supported controls, enforce authorization in their integration and destination systems, and obtain supplier assurance for internal behavior they cannot inspect.
Against the UI/low-code managed agent runtime: a customer-built application integrates the agent API and engineers manage the definition through their delivery process. Builder platforms can also support review and staged deployment.
Against hosted task sessions and persistent managed agents: the application owns session integration, caller binding, event handling and custom-tool execution. Session duration or retained memory alone does not decide which reference applies.

exemplars.name: Claude Managed Agents
exemplars.note: Beta provider-operated harness with agent, environment, session and event APIs. Hosted and self-hosted execution have different boundaries; tunnels and other features have separate availability.

exemplars.name: OpenAI Agents API
exemplars.note: Public beta managed Codex harness with hosted or self-hosted execution. Computer use adds application-handled origin and sign-in approvals; these do not authorize every subsequent action.

exemplars.name: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore managed harness
exemplars.note: GA configuration-driven harness operated by AWS, with selectable model providers. This mode fits the managed loop; AgentCore hosting customer-written agent code has a different ownership boundary.

exemplars.name: Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Managed Agents API
exemplars.note: Google's Antigravity managed harness, currently Pre-GA for testing and evaluation only. The documented terms exclude production and confidential data; customer-written Agent Runtime code is a separate mode.

zones.note: The people the published agent serves, and the team that defined it.
zones.title: User surfaces

zones.note: What we still own on somebody else's platform: the definition that decides what the agent may do, our GitHub Enterprise reached by the vendor's GitHub App, the front end our users call, the tunnel their runtime reaches us through, the gateway that admits it into our systems, and the systems themselves.
zones.title: Enterprise cloud

zones.note: The provider's environment, and where the agent actually runs. A request reaches it through our own front end first, and it reaches back into us through the tunnel. Its connectors to the SaaS we approved sit here too, under agreement. What they operate inside it is assured, not drawn.
zones.title: Vendor platform

zones.note: What the sandbox reaches out to under the environment's allowlist: public repositories, package and skill sources, and the open web. Every edge here is opened from the vendor's side; nothing in this band connects back in.
zones.title: External

zones.note: On a platform we do not operate, this band is most of what "our controls" can mean — and the identity the agent runs as is not one of them by default.
zones.title: Security & governance control plane

blocks.title: Developer
blocks.note: The engineer who writes the definition and the code — the author the delivery pipeline still applies to, which is this page's whole distinction from the low-code sibling.

blocks.title: End user
blocks.note: The person a session runs for, and whose credentials it acts on if we set it up that way.

blocks.title: Application front end
blocks.note: The customer-owned surface an SDK-driven runtime is invoked from — our code, calling their API. User authentication and the delegated session context are bound here, before anything reaches the vendor. It is also the session client: it creates sessions, streams events, answers the approval prompts for tools configured to ask, and dispatches custom tools through our gateway — a path back into our systems that needs neither a tunnel nor a public endpoint, because the request and the result ride the session stream we already hold.

items.label: App & API endpoint
items.note: The published surface our users actually touch.

items.label: Identity binding
items.note: Which of our people a session runs for, established before it starts.

items.label: Tool handlers
items.note: Custom tools are handled here, in our code. The agent emits the call and the session idles; our handler validates the tool name, schema, arguments and call id, dispatches it through our gateway on the session's bound user context, and posts the result back. The vendor sees inputs and outputs, never the credential or the network.

blocks.title: Managed runtime
blocks.note: The provider hosts the agent loop itself — tool-call decisions, error recovery, context compaction — along with session state and a sandbox per session. Defined declaratively over an API rather than shipped as a container, which makes the definition the whole of the behaviour contract. The adoption caveats are product-specific and belong in the exemplar assessment rather than here — retention and compliance eligibility of cloud sessions, vault scoping, and key-management exclusions all vary by provider and change by quarter; verify each per product before relying on it.

items.label: Agent harness
items.note: Their harness running our definition — the loop, context assembly, compaction and retries, theirs to operate. In effect the vendor's coding agent, hosted: the same anatomy as the harnesses we run, with the built-in tools nested beneath.

items.label: Model inference
items.note: Their model, called inside their boundary. It never crosses our AI gateway, so the inference controls we enforce there elsewhere in the catalogue do not apply here and have to be obtained as tenant configuration instead.

items.label: Memory store
items.note: Session and long-term state they hold, whose scope is a configuration flag rather than an architecture.

items.label: Credential vault
items.note: Secrets the provider holds and injects at egress — per-user credentials for MCP servers and values substituted into requests to named hosts — so the sandbox never holds a value. Who may attach a vault, and what happens when no credential matches, vary by product and are verified per exemplar.

items.label: MCP client
items.note: The harness's own MCP client — the party that connects out. Two directions: back into us through the tunnel to our gateway, and to the provider's hosted connectors for the SaaS we approved, called from the vendor's side with the credential drawn from the vault. That second path is how the agent reaches SaaS data; the public web, repositories and packages it reaches from the sandbox under the environment's allowlist. The alternative for any connector is to register it on our gateway instead and declare the gateway's tunnel hostname as the server: same connector, now scoped and recorded at our tier — the choice per connector is which of the two it is.

blocks.title: Native tools
blocks.note: The harness's built-in tools, nested because the loop calling them is not a hop: file and edit tools, the shell, the skills the definition installs, and (switched off here) the hosted browser and computer use where the product offers them — executing in one sandbox per session, the provider's cloud sandbox or, in the self-hosted variant, a worker we run. What they may reach is the environment definition's egress policy, which is why they are drawn rather than assured: the policy is ours. Under this drawing's policy that is an allowlist — web fetch, public source control and the public package sources or the provider's own mirror — so the edges that leave this block are the same as on the sibling SaaS runtimes; everything else is refused.

items.label: File & edit tools
items.note: Read, write, edit, glob and grep across the session's filesystem.

items.label: Shell commands
items.note: Command execution inside the session sandbox, bounded by the environment's egress policy.

items.label: Installed skills
items.note: Packaged instructions and helpers the definition names, downloaded into the sandbox at session start — content that executes as instruction, versioned like code.

items.label: Computer use
items.note: Off in this reference. The hosted browser and desktop toolsets, where the product offers them: the sharpest tool a definition can switch on, with the open web as its reach. Enabling it is a different profile with its own egress and approval controls.

blocks.title: Agent definition & code
blocks.note: Model, prompt, tools, MCP servers and skills, declared and pushed to the provider — and the environment those sessions run in. On a runtime we do not operate these artifacts are very nearly the whole of what we control about the agent, which makes reviewing them a release gate rather than a formality. The hyperscaler variant adds a third artifact, the customer's own loop code, recorded in the escape-hatch scenario.

items.label: Declarative definition
items.note: What the agent may do — model, prompt, tool enablement and approval policy, MCP servers, skills — versioned, so a session pins to one version and a rollback is a pointer flip.

items.label: Environment definition
items.note: Where sessions run and what they may reach: the vendor's cloud sandbox (a worker we run is the recorded variant), and the sandbox's networking policy — an allowlist of the web it may fetch, public source control and the package sources or the provider's mirror, with write methods restricted on hosts the list must permit.

blocks.title: Source control
blocks.note: Our GitHub Enterprise: the code bases the agent reads and changes. Code, instruction files and threads enter the session as instruction; a branch and a draft pull request come back out for a person to review. It sits in our band, and the vendor reaches it only through a GitHub App on named repositories, admitted from its published IPs by our enterprise IP allow list.

items.label: Repositories & instruction files
items.note: The code, and CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, setup scripts, hooks and MCP configuration — content that executes as instruction and is versioned like code because it is code.

items.label: Issues & PR threads
items.note: Writable by anyone the repository admits, read by the session as instruction. Hidden characters and HTML comments carry payloads the human reviewer never sees.

items.label: Pull requests & CI
items.note: The draft the session opens, the review a person gives, the workflows the pull request would fire — and the single branch the session may write.

blocks.title: Tunnel connector
blocks.note: Vendor-supplied software we run inside our own network so their runtime can reach an MCP endpoint that is not publicly exposed. Outbound-only: it dials the vendor and carries their requests in, so no inbound rule is opened and the endpoint stays on a private address. Two things it does not do, on both vendors' own architecture notes: it does not make the data path local — requests and responses still traverse their cloud — and it does not authenticate to the upstream, which we still do ourselves. The tunnel token and the TLS private key on this host are the load-bearing secrets. Each hostname routes to one upstream, and the upstream here is the gateway's aggregate MCP endpoint — one hostname fronts every server the gateway admits, and the vault holds the gateway's own credential for it.

items.label: Outbound connector
items.note: Dials out to the vendor's edge; opens nothing inbound.

blocks.title: AI gateway
blocks.note: The customer-operated crossing where a vendor-hosted agent is admitted into our systems, from the tunnel and from our own custom-tool handlers. The tunnel hands here rather than to the servers themselves, because the tunnel is transport and this is policy: the one component on those paths where the reach is scoped, credentialed and recorded on our terms rather than theirs.

items.label: MCP & API gateway
items.note: Which of our servers a hosted agent may reach, and on whose grants.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: Our own MCP servers and connectors — the repositories, ticketing and systems of record a hosted agent is adopted in order to reach.

blocks.title: Enterprise data
blocks.note: The systems of record behind those servers, reached on grants we scope per session.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: The provider's hosted MCP servers and connectors for the SaaS we approved, called by the runtime's MCP client under our agreement with the credential drawn from the vault. Nothing we run is on this path. A service outside any agreement is not connected.

blocks.title: Source control
blocks.note: Public source control: open repositories a session clones read-only — an upstream dependency, an example, a project to patch. Untrusted like any page: the instruction files and issue text in someone else's repository are someone else's instructions.

items.label: Public repositories
items.note: Cloned read-only, never with the session's write credential.

blocks.title: Public package sources
blocks.note: What a session installs from under the environment's allowlist: the provider's own package mirror where it offers one, otherwise the public registries. Install only pinned versions verified against lockfile hashes or signatures, and fail on a mismatch. A registry is also a write-capable host every allowlist permits.

items.label: Package registries
items.note: PyPI, npm and the rest — pinned versions, verified against lockfile hashes at install.

items.label: Skill & extension hubs
items.note: Skills and plugins the definition names, pinned to reviewed versions.

blocks.title: Open web
blocks.note: What the sandbox searches and fetches under the environment's allowlist. Every page is someone else's text, and it enters a loop nobody is watching as instruction.

items.label: Web search
items.note: Results ranked by someone else, read as context.

items.label: Arbitrary pages
items.note: Visible and hidden text alike, served by whoever owns the page.

blocks.title: Identity services
blocks.note: Three layers to govern: our workload's identity to the vendor (federated, short-lived, never a pasted key), the per-user credentials the vault holds for our own servers, and the worker's environment key where we self-host. Mapping each back to a person and an expiry is ours to maintain, because most runtimes keep no principal per agent. No identity technique is pinned here: the user is bound at our front end, and the grants are enforced at our gateway.

blocks.title: Secrets & key management
blocks.note: Per-user credential vaults on their side and the tunnel host's secrets on ours — with the product-specific caveats (vault scoping, whether customer-managed keys cover vault values) verified per exemplar rather than assumed of the class.

blocks.title: Policy & authorization
blocks.note: What the hosted agent may reach in our systems, decided at our gateway rather than in their console — the per-tool approval their connector configuration defaults to, which is worth leaving on, and run budgets so no session or chain of sessions runs unbounded.

blocks.title: Supply-chain assurance
blocks.note: Definition admission, the behavioural checks in front of every change, staged rollout of the definitions themselves, and the platform assessment behind adopting the runtime at all — the change half of governance, kept apart from the traces.

blocks.title: Observability & response
blocks.note: Their session event log fused with our gateway's record. A trail that exists only in their console is one we cannot query during an incident.

edges.label: GitHub App · IP allowlist
edges.note: Both directions of our GitHub Enterprise Cloud tenant, on a GitHub App installed on named repositories and admitted by the enterprise IP allow list only from the vendor's published IPs; the vendor's git proxy holds the credential outside the sandbox. Inward: the code, instruction files and threads. Outward: the push to the session's own branch and the draft pull request — the only writes the installation allows. It never rides the tunnel or the AI gateway.

edges.label: authored & reviewed
edges.note: The definition arrives through the ordinary delivery pipeline — written, reviewed, versioned — which is the property this whole page's distinction rests on.

edges.label: request / response
edges.note: Our users touch our surface: the front end binds who a session runs for before anything reaches the vendor, and the response returns the same way.

edges.label: session invoke
edges.note: Our code invokes their runtime over the SDK, carrying the delegated user context the front end bound, and the session stream carries everything after: events out, approvals and custom tool results back. The vendor-direct variant — no customer tier at all — is real for one exemplar class and recorded as a deviation, not drawn as a second path.

edges.label: custom tool calls
edges.note: Our handlers dispatch the custom tools the runtime requests through our gateway, carrying the session's bound user context, so the same grants, approvals and record apply as on the tunnel path. An authenticated session event is still an untrusted proposed action.

edges.label: deploy
edges.note: One direction: the definition is pushed into an environment we do not operate. What it declares is the behaviour contract, and reviewing it is the last point at which we decide anything about the agent itself.

edges.label: outbound-only tunnel
edges.note: Their runtime reaching back into us through software they publish and we run. Note the direction: our side dials out, so nothing is opened inbound and the endpoint stays private. The public-endpoint form — their cloud calling an internet-facing URL of ours, admitted by IP allowlist — is recorded as a deviation rather than drawn as a second path.

edges.label: tool call / result
edges.note: The crossing this architecture exists to govern. The tunnel hands to our gateway rather than reaching past it into the tool surface, so the grants are ours to scope and ours to revoke.

edges.label: brokered tool calls
edges.note: Which of our servers a hosted agent may call, on short-lived grants we issue.

edges.label: scoped reads & writes
edges.note: The repositories and records the agent was adopted to work on.

edges.label: hosted MCP & connectors
edges.note: The runtime's MCP client calling the approved SaaS servers and connectors from the vendor's side — the tool list fetched by them, the credential drawn from the vault — and the content those tools return entering the loop. This is the agent's route to SaaS data; the public web, repositories and packages arrive from the sandbox under the environment's allowlist. Nothing we run is on the path; the control is per-tool enablement in the definition, and the alternative per connector is to register it at our gateway and reach it through the tunnel.

edges.label: setup installs
edges.note: The session installing pinned, hash-verified dependencies under the environment's allowlist, from the provider's own package mirror where it offers one, otherwise the public registries; a changed or unpinned package fails the install. The registry is also a write-capable host every allowlist permits, which is what makes it an exfiltration channel.

edges.label: web fetch under egress policy
edges.note: The sandbox's own reach to the web, to the destinations the environment's allowlist permits, and the content that comes back as instruction.

edges.label: clone public repos
edges.note: A read-only clone of a public repository — through the sandbox's egress or the vendor's git proxy, depending on the product — under the same allowlist. The session's scoped write credential belongs to its own approved destinations alone.

risks.note: Tool descriptions fetched vendor-side enter the loop as instruction, from servers named in the definition and vetted by nobody on the path.

A malicious or compromised package or skill runs in the sandbox, with network, as soon as it is installed. Pinning and hash verification stop a changed artifact; they do not make a reviewed version benign.

An agent is an API call away. Without a registry the population is unbounded and invisible, and the definition is the only artifact that ever existed for review. A vault credential that outlives its owner keeps acting as them, because nothing in the platform ties a vault entry to that person's lifecycle.

The session exercises the user's grant, an App installation's, or a shared service identity's — whichever the product uses — and the repository host cannot tell an injected instruction from an intended one. What bounds it is the token's scope: one repository, one branch, no merge.
Their infrastructure exercising our authority. The grant is the only thing bounding it, and the grant is issued at our gateway — which is the entire argument for drawing one.
The delegation boundary: a service credential substituted for the user's context here means every downstream grant is the service's, not the person's.

Issue text, comments, review threads and instruction files enter the session as instruction, and most are writable by people with no commit access. The dominant ingress wherever an agent works on code.

Content a connected service returns enters the loop vendor-side — untrusted ingress on a path with no customer control anywhere, beside the pages the sandbox fetches. The allowlist bounds where the agent reaches; it does not classify what comes back.
A record somebody else authored comes back as a tool result and enters their runtime as instruction — classified at our gateway on the way, which is the only reason it can be.
A fetched page enters a loop nobody is watching. The allowlist bounds which pages the sandbox reaches; nothing on this path classifies what they say.

Requests, context and tool results all live on their side, under their retention terms — and managed memory's scope is a configuration flag: cross-user scope means one user's content shapes another's turn, switched on without anyone deciding it.
The package registries every allowlist permits are write-capable: a package publish carries whatever the sandbox holds to a public index.

A push, a pull request, a reply on the thread — from a loop that reads its own thread. An agent's reply can fire comment-triggered automation, and an automation configured to approve low-risk pull requests removes the gate this drawing rests on.
Writes into systems of record from a loop running somewhere we cannot watch.

mitigations.note: The repository host's access policy decides who may write the code, threads and instruction files the session reads: write access for named people and registered automations, with non- collaborators' content refused or treated as untrusted. The setting that decides whether a public issue is an attack surface.
Our identity provider admits the end user to our front end, and the identity binding decides who the session runs for — the user's own identity carried to the vendor, never a shared service account.

A token that reaches one repository and one branch, cannot push the default branch, mark ready, approve or merge; protected scopes and repository blocklists on the products that have them; a session that can reach only repositories its trigger could already reach.

Per-tool enablement in the definition, and MCP servers admitted only as the definition declares them: the settings that make "the agent reaches SaaS data only through an approved connector" true. Nothing verifies what a declared server serves, and every one of these is configuration the next definition can undo, which is why the definition is reviewed like code.
Which servers, which tools, whose grant — decided at our tier because theirs is not ours to configure.

The gate: a draft pull request a person reviews and merges, an initiator whose approval does not count, workflows that wait for "approve and run", and the agent's own configuration — instruction files, hooks, setup scripts, MCP config — under CODEOWNERS. It approves the output, not the actions taken to produce it: a session's tool calls and network effects have already happened when the reviewer arrives, which is why the sandbox and egress pins exist.

Our gateway owns the gate: a consequential write is refused unless it carries an approval bound to the exact action — surfaced to the approver through our front end, with the vendor's per-tool approval defaults as the second, configured layer.
Every definition registered and reviewed before deploy; there is no other artifact to review. Change-gating on the data path, per the recorded deviation.

Immutable versions, adversarial evaluation before an alias moves, a canary first, and rollback that is a pointer flip — the software-delivery half of this page's distinction, applied to the definition.

The vault: the runtime substitutes each credential at egress, only toward its named server or host, so the sandbox holds a placeholder and the model never sees a value. It is a shared credential for every session the vault is attached to unless we attach per-user vaults, so tenant-scoped delegation is our arrangement, not the runtime's default.

The definition's per-tool permission rules, evaluated by the runtime before each built-in or MCP call executes: deny by default, always-ask on consequential tools, and guardrail floors a builder cannot lower where the platform offers them. A provider classifier or auto-approve mode is not this decision. Custom tools bypass it and are dispatched by our application through our gateway.

Memory scope is a flag on their platform, and the default is wider than most adopters assume. Setting it deliberately is the part we configure; authorized writes, provenance, retention and recovery of that state are assured by assessment or recorded as gaps.

Run limits the runtime enforces on each session — duration, turns or tool calls, and cost where it supports them — plus cumulative limits in our application, because a fresh session resets a per-session cap. A per-session budget is not an organisation-wide spend ceiling.

Their isolation, retention and tenancy assured by assessment rather than drawn — the only representation a vendor-internal control gets — and re-assessed on a clock, because memory scope, guardrail coverage and tool-gateway defaults drift as the platform ships.

One sandbox per session around the built-in tools — the provider's container or microVM, or the worker we run. Inside it: the shell and file tools the definition enables. Outside it: the loop, inference and the MCP client, which the provider operates. Where we self-host, the image, capabilities and process user are ours to harden; the provider's boundary stops at the sandbox.

The environment definition's networking policy, authored by us and enforced by the provider around the sandbox: an allowlist of web fetch, public source control and the public package sources or the provider's own mirror, with write methods restricted on the hosts the list must permit; everything else is refused. Paths it does not see — the MCP client, and the provider's web tools where a product runs them server-side under their own domain list — are verified per product and bounded by the declared tool set. A self-hosted worker's egress is our firewall.

The tunnel token and TLS private key on this host are the load-bearing secrets on the path — issued scoped, rotated like a service credential, and revocable without redeploying the host. The tunnel carries traffic on them but never authenticates to our server; that is the gateway's job.

Tool and connector content returned through this gateway — on the tunnel path and to our custom-tool handlers — is classified here before it goes back to a loop we cannot see, enterprise-data returns included, because many hands wrote those records too. Vendor-direct connector content never crosses it.
Their session event log exported and fused with our gateway's record, and retained on our side — a trail that exists only in their console is one we cannot query during an incident.

Archive the agent, interrupt its running and queued sessions, revoke its vault entries and stop our handlers dispatching for it — the SaaS form of the stop, and the response the credential-outlives-its-owner scenario actually invokes. An alias rollback alone affects new sessions only.

walkthrough.title: A user's request becomes a tool call on our systems
walkthrough.moves: A request through our front end to a runtime somebody else operates, reaching back into our data, and the answer coming home.

steps.label: request, session bound
steps.note: The request arrives at our surface, and the session is bound to one of our people.

steps.label: invoke with user context
steps.note: Our code invokes their runtime, carrying the delegated user context.

steps.label: through the tunnel
steps.note: Their runtime reaches back through software they publish and we run — outbound-only, so nothing is opened inbound. The data path is not local, and the tunnel does not authenticate for us.

steps.label: to our gateway
steps.note: Handed to our gateway rather than reaching past it into the tool surface.

steps.label: per-user grant
steps.note: Admitted to a named server on a short-lived, per-user grant.

steps.label: read/write on our side
steps.note: The read or write happens on our side, which is the only reason it is bounded.

steps.label: record
steps.note: The record comes back.

steps.label: recorded
steps.note: Through the crossing, where the call is recorded against the per-user grant.

steps.label: into the tunnel
steps.note: Back into the connector, bound for their cloud.

steps.label: tool results
steps.note: The tool results land in their runtime, which finishes the turn.

steps.label: completion
steps.note: The completion returns to our front end.

steps.label: attributable reply
steps.note: And to the person the session ran for, attributable end to end.

scenarios.title: The agent works on our code base

steps.label: clone via the GitHub App
steps.note: Admitted only from the vendor's published IPs, on an installation scoped to named repositories.

steps.label: code & instruction files
steps.note: Instruction files and threads arrive as instruction — screened, from approved initiators only.

steps.label: push branch, open draft PR
steps.note: The only writes the App installation allows; a person reviews and merges.

scenarios.title: A credential outlives its owner

steps.label: deploy with vault reference
steps.note: An agent is deployed on a platform whose identity is a vault reference, not a principal.

steps.label: stale credential presented
steps.note: Sessions keep presenting that credential after the person has gone, because nothing in the platform ties it to their lifecycle. The tunnel carries it without looking.

steps.label: reaches our gateway
steps.note: The first hop we govern.

steps.label: noticed & cut
steps.note: Our gateway is where that can be noticed and cut, since it is the only hop we watch.

scenarios.title: A hosted connector returns untrusted content

steps.label: connector call, vendor side
steps.note: The MCP client calls an approved SaaS connector from the vendor's side — no customer control sits anywhere on the path.

steps.label: untrusted content
steps.note: What the service returns — a record someone else wrote — enters the loop as instruction, unclassified, because nothing of ours is on this path.

steps.label: steered tool request
steps.note: A steered loop now asks for our tools. The tunnel carries the request in without judging it — transport, not policy.

steps.label: first tier we control
steps.note: The first tier we control, and the reason its per-call policy cannot assume a well-behaved caller.

steps.label: scope, approval, record
steps.note: Scope, approval and the record are what stand between the steered plan and our data.

scenarios.title: A custom tool runs in our own code

steps.label: request
steps.note: A request that will need something only our systems can answer.

steps.label: session invoke
steps.note: Our code starts the session; the loop decides it needs the custom tool.

steps.label: custom tool call
steps.note: The agent emits the call and the session idles. No tunnel, no public endpoint: the request arrives on the stream our own application already holds — which authenticates the session, not the call.

steps.label: dispatched through our gateway
steps.note: Our handler validates the tool name, schema, arguments and call id, and dispatches it through our gateway on the session's bound user context.

steps.label: scoped, approved, recorded
steps.note: The user's grant, any approval bound to the exact action, and the record apply as they do on the tunnel path.

steps.label: read/write on our side
steps.note: The tool runs against our systems, on our credentials.

steps.label: result
steps.note: The result comes back through the crossing, classified on the way.

steps.label: result to the handler
steps.note: Back to our handler.

steps.label: tool result
steps.note: The handler posts the result back. The vendor sees the inputs and the output, never the credential or the network.

scenarios.title: A fetched page names a package

steps.label: web fetch under the allowlist
steps.note: The session fetches a page on a host the allowlist permits — documentation, an issue, a forum answer.

steps.label: page text enters as instruction
steps.note: The page's visible and hidden text reaches the loop, unclassified.

steps.label: install the package it names
steps.note: The loop installs the package the page recommends, from a registry the allowlist permits — pinned and verified only if the definition insists on it.

steps.label: package runs in the sandbox
steps.note: Its install script runs in the sandbox, with network.

steps.label: publish as exfiltration
steps.note: It publishes what the sandbox holds to the same registry. The list said where the sandbox may talk, not what it may say; method restrictions are what remain.

scenarios.title: Variant: the definition moves to custom code

steps.label: escape hatch shipped
steps.note: In this variant, on a hyperscaler runtime, the team hits a limitation and ships the escape hatch: their sandbox, their identity, but the loop is now our code. That changes who owns the loop and its enforcement, and it inherits only the guardrails it explicitly calls.

steps.label: same path in
steps.note: Calls still arrive the same way, through the connector we run.

steps.label: per-call policy floor
steps.note: Which is why our per-call policy is the floor that survives the migration — the platform's automatic guardrails did not.

deviations.subject: Definition admission, evaluation and staged rollout are pinned on the deploy edge
deviations.reason: All three are management-class capabilities cited from the supply-chain call-out, but what they gate — the definition — genuinely flows through the deploy edge, the ontology's own change-gating exception. The chips sit where the gate closes.

deviations.subject: One exemplar class is vendor-direct and has no customer front end
deviations.reason: Hosted background coding agents take a task and a grant and are driven from the vendor's own surfaces; for that class the endUser reaches the provider directly and the front-end tier this drawing requires does not exist. Since 2026-09-17 that class has its own drawing, the coding & desktop session managed agent runtime, and its products are registered there; this deviation stays as the record of why the two are separate.

deviations.subject: The AI gateway carries tool and data traffic only
deviations.reason: The provider calls its own model inside its own runtime — drawn as the Model inference item on the Managed runtime block, with no Model provider block on this drawing — and nothing fetches skills through our crossing. The gateway is drawn with its one real traffic class rather than the registered aiGatewayTraffic pack, following the low-code builder's precedent: the honest signal that a gateway is not on the model path is its own contents.

deviations.subject: The tunnel absorbs secrets consumption
deviations.reason: Credential hardening (D3-CH) is embodied by the AI gateway, but the load-bearing secrets on this path are the tunnel token and TLS key on the tunnel host — the pin sits where the credentials live, the issuance and rotation story in the governance call-out. The same absorption, for the same reason, as the enterprise chat drawing.

deviations.subject: The public-endpoint return path is recorded, not drawn
deviations.reason: Both first-party vendors also reach a customer MCP endpoint the ordinary way — their cloud calling an internet-facing URL of ours, admitted by allowlisting their IP ranges. That is the same crossing with weaker admission: audience-bound tokens, per-user OAuth and rate limiting on a public listener instead of an outbound-only connector. It is the form to draw where a vendor's tunnel is unavailable (one vendor's tunnel is a research preview with no continuity commitment), and it is recorded here rather than drawn as a second edge into the same gateway.

deviations.subject: The self-hosted sandbox variant is recorded, not drawn
deviations.reason: One exemplar lets tool execution move onto a worker we run — code, filesystem and egress inside our perimeter — while the loop, the model and the orchestration stay with the provider. The worker polls the provider outbound-only, the same shape as the tunnel, and tool inputs and outputs still cross to the loop. It would move the nested Native tools block into our cloud band; it is recorded here until the organisation adopts it, because a drawing that shows both variants at once implies a choice nobody has made. Two facts to carry into that drawing when it comes: placeholder-substituted credentials are not supported there, so secrets fall back to the worker's own custom tools, and the worker can act as the MCP client itself, in which case the provider sees only tool outputs.

deviations.subject: Native tools nest inside the Managed runtime, the exception to the fused-runtime rule
deviations.reason: The ontology keeps vendor-operated fused runtimes flat because we cannot see inside. The API/SDK runtime is the exception, recorded here and in the ontology (2026-09-09): its built-in tools are the vendor's coding-agent tool surface, enumerated in the definition and bounded by an environment egress policy we author, and in the self-hosted variant they execute on a worker we run. What we configure, we draw. The block is provider-kind because the execution is still theirs; web fetch and package installs leave it under the allowlist, and public clones leave from the runtime, because depending on the product they take the sandbox's egress or the vendor's git proxy.

archetypes.title: Persistent managed agents
summary: A vendor-hosted agent that continues across tasks, keeping its memory, files and a logged-in browser, and takes work from approved channels and its own schedules as well as from the person who set it up. Unlike a coding & desktop session, it holds standing connector grants and saved logins, so each consequential action is approved at dispatch rather than through a reviewed pull request. It works through the vendor's connectors and a hosted computer, and reaches our systems only through two crossings: the tunnel to our AI gateway for tool calls, and a GitHub App for our source control.
description:
What sets this pattern apart is that the agent gets its own working computer and is run like a new hire with a laptop. Grok Bot works on a persistent cloud desktop with a browser, filesystem and terminal, and uses any application by computer use — mouse, keyboard and screenshots — wherever no plugin exists. OpenAI's dots work the same way from their own cloud computer and browser, and can be given permission to use the owner's own laptop as well. Files, browser sessions and app logins persist from one task to the next, so the agent returns to work already signed in, the way a person returns to their desk.
That is what makes it hard to govern. Computer use reaches every application the agent is signed in to, not just the APIs a connector scopes: each saved login is a standing grant, and a page, email or document it reads can steer clicks in any open app. The continuing agent is the unit of governance — a new conversation resets none of its owner, audience, schedules, retained memory, files, logins or standing grants, and a team channel can have a wider audience than the person whose grant it uses. Stopping it means halting work, disabling schedules, revoking grants and clearing retained memory, files and browser sessions.
Its key tools: the hosted computer — browser, desktop applications through computer use, and shell; the vendor's connectors to the SaaS we approved (Tool services in the vendor band); package installs and public source control under one egress allowlist; its retained memory; and its schedules. The critical boundary is the way back in, through two controlled crossings: a GitHub App on named repositories of our GitHub Enterprise Cloud, admitted from the vendor's published IPs, for code; and an outbound-only tunnel we run to our AI gateway, for tool calls to our tool servers and data. Letting the agent onto an employee's own laptop would be a third crossing this drawing does not include; keep it disabled by policy.
The baseline reads with scoped accounts and returns drafts. A consequential write — including one made by clicking through an application — needs an authenticated human approval bound to the exact action at dispatch; the vendor's own rules and auto-review help but do not replace it. Where a product cannot enforce that gate, leave the operation unavailable. Provider internals are assessed through vendor assurance, not drawn.
distinguishedBy:
Against the coding & desktop runtime's hosted sessions: a session does one task, started by a person or a repository event, on a per-task grant — usually the initiator's — and its environment is reclaimed; its work is code, gated by a reviewed pull request. This agent continues on standing grants, a shared bot acting on its owner's or a service account, and its work is business SaaS — mail, documents, calendars, the web — gated per action at dispatch.
Against enterprise chat: chat centres on conversations and tenant content; this pattern centres on a continuing agent with retained context, standing authority and recurring work.
Against the API/SDK managed agent runtime: customer software invokes and integrates that loop. This agent is consumed through the vendor's product and approved channels, with no application of ours in front of it.

exemplars.name: OpenAI Dots
exemplars.note: Always-on agents, each with its own cloud computer and browser and apps connected through plugins; with permission, a dot can also use the owner's laptop. Rolling out on Pro, Business Premium and Enterprise plans.

exemplars.name: Grok Bot
exemplars.note: Persistent personal and team bots, each on a cloud desktop with a browser, filesystem and terminal, using computer use wherever no plugin exists. Files, browser sessions and app logins persist, and a user's bots share them.

exemplars.name: Claude Duet
exemplars.note: A proactive agent on its own cloud computer and browser, carrying the person's Claude memory, skills and connectors, sending a morning brief and checking accounts on a schedule; it asks before sending, paying, signing or deleting. Research preview for US Pro and Max accounts.

exemplars.name: Meta Muse
exemplars.note: A personal agent on a dedicated cloud VM with its own browser, files and memory, working on schedules and events; a separate Sentinel agent approves every connector action and all egress. Consumer product, US rollout, also reachable in WhatsApp.

zones.note: The owner and requesters in the vendor's product, and the team channels where anyone the channel admits can give the agent work. Only an authorised approver may approve a consequential action.
zones.title: User surfaces

zones.note: Our GitHub Enterprise, reached by the vendor's GitHub App; the tunnel the agent reaches back through, our gateway where it is admitted to our tool servers, and the systems behind them.
zones.title: Enterprise cloud

zones.note: The agent provider, under our agreement: the product that admits work, the runtime that keeps the agent's state between tasks, and its connectors to the SaaS we approved.
zones.title: Vendor platform

zones.note: What the agent reaches out to under its egress policy: public repositories, the package and skill sources its hosted computer installs from, and the open web its browser reads and acts on. Every edge here is opened from the vendor's side; nothing in this band connects back in.
zones.title: External

zones.note: Customer administration, supplier assurance and response across the continuing agent's lifetime.
zones.title: Security & governance control plane

blocks.title: End user
blocks.note: An authenticated owner or requester; only an authorised approver may approve the proposed action.

blocks.title: Remote device
blocks.note: Team channels the agent belongs to. Anyone the channel admits can give it work, and it answers on its owner's or a service account rather than as the person who typed — the widest admission decision on the drawing.

items.label: Vendor apps
items.note: The vendor's phone and browser apps on the owner's device, where they ask for work and approve it.

items.label: Chat channels
items.note: Slack, Teams and similar team spaces; the channel's membership is the audience for everything the agent posts.

blocks.title: Vendor service
blocks.note: The vendor's product and channel integrations, and the customer-visible configuration surface: who may create, share and invoke an agent, and the schedules it keeps.

items.label: Managed settings
items.note: Membership, agent ownership, sharing and available action modes.

items.label: Remote & scheduled sessions
items.note: Channel requests and the recurring work the agent keeps, each schedule with a named owner, scope and expiry; recurrence does not renew authority.

items.label: Session audit export
items.note: Available product events, exported with documented gaps in tool and browser visibility.

blocks.title: Managed runtime
blocks.note: The hosted agent loop and the state it keeps between tasks. Per-agent, per-user and shared computer or memory scopes must be established from the product; no per-agent VM is assumed.

items.label: Agent harness
items.note: Runs admitted work and consumes tool results within the configured authority.

items.label: Model inference
items.note: Provider-operated inference inside the managed service.

items.label: Memory store
items.note: Memory, conversation history, work files and browser sessions kept between tasks — the property that makes this a different class from a hosted session. Each can have its own sharing and deletion lifetime.

items.label: Credential vault
items.note: The standing authority the agent holds between tasks: connector grants, browser cookies and saved logins. They are distinct credentials; a vault claim need not cover all three.

items.label: MCP client
items.note: Calls the vendor's connectors, and our gateway down the tunnel, on the grants the vault holds for this agent.

blocks.title: Native tools
blocks.note: Hosted file, shell, browser and computer-use operations invoked by the enclosing runtime. Containment represents that local dispatch and result path, as in the other managed-runtime architectures.

items.label: File & edit tools
items.note: Work files may survive individual tasks; restrict accessible material and verify its lifecycle.

items.label: Shell commands
items.note: Commands on the hosted computer, an alternate route to the network beside the browser.

items.label: Browser tools
items.note: Hosted browsing with separately governed cookies, saved accounts and destination rules.

items.label: Computer use
items.note: Mouse, keyboard and screenshots on the hosted desktop, for any application without a plugin — reaching everything the agent is signed in to.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: The vendor's connectors to the SaaS we approved — mail, documents, calendars — called on the agent's standing grants under our agreement. A service outside any agreement is not connected. This baseline enables APIs and connectors only; A2A peers need a reviewed flow before use.

blocks.title: Source control
blocks.note: Our GitHub Enterprise: the code bases the agent reads and changes. Code, instruction files and threads enter the session as instruction; a branch and a draft pull request come back out for a person to review. It sits in our band, and the vendor reaches it only through a GitHub App on named repositories, admitted from its published IPs by our enterprise IP allow list.

items.label: Repositories & instruction files
items.note: The code, and CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, setup scripts, hooks and MCP configuration — content that executes as instruction and is versioned like code because it is code.

items.label: Issues & PR threads
items.note: Writable by anyone the repository admits, read by the session as instruction. Hidden characters and HTML comments carry payloads the human reviewer never sees.

items.label: Pull requests & CI
items.note: The draft the session opens, the review a person gives, the workflows the pull request would fire — and the single branch the session may write.

blocks.title: Tunnel connector
blocks.note: Vendor-supplied software we run inside our own network so the agent's runtime can reach our gateway without an inbound rule: it dials out, holds the connection open and carries the requests in. Transport only — it does not authenticate to the upstream, and the payloads still traverse the vendor's cloud — so it hands to the AI gateway, never to a server or the data. Verify per product that its persistent agents can use the tunnel; where they cannot, this path stays closed.

items.label: Outbound connector
items.note: Dials out to the vendor's edge; opens nothing inbound.

blocks.title: AI gateway
blocks.note: The customer-operated crossing where the agent is admitted to our MCP servers: the one component on the reach-back path where the grant is ours to scope and revoke and the call is recorded on our terms. Not on the inference path: the agent's model calls stay with the vendor.

items.label: MCP & API gateway
items.note: Which of our servers the agent may reach, and on whose grants.

blocks.title: Tool services
blocks.note: Our own MCP servers and connectors — ticketing, documentation, systems of record — that the agent is approved to reach.

blocks.title: Enterprise data
blocks.note: The systems of record behind those servers, reached on grants we scope per agent.

blocks.title: Open web
blocks.note: Search results and the pages the hosted browser reads and acts on. Every page is someone else's text and enters the loop as instruction; a logged-in session there carries the agent's saved authority.

items.label: Web search
items.note: Results ranked by someone else, read as context.

items.label: Arbitrary pages
items.note: Visible and hidden text alike — and the form a disclosure is typed into.

blocks.title: Source control
blocks.note: Public source control: open repositories the agent clones read-only — an upstream dependency, an example, a project to patch. Untrusted like any page: the instruction files and issue text in someone else's repository are someone else's instructions.

items.label: Public repositories
items.note: Cloned read-only, never with a write credential the agent holds.

blocks.title: Public package sources
blocks.note: What the agent installs on its hosted computer: the vendor's own package mirror where it offers one, otherwise the public registries under the allowlist. Install only pinned versions verified against lockfile hashes or signatures. A registry is also a write-capable host every allowlist permits.

items.label: Package registries
items.note: PyPI, npm and the rest — pinned versions, verified against lockfile hashes at install.

items.label: Skill & extension hubs
items.note: Skills and plugins the agent or its owner adds, pinned to reviewed versions.

blocks.title: Identity services
blocks.note: Enrol authorised users and approvers, and remove access when their role changes.

blocks.title: Secrets & key management
blocks.note: Track connector tokens, browser credentials and the tunnel's token and TLS key separately, including revocation at each issuer.

blocks.title: Policy & authorization
blocks.note: Define permitted actions, approval conditions, retained-state policy and continuing-work limits.

blocks.title: Supply-chain assurance
blocks.note: Maintain the approved population and assess provider controls that the customer cannot configure.

blocks.title: Observability & response
blocks.note: Correlate available activity records and exercise stopping work and revoking continuing authority.

edges.label: GitHub App · IP allowlist
edges.note: Both directions of our GitHub Enterprise Cloud tenant, on a GitHub App installed on named repositories and admitted by the enterprise IP allow list only from the vendor's published IPs; the vendor's git proxy holds the credential outside the sandbox. Inward: the code, instruction files and threads, and the events that start or steer work. Outward: the push to the session's own branch and the draft pull request — the only writes the installation allows. It never rides the tunnel or the AI gateway.

edges.label: in a team channel
edges.note: The owner — or anyone the channel admits — giving the agent work where the team already talks.

edges.label: start & steer work
edges.note: The channel talks to the vendor's integration directly; nothing we operate is on the path. Admission is whoever the channel admits, and the agent answers on its owner's or a service account, not as the person who typed.

edges.label: admitted work / status
edges.note: Requests, channel messages and the agent's own schedules enter here; results and proposed actions return for review.

edges.label: scoped API call / result
edges.note: The vendor's connector on one of the agent's standing grants; returned records are untrusted task input.

edges.label: browser action / page
edges.note: The hosted browser's own session and cookies, to allowed destinations only. Connector OAuth restrictions do not constrain this route, and the reply brings untrusted content in.

edges.label: package installs
edges.note: Packages and skills the agent installs on its hosted computer, pinned and hash-verified, from the vendor's own package mirror where it offers one, otherwise the public registries under the allowlist; a changed or unpinned package fails the install. What it installs stays on a computer that persists between tasks. The registry is also a write-capable host every allowlist permits, which is what makes it an exfiltration channel.

edges.label: clone public repos
edges.note: A read-only clone of a public repository from the hosted computer, under the same allowlist. A write credential the agent holds belongs to its own approved destinations alone.

edges.label: outbound-only tunnel
edges.note: The agent reaching back into our systems through software the vendor publishes and we run. Our side dials out, so nothing is opened inbound; the requests still traverse the vendor's cloud. The public-endpoint form — the vendor calling an internet-facing gateway URL — is not part of this baseline.

edges.label: tool call / result
edges.note: Tool calls the tunnel hands to our gateway's aggregate MCP endpoint, never straight to a tool server or the data; git never comes this way — it reaches our GitHub Enterprise Cloud through the vendor's GitHub App: admitted on audience-bound tokens and per-agent grants our own authorization server issued, per-call policy evaluated at the gateway, the servers and tools scoped to a named list, and every call recorded against the grant. The vendor's identity and IP ranges admit the caller; they authorise nothing.

edges.label: brokered tool calls
edges.note: Which of our servers the agent may call, on short-lived grants we issue.

edges.label: scoped reads & writes
edges.note: The records and systems the agent was approved to reach.

risks.note: A malicious or compromised package or skill the agent installs runs on its hosted computer, beside retained files and saved logins, and stays there for later tasks. Pinning and hash verification stop a changed artifact; they do not make a reviewed version benign.
An unregistered persistent agent or schedule continues outside the approved owner and connector inventory.

The session exercises the user's grant, an App installation's, or a shared service identity's — whichever the product uses — and the repository host cannot tell an injected instruction from an intended one. What bounds it is the token's scope: one repository, one branch, no merge.
A channel participant induces work using a broader owner's or shared account's authority.

Their infrastructure exercising our authority, steered by whatever the agent read or kept. The grant is the only thing bounding it, and the grant is issued at our gateway — never let the vendor's tunnel or IP range reach past it.

Issue text, comments, review threads and instruction files enter the session as instruction, and most are writable by people with no commit access. The dominant ingress wherever an agent works on code.
An instruction retained from untrusted content influences later tasks through continuing memory or files.
A connector response embeds instructions that try to redirect the agent's next action.
A returned public page attempts to obtain connected-account actions or disclosure of retained context.
Repeated tasks and retries consume resources after the original requester has stopped watching.
Retained context acquired for one audience is reused in a task or channel with a wider audience.
A logged-in browser exports retained sensitive material through an account unrelated to the current task.
The package registries every allowlist permits are write-capable: a package publish carries whatever the hosted computer holds — retained files, saved tokens — to a public index.

A push, a pull request, a reply on the thread — from a loop that reads its own thread. An agent's reply can fire comment-triggered automation, and an automation configured to approve low-risk pull requests removes the gate this drawing rests on.
A write exceeds the current approved purpose even though the connected account can technically perform it.
A browser operation changes records or sends material beyond the exact action its owner approved.

mitigations.note: The repository host's access policy decides who may write the code, threads and instruction files the agent reads: write access for named people and registered automations, with non- collaborators' content refused or treated as untrusted.
Administer who may create, invoke, share or reschedule agents, and who may change their account grants.

A token that reaches one repository and one branch, cannot push the default branch, mark ready, approve or merge; protected scopes and repository blocklists on the products that have them; a session that can reach only repositories its trigger could already reach.
Limit admitted tools and effective account grants by operation and resource; use read-only accounts for draft work.
Bound file access and browser-account permissions separately; do not attach a write-capable account to read-only work.

Which servers and tools the agent may reach, on whose grant — a per-agent, audience-bound grant our authorization server issued, never the vendor's service identity: one aggregate endpoint fronting a named list, read-mostly unless a write has a named owner.

The gate: a draft pull request a person reviews and merges, an initiator whose approval does not count, workflows that wait for "approve and run", and the agent's own configuration — instruction files, hooks, setup scripts, MCP config — under CODEOWNERS. It approves the output, not the actions taken to produce it: a session's tool calls and network effects have already happened when the reviewer arrives, which is why the sandbox and egress pins exist.

Require an authenticated human decision bound to the exact consequential operation, arguments and target before dispatch. Auto-review or permission to log in is not this gate; leave consequential operations unavailable where it cannot be enforced.
Require a verified second factor for product access and privileged approval sessions; SSO alone is insufficient.

The settings we own on the agent's credentials: short lifetimes, rotation and revocation of the connector grants it holds, and clearing of standing grants, cookies and saved logins on a schedule and when the agent's owner or purpose changes.

The tunnel token and TLS private key on this host are the load-bearing secrets on the path — issued scoped, rotated like a service credential, and revocable without redeploying the host. The tunnel carries traffic on them but never authenticates to our server; that is the gateway's job.
Restrict each connector credential to its designated recipient and audience; do not forward it to another tool or browser route.

Govern retained-state readers and writers, source provenance, correction, retention and recovery. Verify what deletion clears across memory, files and history; restrict sensitive durable use when the product cannot meet the required lifecycle.
Enforce task duration, iteration and tool budgets plus aggregate recurring-work limits; a fresh run must not reset the owner's total allowance.

One destination allowlist for the hosted computer's actual network routes — the browser, and the shell's fetches, clones and package installs — limited to the open web the task needs, public source control and the package sources or the vendor's mirror, with write methods restricted on hosts the list must permit. Verify redirects and alternate fetch tools. Enable these routes only for the data class their enforceable restrictions support; a connector allowlist is not egress control.

Tool content returned through this gateway is classified here before it goes back to a loop we cannot see — and may be kept in its memory. Content from the vendor's own connectors never crosses it, so this pin covers none of theirs.

Register each agent's owner, audience, version, approval state, triggers, tools and grants. Reconcile actual tenant activity against that record and configure admission to deny unapproved agents and grants; inventory alone does not authorise their use.
Verify provider isolation, hidden credential handling, internal screening and retention claims with evidence; record gaps instead of drawing unobservable controls.
Correlate available agent, requester, schedule, tool and gateway records; establish coverage gaps before relying on reconstruction.

Stop active work, disable recurring triggers and queued restarts, revoke connector, browser and gateway grants, and clear retained memory and browser state as a separate, verified step; confirm that work cannot resume on surviving authority.

walkthrough.title: A continuing agent prepares a work summary
walkthrough.moves: Read approved SaaS, our own records and public context, keep only permitted working state, and return a draft to the authorised audience.

steps.label: request a draft
steps.note: Resolve the requester and permitted audience before admitting the task.

steps.label: admit scoped work
steps.note: Apply the continuing agent's current scope and budgets, not the authority of an arbitrary channel member.

steps.label: read approved SaaS
steps.note: Invoke an approved connector on the agent's scoped standing grant.

steps.label: consume records as data
steps.note: Returned records are task input, not instruction; record source and scope for anything retained.

steps.label: tool call down the tunnel
steps.note: The agent needs a record only our systems hold; its MCP client calls back through the connection our side opened.

steps.label: to our gateway
steps.note: Admitted on a per-agent grant we issued, evaluated per call, scoped to a named server list.

steps.label: per-agent grant
steps.note: Admitted to a named server on a short-lived grant.

steps.label: read on our side
steps.note: The read happens on our side, which is the only reason it is bounded.

steps.label: recorded result back
steps.note: The record returns the same way — classified and recorded at our gateway — to the loop.

steps.label: fetch allowed public context
steps.note: The runtime dispatches its nested browser tool; this route has its own egress restrictions.

steps.label: return untrusted page
steps.note: The tool returns page content to its enclosing runtime; the page grants no authority.

steps.label: return draft and provenance
steps.note: Preserve only permitted continuing context, with the configured audience and retention.

steps.label: show draft to authorised audience
steps.note: A completed draft does not authorise sending or publishing it elsewhere.

scenarios.title: The agent works on our code base

steps.label: clone via the GitHub App
steps.note: Admitted only from the vendor's published IPs, on an installation scoped to named repositories.

steps.label: code & instruction files
steps.note: Instruction files and threads arrive as instruction — screened, from approved initiators only.

steps.label: push branch, open draft PR
steps.note: The only writes the App installation allows; a person reviews and merges.

scenarios.title: A consequential browser action needs approval

steps.label: propose exact action
steps.note: Present the operation, account, target and arguments before any effect.

steps.label: request owner approval
steps.note: Use an authenticated approval surface; an untrusted page or channel participant cannot approve.

steps.label: approve this action
steps.note: Bind the decision to the presented action and reject changed or expired proposals.

steps.label: release approved dispatch
steps.note: Refuse the operation if the product cannot enforce the required human gate.

steps.label: perform approved browser action
steps.note: Recheck the browser account and target against the approved proposal before effect.

steps.label: return action result
steps.note: The browser returns status to its enclosing runtime on the same session.

steps.label: report outcome
steps.note: Report the actual effect and available evidence, including failures.

steps.label: deliver receipt
steps.note: The requester receives the outcome; continuing grants remain subject to revocation.

scenarios.title: Standing authority: a channel request and a schedule

steps.label: request from a team channel
steps.note: Anyone the channel admits can give the agent work; nothing we operate is on this path.

steps.label: runs on the owner's grants
steps.note: The agent acts on its owner's or a service account's standing grants, not as the person who typed — the delegation a hosted task session does not have.

steps.label: standing grant, no new consent
steps.note: The connector call needs no fresh consent; the grant was given once and survives between tasks.

steps.label: kept in memory
steps.note: What comes back can be retained and shape later tasks for a different audience.

steps.label: result posted to the channel
steps.note: The output's audience is the channel's membership, wider than the grant's owner.

steps.label: visible to the whole channel
steps.note: Everyone in the channel reads it.

steps.label: next run on a schedule
steps.note: The agent's own schedule starts the next run with nobody present. Recurrence does not renew authority; disabling schedules and revoking grants is part of the stop.

scenarios.title: An installed package tries to publish what the agent holds

steps.label: install a package
steps.note: A task needs a library, and the agent installs it on its hosted computer from a registry the allowlist permits.

steps.label: package runs on the hosted computer
steps.note: Its install script runs beside retained files and saved logins, on a computer that persists into later tasks.

steps.label: publish as exfiltration
steps.note: It publishes what it found to the same registry, a host every allowlist permits. The list said where the computer may talk, not what it may say; method restrictions and watching those hosts for writes are what remain.

deviations.subject: Hosted browser and backend connector routes remain separate
deviations.reason: Provider-hosted tools are shown within Managed runtime using the existing SaaS grammar. The browser has a real outbound route to the open web and separate account state. Local desktop browsing, VPN routing or delegated child agents require their own enforcement and lifecycle review; none inherits connector restrictions automatically.

deviations.subject: The AI gateway carries tool traffic only
deviations.reason: The vendor calls its own model inside its own runtime — drawn as the Model inference item on the Managed runtime block, with no Model provider block on this drawing. The gateway is drawn with its one real traffic class rather than the registered aiGatewayTraffic pack, following the SaaS siblings.

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Pattern-level by design; no vendor facts to date.
overview: This is the architecture where the agent writes: a request arrives, a decision happens, and an effect lands on a system of record in seconds with nobody between them. The organisation's requirements therefore centre on reversibility rather than accuracy — the review question for every design is not "how often is it right" but "what happens when it is wrong, and who can undo it, and how fast."

The requirements below assume the multi-agent workflow's guidance as a sibling: each subagent there is this pattern one level down, and everything here applies inside every one of them. What this pattern adds is the concentrated question of a single fast path — the action catalogue, the approval threshold and the compensating transaction carry the weight a human carries in the chat pattern and durability machinery carries in the workflow pattern.

items.title: Make the action catalogue the policy surface — no arbitrary calls
body: Require a deterministic catalogue: named, parameter-validated actions, each declaring its blast radius and its compensating transaction. An agent that can compose arbitrary API calls has no policy surface at all — reject that design in review, whatever the framework makes convenient. Enforcement is per invocation, outside the loop: this action, this record, this value, now — evaluated by a policy engine the agent cannot edit, not a session-time grant. Evidence: the catalogue definition, and a denied-call log showing the bounds actually fire.

items.title: Tie approval to consequence, and reversal to everything else
body: The approval threshold is keyed to irreversibility and value, never to model confidence — and it must be rare enough that a human actually reads what fires. Below the threshold, the control is the compensating transaction: an action with no reversal path does not belong in the catalogue below the gate. Assessment probe: list the catalogue's actions and demand the compensating transaction for each; any blank cell below the threshold fails the review.

items.title: Give the agent an identity, and broker every credential
body: A distinct, revocable workload identity per agent — actions taken as a shared service account are neither attributable nor separately revocable, and turn every incident response into a full-service outage. The agent tier holds no standing keys for brokered calls: model and tool credentials are brokered at the gateway per call, short-lived and scoped; whatever the in-process handlers hold is the exception to keep small. Effective authority on any call is the intersection of the grant the trigger carried, the agent's identity, the action policy and the target record — never the union. Assessment probe: revoke the agent's identity and confirm the loop stops without touching any other service.

items.title: Scope what the loop reads, because the payload's author is the attacker
body: The payload that starts a run is authored by the party who benefits from the outcome, and record content written months earlier re-enters as context — both are injection paths with a short path to money. Classify inbound payloads before the loop, scope retrieval to the account under discussion rather than to what the service can reach, and keep case memory hard-scoped to one case. Assessment probe: a request against account A that attempts to retrieve account B's records into context.

items.title: Bind identity at the trigger ingress, and admit actions out of band
body: Whose authority a run carries is established at ingress, before the loop runs — a service principal with its own named scope, or the on-behalf-of grant attached to the message. It is the identity every downstream action is taken on behalf of, and the thing that bounds the reachable set. There is no front end to bind it anywhere else. The catalogue itself changes only out of band: actions exist because the registry admitted them, through a review the loop cannot invoke — admission, not discovery — and a definition whose hash changed after admission is refused where the harness loads it. Assessment probe: have the model name a plausible action that was never admitted, and confirm the gateway refuses it.

items.title: Evaluate every change, the prompt included
body: With nobody watching a run, there is no later opportunity to notice a change was wrong: every model, prompt or catalogue change ships through a behavioural evaluation gate first. The system instruction is versioned and owned like the catalogue it governs — a prompt edit is a behaviour change and gets the same review. Behavioural evaluation says nothing about the packages underneath: what the sandbox can install is file-analysed at the mirror before admission — malware and typosquat scanning, not just a digest match.

items.title: Bound the spend, the destinations, and the time to stop
body: Rate and budget ceilings sit at the gateway, sized for a loop that retries in seconds; the write path reaches named destinations only, because unbounded egress is the exfiltration channel a steered agent looks for — and that includes the in-process handlers and the sandbox, whose calls never cross the gateway and are bounded by the workload's network policy instead. The decision audit records action, reasoning, inputs and identity where the agent can append and cannot amend — the basis for reversal and dispute. And the stop must halt the agent and revoke its identity without a deploy, because the loop acts faster than a pipeline ships.
