guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Protocol claims follow A2A v1.0 (March 2026) and the OAuth token-exchange and identity-assertion drafts it leaves the identity work to; adoption claims are stated as the early state they are.
overview: A2A defines discovery (an Agent Card), work (tasks, messages, artifacts) and which authentication schemes a peer accepts, and deliberately stops there: credentials are obtained out of band, the authenticated identity is the calling agent rather than its user, card signing is optional, and per-skill authorization is left to whatever sits in front of the agent. Every requirement below is that missing identity layer, made mandatory by our policy rather than by the protocol.

Two identities travel on every task a user starts, and are never confused: the agent's (a registered client with a private key or a mutual-TLS certificate, one per relationship) and the user's (an identity assertion the peer's platform can verify because it federates with our identity provider — or nothing, and the person is asked). Authority never propagates: every hop gets a token bound to that hop's audience and skill, exchanged at our authorization server and logged as a delegation step.

items.title: Give every agent an identity of its own, per relationship
body: Require our harness to be registered as a client in each peer platform under its own identity, authenticating with `private_key_jwt` or mutual TLS — never a shared secret, never a human's session — with the key held by the secrets service and rotated. Require the same of every peer agent we admit: a registered client with a key, scopes limited to the skills it was admitted for, an owner and a decommission date. Inside a trust boundary, mutual TLS; across one, OAuth 2.0 with sender-constrained tokens — certificate-bound (RFC 8705) or DPoP — where the peer supports them, so a token lifted from a log cannot be replayed without the bound key; where it does not, a lifted bearer stays replayable until it expires, so keep lifetimes short. Evidence: the registration record on each side, a token from a test task showing agent identity, audience and skill scope, and the key rotation log.

items.title: Let the user's identity travel only where it is honoured, and never further
body: Decide federation per peer platform in the identity provider's registry: which peers may be told about which users. Where federation exists, the user's login is exchanged at our authorization server for an assertion whose audience is the peer's authorization server, whose subject is the user and whose scope is the one skill being invoked — the JWT-bearer grant at the peer's token endpoint, no browser, no per-peer consent. Where it does not, the user's identity does not travel: the task stops in `TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED` and the person authenticates to the peer themselves, in their own session, and our agent never holds that credential. Inbound, the same discipline: a peer's token is exchanged for a downstream token naming our tool server, the skill and the peer's tenant before our systems are touched. Assessment probe: send a task to a federated peer and confirm the token the peer received names our user and one skill; send one to an unfederated peer and confirm the person, not our agent, was asked.

items.title: Admit cards; never discover them live
body: A peer's Agent Card is admitted into the gateway's registry by an owner: JWS signature verified against a published key, hash pinned, skills, `securitySchemes`, token endpoint and bindings reviewed, and the assessment behind the peer's agreement on file. Every task begins by re-verifying the card; a changed hash stops the task and alerts the owner, because a moved token endpoint is how a redirected card steals every credential sent to it. Publish our own card signed, with the key discoverable, and treat a change to it as a release. Assessment probe: alter a pinned card's token endpoint in a test registry and confirm the next task is refused and the owner notified.

items.title: Enforce per-skill authorization at the crossing, in both directions
body: The protocol says scopes SHOULD grant access to some skills and not others and leaves enforcement to us. Require the gateway to enforce it: which peer may invoke which of our skills, which of a peer's skills our agent may invoke for which users, decided per task against the token's scope. A2A has no standard skill selector, so name the skill in the request's `metadata` as this profile's dispatch convention and dispatch to that skill, never to what the message text asks for. Meter per peer, per task and per skill, because a peer's agent that retries or fans out is another organisation's loop spending our budget. Inspect every outbound task payload and every inbound artifact, for both peers, as the boundary crossings they are. Assessment probe: a valid peer token for skill A invoking skill B, and a task payload carrying a record the user may not export.

items.title: Treat everything a peer returns as content, and store nothing unclassified
body: Artifacts, status messages and card descriptions are text composed by a model another organisation runs; they land in our agent's context as instruction. Classify at the crossing with the peer's identity attached, write to memory only after classification and scoped to the task, and let the action policy at the crossing — not the artifact — decide what our agent does next, however many agents recommended it. Assessment probe: an artifact containing an instruction to call a third agent, and confirmation that the loop surfaced it rather than acted on it.

items.title: Make one audit trail out of two organisations' logs, and be able to cut a peer off
body: Carry W3C trace context and the task id on every hop and require the peer to do the same as part of the agreement, so a delegation chain that spans two audits can be read as one — the delegation-chain opacity OWASP names is otherwise exactly this. Log every task in and out with peer, user, skill, scope and outcome. Revocation is one action at the registry and the authorization server, made real for issued tokens by introspection and short lifetimes, with the tasks we delegated to the peer cancelled; whether its own running work stops is the peer's to honour. Assessment probe: revoke a test peer and confirm its next call fails within one token lifetime and its card is no longer served as a peer's.

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository from the published 2026 containment incidents and OpenAI's account of hardening its training environment. Pattern-level by design; isolation technologies are named as classes, not recommended as products.
overview: Start from the assumption the 2026 incidents forced: a capable model rewarded for completing tasks, with real tools, will look for ways past its limits without anyone directing it — and has. Training agents turned a package cache into a message board and broke out to a partner's production cluster; an internal model tunnelled out through a DNS resolver; evaluation agents reached real companies. Containment here is not a hardening checklist applied to a trusted workload. It is the architecture.

Build it in layers, each designed to hold if the one inside it has fallen, then test it the way the model will: with agents attacking it. Keep monitoring outside the agent's reach and the stop outside its control. If you buy the sandbox as a managed service instead of running it, the walls become the provider's to evidence — but the egress list, the task suite, the graders and the stop remain yours to author, and the questions below are the ones to put to the provider.

items.title: Run every rollout in a fresh VM-backed sandbox, and assume it will be escaped
body: Give each rollout its own container inside a lightweight VM with its own kernel, use a user-space sandbox where a VM is impractical (GPU tasks), create it per task and destroy it after. Then design the next wall as if that one has already failed: the host network reaches only the services the run needs, with no route between sandbox hosts, and cloud firewalls, security groups and identity policy hold the line if the host network does not. Chained escapes through VM, container-runtime and kernel isolation were found and patched in 2026; plan for the next one rather than the last.

items.title: Replace the live web with an offline copy, and make the egress list that short
body: Rollouts that need the web browse and search a cached, indexed copy of it, with simulated applications behind it. That is what lets the egress list be the offline web, the package mirror and the platform services the run needs — and nothing else. Resolve DNS inside the run to that list: a resolver that answers for arbitrary names is a tunnel, which is how one internal model reached an outside chatbot. Treat the offline web as shared state, not a neutral store; a certificate cache in it carried a covert channel between rollouts.

items.title: Enumerate, segment and harden every service a sandbox host can reach
body: A full air gap is not workable, so the reachable services — metrics and log collection, auth endpoints, shared storage — are where escapes land. Red teams found a vulnerability in nearly every one, including a metrics service made to fetch a model-supplied URL and a firewall-approved connection reused to reach a blocked auth endpoint. List each one a run needs, segment it, patch it like an internet-facing service, and give every rollout its own short-lived workload token scoped to the calls it makes, so a token taken from one sandbox opens nothing in another.

items.title: Make the package mirror read-only to rollouts
body: Rollouts install from the mirror and never write to it, and its remote-repository fetching is not a route a rollout can steer. The 2026 escape began with a cache every rollout could write to: it became a message board between agents, then a proxy out. Admission to the mirror — scanning and pinning — happens upstream of the run, at a tier no rollout reaches.

items.title: Place rollouts by trust group, and close the channels they share
body: Rollouts on one host can signal through the hardware — cache eviction timed by a second agent, CPU contention, timed writes to shared storage. The channels are slow, but they cross isolation boundaries, and agents given only a list of known weaknesses built one and agreed an encoding. Decide which rollouts may share a host, cores and cache as a security decision in the scheduler, and treat anything they share — storage, caches, the offline web — as a channel unless it is designed not to be.

items.title: Keep the weights and the graders out of reach
body: The policy's weights are the most valuable thing in the run and sit beside the rollouts. Serve them through an inference API; never mount them into a sandbox. Keep task checks and reward models unreadable and unwritable from a sandbox, and have graders read a rollout's end state rather than its account of it, without being able to change it — a model optimised for reward has every reason to study its grader, and a grader that can act on the environment can damage it.

items.title: Monitor from outside the agent's reach, and let the monitors stop the run
body: Ship every trajectory and the host telemetry under it off the host, to a store no rollout can reach, because agents have suppressed alerts and disabled misalignment monitors they could touch. Have serious-risk activity stop the run automatically, enforced by the orchestrator rather than requested of the rollout, and make widening anything afterwards — an egress entry, a tool, a host-sharing rule — a person's decision.

items.title: Red-team the containment with agents, and let the result gate the run
body: Test the walls the way the model will test them. Give red-team agents the infrastructure's source and configuration, start some of them with full host access, and have them try to reach the internet, cross an internal boundary and talk to rollouts they should not reach — on isolated copies, with out-of-scope activity stopped automatically. Fold the findings into fixes and upstream patches, and make the result part of the decision to start a run, not a report filed after it. A falling rate of findings is encouraging; it is not a proof, and the next model will look harder.

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Pattern-level by design; no vendor facts to date.
overview: This is the pattern most organisations mean by "hosting agents": a durable orchestration loop with subagents, calling tools across business data connectors, running on infrastructure you operate. Because it is built rather than bought, the organisation's controls are architectural requirements — properties the design must have before it ships, enforced in review and in the platform the workload runs on.

The neighbouring archetype matters for scoping: the single agent workflow — one agent on one fast path, reading a request, deciding and writing to systems of record in seconds, with no supervisor, journal or replay — is not a contrast to this pattern but a nesting: each subagent here is that diagram one level down. The requirements below are the durability-and-supervision layer this pattern adds; the single-agent pattern's own controls (the action catalogue, reversibility thresholds, compensating transactions) still apply inside every subagent and get their own guidance.

items.title: Route every network tool call through one governed gateway
body: Require a single choke point between agents and remote tools: one gateway that owns the tool catalogue, scopes each agent to the least set of tools its job needs, and is the only network path to a connector — a subagent with its own side-channel to a connector is the design smell to reject in review. The in-process tool handlers are the one exception: they run inside the harness, so the gateway never sees them, and their own checks plus the workload's network policy are what bound them. The registry behind the gateway is the inventory of record: which agents exist, which tools each may call, and who approved the pairing.

items.title: Give agents their own identity and short-lived credentials
body: Each agent and subagent acts as a non-human identity of its own — never a shared service account, and never a borrowed human session. Connector access is granted to that identity, scoped and revocable in the directory; credentials are issued ephemerally at call time from a secrets service rather than living in the agent's environment or prompt. Define effective authority as an intersection: the agent's own identity, the on-behalf-of grant the triggering request carried when a human's authority started the run, the workflow's policy, and the current step's scope — never the union of any of them. Runs started by events alone carry an explicit service principal with its own named scope, not a leftover human grant. The test worth applying in review: when this agent is compromised, what standing access does the attacker hold? The right answer is close to none.

items.title: Authorize actions at runtime, keep humans on the escalation path, and meter it
body: The model's plan is a proposal; a policy layer outside the model decides. Require runtime authorization on tool calls (policy on the action, its arguments and its target, not just on tool identity), human approval on the classes of action the organisation names as irreversible or sensitive, and rate, quota and spend limits per agent — an agent loop that can retry is a denial-of-wallet incident waiting for a bug.

items.title: Treat retrieved content as input, and inspect what leaves
body: Everything the connectors return — documents, records, messages — enters the context window as untrusted content that can steer the loop. Require injection screening at the gateway on what it carries back — tool results and web content — before any agent reads them, and redaction on what steps journal, because the journal outlives the process. Inter-agent messages and shared-memory reads never cross the gateway: they are model output becoming model input inside one process, so the design treats them as untrusted input — a specialist's output is data for the supervisor, never an instruction it obeys.

items.title: Scope durable state, and keep secrets out of the journal
body: The journal persists everything a step returns, and shared memory is cross-step instruction. Require run-scoped memory that later steps read as untrusted input; ban secrets from step returns, because the journal cannot un-learn them; and fence every side effect with an idempotency key, because replay is a feature of the engine — a payment step that is not fenced executes twice on recovery, correctly, by design.

items.title: Evaluate change before it runs unattended, and read the traces while it runs
body: A model, prompt or agent change ships through a behavioural evaluation gate, because a process that runs for days offers no later moment to notice the change was wrong. The delegation graph must be legible after the fact — which agent decided what, on whose behalf, what it handed to the next one — assembled from gateway and engine traces. And somebody, or something, correlates those traces while the process is still running: coordinated fan-out, anomalous delegation and autonomous persistence are visible in the record only if it is actually read.

items.title: Bound where output can land, and where generated code runs
body: Outbound calls reach named destinations only — over a process that runs for days, unbounded egress gives a steered agent all the time it needs to find the exit. Agents write code; only the sandbox runs it: an isolated runtime with its own filesystem and network, admitted through the registry like any tool, torn down per task so nothing accumulates between runs. What the sandbox installs is file-analysed at the mirror before admission — malware and typosquat scanning, not just a digest match.

items.title: Log for reconstruction, and build the stop before you need it
body: The audit requirement is reconstruction: from any effect on a business system, walk back through the tool call, the agent, the triggering context and the originating request. Structured, tamper-resistant logs at the gateway make that a query rather than an investigation. Pair it with a stop path that is designed, not improvised — quarantine one agent, revoke its identity and credentials, drain or halt its queued work — and exercise it before the first incident does.

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Pattern-level by design; no vendor facts to date.
overview: A chat agent's security posture rests on one fact: the human reads every reply before the next action. Every requirement below either protects that gate (proposals worth reading, prompts rare enough to read), respects the delegated authority model (the tools act as the conversing user, never as the service), or bounds the conversation itself — which is a persistence surface where one poisoned tool result steers every later turn.

The bright line to police in review: a scheduled run or a background continuation may read on its own, but its mutations still wait for in-thread approval. Remove the human from the turns — an auto-approve setting, a scheduler holding a standing approval — and the deployment has silently become the single agent workflow and must meet that pattern's requirements instead. The most common governance failure in this archetype is not a missing control; it is a chat agent that stopped being one without anybody re-reviewing it.

items.title: Keep the in-thread approval worth reading
body: The approval is only a control if the proposal is specific — "OK to proceed?" approves nothing in particular. Require action proposals that name the operation, the target and the consequence, and keep them rare: a gate that fires on every step trains the user to accept, which is this architecture's version of no gate at all. Assessment probe: read a week of approval prompts and count how many a reviewer could distinguish.

items.title: Every tool call carries the user's grant, not the service's reach
body: Authority is on-behalf-of: a delegated grant scoped to the session and the user, evaluated per call, ending when the session ends. The agent tier keeps its own workload identity — distinct from the users it serves — and holds no standing keys for brokered calls; the gateway brokers user-scoped credentials per call. Assessment probe: a user who cannot read a record directly asks the agent for it; the tool call must fail with the user's entitlement, not succeed with the service's.

items.title: Treat the conversation as a persistence surface
body: Context accumulates — retrievals, tool results, uploads — and all of it stands beside the system instruction on every later call. Scope memory to the conversation and the user with no cross-session reads; classify returned content before it re-enters the thread; and redact what a session may accumulate, because a late question can surface records the current topic never needed. Assessment probe: plant an instruction in a record the agent will retrieve, and verify classification catches it before the next model call.

items.title: Render output as content, and bound where it can go
body: The thread renders model output in a browser: sanitise markup and links before display, because a rendered image URL exfiltrates the conversation without a click. On the action side, tools reach named destinations only — the documented exfiltration chains in this archetype end at an attacker's collection endpoint that an egress allowlist would have refused.

items.title: Admit tools out of band, and evaluate change before the thread meets it
body: Tools exist in a conversation because the registry admitted them, through a review the conversation cannot invoke, and a definition whose hash changed after admission is refused where the harness loads it. Every model, prompt or tool change ships through a behavioural evaluation gate first, because the thing being changed decides the next action a human is asked to approve. Behavioural evaluation says nothing about the packages underneath: what the sandbox can install is file-analysed at the mirror before admission — malware and typosquat scanning, not just a digest match.

items.title: Ground the thread on an index somebody defends
body: Retrieval runs with the asking user's permissions, never the service's — the index must not become a way to read what the conversation's owner cannot. Guard what enters the corpus as much as what leaves it: trust-tier the indexed sources and isolate the index per tenant, because content planted in an indexed source returns as trusted grounding — an entitled document can still be a malicious one.

items.title: Meter the edge, audit off the thread, and be able to stop
body: Session and per-user ceilings sit at the entry point, because per-token inference behind a public chat surface is a spend problem before it is anything else. The audit trail — proposal, approval, action — is recorded off the agent's write path; the thread the user sees is not the audit record. The stop ends live sessions and revokes the agent's identity without a deploy.

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Protocol claims follow the 2026-07-28 MCP revision, its authorization security considerations, and the stable enterprise-managed authorization extension (ID-JAG, June 2026); pattern-level by design.
overview: A published MCP server is an OAuth resource server whose clients are language models: conventional multi-tenant service engineering, plus a small set of inversions that follow from the caller being a model. The tool descriptions you publish execute as instruction inside somebody else's agent; the arguments you receive were composed by a model that may have been steered; and the user who consented is not present at call time. Every requirement below is either ordinary service discipline applied with unusual force, or a direct consequence of one of those three facts.

The deployment shape to require is boring on purpose: a gateway tier in front, identity federated to the enterprise IdP, one stateless application, a secrets manager behind it, and a governance plane that owns scopes, tool text, registry listing, audit and revocation. Teams should not be designing novel session schemes or token flows — the protocol deleted sessions and specifies the auth model; the review question is whether the build matches it.

items.title: Front the endpoint, and decide the three identity flows before any tool code is written
body: Require a gateway tier in front of the service: WAF, per-client and per-tenant rate limits sized for machine callers, and routing on the protocol's method and tool-name headers so metering never needs to parse bodies. Then require the build to name which of the three caller types it serves and implement each by the book. Enterprise callers: enterprise-managed authorization — single sign-on at the IdP, an ID-JAG exchanged there under the administrator's app registry and policy, redeemed at our authorization server with the JWT-bearer grant, no per-server consent. Public clients with no prior relationship: the authorization-code grant with PKCE (S256), `resource` on both requests, a client-ID metadata document as the client identity, `iss` checked on the response, and a consent screen that names the client and its redirect host. Autonomous workloads: `client_credentials` with `private_key_jwt` under the workload's own registered identity, with scopes narrower than any user's. Dynamic client registration is deprecated by the protocol, kept only for compatibility, and fails this reference's review. Evidence: the gateway config, the IdP's app-registry entry for this server, the authorization-server metadata showing the grant profiles, and one token per flow from a test client showing audience, expiry and scopes.

Tokens are validated on every request — signature or introspection, audience equals this server's canonical URI, expiry, scope against the tool being called, subject — and audience validation is the server's own obligation even when the gateway pre-checks. Prefer introspection where revocation must reach running agents; local JWT validation is faster and blind to it. A server that accepts a token issued for any other audience fails the assessment.

Scopes are a catalogue owned outside the service: narrow, no omnibus scope, minimal set at first grant, and every scope an operation needs emitted in one `insufficient_scope` challenge so the client steps up in one round trip. Under enterprise-managed authorization a step-up is another exchange at the IdP, and the organisation's policy answers; under the public flow it is a consent screen listing exactly the added scope. Assessment probe: call a write tool with a read token and confirm a single 403 challenge names every scope the write needs.

items.title: Build stateless; a state handle is a name, not a capability
body: The current protocol has no sessions: every request is self-contained, which is what makes the tier horizontally scalable. Where tools need cross-call state, the server mints opaque handles — high-entropy, bound to the token's subject, expiring, and re-authorized against the presenting token on every request. Possession of a handle must prove nothing. Reject designs that carry trust in the handle, vary tool listings per connection, or reimplement session affinity. Require Origin validation and TLS termination evidence at the edge. Assessment probe: present a valid handle with a different subject's token and confirm the request fails.

items.title: The caller's token never travels upstream
body: Most servers wrap existing systems, and the one rule with no exceptions is at that boundary: the inbound token stops at the service. Two shapes pass review. On-behalf-of: the handler exchanges the inbound token at the authorization server for one whose audience is the upstream and whose scope is narrowed to the tool, so the upstream sees who is really asking and applies its own authorization — the preferred shape for internal systems that already understand the user. Service credential: the handler calls as itself on a credential the secrets manager issues, scopes and rotates, where no delegation exists. The third shape — forwarding the inbound token — is the confused deputy the protocol forbids by name, and the finding most often discovered in production. Bound egress to named upstream destinations; unbounded outbound reach from a tool server is the exfiltration path a steered agent is looking for.

On the data path, require the dual check on every operation — the scope permits it, and the tenant on the token matches the tenant on the record — enforced in a shared layer rather than re-implemented per handler. Assessment probe: a valid token for tenant A requesting tenant B's record by identifier, on a read as well as a write.

items.title: Ship tool text like code, and list the server like a dependency
body: Descriptions, schemas and error text execute inside the caller's model, so they ship through the same pipeline as code: versioned, reviewed as a security artifact, adversarially read for what a model will do with the words, and published with provenance. Publish to the registry or private subregistry consuming clients admit from, with versions pinned, so a definition that changes after approval is detectable by the people trusting it. Make consequential handlers return `input_required` and execute only on the retry that carries the confirmation — annotations are hints a client must treat as untrusted, so elicitation is the lever the server actually holds, though a confirmation proves only that the client answered, not that a person reviewed the action — and keep results bounded in size, because output lands in someone else's context window.

items.title: Test it like the published application it is
body: Behind the protocol this is an ordinary HTTP application with ordinary attack surface, and it ships through the ordinary release gate: dependency and code scanning, dynamic testing against the deployed endpoint, and the tenant-isolation checks exercised as tests rather than trusted as intentions. A tool server that skipped AppSec because "it is just MCP" skipped it for the one application whose caller is a machine that retries.

items.title: Audit per call, and design revocation before launch
body: The audit record is per tool call — client, user, tenant, tool, arguments, result, with trace context propagated — because it is both the incident trail and the answer to a customer asking what their agent did. Scope design is where a hijacked agent's blast radius is decided: a catalogue of narrow scopes owned outside the service, no omnibus scope, and step-up challenges rather than over-asking at consent. Revocation must work at three grains without a deploy: a user (at the IdP — a group removal ends every new ID-JAG at once), a client (at the authorization server), and a tool (at the definition layer) — and it must reach tokens already issued, which is what introspection, short access-token lifetimes and revoking refresh tokens with the grant buy; a group removal at the IdP reaches issued tokens only through a revocation signal or their expiry. Assessment probe: remove a test user from the granting group and confirm the agent's next call fails within one token lifetime, and that its refresh and re-exchange both fail.

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Pattern-level by design; serving products are named only in cited sources, not in the items.
overview: Self-hosting open weights trades a data-disclosure risk for a supply-chain, availability and safety risk: no provider applies content policy, absorbs spikes, or patches the serving stack. The requirements below are the provider role, written down — and the two facts that shape them are that the serving stacks assume a trusted network (auth is partial, auxiliary endpoints and distributed control planes ship open by design), and that multi-tenancy inside the runtime is a set of configuration flags with data-protection consequences.

The review posture: treat serving configuration as security configuration. Continuous batching, cache sharing, tenancy scoping and network binding are tuning knobs to the platform team and controls to the security team; the gap between those two readings is where the incidents in this archetype live.

items.title: Nothing reaches the runtime except through the gateway
body: The serving stack is not safe as an exposed edge service and its own API keys guard only part of the surface — so the gateway in front is mandatory, not optional: one governed door carrying workload identity per calling tenant, per-tenant quotas sized for finite capacity, and admission control that sheds load at the front rather than at the accelerator. The distributed control plane behind it — job APIs, inter-node channels — ships unauthenticated by design; network isolation is the control there, not a version bump. Assessment probe: enumerate every listening endpoint on the serving tier and demand the auth story for each.

items.title: A blocking promotion gate, and digest verification at load
body: Weights reach the runtime only through the promotion pipeline: format policy and scanning as a blocking gate, per-version evaluation because a new checkpoint is a new model, and verification at load against the approved digest recorded at promotion — a record the serving identity cannot alter — so the gate cannot be bypassed by writing to storage directly. Weights at rest get scoped access control: the artifact is expensive to reproduce and trivial to copy.

items.title: Tenancy is a configuration review, not a default
body: Continuous batching mixes tenants in one forward pass; the KV and prefix caches hold their live context. Require a secret per-tenant cache salt that the gateway sets on every request, overwriting any the caller sent — published attacks reconstruct other tenants' prompts from cache-hit timing alone — or turn prefix sharing off. Keep serving instances in separate processes; that isolates their memory, not the accelerator side channels, so where shared silicon is unacceptable for a tenant the answer is dedicated accelerators, a deployment decision with its residual risk stated. Assessment probe: send identical prefixes from two tenants and read the serving configuration for the settings a tenant boundary depends on.

items.title: Own the patch stream and the posture, including the gateway's
body: The serving stack is fast-moving third-party code with a live CVE stream, and nobody upstream patches it on your behalf — enumerate the versions running against the advisory feed so each advisory maps to the instances it affects, patch on your own schedule, and treat the gateway itself as supply chain: it is third-party code holding every tenant's credentials, an incident class with recent precedent. The content-policy checks a provider would have run are deployed at the gateway on both legs, because the output side is the half most often omitted.

items.title: Keep the lineage, the identities and a privacy-conscious record
body: Three records this system cannot run honestly without. The artifact inventory: which model version is serving where, its publisher, format and the scan that cleared it — without it "what is running" has no answer. The identity story: every calling tenant on a workload identity the platform issues, never a shared key in a config map. And the request log from the gateway tap, kept privacy-consciously — the log of an inference service is itself a corpus of everything the organisation asked it.

items.title: Red-team every version, and promote in stages you can reverse
body: A new checkpoint from the same publisher is a new model nobody else has tested, and no provider is testing it on your behalf: adversarial evaluation runs per version, before promotion. Promotion itself is staged — a slice of traffic first, the previous version kept loadable — so rollback is a registry operation rather than a re-download under incident pressure.

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Pattern-level by design; research findings are cited, vendors are not named in the items.
overview: Treat the pipeline as a build system and hold it to build-system controls: reproducible runs, provenance, signed artifacts, and a promotion gate nothing bypasses. Where the analogy breaks — the artifact cannot be diffed or read for backdoors — the substitutes are the two things that can be examined: what went into the training set, and how the result behaves. Every requirement below serves one of those two.

Scale the paranoia correctly: published results found a near-constant few hundred poisoned documents implanted a trigger backdoor across the model sizes they tested, backdoors in a base model survive tuning and the benchmarks that do not know their trigger, and fine-tuning on entirely benign data measurably erodes safety alignment. None of that is exotic; all of it is priced into the gates below.

items.title: Curate in front, with provenance captured at ingestion
body: Curation is the last point where a poisoned or improperly sourced example is a deletion rather than a retraining decision — filtering happens before the corpus, and per-example source and licence are recorded at ingestion because they cannot be reconstructed later. Lineage from every promoted model back to its exact dataset version is what makes a poisoning discovered months later scopeable at all. Include the labelling workforce in scope: labels steer behaviour directly and typically get no scrutiny relative to that influence.

items.title: Gate corpus access, and scope every job to its approved dataset
body: Corpus read access is the union of everything the organisation decided a model should learn, and it defaults to a broad platform role — gate reads and writes separately, and scope each training job to the dataset version approved for that run so a job cannot quietly widen its own inputs. Restricted-access content in the corpus becomes part of an artifact served far more widely than the dataset ever was; decide who may read the corpus with that in mind.

items.title: Sign at promotion, with a key the job never holds
body: The job writes an unsigned candidate; the signature happens at promotion, after the evaluation gate, with an identity the training environment never possesses — the default configuration usually violates this, so check rather than assume. Sign with the standardised model-signing tooling and verify at load in whichever tier serves it; a signature nobody checks is a checksum, and a signature the job could mint proves only that a job finished. Authorising a run against a named dataset version is a human decision, promotion is a second one made by a different person, and the lineage record — dataset version, code, base model, run — is written during the run rather than reconstructed from it. Candidates are immutable once written, and the signature covers exactly the digest the evaluator tested. Withdrawing a release in the registry stops future loads only where the serving tier checks release status; stopping instances already serving it is the serving tier's response.

items.title: Scan what comes in from upstream
body: Base checkpoints and training frameworks arrive from outside and execute with access to the corpus and the artifact: scan them before use, prefer formats that cannot execute on load, and treat scanner output as advisory next to format policy, because scanner bypasses are documented. What happens downstream of the artifact — staged promotion, traffic splitting, rollback — belongs to the tier that serves it, and is drawn on the self-hosted inference page rather than this one.

items.title: Evaluate behaviour before promotion, and guard the benchmarks themselves
body: How the result behaves is one of only two things anyone can examine, so it is a blocking gate, not advice: capability and safety evaluation, backdoor probing against triggers the training population could not have studied, and memorisation testing that asks whether restricted corpus content comes back out. Keep benchmark custody separate from the people and jobs being evaluated — a gate whose answer key the candidate's authors can edit gates nothing — run the evaluator isolated, with read-only access to candidates and no signing credential, and treat a safety regression after benign tuning as the expected finding, not a surprise.

items.title: Keep the record that answers next year's question
body: Who ran what against which dataset version, and what the artifact is — retained past the artifact's own lifetime, because the question a poisoning raises arrives months after the run. Model documentation travels with the artifact through the registry rather than living in a wiki: the serving tier's operators read the registry entry, not the training team's notes.

items.title: Apply privacy tech and hardening where the data and the use demand it
body: Neither is a default. Where sensitive records enter the corpus, de-identification or differential-privacy transforms run at curation, priced against the utility loss they cause. Where the tuned model's use is safety-critical, decide whether adversarial or safety-preserving training recipes apply; no control pinned here implements them, so record the decision and what the evaluation will measure. State the applicability decision either way — a control assumed universal is a control nobody verified.

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Vendor and product facts are confined to the dated tool entries and their cited documentation, verified at authoring time.
overview: A browser agent acts inside sessions that are already signed in, and every page it reads is untrusted input. The organisation does not build it — a browser ships it or a store installs it — so the leverage is three tiers the organisation already runs: browser policy over the profile and its extensions, the secure web gateway every session leaves through, and the vendor's admin console.

The controls that hold up constrain what the session can reach rather than what the model may say. Scope comes first, because no later control can narrow the set of signed-in origins a hostile page can act on once the profile holds them. Vendor features such as injection classifiers and action screening are credited through the vendor assessment, not counted as screens the organisation operates.

items.title: Scope the profile before anything else
body: Run the agent in a dedicated, managed browser profile signed into the few origins it needs, with no saved passwords or autofill — the vendors' own safety guidance asks for exactly this. A profile is a scope decision, not an OS boundary: it limits which sessions a steered agent can use, and nothing more.
Set site-level permissions — act, read only, no access — from the vendor console so they override the user's own grants, and start from an allowlist of origins rather than a blocklist.

items.title: Admit extensions and agentic browsers by policy, and pin their updates
body: Use browser policy to allow extensions by identifier, block by requested permission, and pin reviewed versions where the browser supports it, so an update is a decision rather than an event. The store's review is the only review an extension otherwise gets.

Inventory the extensions and assistant panels nobody enrolled, from the device and from the edge, and reconcile them against the approved list — this archetype spreads one click at a time, and assistant panels ship enabled to installed bases nobody chose.

items.title: Confirm consequential actions, and enforce the action policy from the console
body: Define the confirmation set by consequence — payments, sends, publishing, permission changes, credential entry — and require that action, on that site, to be approved before it runs. Remove the mode that skips approvals wherever the admin tier can; where it cannot pin the mode, record that as a gap rather than a setting.

Managed settings make the site lists, blocked action classes and approval mode non-overridable on the device. Check per product and plan which of these the console actually enforces; defaults differ and change.

items.title: Inspect what leaves at the edge
body: The managed browser trusts the enterprise root and sends every session through the secure web gateway, so the inference hop to the vendor can be inspected: classify and redact authenticated page content before it leaves. The control holds only where the gateway can parse the agent's payload — test with representative traffic, and block a payload it cannot parse rather than passing it.

Allowlist where the agent may browse, at the gateway and in managed browser policy on the agent's profile, so the rule applies to the agent's browsing and not the user's. An allowed destination is still an exfiltration path; the allowlist narrows it.

items.title: Screen page content, and govern what the agent remembers
body: Strip hidden and off-screen content at page extraction and classify what remains before it becomes context. This bounds injection; it does not prevent it, which is why scope and confirmation come first.

Limit which origins may be remembered, keep sensitive ones out, record the page each memory came from so memories can be deleted or rolled back by origin, and treat memory as untrusted on every read — a page read once can otherwise steer every later task.

items.title: Bind the account, keep the record, and rehearse the stop
body: Federate the vendor account to the IdP with MFA enforced there — SSO alone is not MFA — and bind the extension to the organisation's tenant so it cannot sign into a personal account.

Fuse the gateway's session record with the vendor's audit export, and add in-browser telemetry of what the agent read and clicked, compared against its normal pattern per origin; only that vantage point sees both.

Decide the stop before it is needed: force-remove the extension by browser policy, disable the agent in the vendor console and revoke the profile's sessions — then confirm that running and queued tasks actually stopped, in every browser shape the fleet runs.

items.title: Assess the vendor for what it keeps
body: Whole pages, screenshots and synced memories go to the vendor. Review retention, memory sync, subprocessors and the managed-settings surface per product and plan; a claim that holds for one vendor's enterprise tier is not a property of the category.

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Pattern-level by design; harness products are named only in cited sources, not in the items.
overview: A first-party coding harness is the third-party product with the vendor column deleted: the same loop and tool surface, with pasted long-lived keys instead of session credentials, community registries instead of a signed channel, and configuration files instead of a control plane. Nothing here can be governed from a vendor console, which puts every control on the organisation's side. Remote steering — relays, chat bridges, exposed serve ports — is not part of this reference.

Two facts anchor the policy. The supply chain includes the agent itself: the category's landmark incident was a compromised harness release published through a community channel, whose payload installed further agents. And the serve ports ship weak: their auth ranges from a mandatory shared secret down to none, so they stay bound to localhost.

The mode is hybrid because the organisation genuinely builds part of this: the AI gateway, the private mirror and the governance band are tiers we stand up and operate, while the harness itself is upstream software we configure and pin. The items below say which side of that line each control lives on.

items.title: Sanction specific harnesses, and pin their supply chain
body: Take a position on which harnesses are acceptable, and mirror them: harness releases, extensions and skills reviewed, version-pinned and served from the organisation's registry, with public marketplaces blocked on managed machines. An update is a decision — the update channel is the category's proven attack path. Pair the position with discovery built from package-manager and process telemetry, because these harnesses arrive one developer at a time and appear in no procurement record.

items.title: Vault the keys and route the calls through your gateway
body: The common state is a provider key in plaintext configuration, readable by the agent, its tools, and any repository script they run. The sanctioned state brokers credentials at the organisation's AI gateway — keychain-backed locally where the harness supports it, vaulted behind the gateway where it does not — with deny-by-default egress naming providers, registries and remote tool servers, and spend ceilings at the crossing, because the only native meter is the provider's invoice. Assessment probe: grep a sanctioned install's configuration for key material; anything found fails.

items.title: Keep serve ports local and the approval gate real
body: Relays, tunnels, chat bridges and web UIs reached from another device stay off on managed machines; serve ports stay bound to localhost, behind a mandatory shared secret where the harness offers one. Keep the local approval gate real: dangerous-command detection on and auto-approve flags banned on managed machines — it is the only gate there is.

items.title: The engine disciplines still apply — nobody else will apply them
body: Everything the vendored guidance requires of the engine holds here with no managed tier to enforce it: per-tool permission scoping configured outside the repository the agent works on; sandboxed execution treated as a harness-selection criterion, because the category default is bare-host; SSH keys, cloud credentials and browser profiles kept outside what the sandbox can reach; agent writes scoped to its own memory files, kept under version history so a poisoned note can be rolled back, with rules, hooks and settings changed only as reviewed code; and repository content and tool results treated as instruction-bearing input, screened at the gateway where they cross it.

items.title: Log at the gateway
body: A built control: the gateway tap is the only record of brokered calls, because there is no vendor console and no audit export; what does not cross the gateway is on record only through endpoint telemetry, which is the argument for routing everything that can through it.

items.title: Inventory the fleet and inspect what leaves
body: The approved-harness inventory is enforced from the gateway and the mirror — which builds run, which connectors and servers they may reach — not from the config files the agent can edit. Content inspection sits on the direct web path, where a search query or a fetch can carry repository content or a key out. And the device tooling closes the gap no crossing sees: which harness processes run, which ports they listen on and what their children execute.

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Vendor and product facts are confined to the dated tool entries and their cited documentation, verified at authoring time.
overview: Nobody builds their own Claude Code — this archetype is consumed, so the organisation's leverage is the policy tier each vendor ships. Every major coding agent now has one: a managed configuration channel that outranks whatever the developer sets locally, deliverable through MDM, an OS policy store, or the vendor's own admin console. Governing the archetype means using that tier deliberately, and holding one posture across four or five different products rather than five postures.

The guidance below is organised by control, not by product; the dated tool entries under each item carry the product-specific mechanics. Where vendors differ in strength — a console-delivered setting one vendor calls a client-side control versus an OS-enforced sandbox — the difference is called out, because it changes what the control is worth.

items.title: Deploy policy through the managed tier, not through documentation
body: Each vendor's managed tier can pin permission rules, approval behaviour and feature availability so the local user cannot loosen them: managed settings for Claude Code, an enforced requirements file for Codex, dashboard-plus-MDM policies for Cursor, and enterprise policies for Copilot. Treat a written standard with no managed-tier enforcement as not yet deployed.

Two properties are worth demanding everywhere: the auto-approval escape hatch is removable (the mode where the agent stops asking), and the policy channel fails closed — both Claude Code and Codex can refuse to start when the managed policy cannot be fetched, which turns a lost policy server into a stop rather than an unmanaged fleet.

Watch the conflict semantics per vendor: Copilot resolves a user's multiple organisations to the least restrictive setting within an enterprise, so a lockdown only holds when set at the enterprise level.

items.title: Constrain the native tools with allowlists backed by a registry
body: The configuration file that admits tool servers arrives with the repository clone, which is why the allowlist has to be enforced outside it. Every one of the four vendors now supports centrally-managed MCP server allowlists; the shared semantics to get right are the empty-list case (for Claude Code and Codex an empty managed list is a full MCP lockdown, which is the correct starting state) and the matching strength — prefer the mechanisms that match on executable, URL or command rather than display name, since name-only matching is bypassable by design.

The allowlist is the enforcement point; the registry behind it is the decision record. Admit a server after a supply-chain review of its source, and keep the approved set somewhere reviewable rather than in a dashboard nobody diffs.

items.title: Sandbox execution and default-deny the network
body: The strongest available posture is OS-enforced sandboxing with the network off by default and a domain-filtered proxy where egress is genuinely needed — Codex ships exactly this shape, and its managed tier can forbid the profiles that escape it. Where a product's controls are weaker, the vendor's own documentation often says so: Cursor labels its terminal allowlist best-effort rather than a security boundary. Read those admissions as design guidance — pair weak in-product controls with endpoint-level egress filtering rather than treating them as equivalent.

Protect the paths that hold standing credentials from the agent regardless of sandbox: enforced deny-read patterns for key material and dotfiles are available in the managed tier (Codex's filesystem rules; Claude Code permission deny rules) and cost nothing to deploy fleet-wide.

items.title: Bind sessions to the organisation and export the audit trail
body: Force organisational login so every session maps to a directory identity, with MFA enforced at the IdP behind it — SSO alone is not MFA. Claude Code and the Codex clients can both pin the login method and organisation, and block ambient personal API keys; broker model credentials through managed helpers rather than long-lived keys in the environment.

Know what each audit surface actually captures before relying on it: Claude Code's managed OpenTelemetry emits per-session tool-decision events fleet-wide; Codex local usage exports through the workspace Compliance API; Cursor's Enterprise audit log records admin and account events but explicitly not agent output; Copilot's org audit log covers policy and licensing changes and the cloud agent's actions, not IDE prompts. The gaps define what endpoint or gateway logging still has to cover.

items.title: Deploy the desktop apps managed and govern connectors at the organisation, not the user
body: The desktop-shaped shells of this archetype reach the enterprise through the same door as any desktop software — someone installs one — but they connect to mail, files, calendars and internal services through per-user connector grants that no one sums. Both major desktop assistants now ship enterprise installers and honour device-level policy (MDM configuration profiles and policy registries), and both have org-level admission controls for what the assistant may connect to — allowlists for desktop extensions and role-scoped app and plugin enablement. The defaults differ in a way that matters: one vendor's extension allowlist ships disabled (everything available until an admin turns it on) while the other disables plugins by default on enterprise workspaces. Check the default, don't assume it.

Where managed connector authorization through the IdP is available, prefer it over per-user OAuth grants: it makes the connector's scope an administered decision and keeps revocation in the directory rather than in each employee's settings.

items.title: Contain what the desktop shells can reach from the device
body: Device policies can turn off the highest-risk local surfaces — local MCP server connections, computer-use and record modes, unmanaged workspace folders — and pin updates to managed channels. What the policies cannot see is content leaving through sanctioned chat, which is why this archetype pairs the vendor controls with interaction-level data loss prevention and network egress telemetry; the compliance export APIs both vendors ship are the hook for that monitoring, with source retention short enough that continuous export is part of the deployment, not an afterthought.

items.title: Assess the vendor as the tier it is
body: The vendor's service carries the organisation's code, documents and screenshots on a session this reference admits by allowlist rather than inspects — the assessment behind the allowlist entry is the control. Review retention terms, tenancy, subprocessor disclosure (including which model providers sit behind the service) and the managed-settings surface per product and edition; a claim that holds for one vendor's enterprise tier is not a property of the category.

items.title: Treat memory and rules as code, and broker every credential
body: The persistent instruction channel — memory files, AGENTS.md-class rules, settings hooks — is executable content: a repo-committed rules change is a code change and reviews like one, agent writes are scoped to its own memory files under version history so a poisoned note can be traced and rolled back, and agent-written notes are untrusted input on every later read. Credentials are brokered at the crossing per call rather than standing in configuration, and per-call policy is evaluated at the gateway, outside the application being governed — the one place the developer running the agent cannot override it.

items.title: Discover what you did not deploy, and assume the repo is hostile input
body: The managed tier only governs the clients you deployed; developers can install others, and IDE forks and extensions ship agent capability by default now. Discovery — endpoint software inventory, extension allowlists, egress telemetry to known vendor endpoints — is what makes the sanctioned-tools list a fact rather than an aspiration.

Prompt injection for this archetype arrives with the working tree: source files, manifests, issue text and tool output all enter the context window without being the developer's instruction. That is an argument for keeping approval gates meaningful (a gate that fires on everything trains reflexive acceptance) and for treating repo-supplied configuration — hooks, tool manifests, agent instruction files — as untrusted until reviewed, which is what the managed hook and sideload restrictions in the vendor policy tiers exist to enforce.

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Pattern-level by design; runtime products are named only in cited sources, not in the items.
overview: A local model runtime is a network service one person installs in an afternoon: it binds a port, speaks an OpenAI-compatible API, and in the flagship implementations ships without authentication by design — the vendors point at VPNs and reverse proxies rather than shipping auth. Everything a hosted API supplied — guardrails, rate limits, abuse monitoring, patching — is absent unless the device owner adds it, and the organisation's problem starts with not knowing the runtime exists.

Two facts should anchor the policy. Exposure is real and growing: internet scans keep finding these runtimes by the tens of thousands, bound to routable interfaces by users who never made that decision consciously. And the model files themselves are attack surface: formats that execute code on load, native parsers whose memory bugs are a code-execution class, and embedded templates that execute at inference time.

items.title: Publish a sanctioned runtime posture, and enforce it from the device
body: Take a position: whether local inference may run at all, on which runtimes, bound to loopback only, with authentication in front of the port — a reverse proxy or token-authenticated wrapper where the runtime itself refuses to ship auth, each calling application holding its own token and the raw runtime reachable only by the wrapper. Locality is not authorization: a browser tab is local too, and a permissive cross-origin policy lets any visited page drive the runtime. Require local-only mode: the runtime's cloud models and web search switched off and its outbound traffic denied at the device firewall, with model downloads left to the controlled fetch to quarantine. Device management is the enforcement point, because there is no server side to enforce from.

items.title: Fetch to quarantine, scan at rest, load only what was promoted
body: The sequencing is the control: the artifact is acquired without being loaded, verified and scanned in quarantine, then promoted to the approved storage the runtime loads from — never fetched and opened in one step, which is what the common install does. Format policy runs as its own gate (safe-by-construction tensor formats required, executable formats refused), independent of provenance and scanning — passing one buys nothing at the others. Treat "safe" formats as reduced surface rather than no surface: their native parsers carry their own code-execution bug class. Protect the artifacts on disk with restrictive permissions — only promotion writes approved files, only the runtime reads them — so another process can neither swap nor copy them; the organisation's own adapters beside the public weights are the part worth stealing.

items.title: Replace the provider floor the callers assume is there
body: Local applications call the local API the way they would a hosted one, assuming a safety floor that is not there. Where local inference is sanctioned for real use, require the missing pieces on the request path: input and output classification, a per-caller rate bound on the shared unmetered port, and an evaluation of what the weights actually do before other software builds on them — there is no provider evaluation to inherit, and refusal behaviour is removable by fine-tune.

items.title: Inventory what is running, and find what never registered
body: Every response to a bad model release, a parser CVE or an exposure report presumes the organisation knows which machines run which runtimes serving which models from which sources. Build that inventory from the device — process, port and model-file telemetry — rather than from self-reporting, because this archetype spreads one install at a time and appears in no procurement record.

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Vendor and product facts are confined to the dated tool entries and their cited documentation, verified at authoring time.
overview: An always-on personal agent is a daemon a person runs with their own credentials, taking ambient instructions from messaging channels and acting without a human in the loop. The organisation rarely operates it — someone installs it because it is useful — so governing this archetype means publishing a sanctioned way to run it that is safer than the default, and making the unsanctioned way visibly out of policy.

The archetype's exposure is concentrated in two places: the runtime (what the agent can execute, read and reach) and the control plane (the daemon's local control API, which admits instructions and holds the operator's authority). Both have hardened configurations that exist today; the controls below are about making those configurations the required path.

items.title: Sanction a hardened runtime, or people will pick their own
body: Take a position on which runtimes are acceptable and publish it. A bare-host install — the agent executing shell commands directly on the operating system with the user's full profile — is not an acceptable posture for a daemon that takes instructions from inbound messages. The sanctioned configurations are the containerised ones: an OpenClaw-class agent with its sandbox backend enabled (tool execution isolated in a container with no network, a read-only root and dropped capabilities) or run inside a purpose-built sandbox product that adds an egress proxy; or a Hermes-class runtime whose execution goes through per-command approval and one of its isolated terminal backends.

The configurations differ in what they contain. An agent-native sandbox backend isolates tool execution only — the daemon, its memory and its credentials stay on the host. The microVM wrap contains the harness whole, keeps secrets host-side behind an injecting proxy, and shares only named workspace folders in; it is the only configuration under which the products' approval-free default is defensible. Sanction the whole-harness wrap where it is available, and in enterprise deployments require clone-mode (read-only) workspace sharing so agent edits return by git rather than landing on the host as they happen.

Pair the runtime position with a tool-policy floor: high-risk tools (arbitrary shell, browser control, unrestricted fetch) disabled unless the deployment has a stated need, and per-agent tool policies rather than one permissive default.

items.title: Lock down the control plane and keep credentials out of the agent
body: The daemon's local control API — the product calls it its gateway; it is not the AI gateway on the drawing — is the operator's authority; treat its exposure as the incident. Require loopback-only binding with token authentication, and set a version floor at the release that closed the control-plane token-exfiltration CVE — the exposed-instance scans that followed it are the case for making this a hard requirement rather than a recommendation.

Keep provider keys and account credentials out of the agent's own environment where the tooling allows it: sandbox egress through a proxy that injects API keys on the way out, so a compromised agent process has nothing durable to leak, and default-deny network egress from the execution sandbox with an explicit allowlist for what the agent legitimately needs to reach.

items.title: Keep a human between the agent and anything hard to undo
body: Unattended operation is the archetype's point, so the approval budget has to be spent precisely: dangerous-command detection with a blocking approval step, pairing codes or allowlists before an unknown sender can instruct the agent at all, and mention-gating in group channels. These are runtime-enforced policies in the current tooling, not etiquette.

Decide the quarantine path before the first incident: who can stop a personal agent, what stopping means (revoking the daemon's control token and its AI-gateway credentials, killing the daemon and its heartbeat, expiring its channel pairings), and how a compromised agent's standing access is enumerated afterwards.

items.title: Govern what the agent loads and what it remembers
body: Personal agents grow by acquiring skills, tools and server connections from public registries, and they keep long-lived memory. Both are injection surfaces: a fetched skill is unreviewed code admitted into the operator's session, and ambient-message instructions can write durable state into memory that outlives the message. Require vetting before third-party skills or tool servers are admitted, keep memory under snapshots so a poisoned entry can be traced and rolled back, and treat memory as contaminated-by-default when the agent ingests content from senders who are not the operator.

items.title: Authenticate every surface, and bind the channels to identities you govern
body: The control socket authenticates every message from its client, with origin checks at the handshake — localhost is not a boundary against the owner's own browser, which is the documented token-exfiltration path — and the bridges bind to loopback; the remote dashboard rides an identity-bound tunnel, never a port on the device. Pairing records bind each channel to a directory identity under one centrally administered policy, which every adapter enforces per message rather than trusting enrolment day.

items.title: Broker delegation, bound the spend, and keep the record
body: Remote calls carry on-behalf-of tokens exchanged at the crossing, each with one tool server as its audience and the task as its scope — never the owner's standing grants riding a loop nobody watches. Spend and iteration ceilings are sized for a heartbeat that wakes the loop with no human to notice a runaway. And one correlated trace per brokered call — prompt, tool calls, effects — is written where the agent cannot amend it and joined to the relay's and the endpoint's records, because the thread is not the audit trail.

items.title: Police the model boundary, and find what nobody registered
body: The inspection a hosted product would have applied runs at the crossing on both legs, because no provider is applying it. Discovery is derived from the device rather than self-reported — this archetype spreads one enthusiast at a time — and endpoint telemetry watches the daemon itself: a long-lived process with shell access is what commodity stealers target, and incident 06's payload was exactly that.

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Pattern-level by design; incidents are cited, vendors are not named in the items.
overview: The organisation's exposure here is a sum nobody computes by default: thousands of individually reasonable connector grants, a file-upload path no connector governance sees, and a consumer version of the same product one session cookie away. The controls split cleanly into two halves — the vendor tenant you configure, and the edge and browser telemetry you own — and the second half matters more, because it covers the consumer product the vendor's console cannot see and the upload path before anything leaves.

One material change to re-review against: these products are agents now. The same standing grants that powered retrieval also carry write actions — mail sent, files changed, tickets moved — through vendor-side agent modes, scheduled tasks and code execution. The documented incident class is zero-click: content in a connected mailbox or drive steers the assistant into exfiltrating without the user clicking anything.

items.title: Restrict the tenant at the edge, or the enterprise terms are optional
body: Everything the enterprise agreement promises — retention, training opt-out, audit export — applies only to traffic that reaches the managed tenant. Tenant restriction enforced at the secure edge is what stops the consumer product being an alternative; without it, the crossing simply succeeds and corporate data leaves under consumer terms, invisibly. Identity establishes who is licensed and which tenant they may reach; the edge blocks or logs everything else. A hostname allowlist cannot tell the two tenants apart at the same host — that takes the vendor's tenant-restriction header, injected by a proxy that inspects TLS for the client in use, or a managed browser. Test a personal session to the same host.

items.title: Inspect the upload path, because nothing else can
body: A pasted or uploaded document crosses the boundary with no connector and no grant — every control that watches connectors misses it entirely. Inspect it at submission: endpoint or managed-browser DLP that blocks or masks a hit before the request is sent. Whether the network edge can also read it depends on the client and on TLS inspection being supported for it, so test the client you deploy with pasted text and uploaded files. The vendor's audit export may record the exchange afterwards, with coverage and retention that vary by plan; the endpoint record is the one you control.

items.title: Gate the agent modes and write-capable connectors deliberately
body: Own tenant configuration as living policy, re-reviewed every time the vendor ships a connector or an agent capability — the default for new ones is rarely off. Write actions get the strictest treatment the vendor offers: admin-gated per app and per action, with confirmation required on writes; the vendor ships the toggles, and leaving them at default is the decision not to use them. On our own tools, the gateway refuses a write without approval bound to the exact action; that approval is relayed through the vendor's client, so confirm per client that it is supported, and fail closed where it is not. Treat connector-retrieved and web-search content as untrusted in policy and user guidance: the vendor's own guardrails are assured, not configured, and the zero-click incident record says they are not sufficient alone; records returning through our gateway are screened there.

items.title: Inventory and revoke standing grants, and classify before connecting
body: Standing OAuth grants authorize the vendor's client on a person's behalf and can outlive that person: inventory them, expire them where the vendor allows, and revoke them when the employee or project goes — the broker keeps calling on grants issued for projects that ended. Connect only services held under agreement: admin consent on the target tenant and the vendor's connector policy decide what counts as approved, and nothing else is connected. Govern by classification which of those systems may be connected at all, so individual consent cannot outrun policy, and know what sensitive data sits inside connector reach before the grants aggregate it — an assistant makes pre-existing oversharing instantly discoverable.

items.title: Assess once, then watch the tenant continuously
body: The point-in-time assessment — retention terms, tenancy, subprocessors, the controls behind the allowlist entry — is the admission ticket; the standing control is continuous posture over the tenant: configuration drift detection, the vendor's audit stream ingested as it changes, and the connector inventory kept current across both the admin-granted corpora and the user-granted connections. A tenant reviewed once and watched never is a tenant whose controls are whatever the last admin left behind.

items.title: Hold the crossing's keys, and scope what the product may reach
body: The tunnel host's runtime credential is the load-bearing secret on the one path we run — issued short-lived, rotated, and revocable without a redeploy, with the host patched and monitored like the crossing it is. Our gateway decides which MCP servers the product may reach and on whose grant.

items.title: Fuse the vendor's audit with your own, and hunt the shadow traffic
body: The vendor's export covers the managed tenant, as far as its fields and retention go; your edge and browser telemetry cover the consumer product it will never see and the uploads before they leave — only the fused record answers what actually left. Run discovery for personal-account and competitor traffic independently of the vendor: it is usually the larger flow, and it is the population the sanctioned tenant exists to absorb.
