guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Pattern-level by design; products are named only in cited sources and in the tooling registry, not in the items.
overview: Hosted coding agents share one shape: the endpoint engine run in a per-session sandbox on the vendor's compute, started from the vendor's web app (or the same synced session in its desktop or mobile app), a chat surface, a repository event or a schedule. A hand-off from a local session is the endpoint guidance's. The coding profile finishes with a draft pull request; general desktop work finishes at an authorized application or file action. Require approved initiators, an ephemeral sandbox, an egress allowlist an administrator locks, the repository credential kept out of the sandbox where the product supports it, a token that reaches one branch and cannot merge, a reviewer who is not the initiator, and workflows that wait for a person — plus two things to build yourself: an inventory of the sessions, automations and channels somebody enabled, and a stop with a known delay. Which products meet each requirement is dated evidence in the tooling registry, not a property of the class.

What differs from the local twin is custody and attention. The loop runs unattended, so an injected instruction runs to completion; the vendor holds the repository grant, so revocation is a vendor action; egress is the vendor's policy, so the corporate proxy, DLP and IP allowlists never see the traffic; and the human's approval moves from each tool call to the merge. Treat the merge gate as approving the output, never the actions taken to produce it, and put the containment on the sandbox and the egress where those actions happen.

items.title: Decide hosted mode per group, and know who a session runs as
body: Hosted mode is an organisation decision, not a user one: enable it per role or group behind federated login and trusted-device enrolment, and keep the switches that widen it — quick web setup with a personal token, self-hosted runners, remote control — off until a named owner asks. Before any other control is assessed, establish which principal a product's sessions act as: the user (their commits and replies carry their identity), an App with the user as co-author, or a shared service identity for channels and automations. Inventory every App installation, service identity, routine, automation and shared environment with an owner and an expiry, because the vendor keeps no such list and "revoke this agent" is a different operation for each kind. Assessment probe: for one session, name the principal it acted as and the single operation that would have stopped it.

items.title: Only approved initiators start a session
body: The repository host is the ingress. Require that a session can be started or steered only by a person with write access or by a registered automation or schedule with a named owner and a bounded identity — never by a comment from someone the repository merely admits, or by an unregistered App or bot — and confirm the product enforces it rather than documenting it. Treat issue text, comments, review threads and instruction files as untrusted input: hidden characters and HTML comments are filtered, and content from non-collaborators never becomes a standing instruction. Every 2026 incident in this class began with text someone without commit access was allowed to write.

items.title: Lock the egress allowlist, and restrict what the permitted hosts may receive
body: Defaults diverge across products — off in the agent phase on some, allow-all on others — so set the environment's network policy deliberately and lock it at the organisation so a user cannot widen it. Separate the setup phase, which needs registries, from the agent phase, which usually needs nothing. The allowlist bounds where setup reaches, not what it installs: have the reviewed setup script install pinned versions verified against lockfile hashes or signatures, and fail the setup on a mismatch. Then remember the two facts the allowlist does not fix: some traffic may bypass it (verify per product — the vendor's connector service, the git proxy, the inference API), and the hosts every list must permit — the repository host, the package registries — are write-capable, so restrict methods where the product allows and watch those destinations for writes. Confirm the sandbox is one microVM or container per session with no shared filesystem, reclaimed at the end, and that snapshots have a retention you chose. The connector and MCP allowlist belongs in the same locked environment, where the session cannot widen it.

items.title: Keep the repository credential out of the sandbox
body: Prefer the products whose proxy substitutes a scoped credential so the sandbox holds a placeholder; where a product does not, record that the token is in the sandbox and scope it accordingly. Put secrets where the model cannot read them — setup-phase secrets removed before the agent runs, runtime secrets redacted from transcripts and commits — and treat environment variables as visible to the model and to everyone who shares the environment. Verify the plan-gated gaps per product: proxied API credentials exist on some plans and not others.

items.title: One branch, no merge, a reviewer who is not the initiator
body: The session's token reaches one repository and one branch; it cannot push the default branch, mark a pull request ready, approve it or merge it. A human reviews the draft, the initiator's approval does not count toward the required number, and any workflow the pull request would fire waits for "approve and run", and the agent's own configuration — instruction files, hooks, setup scripts, MCP config — sits under CODEOWNERS so a session cannot change what the next one runs. Disable automations that approve pull requests on the agent's behalf, and do not let an agent's replies fire comment-triggered automation. Inside the session, pick the permission mode the tenant allows — unattended runs have no prompt to answer, so remove bypass modes in managed settings and let the environment's allowlists do the work the prompt would have done.

items.title: The gate approves the output; contain the actions
body: By the time a reviewer sees the draft, every tool call, fetch and push the session made has already happened. Write the assessment that way: the merge gate is an output control, and the sandbox, the egress allowlist and the credential proxy are the action controls. Leave the vendor's own classifiers on — hidden-character filtering, auto-mode reviewers, browser safety checks — as a second layer, never the only one, and set session budgets and automation caps so a loop that re-triggers itself on its own replies has a ceiling.

items.title: The gateway is on the tool path only; re-obtain inference controls from the tenant
body: Assume the hosted loop's inference does not pass your gateway: the hosted mode keeps it with the provider, and runner variants may too, so verify per product. Admit the vendor's connector service to your MCP servers at your gateway — through the vendor's outbound-only tunnel where it ships one, so no endpoint of yours faces the internet, and on an allowlisted public endpoint only where it does not — on per-user, audience-bound grants you issue, scoped to a named server list, and classify what returns before it goes back to a loop you cannot see. That classification covers only calls brokered through your gateway; connectors the vendor calls directly return content it never sees, so limit them at the connector allowlist. The tunnel is transport: it authenticates nothing, and its token and TLS key are secrets to rotate. Everything the gateway does for inference elsewhere — model allowlist, prompt inspection, spend ceilings, the prompt-level record — has to be re-obtained as tenant configuration and exported audit. Assess the platform's isolation, retention and tenancy claims like any critical vendor dependency, and re-assess on a clock because the defaults move: egress on or off, self-approving automations, which plan gets proxied credentials, whether the compliance export covers this surface at all.

items.title: Fuse the exports, and define the stop with its delay
body: Export the vendor's session logs and agentic audit events and fuse them with the repository host's record and your gateway's, so one session has one trail from trigger to merge; confirm per product which surfaces the export actually covers, because at least one vendor's compliance export is documented for local and remote sessions but not the hosted coding surface. Decide what persists — agent-written memory merged into later sessions, transcripts shareable outside the organisation, snapshots kept for months — and set each deliberately. Then write down the stop: disabling hosted mode, uninstalling the App or revoking the seat prevents the next session and does not stop the running one, so name the vendor's cancel and how long it takes.

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Pattern-level by design; incidents are cited, vendors are not named in the items.
overview: The unit of risk in this archetype is the population, not the agent: hundreds of near-identical agents, each simple, each holding connector grants, many authored by people who have left. There is no code review between an afternoon's work and something that acts on production data unless the platform's gates are turned on — and several of the platform defaults (sharing scope, agent-to-agent discovery, soft-enabled policy) are set for adoption, not governance.

The decisive technical question when evaluating or configuring any platform in this class: does a published agent execute on its author's credentials or its invoker's? Author-credential execution turns publishing into a privilege grant — a user who could not read a table reads it through an agent someone else built — and no amount of population management compensates for getting this one wrong.

items.title: Build the inventory first; everything else depends on it
body: Every agent, its author, its connector set, its audience, its sharing mode and its last use — the platforms now report this, and the vendors sell fleet-level control planes over it. Pair the inventory with run history per agent and per consumer: it is the basis for retiring what nobody uses, investigating what someone did, and noticing the agents shared to "anyone with the link" on the vendor's own domain, where exposure research keeps finding them by the thousands.

items.title: Decide who may build, and demand invoker-credential execution
body: Restricting who may build is the bluntest and often most effective population control — on several platforms, creating an agent by default needs no more than ordinary user rights. Require per-invoker authorisation so the organisation's existing access model survives publication; where a connection runs on stored credentials whoever invokes the agent, the tools behind it must check the invoker themselves. Use the platforms' per-agent identities: an agent that signs in as its own directory principal can be verified and refused by conditional access one agent at a time, and the same principal is the handle for transferring ownership when authors leave.

items.title: Author connector policy centrally, and gate publication
body: Blocking a connector pairing scales where reviewing agents does not: a source of confidential data plus a path that sends mail is the pairing worth banning outright. Check the enforcement default on whatever platform is in use — some enforce centrally out of the box, others ship policy soft-enabled where makers never feel it. Where the platform offers environments and deployment pipelines with an approver, route consequential agents through them so review stands between an author and an audience; they are the nearest available thing to code review, and they are optional.

items.title: Treat grounding sources as instruction channels
body: A shared agent's knowledge source is frequently a folder anyone can write to — an instruction channel wearing a grounding label, where one planted document steers the agent for every user. Restrict attachable locations to ones with governed write access, govern by classification what connectors may reach at all, and know what sensitive data sits inside connector reach before hundreds of agents find it. Where the platform does not inspect knowledge a maker uploads — the mainstream ones do not — approve what may be uploaded before an agent is published. Screen grounding that returns through your own gateway; the platform's own injection screening is supplier assurance. Check whether agent-to-agent discovery is on and decide deliberately whether it should be: one steered agent recruiting a teammate's stronger connectors is the documented second-order path.

items.title: Publish in stages, and watch the population for drift
body: Publication is delivery: versioned agents, a limited audience before the whole team where the platform offers one, and re-activating the previous version as the rollback; unpublish alone only stops the agent. Over a population of hundreds, drift is the signal worth automating — export each run's tool, connector and retrieval steps, and the agent whose connector mix or run pattern moved from its baseline is the one to quarantine before an incident names it. Test what can be tested: vendor internals are opaque, but a published agent, its policies and its connector boundaries are all black-box testable, and should be.

items.title: Own the tunnel host like the crossing it is
body: Point the platform's tunnel at your AI gateway, never straight at a data source, so every call into your systems meets the same scoping and record. The relay caches connection credentials on a host somebody must patch: rotate those secrets on a schedule, revoke them without redeploying the host, monitor its health, and decommission it deliberately when the last connection moves off it.

items.title: Run it as a programme, and assure what you cannot test
body: Maker governance is ongoing: environments and licensing, lifecycle and ownership transfer, retirement as somebody's actual job — the population grows by default and shrinks only on purpose. The platform's internal execution, isolation and model safeguards are assured the way any critical vendor control is assured, not tested; the settings it exposes and the boundaries a published agent touches can be probed directly. Revisit when the vendor ships the features that change the answer.

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Pattern-level by design; platforms are named only in cited sources, not in the items.
overview: Every provider converged on the same decomposition — runtime, memory, tool gateway, identity, sandbox, observability, evaluation, policy — which means the governance plane most self-built agent architectures never get is exactly what these platforms sell. The organisation's job splits accordingly: require teams to actually use the supplied controls (the platform makes them available, not mandatory), and configure the customer-owned half deliberately rather than accepting defaults.

The consequential engineering choice is between the declarative harness and the code escape hatch. The first inherits the platform's guardrails automatically; the second inherits only what it explicitly calls. Teams start declarative, hit a limitation, move to code, and do not notice which controls stopped applying — make that transition a review event, because the platform will not.

items.title: Use a per-agent identity where the platform mints one, and carry the user's
body: The hyperscaler runtimes mint a revocable principal per agent; the first-party runtimes do not, and the agent acts as whatever its vault holds. Where a principal exists, use it — teams routinely collapse everything back onto one shared service principal, which undoes attribution and per-agent revocation in one stroke. Where it does not, inventory every vault entry and environment key with an owner and an expiry. Either way, require the user's identity to travel from the front end to the tool call: dropping it on the way is the confused-deputy failure this architecture makes easy to avoid and easy to commit. Assessment probe: revoke one agent's credentials and confirm exactly one agent stops.

items.title: The escape hatch is a review event, and gateway coverage is the checklist
body: Tool brokering, scoping, logging and guardrails reach a declarative agent automatically and reach custom code only where it calls the gateway. Where enforcement sits is the platform-evaluation question: the strongest platforms enforce default-deny policy and guardrails at the tool gateway, outside agent code, with floor settings a builder cannot lower — on others the same controls are code the builder must remember to call. Require an explicit coverage check whenever a team takes the code path: which calls route through the gateway, which guardrails still apply, and who verified it.

items.title: Choose the return path deliberately, and put the gateway behind the tunnel
body: A hosted agent reaches our systems one of three ways: a public MCP endpoint their cloud calls (admitted by IP allowlist), an outbound-only tunnel we run inside our network, or a self-hosted worker that executes the tools itself. Prefer the tunnel where the vendor ships one for this surface — both first-party vendors now do — and point it at the AI gateway, never at an MCP server or the data directly: the tunnel is transport, does not authenticate to the upstream, and still carries payloads through the vendor's cloud, so the gateway is the only place scope, grant and record are ours. The tunnel token and TLS key on that host are the load-bearing secrets; rotate them like a service credential. Assessment probe: name every route a session can take into our network — the tunnel and the custom-tool handlers — and confirm each one terminates at the gateway. Vendor-direct connectors never enter our network and never meet the gateway, so they need their own tool and scope settings in the definition.

items.title: The gateway is not on the inference path, so re-obtain those controls from the tenant
body: The runtime calls its own vendor's model inside its own boundary. Every control our AI gateway applies to inference elsewhere — model allowlist, prompt and response inspection, spend ceilings, the prompt-level record — sees none of this traffic. Each has to be re-obtained as tenant configuration (guardrail floors, inference geography, retention and training terms, session budgets — with cumulative limits in your application, because a new session resets a per-session cap) and as exported audit, and re-verified on a clock because the defaults drift. Where a control has no tenant equivalent, record it as a gap in the platform assessment rather than assuming the gateway covers it.

items.title: Memory scope is a reviewed decision, never a default
body: Managed memory's scope — per session, per user, or shared across users — is a configuration flag with a data-protection consequence: cross-user scope means one user's content shapes another's turn, and it looks like a feature. Session or per-user scope is the default posture; cross-user scope is a design exception with a named owner and a written justification.

items.title: Admit definitions like code, and evaluate before every alias move
body: An agent definition — instructions, tool bindings, or loop code — is a deployable artifact that decides what the agent may do; it gets the same review, inventory and provenance as application code, and the population inventory matters because a managed runtime makes agents cheap enough to sprawl. No definition change reaches a production alias without adversarial evaluation, because the definition is the attack surface prompt injection negotiates with.

items.title: Vault the credentials per user, and know what the vault does not cover
body: Per-user credential vaults over a shared service secret, with placeholder substitution where the platform offers it so the agent never holds the value. Verify the two product-specific edges before relying on either: what scope can reference a vault entry, and whether customer-managed keys cover the vault's own secrets — on at least one major platform they do not, and the answer changes by provider and by quarter.

items.title: Bind approvals to exact actions, and name the destinations
body: A consequential write is refused at our gateway unless it carries an approval bound to the exact action, surfaced through our own front end — the vendor's per-tool approval default is the second layer, worth leaving on, never the only one. Outbound actions reach named destinations only. What returns through our gateway — enterprise records and custom-tool results — is classified there before the loop we cannot see treats it as instruction; content from the vendor's own connectors and from the web the sandbox fetches under the environment's allowlist is not, and the hosted browser stays off in this reference.

items.title: Turn on everything observable, export it, and assure the rest
body: The loop is not inspectable; traces are the only window, so all of it is on — steps, tool calls, decisions — and exported out of the provider's console, where it can be correlated with everything else and retained on your schedule. Policy and guardrail configuration is authored through governed intake, not console edits. What remains — the sandbox isolation claim, the runtime's own supply chain — cannot be tested from your side: assure it like any critical vendor dependency, and note the direction of travel toward sandboxes and compute in the customer's own perimeter where the claim is not acceptable.

guidance.attribution: Authored in this repository. Pattern requirements are separate from the dated, sourced implementation coverage of individual products.
overview: Govern the continuing agent, its retained context and its usable authority together. Closing a conversation, stopping compute, disconnecting an app and deleting retained data are different operations. Use scoped reads and draft outputs as the baseline; enable consequential effects only when the required approval and revocation controls are verified.

items.title: Register the owner, audience and continuing authority
body: Record each agent's owner, permitted callers, channels, schedules, tools, account grants, version, approval state and review date. Reconcile the actual tenant population against that record and deny admission to unapproved agents and grants. Where the product cannot enforce that boundary, restrict who may create agents and connect accounts before rollout. Require a second factor for access and privileged approvals. Configure who may create or share agents and change triggers or grants. Test an unauthorised channel participant and a departed owner: neither should start work on surviving authority.

items.title: Verify the account on each path
body: Treat backend OAuth, shared service secrets and browser sessions as separate credentials. Bind connector tokens to their intended recipient and scope account permissions to the task. Keep raw credentials out of prompts and work files. Confirm whether private and group invocations use the caller's account or a shared account; a shared computer is not proof of shared OAuth, and per-user OAuth does not isolate shared files or cookies. Probe both connector and browser routes with an account that lacks the requested access.

items.title: Gate consequential effects at dispatch
body: Require an authenticated approver to see the exact operation, arguments, account and target. Verify that refusal, expiry or altered arguments prevent the effect. Automated review and consent to a browser login do not establish this human gate. Leave writes unavailable when the product cannot enforce it; use read-only accounts and draft outputs.

items.title: Bound retained state across tasks and audiences
body: Identify the actual scope of memory, conversation history, files, browser cookies and saved logins. Configure authorised readers and writers, track source provenance, and establish correction, retention and recovery procedures. Test what remains after ending a task, disconnecting a connector and deleting the agent. Material already acquired may persist independently. Limit sensitive durable use where selective removal or reliable isolation cannot be established; a machine restart is not evidence of data erasure.

items.title: Constrain browser and computer reach separately
body: Apply and test one destination allowlist on the hosted computer's actual routes — the browser, and the shell's web fetches, public repository clones and package installs — including redirects and alternate fetch mechanisms. Restrict write methods on the hosts the list must permit, and install only pinned, verified packages, from the vendor's mirror where it offers one. Limit accessible files and browser accounts independently of connector permissions. If a route cannot enforce the restrictions required by the data class, leave it disabled or use it only with nonsensitive context. Keep local execution, desktop or VPN routes into private networks and agent delegation disabled until their actual paths and authority boundaries receive a separate review; the tunnel below is the one reviewed route into our systems.

items.title: Reach our systems only through the tunnel and our gateway
body: Where the agent needs our own records, admit it down the vendor's outbound-only tunnel to our AI gateway, never to a server or the data directly. Issue per-agent, audience-bound grants at the gateway, scoped to a named server list and read-only unless a write has a named owner, and classify what returns before it reaches a loop that may keep it. The tunnel is transport: it authenticates nothing, and its token and TLS key are secrets to rotate. Confirm the product lets its persistent agents use the tunnel; where it does not, leave this path closed.

items.title: Bound recurring work and verify the stop
body: Set task and aggregate limits for duration, iterations, tool use and spend, and give recurring triggers an owner and expiry. Exercise an incident stop: terminate active work, disable schedules and queued restarts, and revoke connector tokens, browser sessions and gateway grants at their issuers. Verify no new effect occurs. Data deletion is a separate governed step; stopping compute must neither imply erasure nor silently leave authority able to restart.

items.title: Export evidence and assess hidden provider controls
body: Correlate available agent, caller, trigger, approval, tool and downstream events in a customer-controlled record. Test whether a browser action and a scheduled connector call can be reconstructed; document fields or routes the product does not expose. Assess provider isolation, internal screening, credential handling and retention using current evidence. Do not treat those supplier claims as customer-configured runtime controls.

tools.name: Claude Agent SDK

variants.name: @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk (TypeScript)
claude-agent-sdk (Python)
Headless CLI (claude -p) as a subprocess from other languages

summary: A library (Python and TypeScript) that runs the Claude Code agent loop inside the customer's own process: each query() spawns a bundled claude CLI subprocess that owns a shell, a working directory and JSONL transcripts on local disk, and calls the Anthropic API (or Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry, Claude Platform on AWS) with an API key from the host's environment. Nothing is hosted by Anthropic; sandboxing, egress, credential injection, multi-tenant isolation and session persistence are the deployer's responsibility, and the docs describe container, gVisor and Firecracker patterns with a credential-injecting egress proxy.

Its controls are Claude Code's, reachable as options: permissionMode, allowedTools / disallowedTools, a canUseTool callback, programmatic PreToolUse hooks that run before every other check, settingSources to stop reading filesystem settings, mcpServers, maxTurns, and OpenTelemetry export inherited from the environment. Managed policy on the host (MDM, managed-settings.json) and server-managed settings fetched with an organisation credential still apply and cannot be disabled from the SDK; the TypeScript managedSettings option passes policy-tier settings from the host process. Anthropic does not allow third parties to offer claude.ai login through SDK-built products.

facts.label: Plans
facts.value: Anthropic API key (Console), Bedrock (CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK), Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud's Agent Platform (CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX) or Microsoft Foundry (CLAUDE_CODE_USE_FOUNDRY); governed by Anthropic's Commercial Terms.

facts.label: Inference & routing
facts.value: Direct to api.anthropic.com or the provider's regional endpoint; ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL or HTTPS_PROXY route model calls through a proxy that can inject the key outside the container.

facts.label: Data leaving the device
facts.value: Prompts, tool results and file contents to the model provider; OTLP telemetry only to the collector you configure (content redacted unless OTEL_LOG_* opt-ins are set); transcripts on local disk or a SessionStore you provide.

facts.label: Retention & training
facts.value: API: retained data is never used for training without express permission; conversation content is not retained by default except for Covered Models (Claude Fable 5 / 5.1, Mythos 5 / 5.1), which require 30-day retention and are outside ZDR; ZDR available for API organisations. Local transcripts under ~/.claude/projects/ or CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR are swept after cleanupPeriodDays (30 days by default); a SessionStore keeps whatever its adapter's retention keeps.

facts.label: Docs index
facts.value: code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk (overview, permissions, hooks, hosting, secure deployment)

riskNotes.note: The SDK's own guide opens with prompt injection as the threat model and recommends defence in depth: bare-name deny rules, PreToolUse hooks, read-only mounts, --network none containers and a credential-injecting proxy.

Subagents inherit the parent's permission mode (never bypassPermissions unless the parent has it) and hooks fire inside them with agent_id / agent_type; tracing nests subagent spans under the parent tool span only when CLAUDE_CODE_ENHANCED_TELEMETRY_BETA is on.

There is no wall-clock deadline for a session or a subagent, and the stall watchdog (CLAUDE_ASYNC_AGENT_STALL_TIMEOUT_MS) is not one. The bounds are maxTurns (per query and per subagent), maxBudgetUsd (counts subagent spend and stops running background subagents), and the subagent depth (default 3) and concurrency (default 20) limits; cost is a client-side estimate.

Default query() options read user, project and local settings, CLAUDE.md and auto memory from the host filesystem, and load claude.ai connectors when a claude.ai login is present; multi-tenant deployments must set settingSources [] and per-tenant CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR / cwd.

MCP servers are whatever the deployer configures; .mcp.json in the working directory is loaded when the project setting source is on. Managed host policy (allowedMcpServers, strictPluginOnlyCustomization) still applies to SDK sessions.

controls.mechanism: Sessions keyed by session UUID and working directory; settingSources [], CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1 and a per-tenant CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR and cwd; a per-tenant SessionStore whose delete() backs deleteSession(); PreToolUse hooks on Write and Edit as the only place to check a memory write

steps.title: Isolate each tenant's state
body: Pass settingSources [] (Python setting_sources=[]), set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1 and a per-tenant CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR in env, and a per-tenant cwd on every query().

steps.title: Keep one store per tenant and delete on schedule
body: Give each tenant its own SessionStore (or key prefix), implement delete so deleteSession() cascades to subagent transcripts, and set expiry in the backend, because the SDK never deletes from the store.

steps.title: Check writes to memory files
body: Register a hooks.PreToolUse callback with matcher "Write|Edit" that denies or validates writes to CLAUDE.md, .claude/rules and the auto-memory directory.

controls.note: Partial by the rule for this drawing: per-session and per-tenant scoping and deletion are configuration, but nothing ships that validates what a step writes. Auto memory and CLAUDE.md are plain files the agent edits with Write and Edit, and every subagent in a session shares the working directory, so one branch's writes are read as trusted context by the next; the hook is only an attach point for that check. Auto memory loads into the system prompt regardless of settingSources unless it is turned off. SessionStore mirrors transcripts only (memory files and working-directory artifacts need their own storage), its writes are best-effort (mirror_error), and the CLI writes the local transcript first.

original.mechanism: settingSources [] plus CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1 and per-tenant CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR and cwd; SessionStore adapter for transcripts; no memory validation or rollback

steps.title: Isolate tenants' memory and settings
body: Pass settingSources [] (Python setting_sources=[]), set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1 and a per-tenant CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR in env, and a per-tenant cwd on every query().

steps.title: Control where transcripts persist
body: Configure a SessionStore adapter (S3, Redis, Postgres) and alert on mirror_error messages; do not share a store across tenants.

original.note: Isolation only: per-tenant directories and disabled auto-memory bound where memory lives. Nothing validates what is written, detects poisoning or restores a known-good state — recovery is the SessionStore's backups.

controls.mechanism: None in the SDK; an evaluation or red-team platform in the deployer's CI drives query() headless

evidence.title: Agent SDK overview (no evaluation harness or release gate documented)
How the agent loop works (result subtypes to gate on)

controls.note: External (an evaluation or red-team platform in CI): the SDK ships no evaluation harness and nothing that gates a model, prompt or agent-definition change. Integration points: run query() headless in CI with a pinned model and outputFormat, and gate on the result message's subtype, structured output and total_cost_usd; the test set, its protection and the release decision are the platform's.

original.note: The SDK ships no evaluation harness or release gate; build evals in your CI around query() and the result message subtypes yourself.

evidence.title: Vendor docs index, reviewed; no setting for this control (2026-09-10)

controls.mechanism: OpenTelemetry traces from the CLI subprocess (claude_code.interaction, llm_request, tool with blocked_on_user and execution child spans, hook), subagent spans nested under the parent's tool span, W3C trace context injected from the host application, and tool_decision / tool_result / mcp_server_connection log events; OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS and OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT add arguments and results

steps.title: Export all three signals
body: Set CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1, CLAUDE_CODE_ENHANCED_TELEMETRY_BETA=1, OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER, OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER and OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER to otlp and OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT in the container environment or the env option.

steps.title: Capture arguments and results
body: Set OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1 for tool arguments and OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT=1 for file contents and Bash output on the tool span, only where the collector is approved to hold them.

steps.title: Join runs to the application's trace and user
body: Call query() inside an active span so the SDK injects TRACEPARENT, and pass enduser.id and tenant.id in OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES on each query().

steps.title: Surface export failures
body: Set CLAUDE_CODE_OTEL_DIAG_STDERR=1 and read the stderr callback; without it the CLI drops telemetry silently when the collector is unreachable.

controls.note: Native: the CLI traces every turn, model request and tool call, including the wait for permission, nests each subagent's spans under the Agent tool span so the delegation chain is one trace, and exports to the customer's collector. Limits: tracing is beta and span names may change; hook spans need the separate detailed beta tracing; arguments and results appear only with the opt-ins; a killed process loses its unexported batch; memory writes show as Write and Edit tool spans, not memory events; identity attributes name the service credential unless the application injects enduser.id. Emission is not tamper resistance or detection — the collector and SIEM supply those.

original.mechanism: OpenTelemetry traces (claude_code.interaction / llm_request / tool / hook spans), metrics and log events exported by the CLI subprocess; W3C trace context propagated from the host application; OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES for enduser.id / tenant.id

steps.title: Turn on OTLP export
body: Set CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1, OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER / OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER / OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=otlp and OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT in the container environment; add CLAUDE_CODE_ENHANCED_TELEMETRY_BETA=1 for traces.

steps.title: Attribute actions to end users
body: Inject enduser.id and tenant.id through OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES per query() so tool_decision, tool_result and mcp_server_connection events form a per-user audit trail for the SIEM.

original.note: Traces cover interactions, model requests, tool calls and hooks with W3C correlation; content is off unless enabled. Emitting traces is not detection or an audit record — the collector's rules and retention supply those.

original.mechanism: OTLP log events (tool_decision, tool_result, mcp_server_connection, permission_mode_changed) to your collector; transcripts on disk or in a SessionStore; the Console Usage and Cost API

steps.title: Ship security events to the SIEM
body: Export OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=otlp with enduser.id attributes; the events are named with a claude_code. prefix and carry the decision source.

original.note: Records live in your infrastructure; tamper evidence is what your collector provides.

original.mechanism: OTLP events and traces correlated in your SIEM; no vendor-side detections for SDK workloads

steps.title: Build detections on the exported events
body: Correlate tool_decision rejections, permission_mode_changed and mcp_server_connection events with enduser.id in your SIEM.

original.note: The traces and events are the feed; the detections (unexpected tool sequences, egress to new hosts, permission denials spiking) and the response playbook are written in the SIEM. Required fields for that: session id, tool name, decision, host.

controls.mechanism: None in the SDK; an API gateway and IdP in front of the application's endpoint decide who may start, resume or stop a run

evidence.title: Hosting the Agent SDK (inbound auth at a gateway; the subprocess does not listen)
Authentication (Console roles for API-key creation)

controls.note: External (API gateway / IdP): the SDK has no listener and no authorization policy over who may start, steer, resume or cancel a run — the hosting guide puts authentication at a gateway in front of the container and says the agent should not validate user tokens. Integration points: the application's HTTP or WebSocket endpoint that calls query(); the resume session ID, whose ownership the application must check before resuming (see the Python SDK's resume advisory); enduser.id and tenant.id in OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES for attribution. Console roles (the Claude Code role creates only Claude Code keys) govern who mints the model credential, not who may run the agent.

original.mechanism: Authentication of end users happens at your gateway; the agent receives pre-authenticated requests. Claude Console roles and SSO govern who can mint API keys

steps.title: Put user authentication in front of the agent
body: The hosting guide says the agent should not be the component that validates user tokens; terminate auth at a gateway and pass identity as resource attributes.

steps.title: Control who can create API keys
body: Use Console roles (Claude Code role can only create Claude Code keys) and Console SSO for the humans who provision credentials.

original.note: Rated partial on the same rule as the Copilot SDK and Codex SDK: Console roles, SSO and workload identity federation govern who can mint the credentials the agent uses; authentication and authorisation of the application's end users happen at the deployer's gateway, which the SDK does not provide.

original.mechanism: Retrieval runs with whatever filesystem mounts and MCP credentials the deployer grants
original.note: The SDK reads whatever the working directory and MCP servers expose; least-privilege mounts and per-user MCP credentials are your responsibility.

steps.title: Mount only what the task needs
body: Mount code read-only, give each session its own cwd, and use per-tenant MCP credentials so retrieval runs as the requesting user.

controls.mechanism: Inline mcpServers on an AgentDefinition (a server config with its own headers or env for that subagent); agent_id / agent_type on hooks, canUseTool and spans; the process authenticates to Anthropic once, with an API key, apiKeyHelper or a Workload Identity Federation service account

steps.title: Give a subagent its own tool credential
body: Define the subagent's MCP server inline in AgentDefinition.mcpServers with headers carrying a token minted for that agent, and leave that server out of the parent's mcpServers.

steps.title: Federate the workload identity
body: Set ANTHROPIC_FEDERATION_RULE_ID and ANTHROPIC_ORGANIZATION_ID in env so the process exchanges its OIDC token through a Console service account instead of holding ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.

controls.note: Partial by the rule for this drawing: per-agent credentials can be configured (a subagent's inline MCP server config) but every agent shares the process identity — one model credential, one environment and filesystem, and Bash in every subagent runs as the same OS user. agent_id is a runtime label for correlation, not an authenticated principal; no per-agent token is issued, and minting, rotating and revoking per-agent credentials is the application's work.

original.mechanism: Console service accounts with workload identity federation (OIDC exchange, no static keys) identify the workload to Anthropic; no per-agent identity beyond the API key or service account

steps.title: Give the workload a federated identity
body: Exchange the runtime's OIDC token (GitHub Actions, AWS, GCP, Kubernetes, Entra, Okta, SPIFFE) for Claude API access through a Console service account instead of shipping ANTHROPIC_API_KEY; Claude Code reads ANTHROPIC_FEDERATION_RULE_ID and ANTHROPIC_ORGANIZATION_ID.

original.note: The workload identity authenticates the deployment to Anthropic; every agent and subagent in it shares that identity, and tool calls to other systems carry whatever credential the application supplies. A per-agent principal is the application's to mint.

controls.mechanism: apiKeyHelper passed through the settings option (re-run after five minutes and on a 401), Workload Identity Federation (ANTHROPIC_FEDERATION_RULE_ID), ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to a key-injecting proxy, ${VAR} expansion in MCP headers, CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB

steps.title: Fetch short-lived model credentials
body: Pass apiKeyHelper in the settings option pointing at a script that reads your vault (the Agent SDK honours it; CLAUDE_CODE_API_KEY_HELPER_TTL_MS sets the refresh), or use Workload Identity Federation instead of a static ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.

steps.title: Keep secrets outside the agent's container
body: Set ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to a proxy that injects the model key, and route tool calls through a credential-injecting proxy so the agent never holds those secrets.

steps.title: Scrub credentials from agent subprocesses
body: Set CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 in env to strip Anthropic, cloud-provider and other recognised credentials from Bash, hook and stdio MCP server environments.

controls.note: Partial by the rule for this drawing: the SDK takes secret references and helper hooks (apiKeyHelper, env, header variable expansion) but brokers nothing at step time — no credential provider issues a short-lived, scoped credential per tool call, and the proxy pattern keeps secrets outside the agent only where the deployer builds it. Anything passed in env or MCP headers lives in the CLI process; the subprocess inherits the host environment unless the TypeScript env option replaces it (Python only merges over it). The model sees a secret only if a tool returns it.

original.mechanism: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from your secret manager, ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to a key-injecting proxy, apiKeyHelper, workload identity federation; tool credentials via proxy injection

steps.title: Keep credentials outside the agent container
body: Route model calls through a proxy that injects the key (ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL) and outbound tool calls through a TLS-terminating or custom-tool proxy so the agent never holds the secret.

steps.title: Strip secrets from mounted directories
body: Exclude .env, ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, .npmrc, *.pem and similar files before mounting code even read-only.

original.note: Storage is the deployer's secret manager; ephemeral issuance exists only where apiKeyHelper or workload identity federation is used. Readers: the SDK process holds the provider key; shell commands and MCP servers read whatever environment the application passes them; the model sees a secret only if a tool returns it.

controls.mechanism: Declarative deny and ask rules (disallowedTools such as Bash(rm *) and Edit(//secrets/**), permissions.deny / ask in the settings option or a managed-settings file in the image) evaluated before the permission mode on every call, and PreToolUse hooks that run first; each decision is a claude_code.tool_decision event

steps.title: Pass declarative deny and ask rules
body: Set disallowedTools to scoped rules such as Bash(curl *) and Edit(//etc/**), and put permissions.ask entries in the settings option; deny holds in every mode, including bypassPermissions.

steps.title: Lock the rules below the application
body: Bake permissions.deny with allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly into a managed-settings file in the image, or pass them in the TypeScript managedSettings option; managed policy loads whatever settingSources the code passes.

steps.title: Gate every call in a hook
body: Register hooks.PreToolUse callbacks that return permissionDecision "deny", "ask" or "defer"; a hook that times out leaves the tool unrun, and any deny wins over other hooks.

steps.title: Log every decision
body: Export OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=otlp so each claude_code.tool_decision event, with its decision and source, reaches your collector.

controls.note: Native on the Claude Code rule (declarative permissions decide every call outside the model; hooks alone would be partial): deny and ask rules over tool, argument and path patterns are evaluated for every built-in and MCP tool call, in the main agent and its subagents, before any mode can approve it, and ask escalates to the application's canUseTool. Boundaries: Bash rules match the command as written; a bare allowedTools entry pre-approves the whole tool and skips canUseTool; the application can loosen its own options mid-session (setPermissionMode, applyFlagSettings) unless the rules come from managed settings; in-process custom tools are matched by name, with argument checks only in a hook; the auto-mode classifier is a second, non-deterministic gate.

original.mechanism: Programmatic PreToolUse hooks (permissionDecision allow/deny/ask/defer) and deny rules run before every permission mode, including bypassPermissions; filesystem hooks from settings also apply

steps.title: Gate every tool call in a hook
body: Register hooks.PreToolUse callbacks (with matcher patterns) that return permissionDecision "deny" or "ask"; hooks run first in the evaluation order and a deny holds even in bypassPermissions.

steps.title: Add declarative deny rules
body: Pass disallowedTools (bare names remove the tool; Bash(rm *) scopes it) and, when the project source is enabled, permissions.deny in .claude/settings.json.

original.note: The hook API is the enforcement point; the policy is code the application writes. Deny rules are deterministic; a canUseTool decision is whatever the application implements. Subagents inherit hooks; custom tools the application registers are covered only if the hook logic addresses them.

controls.mechanism: The requesting user's token passed per query in an MCP server's headers (the application runs the OAuth flow); built-in file tools read with the process's filesystem permissions, bounded by cwd, mounts and Read rules

steps.title: Pass the requesting user's token to each data server
body: Complete OAuth in your application and put the user's access token in that server's headers in mcpServers for the user's query(); a server left at needs-auth runs without its tools.

steps.title: Fence the built-in file tools
body: Give each user's query its own cwd and read-only mounts, and add Read(//path/**) deny rules in disallowedTools for anything outside the user's scope.

controls.note: Partial on the same rule as the Copilot SDK's per-session token: the SDK carries whatever credential the application puts in a server's headers or env, so retrieval runs with the user's entitlements only when the application obtains and passes that user's token per query — the SDK runs no OAuth flow and no on-behalf-of exchange. Read, Grep, Glob and Bash read with the process's own filesystem permissions, not the requesting user's. Oversharing analysis of the sources is outside the SDK.

original.mechanism: Retrieval runs with whatever filesystem mounts and MCP credentials the deployer grants
original.note: The SDK reads whatever the working directory and MCP servers expose; least-privilege mounts and per-user MCP credentials are your responsibility.

steps.title: Mount only what the task needs
body: Mount code read-only, give each session its own cwd, and use per-tenant MCP credentials so retrieval runs as the requesting user.

controls.mechanism: AgentDefinition tools / disallowedTools (tool names and mcp__server patterns), mcpServers and permissionMode per subagent; CLAUDE_AGENT_SDK_DISABLE_BUILTIN_AGENTS; argument and path rules (disallowedTools Bash(git push *), Edit(//path/**)) apply session-wide

steps.title: Give every subagent an explicit tool list
body: Set tools (and disallowedTools such as mcp__github) on each AgentDefinition; a subagent with no tools field inherits every tool available to subagents.

steps.title: Remove the built-in general-purpose agent
body: Set CLAUDE_AGENT_SDK_DISABLE_BUILTIN_AGENTS=1 in env so Claude can spawn only the agents you defined.

steps.title: Scope arguments for the whole session
body: Add scoped rules such as Bash(git push *) and Edit(//secrets/**) to disallowedTools; they bind the main agent and every subagent.

steps.title: Keep the parent in a mode subagents can narrow
body: Run the parent in default, dontAsk or plan mode; a subagent's permissionMode applies only then, and bypassPermissions is never granted unless the parent has it.

controls.note: Partial by the per-hop rule for this drawing: a subagent's grant narrows by tool name and MCP server only. A specifier in its disallowedTools removes the whole tool, and argument and path rules are session-wide, so a hop cannot carry narrower arguments than its parent except through a PreToolUse hook keyed on agent_type (an attach point). allowedTools pre-approves but does not restrict. Every tool runs with the process's authority; the caller's authority is not carried into the tool.

original.mechanism: allowedTools / disallowedTools, permissionMode (default, dontAsk, acceptEdits, plan, auto, bypassPermissions), mcp__server__tool allow patterns, skills option, per-subagent permissionMode

steps.title: Fix an explicit tool surface
body: Pair allowedTools with permissionMode "dontAsk" so listed tools run and everything else is denied; note allowedTools does not constrain bypassPermissions.

steps.title: Allow MCP tools narrowly
body: Use mcp__<server>__<tool> or mcp__<server>__* entries rather than a broad permission mode; acceptEdits never auto-approves MCP tools.

original.note: Options the application passes, not fleet policy: allowedTools hides tools, permissionMode pre-approves classes of action, and argument limits come only from deny patterns or a canUseTool implementation. bypassPermissions is available to the application unless the host's managed settings disable it; MCP tools follow the same patterns, custom tools are whatever the application registers.

controls.mechanism: Per-server headers and env in mcpServers (and in a subagent's inline mcpServers); sandbox.credentials deny and mask entries in the image's ~/.claude/settings.json, applied even when settingSources excludes user settings; CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB; a credential-injecting egress proxy the deployer runs

steps.title: Scope each credential to one server
body: Put each tool credential in that server's headers or env in mcpServers, or in a subagent's inline server config, rather than in the process environment.

steps.title: Hide credentials from agent commands
body: Add sandbox.credentials deny or mask entries to ~/.claude/settings.json in the image; Claude Code applies them to sandboxed commands even when settingSources excludes user settings.

steps.title: Inject service credentials at a proxy
body: Run a credential-injecting proxy (Envoy credential_injector, mitmproxy, LiteLLM) outside the container and route git and API calls through it.

controls.note: Partial by the rule for this drawing: credential scoping is per server (and per subagent for MCP) only; the process environment, the model credential and the filesystem are shared by every agent in the session, and Bash in any subagent reads them unless scrubbed or sandbox-masked (the sandbox covers Bash only). No on-behalf-of exchange and no passthrough guard: an MCP server receives whatever token the application put in its headers.

original.mechanism: Proxy-injected credentials and custom tools that call authenticated services outside the boundary; per-tenant egress rules at the proxy; no on-behalf-of exchange in the SDK

steps.title: Use the proxy pattern for every service credential
body: Run a credential-injecting proxy (Envoy credential_injector, mitmproxy, LiteLLM) outside the container; give the agent no direct credentials and route git and API calls through it.

original.note: Deployer-built: proxy-injected credentials and per-tenant egress rules exist only where the application's proxy implements them; the SDK itself hands the process whatever environment it starts with. No on-behalf-of exchange, so an agent serving several requesting users needs the application to scope each call.

controls.mechanism: maxTurns on query() and each AgentDefinition; maxBudgetUsd counting subagent spend (refuses new subagents, stops running background subagents, ends the query); CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH (default 3) and CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS (default 20)

steps.title: Cap turns
body: Set maxTurns (Python max_turns) on query() and on every AgentDefinition; unset or 0 means no limit, and the run ends with error_max_turns.

steps.title: Cap spend across the agent tree
body: Set maxBudgetUsd (max_budget_usd); at the cap Claude Code refuses new subagents, stops running background subagents and ends the query with error_max_budget_usd.

steps.title: Cap nesting and fan-out
body: Set CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH and CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS in the env option.

controls.note: Native: turn, spend, depth and concurrency limits are options the SDK enforces, and the budget stops delegated work already running, not only new spawns (TypeScript SDK 0.3.219 / Python 0.2.127 and later). Limits: no wall-clock deadline for a session or subagent; the budget is a client-side cost estimate that counts only the call's own spend (a resume or /clear starts it over), and the response that crosses it is still billed; under streaming input maxTurns restarts for each queued message; sessions with ultracode active are never refused on concurrency.

original.mechanism: maxTurns per query and per subagent AgentDefinition; API organisation spend limits and usage-tier rate limits; per-session cost tracking in the result stream

steps.title: Bound turns and cost
body: Set maxTurns on query() and on each subagent definition (there is no wall-clock deadline); read total_cost_usd from the result message for per-session accounting.

original.note: Sub-limits: iterations (maxTurns per query and per subagent, hard), spend (organisation limits and usage-tier rate limits, hard at the account). No wall-clock or per-session spend cap — cost is reported per session, not enforced, so the application supplies that.

controls.mechanism: PostToolUse hooks returning updatedToolOutput (any tool, both SDKs) and UserPromptSubmit hooks that block a prompt, as attach points for the deployer's classifier; built-in subagent output scanning and web-search summarisation are not configurable

steps.title: Screen tool results before the model reads them
body: Register a PostToolUse hook for WebFetch, Bash, Read and mcp__ tools that sends the result to your injection classifier and returns updatedToolOutput with a quarantine notice.

steps.title: Screen the initiator's request
body: Register a UserPromptSubmit hook that classifies the prompt and blocks it on a hit; a callback that times out blocks the prompt rather than letting it through.

controls.note: Partial by the rule for this drawing: the hooks are attach points; no injection classifier ships or can be switched on. Built in and not configurable: subagent output scanning neutralises harness control tags and turn markers in a subagent's final message but removes nothing, and web search results are summarised. Uncovered: CLAUDE.md, rules, skills and auto memory that enter context without a tool call; updatedToolOutput changes only what Claude sees, and OpenTelemetry keeps the original.

original.mechanism: Claude Code's built-in command parsing, web-search summarisation and sandbox mode; defence in depth recommended via containers and egress proxy

steps.title: Layer the recommended controls
body: Follow the secure-deployment guide: PreToolUse hooks, deny rules, read-only mounts, --network none with a Unix-socket proxy, and gVisor or Firecracker for untrusted content.

original.note: No admin-configurable injection classifier is exposed; auto mode's classifier is available as a permission mode.

controls.mechanism: PostToolUse updatedToolOutput and UserPromptSubmit hooks as the attach point for a detector; OTLP content off unless OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS / OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS / OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT are set; Read deny rules and sandbox.credentials masks keep named paths and secrets out

steps.title: Mask sensitive spans before the model and the journal see them
body: Register a PostToolUse hook that runs your PII and secret detector on the result and returns updatedToolOutput with the spans masked.

steps.title: Keep content out of traces
body: Leave OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS, OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS, OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT and OTEL_LOG_RAW_API_BODIES unset unless the collector is approved to hold the content.

controls.note: Partial by the rule, as for Claude Code and the Copilot SDK: the hooks are the attach point and no detector ships, so nothing is inspected until the deployer attaches one. The telemetry opt-outs and path denies are minimisation, not detection. The journal: the CLI writes the full transcript to local disk under CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR before the SDK mirrors it to a SessionStore; updatedToolOutput changes what Claude sees, OpenTelemetry keeps the original, and the docs do not say which version the transcript keeps.

original.mechanism: Read/Edit deny rules keep named files out; inspection of prompts and outputs is the deployer's proxy or hook

steps.title: Inspect at the proxy or in a hook
body: Use a TLS-terminating proxy or a PreToolUse / UserPromptSubmit hook to scan content; the SDK itself ships no DLP classifier.

original.note: Rated like Claude Code, Gemini CLI and the Copilot SDK: deny rules restrict paths and the hooks are the attach point for a scanner. No scanner ships — until the deployer attaches one, no prompt, upload or output content is inspected.

controls.mechanism: Ask rules and default-mode prompts routed to canUseTool with the tool name, input, toolUseID, agentID and requestId; the call waits until the application answers allow (optionally with updatedInput) or deny; PreToolUse "defer" ends the run with deferred_tool_use (id, name, input) for a later resume

steps.title: Route named actions to a person
body: Put permissions.ask entries such as Bash(git push *) in the settings option and keep the session in default mode; ask rules reach canUseTool even in bypassPermissions.

steps.title: Bind the answer to the exact call
body: Implement canUseTool to show the approver toolName, input, toolUseID and agentID, and return deny when no authenticated approver answers in time.

steps.title: Suspend across a process restart
body: Return permissionDecision "defer" from a PreToolUse hook; the run ends with stop_reason tool_deferred and deferred_tool_use, and on resume the same call fires the hook again for the decision.

controls.note: Native: a built-in primitive holds the exact call — tool, arguments, toolUseID and requestId — until the application answers; the deployer supplies the approver, its UI and its authentication. Boundaries: calls pre-approved by allowedTools, allow rules, acceptEdits or bypassPermissions never reach canUseTool, and dontAsk denies ask rules instead of asking; the auto-mode classifier is not human approval; the callback has no expiry, so the application sets the timeout and fails closed; an allow with updatedInput replaces the arguments, so the approver must see the final ones; defer is ignored when Claude makes several tool calls in one turn.

original.mechanism: canUseTool callback for unresolved calls, ask rules, plan mode, PreToolUse "ask" or "defer" (ends the query for later resumption), AskUserQuestion

steps.title: Route sensitive calls to a human
body: Implement canUseTool (Python can_use_tool) and add ask rules; tools marked anthropic/requiresUserInteraction and org connector tools set to ask always reach the callback.

steps.title: Pause for asynchronous approval
body: Return permissionDecision "defer" from a PreToolUse hook to end the query and resume it after an out-of-band approval.

original.note: The SDK routes the decision to the application; the application must implement an authenticated human approver and fail closed on timeout. Nothing in the SDK ships an approval UI, so the control is complete only in the deployed application.

controls.mechanism: The sandbox option (enabled, failIfUnavailable, allowUnsandboxedCommands, excludedCommands, filesystem denyRead / allowWrite) confining Bash on macOS, Linux and WSL2; the container, gVisor and Firecracker tiers the deployer runs

steps.title: Sandbox every agent command
body: Pass sandbox with enabled true, failIfUnavailable true and allowUnsandboxedCommands false and no excludedCommands, so a missing sandbox stops the run and the model cannot request an unsandboxed command.

steps.title: Keep the repository from widening it
body: Pass settingSources [] (or omit project and local) so a checked-in .claude/settings.json cannot add sandbox.excludedCommands.

steps.title: Put the whole process in an isolation tier
body: Run the SDK in a hardened container (--cap-drop ALL, --read-only, --network none), gVisor or a Firecracker microVM per the isolation table.

controls.note: Partial by core rule 3 and this drawing's rule: the built-in sandbox is off by default and allowUnsandboxedCommands defaults to true (the model may request an unsandboxed run, which falls to canUseTool). With the keys set it confines Bash and its children and the agent cannot step out, but WebFetch, MCP servers, hooks, in-process custom tools and the CLI itself run outside it on the orchestration tier, sharing the host kernel; native Windows has no sandbox. The container, gVisor and VM tiers are the deployer's, and the docs place the SDK application inside that same boundary.

original.mechanism: Claude Code's sandbox settings (Seatbelt / bubblewrap) apply when configured; Anthropic's sandbox-runtime package; documented Docker, gVisor and Firecracker patterns

steps.title: Choose the isolation tier
body: Use sandbox-runtime for lightweight OS-level isolation, hardened Docker (--cap-drop ALL, --read-only, --network none), gVisor for syscall interception or Firecracker microVMs per the isolation table.

steps.title: Size and recycle containers
body: One subprocess per session; start at 1 GiB RAM / 1 CPU, recycle long sessions, and use ephemeral containers for one-off tasks.

original.note: Optional and deployer-built: Claude Code's sandbox applies only when the application configures it, and container, gVisor or Firecracker isolation is the deployer's infrastructure. Inside the boundary: shell commands; outside: MCP servers, WebFetch and the SDK host process.

controls.mechanism: A managed allowedMcpServers list baked into the image's managed settings, with strictMcpConfig so only the servers the application passes are loaded; no registry of agents or servers with owner, version or approval state

steps.title: Pin the admissible servers in managed settings
body: Bake allowedMcpServers (and deniedMcpServers) into a managed-settings file in the image; managed policy loads regardless of settingSources, so a query cannot widen it.

steps.title: Load only the servers the application declares
body: Pass mcpServers built from your registry on each query with strictMcpConfig true, so .mcp.json, user settings, plugins and claude.ai connectors cannot add servers.

steps.title: Remove the built-in subagent if it is not registered
body: Set CLAUDE_AGENT_SDK_DISABLE_BUILTIN_AGENTS=1 so the general-purpose subagent exists only if you declare it.

controls.note: Partial on the registry rule applied to every SDK on this drawing (as toolCodexSdk): an enforced allowlist admits servers, but there is no registry record of agents or tool servers with owner, version or approval state — agents and mcpServers are whatever the application passes to each query, and the agent inventory lives in the organisation's governance platform or MCP gateway. Reconcile with supportedAgents(), mcpServerStatus() and OTEL_SERVICE_NAME.

original.note: No registry of SDK-built agents exists on the vendor side; OTEL_SERVICE_NAME and resource attributes are the only identifiers, so maintain the inventory in your own governance platform.

controls.mechanism: close() on the Query (terminates the CLI subprocess), abortController, interrupt() in streaming mode, stopTask(taskId) for a background subagent, deleteSession() on the SessionStore; revoking the Console API key or federation rule refuses the next model request

steps.title: Terminate a running query
body: Call close() on the Query object (or abort its abortController) to end the query and terminate the CLI subprocess with its subagents.

steps.title: Stop one background subagent
body: Call stopTask(taskId) (Python stop_task) with the task ID from the task notification.

steps.title: Purge what the run stored
body: Call deleteSession() against the SessionStore, which cascades to subagent transcripts when the adapter implements delete, and remove the container's working directory.

controls.note: Partial by the rule for this drawing: the stop is an in-process call by the application that holds the Query handle. close() ends that query and its in-process subagents, but no runtime-level cancel reaches a run on another worker or a session that can be resumed from a SessionStore; interrupt() stops the turn while queued messages still run unless the control request sets cancel_queued; whether commands a Bash tool left running in the background die with the subprocess is not documented. Revoking the API key or federation rule refuses only the next model request (delay not documented), and quarantine and deletion are the deployer's steps.

body: Pass mcpServers in options and set settingSources [] so a checked-in .mcp.json cannot add servers; set strictMcpConfig or disableClaudeAiConnectors to suppress claude.ai connectors.

steps.title: Allow tools per server
body: Grant mcp__<server>__<tool> entries in allowedTools and treat needs-auth / failed statuses in the init message as blockers.

original.note: The application decides which servers a session gets; host managed policy can constrain it where Claude Code's managed settings are deployed. Admission is not integrity — nothing pins the tool descriptions a server returns.

settings.name: ANTHROPIC_FEDERATION_RULE_ID with ANTHROPIC_ORGANIZATION_ID
settings.where: options.env (or the container environment), against a federation rule in Claude Console › Settings › Workload identity
settings.recommended: One federation rule and service account per agent workload, with ANTHROPIC_API_KEY unset
settings.why: No long-lived model key sits in the container, each workload is a separate revocable principal, and archiving its rule refuses the next token exchange.

settings.name: mcpServers (AgentDefinition)
settings.where: options.agents[name].mcpServers, with the server's headers or env
settings.recommended: A server a subagent needs defined inline on that subagent, with a token minted for it, and left out of the parent's mcpServers
settings.why: The credential for that tool is held by the one agent that uses it, so a parent or sibling hijacked by injected text cannot call it.

settings.name: mcpServers headers
settings.where: options.mcpServers[name].headers on each query()
settings.recommended: The requesting user's own OAuth access token, obtained by the application, for every data server
settings.why: Retrieval runs with that user's entitlements in the source system instead of a shared service credential that reaches everything.

settings.name: settingSources
settings.where: options.settingSources (Python setting_sources)
settings.recommended: [] — the application passes everything the agent needs
settings.why: A repository's or host user's settings, hooks, CLAUDE.md, skills and subagents never enter the agent; managed policy still loads.

settings.name: CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY
settings.where: options.env → CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY (or autoMemoryEnabled false in settings)
settings.default: Auto memory on, loaded whatever settingSources says
settings.recommended: "1", unless the application deliberately keeps per-tenant memory
settings.why: Notes one run wrote are not loaded into the next run's system prompt as trusted context.

settings.name: CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR and cwd
settings.where: options.env → CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR, and options.cwd, per tenant
settings.default: ~/.claude and the process directory, shared by every query
settings.recommended: A per-tenant config directory and working directory on every query()
settings.why: Tenants do not share the global config, local transcripts, auto memory or files, so one tenant's session cannot read or seed another's.

settings.name: sessionStore (delete)
settings.where: options.sessionStore, an adapter implementing delete, with expiry set in its backend
settings.recommended: One store or key prefix per tenant, delete implemented, and the backend's retention at 30 days
settings.why: Transcripts live in storage the firm governs, deleteSession() cascades to subagent transcripts, and nothing is kept past the retention you set — the SDK never deletes from the store.

settings.name: permissionMode
settings.where: options.permissionMode (Python permission_mode)
settings.recommended: "default" — calls that need approval reach canUseTool
settings.why: Nothing is auto-approved by mode; acceptEdits and auto are for sandboxed workers only, and dontAsk denies instead of asking.

settings.name: allowDangerouslySkipPermissions
settings.where: options.allowDangerouslySkipPermissions (TypeScript)
settings.recommended: false
settings.why: bypassPermissions cannot be set at startup or switched to later with setPermissionMode(), so no code path runs every tool unapproved.

settings.name: disallowedTools
settings.where: options.disallowedTools (Python disallowed_tools)
settings.recommended: Bare names for tools the agent never needs, and scoped rules for secret paths and risky commands — Read(./.env*), Edit(//etc/**), Bash(git push *)
settings.why: Deny rules hold in every permission mode, bypassPermissions included, for the main agent and every subagent.

settings.name: canUseTool
settings.where: options.canUseTool, with permissions.ask rules in options.settings
settings.default: Unset (calls that would prompt are denied)
settings.recommended: A callback that shows the tool, final input and agentID to an authenticated approver and returns deny on timeout
settings.why: Each call an ask rule or default mode routes there waits for a person; an allowedTools bare name skips it, so pre-approve with specifiers only.

settings.name: hooks.PreToolUse
settings.where: options.hooks.PreToolUse, a callback returning permissionDecision
settings.recommended: A policy callback on every consequential tool that checks the principal, tool and arguments and returns deny or ask
settings.why: It runs before every other check, and its deny wins; a hook that times out leaves the tool unrun.

settings.name: managedSettings
settings.where: options.managedSettings (TypeScript), or managed-settings.json baked into the container image
settings.recommended: permissions.deny for secret paths, allowedMcpServers with allowManagedMcpServersOnly, and sandbox.network.allowManagedDomainsOnly
settings.why: Policy-tier rules that a later setPermissionMode() or applyFlagSettings() call cannot loosen; on a host with admin-deployed managed settings they are ignored unless that policy sets parentSettingsBehavior merge.

settings.name: tools (AgentDefinition) with CLAUDE_AGENT_SDK_DISABLE_BUILTIN_AGENTS
settings.where: options.agents[name].tools; options.env → CLAUDE_AGENT_SDK_DISABLE_BUILTIN_AGENTS
settings.default: A subagent with no tools inherits every tool; the general-purpose subagent is always available
settings.recommended: An explicit tools list on every subagent, and "1"
settings.why: Claude can spawn only the agents you defined, each holding only the tools its task needs.

settings.name: strictMcpConfig
settings.where: options.strictMcpConfig (Python strict_mcp_config)
settings.recommended: true, with mcpServers built from your registry and stdio servers on pinned versions
settings.why: Project .mcp.json, user settings, plugin servers and claude.ai connectors cannot add servers the application did not declare.

settings.name: sandbox (enabled, failIfUnavailable, allowUnsandboxedCommands)
settings.where: options.sandbox
settings.recommended: true / true / false, with no excludedCommands
settings.why: Bash and its children run in the OS sandbox, a host that cannot sandbox stops, and the model cannot ask to run a command outside it; WebFetch, MCP servers and hooks stay outside.

settings.name: CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB
settings.where: options.env → CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB
settings.why: Strips credentials from the environment of every Bash command, hook and stdio MCP server, so an injected command finds no keys to read.

settings.name: maxTurns
settings.where: options.maxTurns (Python max_turns), and maxTurns on each AgentDefinition
settings.recommended: A cap sized to the task on the query and on every subagent
settings.why: A looping agent ends with error_max_turns instead of running on.

settings.name: maxBudgetUsd
settings.where: options.maxBudgetUsd (Python max_budget_usd)
settings.recommended: A cap sized to what one run should cost, with headroom
settings.why: At the cap new subagents are refused, running background subagents stop and the query ends; the estimate is client-side and can pass the cap.

settings.name: hooks.PostToolUse (updatedToolOutput)
settings.where: options.hooks.PostToolUse for WebFetch, WebSearch, Bash, Read and mcp__ tools
settings.recommended: Your injection classifier and PII / secret detector on every tool that returns external content, replacing hits through updatedToolOutput
settings.why: Injected instructions and sensitive spans are removed before the model reasons over the result; OpenTelemetry keeps the original.

settings.name: hooks.UserPromptSubmit
settings.where: options.hooks.UserPromptSubmit
settings.recommended: A classifier on the initiator's prompt that blocks on a hit
settings.why: An injected or policy-breaking request relayed from an end user is stopped before the first model call.

settings.name: sandbox.network.allowedDomains with strictAllowlist
settings.where: options.sandbox.network.allowedDomains, strictAllowlist (or the same keys in managedSettings)
settings.recommended: Your source control, package mirror and approved APIs / true
settings.why: Sandboxed commands reach only listed hosts instead of prompting; strictAllowlist is honoured from managed or --settings sources and does not gate WebFetch.

settings.name: ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL and HTTPS_PROXY
settings.where: options.env, or the container environment
settings.default: Direct to api.anthropic.com and the internet
settings.recommended: A credential-injecting proxy outside the container, with the container on --network none or a subnet that reaches only the proxy
settings.why: Keys for the model and other services are added after traffic leaves the agent, and every destination is allowlisted and logged at the proxy.

settings.name: CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY with OTEL exporters
settings.where: options.env → CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY, CLAUDE_CODE_ENHANCED_TELEMETRY_BETA, OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER, OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER, OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT
settings.recommended: "1", exporting traces, metrics and logs over OTLP to your collector, with enduser.id in OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES
settings.why: Every turn, model request, tool call and permission decision — subagents nested under the parent — lands in the SIEM keyed to the end user.

settings.name: OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS, OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS, OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT, OTEL_LOG_RAW_API_BODIES
settings.where: options.env
settings.recommended: Leave unset, unless the collector is approved to hold client material
settings.why: Telemetry stays structural, so prompts, file contents and tool results do not land in the observability pipeline.
