summary: Cloud Agents (formerly Background Agents) run the Cursor agent in a Firecracker microVM in a dedicated AWS account, one VM boundary per agent rather than a shared process sandbox. They clone repositories through a Cursor GitHub / GitLab / Bitbucket / Azure DevOps app an account admin connected, work on a branch and hand back a draft pull request. Triggers are the web app, iOS, the Desktop Cloud dropdown, @cursor in Slack, Linear, GitHub or Bitbucket, the Cloud Agents API (public beta) and Automations that fire on schedules, source-control, Slack, Linear, Sentry, PagerDuty or webhook events. Bugbot, Security Agents and Approval Agents are Cloud Agents wired to pull-request events; Self-Hosted Machines move tool execution onto customer workers while the agent loop and inference stay in Cursor's cloud.

Inference runs on Cursor's hosted providers under Privacy Mode (Cloud Agents do not support Legacy Privacy Mode and never train on accessed code). Code is stored temporarily while a run executes; conversation state is retained indefinitely by default until deleted, VM snapshots are deleted after 30 days unused (each start or resume extends that). Data at rest is AES-256 with per-agent keys, TLS 1.2+ in transit, and Enterprise teams can bring a customer-managed KMS key (CMEK/BYOK). Egress leaves from published CIDR ranges (docs/ips.json) and a fixed three-IP git proxy; AWS PrivateLink or Cloudflare Tunnel reach private git servers and registries.

The admin surface is the dashboard's Cloud Agents section plus Enterprise settings: a network-access policy (Allow all / Default + allowlist / Allowlist only) that admins can lock org-wide, Runtime Secrets that are redacted from transcripts, tool output and commits, OIDC federation (issuer api.cursor.com, 5-minute RS256 tokens) so agents assume cloud roles without stored credentials, Protected Git Scopes (the editor's Repository Blocklist does not reach Cloud Agents), and admin toggles for agent summaries in Slack, Team follow-ups, Computer use and self-hosted placement. The default network policy is allow-all, and an Approval Agent can be configured to approve low-risk pull requests itself — both defaults an organisation should decide on deliberately.

facts.label: Plans
facts.value: Any paid Cursor plan can run Cloud Agents. Enterprise-only: network-policy lock, CMEK, PrivateLink / Cloudflare Tunnel, service accounts, Team Pools for Self-Hosted Machines, audit log and SIEM, OpenTelemetry export, Computer use toggle, Cloud Agent retention policies (early access). The Admin API, Bugbot Admin API included, is available on Teams and Enterprise.

facts.label: Inference & routing
facts.value: Self-Hosted Machines keep inference and planning in Cursor's cloud and send only the content the agent needs; workers connect outbound to api2.cursor.sh, api2direct.cursor.sh and the artifacts S3 bucket.

facts.label: Data leaving the device
facts.value: Nothing runs on the developer's device; the repository, secrets and environment live in the VM. Slack, GitHub and Linear see agent summaries and diffs (file paths included) unless the Display agent summary toggles are off; Slack Connect guests are governed by a separate external-channels toggle.

facts.label: Data retention / training
facts.value: Privacy Mode always: Cursor never trains on code accessed by Cloud Agents or on their prompts and responses. Conversation state is retained indefinitely by default and deletable on demand; VM snapshots auto-delete after 30 days of inactivity; the runtime workspace is recycled when idle. Secrets are KMS-encrypted at rest.

facts.label: Docs index
facts.value: Cloud Agents documentation (overview, security, secrets and network, identity, settings, private connectivity, self-hosted, automations, API).

facts.label: Isolation
facts.value: Firecracker microVMs in a dedicated AWS account segregated from other Cursor services; one VM boundary per agent.

facts.label: Egress
facts.value: Published CIDR ranges per cluster (us3p, us4p, us5p) at cursor.com/docs/ips.json and a three-IP git egress proxy (184.73.225.134, 3.209.66.12, 52.44.113.131); the default network allowlist matches the desktop sandbox's defaults.

facts.label: Private connectivity
facts.value: AWS PrivateLink (endpoint service com.amazonaws.vpce.us-east-1.vpce-svc-054b15427d4bea2b7 for the api2.cursor.sh webhook path) or Cloudflare Tunnel for GitHub Enterprise Server, GitLab Enterprise, Bitbucket Data Center and package registries; shared by Cloud Agents, Bugbot and backend services; Enterprise only, arranged via hi@cursor.com.

facts.label: Cursor Origin (excluded surface)
facts.value: Cursor's git forge, early beta since 2026-08-17 on Pro, Teams and Enterprise, mirroring a GitHub repository one-way (GitHub stays the source of truth); admins can disable Origin for the team from the dashboard, and a namespace must be claimed before enabling. Left out of the registry as code hosting rather than an agent runtime; treat repositories mirrored into Origin as a code-egress path to review.

facts.label: Vendor ownership
facts.value: SpaceX closed its acquisition of Anysphere (Cursor) on 2026-08-15; Cloud Agent infrastructure and subprocessors should be re-confirmed under the new owner.

riskNotes.note: A Cloud Agent reads repository content, PR comments, Slack threads and Linear issues as instructions and can browse the web; the vendor's stated mitigations are egress restriction, Runtime Secret redaction and the draft-PR gate. The default network policy is allow-all, so the first mitigation only exists once an admin locks Allowlist only.

The GitHub App is installed with eight permission categories including Administration; the agent can only reach repositories the triggering user could, but Automations run under the `cursor` account or a service account and Approval Agents can approve PRs on their own criteria — a machine identity approving machine-authored changes unless you keep approvals off.

Agent summaries and diffs are posted into Slack, GitHub and Linear by default; conversation state persists indefinitely. Turn off Display agent summary in external channels, mark credentials as Runtime Secrets and set a deletion routine through the API.

Anyone on a paid plan can create Automations and any team member can create Private ones that run as and bill to themselves; Protected Git Scopes, admins' ability to view and disable Private automations, and an admin switching Run as to Service account are the levers that bring them under the team.

controls.mechanism: Source-control connection by a Cursor admin plus the Git provider admin's app install on chosen repositories; Protected Git Scopes (dashboard Integrations tab); Team follow-ups; Allow Personal Machines (Remote Control) and Allow / Require Self-Hosted Machines under Dashboard → Cloud Agents → Self-Hosted

steps.title: Gate Cloud Agents behind the source-control connection
body: Cloud Agents start only after a Cursor admin connects source control and a Git provider admin installs the Cursor app on the repositories you choose; each user then connects their own Git account, and a run never reaches a repository the triggering user could not already reach.

steps.title: Lock the Git organisation to your Cursor organisation
body: Claim the scope under Protected Git Scopes from the dashboard's Integrations tab (a team admin who is also a Git provider admin) so only your teams run Cloud Agents, automations and Bugbot on it; the Repository Blocklist covers only the editor and CLI, not Cloud Agents, automations or Bugbot.

steps.title: Decide who may steer a running agent
body: Set Team follow-ups in the Cloud Agents security settings to Disabled or Service accounts only; All lets any teammate with repository access instruct an agent that holds another user's secrets.

steps.title: Keep Allow Personal Machines off until someone owns it
body: Leave Allow Personal Machines, the team's Remote Control setting, off under Cursor Dashboard → Cloud Agents → Self-Hosted; while it and Allow Self-Hosted Machines are off, Cloud Agents cannot run on members' machines.

controls.note: Rated partial on the hosted rule. Enablement is organisation-level only: the gate is the admin's source-control connection, and no per-role or per-group Cloud Agents switch is documented, so any paid member with repository access can start runs. The trigger condition is not admin-configurable: @cursor in Slack, GitHub, Bitbucket and Linear admits any linked Cursor user with access to the repository, automation "Comment added" triggers name no restriction on the commenter, and Bugbot runs for all contributors to enabled repositories. The widening switches are admin-controlled and enforced by Cursor's control plane: Allow Personal Machines (Remote Control), Allow / Require Self-Hosted Machines (https://cursor.com/docs/cloud-agent/self-hosted), Team follow-ups, Computer use and Sync Skills for Cloud Agents. Protected Git Scopes covers cloud and self-hosted GitHub and GitLab.

original.mechanism: Team SSO / SCIM; source-control connection by an account admin; Protected Git Scopes; Remote Control and Self-Hosted enablement under Dashboard → Cloud Agents

steps.title: Gate who can trigger agents
body: Members authenticate through the team's SSO; a Cursor account admin must connect GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket or Azure DevOps before any agent can clone, and the GitHub App can be installed on Selected repositories only.

steps.title: Lock your git organisation to your Cursor organisation
body: Enable Protected Git Scopes (needs GitHub org owner or admin) so only your Cursor teams can use those repositories with Cloud Agents and Bugbot.

steps.title: Decide on Remote Control and self-hosted workers
body: Under Cursor Dashboard → Cloud Agents → Self-Hosted enable or disable Remote Control for members; enabling it also enables the team's self-hosted worker access.

controls.mechanism: Automations list (team admins view and disable Private automations); Run as → Service account with automation-<id> service accounts; Cloud Agents dashboard Environments view; Bugbot /bugbot/repos

steps.title: Bring automations under the team
body: Team admins can view and disable any automation, Private ones included, and only admins can set Run as to Service account, which gives the automation its own service account billed to the team pool.

steps.title: Review shared environments
body: The Environments view in the Cloud Agents dashboard lists each saved environment with its repositories, install script, runtime and build secrets, network access and version history.

steps.title: Enumerate what Bugbot is enabled on
body: List repositories and their settings with /bugbot/repos and set enabled or manualTriggerOnly per repository with /bugbot/repo/update, using a team Admin API key.

controls.note: Partial on the hosted rule. The dashboard lists automations, environments, self-hosted workers and service accounts, but nothing is denied for being unlisted: any paid member can start runs or create a Private automation billed to themselves, and there is no approval state or declared-capability record. Cursor's control plane holds the inventory; reconciliation against the organisation's register is the organisation's.

original.mechanism: Dashboard → Cloud Agents and Automations lists; service accounts visible to admins; Bugbot repository list via /bugbot/repos

steps.title: Bring automations under the team
body: Admins can view, disable and promote automations to Team Owned (regenerates webhook keys and OAuth); Private and Team Visible automations otherwise bill and belong to their creator.

steps.title: Enumerate what Bugbot is enabled on
body: List repositories and settings with /bugbot/repos and set enabled or manualTriggerOnly per repository with /bugbot/repo/update.

original.note: No approval workflow or declared-capability record; the lists are inventories, not a register with reconciliation.

controls.mechanism: Enterprise team hooks (preToolUse, beforeShellExecution) as the only per-call gate; Computer use team toggle; per-automation tools; Cursor app on Selected repositories and Protected Git Scopes

steps.title: Scope repository reach
body: Install the Cursor app on Selected repositories only and claim the Git organisation under Protected Git Scopes; the Repository Blocklist does not apply to Cloud Agents, automations or Bugbot.

steps.title: Switch off built-in capabilities the team does not need
body: In the Cloud Agents dashboard's Team feature settings turn off Computer use (Enterprise); changes apply to new agents immediately.

steps.title: Give each automation only the tools it needs
body: Enable only the automation tools a workflow needs (Send to Slack, Read Slack channels, MCP server, Memories, Computer use); an MCP server tool exposes every tool that server offers.

steps.title: Distribute a deny hook from the dashboard
body: Publish an Enterprise team hook on preToolUse (Shell, Read, Write, MCP tools, Task) that returns deny for disallowed tools or arguments; any deny wins over project hooks. Dashboard hooks take no failClosed, so a hook that crashes or times out lets the call through unless the repository's .cursor/hooks.json sets it.

controls.note: Rated partial on the rule applied to every vendor. Cursor ships no declarative per-tool or per-argument permission rules for Cloud Agents and the agent auto-runs every terminal command, so per-call allow and deny exists only as org-written hook code (an attach point) distributed as Enterprise team hooks, which do not run during the read-only exploratory turns and cannot use beforeMCPExecution in the cloud. The product-enforced levers bound repositories (app installation, Protected Git Scopes; the editor's Repository Blocklist does not apply here), network (Lock Network Access Policy) and whole capabilities (Computer use, per-automation tools). Cursor does not scope the repository token to one branch; default-branch protection is the forge's branch protection. The Enterprise MCP allowlist page does not state that it applies to Cloud Agents, and users can add personal MCP servers at cursor.com/agents, so the connector allowlist is not credited here.

original.mechanism: GitHub App scope (Selected repositories; access never wider than the triggering user); Protected Git Scopes; Repository Blocklist; Team feature settings (Long running agents, Computer use); per-automation tool enablement; MCP allowlist

steps.title: Scope repository reach
body: Install the GitHub App on Selected repositories, keep the Repository Blocklist for sensitive repos, and rely on the rule that a Cloud Agent can only reach repositories the triggering user could.

steps.title: Manage the blocklist by API
body: Read and update repository blocklist glob patterns through /settings/repo-blocklists/repos.

steps.title: Switch off tools the team does not need
body: In Cloud Agent dashboard settings disable Computer use and Long running agents, and set Team follow-ups to Disabled or Service accounts only.

steps.title: Keep the MCP allowlist in force
body: The Enterprise MCP Configuration applies to cloud runs; Automations only get the tools (PRs, Slack, MCP, memory, computer use) you enable per automation.

original.note: Repository scope, blocklists and Protected Git Scopes limit resources; per-automation tool enablement hides tools; there is no pre-approval layer because runs are unattended. MCP tools follow the MCP allowlist.

original.mechanism: Command-based repository hooks (beforeShellExecution, beforeMCPExecution, preToolUse) with failClosed run in cloud agents once the environment is writable; Enterprise MCP Configuration Tools field; Protected Git Scopes and Repository Blocklist

steps.title: Commit fail-closed command hooks
body: Cloud agents run command-based hooks from the repository (prompt-based hooks are not supported there); set failClosed true on beforeShellExecution and beforeMCPExecution so a crashed or timed-out hook blocks rather than allows.

steps.title: Restrict MCP tools centrally
body: Use the Tools field per server in the Enterprise MCP Configuration to name the tools a server may run; it applies to Cloud Agents as well as the IDE.

original.note: Rated partial on the same rule as Copilot cloud: the hooks are repository code, writable by anyone with push access, not enterprise policy, and they do not run during the read-only exploratory turns a run starts with. The deterministic administrator rules bound tools and repositories, not individual shell commands.

original.mechanism: Enterprise MCP Configuration: allowlist by full command string or URL with wildcards, per-server network mode (Allow all, Allowlist, Deny all, No sandbox) and Tools field; applies to Cloud Agents

steps.title: Allowlist servers for cloud runs
body: Add each permitted server by command string or URL pattern in the Enterprise MCP Configuration and give local servers an Allowlist or Deny all network mode; the configuration applies to Cloud Agents and Bugbot as well as the IDE.

original.note: Rated native on the same rule as Cursor in the IDE: admission by identity, organisation-wide. Admission is not integrity — nothing pins the tool descriptions a server returns or detects a changed implementation between runs.

controls.mechanism: Draft pull request a person reviews and merges in the forge; PR Routing & Approval with risk-based approval left off; automation Comment on pull request tool with approvals disabled; Team follow-ups

steps.title: Keep the merge gate human
body: In PR Routing & Approval use routing only, or set approval criteria and Maximum Risk Threshold deliberately, because the agent can approve low-risk PRs; keep required human review in your forge.

steps.title: Keep automations from approving
body: Leave approvals off on the Comment on pull request tool; with approvals enabled the agent can approve, request changes and dismiss reviews.

steps.title: Restrict who can steer a running agent
body: Set Team follow-ups to Disabled or Service accounts only so only the creator can add instructions from Slack or the web.

controls.note: Partial by the hosted rule. A draft pull request a person reviews and merges approves the output, not the actions: Cloud Agents auto-run terminal commands, network calls and tool calls with no per-action approval (a preToolUse hook's ask is not enforced today), and all of it has happened when the reviewer arrives. PR Routing & Approval and automations with approvals enabled are AI reviewers and never count as human approval.

original.mechanism: Draft pull request as the review gate; Team follow-ups; Approval Agent approval toggle; Bugbot manualTriggerOnly

steps.title: Keep the PR gate human
body: Cloud Agents deliver draft PRs; branch protection in your forge is the deterministic gate. If you deploy PR Routing & Approval, leave approvals off unless you accept machine approval of low-risk PRs.

steps.title: Restrict who can steer a running agent
body: Set Team follow-ups to Disabled or Service accounts only so only the owner can add instructions from Slack or the web.

original.note: The human gate is the pull request; commands, network access and tool calls taken while the agent runs are not individually approved.

controls.mechanism: Enterprise team hooks as the attach point (postToolUse updated_mcp_tool_output replaces stdio MCP results, beforeReadFile can block reads); vendor containment layers (egress allowlist, Runtime Secret redaction, .cursorignore, draft pull request)

steps.title: Screen MCP results with a team hook
body: Distribute an Enterprise team hook on postToolUse that sends stdio MCP output to your inspector and returns updated_mcp_tool_output to replace a flagged result before the model sees it; use beforeReadFile to deny reads of untrusted paths.

steps.title: Apply the vendor's containment layers
body: Lock Allowlist only egress, mark credentials as Runtime Secrets, add sensitive paths to .cursorignore and keep the draft pull request gate; these are the documented prompt-injection layers.

controls.note: Partial on the rule. Cursor classifies nothing it feeds a Cloud Agent: repository files, PR and issue threads, Slack messages and fetched pages enter context unscreened. The only screening point is org-written hook code, and postToolUse can replace output only from stdio MCP servers in the VM: HTTP MCP servers run on Cursor's backend, where postToolUse receives {"redacted": true} and cannot replace the result, and shell output and web content cannot be replaced either; hooks do not run during the read-only exploratory turns. The vendor's layers contain an injection's effect rather than detect it. Automation pull-request triggers skip fork PRs; CODEOWNERS on .cursor/ is a forge process control. CVE-2026-61613 showed attacker web content reaching an unauthenticated agent endpoint inside the VM (fixed 2026-03-31).

original.mechanism: Egress allowlist, Runtime Secret redaction and draft-PR gating (vendor's listed mitigations); Team and Enterprise hooks run in cloud agents

steps.title: Apply the vendor's three mitigations
body: Lock Allowlist only egress, mark credentials as Runtime Secrets and keep the draft-PR gate; these are the documented prompt-injection mitigations for Cloud Agents.

steps.title: Run enterprise hooks in the cloud
body: Team hooks distributed from the dashboard and Enterprise-managed hooks also run in cloud agents, so beforeShellExecution and beforeSubmitPrompt checks apply there.

original.note: No classifier over retrieved web, PR or Slack content; CVE-2026-61613 showed attacker web content reaching an unauthenticated agent endpoint inside the container (fixed 2026-03-31).

controls.mechanism: Vendor evidence (cursor.com/security, trust.cursor.com, the Cloud Agents security overview) consumed by the organisation's TPRM platform

evidence.title: Cursor security page (AIUC-1, ISO/IEC 27001:2022, ISO/IEC 42001:2023, SOC 2 Type II, annual third-party penetration testing; reports on request at trust.cursor.com), checked 2026-09-25
Cloud Agents security overview (isolation, encryption, retention, Trust Center link)

controls.note: External: Cursor offers no assessment workflow; the organisation's TPRM platform consumes the evidence. Record the per-agent Firecracker microVMs in a separate AWS account, the shared egress ranges, conversation state kept indefinitely by default (a 90-day Enterprise cap is in early access), subprocessors from the Trust Center and the SpaceX ownership change, and re-assess when Cloud Agent defaults move (egress Allow all, self-approving PR agents). Configuration read APIs exist (/settings/repo-blocklists/repos, /teams/audit-logs) but the network-policy lock and the Display agent summary toggles have no documented API, so posture checks read the dashboard.

original.mechanism: Vendor evidence (trust portal, cursor.com/security, published egress ranges) consumed by the organisation's TPRM platform

steps.title: Refresh the assessment for the hosted runtime
body: Record the dedicated-AWS-account and Firecracker isolation, the shared egress ranges, sub-processors, SOC 2 / ISO 27001 / ISO 42001 / AIUC-1 and the SpaceX ownership change.

original.mechanism: Admin API endpoints (/teams/model-access/configuration, /teams/audit-logs, /settings/repo-blocklists/repos) polled by an SSPM product
original.note: Cursor exposes configuration read APIs but ships no posture checks; the network-policy lock, Privacy Mode enforcement and Display-summary toggles are dashboard-only and must be verified manually.

evidence.title: Vendor docs index, reviewed for the integration point (2026-09-10)

controls.mechanism: Team Settings → OpenTelemetry Export (cloud_agents, model_usage and tool_calls families; opt-in Allow conversation content export with Tool I/O, one record per side of every MCP and builtin tool call); Cloud Agents API run stream; Enterprise audit log

steps.title: Export Cloud Agent telemetry
body: In Team Settings → OpenTelemetry Export create a destination and keep the cloud_agents, model_usage and tool_calls families on; cloud_agent.* logs carry setup, artifact, pull request and MCP-auth events keyed by the bc- agent id.

steps.title: Add prompts and responses
body: Turn on Allow conversation content export for the team and Conversation content on the destination to stream scrubbed user prompts and final assistant responses; off by default, no backfill.

steps.title: Export every tool call
body: On the destination turn on Conversation content and Tool I/O (Prompts and Responses can stay off); every finished MCP and builtin call (shell, read, edit, grep, fetch, Task) arrives as cursor.conversation.tool_io records with cursor.tool.name, scrubbed arguments and result, joined by cursor.tool_call.id and cursor.conversation.id.

steps.title: Capture per-step tool calls at run time
body: Stream each run with GET /v1/agents/{id}/runs/{runId}/stream and archive its tool_call events (name, args, result) before X-Cursor-Stream-Retention-Seconds lapses.

steps.title: Stream Cloud Agent audit events
body: The Enterprise audit log records Cloud Agent environment creation, updates, restores and lifecycle changes plus MCP configuration and Slack links; stream it to a SIEM, webhook or S3.

controls.note: Native on the hosted rule: an admin turns on server-side OTel export, and with the opt-in Tool I/O toggle every finished MCP and builtin tool call a Cloud Agent makes (Task subagents included, under their own bc- id) arrives as a per-call record with tool name, scrubbed arguments and result, correlated by cursor.tool_call.id, cursor.conversation.id and turn id; members cannot switch it off. Limits: each side is an 8 KiB excerpt, scrubbing is best effort, records are exported when the turn ends (order by record timestamp), delivery is at-least-once with no backfill or trace ids, subagent prompts are not exported, and no per-call allow or deny decision is recorded, so a hook that denies must log it itself. The run stream and transcript remain a per-owner pull bounded by a retention window. Audit logs are control-plane only and exclude agent responses and code. Enterprise only.

original.mechanism: Team Settings → OpenTelemetry Export (cloud agent lifecycle, tool-call and token events); run stream via GET /v1/agents/{id}/runs/{runId}/stream; Automations run history

steps.title: Export lifecycle and tool events
body: Configure an OTLP/HTTP destination; logs include cloud agent lifecycle events, hook and plugin activation and builtin / MCP tool-call counts, with no prompt content, trace context or backfill.

steps.title: Capture transcripts at run time
body: Stream each run with the SSE endpoint and archive it; the API keeps run history per agent with pagination.

original.note: No structured trace of reasoning steps, memory reads or handoffs is exported; Grok Bot's Action Recording does not apply to Cloud Agents.

original.mechanism: Enterprise Audit Log with SIEM streaming; Admin API /teams/audit-logs

steps.title: Stream Cloud Agent audit events
body: The audit log records Cloud Agent environment creation, updates, restores and lifecycle changes, repository mappings, MCP authentication and Slack links; stream it to your SIEM.

steps.title: Query the audit log by API
body: Pull audit events programmatically from /teams/audit-logs with an Admin API key.

original.note: Agent responses and generated code are explicitly not logged; retention and tamper-evidence are not stated on the page fetched.

controls.mechanism: Conversation state kept indefinitely by default; Enterprise Cloud Agent retention policy (Indefinite or 90 days, early access); Delete Agent API; snapshots expire after 30 days unused; automation Memories; Sync Skills for Cloud Agents team switch

steps.title: Cap conversation retention
body: Enterprise admins set the Cloud Agent retention policy to 90 days in Team Settings on the Cloud Agents dashboard (early access); otherwise delete transcripts with the Delete Agent API. Snapshots cannot be deleted on demand.

steps.title: Turn automation memory off or review it
body: Memories are enabled by default per automation; disable them where input is untrusted, or view, edit and delete memory files from the tool configuration UI.

steps.title: Stop personal skills reaching cloud runs
body: Turn Sync Skills for Cloud Agents off under Security & Identity to disable personal skill sync for everyone.

controls.note: Partial on the rule. Admins can cap transcript retention (Enterprise, early access) and switch off personal-skill sync, and an automation's owner can disable or edit its memory, but memory writes are not validated or gated (the docs warn untrusted input can plant misleading memories), there is no team-wide memory switch, and instruction sources (.cursor rules, AGENTS.md, repository skills) are repository content any committer can change. Snapshots, which can include .env.local files, persist until 30 days of inactivity (each start or resume extends the window); transcripts are visible to teammates who have repository access.

original.mechanism: Conversation state retained indefinitely, deletable on demand; agent archive / DELETE via API; Automations persistent memory as an opt-out tool (enabled by default)

steps.title: Delete what you do not need
body: Archive or DELETE /v1/agents/{id} when work is merged; VM snapshots are removed after 90 days idle but conversation state is not.

steps.title: Turn memory off where not needed
body: Memories are enabled by default for each automation; disable the persistent-memory tool on automations that do not need it.

original.note: No validation, quarantine or rollback of memory content; the control is deletion.

controls.mechanism: Monthly additional usage limit (The X Subscription, admin-only on Teams) or, on legacy plans, the Spending tab Monthly Limit with Only Admins Can Edit Usage Settings; Enterprise member and group spend-limit overrides (/teams/user-spend-limit); vendor-fixed run limits

steps.title: Cap spend and lock the setting
body: On The X Subscription set Monthly additional usage limit under Additional usage credits at grok.com/dashboard/billing (fixed or per seat; only team admins can change it). On legacy plans set the team limit in the Spending tab and enable Only Admins Can Edit Usage Settings under Permissions. On Enterprise add member or group overrides.

steps.title: Set member limits by API
body: Set or read per-member spend limits (Enterprise) through /teams/user-spend-limit.

controls.note: Partial on the hosted rule. The caps are financial and enforcement is not instant (the spend-limit page says usage can briefly exceed a limit); whether a Cloud Agent already running stops at the cap is not documented. No admin-set run duration, concurrency, fan-out or per-automation budget exists (the Long running agents team toggle is gone from the settings page; long work is now started with /goal, which no admin setting governs); the fixed limits are the vendor's (one active run per agent, at most 10 automatic CI-fix follow-ups per PR, subscriptions that last at most 180 days). Automations that Run as a service account bill the team pool; Run as Me bills the creator.

original.mechanism: Usage-Based Pricing Settings (monthly team limit, admin-only changes); per-member spend limits (Enterprise) via /teams/user-spend-limit; API rate limits; one active run per agent

steps.title: Cap spend per team and member
body: Set the monthly team spending limit and, on Enterprise, individual limits per member from the dashboard; usage-based Cloud Agent, Bugbot and Automation runs draw from these pools.

steps.title: Set member limits by API
body: Set or read per-member spend limits (Enterprise) through /teams/user-spend-limit.

original.note: Limits are financial; there is no cap on tool-call depth or run duration beyond the Long running agents toggle.

controls.mechanism: POST /v1/agents/{id}/runs/{runId}/cancel by the agent's owner; admin disable of any automation; service-account archive; /teams/remove-member; Bugbot enabled false

steps.title: Cancel the run
body: The agent's owner, or the service account that started it, cancels with POST /v1/agents/{id}/runs/{runId}/cancel; cancellation is terminal and the run moves to CANCELLED.

steps.title: Disable the automation
body: Team admins can disable any automation, Private ones included; an automation that runs as a service account stops running if that account is archived.

steps.title: Revoke the principal
body: Archive the service account to revoke every API key it holds while keeping the record for audit.

steps.title: Switch Bugbot off per repository
body: Set enabled false through /bugbot/repo/update with a team Admin API key.

controls.note: Partial by the hosted rule. Only an agent's owner, or whoever holds the service-account key that started it, can cancel a run in flight; the docs give administrators no way to stop a teammate's running agent. Disabling automations, archiving service accounts, removing members (/teams/remove-member, Enterprise) and switching Bugbot off prevent the next run; whether they stop one already running, and how quickly, is not documented. Cancelling does not undo commits already pushed. On Self-Hosted Machines, stopping the worker is the organisation's own complement.

original.mechanism: POST /v1/agents/{id}/runs/{runId}/cancel; archive / delete agent; disable automation; archive service account (revokes keys); /teams/remove-member; Bugbot enabled=false

steps.title: Stop a run and revoke its identity
body: Cancel the run, then archive or delete the agent; archive the service account to revoke every key it holds while keeping the record for audit.

steps.title: Disable the integration
body: Admins can disable any automation from the dashboard and set enabled false per repository for Bugbot through /bugbot/repo/update.

original.note: Cancelling a run stops active work; archiving the service account revokes future access. A run already pushing a commit completes that push.

controls.mechanism: Firecracker microVM per agent in an AWS account separate from Cursor's production infrastructure; runtime workspace recycled on idle timers, snapshots deleted after 30 days of inactivity

steps.title: Rely on per-agent microVMs and let them recycle
body: Each agent runs in its own Firecracker-based VM in a separate AWS account and cannot see another agent's code, environment or state; the workspace is recycled once the run goes idle.

controls.note: Native on the hosted rule: one microVM per agent, created for it and reclaimed on idle timers, documented by the vendor. Boundary: follow-up runs on the same agent reuse its VM and snapshot, and snapshots (which can include .env.local files) persist until 30 days of inactivity. Inside: commands, Docker builds, stdio MCP servers and computer use. Outside: the model and HTTP MCP servers, whose calls are proxied through Cursor's backend. Allow or Require Self-Hosted Machines moves tool execution onto your workers, where isolation is yours.

original.mechanism: Firecracker microVM per agent in an AWS account separate from Cursor's production infrastructure; workspace recycled after the run goes idle, snapshots expire after 90 days of inactivity

steps.title: Rely on per-agent microVMs and let them recycle
body: Every agent gets a dedicated environment isolated from other agents and users; do not extend idle timers beyond what a run needs, because the workspace persists until the timer lapses.

original.note: Inside the boundary: commands, Docker builds, local MCP servers and computer use when enabled. Outside: the model and remote MCP servers. Self-hosted runners (Dashboard > Cloud Agents > Self-Hosted) move the sandbox onto your infrastructure, where isolation is yours.

controls.mechanism: Network access modes Allow all network access (default), Default + allowlist and Allowlist only, set per user, per environment or as a team default; Enterprise Lock Network Access Policy

steps.title: Set Allowlist only and lock it
body: In the Cloud Agents dashboard set the team default to Allowlist only, then enable Lock Network Access Policy (Enterprise) so members cannot override it; Cursor services and your source-control provider stay reachable.

steps.title: Keep environments on the team policy
body: Leave saved environments on Inherit settings or Inherit settings + environment allowlist, and add cloud-agent-artifacts.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com exactly, never a regional wildcard.

controls.note: Native on the hosted rule: an admin-authored allowlist, lockable by an Enterprise admin, enforced by Cursor around the VM for cloning, package downloads, API calls, web access and artifact uploads. Bypasses: Cursor's own services and the source-control provider stay reachable in every mode, HTTP MCP calls leave from Cursor's backend, and inference is outside. The default is Allow all, locking is Enterprise only, no separate setup-phase policy is documented, and the page does not say whether the lock overrides an environment that defines its own mode, so keep environments inheriting. Private resources behind Tailscale, Cloudflare Tunnel or PrivateLink still need allowlist entries; egress IP ranges are shared (cursor.com/docs/ips.json).

original.mechanism: Network access modes Allow all (default), Default + allowlist and Allowlist only, set per user, per environment or as a team default; Enterprise Lock Network Access Policy; per-server network modes for local MCP servers in the Enterprise MCP Configuration

steps.title: Set Allowlist only and lock it
body: In Team settings choose Allowlist only with the domains agents need, then enable Lock Network Access Policy so members and environments cannot widen it; core Cursor services and your source-control provider stay reachable.

steps.title: Make environments inherit the policy
body: Saved environments can inherit the user or team policy, add an environment allowlist or define their own mode; keep them on inheritance so the lock applies.

original.note: Covers cloning and pushing, package downloads, API calls, web access and artifact uploads from the VM. The default is allow-all, so the restriction must be set deliberately; private resources are reached through Tailscale, Cloudflare Tunnel or PrivateLink and still pass the allowlist. Published egress ranges are at cursor.com/docs/ips.json.

controls.mechanism: Secrets tab types (Environment Variable, Runtime Secret, Build Secret) scoped to team, user or environment; HTTP MCP credentials held on Cursor's backend; OIDC 5-minute tokens; CURSOR_AWS_ASSUME_IAM_ROLE_ARN with 1-hour STS credentials

steps.title: Keep build credentials out of the agent
body: Store registry and build-time credentials as Build Secrets (Docker build only) and sensitive runtime values as Runtime Secrets, which are replaced with [REDACTED] in tool results, the transcript, commits and commit messages.

steps.title: Scope secrets to one environment
body: Use environment-scoped secrets so a credential reaches only agents that use that environment.

steps.title: Prefer HTTP MCP servers
body: HTTP server configurations, headers and tokens never enter the VM and tool calls are proxied through Cursor's backend; stdio servers expose their environment to the agent.

steps.title: Federate cloud access instead of storing keys
body: Mint OIDC tokens from the VM socket (valid five minutes) and scope the assumed role to what you would grant the whole run.

controls.note: Partial on the hosted rule. Build Secrets are kept out of the agent's runtime and HTTP MCP credentials stay on Cursor's backend, but Runtime Secrets are environment variables inside the VM (redacted from the transcript and commits, readable by any command the agent runs and in the VM terminal), and any process on the VM can mint the run's OIDC token. How the repository credential reaches a Cursor-hosted VM is not documented (the git egress proxy fixes source IPs; nothing says it substitutes the credential), so treat it as present in the sandbox; on Team Pool workers --mint-github-token places a short-lived GitHub token on the worker. With Team follow-ups set to All, a teammate can steer an agent that holds another user's secrets.

original.mechanism: Runtime Secrets redacted from the transcript, tool output and commits; encrypted storage with per-agent KMS keys; short-lived OIDC tokens (five minutes) minted inside the run for cloud federation instead of stored keys

steps.title: Federate instead of storing cloud keys
body: Verify tokens from the issuer https://api.cursor.com and scope the assumed role to what you would grant the whole run; the token carries cloud_agent_id, repo_urls, owner and team claims.

steps.title: Mark values as Runtime Secrets
body: Store credentials as Runtime Secrets so their values are stripped from transcript, tool output and commits and never reach the model.

original.note: Rated partial because the boundary is the transcript, not the execution: a Runtime Secret remains readable by any command in the VM, and any process that can reach the socket — the agent, code it runs, hooks — can mint the OIDC token, which identifies the run, not a process. No on-behalf-of exchange: a run acts as the GitHub App and the triggering user's repository reach.

original.mechanism: Secrets tab per environment — Environment Variables, Runtime Secrets (redacted), Build Secrets (Docker build only); KMS at rest; OIDC short-lived tokens

steps.title: Mark credentials as Runtime Secrets
body: In the environment's Secrets tab store credentials as Runtime Secrets so values are replaced with [REDACTED] in tool results, transcript, commits and commit messages; use Build Secrets for values only the Docker build should see.

steps.title: Prefer federated tokens to stored keys
body: Replace long-lived cloud keys with AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity against the Cursor OIDC issuer; tokens expire in five minutes.

original.note: Runtime Secrets are readable by commands the agent runs (redacted in logs, not from the shell); Build Secrets are readable by the Docker build only; OIDC tokens are the ephemeral path. The model sees a Runtime Secret if a command prints it.

controls.mechanism: Secrets tab (encrypted at rest and in transit, scoped to team, user or environment); service-account keys shown once, rotatable and archivable; OIDC and STS short-lived credentials; Cursor-issued Cloudflare Tunnel token for Enterprise private connectivity

steps.title: Keep secrets in the Secrets tab
body: Store credentials in the Secrets tab rather than the repository or a snapshot, as Runtime Secrets or Build Secrets; plain Environment Variables are visible to the agent.

steps.title: Replace static cloud keys with short-lived ones
body: Federate with OIDC tokens (five minutes, no refresh) instead of storing cloud access keys.

steps.title: Rotate automation keys
body: Rotate a service account's API key from Dashboard → Settings → API Keys → Service Accounts (the old key is invalidated immediately) and archive the account to revoke all its keys.

steps.title: Treat the private-connectivity tunnel token as a service credential
body: For Cloudflare Tunnel private connectivity Cursor creates the tunnel and shares the token through a 1Password share; keep it out of email and chat and agree rotation and revocation with Cursor.

controls.note: Partial on the hosted rule. Secrets are encrypted and scoped per team, user or environment, and MCP env, headers and client secrets are write-only after saving, but the docs do not say Cloud Agent secrets are write-only, Environment Variable secrets are visible to the agent by design, and Runtime Secrets are readable inside the VM. Short-lived issuance exists for cloud roles (OIDC five minutes, STS one hour) and for Team Pool GitHub tokens, not documented for the repository credential on Cursor-hosted VMs. Tunnel: a vendor tunnel exists for Enterprise private connectivity (Cloudflare Tunnel, token issued by Cursor) with no documented rotation or revocation; tunnels an organisation runs inside the VM (Tailscale, cloudflared) keep their tokens as Cursor Secrets, which the setup page says to rotate after testing.

settings.name: Protected Git Scopes
settings.where: Dashboard › Integrations › Protected Git Scopes
settings.recommended: Every GitHub and GitLab organisation or group the firm owns, claimed
settings.why: Only your Cursor teams can run Cloud Agents, automations and Bugbot on those repositories, even an outside Cursor account whose user has Git access.
settings.requires: Teams or Enterprise; a team admin who is also a Git provider admin

settings.name: Selected repositories
settings.where: GitHub › Cursor app installation › Repository access (or the GitLab / Bitbucket / Azure DevOps equivalent)
settings.recommended: Selected repositories — those cleared for Cloud Agents
settings.why: The app clones and pushes only where it is installed, so a run cannot reach a client repository nobody chose.

settings.name: Team follow-ups
settings.where: Dashboard › Cloud Agents › Security settings › Team follow-ups
settings.recommended: Service accounts only
settings.why: A teammate cannot steer an agent that runs with another person's secrets and tokens; shared service-account agents stay collaborative.

settings.name: Run as
settings.where: Automations › automation › Share › Run as
settings.recommended: Service account for every team automation
settings.why: The automation gets its own automation-<id> service account that admins manage, disable or archive, instead of running on a member's personal auth.

settings.name: Allow Self-Hosted Machines and Require Self-Hosted Machines
settings.where: Dashboard › Cloud Agents › Self-Hosted
settings.recommended: Off / Off, unless you run Team Pools, then On / On
settings.why: Runs stay in per-agent Cursor microVMs under the locked network policy, which does not reach self-hosted workers.

settings.name: Allow Personal Machines
settings.where: Dashboard › Cloud Agents › Self-Hosted
settings.default: Off on Teams and Enterprise until an admin enables it
settings.recommended: Off
settings.why: Cloud Agent runs and Remote Control cannot execute on members' laptops with their local credentials.

settings.name: Automatically allow Projects to place their work
settings.where: Dashboard › Cloud Agents › Security settings
settings.recommended: Off
settings.why: A Project agent asks in chat before starting work on a self-hosted machine or pool it has not used.

settings.name: Allow VM sharing
settings.where: Dashboard › Cloud Agents
settings.recommended: Off
settings.why: Teammates cannot open a live workspace terminal on a self-hosted worker as that worker's OS user.

settings.name: Cloud agent retention policies
settings.where: Dashboard › Cloud Agents › Team Settings › retention policy
settings.recommended: 90 days
settings.why: Transcripts with client code and tool output are deleted after 90 days instead of kept forever; snapshots still expire after 30 days idle.

settings.name: Display agent summary in external channels
settings.where: Dashboard › Cloud Agents › Security settings
settings.recommended: Off
settings.why: File-diff images and code snippets are not posted into Slack Connect or channels with guests.

settings.name: Sync Skills for Cloud Agents
settings.where: Team dashboard › Settings › Security & Identity
settings.recommended: Off
settings.why: Unreviewed personal skills from members' laptops do not ride into cloud runs; shared skills go through the team marketplace.

settings.name: Memories
settings.where: Automations › automation › tools › Memories
settings.recommended: Off on automations triggered by Slack, webhooks, PR comments or other untrusted input
settings.why: Text from an attacker cannot be written into MEMORIES.md and replayed into every later run.

settings.name: Runtime Secret and Build Secret
settings.where: Dashboard › Cloud Agents › Secrets (type per secret; team, user or environment scope)
settings.recommended: Runtime Secret for credentials, Build Secret for registry tokens, environment-scoped; never Environment Variable for a secret
settings.why: Credentials are redacted from tool results, transcripts and commits, and build-time tokens never enter the running agent.

settings.name: OIDC tokens
settings.where: Your cloud or Vault trust policy for issuer https://api.cursor.com, conditioned on team_id and repo_urls
settings.recommended: Federate cloud access with OIDC, trusting only your team_id and the repositories that need the role
settings.why: Agents get a five-minute token for a scoped role instead of a long-lived cloud key in Secrets.

settings.name: Secret sync
settings.where: Dashboard › Cloud Agents › Self-Hosted
settings.recommended: Off; pool workers use their own credentials
settings.why: Team and user secrets are not copied as environment variables onto every pool worker started with --sync-dashboard-secrets.

settings.name: Computer use
settings.where: Dashboard › Cloud Agents › Team feature settings
settings.recommended: Off, unless a team has a use for it
settings.why: New agents cannot drive a browser or desktop against internal services; changes apply to new agents immediately.

settings.name: Team hooks
settings.where: Web dashboard › Team content › Hooks
settings.recommended: preToolUse and beforeShellExecution hooks calling your policy service; postToolUse and beforeReadFile hooks calling your injection screening
settings.why: The only per-call deny and the only content screen in a Cloud Agent; they do not run in read-only exploratory turns and beforeMCPExecution is unavailable in the cloud.

settings.name: Comment on pull request (approvals)
settings.where: Automations › automation › tools › Comment on pull request
settings.recommended: Approvals off
settings.why: An automation cannot approve, request changes on or dismiss reviews of pull requests, often its own.

settings.name: Risk-based approval
settings.where: Automations › PR Routing & Approval (approval criteria, Use Risk Score, Maximum Risk Threshold)
settings.recommended: Routing only — no approval criteria — with required human review in the forge
settings.why: A model never counts as the approving reviewer for agent-authored changes.

settings.name: Team-level settings (Network access)
settings.where: Dashboard › Cloud Agents › Network access
settings.recommended: Allowlist only — your source control, package mirror, approved APIs and cloud-agent-artifacts.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com exactly
settings.why: A prompt-injected agent that auto-runs every command can send code only to hosts you listed; the same list sets the desktop sandbox defaults.

settings.name: Lock Network Access Policy
settings.where: Dashboard › Cloud Agents › Network access
settings.default: Unlocked (users can set their own mode)
settings.recommended: Locked
settings.why: Members cannot switch their own agents back to Allow all network access.

settings.name: Inherit settings
settings.where: Dashboard › Cloud Agents › Environments › environment › Network access
settings.recommended: Inherit settings, or Inherit settings + environment allowlist
settings.why: An environment that sets its own mode overrides the team default, so saved environments cannot reopen allow-all egress.

settings.name: OpenTelemetry Export
settings.where: Team Settings › OpenTelemetry Export › destination (cloud_agents, model_usage and tool_calls families)
settings.recommended: A destination at your collector with every family on
settings.why: Setup, commit, pull-request and MCP-auth events for each bc- agent reach the SIEM server-side, keyed to the person or service account.

settings.name: Allow conversation content export and Tool I/O
settings.where: Team Settings › OpenTelemetry Export › Allow conversation content export; destination › Conversation content › Prompts, Responses, Tool I/O
settings.recommended: Team opt-in on; on the destination Tool I/O on, Prompts and Responses off
settings.why: Every MCP and builtin tool call's scrubbed arguments and results reach the SIEM without exporting prompt text; turn prompts on only for an investigation.

settings.name: Streaming audit logs
settings.where: Arranged with hi@cursor.com — Splunk HEC, Sumo Logic, HTTPS webhook or S3
settings.recommended: On, to your SIEM
settings.why: Cloud Agent environment changes, MCP configuration and Slack links are recorded outside Cursor's dashboard.

settings.name: Monthly additional usage limit
settings.where: grok.com/dashboard/billing › Additional usage credits (legacy plans › Spending › Monthly Limit with Only Admins Can Edit Usage Settings)
settings.recommended: A per-seat team limit set by admins, with Enterprise member overrides for heavy users
settings.why: A runaway automation or agent loop stops at a known spend; enforcement is not instant and a running agent may finish past it.

tools.name: Cursor

variants.name: Cursor IDE
Cursor CLI (agent)
Cursor for iOS / Web — Remote Control of a local agent

summary: Cursor is a VS Code-derived IDE and a companion CLI (installed as `agent`) that run an agent on the developer's machine with the developer's own credentials. Inference is never local: prompts and code context go to Cursor's backend (api2/api5.cursor.sh) and on to the model providers Cursor routes to, most under zero-data-retention terms, with Privacy Mode on by default for Enterprise teams and enforceable so members cannot switch it off. The Remote Control variant (Cursor 3.9.8+, iOS / web) moves only the agent loop to Cursor's cloud; terminal, file and git tool calls still execute on the developer's computer.

Admin control has two channels. MDM device policies (AllowedTeamId, AllowedExtensions, WorkspaceTrustEnabled, UpdateMode, ExtensionGalleryServiceUrl) ship as a macOS .mobileconfig, Windows ADMX or ~/.cursor/policy.json on Linux, and MDM can also drop ~/.cursor/permissions.json and an enterprise hooks.json. The Enterprise team dashboard pushes Run Mode policy, Model Access Control, MCP Configuration, Team Rules, Team hooks (synced every thirty minutes), Repository Blocklist, Protected Git Scopes, Browser Controls and .cursor Directory Protection; dashboard and hard-coded sandbox rules cannot be weakened by user or project files.

Two things leadership should hold onto. First, the docs are candid that the Auto-review classifier "can make mistakes" and that .cursorignore "is not a security boundary" — the hard controls are the sandbox policy, the CLI's permissions.deny rules and hooks that fail closed. Second, the local sandbox has had a steady run of escapes in 2026 (git hooks, .claude hook files, working-directory and symlink canonicalisation, privileged Docker containers, tampered venvs), all fixed by 3.0–3.1.2, plus an unfixed Windows C:\ProgramData\Cursor\hooks.json trust issue reported to Cursor in January 2026 and still unresolved, with no CVE assigned. Anysphere became a SpaceX subsidiary on 2026-08-15, which changes the vendor-risk file.

facts.label: Plans
facts.value: Hobby, Pro, Pro+, Ultra, Teams and Enterprise. Nearly every admin control on this entity is labelled Enterprise: SCIM, MDM policies, Model Access Control, MCP Configuration, Run Mode policy, Repository Blocklist, .cursor Directory Protection, Browser Controls, audit log, SIEM streaming, OpenTelemetry export, Admin API and service accounts.

facts.label: Inference & routing
facts.value: Cloud-hosted only. The app talks to Cursor backends (*.cursor.sh, *.cursorapi.com, *.cursor-cdn.com, *.cursorvm.com; api2.cursor.sh for API, api5.cursor.sh for agent traffic) over TLS 1.2+ with certificate pinning, defaulting to HTTP/2 with an HTTP/1.1 SSE fallback; SSL inspection of these domains is documented as a cause of agent failures.

facts.label: Data leaving the device
facts.value: Prompts and code context for every LLM request; the codebase index; MCP traffic to whatever servers are configured (terminal and MCP tools cannot be stopped by .cursorignore). Cloud Agents are the only feature that stores code, temporarily while a run executes. With Privacy Mode on, code is never used for training by Cursor or providers; models that keep inputs for provider-side safety review (Claude Fable 5/5.1) are disabled until an admin approves them.

facts.label: Data retention / training
facts.value: Privacy Mode is on by default for Enterprise teams and enforceable org-wide; most models run under zero-data-retention agreements, ZDR does not apply when members bring their own API keys, and Claude Fable models retain inputs and outputs for Anthropic harm-prevention review (not training). Sub-processors are listed on the trust portal.
