tools.name: Grok Bot

variants.name: Grok Bot personal agents in Cursor
Grok Bot shared Bots
variants.note: A shared Bot uses the apps and secrets its owner added for everyone who chats with it, and asks before using a member's own accounts; shared Bots always run in the cloud.

variants.name: Grok Bot in Slack

summary: Persistent personal and shared Bots operated by Cursor. Personal Bots belonging to one user share a hosted computer, files and browser sessions across tasks. Shared Bots (formerly Team Bots) add the owner's apps, secrets and team memory, with private per-member chats and channel-specific computer and approval behavior.

Backend connectors, signed-in browsers, optional local commands and desktop network routing have separate authority boundaries. Enterprise network policy and connector policy must be configured separately. Terminating compute preserves durable state and does not revoke access.

Enterprise administration includes access controls, Action Recording and Auto-review enforcement. Automated review screens selected actions; it does not establish human approval or complete coverage of memory writes. Existing controls retain their individual verification dates; this October refresh covers placement, Team Bots and telemetry.

facts.label: Plans
facts.value: Early beta from 2026-08-11 for Cursor Ultra, SuperGrok Heavy and Cursor Teams Premium, widened on 2026-08-26/27 to all SuperGrok, Cursor Pro and Cursor Teams plans (Cursor's docs now say every paid individual Cursor plan, Cursor Teams, or a linked individual SuperGrok, SuperGrok Plus, SuperGrok Heavy or X Premium+ subscription, with weekly usage). Most organisational controls are Enterprise only (the enable switch, Network Controls, Team Setup, Team Secrets, Action Recording, Enforce Auto-review, audit logs, OpenTelemetry Export, SCIM); Team Rules, Cloud Agent delegation, template sharing and the local-execution ceiling are on Teams too, and on self-serve Teams Grok Bot cannot be switched off.

facts.label: Inference & routing
facts.value: Cursor's hosted providers; Privacy Mode terms apply uniformly, including to Grok 4.5. Computers run in the United States today; custom residency requires the account team.

facts.label: Data leaving the device
facts.value: Mostly nothing runs locally: files, browser sessions, memory and shell state live on the cloud computer, except commands and file transfers a Bot runs on the member's machine through the desktop app (per-command approval by default); connector tokens stay on Cursor's backend and are never stored on the computer; internet egress uses shared ranges that identify Grok Bot traffic rather than your team.

facts.label: Data retention / training
facts.value: Deletion follows the DPA — data is deleted or returned within 30 days of written direction after the service ends; Bot memory and files persist across sessions by design. Privacy Mode means code is not used for training.

facts.label: Docs index
facts.value: Grok Bot documentation (overview, Teams and Enterprise, security, security FAQ, private networks, settings).

facts.label: Isolation
facts.value: Personal Bots share a per-user Firecracker computer. In a member's own chat or Slack DM a shared Bot usually works on that member's computer (sometimes a separate one for that conversation); in Slack channels, threads and group chats it uses one shared computer of its own. Verify the applicable conversation mode rather than assuming per-Bot isolation.

facts.label: Vendor ownership
facts.value: Grok Bot is the first joint product after SpaceX's acquisition of Anysphere (closed 2026-08-14); the SpaceXAI docs mirror Cursor's and state that Anysphere operates the service.

riskNotes.note: Pages, messages and shared memory can carry hostile instructions. Signed-in browsers and permitted connectors expose downstream authority; automated action review does not eliminate injection or replace destination authorization.

Personal OAuth authority and a shared Bot's owner-added apps and secrets differ. Check the caller, channel audience and effective destination credential before any action or delegation; shared secrets can authorize every teammate.

Persistent memory, files and browser sessions accumulate on a US-hosted computer that all of the user's Bots share; Action Recording is off by default, so what a Bot did with that data is not recorded unless an admin turns it on.

Grok Bot is bundled with individual paid plans, so members with personal accounts get it outside the organisation's switch; AllowedTeamId on managed devices and the org-wide switch with Manage Group Access are the containment.

items.title: Separate personal authority from shared Bot resources
body: A shared Bot uses the apps and secrets its owner added for everyone who chats with it; in a member's own chat it asks before using that member's accounts, and in Slack channels and group chats it uses only the owner's apps. Approval cards go to the person the Bot is answering; chats where nobody can answer run without Auto-review unless Enforce Auto-review is on.

links.title: Shared Bots: apps, secrets, computers and approvals

items.title: Treat isolation and screening as bounded supplier safeguards
body: Personal Bots share their user’s computer; this is not per-Bot isolation. Auto-review checks selected actions, not every incoming document or memory write. Inventory and SSO do not create a separate authenticated principal for each Bot.

items.title: Control optional local paths and delegated work
body: Local command execution and routing through a desktop are separate switches. Cloud Agent delegation starts separate hosted coding work with its own controls; include child work when responding to an incident.

controls.mechanism: Enable Grok Bot switch with Manage Group Access on the Grok Bot dashboard page (Enterprise); Cloud Agents, Public template sharing, Execution on Local Computer and Allow Local Egress capability switches; group Grok Bot tabs that can only widen; /grok-bot/access and /grok-bot/capabilities in the Admin API

steps.title: Decide who gets Bots
body: On the Grok Bot page of the Cursor dashboard turn Enable Grok Bot on and use Manage Group Access to limit it to specific groups (Enterprise); turning it off blocks every member without deleting their computers.

steps.title: Close the widening switches
body: On the same page turn Cloud Agents off, keep Public template sharing off, set Execution on Local Computer to Never allow and turn Allow Local Egress off (Enterprise); a group's Grok Bot tab can only widen these for its members.

steps.title: Manage access as code
body: Set /grok-bot/access to mode limited with group IDs, and the cloudAgents, templateSharing, localExecution and localEgressAllowed fields of /grok-bot/capabilities, with an admin-scoped key.

controls.note: Rated partial on the hosted rule. On Enterprise, enablement is per group and the widening switches are admin-owned (a group can only widen them, and a member in several groups gets the most permissive result), but who can wake a Bot is not an admin setting: a routine's Slack listener starts a run on any matching message in the channel, and routines can also fire on GitHub notifications. On self-serve Teams Grok Bot is on for every member with no switch to turn it off, and personal paid plans bring it outside the organisation's switch. Enforced by Cursor's control plane; sign-in follows the team's Cursor SSO, so device-aware IdP policies gate the member's device, not the hosted computer.

original.mechanism: Organisation-wide switch on the Grok Bot page with Manage Group Access; SSO and SCIM 2.0 (Enterprise)

steps.title: Decide who gets Bots
body: Use the organisation-wide switch on the Grok Bot dashboard page and Manage Group Access to enable it for specific groups; provision and deprovision through SCIM 2.0.

controls.mechanism: Audit log events grok_bot_created, grok_bot_lifecycle, grok_bot_routine, grok_bot_resource and grok_bot_team_setup_manifest; Grok Bot Computers for organisation admins

steps.title: Inventory Bots and routines from the audit log
body: Filter the Audit Log by the Grok Bot application; grok_bot_created, grok_bot_lifecycle and grok_bot_routine record each Bot and routine (automation_id, name, trigger_type) with the member who acted, and the log streams to a SIEM.

steps.title: Inventory and clean up computers
body: Organisation admins search members under Grok Bot Computers → Manage, and turn on Terminate Inactive Computers to reclaim computers idle for 30 days.

controls.note: Partial on the hosted rule. The audit trail records each Bot and routine with its owner, but the docs describe no admin list of Bots and routines, no approval state, and nothing unregistered is denied: any member with access creates Bots and routines at will. Public template sharing (off by default on Enterprise) limits what leaves the team, not what is created.

original.mechanism: Computer management (look up any member's computer, creation and last-active times); audit log of Bot creation and member access changes

steps.title: Inventory computers and Bots
body: Organisation admins can look up any member's computer, see when it was created and last active, and read Bot creation and access-change events in the audit log.

original.note: No approval step or declared-capability record per Bot.

controls.mechanism: Team connector policy (Plugins & MCPs) and the Enterprise MCP allowlist; Network Controls; Execution on Local Computer ceiling; Cloud Agents switch; Enforce Auto-review with team Auto-review rules

steps.title: Restrict connectors
body: Set which servers members can use from the Team Marketplace on the dashboard's Plugins & MCPs page and, on Enterprise, the MCP allowlist; a blocked connector shows Disabled by team admin on every Bot.

steps.title: Set a locked network policy
body: Choose Team allowlist only in Network Controls on the Grok Bot page and lock the team policy so directory-group policies cannot replace it (Enterprise).

steps.title: Cap local execution and delegation
body: Set Execution on Local Computer to Never allow and turn the Cloud Agents switch off unless Bots need them.

steps.title: Lock the reviewer on
body: Turn on Enforce Auto-review and add team rules with Configure Rules (Enterprise); members see them as locked rows and can only add stricter personal rules.

controls.note: Rated partial on the rule applied to every vendor. The product-enforced limits are per connector (allow or block a server), per destination (Network Controls) and per capability (local execution, Cloud Agent delegation, local egress). There is no admin rule over built-in tool calls by name and arguments: shell, browser and computer use inside the hosted computer are gated only by Auto Review, and team Auto-review rules are natural-language allow and block instructions the reviewer model interprets (the Admin API takes up to 20 of each), not deterministic matches. A group can lift Enforce Auto-review with Don't enforce for this group. Blocking a plugin does not block the service's website. A Bot's reach is its member's accounts and every login on the shared computer.

original.mechanism: Network Controls (four modes, team allowlist); Team Setup; Auto-review Ask first / Allow automatically rules; Execution on Local Computer (Always allow / Ask every time / Never allow); Bot access bounded by its owner

steps.title: Set a network policy
body: Pick one of the four Network Controls modes; teams without a policy default to allow-all, and the policy is separate from Cloud Agent network settings and applies when a computer is created or recreated.

steps.title: Write Auto-review rules
body: Ask first rules always stop matching actions and Allow automatically rules let them proceed when the reviewer finds no safety concern; admins set team rules and members may only add stricter personal ones.

steps.title: Restrict execution on the member's own machine
body: Set Execution on Local Computer to Ask every time or Never allow; the default is Always allow, and the more restrictive of the admin and member setting wins.

original.note: Network Controls limit destinations, Ask first and Allow automatically rules pre-approve or gate actions, and the local-execution setting caps what a Bot may run on a member's machine. Tools are not individually hidden; a Bot's reach is its owner's.

original.mechanism: Team-wide Ask first rules always stop matching actions; Never allow for Execution on Local Computer; Auto-review (an AI reviewer) evaluates everything else and can allow, require approval or deny; login, 2FA and payment always handed to the member

steps.title: Write Ask first rules for the actions that must stop
body: Ask first rules always stop matching actions and win over Allow automatically when rules conflict; admins set team rules and members may add only stricter ones.

steps.title: Deny local execution where the microVM must hold
body: Set Execution on Local Computer to Never allow; the default Always allow delegates the decision to the member.

original.note: The deterministic part is Ask first and Never allow; Auto-review is a classifier that the docs say does not review all side effects, such as memory writes. Rules match actions, not shell commands individually, and the MCP allowlist decides which connector tools exist at all.

original.mechanism: Enterprise MCP allowlist under the team's connector policy; a blocked connector shows as Disabled by team admin on every Bot

steps.title: Allowlist connectors and MCP servers for the team
body: Set the connector policy and MCP allowlist on the Grok Bot page; any permitted connector is available to every Bot a member runs and a blocked one is disabled for all of them.

original.note: Enterprise only. Rated native on the same rule as Cursor: admission by identity, organisation-wide. Admission is not integrity — nothing pins what a permitted server serves.

controls.mechanism: Approval cards (Allow once, Always allow, Deny) raised by Auto Review; Enforce Auto-review and team Auto-review rules (Enterprise); Execution on Local Computer Ask every time; login, 2FA and payment handed to the member

steps.title: Lock Auto Review on
body: Turn on Enforce Auto-review on the Grok Bot page (off by default) and do not use Don't enforce for this group on any group.

steps.title: Add Ask first team rules
body: Use Configure Rules on the Grok Bot page to add Ask first rules for production deployments, external email, payments and accepting legal terms; Ask first wins when rules conflict.

steps.title: Force per-command approval on members' machines
body: Set the Execution on Local Computer ceiling to Ask every time or Never allow; the local approval card shows the exact command.

steps.title: Check who can approve on shared Bots
body: A shared Bot's approval card goes only to the person it is answering, in their own chat, a Slack thread or a group chat; turn on Enforce Auto-review so shared Bots in chats where nobody can answer an approval do not run without it.

controls.note: Partial: approval cards support human decisions for personal and owner conversations, but Auto-review is a model-based action reviewer. On shared Bots the person being answered approves in their own chat, Slack thread or group chat, but chats where nobody can answer an approval run without Auto-review unless it is enforced; do not infer a human gate there. Local execution set to Ask every time covers local commands only. Natural-language rules are not deterministic action matching.

original.mechanism: Team-wide Ask first rules (the human gate); Enforce Auto-review (Enterprise, off by default, an AI reviewer); local-execution ceiling; login, 2FA and payment always handed to the member

steps.title: Add team-wide Ask first rules
body: On the Grok Bot page add Ask first rules for the actions a person must approve; they apply to every member's Bots and win over Allow automatically when rules conflict. This is the human gate — Auto-review can allow an action without anyone seeing it.

steps.title: Enforce Auto-review
body: Turn on Enforce Auto-review so members cannot switch the AI reviewer off; it evaluates shell commands, plugin calls, computer use, automation writes and delegation and can allow, require approval or deny. An allow verdict is automatic, not human, review.

steps.title: Set the local-execution ceiling
body: Always allow, Ask every time or Never allow for local execution on the Grok Bot page is the team's ceiling; a member's own stricter setting still applies, so the ceiling is not every member's effective default.

original.note: Enforce Auto-review guarantees automatic review, not human review; the docs state Auto-review does not review all side effects, such as memory writes.

controls.mechanism: Vendor evidence (Grok Bot security Certifications section, trust.cursor.com, the DPA) consumed by the organisation's TPRM platform

evidence.title: Grok Bot security (ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO/IEC 42001 by Schellman with Grok Bot in the current scope; US-only hosting; DPA 30-day deletion), checked 2026-09-25
Grok Bot security, SpaceXAI docs mirror
Cursor security page (SOC 2 Type II, AIUC-1 and ISO certifications for Cursor)

controls.note: External: the organisation's TPRM platform consumes the evidence. Record US-only hosting outside Cursor's US data residency program, shared egress ranges, the DPA's 30-day deletion term, a model allowlist whose enforcement is not guaranteed, the SpaceXAI co-branding, and that the Grok Bot pages name ISO 27001 and 42001 scope but not SOC 2 (cursor.com/security lists SOC 2 Type II for Cursor without naming Grok Bot). Access, capabilities, network policy and Enforce Auto-review are readable through the Admin API (/grok-bot/*) for posture checks; Team Secrets and Action Recording's store are not.

original.mechanism: Vendor evidence (Cursor trust portal, ISO 27001/42001, DPA) consumed by the organisation's TPRM platform

steps.title: Assess the new surface
body: Record US-only hosting, shared egress ranges, the DPA's 30-day deletion term, the SpaceXAI co-branding and Anysphere's ISO 27001 / 42001 certifications.

original.mechanism: Dashboard-only settings verified manually or through an SSPM product
original.note: Network Controls, Enforce Auto-review and Action Recording have no documented API; posture checks must read the dashboard.

evidence.title: Vendor docs index, reviewed for the integration point (2026-09-10)

controls.mechanism: Enterprise Action Recording and server-side OpenTelemetry Export, with separate opt-ins for conversation content and MCP Tool I/O

steps.title: Enable action recording and export
body: Enable Action Recording and configure the Enterprise OpenTelemetry destination. Keep action records for correlation with exported tool content.

steps.title: Choose content export deliberately
body: Enable Allow conversation content export for the team and Conversation content for the destination. Enable Tool I/O separately for hosted MCP arguments and results; it defaults off.

controls.note: Standard action records omit tool payloads. Opt-in conversation export can include prompts and responses, and the separate Tool I/O toggle adds hosted MCP arguments/results. Content is scrubbed and truncated; redaction cannot guarantee removal of every secret. Other shell/browser payloads are not thereby fully captured. Disabled periods are not backfilled.

original.mechanism: Action Recording (Enterprise, off by default) plus OpenTelemetry Export tagged cursor.surface=grok_bot

steps.title: Record Bot actions
body: Turn on Action Recording on the Grok Bot page to capture Bot actions including scrubbed shell commands, then enable OpenTelemetry Export so shell, browser, tool-call and computer-use events reach your collector.

steps.title: Export the events
body: Configure Team Settings → OpenTelemetry Export; Grok Bot actions arrive as logs with no prompt content.

original.note: Action Recording captures what the Bot did on its computer; OTel export carries lifecycle and tool events. Neither is detection — the recordings and events feed a tool the organisation runs.

original.mechanism: Enterprise audit log covering Grok Bot control-plane events; SIEM streaming

steps.title: Stream Grok Bot audit events
body: Audit logs cover admin, security and authentication events plus Bot creation, member access changes, Team Setup manifests, MCP authentication, Slack account links and routines.

original.note: Control-plane events only — Bot actions are in Action Recording, not the audit log. Retention and tamper evidence are not stated; the SIEM stream is the durable record.

controls.mechanism: Bot memory persists by design with no admin switch; Team Rules and Group Rules always required; Grok Bot Computers Delete VMs and Data (organisation admins, Enterprise)

steps.title: Lock the instruction sources
body: Add Team Rules on the Grok Bot page scoped to Grok Bot; rules applied to Grok Bot are always required and members cannot turn them off.

steps.title: Wipe a member's state when needed
body: Under Grok Bot Computers → Manage → Manage selected, Delete VMs and Data removes the computer and its durable data; Terminate VMs and Recreate VMs keep the disk.

controls.note: Partial on the rule. Admins can lock instruction sources (Team Rules and Group Rules) and wipe a member's computer, but no admin setting disables or scopes Bot memory, memory writes are not validated and Auto Review does not review them, and the shared durable disk (files, browser sessions, logins) persists across sessions for every Bot the member runs. Deleting a Bot removes its profile, conversation and routines, not files or sign-ins on the computer; a shared Bot template carries identity, description, skills and routines.

original.mechanism: Per-user microVM; admin computer termination; separate user accounts for separate credentials

steps.title: Terminate a computer to reset state
body: Organisation admins can terminate any member's computer; provision separate Cursor user accounts where workloads must not share memory, files or browser sessions.

original.note: Memory persists by design and Auto-review does not evaluate memory writes; there is no validation, expiry or rollback.

controls.mechanism: Monthly additional usage limit (grok.com/dashboard/billing on The X Subscription; legacy plans use the On-demand monthly limit, set as Spending → Monthly Limit) and Enterprise member spend limits; weekly included usage per plan; no separate Grok Bot spend cap; 50 routines per Bot

steps.title: Cap additional usage
body: On The X Subscription set Monthly additional usage limit under Additional usage credits at grok.com/dashboard/billing. On legacy plans set Monthly Limit under Spending on cursor.com/dashboard (shown in Grok Bot as On-demand monthly limit), or turn on-demand off so Grok Bot stops when weekly usage runs out.

steps.title: Lock the setting and set member limits
body: On The X Subscription only team admins can change the team limit; on legacy plans enable Only Admins Can Edit Usage Settings under Permissions in the Spending tab. On Enterprise, set member or group overrides.

controls.note: Partial on the hosted rule. The only lever is the account's additional-usage limit (on-demand limit on legacy plans) and Enterprise member limits: the teams page says a separate Grok Bot spend cap is not available, and the plans page says the limit is not a hard stop in the middle of a run (a Bot already working can finish past it). Weekly included usage and the 50-routines-per-Bot cap are vendor-fixed, and no admin-set routine frequency, action count, duration or concurrency limit is documented.

original.mechanism: Weekly usage allowances per plan; Cursor team spend limits

steps.title: Cap spend through the team
body: Grok Bot usage draws on plan allowances that reset weekly with on-demand billing beyond them; team and per-member spend limits in the Cursor dashboard bound the cost.

original.note: No limit on routine frequency, action count or task duration is documented.

controls.mechanism: Grok Bot Computers → Terminate VMs (organisation admins, Enterprise); Manage Group Access or Enable Grok Bot off (/grok-bot/disable); member removal; identity-provider session revocation

steps.title: Stop running work
body: Open Grok Bot Computers → Manage, select members, and choose Manage selected → Terminate VMs; running work stops, the operation runs on Cursor's side, and a progress card reports each member as complete, skipped or failed.

steps.title: Keep it stopped
body: Terminating does not remove access, so turn the member's group off in Manage Group Access or turn Enable Grok Bot off, remove the member from the team, and revoke their identity-provider sessions.

controls.note: For personal/member computers, an organisation admin or Enterprise team admin (Enterprise only) can stop running Bots for any member, in bulk, from the vendor control plane, and the dashboard reports each stop as complete or failed. Delay: no time bound is published (members are processed in batches and large operations take a while), so the per-member result is the evidence. A terminated computer restarts on the member's next message on the same durable disk, and the enable switch and group removal block future work without saying whether they stop a running turn, so pair terminate with access removal. Stopping does not undo completed actions; grok_bot_vm and grok_bot_vm_bulk audit events record the kill. Termination coverage for shared Bot computers and independently running delegated Cloud Agents must be verified separately; the personal-computer operation does not establish an atomic stop across those paths.

original.mechanism: Organisation-wide switch; Manage Group Access; computer termination by admins; SCIM deprovisioning

steps.title: Stop a Bot or the whole feature
body: Terminate the member's computer from computer management, remove the group in Manage Group Access, or flip the organisation-wide switch off.

original.note: Terminating a member's computer stops active work on it; the organisation-wide switch and group removal block future work and the docs state no propagation delay, so measure it.

controls.mechanism: Network Controls (Enterprise) with No policy, Allow all network access, Defaults plus team allowlist and Team allowlist only, domains and IP ranges with ports, directory-group policies and a lock; /grok-bot/network (egressMode, locked); Allow Local Egress

steps.title: Set Team allowlist only and lock it
body: In Network Controls on the Grok Bot page choose Team allowlist only, list the domains and IP ranges Bots need, and lock the team policy so group policies cannot replace it; running computers apply changes within about a minute.

steps.title: Keep desktop routes and networking clients inside the policy
body: Turn Allow Local Egress off unless members need Route egress through this desktop, and add a Team Setup networking client's coordination servers, relays and gateways to the allowlist.

steps.title: Manage the policy as code
body: PUT /grok-bot/network with egressMode network_settings_only and locked true.

controls.note: Native on the hosted rule: an admin-authored allowlist, lockable over directory-group policies, enforced by Cursor on all traffic from the Bot computer and applied to running computers within about a minute. Enterprise only; teams without a policy allow all destinations. Bypasses: connector calls run from Cursor's connector backend outside the computer's policy (blocking a plugin and blocking its website are separate controls), delegated Cloud Agents follow Cloud Agent network settings, and inference is outside. Traffic leaves from static ranges shared across Grok Bot customers unless routed through a member's desktop or your networking client.

original.mechanism: Network Controls (Enterprise): No policy, Allow all, Defaults plus team allowlist, Team allowlist only, with domains and IP ranges with ports; directory-group policies with a lock; private networks through desktop routing or Team Setup networking clients

steps.title: Set Team allowlist only and lock it
body: Pick Team allowlist only on the Grok Bot page, list the domains and IP ranges Bots need, and lock the policy so directory groups cannot override it; the policy applies when a computer is created or recreated.

steps.title: Keep private-network routes inside the allowlist
body: Desktop routing and Team Setup clients (Tailscale, Cloudflare Tunnel) give reach into private networks but do not replace the destination allowlist; add coordination servers, relays and gateways to it.

original.note: Enterprise only; teams without a policy allow all destinations. Covers all traffic from the Bot computer, which egresses through Cursor's shared static ranges unless routed through a member's desktop. Connector calls run from Cursor's backend, outside the computer's policy.

controls.mechanism: Backend connector token custody is documented; credential recipient/audience enforcement is not established.

evidence.title: Connector credentials and browser authority

controls.note: Keeping OAuth tokens out of the computer supports credential hardening. It does not by itself prove that credentials can reach only designated recipients. Confirm recipient binding and non-forwarding before crediting this control; shared browser sessions remain separately usable.

original.mechanism: Connector OAuth tokens stay on Cursor's backend and are never stored on the computer; Bots invoke tools without receiving tokens; a secure secret request masks an entered value and keeps it out of the transcript

steps.title: Keep credentials off the computer
body: Connect tools through connectors so tokens stay on the backend, and enter one-off secrets through the secure secret request rather than in chat.

original.note: Covers connector tokens. The member's logged-in browser sessions on the durable disk are inside the boundary — a Bot acts with them — so web credentials are isolated only by terminating the computer. A Bot acts as its owner; there is no on-behalf-of exchange.

original.mechanism: Connector OAuth tokens held on Cursor's backend, never on the computer; login, 2FA and payment handed to the member

steps.title: Rely on backend-held connector tokens
body: Bots invoke connector tools without receiving OAuth tokens and tokens are never stored on the computer; credentials typed during browser sessions are outside this model, so hand those steps to the member.

original.note: No vault or just-in-time issuance for secrets the Bot uses inside its shell or browser sessions.

controls.mechanism: Team Secrets (Enterprise; encrypted, never shown again after saving, admin-managed, up to 100 per team); write-only per-Bot Secrets; connector OAuth tokens on Cursor's backend; no vendor tunnel (the organisation's own networking client through Team Setup)

steps.title: Store fleet credentials as Team Secrets
body: Add each credential under Team Secrets on the Grok Bot page as a name and value; Cursor stores it encrypted, never shows it again, and Replace rotates it on the next script run.

steps.title: Roll a rotation out now
body: Run Recreate VMs from Grok Bot Computers so Team Setup re-runs with the rotated value instead of waiting for the periodic refresh.

steps.title: Scope the networking-client credential
body: Prefer interactive login in the computer's browser; a reusable tagged Tailscale auth key stored as a Team Secret joins every team computer under the same tags, so scope its ACLs and revoke computers from your own admin console.

controls.note: Partial on the hosted rule. Team Secrets and per-Bot secrets are encrypted and write-only, and Team Secrets are admin-scoped to setup scripts with output redaction, but a rotation reaches computers only when scripts re-run, a Team Secret spans the whole team (there are no group-level secrets), and the credentials a Bot actually uses in the browser are long-lived web sessions on the durable disk rather than short-lived issued tokens. Tunnel: Grok Bot has no vendor tunnel or connector; private reach is a member's desktop route or the organisation's own networking client installed by Team Setup, whose key is issued, rotated and revoked in that vendor's console, not Cursor's. Team Secrets are dashboard-only (not in the Admin API).

controls.mechanism: Grok Bot sign-in is the member's Cursor account through the team's SAML 2.0 SSO, which can be required for every member (blocking password login); MFA and device-aware sign-in policy are set on the existing Cursor app in the IdP; SCIM deprovisioning (Enterprise)

steps.title: Require SSO for the team
body: In Team Settings › Single Sign-On (SSO) (Enterprise org admins use the Organization's Settings) complete SSO-Provider Connection Settings and Domain Verification Settings so members on the domain sign in through the IdP.

steps.title: Enforce MFA on the Cursor app in the IdP
body: In Okta or Entra ID require MFA and a managed device on the existing Cursor app (there is no separate Grok Bot app), and add a separate higher-priority rule, password plus a second factor, for the IdP apps the Bot's Linux computer browser opens.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor (as on toolCursor): Grok Bot inherits Cursor SSO, so the IdP's MFA policy governs each member's interactive sign-in, but MFA is configured in the IdP, not in Cursor, and a device-aware policy gates the member's device, not the hosted computer. Paths the IdP's MFA does not see: work that starts without a sign-in (a routine's Slack listener or GitHub notification, and messages from a linked Slack account, which rest on Slack's own sign-in); personal paid plans outside the organisation's SSO; and sign-ins inside the computer's browser, where FastPass and device-compliance rules cannot be met, so that session's rule is password plus a second factor.

controls.mechanism: Inference Hooks (Enterprise, beta): each governed Grok Bot model request (every step of a turn, subagents, conversation summaries and routines) is sent as a signed frame with the conversation so far to the organisation's AI security server and held for an allow or deny verdict; Enforce Verdicts, Mode (Shadow Mode default, Allow the Request fails open, Block the Request fails closed), Verdict Timeout and Requests Inspected (%)

steps.title: Point the hook at your AI security server
body: On the Grok Bot page › Security & Compliance › Inference Hooks select Set Up Endpoint, choose your vendor or Custom Endpoint, enter the endpoint URL and headers, give the whsec_ signing secret to the server and run Test Connection.

steps.title: Enforce after a shadow trial
body: Turn on Enforce Verdicts, review denials in the audit log while in Shadow Mode, then set Failure Handling › Mode to Allow the Request (Block the Request to fail closed) with Requests Inspected at 100%.

controls.note: Partial on the rule applied to every vendor (as on toolClaudeCowork): an inline attach point that stops the model request on the server's deny, partial until the organisation's server does the classifying. Tool results, fetched pages and connector returns are inspected only when they come back in the next model request, after the tool has run; model responses, system prompts, tool definitions and ancillary calls (Auto Review, memory saving, chat titles) are never sent; Shadow Mode, the default, blocks nothing; Allow the Request fails open on timeouts and errors, and every mode fails open when Cursor cannot load the settings or pauses hooks itself; a Requests Inspected share below 100% skips the rest; Cloud Agents a Bot delegates to are not covered.

settings.name: Enable Grok Bot with Manage Group Access
settings.where: Cursor dashboard › Grok Bot › Enable Grok Bot › Manage Group Access
settings.default: Off on Enterprise (on for every member on Teams, with no switch)
settings.recommended: On, limited to the groups approved for Grok Bot
settings.why: Only named cohorts get standing Bots, and turning a group or the switch off blocks their members without deleting computers.

settings.name: Device-aware sign-in policy
settings.where: Your IdP › Cursor app › authentication policy or Conditional Access
settings.recommended: Managed device and MFA required for Cursor sign-in, with a separate scoped rule for the Bot computer's Linux browser
settings.why: Grok Bot sign-in goes through Cursor SSO, so only managed devices reach it; the scoped rule avoids turning device trust off company-wide for the hosted browser.

settings.name: SCIM
settings.where: Team Settings › SCIM, with the Cursor SCIM app in your IdP
settings.recommended: On, driven by the IdP group that grants Grok Bot
settings.why: A leaver is deprovisioned from Grok Bot with their account; revoking IdP sessions also ends their sign-ins inside the hosted browser.

settings.name: Manage Shared Bots
settings.where: Grok Bot page › Shared Bots › Manage Shared Bots › Access
settings.recommended: Each shared Bot limited to the people or groups who need it
settings.why: Secrets, apps and files the owner adds to a shared Bot are usable in every teammate's chat, so access decides who borrows that authority.

settings.name: Connector policy
settings.where: Dashboard › Plugins & MCPs (Team Marketplace), plus the MCP allowlist in MCP Configuration
settings.recommended: Only the connectors the firm has approved, matched by the MCP allowlist
settings.why: Any permitted connector is available to every Bot a member runs; a blocked one shows as Disabled by team admin.

settings.name: Cloud Agents
settings.where: Grok Bot page › Cloud Agents (Admin API /grok-bot/capabilities cloudAgents)
settings.recommended: Off, unless Bots need to delegate coding work
settings.why: Bots cannot start separate Cloud Agent runs that keep going under different controls when the Bot is stopped.

settings.name: Execution on Local Computer
settings.where: Grok Bot page › Execution on Local Computer (Admin API /grok-bot/capabilities localExecution)
settings.default: Always allow (leaves it to each member, whose own default is ask)
settings.recommended: Never allow
settings.why: A hosted Bot cannot run commands or move files on a member's laptop with that member's local credentials.

settings.name: Agent Email
settings.where: Grok Bot page › Bot Capabilities › Agent Email
settings.recommended: Off
settings.why: Bots get no mail.grokbot.com mailbox outside the firm's mail system to send from or be triggered by.

settings.name: Allow Sudo on Bot Computers
settings.where: Grok Bot page › Bot Computers › Allow Sudo on Bot Computers
settings.recommended: Off
settings.why: A Bot cannot run commands as root to remove the tooling Team Setup Scripts installed; Team Setup itself still runs with sudo.

settings.name: Team Rules
settings.where: Grok Bot page › Team Rules (scoped to Grok Bot)
settings.recommended: A few short rules such as never moving company data to personal accounts
settings.why: Rules applied to Grok Bot are always required, so members cannot switch off the firm's instructions; they guide the Bot and do not enforce.

settings.name: Enforce Auto-review
settings.where: Grok Bot page › Enforce Auto-review (and no group set to Don't enforce for this group)
settings.recommended: On, with no group exemption
settings.why: Members cannot turn the action reviewer off, and shared Bots in chats nobody can approve no longer run without it.

settings.name: Auto-review rules
settings.where: Grok Bot page › Configure Rules
settings.recommended: Ask first for production deployments, external email, payments and accepting legal terms; Allow automatically rules kept narrow
settings.why: Those actions stop for the member's approval on every Bot, and Ask first wins over any member rule; the reviewer is a model, not a deterministic match.

settings.name: Inference Hooks
settings.where: Grok Bot page › Security & Compliance › Inference Hooks (Enforce Verdicts, Failure Handling › Mode)
settings.recommended: Enforce Verdicts on with Mode Allow the Request, after a Shadow Mode trial
settings.why: Your AI security server can refuse a model request carrying injected content or data your DLP policy blocks; regulated teams pick Block the Request to fail closed.

settings.name: Team Secrets
settings.where: Grok Bot page › Team Secrets
settings.recommended: Every credential Team Setup Scripts need, stored here and read from the environment, never written into a manifest
settings.why: Values are encrypted and never shown again, exist only in the script's process and are redacted from script output.

settings.name: Grok Bot Network Access
settings.where: Grok Bot page › Network › Grok Bot Network Access (with Lock for all groups)
settings.recommended: Team Allowlist Only, locked, listing the firm's SaaS and the research sites teams need; wider cohorts get a group policy
settings.why: A Bot with signed-in browsers can send data only to hosts you listed, and changes reach running computers within about a minute.

settings.name: Apply to MCP servers
settings.where: Grok Bot page › Network › Grok Bot Network Access › Apply to MCP servers
settings.recommended: On, with each approved connector's API hosts on the allowlist
settings.why: Remote and built-in connectors, which Bots reach from Cursor's servers, are held to the same allowlist as the computer.

settings.name: Allow Local Egress Routing
settings.where: Grok Bot page › Bot Computers › Allow Local Egress Routing
settings.recommended: Off
settings.why: Members cannot route Bot traffic through their own desktop and around the team network policy; active routes stop within five minutes.

settings.name: Terminate Inactive Computers
settings.where: Grok Bot page › Bot Computers › Terminate Inactive Computers
settings.recommended: On
settings.why: A computer holding files and signed-in sessions shuts down after 30 days without a message, and routines alone do not keep it alive.

settings.name: Public template sharing
settings.where: Grok Bot page › Public template sharing
settings.default: Off on Enterprise, allowed on other plans
settings.recommended: Off
settings.why: A Bot template with its skills and routines cannot be published outside the team; Cursor enforces it server-side, including on templates already public.

settings.name: Page sharing
settings.where: Grok Bot page › Sharing › Page sharing
settings.recommended: Anyone on the team
settings.why: Pages stay shareable inside the firm only; there is no outside-the-team option to close.

settings.name: Action Recording
settings.where: Grok Bot page › Action Recording
settings.recommended: On
settings.why: Every tool call, who or what allowed it, shell commands, navigations, messages sent and delegations are recorded for 90 days and can be exported.

settings.name: OpenTelemetry Export
settings.where: Team Settings › OpenTelemetry Export › destination (grok_bot_agent_actions family)
settings.recommended: A destination at your collector with every family on
settings.why: Action Recording events never appear on the Audit Log page; this is the only way they reach the SIEM.

settings.name: Allow conversation content export and Tool I/O
settings.where: Team Settings › OpenTelemetry Export › Allow conversation content export; destination › Conversation content › Prompts, Responses, Tool I/O
settings.recommended: Team opt-in on; on the destination Tool I/O on, Prompts and Responses off
settings.why: Hosted connector calls carry their scrubbed arguments and results into the SIEM without exporting the member's prompt text.

settings.name: Streaming audit logs
settings.where: Arranged with hi@cursor.com — Splunk HEC, Sumo Logic, HTTPS webhook or S3
settings.recommended: On, to your SIEM
settings.why: Bot creation, routines, access changes and Team Setup manifests land in the SIEM as an inventory of what each member runs.

settings.name: Monthly additional usage limit
settings.where: grok.com/dashboard/billing › Additional usage credits (legacy plans › Spending › Monthly Limit, shown in Grok Bot as On-demand monthly limit)
settings.recommended: A per-seat team limit set by admins
settings.why: Routines and long Bot runs stop at a known spend; there is no Grok Bot-specific cap and a running Bot can finish past the limit.

tools.name: llama.cpp server (llama-server)

variants.name: llama-server / llama serve (prebuilt binary, install.sh, package managers or source build)
variants.note: The `llama` binary's `serve` subcommand (and the standalone llama-server) loads one GGUF from a path (-m), a Hugging Face repository (-hf), a URL (-mu) or Docker Hub (-dr) and serves it on 127.0.0.1:9931 with a built-in web UI. Started with no model it runs in router mode, loading and unloading models from the cache, --models-dir or a --models-preset file on request. install.sh installs per user to ~/.llama-app and ~/.local/bin/llama.

variants.name: llama cli (terminal chat)
variants.note: Interactive chat over the same loader and the same -hf / -m model sources, with no listener; its risks are the model-file ones of this entry.

variants.name: Llama app (macOS menu bar, Windows tray)
variants.note: A minimalist desktop app built on llama.cpp that downloads models, serves them through `llama serve` on localhost:9931 and opens the web UI; its own settings are not documented on llama.app/docs.

variants.name: ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server container images
variants.note: Server-only images per backend (CPU, CUDA 12/13, ROCm, MUSA, SYCL, Vulkan, OpenVINO, s390x). The documented `docker run` passes --host 0.0.0.0 and publishes -p 8080:8080 on every host interface; publish on 127.0.0.1 instead.

summary: Open-source (MIT, "The ggml authors") C/C++ inference engine for GGUF models and its HTTP server, maintained by the ggml-org project, whose company ggml.ai was acquired by Hugging Face in 2026. `llama serve` / llama-server exposes OpenAI-compatible /v1 (chat completions, completions, responses, embeddings, rerank), Anthropic-compatible /v1/messages, native llama.cpp endpoints and a web UI on http://127.0.0.1:9931; builds are numbered b<N> (b11941 current on 2026-10-30).

Inference runs on the device's CPU or GPU (CUDA, Metal, ROCm, Vulkan, SYCL and others) and no telemetry is documented. What leaves the device is what the operator configures: model downloads from Hugging Face, Docker Hub or a URL, remote image URLs the server fetches for multimodal requests, offload to remote ggml rpc-servers (--rpc), and the experimental peer-to-peer tunnel (--connect).

Every control is a launch flag or its LLAMA_ARG_* environment variable, so whoever starts the process sets policy: loopback bind by default, optional static API keys (--api-key, --api-key-file) checked on every route except /health and web-UI assets, optional TLS, and CORS that by default reflects any origin with credentials. The project's SECURITY.md says not to use llama-server on an untrusted network, and its private disclosure program is disabled — fixes arrive as public pull requests.

facts.label: Plans
facts.value: Free and open source (MIT). No paid tier, licence key, account or vendor console; the operator runs and configures everything. The Llama desktop app and llama.app installer are free.

facts.label: Inference & routing
facts.value: On the local machine's CPU and GPUs; one model per server process, or router mode forwarding each request to a child instance per model (model instances inherit the router's flags and environment). --rpc host:port offloads tensors to remote ggml rpc-servers.

facts.label: Data leaving the device
facts.value: Model files from Hugging Face (-hf, POST /models in router mode), a URL (-mu) or Docker Hub (-dr), through HTTPS_PROXY when set; image_url parts given as remote URLs, which the server fetches; tensors and graphs sent to --rpc servers; traffic over the experimental --connect tunnel; and stdio MCP servers started with --mcp-servers-config. No usage telemetry is documented. --offline forces the cache and prevents network access.

facts.label: Retention & training
facts.value: No vendor receives prompts or data. Downloaded models stay in LLAMA_CACHE (default ~/Library/Caches/llama.cpp on macOS, %LOCALAPPDATA%\llama.cpp on Windows, $XDG_CACHE_HOME or ~/.cache/llama.cpp on Linux) until deleted. Prompt state reaches disk only through --slot-save-path (KV cache files), --log-prompts-dir (debugging) or verbose logging; prompt caching otherwise lives in memory (--cache-ram, default 8192 MiB).

facts.label: Docs index
facts.value: llama.app/docs (introduction, installation, CLI, server, web UI, API; .md variant of each page) and the repository's tools/server/README.md, the generated reference of every server flag.

facts.label: Local endpoint
facts.value: http://127.0.0.1:9931 (--host and --port; LLAMA_ARG_HOST, LLAMA_ARG_PORT); the Docker guide's example still uses --host 0.0.0.0 -p 8080:8080. GET /health answers without a key; requests without a valid key get 401 "Invalid API Key" once --api-key is set.

facts.label: Security policy
facts.value: "The private security disclosure program is disabled until further notice" — patches go in as public PRs. Covered topics exclude the Web UI, experimental features, features not recommended for untrusted environments (router, MCP) and denial of service; the policy tells operators to sandbox untrusted models, confirm the hash of downloaded weights and not to expose llama-server or the RPC backend to untrusted networks.

facts.label: Vendor ownership
facts.value: ggml-org on GitHub ("a team of volunteers on a reasonable-effort basis"); ggml.ai, founded in 2023 by Georgi Gerganov to support ggml development, was acquired by Hugging Face in 2026.

facts.label: Release cadence
facts.value: Builds are published continuously as b<N>; install.sh resolves "latest" from Hugging Face and LLAMA_VERSION pins a build; it checks that the binary reports that build, not a signature.

items.title: Server baseline for a managed device or shared host
body: Launch from a managed unit or script with --host 127.0.0.1 (the default, set explicitly), --api-key-file pointing at a file only the service account reads, --cors-origins localhost and --no-cors-credentials, and keep --tools, --agent, --mcp-servers-config, --ui-mcp-proxy, --connect, --props, --rpc and --slot-save-path unset.

Bound the work any caller can ask for: -np (slots), -c (context), -n (tokens per request) and -to (timeout), and in router mode --models-max; the API key is shared by every caller, so per-caller quotas and identity belong to a gateway in front.

A server reached from other machines needs TLS (--ssl-key-file and --ssl-cert-file on an SSL build, or a TLS-terminating proxy) and an authenticating reverse proxy, because SECURITY.md does not cover the web UI, router or DoS and says not to expose llama-server to untrusted networks.

items.title: Model supply chain
body: -hf, -mu, -dr and router POST /models download straight into the loadable cache with no digest check (the download code stores the server's ETag for cache freshness only). For a promotion flow, fetch and scan outside llama.cpp, record the sha256, place approved GGUFs in a directory only the promotion job can write, and serve them with -m or --models-dir and --offline.
Each GGUF carries a Jinja chat template that runs on every request (--jinja is on by default); serve reviewed models with --chat-template-file pointing at a reviewed template.

links.title: llama-server — Using multiple models (model sources, router download and delete)
llama.cpp download code (ETag cache handling, offline mode)

riskNotes.note: GGUF only, so no pickle path; the live class is the native GGUF and vocabulary parser — CVE-2025-49847, CVE-2025-53630, CVE-2026-27940 (a bypass of the 53630 fix) and CVE-2026-116840 (a second bypass) all turn a crafted model file into heap corruption — plus the model's Jinja chat template, which runs on every request. SECURITY.md says there is no reliable way to detect a malicious model and to sandbox untrusted ones.

-hf accepts any Hugging Face repository and falls back to the first file in the repo when the requested quant is missing; nothing verifies a digest or signature, so the file is whatever the hub (or a proxy) served. SECURITY.md leaves hash confirmation to the operator.

One slot pool (-np) and context are shared by every caller, -n defaults to unlimited, and SECURITY.md does not treat denial-of-service bugs as vulnerabilities; several 2026 CVEs (CVE-2026-52130, CVE-2026-52132) are request-triggered crashes.

In router mode GET /models lists every cached model with its file path, and POST /models and DELETE /models change the cache for anyone holding the shared key — or anyone at all when no key is set; --tools read_file and the stdio MCP servers can read any file the process can.

A fast-moving native codebase with about forty CVEs published in 2025–26, including critical memory-safety bugs reachable over HTTP (CVE-2026-43632, CVE-2026-107183) and over the RPC backend (CVE-2026-34159, CVE-2026-118375), and no private disclosure channel while the program is disabled.

Prompts reach disk through --slot-save-path, --log-prompts-dir or -v; leave the device through --rpc and --connect; and remote image_url parts make the server fetch arbitrary URLs, with no domain allowlist flag documented.

What is served can change at runtime: router POST /models downloads and /models/load loads any repository, POST /lora-adapters rescales loaded adapters (and each request's lora field overrides it), and --props enables POST /props; a GGUF swapped on disk is served on the next load with no check.

controls.mechanism: Loader surface limited to GGUF (no pickle or Python model code); --check-tensors validates tensor data for invalid values; --chat-template-file replaces the model's embedded Jinja template; no content scan, quarantine or digest check

steps.title: Serve only promoted files
body: Start the server with -m <path> or --models-dir <dir> on a directory only the promotion job can write, with --offline, instead of -hf, -mu or -dr, so nothing reaches the loader without passing the scanner.

steps.title: Replace the embedded chat template
body: Pass --chat-template-file with a reviewed Jinja template for each served model, so the template shipped in the GGUF metadata does not run on every request.

steps.title: Check tensors at load
body: Add --check-tensors so tensor data with invalid values is refused at load; it is a sanity check, not malware detection.

controls.note: Partial on this drawing's rule (native needs verification before load; partial covers safe formats without it), the same rule as toolLmStudio. The pickle and remote-code axis is closed by construction — GGUF is the only model format — but nothing inspects a file before load: -hf, -mu, -dr and the router's POST /models download straight into the loadable cache, and the GGUF parser itself is the attack surface (four parser CVEs in 2025–26, two of them bypasses of an earlier fix). The model's Jinja template executes on every request unless replaced. SECURITY.md: "there are no reliable methods to detect malicious models" and untrusted models belong in a sandbox. Format and content inspection at quarantine is an external model scanner in the promotion pipeline.

controls.mechanism: --api-key / --api-key-file (static bearer or x-api-key keys, checked on every route except /health, /v1/health and web-UI assets) and loopback bind by default (--host 127.0.0.1); optional TLS (--ssl-key-file, --ssl-cert-file); --cors-origins (default: reflect any origin with credentials)

steps.title: Require a key on every launch
body: Start the server with --api-key-file pointing at a file of keys readable only by the service account (LLAMA_ARG_API_KEY_FILE), one key per consuming application or the gateway's only.

steps.title: Pin the bind to loopback
body: Pass --host 127.0.0.1 explicitly (the default) and never --host 0.0.0.0 as in the Docker example; publish containers on 127.0.0.1 only.

steps.title: Restrict browser origins
body: Pass --cors-origins localhost (or the exact front-end origin) and --no-cors-credentials, because the default reflects any Origin with credentials allowed.

controls.note: Partial on this drawing's rule — a shared key is not per-caller identity (the toolVllm rule; toolLmStudio is partial on its tokens too, toolOllama external with none). The operator can require a key at launch, and whoever controls the launch (systemd unit, MDM-delivered script) controls the policy, so unlike a desktop toggle it can be enforced; but the key admits a bearer without naming a caller, any key in the list is accepted, /health and the web-UI assets skip the check, and with no key every route is open. The default CORS policy reflects any origin with credentials — harmless only while the server is stateless, which --tools, --agent and MCP undo (they switch the default to localhost). Host-header validation against DNS rebinding is not documented. The Llama desktop app's own settings are not documented. Per-caller identity is an authenticating reverse proxy or gateway that holds the only key (external).

controls.mechanism: A guardrail proxy or AI gateway on the request path, optionally calling a safety classifier served by a second llama-server; the runtime ships no content classification

evidence.title: llama-server README (no guardrail, moderation or content-policy setting)
llama.cpp SECURITY.md — Untrusted inputs (pre-analysis and sanitisation are the deployer's)

controls.note: External: llama-server returns the raw completion; grammars and JSON schemas constrain format, not content, and a system prompt is an instruction to the model. SECURITY.md puts input validation, filtering and prompt-injection detection on the deployer. Integration point: point applications at the gateway and keep llama-server on loopback with the gateway holding the only API key; a caller that reaches the port directly skips the classification.

controls.mechanism: Server-wide limits: -np slots (default auto), -c context, -n tokens per request (default unlimited), -to read/write timeout (default 3600 s), --threads-http, and in router mode --models-max (default 4); nothing per caller or key

steps.title: Bound slots and context
body: Set -np (LLAMA_ARG_N_PARALLEL) and -c (LLAMA_ARG_CTX_SIZE) explicitly for the hardware instead of the automatic values.

steps.title: Cap tokens and time per request
body: Set -n (LLAMA_ARG_N_PREDICT) to a ceiling instead of -1 (unlimited) and lower -to (LLAMA_ARG_TIMEOUT) from its 3600-second default.

steps.title: Bound the router
body: In router mode set --models-max so callers cannot load more models at once than the machine holds.

controls.note: Partial on this drawing's rule: global slot, context, token and time limits, not per caller — the same rule as toolOllama and toolLmStudio. One caller can occupy every slot, and the API key carries no quota. SECURITY.md tells multi-tenant operators to add rate limits themselves and does not treat DoS bugs as vulnerabilities. Per-caller or per-key quotas need an AI or API gateway in front (external).

controls.mechanism: Model files in LLAMA_CACHE or the --models-dir directory with the OS's file permissions; not content-addressed and not digest-checked; the API key gates the router's POST /models (download) and DELETE /models

evidence.title: llama-server README — Using multiple models (cache, --models-dir, POST and DELETE /models)
llama.cpp cache directory resolution (LLAMA_CACHE and per-OS defaults)

controls.note: External on this drawing's rule (partial needs at least a digest on download or content-addressed storage, which is what puts toolOllama at partial; toolLmStudio is external on the same rule). Files sit under the user's cache directory by repository and file name, readable and replaceable by any process of that user, and are loaded without a check. The product's contributions are the location (LLAMA_CACHE, --models-dir on a directory the server account owns), the API key on the router's download and delete endpoints, and leaving --slot-save-path unset so KV-cache state (conversation content, and the CVE-2026-43629 restore path) is not written to disk. Permissions and swap detection are OS controls and file-integrity monitoring.

controls.mechanism: The decision lives in the organisation's GRC / AI governance register; inputs are SECURITY.md's covered-topics list and secure-use guidance, and the device settings that enforce it are --offline, the model source flags, HTTPS_PROXY and LLAMA_VERSION

evidence.title: llama.cpp SECURITY.md (disclosure disabled; covered topics; using llama.cpp securely)
ggml.ai (maintainer company, acquired by Hugging Face in 2026)
llama.app install.sh (LLAMA_VERSION pin)

controls.note: External: whether local inference may run, from which sources and on which machines is recorded in the GRC or AI-governance platform. Vendor evidence is thin and specific: no assurance report or trust page; a security policy whose private disclosure program is "disabled until further notice", which excludes the web UI, router, MCP, experimental features and DoS from coverage, and which says not to expose llama-server or the RPC backend to untrusted networks. CVEs reach NVD through the repository's earlier GitHub advisories, VulnCheck and VulDB. Device settings that enforce the decision: --offline and -m / --models-dir in place of -hf, HTTPS_PROXY so downloads pass a proxy allowlist, and LLAMA_VERSION on the installer.

controls.mechanism: Third-party EDR over the llama / llama-server process and router child instances; integration points are TCP 9931, GET /health, --log-file / --log-jsonl, --metrics and the install paths

evidence.title: llama-server README — logging flags, /health, /metrics, /slots
llama.app install.sh (~/.llama-app and ~/.local/bin/llama)

controls.note: External: llama.cpp writes operational logs but no security telemetry and has no self-protection. Integration points: the `llama serve` / llama-server process (and in router mode one child process per loaded model, inheriting the router's environment); TCP 9931 by default; --log-file and --log-jsonl for structured logs; --metrics for Prometheus counters; the Llama app in the menu bar or tray; ~/.llama-app and ~/.local/bin/llama from install.sh; and stdio MCP children started with --mcp-servers-config, which run with the server's privileges. -v and --log-prompts-dir write prompt content and should stay off.

controls.mechanism: Local list endpoints for fleet tooling to collect: router GET /models (id as <repo>:<quant>, file path, status, load arguments), GET /v1/models (id defaults to the model file path), GET /props; no digest

steps.title: Collect each server's model list
body: Have the MDM or EDR agent call GET /models (router mode) or GET /v1/models with the API key on a schedule and ship id, path and status to the inventory.

steps.title: Hash what the paths point to
body: Have the same job sha256 each file under the reported paths and LLAMA_CACHE, since llama.cpp records no digest of its own.

controls.note: Partial on this drawing's rule, calibrated as toolVllm is: the server names the source (a Hugging Face repository and quant in router mode, the file path otherwise) but no digest, revision or licence, so the inventory job must hash the files itself; toolOllama is partial with digests, toolLmStudio external with neither. --alias and --tags present any name, and a single-model server reports only the path it was started with. Nothing aggregates across machines.

controls.mechanism: EDR/MDM software inventory and network scanning for the llama binary, the Llama app, the container images, the model cache and TCP 9931 answering /health

settings.name: --host
settings.where: llama serve / llama-server --host, or LLAMA_ARG_HOST
settings.recommended: 127.0.0.1, set explicitly by the managed launch
settings.why: Only processes on the device reach the API; a team server goes behind an authenticating proxy, never --host 0.0.0.0 as in the Docker example.

settings.name: --api-key-file
settings.where: llama-server --api-key-file <file> (LLAMA_ARG_API_KEY_FILE), or --api-key (LLAMA_API_KEY)
settings.recommended: A key file readable only by the service account, one key per consuming application or the gateway's only
settings.why: Every route but /health and the web-UI assets needs a key, so another local process or a web page cannot download, load or call models; a file keeps keys out of the process list.

settings.name: --ssl-key-file / --ssl-cert-file
settings.where: llama-server --ssl-key-file --ssl-cert-file (SSL build)
settings.recommended: Set whenever the server is reached from another machine without a TLS-terminating proxy
settings.why: The API key and prompts are not sent in clear text across the network.

settings.name: --cors-origins
settings.where: llama-server --cors-origins, or LLAMA_ARG_CORS_ORIGINS
settings.recommended: localhost, or the exact origin of the approved front end
settings.why: A web page open in the user's browser cannot drive the local API; the default is safe only while the server is stateless and read-only.

settings.name: --cors-credentials / --no-cors-credentials
settings.where: llama-server --no-cors-credentials, or LLAMA_ARG_CORS_CREDENTIALS=false
settings.recommended: --no-cors-credentials
settings.why: Cross-origin requests cannot ride the browser's credentials; clients send the API key as a header and do not need them.

settings.name: --ui / --no-ui (--webui / --no-webui)
settings.where: llama-server --no-webui, or LLAMA_ARG_UI=false
settings.recommended: --no-webui on servers that only feed applications
settings.why: The web UI is outside the project's security coverage and its assets skip the API key; a person who chats in it on their own device can keep it on loopback.

settings.name: --tools
settings.where: llama-server --tools, or LLAMA_ARG_TOOLS
settings.recommended: Unset
settings.why: The experimental tools (read_file, write_file, edit_file, exec_shell_command) expose file and shell access over the API; the flag says not to enable it in untrusted environments.

settings.name: -ag, --agent
settings.where: llama-server --agent, or LLAMA_ARG_AGENT
settings.recommended: Disabled
settings.why: Turns on the MCP CORS proxy and every built-in tool at once, including shell commands on the host.

settings.name: --mcp-servers-config / --mcp-servers-json
settings.where: llama-server --mcp-servers-config <mcp.json>, or LLAMA_ARG_MCP_SERVERS_CONFIG
settings.recommended: Unset
settings.why: Each declared stdio server is a child process with the server's privileges that the model can call; experimental and outside the security policy's coverage.

settings.name: --ui-mcp-proxy
settings.where: llama-server --ui-mcp-proxy, or LLAMA_ARG_UI_MCP_PROXY
settings.recommended: Disabled
settings.why: The server does not act as a CORS proxy for the web UI to reach remote MCP servers; the flag says not to enable it in untrusted environments.

settings.name: --connect
settings.where: llama-server --connect, or LLAMA_ARG_CONNECT
settings.recommended: Disabled
settings.why: The experimental llama-connect tunnel would make the server reachable from outside the device without an inbound port or the organisation's proxy.

settings.name: --rpc
settings.where: llama-server --rpc host:port,..., or LLAMA_ARG_RPC
settings.recommended: Unset
settings.why: Model tensors and prompts are not sent to remote rpc-servers, an unauthenticated channel SECURITY.md says not to use on untrusted networks.

settings.name: --props
settings.where: llama-server --props, or LLAMA_ARG_ENDPOINT_PROPS
settings.recommended: Disabled
settings.why: Callers cannot change the server's global properties through POST /props.

settings.name: --slots / --no-slots
settings.where: llama-server --no-slots, or LLAMA_ARG_ENDPOINT_SLOTS=false
settings.recommended: --no-slots on servers with more than one consuming application
settings.why: One caller cannot read the per-slot state and sampling parameters of other callers' requests.

settings.name: --slot-save-path
settings.where: llama-server --slot-save-path, or LLAMA_ARG_SLOT_SAVE_PATH
settings.recommended: Unset
settings.why: Conversation KV state is not written to disk by API callers, and crafted state files there were a heap-overflow path (CVE-2026-43629).

settings.name: --media-path
settings.where: llama-server --media-path
settings.recommended: Unset
settings.why: Requests cannot read local files through file:// image URLs.

settings.name: --log-prompts-dir
settings.where: llama-server --log-prompts-dir
settings.recommended: Unset
settings.why: Prompts and client material are not written to a directory on disk; the flag is for debugging only.

settings.name: -lv, --verbosity / -v, --verbose
settings.where: llama-server -lv N (LLAMA_ARG_LOG_VERBOSITY); never -v
settings.recommended: 3 (info)
settings.why: Logs stay operational; -v sets verbosity to infinity and logs every message, for debugging only.

settings.name: --log-jsonl / --log-file
settings.where: llama-server --log-jsonl (stdout) or --log-file <path> (LLAMA_ARG_LOG_FILE), with --log-timestamps
settings.recommended: --log-jsonl with timestamps, collected by the platform's log shipper
settings.why: Server events reach the EDR or SIEM as structured records with times, for investigation and version tracking.

settings.name: --metrics
settings.where: llama-server --metrics, or LLAMA_ARG_ENDPOINT_METRICS
settings.recommended: Enabled on shared servers, scraped by monitoring with the API key
settings.why: Load and throughput counters show a caller saturating the server, without exposing prompt content.

settings.name: -m, --model / --models-dir
settings.where: llama-server -m <path> (LLAMA_ARG_MODEL) or --models-dir <dir> (LLAMA_ARG_MODELS_DIR), in place of -hf, -mu or -dr
settings.default: Whatever the launch names, including Hugging Face repositories with -hf
settings.recommended: A local path in a directory only the promotion job can write
settings.why: Only files that passed the scanner and were hashed reach the GGUF parser; -hf would fetch any repository straight into the loadable cache.

settings.name: --offline
settings.where: llama-server --offline, or LLAMA_ARG_OFFLINE
settings.recommended: On for managed servers
settings.why: The server uses only cached or local files and makes no download, so a request or a flag cannot pull a new model.

settings.name: HTTPS_PROXY
settings.where: Environment of commands that download models → HTTP_PROXY / HTTPS_PROXY (NO_PROXY for exceptions)
settings.recommended: The corporate proxy, with huggingface.co on its allowlist
settings.why: Any download that is allowed passes the proxy's source allowlist and logging.

settings.name: -hft, --hf-token / HF_TOKEN
settings.where: llama-server --hf-token, or HF_TOKEN from the secret store
settings.default: The HF_TOKEN environment variable, if set
settings.recommended: Unset on serving hosts; a read-only, fine-grained token only on the promotion job that downloads
settings.why: A token on the serving host is exposed to anything that compromises the process, and is not needed once models are local.

settings.name: --chat-template-file
settings.where: llama-server --chat-template-file <reviewed.jinja>
settings.default: The template from the model's GGUF metadata
settings.recommended: A reviewed template for each served model
settings.why: A poisoned template embedded in a downloaded GGUF does not run on every request.

settings.name: --check-tensors
settings.where: llama-server --check-tensors
settings.recommended: true
settings.why: A model with invalid tensor values is refused at load; it is a sanity check, not malware detection.

settings.name: -np, --parallel
settings.where: llama-server -np N, or LLAMA_ARG_N_PARALLEL
settings.recommended: Set explicitly to what the hardware serves
settings.why: Bounds concurrent requests; slots are shared by every caller, so per-caller limits need a gateway.

settings.name: -c, --ctx-size
settings.where: llama-server -c N, or LLAMA_ARG_CTX_SIZE
settings.recommended: Set explicitly for the hardware
settings.why: Bounds the context requests share, so callers cannot claim a model's full window on a machine sized for less.

settings.name: -n, --predict, --n-predict
settings.where: llama-server -n N, or LLAMA_ARG_N_PREDICT
settings.recommended: A ceiling sized to the workload (for example 4096)
settings.why: One request cannot generate without end and hold a slot from every other caller.

settings.name: -to, --timeout
settings.where: llama-server -to N, or LLAMA_ARG_TIMEOUT
settings.why: Slow or stalled connections are dropped after ten minutes instead of an hour.

settings.name: --models-max
settings.where: llama-server --models-max N (router mode), or LLAMA_ARG_MODELS_MAX
settings.recommended: Set to what the machine can hold, never 0 (unlimited)
settings.why: Callers naming models cannot force more into memory than the host serves.

settings.name: GET /models (router) / GET /v1/models
settings.where: Called with the API key by the MDM or EDR agent on a schedule
settings.recommended: Collected from every device and server into the AI inventory, with each reported file hashed
settings.why: The organisation sees which repository, quant and file each server can serve, and spots one that was never approved.

settings.name: LLAMA_VERSION
settings.where: curl -LsSf https://llama.app/install.sh | LLAMA_VERSION=b<N> sh
settings.recommended: The build your vulnerability management has approved, moved forward as fixes land
settings.why: Devices run a build someone checked against the CVE stream, which is fast-moving and has no private disclosure channel.

variants.name: Copilot Chat on github.com (immersive and panel)
Copilot Chat in GitHub Mobile
Copilot Spaces (curated context, organisation-owned or personal)

summary: Copilot on github.com and GitHub Mobile answers over repositories, issues and PRs the user can see, attaches images and PDFs, searches the web when the policy allows, and acts through preconfigured GitHub tools (branches, file updates, issues). Since 2026-10-28 paid seats get the Copilot in the cloud experience: the same conversation can plan and make changes in a cloud sandbox (the default) or on GitHub Actions and continue in the Copilot app, VS Code or the CLI, and cloud sandbox sessions can use repository and personal MCP servers and Copilot connectors. Copilot Free keeps the older Copilot Chat experience. Spaces bundle repositories, files, issues and uploads as reusable context.

Inference runs on the Copilot API with enterprise-enabled models; retrieval runs with the user's own permissions (viewers of a Space only see sources they can access; without write access a session is read-only). Conversations are stored by GitHub: for the life of the account in cloud sandbox sessions, 28 days in sessions on GitHub Actions. Business and Enterprise prompts are not used for training.

Admin levers are the unified "Copilot in the cloud" policy (it replaced the Copilot cloud agent, Copilot Chat in GitHub and Copilot Chat in GitHub Mobile policies), the web search, models, MCP servers in Copilot and Copilot Memory policies, content exclusion, the managed-settings keys that cloud sandbox sessions read (permissions, allowedMcpServers), and, for Enterprise Managed Users, the enterprise access-restriction header. Spaces have no dedicated policy on the pages fetched; the MCP registry restriction does not apply to cloud sessions.

facts.label: Plans
facts.value: All plans; Business and Enterprise gate it with the Copilot in the cloud policy (AI controls > Copilot > Configure features & clients), which replaced the Copilot cloud agent, Copilot Chat in GitHub and Copilot Chat in GitHub Mobile policies. Copilot Free keeps the older Copilot Chat experience.

facts.label: Inference & routing
facts.value: Copilot API; models selectable per conversation within the enterprise Configure models policy; enterprise BYOK custom models appear in Chat; data-resident routing under the data residency policy.

facts.label: Data leaving the browser
facts.value: Prompts, attached files, repository context and (when enabled) web search results to the Copilot API; nothing runs on the device.

facts.label: Data retention / training
facts.value: Chat data is kept for the life of the account in cloud sandbox sessions and 28 days in GitHub Actions-based sessions; Business and Enterprise data is not used for training.
