tools.name: Ollama

variants.name: Ollama for macOS (app, menubar server and CLI)
variants.note: The app starts `ollama serve` itself and merges its own Settings into the server environment: "Expose Ollama to the network" sets OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0 over any launchctl value; the Cloud toggle is greyed out when OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD forces cloud off. Models and logs live under ~/.ollama.

variants.name: Ollama for Windows (app, tray server and CLI)
variants.note: Installs per user under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Ollama without Administrator rights and auto-downloads updates; inherits user and system environment variables. Same app Settings as macOS.

variants.name: Ollama for Linux (CLI and ollama.service)
variants.note: The standard installer creates an `ollama` system user with home /usr/share/ollama and a systemd unit running `ollama serve` as that user; configuration is Environment= lines in a root-owned override.conf.

variants.name: Ollama Docker image (ollama/ollama)
variants.note: The image sets OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0:11434 and the documented `docker run -p 11434:11434` publishes the port on every host interface; publish as -p 127.0.0.1:11434:11434 to keep it on loopback.

summary: Open-source (MIT) local model runtime: a daemon (`ollama serve`) that pulls open-weights models by name from the ollama.com library or Hugging Face (hf.co/{user}/{repo}), stores them as content-addressed blobs, and serves them on http://127.0.0.1:11434 through its own API plus OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible endpoints. Shipped as a macOS and Windows desktop app, a Linux CLI and systemd service, and a Docker image; current release v0.34.4 (2026-09-23).

Inference runs on the device and local prompts do not leave it. Signed in to ollama.com (`ollama signin`), the same local API also serves cloud models (names ending -cloud or :cloud) and web search, which forward the prompt to Ollama's cloud; OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD=1 or disable_ollama_cloud in ~/.ollama/server.json turns both off. Model pulls, app updates and limited usage metadata are the other outbound traffic.

Every control is an environment variable of the server process, delivered by systemd override, launchctl or Windows environment variables: OLLAMA_HOST (bind), OLLAMA_ORIGINS (browser origins), OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL and OLLAMA_MAX_QUEUE (global load), OLLAMA_MODELS (store), OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD and OLLAMA_REMOTES (cloud egress). The local API has no authentication at all, so any caller that reaches the port can pull, create, copy, delete and push models as well as run them.

facts.label: Plans
facts.value: The runtime is free and open source. ollama.com accounts (Free, Pro $20/mo, Max $100/mo, Team $500/mo, Enterprise custom) meter cloud-model use only; Team adds centralised billing and administration, Enterprise adds model access controls and cost budgets for users and API keys — all on the cloud side.

facts.label: Inference & routing
facts.value: Local CPU/GPU by default. With the machine signed in, a cloud model name (gpt-oss:120b-cloud, gemma4:cloud) sent to the local API is forwarded to Ollama's cloud; OLLAMA_REMOTES lists the hosts remote models may reach (default ollama.com). Direct cloud calls to https://ollama.com/api need OLLAMA_API_KEY and no local install (excluded here).

facts.label: Data leaving the device
facts.value: Local runs: "We don't see your prompts or data when you run locally." Outbound traffic is model pulls over HTTPS (HTTPS_PROXY honoured; HTTP_PROXY discouraged), macOS/Windows update downloads, and limited device and usage metadata (app version, request counts). Cloud models and web search send prompts and queries to Ollama; OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD=1 or "disable_ollama_cloud": true in ~/.ollama/server.json disables both and the log shows "Ollama cloud disabled: true".

facts.label: Retention & training
facts.value: Cloud prompts and responses are processed transiently, not stored beyond the request and not used for training; cloud compute is primarily in the United States with overflow to Europe and Singapore (privacy policy updated March 2026; pricing page). Locally, model files and the ed25519 identity key sit under ~/.ollama (/usr/share/ollama/.ollama for the Linux service) until removed.

facts.label: Docs index
facts.value: docs.ollama.com (machine-readable index at /llms.txt; OpenAPI at /openapi.yaml)

facts.label: Local endpoint
facts.value: http://127.0.0.1:11434 — native /api, OpenAI-compatible /v1 and Anthropic-compatible /v1/messages on one port; GET / answers "Ollama is running". "The local API at http://localhost:11434 does not require authentication."

facts.label: Updates
facts.value: macOS and Windows apps auto-download updates (user Settings toggle "Auto-download updates"); Linux re-runs install.sh, and OLLAMA_VERSION pins the version it installs. The Windows updater verified no signature before CVE-2026-42248 was reported.

facts.label: Exposure research
facts.value: Cisco Talos found 1,139 internet-exposed Ollama servers by Shodan (September 2025); SentinelLABS and Censys observed 175,108 unique Ollama hosts in 130 countries over 293 days (January 2026); Cyera cites roughly 300,000 exposed servers without naming its source (May 2026).

items.title: Delivering the runtime's security settings by device management
body: Linux: Environment="OLLAMA_HOST=127.0.0.1:11434" (and OLLAMA_ORIGINS, OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD, OLLAMA_MAX_QUEUE) in /etc/systemd/system/ollama.service.d/override.conf, then systemctl daemon-reload and restart; the file is root-owned, so this is the one platform where the setting holds against the user.

macOS: the app reads variables set with launchctl setenv, which an MDM script must reapply at each login; the app's own Settings then override OLLAMA_HOST when "Expose Ollama to the network" is on, so pair the variable with a compliance check that port 11434 listens only on 127.0.0.1. OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD set this way does lock the Cloud toggle.
Windows: the app inherits user and system environment variables; set them as system variables by policy, because user variables are user-writable, and restart the app.

links.title: FAQ — How do I configure Ollama server?
Desktop app server launcher (Expose → OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0, cloud setting → OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD)

riskNotes.note: Ollama imports only GGUF and Safetensors, so the pickle axis is closed by construction; the live class is the native GGUF parser. CVE-2026-7482 (Bleeding Llama) read past the heap from a crafted GGUF sent to the unauthenticated /api/create, and CVE-2025-0312/0315/0317 crashed the server the same way. Chat templates are Go templates selected from Ollama's list or shipped in the model's template layer, not Jinja.

Pulls are by name from the ollama.com library, any user namespace pushed there, or hf.co/{user}/{repo}. The sha256 check compares each layer with a manifest from the same registry, so it proves the transfer, not the publisher; no signature is verified. CVE-2025-51471 showed a malicious registry's WWW-Authenticate realm could steal the client's authentication token during a pull.

One global queue (OLLAMA_MAX_QUEUE 512) and OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL 1 per model are shared by every caller, and callers can raise num_ctx and pin models with keep_alive -1. Exposed hosts are counted by Cisco Talos (1,139, 2025), SentinelLABS with Censys (175,108, 2026) and Cyera (about 300,000, unsourced, 2026).

Any caller of the port can POST /api/push to copy a local model, including an organisation's fine-tune, to a registry it names — the exfiltration step of Cyera's Bleeding Llama chain; on macOS and Windows the blobs sit in ~/.ollama/models, readable by every process of the user.

Fast-moving native serving code with a steady CVE stream (twelve GitHub Advisory Database entries published 2025–26), and an auto-updater that on Windows 0.12.10–0.17.5 verified no signature and let response headers steer the write path (CVE-2026-42248, CVE-2026-42249, reported by CERT Polska).

A -cloud or :cloud model name, or the app's web search, sends the prompt to Ollama's cloud through the same local API once the machine is signed in; OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD=1 is the device-level off switch. OLLAMA_DEBUG_LOG_REQUESTS writes request bodies to a temporary directory and should stay off.

/api/create, /api/copy and /api/delete need no authentication (recorded as CVE-2025-63389), so any local process or web-exposed caller can repoint a model name; a blob swapped on disk is not re-hashed at load.

controls.mechanism: Built into the pull path: `ollama pull` / POST /api/pull recomputes the sha256 of every newly downloaded layer against the registry manifest and deletes a mismatched blob; imports (Modelfile FROM) accept only GGUF and Safetensors, with no pickle loader. No content scanning and no quarantine step.

steps.title: Pull only over the verified path
body: Acquire models with `ollama pull <name>` or POST /api/pull and never set the request's insecure field ("Allow downloading over insecure connections"), so every layer arrives over TLS and is hashed against its manifest.

steps.title: Keep the pull-time digest check intact
body: Run v0.32.10 or later: the pull handler re-hashes each layer that was not already on disk and removes a blob whose sha256 differs, and v0.32.10 fixed the check being skipped when an OCI manifest's config and layer share a digest.

steps.title: Scan third-party files before `ollama create`
body: Stage GGUF or Safetensors files outside OLLAMA_MODELS, scan them with a model-file scanner, and only then import with a Modelfile `FROM /path/to/file.gguf` (or a Safetensors directory) and `ollama create`; Ollama has no importer for pickle-based checkpoints.

controls.note: Partial on this drawing's rule — safe formats by construction and a digest check on pull only. The digest is compared with a manifest from the same registry that served the blob, so it proves the transfer, not the publisher or the content; layers already on disk skip it, and nothing re-hashes at load. There is no content inspection and no quarantine: `ollama pull hf.co/{user}/{repo}` fetches an arbitrary community GGUF and makes it loadable in one step, and any caller of the unauthenticated API can upload a blob to /api/blobs and /api/create a model from it — the route CVE-2026-7482's crafted GGUF took into the native parser. A model scanner at a quarantine directory or a scanning registry mirror (external) is the missing half.

controls.mechanism: No caller authentication on the local API; an authenticating reverse proxy in front of an Ollama pinned to 127.0.0.1:11434 is the integration point, with OLLAMA_HOST (default 127.0.0.1:11434), OLLAMA_ORIGINS (a disallowed Origin is refused with 403) and Host validation while bound to loopback as the configuration around it

steps.title: Pin the bind to loopback
body: Set OLLAMA_HOST=127.0.0.1:11434 explicitly in the server environment (Environment= in /etc/systemd/system/ollama.service.d/override.conf on Linux, launchctl setenv on macOS, a system variable on Windows) rather than relying on the default.

steps.title: Keep the desktop app's network exposure off
body: Leave Settings → "Expose Ollama to the network" off on macOS and Windows: when on, the app starts the server with OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0, overriding the variable you set; it is a per-user setting, so verify the listener with a compliance check.

steps.title: Allow only named browser origins
body: Leave OLLAMA_ORIGINS unset or list exact origins, never * or the chrome-extension://* style wildcards the FAQ shows; the defaults already admit localhost, 127.0.0.1 and 0.0.0.0 on any port.

steps.title: Publish the container port on loopback
body: Run the ollama/ollama image with -p 127.0.0.1:11434:11434, not the documented -p 11434:11434, because the image sets OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0:11434 and Docker then publishes on every host interface.

evidence.title: Ollama API — Authentication ("The local API at http://localhost:11434 does not require authentication")
Ollama FAQ — How can I use Ollama with a proxy server? (Nginx, Host localhost:11434)

controls.note: External on this drawing's rule: "The local API at http://localhost:11434 does not require authentication", so any local process is a full caller (pull, create, copy, delete, push), and caller identity can only come from a proxy that authenticates each calling application. Integration point: keep OLLAMA_HOST on 127.0.0.1:11434 so only the proxy on the same host reaches it, with the proxy setting Host localhost:11434 as in the FAQ's Nginx example; any local process that calls the port directly still bypasses the proxy, and a host firewall on 11434 is the backstop. `ollama signin` and ollama.com API keys authenticate this machine to Ollama's cloud (cloud models, private pulls, push), not callers of the local port, and the OLLAMA_AUTH variable only makes the CLI sign its own requests; the server code checks no caller credential. The built-in configuration around it: Host validation (the DNS-rebinding fix for CVE-2024-28224) runs only while bound to loopback and accepts the machine's hostname, *.localhost, *.local and *.internal names and private IP literals; a routable bind skips it. The origin check applies only to requests that carry an Origin header, and the default list (per source) also admits file://*, app://*, tauri://*, vscode-webview://* and vscode-file://*. Only the Linux systemd override is out of the user's reach; launchctl values are overridden by the app's Expose toggle and Windows user variables are user-writable, and the app's stored Browser setting (no Settings toggle; reset to off by "reset to defaults") sets OLLAMA_ORIGINS=* when true (source, 2026-10-30).

controls.mechanism: A guardrail proxy or AI gateway on the request path, optionally calling a safety-classifier model served by the same Ollama (llama-guard3, shieldgemma); the runtime ships no content classification

evidence.title: Ollama docs index (no guardrail, moderation or content-policy setting)
Ollama library — llama-guard3 (content safety classification of LLM inputs and responses)

controls.note: External: Ollama returns the raw completion; it has no harm-category, denied-topic or policy classifier and no hook between the API and the model runner to attach one. A Modelfile SYSTEM prompt is an instruction to the model, not a control, and callers can send their own system message. The library hosts classifier models, but invoking them on every request and blocking on the verdict is the gateway's job. Integration point: point applications at the gateway and keep Ollama on loopback; a caller that reaches port 11434 directly skips the classification.

controls.mechanism: Server-wide OLLAMA_MAX_QUEUE (default 512, then HTTP 503), OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL (default 1 per model), OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS and a default OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH; nothing per caller or key

steps.title: Cap the shared queue
body: Set OLLAMA_MAX_QUEUE in the server environment (systemd override.conf, launchctl setenv, system environment variable) so requests beyond it are rejected with 503 instead of queuing without bound.

steps.title: Bound concurrency and resident models
body: Set OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL and OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS to what the machine can serve; memory scales with OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL × OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH.

steps.title: Set a default context window
body: Set OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH explicitly in the server environment (or the app's Context length slider) instead of relying on the VRAM-based default.

controls.note: Partial on this drawing's rule: global concurrency, queue and context limits, not per caller — Ollama has no caller identity to meter against. One caller can fill the queue for all, raise options.num_ctx per request and pin models with keep_alive -1 (FAQ), so the context default is not a ceiling. The two vendor pages disagree on that default (FAQ: 4096 tokens; Context length page: 4k, 32k or 256k by VRAM), so set it. Per- caller or per-key quotas need an AI or API gateway in front (external). Plan concurrency limits and Enterprise budgets on ollama.com apply to cloud models only.

controls.mechanism: Content-addressed store (models/blobs named sha256-<digest>, referenced by manifests) under OLLAMA_MODELS; digest verified on pull only; the Linux service runs as the dedicated ollama user owning /usr/share/ollama/.ollama/models, while macOS and Windows keep models in the user's ~/.ollama

steps.title: Run the Linux service as its own account
body: Install with the standard installer (or useradd -r -s /bin/false -U -m -d /usr/share/ollama ollama and User=ollama in ollama.service) so the model store belongs to the ollama account, not to users.

steps.title: Move the store to a restricted directory
body: Set OLLAMA_MODELS to a directory only the serving account can write, and on Linux run sudo chown -R ollama:ollama <directory> as the FAQ describes.

controls.note: Partial on this drawing's rule: content-addressed and digest-checked on download only, with permissions left to the OS. Nothing re-hashes a blob when it is loaded, so a file swapped under models/blobs is served on the next load; on macOS and Windows the store sits in the user's home, readable and writable by any process running as the user, including org fine-tunes. The unauthenticated API is a second path to read or replace models (/api/push, /api/copy, /api/delete, /api/create). File-integrity monitoring over the blobs directory, re-hashing each file against its sha256-<digest> name, is the external half. Same rule as toolLmStudio, rated external there because its store is neither content-addressed nor digest-checked.

controls.mechanism: GRC / AI governance platform holds the decision; the device settings that enforce it are OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD (or disable_ollama_cloud), OLLAMA_REMOTES, HTTPS_PROXY for pulls, OLLAMA_MODELS and the Linux OLLAMA_VERSION pin

evidence.title: Ollama SECURITY.md (report to hello@ollama.com; user best practices)
Ollama release notes
Ollama environment variables (OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD, OLLAMA_REMOTES), printed by `ollama serve --help`
Ollama FAQ — disable cloud features; behind a proxy

controls.note: External on this drawing's rule: the runtime cannot assess itself, so whether local inference may run, from which sources and on which machines is recorded in the GRC or AI-governance platform. Inputs Ollama publishes: SECURITY.md (private report to hello@ollama.com, a three-line best-practice list, no bounty), GitHub release notes and the privacy policy. It publishes no repository security advisories — its 2025–26 CVEs reach the GitHub Advisory Database through NVD, CERT Polska, VulDB and researchers — and no release-signing statement. Device settings that enforce the decision: OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD=1 (cloud models and web search off), OLLAMA_REMOTES (hosts remote models may reach, default ollama.com), HTTPS_PROXY so pulls from ollama.com and hf.co pass a proxy allowlist, a pre-approved OLLAMA_MODELS store, and OLLAMA_VERSION on the Linux installer; "Auto-download updates" is a user setting.

controls.mechanism: Third-party EDR over the ollama server process and the inference processes it spawns; integration points are port 11434, the ollama.service unit, the server.log / app.log paths and the %TEMP%\ollama* executables on Windows

evidence.title: Ollama troubleshooting — log locations per platform
Ollama for Windows — install, log and temporary-executable paths
Ollama for macOS — file locations

controls.note: External: Ollama writes operational logs but no security telemetry and has no self-protection. Integration points: the `ollama serve` process (Linux systemd ollama.service running as User=ollama; started by Ollama.app on macOS and `ollama app.exe` on Windows) and its per-model inference child processes; TCP 11434; logs in ~/.ollama/logs/server.log and app.log (macOS), %LOCALAPPDATA%\Ollama\server.log, app.log and upgrade.log (Windows), journalctl -u ollama (Linux), docker logs (container). Windows stages temporary executables in %TEMP%\ollama* directories, so EDR should trust the signer and path, not the name. GET /api/version or `ollama -v` gives the version for vulnerable-version discovery. OLLAMA_DEBUG raises log detail; OLLAMA_DEBUG_LOG_REQUESTS writes request bodies to disk and should stay off.

controls.mechanism: Local list APIs for fleet tooling to collect: `ollama ls` / GET /api/tags (name, sha256 digest, size, modified_at, format, family, parameter_size, quantization_level, remote_host for cloud models), POST /api/show (license, template, parameters, model_info), GET /api/ps and GET /api/version

steps.title: Collect each device's model list
body: Have the MDM or EDR agent call GET http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/tags (or run `ollama ls`) on a schedule and ship name, digest, size, modified_at and details to the inventory.

steps.title: Record licence, template and parameters
body: POST /api/show with each model name to capture license, template, parameters, capabilities and model_info for the bill of materials.

steps.title: Record the runtime version
body: GET /api/version on each device so the inventory ties models to the runtime build that serves them.

controls.note: Partial on this drawing's rule: a local list API with digests that fleet tooling can collect; the product has no fleet inventory. The source is only implicit in the name (a bare library name, a user/model namespace anyone can push, or an hf.co/ prefix), not a signed provenance record, and a model built with `ollama create` from a local GGUF records no upstream at all. The listed digest identifies content on this machine, not the publisher. Same rule as toolLmStudio, rated external there because its lists carry no digest or source.

controls.mechanism: EDR/MDM software inventory and network scanning for the Ollama app and binary, its service and data directories, and TCP 11434 answering "Ollama is running"

evidence.title: Ollama for macOS — file locations
Ollama for Windows — per-user install without Administrator
Ollama for Linux — binary, service and user
Ollama server routes (GET / returns "Ollama is running")

controls.note: External: Ollama registers itself nowhere the organisation controls. Discovery points: /Applications/ Ollama.app and /usr/local/bin/ollama (macOS); %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Ollama, installed per user without Administrator, so it can be missing from the software catalogue (Windows); /usr/bin/ollama, the ollama user and ollama.service (Linux); the ollama/ollama container image; ~/.ollama directories with an id_ed25519 key; the login item or Startup app entry; and TCP 11434 answering GET / with "Ollama is running" and GET /api/version. Signed-in cloud use shows as traffic to ollama.com at the SSE.

controls.mechanism: An evaluation / red-team harness run against the candidate model on a staging instance before its digest is approved; Ollama ships no model evaluation

evidence.title: Ollama docs index (no evaluation or model-testing feature)
Ollama OpenAI compatibility (http://localhost:11434/v1 for harnesses)

controls.note: External: nothing in Ollama tests what weights do, and a pull makes a model servable at once. Integration point: a harness calls the candidate through the OpenAI-compatible /v1 or native /api/chat endpoint on a staging instance with its own OLLAMA_MODELS, and the governance band approves the resulting digest; the gate lives with the harness and the approval record, not the runtime. Refusal behaviour is whatever the weights carry, and abliterated or uncensored variants are one pull away.

controls.mechanism: Built into the pull path: `ollama pull` / POST /api/pull reports "verifying sha256 digest", re-hashes each newly downloaded layer against the digest in the registry's manifest and deletes a mismatched blob; no signature is checked and nothing re-hashes at load

steps.title: Pull only over TLS
body: Never set the pull request's insecure field ("Allow downloading over insecure connections"), so the manifest and every layer arrive over HTTPS before they are hashed.

steps.title: Keep the pull-time digest check intact
body: Run v0.32.10 or later, where the pull handler always verifies a layer whose digest is shared with the config entry, and leave blob verification to the pull rather than copying blobs in by hand.

controls.note: Partial on this drawing's rule — a digest check on download, no signature and no verify-at-load. The sha256 of each layer is compared with a manifest served by the same registry as the blob, so it proves the transfer, not the publisher; layers already on disk are skipped, and a blob changed under models/blobs is served on the next load. Ollama checks no model-signing bundle. Verification against an approved digest (the promotion record) is external: an MDM or EDR job compares GET /api/tags digests with the approved list. Same rule as toolVllm (pinned revisions, no verification) and toolLmStudio (no digest at all, external).

settings.name: OLLAMA_HOST
settings.where: Server environment → OLLAMA_HOST (Environment= in /etc/systemd/system/ollama.service.d/override.conf; launchctl setenv; Windows system variable)
settings.recommended: 127.0.0.1:11434, set explicitly
settings.why: The API authenticates no caller, so a routable bind hands pull, create, delete and push to anyone on the network; a team server goes behind an authenticating proxy instead.

settings.name: Expose Ollama to the network
settings.where: Ollama app (macOS, Windows) › Settings › Expose Ollama to the network
settings.recommended: Off
settings.why: When on, the app starts the server with OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0 over any value you set; it is a per-user toggle, so check the listener stays on 127.0.0.1.

settings.name: OLLAMA_ORIGINS
settings.where: Server environment → OLLAMA_ORIGINS
settings.default: Unset (localhost, 127.0.0.1 and 0.0.0.0 on any port, plus app://, file://, tauri:// and vscode-webview:// origins)
settings.recommended: Unset, or exact origins of approved local apps — never * or chrome-extension://*
settings.why: A web page or any browser extension in the user's browser cannot drive the local API, which would let it pull, delete or push models.

settings.name: docker run -p 11434:11434
settings.where: docker run / compose ports for the ollama/ollama image
settings.default: The documented -p 11434:11434 (every host interface; the image sets OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0:11434)
settings.why: The container listens on all its interfaces, so the publish rule is what keeps the unauthenticated port off the host's network.

settings.name: OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD / disable_ollama_cloud
settings.where: Server environment → OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD=1, or ~/.ollama/server.json → "disable_ollama_cloud" (app › Settings › Cloud then shows it forced off)
settings.default: Unset (cloud models and web search available once signed in)
settings.recommended: OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD=1 on managed devices
settings.why: A -cloud model name or web search would otherwise send the prompt to Ollama's cloud through the same local API; teams approved for Ollama Cloud get an exception.

settings.name: OLLAMA_REMOTES
settings.where: Server environment → OLLAMA_REMOTES
settings.recommended: Unset (ollama.com only)
settings.why: Remote models can be forwarded only to the listed hosts, so no other inference host can be added through a model definition.

settings.name: HTTPS_PROXY
settings.where: Server environment → HTTPS_PROXY, with the proxy CA installed as a system certificate
settings.recommended: The corporate proxy, with ollama.com and hf.co pulls on its allowlist
settings.why: Model pulls pass the proxy's source allowlist and logging; the FAQ says not to set HTTP_PROXY, which can break client connections.

settings.name: insecure (Allow downloading over insecure connections)
settings.where: POST /api/pull request body → insecure; ollama pull --insecure
settings.recommended: false — never set
settings.why: Keeps the manifest and layers on TLS, so the pull-time sha256 check is against a manifest an on-path attacker could not rewrite.

settings.name: OLLAMA_MODELS
settings.where: Server environment → OLLAMA_MODELS (app › Settings › Model location sets the same)
settings.recommended: A directory only the serving account can write (sudo chown -R ollama:ollama on Linux)
settings.why: Other users and processes cannot swap a blob or copy an organisation fine-tune out of the store; on macOS and Windows the user's own processes still can.

settings.name: User=ollama
settings.where: /etc/systemd/system/ollama.service → [Service] User= and Group= (created by the standard installer)
settings.recommended: ollama — a dedicated non-login account
settings.why: The server, its model store and its ed25519 key belong to a service account rather than to whoever is logged in.

settings.name: OLLAMA_MAX_QUEUE
settings.where: Server environment → OLLAMA_MAX_QUEUE
settings.recommended: 512, set explicitly; lower on a shared server
settings.why: Requests beyond the queue get HTTP 503 instead of piling up; it is one global queue, so per-caller limits need a gateway.

settings.name: OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL
settings.where: Server environment → OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL
settings.recommended: 1 on a workstation; sized to memory on a server
settings.why: Memory scales with parallel requests × context length, so an unbounded value lets callers exhaust the host.

settings.name: OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS
settings.where: Server environment → OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS
settings.default: 3 × the number of GPUs, or 3 for CPU inference
settings.recommended: Set explicitly to what the machine can hold
settings.why: Bounds how many models callers can force into memory at once by naming them.

settings.name: OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH
settings.where: Server environment → OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH (app › Settings › Context length sets the same)
settings.default: 4096 per the FAQ; 4k, 32k or 256k by VRAM per the Context length page
settings.recommended: Set explicitly for the hardware (for example 32768)
settings.why: The vendor pages disagree on the default, so set it; callers can still raise num_ctx per request, so it is a default, not a ceiling.

settings.name: OLLAMA_DEBUG_LOG_REQUESTS
settings.where: Server environment → OLLAMA_DEBUG_LOG_REQUESTS
settings.recommended: Unset
settings.why: When on, inference request bodies and replay curl commands are written to a temporary directory, putting prompts and client material on disk.

settings.name: Auto-download updates
settings.where: Ollama app (macOS, Windows) › Settings › Auto-download updates
settings.recommended: On
settings.why: Fixes for the GGUF-parser and API CVEs land without waiting for the user; the Windows updater's own signature gap (CVE-2026-42248) is fixed by updating past it.

settings.name: OLLAMA_VERSION
settings.where: Linux install script → curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | OLLAMA_VERSION=<version> sh
settings.recommended: The release your vulnerability management has approved
settings.why: Servers run a version someone checked against the advisory stream, not whatever the script fetched that day.

settings.name: ollama signin
settings.where: ollama signin / app › Settings › Ollama account; keys at ollama.com › Settings › Keys
settings.recommended: Not signed in on managed devices outside teams approved for Ollama Cloud; remove the device key at ollama.com when it leaves
settings.why: The device key is what lets the machine push models to ollama.com and run cloud models, so an unsigned device cannot publish an organisation fine-tune there.

settings.name: List models (GET /api/tags)
settings.where: GET http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/tags (or ollama ls), called by the MDM or EDR agent on a schedule
settings.recommended: Collected from every device into the AI inventory, with digests compared to the approved list
settings.why: The organisation sees which models, by sha256 digest, each device can serve, and spots one that was never approved.

tools.name: OpenAI Agents API

variants.name: Agents API with OpenAI-hosted sandboxes
Agents API with a self-hosted executor (codex exec-server on your infrastructure or a partner sandbox)
variants.note: The harness and inference stay at OpenAI; shell, files and local MCP run where the executor runs. Outbound-only connection; the executor key can only connect environments.

summary: OpenAI's managed Codex harness behind an API (header OpenAI-Beta agents=v1): you define an agent (model, instructions, tools, MCP servers, skills, plugins), optionally an environment (OpenAI-hosted Linux sandbox, or none, or a self-hosted executor), and run sessions that stream events; the vendor runs the loop, compaction, recovery, subagents and the sandbox. Function tools invert the loop — the session pauses with requires_action until your code returns the result — where the application can enforce human approval for its functions. Hosted sandboxes have network enabled by default, a "restricted" mode of up to 100 exact hostnames, and expire after an hour idle; files under /workspace/outputs survive as artifacts.

Governance is API-native and thin: allowed_tools per MCP server, vaults that hold MCP bearer tokens, OAuth grants and sandbox API secrets (substituted at egress for named hosts) the agent never receives, a restricted executor key, a dashboard trace view with a pull-based OTLP JSON export per session, and no general per-action policy language or per-agent principal. Hosted browser use exposes origin and sign-in approval requests to the application; this does not establish approval for every browser action or for other hosted tools. Sessions persist until deleted; the API supports US data residency only and is not eligible for zero data retention, self-hosting included.

facts.label: Plans
facts.value: Any API organisation; public beta. Billed at model API rates plus standard container rates for hosted sandboxes.

facts.label: Inference & routing
facts.value: OpenAI models only, called inside OpenAI's runtime; no BYO model or customer gateway.

facts.label: Data leaving the environment
facts.value: Instructions, input, tool inputs and outputs, and the sandbox's files go to OpenAI; with a self-hosted executor the shell and files stay on your side while tool inputs and outputs still cross to the harness.

facts.label: Retention & training
facts.value: /v1/agents state is retained until deleted and is not ZDR-eligible; data residency is United States only; business terms do not train on API data.

facts.label: Docs index
facts.value: developers.openai.com Agents API guide (overview, architecture, environments, tools, sessions, observability)

items.title: Choose the network mode per environment template
body: Hosted sandboxes default to network enabled. Set restricted with an explicit allowed_domains list (exact hostnames, no wildcards) in the environment template; session overrides cannot broaden a template's policy.

items.title: Keep credentials in vaults and out of the sandbox
body: Attach vaults for MCP bearer tokens and OAuth grants; keep the API key outside the sandbox (reserved environment names are rejected) and give executors only the restricted environment key.

items.title: Bind browser approvals to the caller and pending request
body: When computer use is enabled, handle origin-access and sign-in requests in the application. Verify caller/session ownership and the current request_id before returning a decision; remove obsolete approval controls. Origin admission is not approval of every later action. Cancelling a request does not stop the task.

riskNotes.note: Web search and MCP results enter the hosted loop unclassified; the sandbox's default network policy is enabled, so a fetched page is instruction until restricted.
Sessions and published artifacts persist on OpenAI's side until deleted, US-only, with no ZDR; sandbox files last while the sandbox does; environment variables are readable by the model.
Plugins, skills and MCP servers are named in the definition and fetched or connected by the harness; nothing verifies what a declared server serves.

controls.mechanism: environment.type openai_hosted: one OpenAI-hosted Linux sandbox per session (its own /workspace, shared by the root agent and its subagents, deleted on session delete or after an hour without keep-alives); or environment.type self_hosted, where codex exec-server runs on compute you provide

steps.title: Give each session its own hosted sandbox
body: Set environment.type openai_hosted; each session gets a separate workspace, and the sandbox can be deleted after an hour without activity or keep-alives (not configurable) or when you delete the session.

steps.title: Separate trust boundaries by environment and project
body: Use separate environments for users or workloads that must not share data and a dedicated OpenAI project for each application or workload, as the sandbox security guide says.

steps.title: Harden self-hosted compute yourself
body: With environment.type self_hosted the executor runs on your container, laptop or partner sandbox; isolate it by user or workload, because agents sharing an environment share its files and credentials.

controls.note: Native on the runtime rule: a per-session sandbox the vendor provisions and reclaims. Inside the boundary: bash, apply-patch, file tools, packages, setup commands, and stdio or environment-origin MCP servers. Outside: the harness, inference, web search and service-origin MCP connections, which run in OpenAI's service. The isolation technology is not named beyond a "sandbox" billed at container rates, subagents share the session's sandbox rather than getting their own, and physical cleanup after a session delete may continue asynchronously. environment.type self_hosted moves the boundary to the deployer (image, privileges and cleanup are yours; deleting the session does not stop that compute); environment.type none removes the shell and file tools altogether.

original.mechanism: OpenAI-hosted Linux sandbox per session (Python, Node, CLI tools) or a self-hosted executor
original.note: Isolation technology is not documented beyond "isolated compute environments"; the security guide recommends separate environments per user or workload.

steps.title: Use one environment per trust boundary
body: Create separate environments for users or workloads that must not share data; hosted sandboxes expire after one hour of inactivity and cannot be extended.

controls.mechanism: environment.network.access enabled | disabled | restricted with allowed_domains (1–100 exact hostnames) on an openai_hosted environment or environment template; web_search mode and allowed_domains bound the search tool separately

steps.title: Restrict the hosted sandbox's network
body: Set environment.network.access to disabled, or to restricted with allowed_domains listing exact hostnames (no wildcards, protocols, paths or ports; subdomains and redirect targets need their own entries); enabled is the default.

steps.title: Save the policy in an environment template
body: Put the network policy in an environment template and pass environment_template_id; a session's network override cannot broaden the template's policy.

steps.title: Bound web search on the tool
body: Leave web_search out of agent.tools or set mode disabled; where search is needed use cached mode and an allowed_domains list of up to 100 domains.

controls.note: Native on the runtime rule: an exact-host allowlist the vendor enforces around the hosted sandbox. Paths it does not see: web search (its own mode and domain list), service-origin MCP connections (the default connection_origin, made from OpenAI's service) and inference. Hosted stdio MCP servers require enabled access, so an agent that uses one cannot run restricted. The policy belongs to whoever creates the session — the template is optional — and the API reference gives the default as enabled for beta requests but disabled for GA requests, so set it explicitly. A self-hosted executor's egress is your firewall; it needs api.openai.com and wss://codex-cloud-environments.chatgpt.com.

original.mechanism: environment.network enabled (default) | disabled | restricted with allowed_domains
original.note: Restricted lists up to 100 exact hostnames; hosted stdio MCP requires enabled; templates cannot be broadened by a session.

steps.title: Restrict the hosted sandbox's network
body: Set network to disabled or restricted on the environment template and list the hosts the setup commands and tools genuinely need.

controls.mechanism: Vault credentials attached per session with vault_ids: static_bearer or mcp_oauth bound to an MCP server URL and presented by OpenAI's service, and environment_variable credentials whose placeholder a network proxy replaces only for the credential's allowed_hosts

steps.title: Substitute sandbox secrets at egress
body: Create an environment_variable credential (auth.secret_name, auth.secret_value, auth.networking.type limited, auth.networking.allowed_hosts) so hosted sandbox code sees a placeholder and the proxy supplies the secret only to those hosts over HTTPS on 443 or 8443.

steps.title: Bind MCP credentials to their server
body: Store static_bearer or mcp_oauth credentials with mcp_server_url and set the MCP tool's credential_id when several attached credentials match that URL.

steps.title: Keep each user's grant in its own vault
body: Store the mcp_oauth grant from your own consent flow in a vault per end user or tenant and pass only that vault in vault_ids for that user's sessions.

controls.note: Native on the runtime rule: credentials are held outside the sandbox and injected per destination, and per-user scoping is available by attaching per-user vaults. That is the application's arrangement, not the default: a vault's credentials are presented for every session it is attached to, vaults are project-scoped, and the docs do not say whether attaching one at session creation needs a vaults permission. Not covered: self-hosted environments, environment-origin HTTP MCP and stdio MCP (inline authorization or transport.env_vars, readable by code in the environment) and function tools (the credential stays in your handler); the docs say to run your own trusted proxy there. The placeholder only works in HTTPS request headers, and an environment credential is fixed when the session is created, so a rotation reaches only new sessions.

original.mechanism: Vaults for MCP credentials (service-originated connections only); restricted executor key
original.note: Applies to MCP connections the harness makes; environment variables you inject are visible inside the sandbox.

steps.title: Attach vaults instead of headers
body: Store bearer tokens and OAuth grants in a vault bound to the MCP server URL and attach vault_ids to the session; retrieving a vault never returns secret values.

controls.mechanism: Write-only vault credentials; workload identity federation to a project service account for short-lived API tokens; maximum API key lifetime, API Key Governance and IP allowlist in Platform settings; a connect-only environment key for self-hosted executors; no vendor tunnel for this API

steps.title: Keep tool secrets in vaults
body: Retrieving a vault or credential never returns its secret; replace a secret with POST /v1/vaults/{vault_id}/credentials/{credential_id} and delete credentials or the vault when they are no longer needed.

steps.title: Replace stored API keys with federation
body: In Organization Settings > Security > Workload Identity Provider create a provider and a service account mapping, narrowed by Permissions, so the application exchanges its own OIDC, SPIFFE or X.509 identity for a short-lived OpenAI access token.

steps.title: Bound the keys that remain
body: In Platform settings set a maximum API key lifetime for the organization or project and use API Key Governance to allow only service-account keys; both apply to new keys only.

steps.title: Pin keys to your egress addresses
body: Under Settings > Security > IP allowlist enable an organization or project allowlist so a leaked key fails with ip_not_authorized from any other address.

controls.note: Partial by the runtime rule. The vault and federation halves hold: vault values are write-only, saved agents store no credentials, inline MCP authorization is encrypted and omitted from the returned session, and federation gives the application a short-lived token instead of a stored key. The tunnel half does not: Secure MCP Tunnel documents ChatGPT, Codex and the Responses API (a tunnel_id on the MCP tool) but this API's MCP tool has no tunnel field, so the private path is a self-hosted executor dialling out on its environment key — limited to connecting environments, but readable by agent-generated code in that environment and with no rotation procedure beyond "rotate or revoke it when needed". Anything placed in environment.env or passed to a stdio MCP server is a secret the agent's code can read.

original.mechanism: Environment env vars (reserved names rejected); vaults for MCP; executor-scoped CODEX_API_KEY
original.note: Vaulted MCP credentials are write-only; anything passed as an environment variable is a stored secret readable by the model.

steps.title: Keep the API key outside the sandbox
body: The docs reject OPENAI_API_KEY, PATH and CODEX_* as environment names and tell you to keep the key outside; executors use a key that can only connect environments.

controls.mechanism: allowed_tools on each mcp entry in agent.tools; web_search mode (disabled | cached | live) and allowed_domains; tools left out of agent.tools are off; environment.type none removes the built-in shell and apply-patch tools

steps.title: Allowlist tools per MCP server
body: Set allowed_tools on each mcp entry in agent.tools; every tool the server publishes is callable when it is omitted.

steps.title: Leave web search out or narrow it
body: Omit web_search from agent.tools (or set mode disabled); where it is needed use cached mode and allowed_domains.

steps.title: Drop the built-in shell where it is not needed
body: Set environment.type none so the built-in Bash and apply-patch tools, workspace files and executor MCPs are unavailable; with an environment attached they cannot be switched off one by one.

controls.note: Partial by the runtime rule: per-tool on/off exists for MCP tools and web search has a domain list, but MCP tool-name admission does not establish argument-level authorization. Browser origin/sign-in approvals have a separate, narrower scope. The built-in shell and file tools come with any environment, subagents inherit the MCP tools, credentials and allowed tools, and programmatic tool calling lets model-generated code call the same tools. It all lives in the definition, and the next definition can undo it: the key that creates sessions (api.agents.write) can pass any inline agent, and no tenant restriction on definition changes is documented for this API (project hosted-tool permissions are documented for project workloads without naming the Agents API, so they are not credited). allowed_tools admits tool names; nothing verifies what a declared server serves.

original.mechanism: allowed_tools per MCP server; tool enablement in the agent definition; template network policy

steps.title: Allowlist tools per server
body: Declare allowed_tools on each MCP server entry and keep secrets out of reusable agent definitions, plugin archives and logs.

original.mechanism: server_url, allowed_tools, connection_origin service | environment
original.note: Admission is the definition; the harness verifies nothing about what a declared server serves.

steps.title: Pin servers and origins
body: Name servers by URL with allowed_tools; use connection_origin environment for servers reachable only from your own network.

controls.mechanism: Application-executed function tools pause for results; hosted computer use also exposes origin-access and browser-authentication approval requests

steps.title: Gate consequential custom actions before execution
body: Require an authenticated human decision in the function handler before executing the requested effect. Bind the decision to the caller, session, function arguments and pending call.

steps.title: Handle browser consent at its documented scope
body: Present origin and sign-in requests to the authorized user and answer the current request_id. Treat origin admission and login consent separately from approval of later destructive or external effects.

controls.note: Partial: the application supplies authenticated approval handling and expiry. Browser origin/sign-in consent does not prove an approval gate for each subsequent action. Other hosted tools need their own documented restrictions; a function-tool checkpoint does not cover bypass routes.

original.mechanism: Function-tool pause (agent.session.requires_action) answered by your code
original.note: A checkpoint for tools you execute; no MCP approval gate is documented for this API, so hosted tool calls run without one.

steps.title: Route consequential actions through function tools
body: The session emits requires_action and idles until you return the tool result, which is where an approval can be bound to the exact action.

controls.mechanism: GET /v1/agents/sessions/{session_id}/traces (OTLP JSON with agent, generation and tool spans); session items, turns and subagent item endpoints; the event stream and session webhooks; Logs → Agents in the dashboard

steps.title: Export each session's traces as OTLP
body: With trace export enabled for the organization and a project key holding api.traces.read (or api.agents.read), page GET /v1/agents/sessions/{session_id}/traces and send the OTLP JSON to your collector; list sessions by agent_id to export per agent.

steps.title: Archive items and turns
body: List session items, turns and each subagent's items (order asc with the after cursor) to keep messages, tool calls and results in your own store.

steps.title: Pull on webhooks
body: Subscribe to agent.session.created, action_required, in_progress, idle and failed and collect traces and items when a turn ends; session deletion has no webhook.

controls.note: Native on the runtime rule: programmatic export of each turn's model inputs and outputs and its tool calls with arguments and results, MCP calls and subagent work included, as OTLP. Limits: export is pull-only and "does not set up automatic delivery", traces are built after a turn ends, fields are recorded "when available", trace export must be enabled for the organization (the page does not say how), coordination items can omit inter-agent message content, command-output truncation is not reported, and trace retention is not documented. The record the organisation can rely on is the one it pulls.

original.mechanism: Agents log view and tracing dashboard on the platform
original.note: The public beta exposes no tracing configuration or external trace exporters; usage per turn is best-effort.

steps.title: Read sessions in the dashboard
body: Turns, tool calls, subagents and usage are shown per session under the Agents logs; there is no export.

original.mechanism: Persisted session events retrievable by API; webhooks for session lifecycle
original.note: Retrievable, not exported; retention period for events not documented.

steps.title: Persist events on your side
body: Retrieve session items by API and subscribe to session webhooks (created, action_required, in_progress, idle, failed) to keep your own record.

controls.mechanism: agent.session.input.cancel on the session events endpoint; DELETE the session; delete vault credentials or the vault; revoke the project API key or environment key; stop self-hosted compute yourself

steps.title: Cancel the running turn
body: Send an agent.session.input.cancel event to the session; the turn ends as agent.session.turn.cancelled and the session and its earlier work remain.

steps.title: Delete the session
body: Delete the session to remove it from the API and request sandbox cleanup (physical cleanup can continue asynchronously); stop self-hosted compute separately.

steps.title: Revoke what it held
body: Delete its vault credentials or vault, revoke those tokens with their providers, and revoke the project API key or environment key its sessions used.

controls.note: Partial by the runtime rule: a running turn can be cancelled by API, which stops active work though no time bound is published, but revocation does not reach running work — the vault page says deleting stored credentials neither revokes the provider tokens nor stops a running session — and there is no per-agent disable: deleting a saved agent does not stop a key from starting a session with an inline definition, so the only block on new sessions is revoking the key or its api.agents.write permission. Deleting a session neither stops self-hosted compute nor emits a webhook, and whether cancel stops running subagents or sandbox commands is not stated.

original.mechanism: Delete the session; revoke the API key
original.note: Deleting a session neither stops its environment nor emits a deletion webhook; stop the environment separately.

steps.title: Stop the environment, not just the session
body: The lifecycle guide says deleting a session does not stop its environment; stop or delete the environment and revoke the key.

controls.mechanism: OpenAI Trust Portal evidence and the API data-controls page, consumed by the organisation's TPRM platform

evidence.title: OpenAI Trust Portal
Data controls in the OpenAI platform — /v1/agents retention and ZDR eligibility
Agents API overview — US data residency only, no ZDR

controls.note: External: the assessment runs in the organisation's TPRM platform. The trust portal lists SOC 2 Type 2, SOC 3, ISO/IEC 27001, 27017, 27018, 27701 and 42001, CSA STAR, PCI DSS, FedRAMP 20x, a pentest report and a security whitepaper, scoped to OpenAI's API among other services; the Agents API is not named as its own scope. Product-specific: /v1/agents keeps application state until deleted and is eligible neither for Zero Data Retention nor for Private Retention with Private Safety Processing, data residency is United States only, and a self-hosted sandbox changes neither; BAA eligibility for this API is not stated. The API is in beta and the reference already lists different defaults for GA requests, so re-assess when it goes GA.

original.mechanism: Trust portal reports; no tenancy-configuration readback for this surface
original.note: An SSPM-class product would need an API to read agent, environment and vault configuration; only list endpoints exist.

steps.title: Review the trust portal
body: SOC 2 Type 2 and ISO 27001/27017/27018/27701 reports are on the trust portal.

controls.mechanism: Saved agents (POST /v1/agents: project-scoped, with name, metadata, created_at, updated_at) listed by GET /v1/agents; environment templates, vaults and sessions (filterable by agent_id) listable; no approval state, and nothing refuses an unsaved inline definition

steps.title: Register each definition as a saved agent
body: Create agents with a name and metadata (owner, change ticket, release), start sessions with agent_id, and list, update or delete them through the agents endpoints.

steps.title: Reconcile sessions against the registry
body: List sessions with the agent_id filter for each saved agent and treat sessions created from an inline agent definition as unregistered.

steps.title: Keep one project per workload
body: Create a dedicated OpenAI project for each application or workload so its agents, sessions and vaults list together and its keys reach nothing else.

controls.note: Partial by the runtime rule: a listable, project-scoped inventory with metadata exists, but nothing gates it. Any key with api.agents.write — which every session-running application needs — can create, update or delete a saved agent, or skip the registry by defining the agent inline at session creation; there is no approval state, version history or owner field beyond metadata, and the RBAC permission table lists no Agents API permission for user roles. MCP servers, skills and plugins are declared inside definitions and templates rather than registered. Change-gating is the organisation's pipeline.

controls.mechanism: None: a saved agent is updated in place (updated_at, no version field or history); each session copies the saved configuration when it is created and keeps it

evidence.title: Configuring Agents — saved-agent updates apply only to new sessions
Create an agent — agent object fields
Evals platform deprecation notice

controls.note: None: this API has no versions, aliases, traffic splitting, evaluation hook or rollback. What it contributes is containment of change — saved-agent updates reach only new sessions, and a running session cannot change its tools, instructions or multi_agent setting. What stands in is the organisation's pipeline: the definition kept as code, a new saved agent per release, the application choosing agent_id per request for a canary and switching back to roll back, and evaluation run before the switch. OpenAI's Evals platform becomes read-only on 2026-10-31 and shuts down on 2026-11-30.

controls.mechanism: Customer MCP gateways and function handlers can enforce caller, tool, argument and resource policy; browser origin/sign-in approval is a narrower native mechanism

evidence.title: MCP connections — allowed_tools, connection_origin, server_url
Functions — required_actions and tool results
Configuring Agents — inline and saved definitions
Computer use: bounded browser approvals

controls.note: External for general action policy: evaluate permitted effects in the gateway or application handler before dispatch. MCP tool-name admission and browser origin consent do not supply argument/resource authorization for every operation. Do not assume that browser approval support also gates hosted shell, file tools, web search or delegation.

controls.mechanism: No memory store; state is per session — conversation items, automatic compaction, the sandbox's /workspace for its lifetime and published artifacts — held in the project until DELETE session or artifact delete

steps.title: Keep one session per conversation and delete it when done
body: Store each session ID with the one user conversation it serves and delete the session when that conversation ends; sessions persist until deleted.

steps.title: Delete published artifacts
body: Artifacts under /workspace/outputs survive sandbox expiry; delete each one through the session Artifacts API when it is no longer needed.

controls.note: Partial: the runtime has no persistent memory feature, so the pin's shared-memory default does not arise here; the state in scope is each session's conversation, its compaction and its sandbox files, separated per session and deletable by API. Nothing validates what enters that state — a tool result or fetched page stays in context and in compaction for later turns — and separation beyond the session is the project, whose sessions are listed together. The root agent and its subagents share one sandbox. Which user continues which session is the application's choice.

controls.mechanism: No injection screening in the runtime; MCP responses can be classified by a gateway named as the server_url, and function-tool results by the application before it posts them

evidence.title: MCP connections — server_url and connection_origin
Web search — mode and allowed_domains
Misalignment monitoring — request coverage

controls.note: External by the rule applied to every vendor: no injection classifier is configurable over user input, tool results or fetched content, and no hook lets the deployer screen a hosted tool's result before the model reads it. Integration points: an AI or MCP gateway named as the MCP server_url that classifies responses before returning them; function-tool results the application screens before posting agent.session.input.tool_result; user input, which passes through the application first. Web search results and shell output enter context unscreened — mode disabled or cached and allowed_domains reduce exposure, they do not classify. The vendor's misalignment monitoring is documented for the Responses API, not this API, and reviews actions asynchronously rather than screening input.

controls.mechanism: Organisation and project roles, custom roles and IdP-synced groups (RBAC) in OpenAI Platform settings; project membership; restricted project keys whose permissions (api.agents.read, api.agents.write, api.vaults.*, api.responses.write) bound what an application may do

steps.title: Grant access through groups and custom roles
body: In Organization settings › Roles and Groups create custom roles and assign them to IdP-synced groups, keeping Owner to a named few; access is the union of every role a user holds.

steps.title: Keep each agent application in its own project
body: Create a dedicated project per agent application and give its key only api.agents.read, api.agents.write and api.responses.write, with the vault permissions only on the provisioning service.

controls.note: Native on the authorisation rule: the organisation administers who may use and change each project and what each key may do, and OpenAI enforces it. Boundary: the project is the smallest unit. The RBAC permission table lists no Agents API area (only Agent Builder), so people's rights over agents, sessions and vaults follow project roles, and any key with api.agents.write can start sessions on every agent in the project; role changes take up to 30 minutes to apply. Which end user a session acts for is the application's to authorise.

controls.mechanism: Project and organisation monthly spend limits with Enforce a hard limit (429 project_spend_limit_exceeded); custom project rate limits; multi_agent.max_concurrent_subagents (default 6); environment.container_size (small 1 vCPU / 1 GB to large 4 vCPU / 16 GB); hosted sandboxes deleted after an hour without activity or keep-alives (not configurable)

steps.title: Enforce a hard spend limit on the agent project
body: In Project settings › Limits › Spend select Edit spend limit, enter the Monthly spend limit and turn on Enforce a hard limit, with spend alerts below it.

steps.title: Bound fan-out and sandbox size
body: Set multi_agent max_concurrent_subagents to the number the task needs (or omit multi_agent) and choose the smallest environment.container_size that runs it.

controls.note: Partial on the resource-consumption rule (as on toolVertexAgentEngine): the organisation can cap a project's monthly spend and request rate, and the session caps subagent concurrency and sandbox size, but no per-session or per-turn budget for tokens, turns or run time is documented, so one runaway session draws on the whole project's allowance until the monthly limit stops every session at once. Hard limits are not instantaneous (a small amount of extra usage can pass while the state propagates); spend alerts do not stop anything; the one-hour sandbox expiry needs inactivity and is not settable. Per-session ceilings are the application's to enforce, for example by cancelling a turn.

settings.name: Dedicated OpenAI project
settings.where: platform.openai.com › Organization settings › Projects
settings.recommended: A dedicated project per agent application, holding its keys, vaults, environments and sessions
settings.why: Agents, sessions and vaults are project-scoped, so one application's keys and stored credentials reach nothing else.

settings.name: Roles and Groups (RBAC)
settings.where: platform.openai.com › Organization settings › Roles and Groups, and each project's roles; groups synced by SCIM
settings.recommended: Custom roles assigned to IdP-synced groups; Owner held by a named few
settings.why: Access is the union of every role a user holds, so grants go through groups you can audit; changes take up to 30 minutes.

settings.name: api.agents.read, api.agents.write and api.responses.write
settings.where: Permissions of the application's restricted project key
settings.recommended: Only these on the application key; api.vaults.read and api.vaults.write only on the service that provisions vaults
settings.why: A leaked application key can run sessions but cannot read or change the project's other resources.

settings.name: API Key Governance
settings.where: platform.openai.com › Platform settings › API Key Governance (organization or project)
settings.recommended: Service-account keys only
settings.why: Agent applications authenticate as a project service account, not with a key tied to a person who may leave.

settings.name: Maximum API key lifetime
settings.where: platform.openai.com › Platform settings (organization, or the project)
settings.recommended: 90 days
settings.why: New keys must expire within the limit, so a copied key stops working; a project limit cannot exceed the organization's.

settings.name: Workload Identity Provider (service account mapping)
settings.where: platform.openai.com › Organization Settings › Security › Workload Identity Provider
settings.recommended: One mapping per application workload to its project service account, wherever it runs on a supported cloud or Kubernetes
settings.why: The application trades its own OIDC, SPIFFE or X.509 identity for a short-lived token, so no stored API key exists to leak.

settings.name: IP allowlist
settings.where: platform.openai.com › Settings › Security › IP allowlist (project or organization)
settings.recommended: On for production agent projects, listing every egress address that calls the API
settings.why: A leaked key fails with ip_not_authorized from anywhere else; it does not restrict platform.openai.com sign-in.

settings.name: Environment key (CODEX_API_KEY)
settings.where: platform.openai.com › Agents › Environments › Keys, passed into the self-hosted executor as CODEX_API_KEY
settings.recommended: A separate environment key per executor fleet; the application key never enters the sandbox
settings.why: Agent-generated code can read the environment key, which only connects environments and authorizes no other API action.

settings.name: environment.type
settings.where: Session or saved-agent environment — openai_hosted, self_hosted or none
settings.recommended: openai_hosted, one sandbox per session; none for agents that need no shell or files
settings.why: Agent-written code runs in a sandbox OpenAI provisions and reclaims, not on your hosts; none removes the built-in Bash and apply-patch tools.

settings.name: network.access and allowed_domains
settings.where: environment.network on an openai_hosted environment or environment template
settings.recommended: restricted, with allowed_domains listing your package mirror and the task's exact hosts
settings.why: Sandbox code reaches only the listed hostnames (1–100, no wildcards), so injected instructions cannot send data to arbitrary hosts.

settings.name: environment_template_id
settings.where: Session create, referencing a saved environment template
settings.recommended: Every production session starts from a template that holds the network policy
settings.why: A session's network override cannot broaden the template's policy, so a caller cannot widen egress per request.

settings.name: vault_ids (static_bearer and mcp_oauth credentials)
settings.where: Session create; credentials stored in a vault and bound to the MCP server URL
settings.recommended: One vault per end user or tenant, attached only to that user's sessions
settings.why: OpenAI's service presents the token to the MCP server and the agent never sees it; one user's grant never serves another user's session.

settings.name: auth.networking.allowed_hosts (environment_variable credential)
settings.where: Vault credential of type environment_variable with auth.networking.type limited
settings.recommended: The exact API host that needs the secret, nothing broader
settings.why: Sandbox code holds only a placeholder; the egress proxy supplies the real secret to the listed hosts over HTTPS.

settings.name: allowed_tools
settings.where: Each mcp entry in agent.tools
settings.recommended: The approved tool names for each server
settings.why: The agent can discover and call only the listed tools, so a server that adds a tool later does not widen the agent.

settings.name: web_search mode and allowed_domains
settings.where: The web_search entry in agent.tools
settings.default: live, with no domain filter, when web_search is included
settings.recommended: Included only for agents whose task needs the web, live, with allowed_domains when the sources are known
settings.why: Search results enter the loop unclassified; agents that do not need the web do not get that path.

settings.name: automations tool
settings.where: {"type": "automations"} in agent.tools
settings.recommended: Left out unless the workflow needs the agent to schedule its own follow-ups
settings.why: An agent holding it can schedule future runs that start with nobody present.

settings.name: agent.session.requires_action (function tools)
settings.where: The application's function-call handler
settings.recommended: Consequential functions run only after an authenticated person approves those arguments for that pending call
settings.why: The session pauses until your code returns a result, so your application is the gate for every effect it implements.

settings.name: computer_use_approval_request (browser_origin_access)
settings.where: Session required_actions, answered with agent.session.input.computer_use_approval_request_result for the same request_id
settings.recommended: Shown to the authorised user for each new origin; deny or cancel when nobody answers
settings.why: The hosted browser reaches only origins a person approved; origin approval is not approval of each later action.

settings.name: Saved agents (agent_id)
settings.where: POST /v1/agents with name and metadata; sessions started with agent_id
settings.recommended: Every production definition saved with owner and change reference in metadata, sessions started by agent_id
settings.why: The project's agent list becomes a register to reconcile sessions against; inline definitions show up as unregistered.

settings.name: Export session traces (GET /v1/agents/sessions/{session_id}/traces)
settings.where: A project key with api.traces.read (or api.agents.read), paged as OTLP JSON
settings.default: Tracing on for new sessions; export is pull-only
settings.recommended: Every finished turn's trace pulled into your collector, triggered by session webhooks
settings.why: Model inputs, tool calls and results land in your own store; the export does not set up automatic delivery.
settings.requires: Trace export enabled for the organization

settings.name: Session webhooks
settings.where: Project webhook endpoint subscribed to Agents API events, verified with OPENAI_WEBHOOK_SECRET
settings.recommended: Subscribed to the session lifecycle events, signatures verified before processing
settings.why: Trace and item collection runs when each turn ends, and an unsigned request cannot trigger your handler.

settings.name: Audit logs
settings.where: Admin API GET /v1/organization/audit_logs with an admin key
settings.recommended: Pulled into the SIEM by a collector that alone holds the admin key
settings.why: Key, role, project and configuration changes around the agent application are recorded outside the project they govern.

settings.name: agent.session.input.cancel
settings.where: Session events endpoint
settings.recommended: Wired to an operator stop control in the application
settings.why: The running turn ends as agent.session.turn.cancelled; deleting vault credentials or keys does not stop work already running.

settings.name: Delete a session
settings.where: DELETE /v1/agents/sessions/{session_id}; published artifacts deleted through the session Artifacts API
settings.recommended: Deleted when the conversation it serves ends, its artifacts first
settings.why: /v1/agents state is kept until deleted and is not eligible for zero data retention, so deletion is the only retention control.

settings.name: Monthly spend limit (Enforce a hard limit)
settings.where: platform.openai.com › Project settings › Limits › Spend › Edit spend limit
settings.recommended: A monthly limit on each agent project with Enforce a hard limit on, and spend alerts below it
settings.why: A runaway or hijacked session cannot run up spend past the cap; requests then fail with project_spend_limit_exceeded, and alerts alone stop nothing.

settings.name: multi_agent.max_concurrent_subagents
settings.where: Agent definition or session create › multi_agent
settings.default: 6 when delegation is enabled; delegation off when multi_agent is omitted
settings.recommended: Omitted unless the task delegates; otherwise the smallest number it needs
settings.why: One session cannot fan out into many parallel subagents, each making its own model calls.
