tools.name: ChatGPT desktop app and Work Local

variants.name: ChatGPT desktop app (macOS, Windows MSIX, Linux preview)
variants.note: One app bundles Chat, Work and Codex. Chat and cloud Work show the same synced chats as the web (toolChatgptWeb); the Codex view is toolCodex. This record is what the app executes or reaches on the device.

variants.name: Work Local (local orchestration and execution)
Local computer access with Work Cloud (cloud orchestration, steps run on the connected computer)
variants.note: Allowed by Admin Console > Permissions > Work Cloud > Allow local computer access; needs desktop app 26.929 or later and Sign in with ChatGPT (API keys and Codex access tokens do not enable it).

variants.name: Computer Use (macOS and Windows; Locked Use on macOS)
Built-in browser (in-app browser pane and Browser Use)
Remote control from the ChatGPT mobile app (phone steers the desktop host)
ChatGPT browser extension (Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera, Vivaldi)
variants.note: Driven from the desktop app (side chat, tab mentions, browser control in signed-in sessions); the admin levers recorded here are the desktop app's (External browser use, managed Browser Use site policies). Browser extensions are assessed on the agentic browser drawing (archAgenticBrowser), not here.

summary: The ChatGPT desktop app's local reach: Work Local, where a task reads files, edits them and runs shell commands under the Codex sandbox and approval settings; local computer access with Work Cloud, where OpenAI's cloud coordinates the task and the connected computer executes the steps that need it; Computer Use operating native apps (Screen Recording and Accessibility on macOS, the active desktop on Windows, optional Locked Use on a locked Mac); the built-in browser and the browser extension acting in browser sessions on the machine; Appshots; Computer History; and device remote control from a phone. As a chat client the app shows the same synced chats as the web (toolChatgptWeb); its Codex view is toolCodex.

Inference is at OpenAI for every mode: the vendor states that local execution does not mean offline or device-only inference, and that file excerpts, prompts, screenshots, browser content and tool results may be sent to OpenAI to complete a task. Local Work conversations stay on the computer; cloud Work conversations sync. The local runtime is the Codex runtime the app shares with toolCodex.

Two admin planes. Workspace permissions in Admin Console > Permissions decide who may work locally (Use Work locally, or Allow members to use Codex and Work Locally), whether cloud tasks may reach the computer (Allow local computer access under Work Cloud, which interrupts running turns when turned off) and who may enable Computer History. Runtime requirements constrain the device: Admin Console > Agent security (a Global baseline with Local overrides — Desktop feature availability, Desktop browser controls with Site rules, Desktop app controls with App rules and Allow use while locked, Policy guardrails, Manage Networking) delivered at ChatGPT sign-in, the system requirements.toml, legacy managed_config.toml, and macOS MDM under com.openai.codex, which ranks highest; sign-in restrictions are honoured only from MDM or the system file. Work cloud containers do not inherit any of these local requirements.

facts.label: Plans
facts.value: The desktop app is on every ChatGPT plan, Free included; Work Local and the admin controls need an eligible Business, Enterprise or Edu workspace. Computer Use is on macOS and Windows in supported regions, not in the Linux preview; Computer History is macOS-only on Pro, Business and Enterprise.

facts.label: Inference & routing
facts.value: Model calls go to OpenAI. With local computer access with Work Cloud the cloud coordinates and the computer executes; model_provider and model_providers are not supported in managed requirements or configuration for that mode.

facts.label: Data leaving the device
facts.value: Relevant file excerpts, prompts, screenshots, Appshots, browser content and tool results may be sent to OpenAI services to complete a task; a browser or app already signed in exposes that account's permissions.

facts.label: Retention & training
facts.value: Local Work conversations stay on the computer and do not follow hosted retention settings by assumption; Computer History writes plain-text memory files under ~/.codex/memories that it does not encrypt; local computer access with Work Cloud offers no strict zero data retention. Business data is not used for training by default.

facts.label: Docs index
facts.value: learn.chatgpt.com/docs/enterprise/chatgpt-work-local-security and managed-configuration

items.title: Managed deployment and update control
body: Windows ships only as a Store-signed MSIX (no MSI or standalone EXE), deployable via Intune, MECM or winget with offline packages available; macOS deploys from the enterprise DMG, with device management arriving through the com.openai.codex MDM payload rather than a dedicated packaging guide. The built-in updater is disabled with an enforced requirements.toml feature pin, targeted by group, user or platform from the managed-configs console.

items.title: Desktop requirements in Agent security
body: Desktop feature availability forces off the In-app browser, Browser use, External browser use (the browser extension) or Computer use, and blocks user opt-in to Full CDP access; Desktop browser controls set site rules for access, uploads, downloads and Debug/CDP with approval duration; Desktop app controls set Computer Use app rules by macOS bundle ID, Windows AUMID or signed Windows executable, Save app approvals and Allow use while locked. Appshots and device remote control are set with Edit as TOML.

Browser Use rules do not cover Computer Use operating a browser as a native app; deny the browser in App rules or force Computer use off to close that path. MDM changes are read at the next launch, and a background refresh of cloud requirements does not change a task already running.

links.title: Managed configuration — control browser and Computer Use

riskNotes.note: The built-in browser, the browser extension and Computer Use read pages and app content as context while acting in signed-in sessions; the vendor tells users to treat page content as untrusted, and the only admin levers are feature force-offs, site and app rules, and approval settings.

Locked Use lets an approved Computer Use turn unlock a Mac nobody is watching, and saved app and site approvals ("Allow for all sites" in the extension) remove later prompts unless the persistent-approval requirements are deployed.
Appshots include text beyond the visible window, browser history can be read into a task, and Computer History keeps unencrypted memory files readable by other programs running as the user.
Computer Use sees whatever is on screen in an approved app, and a restriction on direct file access does not restrict the files that app can open.

With local computer access a cloud task reaches the computer from web or mobile, and device remote control steers local sessions from a phone; if the computer is offline the task can continue in a cloud container that does not enforce the local requirements.
The app shares the Codex runtime and its %ProgramData%\OpenAI\Codex configuration path, the subject of the 2026 Cymulate config-trust report.

controls.mechanism: allowed_login_methods = ["chatgpt"] and allowed_chatgpt_workspaces in the system requirements.toml or macOS MDM (cloud-managed values are ignored); MFA itself is enforced by the organisation's SSO IdP

steps.title: Pin the desktop app to the org workspace
body: In the system requirements.toml or MDM com.openai.codex requirements_toml_base64 set allowed_login_methods = ["chatgpt"] and allowed_chatgpt_workspaces = ["<workspace-uuid>"]; both apply before credentials load and are ignored in cloud-managed requirements.

steps.title: Enforce MFA in the identity provider
body: ChatGPT has no workspace-wide MFA enforcement, so require SSO with MFA at the IdP and manage SSO in the Global Admin Console.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor (as on toolCodex): the local runtime can be pinned to the org's ChatGPT workspace, so the IdP's MFA policy governs each interactive sign-in, but MFA is configured in the IdP — the admin FAQ states ChatGPT doesn't provide workspace-wide MFA enforcement. Local computer access with Work Cloud needs Sign in with ChatGPT in the intended workspace (API keys and Codex access tokens do not enable it). The pin holds only on machines that carry the system file or MDM payload; an unmanaged install signs in to whatever account the user chooses.

controls.mechanism: Agent security Desktop browser controls (Site rules: access, uploads, downloads, Debug/CDP) and Desktop app controls (App rules by bundle ID, AUMID or signed executable), [rules] prefix_rules for local shell commands, managed hooks in local-only threads and mcp_tool hooks on the cloud orchestrator

steps.title: Write the site rules
body: In Admin Console > Agent security > Requirements > Desktop browser controls > Site rules edit the Default row and add origin rules with Site access, Uploads, Downloads and Debug/CDP set to Allow or Block.

steps.title: Write the app rules
body: Under Desktop app controls > App rules set the Default row and add rules by macOS bundle ID, Windows AUMID or Windows executable publisher and product name, including a deny for the browsers if Computer Use must not drive them.

steps.title: Gate tool events with an MCP hook
body: For local computer access with Work Cloud configure mcp_tool hook handlers in Global requirements.toml; command, prompt and local or plugin hooks are not supported with cloud orchestration.

controls.note: Partial on the rule applied to every vendor (as on toolCodex): deterministic allow and deny rules exist per site and per app, enforced by the app, and a user approval cannot override an administrator's denial; when several origin patterns match the most restrictive value wins. But they decide whether a site or app may be used and which transfers are allowed, not which action is taken in it; Computer Use operating a browser escapes Browser Use site rules entirely; a PreToolUse callback error, timeout or malformed response fails the hook without blocking the tool; command prefix rules cover shell commands only. Rules arrive with the policy and a running task may not pick up a change.

controls.mechanism: Vendor evidence from the OpenAI Trust Portal and the ChatGPT Work enterprise security whitepaper, consumed by the organisation's TPRM platform

evidence.title: OpenAI Trust Portal (SafeBase) — SOC 2, ISO, pentest and subprocessor artifacts (2026-10-30)
ChatGPT Work enterprise security whitepaper (linked from Work local security, 2026-10-30)

controls.note: External by the rule applied to every vendor: the assessment runs in the organisation's TPRM platform from the same portal evidence as toolChatgptWeb. Assess the desktop binary separately from the service — what it can read on the device (Screen Recording and Accessibility grants, the Locked Use authorization plugin, the browser extension's all-sites permissions) and the release clock, since older app versions get no separate security patches.

controls.mechanism: Managed hooks (UserPromptSubmit and PreToolUse in local-only Work threads; mcp_tool hooks with cloud orchestration) as the attach point for the organisation's inspector; deny_read, allow_appshots = false and site Uploads rules as minimisation only

steps.title: Attach your inspector to managed hooks
body: In Agent security > Edit as TOML define managed hooks with allow_managed_hooks_only = true for local-only threads, or mcp_tool handlers for local computer access with Work Cloud, calling the organisation's DLP service.

steps.title: Keep secrets paths and window captures out
body: Set [permissions.filesystem] deny_read for credential paths and, for the most sensitive teams, allow_appshots = false in Global requirements.toml.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: a hook that can block is an attach point and the detection is the organisation's; the desktop app itself detects nothing. Prisma AIRS external guardrails scan Codex prompts only (toolCodex), not Work. Boundaries: hooks see what reaches the model as tool events, not every screenshot or page the agent views; a hook error or timeout does not block; Computer Use reads files through apps, so deny_read does not bound it. deny_read, Appshots off and blocked uploads keep data out (minimisation, credited here) but inspect nothing. The vendor tells admins to apply endpoint, proxy and DLP controls to the device and workflow.

controls.mechanism: Agent security Desktop feature availability (In-app browser, Browser use, External browser use, Computer use: Force off; Full CDP access: Block user opt-in), Site rules, App rules, [mcp_servers] identity allowlist, features.apps / features.plugins and filesystem deny_read in requirements.toml

steps.title: Force off the surfaces you do not use
body: In Admin Console > Agent security > Global > Requirements > Desktop feature availability set In-app browser, Browser use, External browser use or Computer use to Force off, and Full CDP access to Block user opt-in.

steps.title: Scope sites and apps
body: Use Site rules (access, uploads, downloads, Debug/CDP) and App rules (default_app_access with per-app allow or deny) to bound what Browser Use and Computer Use may touch.

steps.title: Scope local tools and paths
body: Add an [mcp_servers.<id>] identity allowlist, features.apps or features.plugins = false where needed, and [permissions.filesystem] deny_read in requirements.toml.

controls.note: Native by the rule applied to every vendor (as on toolCodex): each local surface can be forced off and the rest scoped by site, app, MCP server, path and permission profile in requirements users cannot loosen, enforced by the app and local runtime on the device. Boundaries: Force off and allow rules do not override product or rollout availability; the browser path, the built-in browser pane and native Computer Use are separate controls and each needs checking; managed in_app_browser and allow_browser_and_computer_use requirements are rejected for local computer access with Work Cloud, where app-side checks still apply; a device without the requirements is unscoped.

controls.mechanism: The Codex OS sandbox around Work Local's direct file reads, edits and shell commands, pinned by Agent security Policy guardrails > Sandbox modes (allowed_sandbox_modes); Computer Use, the browsers and the extension run outside it

steps.title: Remove full access from local work
body: In Admin Console > Agent security > Global > Requirements > Policy guardrails set Sandbox modes to read-only and workspace-write (allowed_sandbox_modes = ["read-only", "workspace-write"]).

steps.title: Deny the credential paths
body: Set [permissions.filesystem] deny_read for ~/.ssh, cloud CLI credentials and "/**/*.env"; while deny rules exist the runtime keeps commands sandboxed.

controls.note: Partial on the rule applied to every vendor (as on toolCodex): direct file reads, file edits and shell commands follow the task's sandbox and approval settings, so the sandbox can be required for them, but an approved escalation runs outside it. Outside the boundary by design: Computer Use acts through an approved native application under that application's permissions (the vendor notes a direct-file restriction does not restrict what the app can open), the built-in browser keeps its own profile, the extension and Computer Use act in signed-in sessions, and the app process itself. If the computer is offline a cloud-coordinated task can continue in a cloud container that does not enforce local requirements.

controls.mechanism: Computer History role permission (off by default, member opt-in), features.memories pin and allow_managed_hooks_only in requirements.toml; local memory files are not validated or encrypted

steps.title: Gate Computer History by role
body: In Workspace Settings > Permissions & roles leave Enable Computer History off, or turn it on only for approved roles; each member must still opt in on macOS.

steps.title: Pin local memories deliberately
body: Set [features] memories = false in requirements.toml where agent-written local memory is not wanted; Computer History requires Memories.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: an administrator can keep Computer History unavailable and pin local memories off, but nothing validates or quarantines what is written. Computer History turns on-screen app and website activity into plain-text Markdown memory files under ~/.codex/memories/extensions/skysight/ that it does not encrypt and other programs running as the user may read; temporary event files are kept up to 48 hours. Browser control follows the member's Memories setting.

controls.mechanism: Managed hooks (local-only threads) and mcp_tool hooks on the cloud orchestrator as the attach point; vendor model safety monitoring and browser auto-review, neither admin-tunable

steps.title: Screen tool results in a managed hook
body: Define the organisation's classifier as a managed hook in Agent security > Edit as TOML (mcp_tool handlers for local computer access with Work Cloud) and test its failure behaviour.

steps.title: Cut the riskiest content paths
body: Block browser-history access with browser_use.allow_history_access = false and restrict sites with Site rules where untrusted pages need not be read.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor (as on toolCodex): hooks are an attach point whose classifier the organisation supplies, and a hook error or timeout fails without blocking. Page content, screenshots and app text read by Browser Use, the extension and Computer Use reach the model without an admin-configurable screen; the vendor's model safety monitoring continues when browser auto-review is disabled but is not tunable or reported. Prisma AIRS covers Codex prompts only.

controls.mechanism: cli_auth_credentials_store = "keyring" for the shared local runtime (system requirements.toml or MDM), filesystem deny_read for credential paths; the browser extension and Computer Use act in the user's signed-in sessions

steps.title: Keep the runtime credential in the OS store
body: In the system requirements.toml or MDM requirements set cli_auth_credentials_store = "keyring"; cloud-managed requirements ignore it.

steps.title: Deny the credential paths
body: Set [permissions.filesystem] deny_read for SSH keys, cloud CLI credentials and .env files.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: the local runtime's sign-in credential can be forced into the OS credential store (shared with toolCodex; how the desktop app's own window session is stored is not documented separately) and credential paths can be denied to direct file tools. Nothing holds credentials outside the agent: the extension reads and acts in the regular browser profile's signed-in accounts, Computer Use operates apps already signed in, and the built-in browser keeps whatever the member signs into in its own profile. Use password manager (a workspace capability, on toolChatgptWeb) keeps the password manager out of the in-app and cloud browsers.

controls.mechanism: requirements.toml [mcp_servers.<id>] identity allowlist and [marketplaces] restrict_to_allowed_sources for the local runtime

steps.title: Allowlist local MCP servers by identity
body: In Agent security > Edit as TOML add [mcp_servers.<id>] identity entries (stdio by executable and args, HTTP by url); a server that does not match is disabled.

steps.title: Restrict plugin sources
body: Set [marketplaces] restrict_to_allowed_sources = true with your Git sources and refs.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor (as on toolCodex): an allowlist admits servers but verifies nothing they serve; nothing scans or pins tool definitions. Desktop-only plugins and locally provided tools may follow different installation paths, and plugins that provide browser or Computer Use capabilities need their own availability review.

controls.mechanism: Per-app Computer Use approval and per-site browser approval with sensitive-action confirmation; requirements computer_use.allow_persistent_approval, browser_use.allow_global_persistent_approval, per-origin persistent_approval and access_approval_lifetime, browser_use.disable_auto_review and computer_use.allow_locked_computer_use

steps.title: Stop saved approvals
body: In Agent security set Desktop app controls > Save app approvals off and Desktop browser controls > Save site approvals off (computer_use.allow_persistent_approval = false, browser_use.allow_global_persistent_approval = false).

steps.title: Bound site approvals to the turn
body: In each site rule set Approval duration to This turn (access_approval_lifetime = "turn") and persistent_approval = false.

steps.title: Keep Computer Use attended
body: Under Desktop app controls set Allow use while locked to Disabled (computer_use.allow_locked_computer_use = false).

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: a present person approves each new app and each new site, and ChatGPT asks before sensitive browser actions such as submitting information, purchases, permission changes or deletions, but the approval is per app or site, not per action; browser auto-review is an automated reviewer unless disabled; saved approvals ("Always allow" apps, "Allow for all sites" in the extension) remove later prompts unless the requirements remove them, and disabling saved approvals still permits approvals for the current session. Locked Use lets an approved turn continue on a locked Mac; the requirement does not turn off Locked Use already enabled. Orchestrator approval policies stay in Global.

controls.mechanism: Admin Console > Plugins catalogue (Computer Use and browser plugins included), enforced on the device by the [mcp_servers] and [marketplaces] allowlists

steps.title: Keep local tools on the allowlist
body: Set the [mcp_servers] identity allowlist and [marketplaces] restrict_to_allowed_sources in requirements.toml so unlisted local servers and sources are disabled.

steps.title: Review browser and Computer Use plugins in the catalogue
body: Treat plugins that provide browser or Computer Use capabilities as their own availability and installation review in Admin Console > Plugins.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor (as on toolCodex): the workspace catalogue records approved plugins and requirements refuse unlisted servers and sources, but the client-side lists carry no owner or approval record, and nothing inventories what runs on a machine without the requirements.

controls.mechanism: Local executor OpenTelemetry ([otel] as a managed default) including Browser Use capability-check events, plus Compliance API conversation_message and codex_log records for local computer access with Work Cloud

steps.title: Point the local executor at the org collector
body: Ship [otel] exporter = "otlp-http" to your collector with log_user_prompt = false in managed_config.toml or MDM config_toml_base64.

steps.title: Collect the cloud records separately
body: Pull conversation_message and codex_log events from the Compliance API for tasks using local computer access with Work Cloud.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: the local executor exports supported execution events, and in supported versions Browser Use emits events for site access, upload and download decisions with the decision source. Missing: cloud orchestration events never reach the OTel collector; OpenAI does not store a separate complete record of extension actions; the vendor says these sources do not establish a complete record of every local command, file operation, screenshot, approval or external action; [otel] is a managed default users can change. Capture only: tamper resistance is the receiving store's.

controls.mechanism: None in product; EDR or MDM software inventory finds the desktop app and browser extension, and SSE or CASB finds personal-account use

evidence.title: Managed configuration — allowed_chatgpt_workspaces refuses other workspaces (prevention, 2026-10-30)
Windows deployment — MSIX package identity for inventory (2026-10-30)

controls.note: External by the rule applied to every vendor (as on toolCodex): find the desktop app (DMG, MSIX, the Linux .deb and .rpm preview) and the ChatGPT browser extension with EDR, MDM or browser-management inventory, and personal-account use with SSE or CASB. The workspace pin in the system requirements or MDM is prevention on managed machines, credited here only.

controls.mechanism: Allow local computer access Off (interrupts running turns), Use Work locally Off, Desktop feature availability Force off, allow_remote_control = false, and the user's own stop

steps.title: Cut cloud tasks off from the computer
body: In Admin Console > Permissions > Work Cloud turn off Allow local computer access; currently running turns are interrupted and new turns continue in the cloud without local files.

steps.title: Turn local Work off
body: Set Use Work locally (or Allow members to use Codex and Work Locally) to Off in the workspace default and every role that grants it; one remaining On keeps access.

steps.title: Force the local surfaces off
body: Set Computer use, Browser use and External browser use to Force off in Desktop feature availability and allow_remote_control = false, then have members restart the app.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: turning off Allow local computer access is documented to interrupt currently running turns, but no page says a purely local Work task stops when Use Work locally is turned off; requirement changes load at the next client start (MDM is read at launch, a background refresh does not change a running task) and some desktop settings need a restart. The member can stop a task at any time; otherwise the operator or EDR ends the process. Measure the stop before relying on it.

controls.mechanism: EDR on the endpoint; the app exposes OS permission grants (Screen Recording, Accessibility), the Locked Use authorization plugin and local OTel events for correlation

evidence.title: ChatGPT Work local security — Computer Use permissions and Locked Use authorization plugin (2026-10-30)
Computer Use — macOS permissions, Windows foreground use (2026-10-30)

controls.note: External by the rule applied to every vendor: the app does not analyse process behaviour; the organisation's EDR does. Integration points: Screen Recording and Accessibility (TCC) grants and the macOS authorization plugin that Locked Use installs are visible to MDM and EDR; local commands run as children of the Codex runtime (see toolCodex); local OTel events can be joined to EDR telemetry. Detections worth writing: non-admin writes under %ProgramData%\OpenAI\Codex (Cymulate, 2026-08, no OpenAI CVE) and Locked Use enablement on managed Macs.

controls.mechanism: [application.network] exact-domain allowlist for the desktop app's own requests, [experimental_network] for local commands (Manage Networking), Browser Use origin rules; Computer Use native-app traffic is outside all three

steps.title: Allowlist local command destinations
body: In Admin Console > Agent security > Requirements turn on Manage Networking and Only allow domains added by admins, with Allow entries for your source control, package mirror and approved APIs.

steps.title: Restrict the app's own destinations
body: In Global requirements.toml set [application.network] enabled = true with exact "allow" domains in [application.network.domains]; requests must be HTTPS or WSS and subdomains are not implied.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: admin-owned allowlists exist for local commands and for the desktop app's own requests, but [experimental_network] is experimental with limited Windows support, [application.network] does not restrict native modules or spawned processes and is not supported by local computer access with Work Cloud, and browser policy checks do not route browser traffic through the command proxy. Computer Use and native-app traffic follow no product egress rule. An endpoint firewall or SSE policy covers the rest.

controls.mechanism: Endpoint anti-malware and the package mirror; the app scans nothing it downloads, and site rules can block downloads (admission, not analysis)

evidence.title: Browser — downloads go to the system Downloads folder (2026-10-30)
Managed configuration — site rules Downloads Allow or Block (2026-10-30)

controls.note: External by the rule applied to every vendor (as on toolCodex): nothing in the app scans files the built-in browser downloads to the Downloads folder, files a task fetches or plugins it installs. Endpoint anti-malware and EDR analyse downloaded files; a package mirror with scanning covers dependencies local commands install. Site-rule Downloads Block and marketplace source pinning are admission controls, not file analysis. No model weights load on the device.

settings.name: Use Work locally (or Allow members to use Codex and Work Locally)
settings.where: Admin Console › Permissions › Work Local (or the combined Codex and Work Local section)
settings.recommended: On only for groups on managed devices that carry the Agent security or MDM requirements
settings.why: Work Local reads files, drives apps and sends excerpts and screenshots from the device; the combined control also grants local Codex.

settings.name: Allow local computer access
settings.where: Admin Console › Permissions › Work Cloud › Allow local computer access
settings.recommended: Off until the Agent security Global baseline is reviewed; then On for Work Local groups only
settings.why: Cloud-orchestrated tasks reach the connected computer's files and tools; turning it off interrupts running turns, so it doubles as a stop.

settings.name: allowed_login_methods and allowed_chatgpt_workspaces
settings.where: System requirements.toml or macOS MDM (com.openai.codex); ignored in cloud-managed requirements
settings.recommended: ["chatgpt"] and your workspace UUID
settings.why: The desktop app's local runtime signs in only to the corporate workspace, not a personal account or API key.

settings.name: cli_auth_credentials_store
settings.where: System requirements.toml or macOS MDM requirements_toml_base64 → cli_auth_credentials_store
settings.recommended: "keyring"
settings.why: The local runtime's cached ChatGPT credential lives in the OS credential store rather than a readable file a command could copy; cloud-managed values are ignored.

settings.name: Desktop feature availability
settings.where: Admin Console › Agent security › Global › Requirements › Desktop feature availability (In-app browser, Browser use, External browser use, Computer use, Full CDP access)
settings.recommended: Full CDP access set to Block user opt-in; the others allowed
settings.why: Browser and computer use stay available with their approvals, while developer-level control of the browser is removed.

settings.name: Site rules (Site access, Downloads, Uploads, Debug/CDP)
settings.where: Admin Console › Agent security › Requirements › Desktop browser controls › Site rules, or [browser_use.default_origin_policy] and [browser_use.origins]
settings.recommended: Default row Site access Allow with Debug/CDP Block; Block rules for the file-sharing and webmail sites your proxy already blocks
settings.why: The agent's browser cannot be talked into a site the firm forbids, and a member's approval cannot override the admin's Block.

settings.name: App rules (App access)
settings.where: Admin Console › Agent security › Requirements › Desktop app controls › App rules, or [computer_use] default_app_access with macos.bundle_ids, windows.aumids and windows.exes
settings.default: No app rules (each app approved by the member)
settings.recommended: Default row Allow; Block for the web browsers and the password manager
settings.why: Computer Use cannot drive a browser outside the Browser use site rules or open the password vault; other desktop apps stay usable.

settings.name: computer_use.allow_persistent_approval
settings.where: Agent security › Global › Edit as TOML, or requirements.toml → [computer_use] allow_persistent_approval
settings.recommended: false
settings.why: Approval to drive a desktop app lasts for the session, not for every later task.

settings.name: browser_use.allow_global_persistent_approval
settings.where: Agent security › Global › Edit as TOML, or requirements.toml → [browser_use]
settings.recommended: false
settings.why: Members cannot give the local browser standing access to every site; each origin is approved on its own.

settings.name: Allow use while locked
settings.where: Admin Console › Agent security › Global › Requirements › Desktop app controls, or [computer_use] allow_locked_computer_use
settings.recommended: Disabled
settings.why: Computer use cannot keep driving apps on a Mac nobody is watching; it does not turn off Locked Use already enabled.

settings.name: browser_use.allow_history_access
settings.where: Agent security › Requirements › Desktop browser controls › Browser history, or requirements.toml → [browser_use] allow_history_access
settings.recommended: false
settings.why: Internal URLs, search terms and signed-in activity in browsing history never enter a task's context, where injected page content could copy them out.

settings.name: allow_appshots
settings.where: Agent security › Global › Edit as TOML, or a local requirements source → allow_appshots
settings.recommended: Unset — Appshots are a member-initiated attachment of the frontmost window
settings.why: Treated like attaching a file; regulated teams set false, since an Appshot carries the window's text beyond what is visible.

settings.name: Enable Computer History
settings.where: Workspace Settings › Permissions & roles › Computer History › (role) › Enable Computer History
settings.recommended: Off
settings.why: Turns recent on-screen app and website activity into memories ChatGPT and Codex can use, which on a consultant's Mac is client material.
settings.requires: Business or Enterprise (by role on Enterprise)

settings.name: Sandbox modes (allowed_sandbox_modes)
settings.where: Admin Console › Agent security › Global › Requirements › Policy guardrails › Sandbox modes
settings.recommended: ["read-only", "workspace-write"]
settings.why: Local Work's file edits and shell commands stay inside the OS sandbox; full access is refused.

settings.name: Managed hooks (allow_managed_hooks_only; mcp_tool handlers for local computer access)
settings.where: Agent security › Global › Edit as TOML → [hooks], allow_managed_hooks_only
settings.default: Unset (user, project and plugin hooks run in local-only threads)
settings.recommended: allow_managed_hooks_only = true, with your inspection hook where you run one
settings.why: Only hooks the firm deploys run, and with cloud orchestration only admin mcp_tool hooks are supported at all; test failure behaviour, since an error does not block.

settings.name: mcp_servers.<id>.identity
settings.where: Agent security › Global › Edit as TOML → [mcp_servers.<id>] identity
settings.recommended: Your approved servers, stdio by executable and args, HTTP by url
settings.why: A local MCP server whose name and identity are not on the list is disabled, plugin-bundled servers included.

settings.name: Manage Networking with Only allow domains added by admins
settings.where: Admin Console › Agent security › Requirements › Manage Networking ([experimental_network] enabled, managed_allowed_domains_only, domains)
settings.recommended: On / On, allowing your source control, package mirror and approved APIs
settings.why: Local commands reach only admin-listed hosts; experimental, so validate per client version and hold back on Windows.

settings.name: application.network
settings.where: Agent security › Global › Edit as TOML → [application.network] enabled, [application.network.domains]
settings.recommended: Absent — enforce the app's destinations at the corporate proxy
settings.why: The exact-domain list must name every OpenAI and plugin host, does not cover native modules or spawned processes, and is unsupported with local computer access; regulated teams enable it after testing.

settings.name: otel.exporter
settings.where: managed_config.toml or MDM config_toml_base64 → [otel] exporter, environment, log_user_prompt
settings.recommended: otlp-http to your collector, log_user_prompt = false
settings.why: Local execution and Browser Use decision events reach the SIEM; cloud orchestration events never do, so collect the Compliance API as well.

settings.name: allow_remote_control
settings.where: Agent security › Global › Edit as TOML, or a local requirements source → allow_remote_control
settings.recommended: false, unless a team needs to steer local sessions from a phone
settings.why: A local session with the member's files and signed-in apps cannot be driven from another device; SSH remote connections are separate.

settings.name: features.in_app_updates
settings.where: Agent security or Managed configuration › requirements.toml → [features] in_app_updates
settings.recommended: Unset — keep the built-in updater on
settings.why: Older app versions get no separate security patches; turn it off only where your deployment tool ships every release promptly.

summary: One agent across the CLI, the IDE extension and the ChatGPT desktop app, configured through TOML with a documented precedence chain and a genuine enterprise enforcement layer: an admin-authored requirements.toml that constrains approval policies, sandbox profiles, network, MCP servers and feature flags, and that users cannot override.

Inference runs at OpenAI; the local runtime executes commands inside an OS sandbox (Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap plus seccomp on Linux, a native Windows sandbox) and sends prompts, file excerpts, command output and — when browser or computer use is on — screenshots and page content to OpenAI services. Work Local is explicit that "local execution does not mean offline or device-only model inference". Structured OTel export is opt-in; a separate anonymous usage and health ping to OpenAI is on by default.

Requirements arrive by four channels, highest precedence first: macOS MDM (com.openai.codex requirements_toml_base64), legacy managed_config.toml fields the client reads as requirements, the Agent security policy authored in the Admin Console (a Global baseline with Local and Codex Cloud environment overrides, delivered as a cloud bundle at ChatGPT sign-in), then the system requirements.toml (/etc/codex or %ProgramData%\OpenAI\Codex). Sign-in restrictions are honoured only from MDM or the system file. A cloud bundle that cannot be fetched and has no valid cache returns an error rather than starting without that layer. Codex Remote, the GitHub Action and Codex Security are shells of the same runtime; Codex cloud and the SDK are separate entities below.

facts.label: Plans
facts.value: Codex is in Free, Go, Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu; API-key sign-in pays per token and loses cloud features (GitHub reviews, Slack). Business, Enterprise and Edu add admin controls, Compliance API audit and spend limits.

facts.label: Inference & routing
facts.value: Model calls go to OpenAI; chatgpt_base_url and model_providers.<id>.base_url can redirect to a proxy, and "Codex respects workspace residency settings when you sign in with ChatGPT".

facts.label: Data leaving the device
facts.value: Prompts, relevant file excerpts, screenshots, browser content and tool results may be sent to OpenAI to complete a task; not every local file operation, screenshot or browser action appears in the Compliance API.

facts.label: Docs index
facts.value: learn.chatgpt.com/docs (Codex, configuration, enterprise, security sections)

facts.label: Data retention / training
facts.value: Workspace audit records are retained up to 30 days for the Compliance API; the BAA does not cover Codex cloud. API-key usage falls under the API data policy (no training by default, 30-day abuse-monitoring logs, ZDR by approval).

items.title: Admin-enforced requirements.toml
body: Requirements arrive by system file (/etc/codex/requirements.toml on Unix, %ProgramData%\OpenAI\Codex\requirements.toml on Windows; the lowest-precedence channel), as an Agent security policy authored in Admin Console > Agent security (Requirements and Defaults, a Global baseline with Local and Codex Cloud environment overrides) and delivered at sign-in, or via macOS MDM under com.openai.codex (base64-encoded TOML; the highest-precedence channel). Agent security replaces Policies & Configuration. If the cloud bundle cannot be fetched and no valid cache exists, the load returns an error rather than starting without the cloud layer.

Enforceable keys cover the surfaces that matter: allowed_approval_policies and allowed_permission_profiles with default_permissions (e.g. pin ":workspace" and allow only read-only and workspace profiles), filesystem deny_read patterns for secrets paths, prefix command rules, managed hooks with allow_managed_hooks_only, experimental network domain allow/deny lists, and feature pins that disable computer use and browser surfaces org-wide.

items.title: Sandbox, approvals and network posture
body: Sandboxing is OS-enforced (Seatbelt on macOS, bwrap plus seccomp on Linux, a native Windows sandbox) with permission profiles from read-only through workspace-write to an explicit danger-full-access escape hatch. The agent runs with network access off by default; enabling it can route through a domain-filtering proxy, and .git, .codex and .agents stay read-only inside writable roots. In Codex cloud, current environments limit public internet with Enable all public internet access off and an Additional allowed domains list; Codex Cloud (Legacy) environments block internet during the agent phase by default, with allowlists and method restrictions.

links.title: Codex Cloud environments — connect to services

items.title: Workspace gating and compliance export
body: Workspace admins gate local Codex (desktop app, CLI and IDE extension together) with "Allow members to use Codex locally" — "Allow members to use Codex and Work Locally" where the workspace shows the combined Codex and Work Local section — and Codex cloud with "Use Codex in the cloud", through the workspace default and custom roles assigned to manual or SCIM-synced groups. Role grants combine additively, so On in any one role grants access. Codex usage, including the local clients, exports through the Compliance API alongside workspace audit and authentication logs.

riskNotes.note: The vendor's own guidance says prompt injection can make the agent fetch and follow untrusted instructions when network access or web search is on; the 2026 web.run research chained exactly that into out-of-sandbox execution on Windows.
--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox (--yolo) removes both boundaries; the admin answer is allowed_approval_policies and allowed_sandbox_modes in requirements.toml, which users cannot loosen.
Plugins bundle MCP servers, skills and hooks from Git marketplaces; without marketplaces.restrict_to_allowed_sources and an [mcp_servers] identity allowlist any developer can add a tool source.
Three 2026 sandbox findings (git show allowlist, Docker socket, ProgramData config trust) were escapes through components the sandbox trusted, not model failures.
File excerpts, screenshots and browser content leave the device on every task; deny_read globs and shell_environment_policy are the only in-product data minimisation.

controls.mechanism: allowed_login_methods = ["chatgpt"] and allowed_chatgpt_workspaces in the system requirements.toml or macOS MDM (cloud-managed values are ignored); MFA itself is enforced by the organisation's SSO IdP

steps.title: Pin every client to the org workspace
body: In /etc/codex/requirements.toml, %ProgramData%\OpenAI\Codex\requirements.toml or MDM com.openai.codex requirements_toml_base64, set allowed_login_methods = ["chatgpt"] and allowed_chatgpt_workspaces = ["<workspace-uuid>"]; Codex ignores both keys in cloud-managed requirements and refuses to start when no permitted login remains.

steps.title: Enforce MFA in the identity provider
body: ChatGPT has no workspace-wide MFA enforcement, so require SSO with MFA at the IdP and manage SSO in the Global Admin Console.

steps.title: Bound the token paths that skip the IdP
body: In Workspace settings > Permissions & roles grant "Allow users to create personal access tokens" only to named owners and set "Access token expiration limit"; revoke tokens at chatgpt.com/admin/access-tokens.

steps.title: Leave device-code login off unless needed
body: codex login --device-auth works only after a workspace admin enables device code login in ChatGPT workspace permissions.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: Codex pins the local client to the org's ChatGPT workspace, so the IdP's MFA policy governs each interactive browser sign-in, but MFA is configured in the IdP, not the product — the admin FAQ states ChatGPT doesn't provide workspace-wide MFA enforcement (Codex cloud requires MFA only for email-and-password accounts). Paths that skip the IdP prompt: Platform API keys (blocked by allowed_login_methods = ["chatgpt"]; "api" also admits Amazon Bedrock), Codex access tokens and service-account tokens (bounded by the expiration limit for new tokens only; the page warns an earlier dialog can offer No expiration), cached ChatGPT credentials that refresh automatically (lifetime not documented), device-code login (admin-enabled) and workload identity. Personal accounts are refused by allowed_chatgpt_workspaces, which also applies to access tokens. The pin holds only on machines that carry the system file or MDM payload; whether SSO-only sign-in can be enforced is on Help Center pages that returned 403.

original.mechanism: requirements.toml forced_login_method / forced_chatgpt_workspace_id (config) and allowed_login_methods / allowed_chatgpt_workspaces (managed), plus workspace roles and SCIM groups

steps.title: Pin the sign-in method and workspace
body: Set forced_login_method = "chatgpt" and forced_chatgpt_workspace_id = "<uuid>" so the client cannot run on a personal account or an API key.

steps.title: Enforce it from the managed bundle
body: In requirements.toml use allowed_login_methods = ["chatgpt"] and allowed_chatgpt_workspaces as the UUID allowlist; deliver by MDM, cloud policy or the system path.

steps.title: Gate Codex Local by role
body: In Workspace settings > Permissions & roles, set the Codex Local / Work Local permission per role; an explicit Off in any role denies even when another grants.

controls.mechanism: requirements.toml [rules] prefix_rules (decision "prompt" or "forbidden") and a managed [hooks] PreToolUse hook with allow_managed_hooks_only = true and [features].hooks = true

steps.title: Enforce restrictive command rules
body: In requirements.toml add [rules] prefix_rules with decision "forbidden" or "prompt" (requirements rules can't allow); they merge with .rules files and the most restrictive decision wins.

steps.title: Deploy a managed PreToolUse hook
body: Define [[hooks.PreToolUse]] in requirements.toml with hooks.managed_dir, set allow_managed_hooks_only = true and [features].hooks = true, and ship the script by MDM (Codex doesn't distribute it).

steps.title: Deny from the hook
body: Return permissionDecision "deny" (or exit code 2); matchers cover Bash, apply_patch, MCP tool names and other local function tools, not hosted tools such as WebSearch.

steps.title: Test the rule set
body: Run codex execpolicy check --rules <file> -- <command> to see the strictest decision and the matching rules before deploying.

controls.note: Partial: the declarative [rules] layer covers shell command prefixes only (the Rules page frames it as controlling commands run outside the sandbox), and the only per-call gate over files and MCP tools is the organisation's own hook script. The vendor says hosted tools skip the hook path, "some specialized tool paths can opt out" and hooks are "a useful guardrail, not a complete enforcement boundary"; a PreToolUse "ask" is not supported and fails open (the call continues), so escalate-to-human exists only through prompt rules for shell prefixes. Enforced on the device by the Codex runtime from requirements.toml, which users can't override; decisions reach the org's collector as codex.tool_decision only when OTel export is configured. The Guardian auto-review is a classifier, not a rule. What an allowed MCP server does downstream is outside.

original.mechanism: requirements.toml [rules] (forbidden / prompt) and managed [hooks] with allow_managed_hooks_only

steps.title: Write managed command rules
body: Add [rules] entries in requirements.toml with decision "forbidden" or "prompt" for command prefixes; users cannot weaken them.

steps.title: Add a PreToolUse or PermissionRequest hook
body: A managed hook returning permissionDecision "deny" (or exit code 2) blocks the call; set allow_managed_hooks_only = true so user, project and plugin hooks are ignored.

original.note: [rules] forbidden entries are deterministic; managed hooks are an integration point. The Guardian reviewer is a classifier, not a rule. MCP tool calls pass the rules; a server's own actions are outside them.

controls.mechanism: Vendor evidence from the OpenAI trust portal consumed by the organisation's TPRM platform

evidence.title: OpenAI Trust Portal (SafeBase) — SOC 2, ISO, pen-test and subprocessor artifacts (2026-09-25)
OpenAI Trust Portal — Security Whitepaper, linked from the Codex docs as the Codex security white paper

controls.note: External: the assessment runs in the organisation's TPRM platform. The trust portal lists a SOC 2 Type 2 report (described as covering the ChatGPT and API products), ISO 27001, 27017, 27018 and 27701 and ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certifications, a Pentest Report, CSA STAR Level 1, the subprocessor list and a Security Whitepaper; most reports require an access request. Codex is not named as its own SOC 2 scope, so the assessment inherits the ChatGPT scope. API-key sign-in moves Codex under the API organisation's data terms instead of the workspace's.

original.mechanism: Vendor evidence from trust.openai.com consumed by the organisation's TPRM platform
original.note: OpenAI publishes SOC 2 Type 2 (scope includes API Platform, ChatGPT Enterprise, Edu and Team), ISO 27001/27017/27018/27701/42001, pen-test reports and the subprocessor list on the trust portal; Codex is not named separately, so the assessment inherits the ChatGPT Enterprise scope.

steps.title: Pull vendor evidence
body: Request the SOC 2 report, pen-test summary and subprocessor list from the trust portal and load them into the TPRM record.

controls.mechanism: Prisma AIRS under Admin Console > Policy & security > External guardrails (prompt scanning, Block mode) and managed UserPromptSubmit / PreToolUse hooks; deny_read and shell_environment_policy are minimisation only

steps.title: Connect Prisma AIRS as the prompt inspector
body: In Admin Console (admin.openai.com) > Policy & security > External guardrails > Prisma AIRS, enter the API key, security profile and endpoint URL, choose Enforcement mode Block and On AIRS failure Block prompts, select Save connection and Test connection, then turn on Enable Prisma AIRS.

steps.title: Close the uncovered sign-in path
body: Set allowed_login_methods = ["chatgpt"] and allowed_chatgpt_workspaces in the system requirements.toml or MDM, because sessions signed in with a Platform API key are not scanned.

steps.title: Inspect prompts and tool arguments in managed hooks
body: A managed UserPromptSubmit hook can block a prompt and a PreToolUse hook can deny a Bash, apply_patch or MCP call after the org's own detector reads it.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: Codex hands content to an inspector the organisation runs rather than detecting it itself. Prisma AIRS scans newly submitted prompt text across the desktop app, CLI, IDE extension and cloud when users sign in to the configured workspace; it does not scan assistant responses, tool calls, tool results, files or images, access must be enabled by the OpenAI account team, and the default On AIRS failure is Allow prompts. Hooks are an attach point that sees prompts and local tool arguments, not hosted tools. Codex itself only redacts secrets from generated memory fields. [permissions.filesystem] deny_read and shell_environment_policy keep named paths and variables away from the agent (data minimisation, credited here) but inspect nothing; endpoint DLP or an AI gateway covers the rest.

original.mechanism: permissions.filesystem.deny_read globs and shell_environment_policy in requirements.toml
original.note: These stop the agent reading named paths and environment variables; nothing in the product inspects prompt or upload content. Endpoint DLP is external.

steps.title: Deny reads of secret paths
body: Set [permissions.filesystem] deny_read globs (SSH keys, cloud credentials, .env); full-access profiles are rejected while deny-read rules exist.

steps.title: Strip secrets from the shell environment
body: Set shell_environment_policy.inherit = "core" and exclude patterns so tokens in the developer's environment never reach subprocesses.

controls.mechanism: Managed PostToolUse hook (attach point), Prisma AIRS prompt scanning, and allowed_web_search_modes in requirements.toml

steps.title: Screen tool output in a managed PostToolUse hook
body: A PostToolUse hook returning decision "block" (or continue false) replaces the tool result with the hook's feedback before the model continues; it covers Bash, apply_patch, MCP and local function tools.

steps.title: Scan submitted prompts with Prisma AIRS
body: Under Admin Console > Policy & security > External guardrails, a Prisma AIRS security profile with prompt injection detection in Block mode stops flagged prompts before they reach the model.

steps.title: Keep web search on the cached index
body: Set allowed_web_search_modes = ["cached"] (or [] to allow only disabled) so live web search is unavailable even in full-access sessions.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: the product-side path is a post-tool hook that can replace a tool result before the model reasons over it — an attach point whose classifier the organisation supplies — plus Prisma AIRS, which screens user prompts only, not tool results, files or fetched pages. Hosted web search skips the hook path. The Guardian auto-review judges proposed actions (credited under action policy) and GPT-6 safety monitoring pauses a task after the fact; neither screens input before it enters context. Cached web search reduces exposure to live content without classifying it. An AI or MCP gateway classifier on the brokered path covers the rest.

original.mechanism: Guardian automatic review (allowed_approvals_reviewers, guardian_policy_config) and the browser sign-in review model
original.note: The vendor ships a reviewing model for out-of-sandbox requests and for browser sign-in pages, and warns that refusal is probabilistic; no admin-tunable classifier on inputs.

steps.title: Decide whether automatic review may replace the human
body: allowed_approvals_reviewers controls whether ["auto_review"] is permitted; guardian_policy_config overrides the review policy text.

steps.title: Keep web access off where it is not needed
body: Network access defaults off in workspace-write; the docs say prompt injection can make the agent fetch and follow untrusted instructions once it is on.

controls.mechanism: requirements.toml [allowed_permission_profiles] with managed default_permissions and profile filesystem rules, [permissions.filesystem] deny_read, [rules] prefix_rules, [mcp_servers] identity allowlist, apps.<id> requirements and [features] / [browser_use] / [computer_use] pins

steps.title: Fix the permission profile set
body: Set default_permissions = ":workspace" (or a managed custom profile) and [allowed_permission_profiles] without ":danger-full-access"; omitted profiles are denied (Codex 0.138.0 or later).

steps.title: Scope paths inside the managed profile
body: In [permissions.<name>.filesystem] mark globs such as "**/*.env" = "deny", and add [permissions.filesystem] deny_read for paths no profile may read.

steps.title: Scope commands, MCP servers and app tools
body: Use [rules] prefix_rules (prompt or forbidden), the [mcp_servers.<id>] identity allowlist, and apps.<id>.enabled = false or apps.<id>.tools.<tool>.approval_mode in requirements.toml.

steps.title: Pin high-agency surfaces off
body: Set [features] computer_use, browser_use, browser_use_external, browser_use_full_cdp_access and in_app_browser = false, or restrict sites with [browser_use.origins] policies.

controls.note: Native: shell commands (by prefix), filesystem paths, MCP servers, app tools and the browser and computer-use surfaces are all scoped in requirements.toml, which users can't loosen, and Full access is removable. Enforced by the Codex runtime on the device; principal scoping comes from assigning cloud-managed requirements to groups. Limits: per-tool deny within an allowlisted MCP server is not a requirements key (enabled_tools / disabled_tools live in user config.toml), so use a managed PreToolUse matcher such as mcp__server__tool; [rules] can only restrict; on native Windows managed deny_read covers direct file tools but not shell subprocess reads; [[remote_sandbox_config]] can widen sandbox modes by hostname, which is not authenticated device proof; clients older than 0.138.0 ignore profile allowlists.

original.mechanism: allowed_permission_profiles, default_permissions, allowed_sandbox_modes, [mcp_servers] enabled_tools / disabled_tools and [features] pins in requirements.toml

steps.title: Fix the permission profile set
body: Set allowed_permission_profiles (the complete allowlist; omitted profiles are denied) and default_permissions = ":workspace"; add allowed_sandbox_modes.

steps.title: Scope MCP tools per server
body: In each [mcp_servers.<name>] set enabled_tools or disabled_tools and a default_tools_approval_mode.

steps.title: Pin high-agency features off
body: Set [features] computer_use = false, browser_use = false and browser_use_full_cdp_access = false where the fleet does not need them.

original.note: enabled_tools/disabled_tools hide MCP tools, permission profiles and sandbox modes limit filesystem and network reach, feature pins remove surfaces; approval policy pre-approves. All enforced by requirements.toml, which users cannot loosen.

controls.mechanism: OS sandbox around spawned commands (Seatbelt / bubblewrap plus seccomp / native Windows sandbox), required by [allowed_permission_profiles] without ":danger-full-access" or allowed_sandbox_modes, with windows.allowed_sandbox_implementations = ["elevated"]. Credential paths: requirements.toml [permissions.filesystem] deny_read for credential paths (OS-enforced for sandboxed commands), shell_environment_policy as a managed default, and mcp_servers.<id>.env_vars allowlists

steps.title: Remove the escape hatch
body: Omit ":danger-full-access" from [allowed_permission_profiles], or set allowed_sandbox_modes = ["read-only", "workspace-write"], so --sandbox danger-full-access and --yolo are refused.

steps.title: Decide what may escalate out of the sandbox
body: Under on-request, add [rules] prefix_rules with decision forbidden for command prefixes that must never run outside the sandbox, or pin allowed_approval_policies = ["never"] to refuse every escalation.

steps.title: Require the stronger Windows sandbox
body: Set [windows] allowed_sandbox_implementations = ["elevated"] so native Windows runs commands as dedicated lower-privilege sandbox users rather than the weaker unelevated fallback.

steps.title: Install bubblewrap on Linux and WSL2
body: Package bwrap on every Linux host; without it Codex falls back to a bundled helper that needs unprivileged user namespaces, and surfaces a startup warning when neither works.

steps.title: Deny the credential paths
body: Set [permissions.filesystem] deny_read for ~/.ssh, cloud CLI and git-credential files and "/**/*.env"; while deny rules exist the runtime rejects full access and keeps commands sandboxed.

steps.title: Strip secrets from spawned commands
body: Set [shell_environment_policy] inherit = "core", ignore_default_excludes = false and filters such as "AWS_*" = "exclude", shipped to every client as a managed default.

steps.title: Pass MCP servers only the variables they need
body: List each stdio server's variables in mcp_servers.<id>.env_vars instead of letting it inherit the developer's environment.

controls.note: Partial on the rule applied to every vendor (Cursor, Claude Code): the sandbox can be required but is not fail-closed, because under on-request approval a command that needs to go beyond the boundary is run outside it once the user approves the escalation. The only admin-pinnable way to refuse escalations is allowed_approval_policies = ["never"], which also removes human approval; the granular policy's sandbox_approval = false rejects them while keeping other prompts, but requirements.toml is not documented to pin it. Inside the boundary: the OS sandbox wraps every command the agent spawns and their children, and requirements.toml stops users choosing full access; in workspace-write, .git, .agents and .codex under writable roots stay read-only and network is off by default. Platforms: Seatbelt on macOS, bwrap plus seccomp on Linux and WSL2 (fail-closed behaviour without bwrap or user namespaces is not documented), elevated or unelevated sandbox on native Windows; inside Docker the sandbox may not start and the vendor tells users to make the container the boundary. Outside the boundary: the Codex process itself, MCP servers, hooks, web search and browser or Computer Use, which have their own controls; [[remote_sandbox_config]] can widen modes on matching hosts. Three 2026 escapes (git show allowlist, Docker socket, ProgramData config trust) are in advisories. Credential paths: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: read-denies are admin-locked and OS-enforced for sandboxed commands on macOS and Linux, but on native Windows managed deny_read applies to direct file tools only, not shell subprocess reads. Environment stripping is a managed default users can change during a run, and by default (ignore_default_excludes = true) variables named KEY, SECRET or TOKEN pass through; ship the policy in managed_config.toml or MDM config_toml_base64. Nothing holds credentials outside the agent and injects them per destination: commands still inherit whatever the developer's account reaches that no rule names — the git credential helper, cloud CLI config, the ssh-agent socket (Unix sockets are allowlist-only when the managed network proxy is active; otherwise not documented) — and Computer Use or the Chrome extension act in signed-in browser sessions. A dev container or secretless credential broker is the external fix.

original.mechanism: OS sandbox (Seatbelt / bubblewrap+seccomp / Windows sandbox) selected by sandbox_mode and pinned by allowed_sandbox_modes
original.note: Three 2026 escapes (git show allowlist, Docker socket, ProgramData config trust) sit in advisories; the Docker-socket one is by design unless a socket is explicitly allowed. Inside the boundary: commands the agent runs. Outside: browser tools, web search and MCP servers, which are bounded by their own controls. Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap plus seccomp on Linux, a native Windows sandbox.

steps.title: Understand the boundary
body: workspace-write keeps writes inside the workspace and network off; .git, .agents and .codex under writable roots stay read-only.

steps.title: Remove the escape hatch
body: Pin allowed_sandbox_modes to ["read-only", "workspace-write"] so danger-full-access and --yolo are unavailable.

original.mechanism: cli_auth_credentials_store, scoped access tokens and service accounts
original.note: Locally the agent acts as the signed-in developer with that developer's file and git rights; there is no on-behalf-of exchange. Automation can run as a service account so runs attribute to a non-human identity.

steps.title: Keep credentials out of auth.json
body: Set cli_auth_credentials_store = "keyring" (or "ephemeral" for CI) in requirements.toml.

steps.title: Run automation as a service account
body: Create a service account, assign it plugins and a role, and issue CODEX_ACCESS_TOKEN from its Access tokens section (CLI 0.142.0+).

controls.mechanism: requirements.toml [features].memories pin, the Computer History role permission, allow_managed_hooks_only, and read-only .codex / .agents inside the sandbox; AGENTS.md sources are not admin-lockable

steps.title: Pin local memories off or on deliberately
body: Set [features] memories = false in requirements.toml to keep agent-written memories out of managed clients; local memories are off by default.

steps.title: Gate Computer History by role
body: In Workspace Settings > Permissions & roles turn on Enable Computer History only for approved roles; it is off by default for Business and Enterprise and each member must still opt in.

steps.title: Load only managed hooks
body: Set allow_managed_hooks_only = true so user, project, session and plugin hooks are skipped.

steps.title: Keep instruction files under review
body: Codex merges ~/.codex/AGENTS.md (or AGENTS.override.md) with repo AGENTS.md files up to project_doc_max_bytes (32 KiB); review them as code.

controls.note: Partial: an administrator can switch agent-written memory off, gate Computer History, restrict hooks to managed ones, and the sandbox keeps .codex and .agents read-only to the agent's own commands; untrusted projects skip project .codex config, hooks and rules. Instruction sources cannot be locked — there is no admin-owned AGENTS.md and a user's AGENTS.override.md wins at its level — and memory contents are not validated or gated: Codex only redacts secrets from generated memory fields. memories.disable_on_external_context (keeps chats that used MCP or web search out of memory generation) and history.persistence are user config.toml keys, not requirements. Stores live under CODEX_HOME on the device.

original.mechanism: history.persistence and the Computer History role permission
original.note: Codex keeps session transcripts under CODEX_HOME and, on the desktop app, a searchable Computer History; there is no admin validation or quarantine of that store.

steps.title: Disable local transcript persistence
body: Set [history] persistence = "none" (and max_bytes) in the managed config.

steps.title: Gate Computer History by role
body: Workspace settings > Permissions & roles carries the Computer History permission.

original.mechanism: AGENTS.md hierarchy with project_doc_max_bytes and project trust
original.note: Instructions load from ~/.codex/AGENTS.md then repo-root-to-cwd AGENTS.md files; project config loads only for trusted projects. There is no admin-owned instruction file.

steps.title: Own the instruction files
body: Keep AGENTS.md under code review; AGENTS.override.md wins at each level and project_doc_max_bytes (32 KiB default) truncates the merged set.

controls.mechanism: cli_auth_credentials_store = "keyring" and allowed_login_methods = ["chatgpt"] in the system requirements.toml or MDM, the workspace Access token expiration limit, and workload identity federation

steps.title: Require the OS credential store and forbid API keys
body: In the system requirements.toml or MDM set cli_auth_credentials_store = "keyring" and allowed_login_methods = ["chatgpt"]; cloud-managed requirements ignore both keys.

steps.title: Cap access-token lifetime
body: In Workspace settings > Permissions & roles set "Access token expiration limit"; owners and admins revoke any token at chatgpt.com/admin/access-tokens.

steps.title: Use federation instead of stored tokens for automation
body: Set OPENAI_FEDERATION_RULE_ID and OPENAI_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE (an OIDC token or SPIFFE JWT-SVID) so the workload authenticates without a stored Codex credential.

controls.note: Native for the product's own credential: it can be forced into the OS credential store (keyring fails rather than falling back to the plaintext ~/.codex/auth.json), ChatGPT sign-in tokens refresh automatically, workload identity and model_providers.<id>.auth.command give keyless or rotating options, and an admin can forbid API keys and bound new access tokens. Enforced on the device by the Codex runtime, only where the system file or MDM payload is present. Limits: the expiration limit applies to new tokens and the page warns an earlier Codex-only dialog can offer No expiration; MCP server credentials (bearer_token_env_var, mcp_oauth_credentials_store) are user config, not requirements; the workload identity page cited on 2026-09-10 now returns 404, so its token lifetime is not re-verified.

original.mechanism: OS keyring credential store, workspace access-token expiration limit, workload identity federation

steps.title: Cap token lifetime
body: Owners set "Access token expiration limit" in Permissions & roles; tokens are created at chatgpt.com/admin/access-tokens with a required expiry.

steps.title: Replace stored tokens with federation
body: Exchange an OIDC or SPIFFE token via OPENAI_FEDERATION_RULE_ID / OPENAI_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE; the resulting token never lasts longer than one hour.

original.note: The keyring stores the sign-in credential; federation is the ephemeral path for automation. Shell commands read the developer's environment unless shell_environment_policy strips it, and the model sees a secret only if a command prints it.

controls.mechanism: requirements.toml [mcp_servers.<id>] identity allowlist (command executable and args, or url) and [marketplaces] restrict_to_allowed_sources with Git source and ref rules

steps.title: Allowlist MCP servers by name and identity
body: Add [mcp_servers.<id>] identity = { command = ... } for stdio or { url = ... } for streamable HTTP; a server whose name or identity doesn't match is disabled and an empty table disables all.

steps.title: Pin stdio invocations
body: Use the structured identity.command form with executable and args entries (match "exact", "prefix" or "regex") so the approved argument list, including a versioned package, must match.

steps.title: Restrict plugin sources
body: Set [marketplaces] restrict_to_allowed_sources = true with allowed_sources Git url and exact ref rules; unmatched marketplace adds, installs and refreshes are rejected.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: an allowlist admits servers but verifies nothing they serve. Exact argument matching can pin a package version for stdio servers only, and the match ignores cwd, env and env_vars; URL-matched remote servers stay unpinned. Nothing scans tool descriptions, hashes tool definitions or re-gates a server whose definitions change (hash-based trust review covers hooks, not MCP tools). Plugin-bundled servers use plugins.<plugin>.mcp_servers.<server>.identity. Enforced by the Codex runtime on the device from requirements.toml; an MCP gateway or registry supplies definition scanning and pinning.

original.mechanism: requirements.toml [mcp_servers] identity allowlist and [marketplaces] restrict_to_allowed_sources

steps.title: Allowlist MCP servers by identity
body: A server is enabled only when both its name and identity match an approved [mcp_servers] entry; an empty table disables all MCP servers.

steps.title: Restrict plugin sources
body: Set [marketplaces] with restrict_to_allowed_sources = true and pin features.plugins; unmatched marketplace operations are rejected.

original.note: Admission by identity: the [mcp_servers] allowlist and marketplace source restriction. Admission is not integrity — nothing pins the tool descriptions a server returns or detects a changed implementation.

controls.mechanism: allowed_approval_policies = ["on-request"], allowed_approvals_reviewers = ["user"], profiles without full access, [rules] prefix_rules decision "prompt", and browser / computer-use persistent-approval pins

steps.title: Remove the no-prompt modes
body: Set allowed_approval_policies = ["on-request"] and omit ":danger-full-access" from [allowed_permission_profiles] so "never", Full access and --yolo are refused.

steps.title: Make the reviewer a person
body: Set allowed_approvals_reviewers = ["user"]; "auto_review" routes approvals to a reviewer agent.

steps.title: Force a prompt for named commands
body: Add [rules] prefix_rules with decision = "prompt" (for example git push and commit); a managed prompt beats a user's allow rule for the same prefix.

steps.title: Stop saved approvals in the browser and Computer Use
body: Set browser_use.allow_global_persistent_approval = false and computer_use.allow_persistent_approval = false.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: a present person sees the exact command for each escalation, and an admin can remove never, Full access and the AI reviewer, but approval fires only for actions that leave the sandbox — commands inside it run unprompted unless a managed prompt rule names them. Users can still persist prefix allow rules to ~/.codex/rules/default.rules and accept Smart-approval suggestions; no requirement disables that, so a managed rule wins only for the prefixes the admin names. Scheduled tasks run with approval_policy "never" wherever requirements allow it. Enforced on the device by the Codex runtime.

original.mechanism: allowed_approval_policies and allowed_approvals_reviewers in requirements.toml, and the permission modes

steps.title: Require approval outside the sandbox
body: Set allowed_approval_policies = ["on-request"] so "never" is unavailable. Do not list "untrusted" — approval_policy = "untrusted" is retired and must be removed from managed defaults and user, project and profile configuration; project trust is now trust_level in project configuration.

steps.title: Make the reviewer a person
body: An "on-request" policy alone lets the reviewer be the automatic (AI) reviewer. Set allowed_approvals_reviewers = ["user"] where a human must decide; ["auto_review"] requires automatic review instead, and listing both leaves the choice to the user.

steps.title: Keep Full access out of the mode picker
body: Ask for approval, Approve for me (auto-review) and Full access are the user modes; admins decide which profiles the workspace allows.

original.note: Approval is requested only for actions that leave the sandbox; commands inside the permitted sandbox boundary run without a new prompt.

controls.mechanism: Admin > Plugins marketplace import with a per-role Installation policy, enforced on clients by the requirements.toml [marketplaces] and [mcp_servers] allowlists

steps.title: Keep the workspace plugin catalogue
body: Admin > Plugins > Add > Import marketplace from GitHub, optionally pinned to a branch, tag or commit; set Installation policy to Available or Installed per role.

steps.title: Refuse what the catalogue doesn't list
body: Set [marketplaces] restrict_to_allowed_sources = true and an [mcp_servers] identity allowlist in requirements.toml so unlisted sources and servers are rejected or disabled.

controls.note: Partial: the workspace catalogue records approved plugins with a role policy and a pinned source, and requirements refuse unlisted marketplace sources and MCP servers, but the client-side lists carry no owner, version or approval record and are not reconciled with the catalogue. Plugins are not available in the IDE extension. Nothing inventories agents or MCP servers a developer runs on a machine without the requirements file.

original.mechanism: Admin > Plugins marketplace import and the [mcp_servers] approved identities
original.note: Approved plugins and MCP servers are recorded centrally; nothing inventories the local agents or MCP servers a developer runs outside that list.

steps.title: Manage the plugin catalogue
body: Admin > Plugins imports a GitHub marketplace, syncs daily and sets Available or Installed per role.

controls.mechanism: None in product; EDR / MDM software inventory and SSE / CASB find unmanaged installs and personal-account use

evidence.title: Managed configuration — allowed_chatgpt_workspaces refuses other workspaces (prevention, 2026-09-25)
ChatGPT Work admin FAQ — identity features listed, no discovery of unmanaged use (2026-09-25)

controls.note: External: find unmanaged installs (the codex binary, npm @openai/codex, the openai.chatgpt IDE extension, the ChatGPT desktop app and MSIX) with EDR or MDM software inventory, and personal-account or unmanaged workspace use of chatgpt.com with SSE / CASB. The vendor lists domain verification among identity features, but no page fetched documents discovery of personal accounts on the org's domain (the Help Center pages returned 403). allowed_chatgpt_workspaces in the system requirements.toml is prevention on managed machines, credited here only.

original.mechanism: None in product; forced workspace login turns personal-account use into a detectable violation
original.note: Discover unmanaged installs (npm @openai/codex, the openai.chatgpt extension, the MSIX) with EDR or software inventory; allowed_chatgpt_workspaces then blocks personal accounts.
