controls.mechanism: [otel] exporter / trace_exporter delivered as a managed default (managed_config.toml or MDM config_toml_base64) and the workspace Compliance API

steps.title: Point every client at the org collector
body: Ship [otel] exporter = "otlp-http" pointed at your collector, environment = "prod" and log_user_prompt = false in /etc/codex/managed_config.toml or MDM config_toml_base64.

steps.title: Know what the events carry
body: Events include codex.conversation_starts, codex.user_prompt (redacted by default), codex.tool_decision (approved or denied, config or user) and codex.tool_result, tagged with the conversation id.

steps.title: Collect workspace records continuously
body: Pull the append-only compliance log stream with COMPLIANCE_API_KEY into the SIEM; the Admin API reference defines which Codex events it covers.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: OTel carries per-session model, prompt and tool-decision events with correlation and prompt redaction, but [otel] is not a requirements.toml key — it arrives as a managed default that users can change during a run — and export is off by default and flushes on shutdown. The Compliance API is the workspace audit channel, and the Work Local page warns that not every local file operation, screenshot, browser action or approval appears there; its event list is in the Admin API reference, which returned 403. Capture only: tamper resistance is the receiving store's job.

original.mechanism: [otel] OTLP export from the client and the workspace Compliance API
original.note: The Compliance API keeps records 30 days; Work Local warns that not every local file operation, screenshot or browser action appears there. OTel is opt-in per client.

steps.title: Export client events
body: Set [otel] exporter = "otlp-http" or "otlp-grpc" with your endpoint; log_user_prompt defaults to false (redacted).

steps.title: Pull workspace records
body: Use the Compliance API with COMPLIANCE_API_KEY; the Admin API reference is the source of truth for event coverage and retention.

controls.mechanism: Codex Local role permission, access-token and service-account revocation, and allow_remote_control = false in requirements.toml

steps.title: Turn local Codex off for the affected roles
body: In Workspace settings > Permissions & roles set "Allow members to use Codex locally" (or "Allow members to use Codex and Work Locally") to Off in the workspace default and in every custom role that grants it — role grants are additive, so On in any one role keeps access; for one person, remove them from every granting group in the IdP or from the workspace.

steps.title: Revoke automation credentials
body: Revoke tokens at chatgpt.com/admin/access-tokens; removing local permission only suspends them, while disabling or deleting a service account revokes all of its tokens.

steps.title: Cut phone steering
body: Set allow_remote_control = false in requirements.toml to disable device remote control.

controls.note: Partial: every lever blocks new access rather than stopping a session in progress. Custom-role changes take about five minutes to appear and revoked tokens can no longer start new authenticated runs; whether a running local session stops is not documented, so the delay for active work is not documented and the operator or EDR kills the process. Requirement changes load at the next client start (a background refresh doesn't replace the loaded policy, MDM is read at launch), and the admin FAQ says managed configuration isn't an access-revocation mechanism. The vendor's asynchronous safety monitoring can pause a task but is not an admin action.

original.mechanism: Role permission off, token revocation, service-account disable, federation rule disable

steps.title: Turn the surface off
body: Set "Allow members to use Codex locally" (or the combined Codex and Work Locally toggle) to Off for the affected roles.

steps.title: Revoke automation credentials
body: Owners and admins revoke any workspace access token; disabling a service account revokes all of its tokens.

original.note: The role toggle and token revocation block future access; a running local process and the commands inside its sandbox are not stopped remotely — the operator stops the process. A cloud-managed requirements bundle is re-fetched on its own schedule, so treat that interval as the cessation delay.

controls.mechanism: EDR on the endpoint; Codex exposes process identity (sandbox-exec, bwrap, dedicated Windows sandbox users) and OTel tool events for correlation

evidence.title: Agent approvals & security — sandbox-exec on macOS, bwrap on Linux, OTel event catalogue (2026-09-25)
Windows sandbox — elevated mode runs commands as dedicated lower-privilege sandbox users (2026-09-25)
Configuration Reference — log_dir enforceable in requirements.toml (2026-09-25)

controls.note: External: Codex does not analyse process behaviour; the organisation's EDR does. Integration points: agent commands run as children of the Codex process under sandbox-exec on macOS and bwrap on Linux, the elevated native Windows sandbox runs them as dedicated lower-privilege sandbox users, OTel codex.tool_decision and codex.tool_result events can be joined to EDR telemetry, log_dir can be enforced in requirements.toml, and a managed PreToolUse hook can log each command. Detections worth writing from the advisories: batch or executable files created in project roots (the web.run node.bat chain), Docker-socket use from the agent, and non-admin writes under %ProgramData%\OpenAI\Codex (pre-create and ACL it; Cymulate, 2026-08, no Codex CVE).

original.mechanism: EDR rules around the runtime; no vendor hook for endpoint security products
original.note: Watch for batch or executable files created in project roots (web.run node.bat chain), Docker-socket use from the agent, and non-admin writes under %ProgramData%\OpenAI\Codex; pre-create and ACL that directory (Cymulate ProgramData config-trust report, 2026-08; no Codex CVE assigned).

controls.mechanism: requirements.toml [experimental_network] (enabled, managed_allowed_domains_only, domains) over sandboxed commands, with command network off by default

steps.title: Enforce a managed domain allowlist
body: Set [experimental_network] enabled = true and managed_allowed_domains_only = true with [experimental_network.domains] "allow" and "deny" entries; deny wins.

steps.title: Keep command network off where it isn't needed
body: sandbox_workspace_write.network_access defaults to false; the managed proxy never grants network a sandbox keeps off.

steps.title: Close the paths the proxy doesn't see
body: Use allowed_web_search_modes, features.apps = false, the [mcp_servers] allowlist and [browser_use] origin policies for web search, connectors, MCP servers and the browser.

controls.note: Partial: the admin-owned allowlist is enforced on commands inside the sandbox, but the vendor marks [experimental_network] experimental, says not to enable it broadly without validation, and calls Windows support limited; DNS-rebinding protection is best effort. It does not filter web search, apps and connectors, MCP server connections, native-app traffic from Computer Use, or Codex's own model and service requests; browser tools check managed denies separately. An endpoint firewall or SSE policy covers the rest.

original.mechanism: [experimental_network] managed_allowed_domains_only and sandbox_workspace_write.network_access
original.note: Domain rules apply to command proxying inside the sandbox, not to browser tools, web search or MCP servers; those need a network-layer control.

steps.title: Allowlist domains for sandboxed commands
body: In requirements.toml set [experimental_network] allowed and denied domains with managed_allowed_domains_only = true.

steps.title: Keep network off by default
body: sandbox_workspace_write.network_access = false is the default; features.network_proxy adds allow/deny domain maps when it is on.

controls.mechanism: Package mirror or artifact repository with malware scanning; Codex's integration point is the [experimental_network.domains] allowlist that forces sandboxed installs through the mirror

evidence.title: Managed configuration — [experimental_network] domains and [marketplaces] allowed_sources (2026-09-25)
Plugin management — marketplace import pinned to a branch, tag or commit, no scanning (2026-09-25)
Configuration Reference — features.skill_mcp_dependency_install on by default (2026-09-25)

controls.note: External: Codex scans nothing it downloads or installs — plugins, skills, MCP dependencies installed for skills (features.skill_mcp_dependency_install, on by default) or packages its commands fetch. Admission scanning belongs at the organisation's package mirror; the integration point is an [experimental_network.domains] allowlist that admits only the mirror for sandboxed commands, with registry variables set through shell_environment_policy as a managed default. [marketplaces] allowed_sources pins plugin Git sources and refs, which is admission, not file analysis. No model weights load in Codex; inference is remote unless a user points model_provider at a local server, which loads them itself.

original.note: No model artifacts are loaded by the product; inference is remote. model_provider can point at a local server (ollama, lmstudio) — that server, not Codex, loads the weights, and scanning them is the obligation of whoever runs it.

settings.name: allowed_login_methods
settings.where: requirements.toml (/etc/codex or %ProgramData%\OpenAI\Codex) or MDM requirements_toml_base64 → allowed_login_methods
settings.default: Unset (ChatGPT and API-key sign-in both allowed)
settings.recommended: ["chatgpt"]
settings.why: Managed devices refuse Platform API keys (and Amazon Bedrock), so every session signs in through the workspace and the IdP's MFA; cloud-managed values are ignored.

settings.name: allowed_chatgpt_workspaces
settings.where: requirements.toml or MDM requirements_toml_base64 → allowed_chatgpt_workspaces
settings.recommended: Your ChatGPT workspace UUID
settings.why: A personal ChatGPT account, another firm's workspace, or a Codex access token from either is refused before credentials load.

settings.name: cli_auth_credentials_store
settings.where: requirements.toml or MDM requirements_toml_base64 → cli_auth_credentials_store
settings.recommended: "keyring"
settings.why: The cached ChatGPT credential lives in the OS credential store rather than a readable CODEX_HOME/auth.json that a command or another process could copy.

settings.name: Allow members to use Codex locally
settings.where: Workspace settings › Permissions & roles › Codex Local (or "Allow members to use Codex and Work Locally" under Codex and Work Local)
settings.recommended: On for the custom role assigned to the IdP group licensed for Codex; Off in the workspace default
settings.why: Only that group can run the desktop app, CLI and IDE extension on the workspace, and turning it off suspends the local clients and their access tokens at once.

settings.name: Enable Directory Sync
settings.where: Workspace settings › Identity & access › Enable Directory Sync
settings.recommended: On, with the Codex group provisioned from the IdP
settings.why: A leaver removed in the IdP loses the seat and group roles at the next sync instead of waiting for someone to remove them by hand.

settings.name: Allow users to create personal access tokens
settings.where: Workspace settings › Permissions & roles › Access tokens (or "Allow members to use Codex access tokens" under Codex Local)
settings.recommended: On only for the role held by named automation owners
settings.why: An access token starts Codex runs as its creator without the IdP prompt, so only people who own an automation and its rotation hold one.

settings.name: Access token expiration limit
settings.where: Workspace settings › Permissions & roles › Access tokens (or the Codex Local section)
settings.recommended: 90 days
settings.why: Caps how long a leaked token works; the limit applies to new tokens only, so revoke older no-expiry tokens at chatgpt.com/admin/access-tokens.

settings.name: Enable device code login
settings.where: ChatGPT workspace permissions (workspace admin)
settings.recommended: Off, unless a team signs in on headless hosts
settings.why: Device-code sign-in can be completed from any browser for a session on another machine, the pattern device-code phishing relies on.

settings.name: permissions.filesystem.deny_read
settings.where: requirements.toml (Agent Security › Edit as TOML, MDM or system file) → [permissions.filesystem] deny_read
settings.recommended: ["/**/*.env", "~/.ssh", "~/.aws", "~/.config/gcloud"] plus your signing-key paths
settings.why: Keys and tokens never reach the model, and while a deny rule exists the runtime refuses full access so it can enforce it; on native Windows it covers file tools, not shell reads.

settings.name: shell_environment_policy
settings.where: /etc/codex/config.toml or managed_config.toml (MDM config_toml_base64) → [shell_environment_policy]
settings.recommended: inherit = "core", ignore_default_excludes = false, filters excluding AWS_*, AZURE_*, GITHUB_*, *_TOKEN, *_SECRET, *_PASSWORD
settings.why: Commands Codex spawns do not inherit the developer's cloud and Git tokens; it is a default users can change, so pair it with deny_read.

settings.name: Enable Prisma AIRS
settings.where: Admin Console › Policy & security › External guardrails › Prisma AIRS (Enforcement mode, On AIRS failure)
settings.default: Off; Enforcement mode Block, On AIRS failure Allow prompts
settings.recommended: On, Enforcement mode Block, On AIRS failure Allow prompts
settings.why: Prompts in the app, CLI, IDE and cloud are scanned for secrets and injection by your own AIRS profile before the model sees them; regulated teams set On AIRS failure to Block prompts.
settings.requires: Prisma AIRS licence, access enabled by the OpenAI account team

settings.name: memories.disable_on_external_context
settings.where: config.toml or managed_config.toml → [memories] disable_on_external_context
settings.default: false (memories themselves are off by default)
settings.recommended: true wherever memories are turned on
settings.why: A thread that read MCP output or web results is not distilled into memory, so injected text cannot persist into later sessions.

settings.name: allowed_permission_profiles with default_permissions
settings.where: requirements.toml → default_permissions, [allowed_permission_profiles]
settings.recommended: default_permissions = ":workspace"; allow ":read-only" and ":workspace", omit ":danger-full-access"
settings.why: The full-access profile — and with it --yolo — is refused, so every command runs in the OS sandbox; needs Codex 0.138.0 or later, older fleets use allowed_sandbox_modes.

settings.name: Approval policies (allowed_approval_policies)
settings.where: Admin Console › Agent security › Global › Requirements › Policy guardrails › Approval policies
settings.recommended: ["untrusted", "on-request"]
settings.why: Removes --ask-for-approval never, so the agent still stops for escalations and prompt rules; "untrusted" here only keeps the stricter approvals of projects marked trust_level = "untrusted", as approval_policy = "untrusted" is retired.

settings.name: allowed_approvals_reviewers
settings.where: requirements.toml → allowed_approvals_reviewers
settings.recommended: Unset — developers may hand escalations to automatic review
settings.why: Keeps approval friction manageable under the managed review policy below; regulated teams set ["user"] so a person answers every escalation.

settings.name: guardian_policy_config
settings.where: requirements.toml (Agent Security › Global › Edit as TOML) → guardian_policy_config
settings.recommended: Your trusted internal destinations and deny rules for credential exposure and uploads to unapproved file-sharing services
settings.why: Automatic review judges each escalation against the firm's own risk rules, and the managed text beats any local [auto_review].policy.

settings.name: rules.prefix_rules
settings.where: requirements.toml (Agent Security › Global › Edit as TOML) → [rules] prefix_rules
settings.recommended: "forbidden" for destructive and credential commands (rm -rf, cloud CLI auth); "prompt" for git push
settings.why: Managed rules merge with project .rules files and the most restrictive decision wins, so a repository cannot allow what the firm forbids.

settings.name: allow_managed_hooks_only
settings.where: requirements.toml → allow_managed_hooks_only
settings.default: Unset (user, project, session and plugin hooks run)
settings.recommended: true
settings.why: A cloned repository's or plugin's hooks are commands on the developer's machine; only hooks from managed layers run.

settings.name: mcp_servers.<id>.identity
settings.where: requirements.toml (Agent Security › Global › Edit as TOML) → [mcp_servers.<id>] identity
settings.recommended: Your approved servers, stdio by executable and args, HTTP by url
settings.why: A server whose name and identity are not on the list is disabled wherever it is configured, plugin-bundled servers included.

settings.name: marketplaces.restrict_to_allowed_sources
settings.where: requirements.toml → [marketplaces] restrict_to_allowed_sources, allowed_sources
settings.recommended: true, with your organisation's plugin repository pinned by Git URL
settings.why: Plugins — which bundle skills, MCP servers and hooks — are added, installed and refreshed only from sources you curate.

settings.name: Installation policy
settings.where: Admin › Plugins › (imported plugin) › Installation policy, per role
settings.recommended: Available for the roles that need each approved plugin; plugins outside your marketplace disabled
settings.why: The workspace plugin directory, imported from your Git marketplace, is the catalogue developers install from; installing a plugin still needs each app allowed.

settings.name: Upload plugins with custom MCP servers / Create plugins with MCPs
settings.where: Workspace settings › Permissions & roles (search "plugins")
settings.recommended: On only for the role held by your plugin maintainers
settings.why: Members cannot introduce a custom MCP connection into the workspace outside the reviewed catalogue.

settings.name: Computer use
settings.where: Admin Console › Agent security › Global › Requirements › Desktop feature availability › Computer use (features.computer_use)
settings.recommended: Force off
settings.why: Stops the agent driving native desktop apps — including a browser as a native app, outside Browser Use site rules; regulated teams also force off Browser use and External browser use.

settings.name: browser_use.allow_global_persistent_approval
settings.where: requirements.toml (Agent Security › Edit as TOML) → [browser_use] allow_global_persistent_approval
settings.recommended: false
settings.why: Browser Use cannot create or honour an "Always allow" that covers every site, such as downloads from anywhere; per-site approvals still work.

settings.name: windows.allowed_sandbox_implementations
settings.where: requirements.toml → [windows] allowed_sandbox_implementations
settings.recommended: ["elevated"]
settings.why: Native Windows commands run as dedicated lower-privilege sandbox users and never fall back to the weaker unelevated sandbox.

settings.name: sandbox_workspace_write.network_access
settings.where: config.toml or managed_config.toml → [sandbox_workspace_write] network_access
settings.recommended: false — don't turn it on fleet-wide
settings.why: Sandboxed commands start with no network, so an injected command cannot post code or secrets out; the managed proxy below is the route for workflows that need hosts.

settings.name: Managed networking with Only allow domains added by admins
settings.where: Admin Console › Agent security › Requirements › Network use controls ([experimental_network] enabled, managed_allowed_domains_only, domains)
settings.recommended: On / On, allowing your source control, package mirror and approved APIs
settings.why: Sandboxed commands reach only admin-listed hosts and users cannot widen the list; experimental, so validate per client version and hold back on Windows.

settings.name: features.respect_system_proxy
settings.where: config.toml or managed_config.toml (MDM config_toml_base64) → [features] respect_system_proxy
settings.recommended: true on devices behind the corporate proxy or PAC
settings.why: The Codex runtime's own requests pass the proxy that holds your allowlist and tenant restriction; it does not cover shell commands or plugins.

settings.name: otel.exporter and otel.trace_exporter
settings.where: managed_config.toml or MDM config_toml_base64 → [otel] exporter, trace_exporter, environment
settings.recommended: otlp-http to your collector, environment = "prod"
settings.why: Run, approval and tool-decision events from every client land in the SIEM; project .codex/config.toml cannot reroute them.

settings.name: otel.log_user_prompt
settings.where: managed_config.toml or MDM config_toml_base64 → [otel] log_user_prompt
settings.recommended: false
settings.why: Tool decisions are logged without the prompt text, keeping client material out of the SIEM; turn on only for an investigation.

settings.name: Compliance API
settings.where: Admin API (COMPLIANCE_API_KEY) → append-only compliance log stream

summary: Codex Cloud runs coding tasks in OpenAI-hosted VMs started from a published cloud environment — the GitHub repositories, dependencies, tools and access settings Codex prepares and tests with the user — from the web, mobile or desktop app, the CLI, Slack (Cloud delegation through @ChatGPT) or a schedule. Each task gets its own workspace from the published environment, and its saved VM state is recoverable for up to seven days. Codex Cloud (Legacy) — containers from the universal image plus a setup script, cached for up to 12 hours — still runs Code Review and the GitHub, GitLab and Linear integrations and is planned for deprecation. The same hosted harness is what ChatGPT Work calls Work Cloud, which the vendor describes as VM-backed sandboxes on OpenAI infrastructure.

Inference and execution are both at OpenAI: the repository, environment variables and the prompt leave the organisation, and the agent's output returns as changes to commit or a pull request for a human to merge. Public internet is set per environment (Enable all public internet access, Enable package manager domains, Additional allowed domains), independently of a Tailscale VPN; service credentials go in as HTTP secrets that the proxy substitutes only for their allowed HTTPS domains, or as short-lived OIDC credentials. In Legacy environments agent-phase internet is off by default (or On with a domain allowlist and GET/HEAD/OPTIONS only), and secrets reach setup scripts only.

Admin gating is by workspace permission (Use Codex in the cloud, off by default for Enterprise; Manage workspace environments; Allow event-triggered scheduled tasks), by Agent security's Codex Cloud override (sandbox modes, managed networking), by environment (repositories, internet, secrets, Who can use) and, for the Legacy integrations, by connector setting (Codex for Linear). Compliance API records are retained 30 days; the BAA does not cover Codex cloud.

riskNotes.note: The Legacy internet-access page shows hidden instructions in fetched web content driving secret exfiltration; the mitigation is Enable all public internet access off with a narrow allowed-domain list (Legacy: the default Off and GET-only methods).

A shared environment's published filesystem, VPN identity and environment-owned credentials reach every user it is shared with; in Legacy environments cached containers are shared for up to 12 hours, so anything a setup script writes is visible to the next user's task.
Output is a diff or PR, but automatic reviews and event-triggered scheduled tasks act without a prompt; scope the GitHub app's repositories and the Allow event-triggered scheduled tasks permission.
Members with cloud access can create and edit their own environments, and only Manage workspace environments restricts editing shared ones; Legacy setup scripts always run with internet on.

controls.mechanism: The Use Codex in the cloud and Manage workspace environments role permissions, Who can use per environment, the "Allow event-triggered scheduled tasks" permission, Codex for Linear in connector settings (Legacy), and per-repository code review settings

steps.title: Grant cloud access by role
body: In Workspace settings > Permissions & roles grant Use Codex in the cloud (off by default for Enterprise) through the custom role for the approved group, and Manage workspace environments (off by default) only to environment owners; role grants are additive, so check every role a member holds.

steps.title: Share environments deliberately
body: Under Privacy > Who can use keep an environment to Only me until its files and credentials are reviewed; sharing lets colleagues start tasks from it without letting them edit it.

steps.title: Enable Legacy integrations only where wanted
body: Codex in Linear needs Codex cloud chats on in workspace settings and Codex for Linear enabled in connector settings; leave both off unless a team uses it.

steps.title: Gate event triggers
body: Grant the "Allow event-triggered scheduled tasks" permission only to roles that should start runs from Gmail, Slack or GitHub events.

steps.title: Decide which repositories review automatically
body: In Codex settings (chatgpt.com/settings/code-review) choose the repository and turn on Automatic review under Review code; configuring it needs GitHub push or admin permission on the repository.

controls.note: Partial: hosted sessions are granted by role (Use Codex in the cloud and Manage workspace environments are documented role permissions, and where Codex Cloud RBAC applies Slack delegation needs both the Slack deployment's service account and the requesting user to hold cloud access), but who may start or steer a session from an integration is not documented as configurable — the docs do not restrict an @codex mention in a GitHub pull request or GitLab merge request or a Linear assignment to people with write access, and no setting excludes Apps, bots or non-collaborators (GitLab's Review my, team or all MRs policy scopes automatic reviews, not invocation). Widening switches are partly admin-owned: personal access tokens are a workspace permission and device remote control is a local requirement (allow_remote_control); Codex cloud requires MFA only for email-and-password accounts.

steps.title: Put credentials in Secrets, not variables
body: Secrets get an additional layer of encryption, are only available to setup scripts and are removed before the agent phase; environment variables persist.

original.note: Environment secrets are readable by the setup script only and are not present when the agent runs; environment variables are readable by the agent's commands and so by the model. Stored secrets, not ephemeral issuance.

controls.mechanism: HTTP secrets substituted by the proxy, OIDC connections for short-lived cloud credentials, encrypted Legacy environment secrets, the never-shown-again GitLab connector token with admin revoke and regenerate, and Secure MCP Tunnel's runtime API key scoped by Platform Tunnels permissions with optional control-plane mTLS

steps.title: Use OIDC instead of stored cloud keys
body: In the environment's Advanced > OIDC settings attach a connection whose provider trust and permissions you control, so tasks obtain short-lived credentials for that identity.

steps.title: Store Legacy setup credentials as Secrets
body: Legacy environment secrets get an additional layer of encryption, are decrypted only for task execution and are removed before the agent phase.

steps.title: Rotate the GitLab connector token
body: In Codex Cloud > Settings > Connectors revoke the service-account token and generate a new one; a saved token is encrypted and never shown again.

steps.title: Scope the tunnel credential
body: Grant Tunnels Read + Use only to the identity running tunnel-client, keep its runtime API key in a secret store, and add control-plane mTLS where required.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: HTTP secrets never reach a process, OIDC credentials are short-lived, and Legacy secrets are encrypted and setup-only, but whether a saved secret can be read back is not documented, and environment variables are plain values visible to the agent and to everyone sharing the environment. The GitLab connector token is encrypted, never shown again and admin-rotatable, but it is an api-scoped personal access token whose lifetime the org sets in GitLab; how the GitHub credential is held and how long it lives is not documented. A vendor tunnel exists: Secure MCP Tunnel serves ChatGPT, Codex and the Responses API, tunnel-client authenticates to OpenAI with a runtime Platform API key and optional control-plane mTLS, access is scoped by Platform RBAC (Tunnels Read, Use, Manage) and tunnel changes appear in Platform audit logs, but the tunnel page documents no rotation or revocation procedure for that key, and it does not say whether Codex cloud sessions can call a tunnel-backed server.

settings.name: Use Codex in the cloud
settings.where: Workspace settings › Permissions & roles › Codex Cloud
settings.recommended: On only for the custom role assigned to the approved IdP group
settings.why: Hosted sessions run only for people the firm chose, and turning it off for a role stops new cloud tasks for that group.

settings.name: Manage workspace environments
settings.where: Workspace settings › Permissions & roles › Codex Cloud › Manage workspace environments
settings.recommended: On only for named environment owners
settings.why: Shared environments fix the repositories, network rules, secrets and VPN every task inherits, so only their owners can change them.

settings.name: Enable Directory Sync
settings.where: Workspace settings › Identity & access › Enable Directory Sync
settings.recommended: On, with the Codex Cloud group provisioned from the IdP
settings.why: A leaver removed in the IdP loses cloud access at the next sync, and role grants follow the directory group.

settings.name: Allow event-triggered scheduled tasks
settings.where: Workspace settings › Permissions & roles
settings.recommended: On only for roles that run approved automations
settings.why: An event from Gmail, Slack or GitHub can start a cloud run with no person present; keep that to teams with a reviewed trigger.

settings.name: Repository access
settings.where: GitHub › organisation or account Settings › installed GitHub Apps › (the app Codex connects through) › Configure › Repository access
settings.recommended: Only select repositories — those the teams using Codex Cloud work in
settings.why: A cloud task can check out and push only to repositories the app was granted, whatever the prompt asks for.

settings.name: Require pull request reviews before merging
settings.where: GitHub › repository Settings › Branches (or Rulesets) › default branch
settings.recommended: On, with at least one approving review on the default branch
settings.why: Codex output lands as a branch or pull request, and a person must approve it before it merges; Codex respects the source system's protections.

settings.name: Allowed sandbox modes
settings.where: Admin Console › Agent Security › (policy) › Codex Cloud › Requirements → allowed_sandbox_modes
settings.recommended: ["read-only", "workspace-write"]
settings.why: An approved full sandbox escalation bypasses the managed command proxy, so the cloud executor never runs unsandboxed.

settings.name: Enable Prisma AIRS
settings.where: Admin Console › Policy & security › External guardrails › Prisma AIRS (Enforcement mode, On AIRS failure)
settings.default: Off; Enforcement mode Block, On AIRS failure Allow prompts
settings.recommended: On, Enforcement mode Block, On AIRS failure Allow prompts
settings.why: Cloud task prompts are scanned for injection and sensitive data by your AIRS profile before the model sees them; regulated teams set On AIRS failure to Block prompts.
settings.requires: Prisma AIRS licence, access enabled by the OpenAI account team

settings.name: HTTP secrets
settings.where: Settings › Codex Cloud › Environments › (environment) › HTTP secrets › Manage (Key, Value, Allowed domains)
settings.recommended: Every service credential as an HTTP secret bound to its own allowed domain; none as environment variables
settings.why: Programs see a placeholder and the proxy substitutes the real value only for the allowed HTTPS destination, so an injected command cannot read or forward the key.

settings.name: OIDC
settings.where: Settings › Codex Cloud › Environments › (environment) › Advanced › OIDC
settings.recommended: An OIDC connection to a least-privilege cloud role in place of stored cloud keys
settings.why: Tasks get short-lived cloud credentials from your provider's trust policy, scoped to that role, instead of a long-lived key in the environment.

settings.name: Who can use
settings.where: Settings › Codex Cloud › Environments › (environment) › Privacy › Who can use
settings.recommended: Your workspace, once the prepared files and environment-owned credentials are reviewed; Only me until then
settings.why: Colleagues start from the published filesystem and its VPN and cloud identities, so anything left in it reaches every user.

settings.name: Enable all public internet access
settings.where: Settings › Codex Cloud › Environments › (environment) › network settings
settings.recommended: Off
settings.why: Tasks reach only the package registries and hosts you list, closing the open path for exfiltration and for injected instructions fetched from the web.

settings.name: Additional allowed domains
settings.where: Settings › Codex Cloud › Environments › (environment) › network settings (with Enable package manager domains)
settings.recommended: Your package mirror and the exact hosts the workflow needs; Enable package manager domains off where the mirror is listed
settings.why: Dependencies come through the firm's scanned mirror and nothing else outside the VPN is reachable.

settings.name: Manage Networking with Only allow domains added by admins
settings.where: Admin Console › Agent Security › (policy) › Codex Cloud › Requirements › Network use controls
settings.recommended: On / On, with the same allow entries as your environments
settings.why: A workspace-wide ceiling that environment owners cannot widen; it does not override a stricter environment setting.

settings.name: Agent internet access
settings.where: Codex Cloud (Legacy) › chatgpt.com/codex/settings/environments › (environment) › Agent internet access, Domain allowlist, Allowed HTTP methods
settings.recommended: Off; where a task needs it, On with the None preset plus named domains and GET, HEAD, OPTIONS only
settings.why: The legacy agent phase that runs Code Review and the GitHub and Linear integrations cannot post code or secrets to an attacker's server.

settings.name: Secrets
settings.where: Codex Cloud (Legacy) › chatgpt.com/codex/settings/environments › (environment) › Environment variables and secrets
settings.recommended: Setup credentials as Secrets, never as environment variables
settings.why: Secrets reach setup scripts only and are removed before the agent phase, whereas variables stay readable for the whole task.

settings.name: User usage limits
settings.where: Workspace settings › usage and spend controls › User usage limits (workspace default, group limits, individual overrides)
settings.recommended: A monthly workspace default sized to normal use, with higher group limits for heavy teams
settings.why: A runaway or hijacked account stops at its allowance instead of consuming the workspace's credits.
settings.requires: Enterprise or Edu (Business uses credits and spend controls)

settings.name: Workspace overage limit
settings.where: Workspace settings › usage and spend controls › Workspace overage limit
settings.recommended: A set amount agreed with finance — not No limit
settings.why: Usage past the credit allocation stops at a known ceiling; No limit isn't a zero-spend cap and usage alerts only notify.

settings.name: Compliance API
settings.where: Admin API (COMPLIANCE_API_KEY) → append-only compliance log stream
settings.recommended: On, streamed continuously into your SIEM or eDiscovery store
settings.why: Cloud task records are retrievable centrally under your own retention and legal hold, not only in each task's log.
