tools.name: Codex SDK

variants.name: @openai/codex-sdk (TypeScript)
openai-codex (Python)

summary: The SDK embeds the Codex agent in customer-hosted automation. The TypeScript library spawns the codex CLI (codex exec) and reads JSONL events over stdin/stdout; the Python library drives a local codex app-server over JSON-RPC and pins its own CLI runtime. Both expose a thread/turn API with sandbox presets (read-only, workspace-write, full access) settable per thread or per turn, and model selection. Inference is at OpenAI; execution is wherever the host runs.

Because both drive the Codex CLI runtime, the host's config.toml and any requirements.toml apply, and per-client config overrides are passed as --config flags; an omitted sandbox falls back to the runtime's configured default (read-only for codex exec). Python threads start with ApprovalMode.auto_review, so a reviewer agent answers escalations unless deny_all is passed. Unattended runs authenticate with CODEX_API_KEY (TypeScript), a service-account CODEX_ACCESS_TOKEN or workload identity federation, which is the credential story that distinguishes this entity from the interactive shells.

facts.label: Plans
facts.value: API-key usage bills at API rates; ChatGPT sign-in and service-account tokens use the workspace plan.

facts.label: Inference & routing
facts.value: The SDK controls a local runtime that calls OpenAI; model_provider / base_url overrides in config.toml apply.

facts.label: Data leaving the device
facts.value: Prompts, file contents the agent reads and command output go to OpenAI as with the CLI.

facts.label: Docs index
facts.value: learn.chatgpt.com/docs/codex-sdk

facts.label: Data retention / training
facts.value: API-key traffic falls under the API data policy — not used for training by default, 30-day abuse-monitoring logs, ZDR by approval.

riskNotes.note: agents.max_concurrent_threads_per_session is the only vendor bound on subagent fan-out; task duration and spend are yours to cap.
full_access is one argument away in the SDK; pin allowed_sandbox_modes on the host so the preset is rejected.
Runs act as whichever token the host holds; use a service account so actions attribute to the automation, not an engineer.
MCP servers and plugins configured on the host are inherited by SDK threads; allowlist them in requirements.toml.

controls.mechanism: Per-thread rollout files under CODEX_HOME (a per-tenant CODEX_HOME through the client's env), Python ephemeral threads, app-server thread/delete, and ExternalMessage for content from other agents; nothing validates stored state

steps.title: Give each tenant its own state root
body: Set CODEX_HOME in the client's env (TypeScript new Codex({ env }), Python CodexConfig(env=...)) to an existing per-tenant directory so sessions, logs, config and auth never share a root.

steps.title: Mark other agents' output as untrusted
body: Pass content from another agent, tool or application as ExternalMessage(tool_name=..., content=...) so it reaches the model with tool-level authority, below user and developer instructions.

steps.title: Keep short-lived runs off disk and delete the rest
body: Start Python threads with ephemeral=True, and remove stored threads with the app-server's thread/delete, which deletes the rollout files of the thread and its spawned descendants.

controls.note: Partial on the architecture rule (per-thread scoping, contents unvalidated). Threads are separate rollout files keyed by thread id, a per-tenant CODEX_HOME separates tenants, and delete exists at the app-server (the Python SDK exposes archive only, the TypeScript SDK neither). Nothing validates what a step writes: thread history, AGENTS.md files and memories are read back unscreened, and resumeThread / thread_resume opens any thread id the process can reach, so ownership checks are the host application's. ExternalMessage lowers the authority of another agent's text but does not screen it, and its tool name is not proof of identity. features.memories is off by default. Enforced by the Codex runtime on the host.

original.mechanism: Thread persistence (resumeThread) and history.persistence on the host

steps.title: Disable persisted transcripts on the host
body: Set [history] persistence = "none" if threads must not survive the process.

original.note: Retention only: thread persistence and history settings decide what is kept on the host. Nothing validates or restores it.

controls.mechanism: None in the SDK; an evaluation platform or CI suite runs SDK turns and gates the release, reading outputSchema structured output and the turn's items and usage

evidence.title: Codex SDK — thread/turn API, no evaluation harness or release gate (2026-09-25)
TypeScript SDK README — outputSchema structured output and streamed turn events (2026-09-25)

controls.note: External: the SDK ships no evaluation harness and nothing that can hold a model, prompt or agent change until tests pass. The integration point is the turn result — outputSchema makes the final response conform to a JSON schema, and the result carries the items, status and token usage — which an evaluation platform or the deployer's CI scores before promotion. Model and agent behaviour change with the pinned runtime (Python) or the installed CLI (TypeScript), so pin both and re-run the suite on every upgrade.

original.mechanism: Not offered
original.note: No vendor evaluation harness for SDK agents; structured output and streaming events let you build one.

evidence.title: Vendor docs index, reviewed; no setting for this control (2026-09-10)

controls.mechanism: [otel] exporter and otel.trace_exporter to the deployer's collector (host config.toml or the client's config overrides), plus the SDK event stream (runStreamed items, Python turn.stream notifications) and the rollout files under CODEX_HOME/sessions

steps.title: Export the runtime's telemetry to your collector
body: Set [otel] exporter (logs) and otel.trace_exporter (traces) to otlp-http or otlp-grpc with your endpoint, environment = "prod" and log_user_prompt = false, in the host config.toml or the client's config overrides.

steps.title: Ship the full step record from the stream
body: Consume runStreamed() (TypeScript) or turn.stream() (Python) and forward item events, which carry the command and its output, file changes, and the MCP server, tool, arguments and result, to your store.

steps.title: Attribute runs to the automation
body: Run each workflow as its own service account so runs attribute to it; token creation and account changes appear in workspace audit records.

controls.note: Partial on the architecture rule: the runtime's OTel export carries conversation starts, model requests, tool decisions (approved or denied, by config or user) and tool results (duration, success, output snippet) tagged with the conversation id, to a collector the deployer controls; export is off by default and flushes on shutdown. Tool arguments and subagent handoff correlation are not in the documented event catalogue, and the TypeScript event stream has no subagent items. Full arguments and results exist in the SDK event stream and the local rollout JSONL, which the host application must ship off the host itself. Emission is not detection or tamper resistance — the collector and SIEM supply those.

original.mechanism: Streaming turn events and [otel] export

steps.title: Export OTel logs
body: Set [otel] exporter to otlp-http or otlp-grpc; events carry model and sandbox metadata, with prompts redacted unless log_user_prompt = true.

original.note: Streaming turn events and OTel export give tool and model events per thread; there is no persisted trace store and no detection — the host application keeps and analyses them.

original.mechanism: OTel export plus Compliance API when signed in with a workspace identity

steps.title: Attribute and export
body: Service-account runs appear in workspace analytics and audit records; token creation and configuration changes are tracked through the Admin API.

original.mechanism: OTel stream into the organisation's SIEM
original.note: Detection content is yours; the vendor emits events with model and sandbox metadata.

evidence.title: Vendor docs index, reviewed for the integration point (2026-09-10)

controls.mechanism: Service account with directly assigned workspace roles and groups and a Codex-scoped, expiring access token as the grant a run carries; authorization of who may start, steer or interrupt runs is the host application's

steps.title: Give each workflow its own service principal
body: In Workspace settings > Service accounts (chatgpt.com/admin/service-accounts) create an account and assign its roles, groups and plugins directly; it inherits nothing from its creator.

steps.title: Scope and bound the token the run carries
body: Create the account's token with the Codex scope and a finite expiration (Admin API ttl, under one year and within workspace policy) and pass it to the client as CODEX_ACCESS_TOKEN.

steps.title: Restrict who can manage the principal
body: Share the account with the User, Configure or Manager role only as needed; only workspace owners and admins create, delete or share accounts.

controls.note: Partial: the product administers the grant a run carries — the service account's roles, groups, plugins, token scope and expiry, enforced by OpenAI server-side — but the SDK has no inbound surface and no authorizer, so who may start, steer (turn.steer), interrupt or resume a run is the host application's code behind its IdP or API gateway. Service accounts are available only on pay-as-you-go plans; the API-key path (CODEX_API_KEY) carries an API Platform project key whose access is administered there. The Admin API reference returned 403, so its event coverage is unverified.

original.mechanism: ChatGPT sign-in, service-account tokens or workload identity federation for the host process

steps.title: Authenticate unattended runs without a personal token
body: Exchange an OIDC or SPIFFE JWT-SVID through a federation rule for a short-lived workspace token (never longer than one hour).

original.note: Sign-in, service accounts and workload identity federation authenticate the host process to OpenAI; who may use the deployed application, with what roles, is the application's own identity layer.

original.mechanism: Not offered
original.note: Rated external on the same rule as the Claude Agent SDK: the SDK retrieves nothing itself; the host account and working directory decide what its tools can read, and per-user scoping is the host application's.

evidence.title: Vendor docs index, reviewed for the integration point (2026-09-10)

controls.mechanism: One service account or workload identity federation rule per Codex client process, passed through the client's env; threads and subagents inside a client share it

steps.title: Give each agent workload its own identity
body: Create a service account per agent workload and pass its token as CODEX_ACCESS_TOKEN in that client's env (TypeScript new Codex({ env }), Python CodexConfig(env=...)); runs attribute to the account.

steps.title: Prefer federation over stored tokens
body: Set OPENAI_FEDERATION_RULE_ID and OPENAI_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE (an OIDC token or SPIFFE JWT-SVID) so the workload authenticates without a stored Codex credential.

steps.title: Revoke one agent without the others
body: Revoke a single token, or disable or delete the service account, which revokes all of its active tokens.

controls.note: Partial on the architecture rule: a distinct, separately revocable workload identity per Codex client process is configurable, but the SDK assigns none per agent — every thread in a client and every subagent a thread spawns authenticates as that one principal, and OpenAI attributes runs to the account, not the agent. SCIM can provision service accounts with userType ServiceAccount. The workload identity page cited on 2026-09-10 returned 404 today, so the federated token's lifetime is not re-verified.

original.mechanism: Service accounts and workload identity federation rules

steps.title: Give the automation its own identity
body: Create a service account (SCIM userType "ServiceAccount" is supported) and issue tokens from its Access tokens section; runs attribute to it.

steps.title: Prefer federation over stored tokens
body: Provider and rule creation, updates and archival generate audit events; disabling a rule revokes tokens already issued through it.

original.note: A service account or federated identity is the principal for the host process; every thread and tool call in it shares that principal, so a per-agent identity is the host application's to mint.

controls.mechanism: Workload identity federation or an injected CODEX_ACCESS_TOKEN / CODEX_API_KEY for the runtime's own credential, cli_auth_credentials_store = "ephemeral", and shell_environment_policy to keep it from commands; no step-time broker for tool credentials

steps.title: Authenticate the runtime without a stored secret
body: Set OPENAI_FEDERATION_RULE_ID and OPENAI_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE in the client's env so the workload exchanges its OIDC token or SPIFFE JWT-SVID instead of holding a Codex credential.

steps.title: Keep the credential in memory only
body: Set cli_auth_credentials_store = "ephemeral" in the host's system requirements.toml so the process never writes auth.json; cloud-managed values of this key are ignored.

steps.title: Keep the credential away from the agent's commands
body: Set shell_environment_policy inherit = "core" and ignore_default_excludes = false so variables containing KEY, SECRET or TOKEN are stripped from spawned commands.

controls.note: Partial on the architecture rule: the runtime's own OpenAI credential can be keyless (federation) and kept in memory, but nothing brokers tool credentials at step time — MCP servers read bearer_token_env_var and env_vars from the process environment, and commands inherit whatever shell_environment_policy leaves. By the documented default (ignore_default_excludes = true) variables named KEY, SECRET or TOKEN pass to commands, which covers CODEX_API_KEY and CODEX_ACCESS_TOKEN unless the policy strips them; the non-interactive page warns against setting CODEX_API_KEY job-wide where repository code runs. The TypeScript env option replaces process.env for the CLI (the SDK re-injects CODEX_API_KEY); Python's CodexConfig.env is merged over the inherited environment. Short-lived per-step tool credentials need a secrets manager or workload identity for each tool.

original.mechanism: CODEX_API_KEY / CODEX_ACCESS_TOKEN environment variables, cli_auth_credentials_store = "ephemeral"

steps.title: Keep the credential in memory only
body: Set cli_auth_credentials_store = "ephemeral" so nothing is written to auth.json; supply CODEX_API_KEY or CODEX_ACCESS_TOKEN from your secret manager.

original.note: The environment variable is the host's storage choice; ephemeral mode keeps the credential out of the on-disk store, not out of the process. Commands the agent runs read the host environment unless the sandbox policy strips it.

controls.mechanism: [rules] prefix_rule decisions for shell commands, mcp_servers.<id>.enabled_tools / disabled_tools and tools.<tool>.approval_mode by tool name, and a managed PreToolUse hook in requirements.toml (attach point)

steps.title: Forbid or gate command prefixes
body: Add prefix_rule(pattern = [...], decision = "forbidden" or "prompt") in a .rules file or the requirements.toml [rules] table; rules are experimental and govern commands run outside the sandbox.

steps.title: Limit MCP tools by name
body: Set mcp_servers.<id>.enabled_tools and disabled_tools, and tools.<tool>.approval_mode, in the host config or the client's config overrides.

steps.title: Gate every local tool call with a managed hook
body: Define [[hooks.PreToolUse]] in requirements.toml with allow_managed_hooks_only = true and [features].hooks = true, and return permissionDecision "deny" (or exit code 2) to block the call.

controls.note: Partial on the rule applied to Codex CLI today: the declarative layer is shell command prefixes (experimental, for commands outside the sandbox) and MCP tool names without arguments; the per-call gate over arguments for file edits, MCP and other local tools is the deployer's hook script, an attach point. Hosted tools such as WebSearch skip hooks, "some specialized tool paths can opt out", and permissionDecision "ask" is parsed but unsupported, so the call continues. Non-managed hooks run only after hash-based trust review, which the TypeScript SDK cannot bypass, so ship hooks as managed ones. Escalate-to-human lands in approvals, which neither SDK surfaces to a person (see AML.M0029). Enforced by the Codex runtime on the host, outside the model.

original.mechanism: PreToolUse / PermissionRequest hooks and [rules] on the host

steps.title: Gate tool calls with a hook
body: A PreToolUse hook returning permissionDecision "deny" blocks the call for every SDK thread; managed hooks in requirements.toml cannot be bypassed.

original.note: Hooks and [rules] on the host apply to every thread the SDK opens; the hook logic is the host application's to write and fail closed.

controls.mechanism: None in the SDK; per-user entitlements come from an MCP or data-access gateway, or from one client per user carrying that user's token; service-account plugins scope connectors to the workflow's own account

evidence.title: Codex SDK — no retrieval or identity passthrough in the thread API (2026-09-25)
Service accounts — plugins configured per account, not inherited from the creator (2026-09-25)
Configuration Reference — mcp_servers.<id>.bearer_token_env_var and env_vars (2026-09-25)

controls.note: External on the rule applied to the Claude Agent SDK: the SDK has no on-behalf-of passthrough and no per-call credential hook. Files are read with the host account's rights inside the sandbox profile, MCP servers use the token the host configured for each server, and plugins act as the service account they were configured on. An MCP or data-access gateway that applies the requesting user's entitlements, or a client per user carrying that user's token in bearer_token_env_var, supplies per-user scoping.

original.mechanism: Not offered
original.note: Rated external on the same rule as the Claude Agent SDK: the SDK retrieves nothing itself; the host account and working directory decide what its tools can read, and per-user scoping is the host application's.

evidence.title: Vendor docs index, reviewed for the integration point (2026-09-10)

controls.mechanism: Sandbox preset and additionalDirectories per thread or turn, permission profiles (default_permissions, permissions.<name>.filesystem) and mcp_servers.<id>.enabled_tools through config overrides, custom agent files with their own sandbox_mode and mcp_servers, bounded on the host by requirements.toml

steps.title: Choose the preset per thread
body: Pass Sandbox.read_only or Sandbox.workspace_write (TypeScript sandboxMode) at thread creation or on a turn; the setting applies to that turn and later turns.

steps.title: Scope paths with a permission profile
body: Pass config default_permissions and a permissions.<name>.filesystem table (for example "/path/to/project/.env" = "deny") through the client's config or configOverrides.

steps.title: Limit MCP tools
body: Set enabled_tools / disabled_tools per [mcp_servers.<name>] in the host config or overrides.

steps.title: Narrow subagents
body: Give each custom agent file under .codex/agents/ its own sandbox_mode and mcp_servers; omitted settings inherit from the parent.

controls.note: Partial on the architecture rule: a thread's grant is well scoped by configuration (read or write, filesystem paths, network, shell prefixes, MCP tools by name, the service account's plugins), enforced by the runtime outside the model and bounded host-wide by allowed_sandbox_modes, but a delegation hop is not reliably narrower. Subagents inherit the parent's sandbox, approval and MCP servers unless a custom agent file overrides them, and the subagents page says the parent's live runtime overrides (sandbox and approval choices, including flags such as --yolo) are reapplied to a spawned child even when the custom agent file sets different defaults; the SDKs set the sandbox that way (TypeScript passes --sandbox), so a custom agent's narrower sandbox_mode is not guaranteed. The model chooses which agent type to spawn.

original.mechanism: Sandbox preset per thread or turn; [mcp_servers] enabled_tools

steps.title: Choose the preset per thread
body: Pass Sandbox.read_only or Sandbox.workspace_write at thread creation or on a turn; the setting applies to that turn and later turns.

steps.title: Limit MCP tools
body: enabled_tools / disabled_tools per [mcp_servers.<name>] in the host config.

original.note: Application integration required: the host chooses the sandbox preset per thread and which MCP tools are enabled; requirements.toml on the host is the only fleet-level constraint.

controls.mechanism: Per-server credentials (mcp_servers.<id>.env_vars, bearer_token_env_var), shell_environment_policy for commands, and the TypeScript env option that replaces process.env for the CLI; agents and subagents in a client share the process credentials

steps.title: Pass each MCP server only its own variables
body: List a stdio server's variables in mcp_servers.<id>.env_vars and point an HTTP server at its own token with bearer_token_env_var.

steps.title: Strip credentials from commands
body: Set shell_environment_policy inherit = "core", ignore_default_excludes = false and filters such as "AWS_*" = "exclude".

steps.title: Control what reaches the runtime at all
body: Pass an explicit env to new Codex({ env }) so the CLI does not inherit the Node.js process environment.

controls.note: Partial on the architecture rule (per-server credential config only): each MCP server and the command environment can be limited to the credentials meant for it, but every thread and subagent in a client shares the process's credentials and the runtime's own token, there is no token exchange or audience scoping per agent, and Python's CodexConfig.env adds to the inherited environment rather than replacing it. A per-agent client with its own service account, or a credential broker, is the fix.

original.mechanism: Service-account attribution; no on-behalf-of exchange
original.note: The agent holds one token for the whole run; there is no per-user delegation inside a thread.

steps.title: Attribute runs to the automation identity
body: Tokens from a service account make runs attribute to that account in analytics and audit records.

controls.mechanism: agents.max_concurrent_threads_per_session / agents.enabled, mcp_servers.<id>.tool_timeout_sec, and workspace usage limits or API billing limits at the account; no turn, token or wall-clock cap per run

steps.title: Cap subagent fan-out
body: Set agents.max_concurrent_threads_per_session (or agents.enabled = false) in the host config or the client's config overrides.

steps.title: Bound tool time
body: Set mcp_servers.<id>.tool_timeout_sec (default 60 seconds) for each MCP server.

steps.title: Set workspace spend limits
body: Plan-dependent usage limits and spend controls cover eligible Codex activity; API billing is separate.

controls.note: Partial on the architecture rule: child concurrency and per-tool time are configuration limits, but the SDK options carry no max turns, token or cost budget, or run timeout (the app-server's thread goal tokenBudget is not exposed by either SDK), and concurrency does not bound total children over a run. Wall-clock limits are the host's code (a TypeScript AbortSignal, Python turn.interrupt()); account-level limits are hard but not per run, and the usage-limits page says they are not a universal Codex limit and do not govern API Platform billing.

original.mechanism: agents.max_concurrent_threads_per_session; workspace usage limits

steps.title: Cap subagent fan-out
body: Set agents.max_concurrent_threads_per_session (or agents.enabled = false) in the host config.

steps.title: Set workspace spend limits
body: Plan-dependent usage limits and spend controls cover eligible Codex activity; API billing is separate.

original.note: Sub-limits: concurrency (max_concurrent_threads_per_session, hard) and workspace usage limits (hard at the account). No turn, runtime or spend cap per thread — the host application supplies those.

controls.mechanism: Managed PostToolUse and UserPromptSubmit hooks (attach points), ExternalMessage labelling of other agents' content, and web_search mode; no built-in classifier for SDK runs

steps.title: Screen tool output in a managed PostToolUse hook
body: Return decision "block" (or exit code 2) so Codex replaces the tool result with the hook's feedback before the model continues; it covers shell, apply_patch, MCP and local function tools.

steps.title: Screen inbound prompts
body: A UserPromptSubmit hook can block a prompt before the turn uses it.

steps.title: Keep live web content out
body: Set the thread's webSearchMode to "disabled" or "cached", and allowed_web_search_modes in requirements.toml.

controls.note: Partial on the architecture rule: the hooks are attach points — nothing is classified until the deployer supplies the detector — and hosted web search skips them. ExternalMessage gives another agent's text tool-level authority but does not screen it. Prisma AIRS prompt scanning names the app, CLI, IDE and cloud, not the SDK, excludes Platform API-key sessions (the TypeScript apiKey / CODEX_API_KEY path) and never scans tool results. Headless runs have no person at an approval prompt, so the sandbox and egress rules are the backstop; an AI or MCP gateway classifier covers the rest.

original.mechanism: Sandbox default and network off; Guardian auto-review where approvals are delegated
original.note: Headless runs have no human at the approval prompt, so the sandbox and egress rules are the defence.

steps.title: Keep network off in workspace_write
body: The default workspace-write sandbox keeps network off; the docs warn injection can make the agent fetch untrusted instructions.

controls.mechanism: otel.log_user_prompt = false (trace-content exclusion), managed UserPromptSubmit / PreToolUse / PostToolUse hooks (attach points), ephemeral threads, deny_read and shell_environment_policy (minimisation); no built-in detector for SDK runs

steps.title: Keep prompt text out of telemetry
body: Leave otel.log_user_prompt = false so exported codex.user_prompt events carry length only.

steps.title: Attach a scanner in managed hooks
body: A UserPromptSubmit hook can block a prompt and a PreToolUse hook can deny or rewrite a call (permissionDecision "allow" with updatedInput) after your detector reads it.

steps.title: Deny secret paths
body: [permissions.filesystem] deny_read in requirements.toml applies to SDK threads too.

controls.note: Partial on the architecture rule: log_user_prompt = false is trace-content exclusion (minimisation, not detection), and the hooks are an attach point where a scanner can block or rewrite — no scanner ships. Tool results still reach the rollout JSONL and OTel tool-result snippets unredacted. deny_read, shell_environment_policy and ephemeral threads keep data away from the agent or off disk but inspect nothing. Prisma AIRS is not documented for the SDK and skips API-key sessions.

original.mechanism: deny_read globs and shell_environment_policy on the host

steps.title: Deny secret paths
body: [permissions.filesystem] deny_read in requirements.toml applies to SDK threads too.

original.note: deny_read and shell_environment_policy restrict what the agent can read; nothing inspects prompt, upload or output content — that is the host application's proxy or endpoint DLP.

controls.mechanism: Not applicable — the SDK ships no retrieval store or index

evidence.title: Codex SDK — thread/turn API with no retrieval store or index (2026-09-25)

controls.note: Not applicable: the SDK ships no retrieval corpus, embedding store or index to namespace or screen. Web search is a tool, not a corpus the deployer ingests into (its exposure is under input guardrails). Any corpus an application attaches through MCP or files owns index scoping and ingest trust — record it on that application or MCP server.

original.mechanism: Not applicable
original.note: Conditional: the SDK ships no retrieval store; any RAG the host adds is the host's control to record on the host application.

evidence.title: Vendor docs index, reviewed for applicability (2026-09-10)

controls.mechanism: The runtime's approval requests (item/commandExecution/requestApproval, item/fileChange/requestApproval) bound to the item, command and cwd, triggered by sandbox escalations, prompt rules and MCP approval_mode; neither SDK surfaces them to a person

steps.title: Route approvals to a person through the app-server
body: Build an app-server client that answers item/commandExecution/requestApproval and item/fileChange/requestApproval (itemId, threadId, turnId, command, cwd) with accept or decline.

steps.title: Name the actions that need approval
body: Use prefix_rule decision = "prompt" for commands and mcp_servers.<id>.tools.<tool>.approval_mode = "prompt" for MCP tools.

steps.title: Refuse the AI reviewer
body: Set allowed_approvals_reviewers = ["user"] in requirements.toml, or pass ApprovalMode.deny_all so escalations fail rather than being auto-reviewed.

controls.note: Partial on the architecture rule: the runtime suspends an item and asks with a request bound to that exact item (itemId, command, cwd), but neither SDK lets a person answer it. Python's public ApprovalMode offers deny_all (approval "never") or the default auto_review (a reviewer agent, which never counts), and the client's internal default handler accepts every command and file-change request it receives; the TypeScript SDK runs codex exec, where an action that needs fresh approval fails. Human approval exists only in an app-server client the deployer writes, and fires only for escalations, prompt rules and MCP approval modes — commands inside the sandbox run unprompted. Expiry of a pending approval is not documented.

original.mechanism: approval_policy on the host; the SDK page documents sandbox presets, not an approval callback
original.note: Could not verify an SDK-level approval handler from the fetched page; treat headless runs as unattended.

steps.title: Decide the approval policy for headless use
body: approval_policy "on-request" versus "never" is a host config choice; requirements.toml can forbid "never".

controls.mechanism: OS sandbox of the local runtime (Seatbelt, bwrap plus seccomp, Windows sandbox) with presets per thread, bounded on the host by allowed_sandbox_modes and allowed_approval_policies; commands run on the SDK's host

steps.title: Run threads in read-only or workspace-write
body: Pass Sandbox.read_only or Sandbox.workspace_write (TypeScript sandboxMode); Sandbox.full_access runs without filesystem restrictions.

steps.title: Remove full access and escalation on the host
body: Set allowed_sandbox_modes = ["read-only", "workspace-write"] and allowed_approval_policies = ["never"] in requirements.toml so full access is refused and escalations fail instead of being auto-reviewed.

steps.title: Install bubblewrap on Linux hosts
body: Package bwrap on every Linux host; without it Codex falls back to a helper that needs unprivileged user namespaces and warns at startup when neither works.

steps.title: Run the host in a container
body: Where the sandbox cannot start inside Docker, the vendor says to make the container the isolation boundary.

controls.note: Partial by the core sandbox rule and the architecture rule: the agent can step out by default — Python threads start with ApprovalMode.auto_review, so a reviewer agent approves escalations beyond the sandbox, and full access is one argument away unless requirements.toml removes it. Even when pinned, commands run under an OS sandbox on the same host as the SDK (the orchestration tier), not in a separate runtime; fail-closed behaviour without bwrap or user namespaces is not documented, and inside Docker the sandbox may not start. Outside the boundary: the host application, the Codex process, MCP servers, hooks and web search.

original.mechanism: OS sandbox of the local runtime, presets settable per thread

steps.title: Run in workspace_write or read_only
body: Sandbox.full_access runs without filesystem restrictions; pin allowed_sandbox_modes on the host to exclude it.

original.note: Inside the boundary: commands the local runtime executes, under the preset the host sets per thread. Outside: MCP servers and the host application's own code. The preset is a host decision, so the boundary exists only where the application requests it.

controls.mechanism: requirements.toml [mcp_servers] identity allowlist and [marketplaces] restrict_to_allowed_sources enforced by the runtime, and plugins configured per service account; no inventory of agents built on the SDK

steps.title: Refuse unlisted servers and plugin sources
body: Add [mcp_servers.<id>] identity entries and [marketplaces] restrict_to_allowed_sources = true with allowed_sources in requirements.toml; unmatched servers are disabled and unmatched sources rejected.

steps.title: Configure plugins per service account
body: In the service account's Plugins section add only the plugins the workflow needs; it does not inherit its creator's plugins or connected apps.

controls.note: Partial on the architecture rule (a list without a registry): the host's allowlists are enforced when a thread loads tools, but they carry no owner, version or approval record and are not reconciled with any catalogue. Nothing inventories the agents built on the SDK or the custom agent files under .codex/agents/; keep that registry in the organisation's AI governance platform.

original.mechanism: [mcp_servers] approved identities and [marketplaces] on the host

steps.title: Allowlist tool servers
body: Only servers whose name and identity match an approved [mcp_servers] entry are enabled.

original.note: The host's approved identities are configuration, not an inventory of the agents built on the SDK; record those in the organisation's inventory.

controls.mechanism: Python turn.interrupt() (app-server turn/interrupt) and Codex.close(), TypeScript AbortSignal on run(), and service-account or token revocation; children not documented

steps.title: Interrupt a running turn
body: Start the turn with thread.turn(...) and call interrupt() on the handle; the app-server ends the turn with status "interrupted".

steps.title: Abort a TypeScript turn
body: Pass { signal } (an AbortSignal) in the turn options of run() or runStreamed(); the SDK hands it to the spawned codex exec process.

steps.title: Revoke the identity
body: Disable or delete the service account, which revokes all of its active tokens, or revoke one token.

controls.note: Partial on the architecture rule (in-process abort only): the host can stop the current turn — the app-server ends it as interrupted, the AbortSignal terminates the codex exec child, and Python's close() terminates the app-server — but whether spawned subagent threads and commands already started stop with it is not documented (descendant handling is documented only for archive and delete). Identity revocation blocks new requests; its effect on a turn in flight is not documented. The host application owns the stop path, and its delay is the process signal it sends.

original.mechanism: Token revocation, service-account disable, federation rule disable

steps.title: Revoke at the identity
body: Disabling or deleting the service account revokes all of its tokens; disabling a federation provider or rule revokes tokens issued through it.

original.note: Revocation stops the next request; the host process the SDK runs in, and any command it has already started, continue until the application stops them. The application owns the stop path and its delay.

controls.mechanism: requirements.toml [mcp_servers.<id>] identity allowlist (command executable and args, or url) and [marketplaces] restrict_to_allowed_sources; no hashing of tool definitions

steps.title: Allowlist MCP servers by name and identity
body: Add [mcp_servers.<id>] identity = { command = ... } for stdio or { url = ... } for streamable HTTP; an unmatched server is disabled and an empty table disables all.

steps.title: Pin stdio invocations
body: Use the structured identity.command form with executable and args matchers ("exact", "prefix" or "regex") so the approved argument list, including a versioned package, must match.

steps.title: Restrict plugin sources
body: Set [marketplaces] restrict_to_allowed_sources = true with allowed_sources rules.

controls.note: Partial by the rule applied to every vendor: an allowlist admits servers but verifies nothing they serve. Exact argument matching can pin a package version for stdio servers only (cwd, env and env_vars are not matched), URL-matched remote servers stay unpinned, and nothing scans tool descriptions, hashes tool definitions or re-gates a server whose definitions change. The SDK adds nothing of its own; an MCP gateway or registry supplies definition scanning and pinning.

original.mechanism: [mcp_servers] identity allowlist and marketplaces.restrict_to_allowed_sources

steps.title: Lock MCP and plugin sources
body: An empty [mcp_servers] table disables all servers; restrict_to_allowed_sources rejects unmatched marketplaces.

original.note: Admission by identity through the host's requirements.toml; the SDK adds nothing of its own. Admission is not integrity — nothing pins the tool descriptions a server returns.

controls.mechanism: Command network off by default (sandbox_workspace_write.network_access, TypeScript networkAccessEnabled) and the experimental domain allowlist ([experimental_network] in requirements.toml, or features.network_proxy with permissions.<name>.network.domains)

steps.title: Keep command network off
body: Leave networkAccessEnabled unset or false (sandbox_workspace_write.network_access = false) unless a workflow needs it.

steps.title: Enforce a domain allowlist
body: Set [experimental_network] enabled = true and managed_allowed_domains_only = true with [experimental_network.domains] allow and deny entries in requirements.toml; deny wins.

controls.note: Partial on the rule applied to Codex CLI: the domain allowlist is experimental and covers sandboxed commands only — not web search, apps, MCP servers, Codex's own model and telemetry traffic, or the host application — and full access removes it. Network on or off is the reliable lever; the host's container egress, firewall or proxy covers the rest.

original.mechanism: sandbox_workspace_write.network_access and [experimental_network] domain lists
original.note: Domain rules cover sandboxed commands only, not MCP servers.

steps.title: Allowlist domains
body: [experimental_network] with managed_allowed_domains_only = true in requirements.toml.

controls.mechanism: Package mirror or artifact repository with malware scanning; Codex's integration points are the [experimental_network.domains] allowlist that forces sandboxed installs through the mirror and the pinned runtime

evidence.title: Managed configuration — [experimental_network] domains and [marketplaces] allowed_sources (2026-09-25)
Python SDK FAQ — published builds pin an exact CLI runtime (2026-09-25)
Configuration Reference — features.skill_mcp_dependency_install on by default (2026-09-25)

controls.note: External: Codex scans nothing it downloads or installs — plugins, skills, MCP dependencies installed for skills (features.skill_mcp_dependency_install, on by default) or packages its commands fetch. Admission scanning belongs at the organisation's package mirror; the integration point is an [experimental_network.domains] allowlist that admits only the mirror for sandboxed commands. The Python package pins an exact runtime (openai-codex 0.157.0 requires openai-codex-cli-bin==0.157.0), and CodexConfig(codex_bin=...) or the TypeScript codexPathOverride points at a vetted binary — supply-chain pinning, not file analysis. No model weights load in the SDK.

original.mechanism: Not applicable
original.note: No model artifacts are loaded by the SDK.

evidence.title: Vendor docs index, reviewed for applicability (2026-09-10)

original.mechanism: Pinned runtime (Python SDK) and codex_bin path
original.note: Rated like the Claude Agent SDK: a pinned runtime and codex_bin path fix the binary version, which is supporting evidence for an inventory, not an AI BOM — nothing is signed or manifested, and the plugins, MCP servers and models a session composes are not recorded. Keep the pin and generate the BOM from your lockfile and configuration.

steps.title: Pin the runtime
body: Point CodexConfig(codex_bin=...) at a vetted binary rather than whatever is on PATH.

settings.name: Service accounts
settings.where: Workspace settings › Service accounts (chatgpt.com/admin/service-accounts) › Create, then Plugins, Access tokens, Share
settings.recommended: One service account per workflow, with its own groups, roles and plugins, its token passed as CODEX_ACCESS_TOKEN
settings.why: Runs act and are audited as the automation, not an engineer, and disabling or deleting the account revokes all of its tokens at once.

settings.name: Access token expiration limit
settings.where: Workspace settings › Permissions & roles › Access tokens (or the Codex Local section)
settings.recommended: 90 days
settings.why: Bounds how long a service-account or personal token leaked from a runner keeps working; the limit applies to new tokens only.

settings.name: OPENAI_FEDERATION_RULE_ID with OPENAI_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE
settings.where: The client's env (TypeScript new Codex({ env }), Python CodexConfig(env=...)), with a federation rule configured for the workspace
settings.default: Unset (a stored token or API key)
settings.recommended: Set on every runner that can present an OIDC token or SPIFFE JWT-SVID
settings.why: The workload exchanges its platform identity for a short-lived Codex token, so no long-lived credential sits in the CI secret store.

settings.name: cli_auth_credentials_store
settings.where: Host system requirements.toml → cli_auth_credentials_store
settings.recommended: "ephemeral" on shared or temporary runners
settings.why: The credential stays in process memory and is never written to CODEX_HOME/auth.json for the next job on the runner to read.

settings.name: env
settings.where: TypeScript new Codex({ env }); Python CodexConfig(env=...)
settings.default: Unset (the CLI inherits the whole process environment)
settings.recommended: An explicit map with only the variables the run needs
settings.why: The Codex process — and every command it spawns — does not inherit the service's other keys and tokens from process.env.

settings.name: shell_environment_policy
settings.where: Host config.toml, or the client's config / configOverrides → [shell_environment_policy]
settings.recommended: inherit = "core", ignore_default_excludes = false, filters excluding *_TOKEN, *_SECRET, *_KEY and cloud prefixes
settings.why: Commands the agent runs do not see the runtime's own Codex token or other credentials present in its environment.

settings.name: mcp_servers.<id>.env_vars and bearer_token_env_var
settings.where: Host config.toml or the client's config overrides → [mcp_servers.<id>]
settings.recommended: Each MCP server given only its own variables, and HTTP servers their own token variable
settings.why: A compromised or malicious server cannot read the credentials meant for another server or the runtime.

settings.name: permissions.filesystem.deny_read
settings.where: Host requirements.toml → [permissions.filesystem] deny_read
settings.recommended: ["/**/*.env", "~/.ssh", "~/.aws", "~/.config/gcloud"] plus the runner's secret paths
settings.why: SDK threads cannot read secret files into the model's context, whatever permissions the calling code asks for.

settings.name: CODEX_HOME
settings.where: The client's env → CODEX_HOME (an existing directory)
settings.recommended: A separate directory per tenant or workflow
settings.why: Sessions, logs, config and auth for one tenant never share a root another tenant's runs can read or resume.

settings.name: ephemeral (thread_start)
settings.where: Python codex.thread_start(ephemeral=True)
settings.recommended: True for one-shot jobs
settings.why: Threads that handled client material are not kept on the runner's disk to be resumed or read later.

settings.name: ExternalMessage
settings.where: Python thread.run(ExternalMessage(tool_name=..., content=...))
settings.recommended: Every input from another agent, tool or application passed as an ExternalMessage
settings.why: That content reaches the model as untrusted tool output, below user and developer instructions, instead of as the operator's request.

settings.name: sandbox (Sandbox presets)
settings.where: Python thread_start(sandbox=Sandbox.workspace_write); TypeScript startThread({ sandboxMode })
settings.default: The runtime's configured default (read-only for codex exec)
settings.recommended: Sandbox.workspace_write (read_only for review jobs); never full_access
settings.why: Each thread runs inside the OS sandbox with writes limited to the workspace; full access removes every filesystem restriction.

settings.name: allowed_sandbox_modes
settings.where: Host requirements.toml → allowed_sandbox_modes
settings.recommended: ["read-only", "workspace-write"]
settings.why: Code that asks for full access is refused on that host, so one argument cannot take a thread out of the sandbox.

settings.name: approval_mode (ApprovalMode)
settings.where: Python thread_start(approval_mode=ApprovalMode.deny_all); TypeScript approvalPolicy
settings.recommended: ApprovalMode.deny_all for unattended runs, or an app-server client that routes escalations to a person
settings.why: A request to leave the sandbox fails rather than being approved by another model; commands inside the sandbox still run.

settings.name: rules.prefix_rules
settings.where: Host requirements.toml → [rules] prefix_rules
settings.recommended: "forbidden" for destructive and deploy commands; "prompt" for git push
settings.why: Commands the workflow must never run outside the sandbox are refused however the prompt is phrased; requirements rules cannot allow.

settings.name: PreToolUse and PostToolUse with allow_managed_hooks_only
settings.where: Host requirements.toml → [hooks], [features] hooks = true, allow_managed_hooks_only = true
settings.recommended: A PreToolUse hook calling your policy and DLP check, a PostToolUse hook screening tool output; only managed hooks load
settings.why: Every shell, apply_patch and MCP call can be denied, and every result blocked, by the firm's own checker before the model continues; hosted tools skip hooks.

settings.name: mcp_servers.<id>.identity
settings.where: Host requirements.toml → [mcp_servers.<id>] identity
settings.recommended: The approved servers, stdio by executable and args, HTTP by url
settings.why: A server the code or host config adds outside the list is disabled before any thread can call it.

settings.name: mcp_servers.<id>.enabled_tools / disabled_tools
settings.where: Host config.toml or the client's config overrides → [mcp_servers.<id>]
settings.recommended: The tools each workflow needs, by name
settings.why: Tools a server adds later, or write tools the job does not need, are never exposed to the agent.

settings.name: mcp_servers.<id>.tools.<tool>.approval_mode
settings.where: Host config.toml or the client's config overrides → [mcp_servers.<id>.tools.<tool>]
settings.recommended: "prompt" for tools that change records or send data
settings.why: Consequential MCP calls raise an approval request the application must answer instead of running unattended.

settings.name: marketplaces.restrict_to_allowed_sources
settings.where: Host requirements.toml → [marketplaces] restrict_to_allowed_sources, allowed_sources
settings.recommended: true, with your organisation's plugin repository pinned by Git URL
settings.why: Plugins the runtime loads for SDK threads come only from sources you curate.

settings.name: agents.max_concurrent_threads_per_session
settings.where: Host config.toml or the client's config overrides → [agents]
settings.recommended: An explicit cap sized to the runner (4 is a reasonable start)
settings.why: One run cannot fan out into an unbounded number of subagents and burn the workspace's budget.

settings.name: mcp_servers.<id>.tool_timeout_sec
settings.where: Host config.toml or the client's config overrides → [mcp_servers.<id>]
settings.recommended: The longest a call to that server should take
settings.why: A hung or deliberately slow MCP server cannot hold a run, and its compute, open indefinitely.

settings.name: interrupt()
settings.where: Python thread.turn(...).interrupt(); TypeScript run(input, { signal }) with an AbortSignal
settings.recommended: Wired to your job controller's cancel and to a run-time ceiling
settings.why: An operator or watchdog can stop a running turn at once rather than waiting for it to finish.

settings.name: sandbox_workspace_write.network_access
settings.where: Host config.toml → [sandbox_workspace_write] network_access; TypeScript startThread({ networkAccessEnabled })
settings.recommended: false unless the workflow needs hosts, then through the managed allowlist below
settings.why: Commands start without network, so injected instructions cannot post the repository or secrets out.

settings.name: [experimental_network] with managed_allowed_domains_only
settings.where: Host requirements.toml → [experimental_network] enabled, managed_allowed_domains_only, domains
settings.recommended: true / true, allowing your source control, package mirror and approved APIs
settings.why: Sandboxed commands reach only listed hosts and calling code cannot widen the list; experimental, so validate per runtime version.

settings.name: web_search
settings.where: Host config.toml → web_search; TypeScript startThread({ webSearchMode })
settings.recommended: "cached" — don't pass "live" for jobs over untrusted input
settings.why: Search results come from OpenAI's index rather than arbitrary live pages, cutting exposure to injected web content.

settings.name: otel.exporter and otel.trace_exporter
settings.where: Host config.toml or the client's config overrides → [otel]
settings.recommended: otlp-http to your collector, environment = "prod"
settings.why: Every run's API, approval and tool-decision events land in the SIEM tagged with the conversation id and the service account.

settings.name: otel.log_user_prompt
settings.where: Host config.toml or the client's config overrides → [otel] log_user_prompt
settings.recommended: false
settings.why: Tool decisions are exported without the prompt text, keeping client material out of the SIEM.

tools.name: OpenAI Dots

variants.name: Personal dot in ChatGPT
Personal dot in Slack and Microsoft Teams
variants.note: Owner-directed work with channel-visible output; Microsoft Teams is an invite-only alpha.

summary: A continuing personal agent with a cloud computer, connected apps and cross-task context. It can delegate Codex or Work tasks. Optional local access introduces another execution boundary; a desktop interface alone does not make the loop customer-operated. Local execution on a connected computer runs through the ChatGPT desktop app, whose local reach is the endpoint record toolChatgptDesktop.

This initial record covers documented personal-dot controls. Specialist dots with dedicated organizational identities are focused enterprise pilots; planned Agent 365 integration is not credited as available enforcement.

facts.label: Plans
facts.value: Gradual rollout: Pro 100, Pro 200 and Pro 500 (over 18, outside the EEA, UK and Switzerland); Business Premium and Enterprise worldwide. On Enterprise dots are off by default and a workspace administrator must enable them.

facts.label: Inference & routing
facts.value: OpenAI operates the service. Enterprise model controls and defaults do not apply to the main dot; tasks it delegates to Work or Codex follow those products' controls.

facts.label: Data leaving the device
facts.value: Connected information and task context reach the hosted service. Connecting a local computer additionally permits local files and commands; local browser access is a separate route.

facts.label: Retention & training
facts.value: Dot context persists until deletion; separately stored artifacts have separate lifetimes. Business workspace data is not used for training by default; personal-plan settings differ.

facts.label: Docs index
facts.value: Dots member guide (learn.chatgpt.com/docs/dots) and workspace admin guide.

items.title: Keep persistent and delegated authority distinct
body: Review connected accounts, browser sessions and child tasks separately. A dot's display identity does not establish the effective principal at each destination.

links.title: Dots launch and specialist pilot scope

items.title: Treat automatic review as a bounded safeguard
body: Auto-review checks selected actions. Proactive research uses restricted read-only tools; subsequent actions follow normal action rules. Neither establishes complete input screening.

riskNotes.note: Untrusted pages, connected content and retained context can influence later tasks.
Browser sessions, connected grants and retained context need separate access and deletion decisions.
Check the initiating owner, downstream credential and audience for each delegated or channel-visible effect.

controls.mechanism: Enterprise role permissions govern access to dots and optional capabilities.

steps.title: Limit workspace access
body: In Admin Console > Permissions > Workspace default > Workspace capabilities keep Use dots (Beta) off and grant it through a custom role; grants add up, so check every role assigned directly or through groups.

controls.note: Feature access is separate from downstream app authorization and website sessions.

controls.mechanism: Workspace capability switches and existing plugin/action permissions constrain supported routes.

steps.title: Enable only required capabilities
body: Review Use a browser, Allow network access and Allow computer use (Let agents use cloud computers), Use password manager, Allow local computer access under Use dots, and each app's access and allowed actions in Plugins separately. Apply least privilege in each destination service too.

controls.note: Coarse capability admission does not prove argument-level authorization for every action.

controls.mechanism: Supported actions expose confirmation or handoff rules.

steps.title: Require review for consequential work
body: In Settings > Personalization > Custom rules, select Ask before taking action or Hand off to you for the relevant action, and avoid Take action without asking for anything consequential. Rules stop applying if the workspace turns off Use custom rules for dots.

tools.name: Secure MCP Tunnel (tunnel-client)

variants.name: tunnel-client (binary and ghcr.io/openai/tunnel-client container)

summary: Secure MCP Tunnel lets a private or localhost MCP server serve ChatGPT custom MCP plugins, the Responses API and Codex without inbound exposure: a customer-run tunnel-client polls api.openai.com (or mtls.api.openai.com) over outbound HTTPS, forwards each request to the local stdio or HTTP MCP server, and returns the response through the same tunnel.

The tunnel itself carries no inference; it is the connectivity leg between OpenAI's hosted chat and the organisation's tool server, which is why it sits on the enterprise-chat architecture. Tunnels are created, edited and deleted in Platform tunnel settings and associated with one or more Platform organisations or ChatGPT workspaces; tunnel-client authenticates with a Restricted runtime API key (CONTROL_PLANE_API_KEY, Tunnels Read + Use) created and revoked on the Platform API keys page, optionally adds control-plane mTLS, can present its own mTLS certificate to the MCP server, and supports outbound proxies and custom CA bundles.

Audit is split: tunnel.created / updated / deleted appear in Platform audit logs, but control-plane tunnel traffic is not emitted as Compliance Platform app events; app-level invocation and auth-lifecycle logging still applies when ChatGPT reaches the app through the tunnel.

On this path the target is our own MCP server, and consent there is its OAuth authorisation server's: the tunnel preserves protected-resource and authorisation-server metadata so the flow works, but sets none of its policy. controls.mechanism: Restricted runtime API key (Tunnels Read + Use) read from an env: or file: reference; key expiry and an organisation- or project-level maximum API key lifetime; optional control-plane mTLS binding; revocation on the Platform API keys page or the Admin API

steps.title: Mint a least-privilege runtime key
body: On the Platform API keys page create a Restricted key with Tunnels Read + Use and export it as CONTROL_PLANE_API_KEY; keep OPENAI_ADMIN_KEY and All keys out of the long-lived daemon.

steps.title: Keep the key out of argv and profiles
body: Set control_plane.api_key to file:/run/secrets/... (or env:) mounted from the secrets manager; tunnel-client resolves it at startup and redacts API keys from its support export.

steps.title: Cap the key's lifetime
body: Enforce a maximum API key lifetime at organisation or project level in Platform settings so new runtime keys must expire; rotate by creating the replacement, restarting tunnel-client with it, then deleting the old key.

steps.title: Drop the static key on AWS
body: Where tunnel-client runs on AWS, set control_plane.aws_identity_provider_id and aws_service_account_id (a project service account with Tunnels Read + Use) and leave the static API key unset; the client exchanges its role for a short-lived token kept in memory.

steps.title: Bind the key to a certificate
body: Activate a trust anchor at Organization settings > Security > Mutual TLS for the key's organisation or project and give tunnel-client control_plane.client_cert and client_key; a request with the key but no accepted certificate fails with certificate_required.

steps.title: Give each deployment its own runtime identity
body: On the Platform API keys page create a Restricted key with Tunnels Read + Use for each tunnel-client deployment, owned by a principal in the tunnel-runtime group, and never run the daemon on an admin key or an All key.

steps.title: Authenticate the tunnel to our server
body: Where the MCP server should see the tunnel as a caller, set MCP_CLIENT_CERT and MCP_CLIENT_KEY (MCP-side mTLS, HTTP bindings only) — a static credential that identifies the tunnel, not the user.

controls.note: Native by the drawing rule for a tunnel credential: it is scoped (a Restricted key with Tunnels Read + Use), held as a reference to the host's secret store rather than in the profile, rotatable under an enforced maximum lifetime, bindable to a client certificate so the key alone is not enough, and revocable centrally without redeploying — delete the key on the API keys page or through the Admin API, remove the principal's Tunnels Use, or delete the tunnel. Boundaries: the key is a bearer token sent to OpenAI on every poll and readable by whoever can read the host's environment or secret file; tunnel-client does not encrypt it (custody is the Kubernetes Secret, systemd credential or secrets manager the operator uses) and still accepts a literal value for compatibility; the reference is resolved at startup, so rotation needs a restart, and stdio bindings allow one instance per tunnel ID (a brief gap); the maximum lifetime binds only keys created after it is set; the propagation delay of a revocation is not documented. Other credentials on the path: a connector-forwarded Authorization bearer crosses OpenAI (strict-local-auth is unsupported), while MCP_EXTRA_HEADERS and MCP-side mTLS keep a backend credential on the final hop. The same rule reads Anthropic's MCP tunnel credentials (tokenVersion rotation, Tunnels API key revoked after setup) as meeting the tunnel test. A key created without an expiry, under no enforced maximum, lives until revoked, so a forgotten tunnel keeps polling until its key is revoked or the tunnel is deleted. By default the tunnel does not authenticate to our MCP server at all; MCP-side mTLS or a static MCP_EXTRA_HEADERS value are opt-in and static.

original.mechanism: CONTROL_PLANE_API_KEY from the environment; rotation and revocation in Platform tunnel settings

steps.title: Rotate the runtime key from Platform settings
body: All creation, rotation and revocation happens at platform.openai.com/settings/organization/tunnels.

original.note: The control-plane key is a long-lived stored secret in the host environment, readable by anyone with access to the tunnel-client process; rotation is manual in Platform settings.

controls.mechanism: Tunnel associations to named Platform organisations and ChatGPT workspaces; Tunnels Use held by a named group; tunnel-client exposes only its configured MCP bindings, allowlisted poll channels and labelled Harpoon targets

steps.title: Associate each tunnel narrowly
body: In Platform tunnel settings associate the tunnel only with the ChatGPT workspace and Platform organisations that should list or call it; each association is a context that can reach the server.

steps.title: Hold Use in one group
body: Grant Tunnels Read + Use through a custom organisation role assigned to the group that runs tunnel-client or attaches tunnels to apps, and keep Manage with tunnel managers.

steps.title: Expose only the intended servers
body: Configure only the intended --mcp.server-url or --mcp-command bindings, set control_plane.poll_channels as an allowlist (omitted channels are disabled), and register Harpoon targets by label so callers cannot choose hosts.

controls.note: Partial by the rule: server-level admission is admin-set and enforced — a tunnel serves only its associated contexts, only principals with Tunnels Use can run or attach it, and tunnel-client reaches only its configured bindings and labelled Harpoon targets — but there is no per-tool or read/write scoping, because tunnel-client forwards JSON-RPC unchanged; per-tool and per-group scoping belongs to the MCP gateway behind it and to ChatGPT's plugin and action controls (toolChatgptWeb). Caller authority is preserved: the connector's Authorization header goes only to the configured MCP origin, and OpenAI-internal, IP-forwarding and hop-by-hop headers are dropped; a static MCP_EXTRA_HEADERS credential adds the tunnel's own authority instead. Harpoon also auto-registers OAuth endpoints discovered from the MCP server's metadata when their hosts pass the private-host filters (loopback, RFC 1918 and ULA by default).

original.mechanism: Tunnel association to specific organisations or workspaces; Harpoon exposes only configured targets by label
original.note: Tool-level scoping belongs to the MCP server and the ChatGPT app's action controls.

steps.title: Scope discovery
body: Associate the tunnel only with the organisations or workspaces that should see it; Harpoon is bounded to configured targets, not a general proxy.

controls.mechanism: The MCP server or MCP gateway behind the tunnel enforces the user's entitlements from the connector Authorization header that tunnel-client forwards

evidence.title: tunnel-client architecture — OAuth-protected MCP (checked 2026-09-25)
Secure MCP Tunnel — OAuth

controls.note: The tunnel decides nothing about which records come back; the MCP server behind it does. tunnel-client forwards the connector's Authorization bearer only to the configured MCP origin, so retrieval runs with the user's entitlements when the MCP server validates that token against the source, and OAuth discovery travels through the tunnel so the server can stay private. A static MCP_EXTRA_HEADERS value or MCP-side client certificate authenticates the tunnel, not the user — used alone it turns retrieval into a service-principal read. Corpus scoping is the MCP server's or gateway's; the admin-granted corpus of the pin is toolChatgptWeb's.

original.mechanism: The MCP server behind the tunnel enforces per-user access
original.note: The tunnel forwards the caller's identity context only insofar as the MCP protocol carries it; whether retrieval is delegated or service-owned is decided by how the MCP server behind the tunnel authenticates callers.

evidence.title: Vendor docs index, reviewed for the integration point (2026-09-10)

controls.mechanism: Platform tunnel settings and GET /v1/tunnels list every tunnel with its organisation and workspace associations; tunnel.created / updated / deleted audit events record who changed them

steps.title: Treat the tunnel list as the register
body: List tunnels in Platform tunnel settings or with tunnel-client admin tunnels list (admin key, Tunnels Manage) and record in your registry the MCP server and owner behind each tunnel_id.

steps.title: Reconcile changes from the audit log
body: Pull tunnel.created, tunnel.updated and tunnel.deleted events from GET /v1/organization/audit_logs (event_types filter) to catch tunnels added outside the process.

steps.title: Read what sits behind a tunnel
body: On the tunnel host, /health/mcp reports the MCP server's self-reported name, version and tool names (loopback only) for the registry's capability descriptor.

controls.note: Partial by the rule (list plus enforcement, but no owner or approval record): only a tunnel created under Tunnels Manage and associated with the workspace can be selected, so the list is enforced by construction, but it records only name, description and associations (owner is the audit-log actor, and there is no approval state), and it registers the tunnel, not the MCP server or tools behind it. The ChatGPT apps built on a tunnel are listed in ChatGPT (toolChatgptWeb). Tunnels created in a personal Platform organisation never appear in the corporate list (cap-shadow-ai-discovery). A tunnel can be associated with several organisations or workspaces, and every association can reach the private server, so review associations as part of the register.

original.mechanism: Platform tunnel settings list every tunnel with its associations; tunnel.* audit events

steps.title: Treat tunnel settings as the register
body: Every tunnel endpoint is created and listed in Platform tunnel settings and its lifecycle appears as tunnel.created / updated / deleted in audit logs.

original.note: A register of tunnels and their associations, which is the inventory relevant to this product; the MCP servers behind them are registered where they are approved, not here.

controls.mechanism: None in the product; endpoint inventory and the egress proxy find unregistered tunnel-clients by binary, User-Agent and the tunnel ID in the poll path

evidence.title: tunnel-client README — What it does (control-plane headers; checked 2026-09-25)
Secure MCP Tunnel — personal Platform organisations

controls.note: Nothing in the product lists tunnels or tunnel-clients outside the corporate organisation, and the guide supports tunnels in personal Platform organisations. Integration point for SSE/CASB and EDR: tunnel-client identifies itself on every control-plane call with User-Agent oai-tunnel-client/<version> plus X-Tunnel-Client-Name, X-Tunnel-Client-Version and X-Tunnel-Client-Instance-Id headers and polls GET /v1/tunnels/{tunnel_id}/poll, so an inspecting proxy can extract tunnel IDs and reconcile them against the organisation's tunnel list; endpoint inventory finds the tunnel-client and bundled cloudflared binaries.

original.mechanism: None; the tunnel register shows only sanctioned servers

evidence.title: Vendor docs index, reviewed for the integration point (2026-09-10)

controls.mechanism: Platform audit logs API (tunnel.*, api_key.*, certificate and role events); tunnel-client structured logs, /metrics and client_instance_id correlation on the host; app invocation logs stay on the ChatGPT side

steps.title: Export the control-plane trail
body: Poll GET /v1/organization/audit_logs with an admin key, filtered to tunnel.created, tunnel.updated, tunnel.deleted and api_key.* events, into the SIEM.

steps.title: Ship the tunnel host's own record
body: Run tunnel-client with --log.format json and --log.file (LOG_FILE) forwarded off the host, and scrape /metrics; each process stamps its client_instance_id on control-plane requests and logs.

controls.note: Partial by the rule: only a control-plane admin audit log is exported programmatically. The guide says tunnel control-plane auth, long-poll and response traffic and individual transport requests are not emitted as ChatGPT Compliance Platform app events, so tool calls and their content are recorded on the app path (app invocation logs and APP_AUTH_LOG — toolChatgptWeb) and by our gateway, not by the tunnel. tunnel-client's own logs and metrics are operational (health, readiness, polling, failures); the docs describe no per-call audit event. Raw HTTP logging (--log.http-raw-unsafe) is off by default and unsafe, and the admin UI export is redacted. The host logs are alterable by whoever runs the host, so capture here is not tamper resistance.

original.mechanism: Platform audit logs for tunnel metadata; app-level invocation logs; tunnel-client /metrics and admin UI
original.note: Control-plane tunnel traffic is not emitted as Compliance Platform app events.

steps.title: Combine the three logs
body: Platform audit logs (tunnel.*), ChatGPT app invocation and auth-lifecycle logs, and tunnel-client's own /metrics and loopback-only /ui log export.

controls.mechanism: Stop tunnel-client; revoke the runtime key on the Platform API keys page; delete the tunnel in Platform tunnel settings (Tunnels Manage) or with tunnel-client admin tunnels delete

steps.title: Stop the client
body: Stop the tunnel-client process or scale its deployment to zero; the guide states that requests through the tunnel fail while the client is not connected.

steps.title: Revoke the runtime key
body: Delete the runtime API key on the Platform API keys page or with the Admin API project API key delete method, so no copy of the client can reconnect.

steps.title: Decommission the tunnel
body: Delete the tunnel in Platform tunnel settings or with tunnel-client admin tunnels delete <tunnel_id> --confirm (admin key with Tunnels Manage), which removes it for every associated organisation and workspace.

controls.note: Native by the drawing rule for this path: one operator action, taken outside the agent on a process that runs in our network, stops it; the guide documents that requests fail while the client is disconnected; and revoking the runtime key and deleting the tunnel end every associated workspace's use at once. Boundaries: an MCP call already forwarded completes at the MCP server, which the tunnel cannot cancel; the propagation delay of key revocation, Tunnels Use removal (role changes up to 30 minutes) and tunnel deletion is not documented. The ChatGPT app built on the tunnel and each user's OAuth grant to the MCP server are disabled in ChatGPT (toolChatgptWeb) and at the authorisation server.

original.mechanism: Delete or revoke the tunnel in Platform tunnel settings (Tunnels Read + Manage)

steps.title: Revoke the tunnel
body: Deleting the tunnel endpoint stops every associated organisation and workspace from reaching the server; stop tunnel-client as well.

settings.name: Tunnels — Read, Manage and Use
settings.where: platform.openai.com › Organization settings › Roles (custom role, Tunnels row), assigned through Groups
settings.recommended: Two roles on IdP-synced groups — tunnel managers Read + Manage, runtime users Read + Use — and nobody else
settings.why: Only named managers can create or repoint a tunnel and only named principals can run tunnel-client or attach it to an app; role changes take up to 30 minutes.

settings.name: Associations (Platform organizations and ChatGPT workspaces)
settings.where: Platform tunnel settings › (tunnel) › associated organizations and workspaces
settings.recommended: The owning Platform organization and the corporate ChatGPT workspace, plus only the organizations a reviewed Codex or API flow calls from
settings.why: Every association is another OpenAI context that can list the tunnel and call the private MCP server behind it.

settings.name: CONTROL_PLANE_API_KEY (control_plane.api_key)
settings.where: Profile YAML control_plane.api_key, --control-plane.api-key, or the CONTROL_PLANE_API_KEY environment variable
settings.default: Falls back to OPENAI_API_KEY when unset
settings.recommended: A Restricted key with Tunnels Read + Use, referenced as a file: or env: reference — never an All key or admin key
settings.why: Anyone who reads the daemon's key can run the tunnel; a restricted key reaches nothing else in the organization and stays out of argv and profiles.

settings.name: control_plane.aws_identity_provider_id and control_plane.aws_service_account_id
settings.where: Profile YAML, or CONTROL_PLANE_AWS_IDENTITY_PROVIDER_ID and CONTROL_PLANE_AWS_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_ID
settings.recommended: Set wherever tunnel-client runs on AWS, mapped to a project service account with Tunnels Read + Use, static key settings unset
settings.why: The client trades its AWS role for a short-lived token held in memory, so no long-lived key sits on the host.

settings.name: Maximum API key lifetime
settings.where: platform.openai.com › Platform settings (organization, or the project)
settings.recommended: 90 days
settings.why: New runtime keys must expire, so a copied key stops working; rotate by creating the replacement, restarting the client, then deleting the old key.

settings.name: control_plane.client_cert and control_plane.client_key
settings.where: Profile YAML or --control-plane.client-cert / --control-plane.client-key, with the trust anchor active under Organization settings › Security › Mutual TLS
settings.recommended: On — a client certificate from your internal CA, its trust anchor active for the key's project
settings.why: A leaked runtime key alone no longer connects; the control plane also requires the certificate.

settings.name: MCP_CLIENT_CERT and MCP_CLIENT_KEY
settings.where: --mcp.client-cert / --mcp.client-key, or per channel on --mcp.server-url (HTTP bindings only)
settings.recommended: On wherever the MCP server can validate client certificates
settings.why: The MCP server accepts calls only from the tunnel host; the certificate identifies the tunnel, not the user, so OAuth still decides per user.

settings.name: control_plane.poll_channels
settings.where: Profile YAML, --control-plane.poll-channel or CONTROL_PLANE_POLL_CHANNELS
settings.recommended: Set explicitly to the channels this client serves, e.g. [main]
settings.why: Once set it is an allowlist, so a channel left out — Harpoon included — is never polled.

settings.name: --mcp.server-url and --mcp.command
settings.where: Flags (aliases --mcp-server-url, --mcp-command), MCP_SERVER_URL, or mcp.server_urls / mcp.commands in the profile
settings.recommended: Only the approved MCP servers, each over HTTPS, one binding per channel
settings.why: tunnel-client forwards JSON-RPC unchanged, so its bindings are the whole set of servers OpenAI products can reach through it.

settings.name: --harpoon.target (HARPOON_TARGETS)
settings.where: Flag, HARPOON_TARGETS, or harpoon.targets in the profile
settings.default: No targets (the harpoon channel returns unsupported_channel)
settings.recommended: None, unless a reviewed private REST endpoint needs it; then labelled targets only, plaintext HTTP left off
settings.why: Each target is a private HTTP endpoint agents can call through the tunnel by label; with none registered the channel stays closed.

settings.name: mcp.oauth_trusted_origins
settings.where: Profile YAML, --mcp.oauth-trusted-origin or MCP_OAUTH_TRUSTED_ORIGINS
settings.default: Only the configured MCP server origin
settings.recommended: The exact origin of your authorization server, nothing else
settings.why: OAuth discovery follows only origins you trust, so altered metadata cannot send the sign-in flow to another host.

settings.name: --http-proxy and --ca-bundle
settings.where: --http-proxy (TUNNEL_CLIENT_HTTP_PROXY), --control-plane.http-proxy, --mcp.http-proxy and --ca-bundle (CA_BUNDLE)
settings.default: Environment HTTP_PROXY / HTTPS_PROXY, system trust store
settings.recommended: Through the corporate proxy, with its CA bundle added
settings.why: The tunnel's egress to api.openai.com is inspected and logged like other outbound traffic; stdio bindings ignore proxy settings.

settings.name: --health.listen-addr (HEALTH_LISTEN_ADDR)
settings.where: Flag, environment variable or health.listen_addr in the profile
settings.recommended: 127.0.0.1:8080 — widen only for an orchestrator probe on a trusted network
settings.why: /healthz, /readyz, /metrics and the embedded UI stay off the network.

settings.name: --allow-remote-ui (ALLOW_REMOTE_UI)
settings.where: Flag or environment variable
settings.recommended: false
settings.why: The admin UI, with its log export and live log-level control, answers only loopback clients.

settings.name: --log.http-raw-unsafe and --harpoon.capture-payloads
settings.where: Flags, or LOG_HTTP_RAW_UNSAFE and HARPOON_CAPTURE_PAYLOADS
settings.recommended: false — on only for a controlled debugging session
settings.why: Raw logging can write headers and bodies — bearer tokens and tool payloads — to the log and the admin UI.

settings.name: --log.format and --log.file
settings.where: Flags, LOG_FORMAT and LOG_FILE, or log.format / log.file in the profile
settings.recommended: json to a file shipped to the SIEM, with /metrics scraped
settings.why: The host's record of polling, failures and client_instance_id sits beside the Platform audit log for the same tunnel.

settings.name: Audit logs (tunnel.created, tunnel.updated, tunnel.deleted)
settings.where: Admin API GET /v1/organization/audit_logs with an admin key, filtered by event type
settings.recommended: Pulled into the SIEM, alerting on tunnel.* and api_key.* events
settings.why: A tunnel created, repointed or deleted outside the change process shows up on the next pull; tunnel traffic itself is not a Compliance Platform event.

settings.name: tunnel-client admin tunnels delete
settings.where: tunnel-client admin tunnels delete <tunnel_id> --confirm (admin key with Tunnels Manage), or Platform tunnel settings
settings.recommended: Your incident runbook's first step for a misbehaving server, with the runtime key revoked alongside
settings.why: Requests fail while the client is disconnected, and with the one tunnel record and its key gone no copy of the client can reconnect.
