settings.name: Assignment required
settings.where: Microsoft Entra admin center › Enterprise applications › (your app) › Properties
settings.recommended: Yes — assigned to the groups that use the app
settings.why: Only assigned users and groups can get a token for the app at all, so access is a group decision rather than every account in the tenant.

settings.name: App Service authentication — Require authentication
settings.where: App Service › Authentication › Restrict access
settings.recommended: Require authentication, Microsoft Entra ID as the provider
settings.why: The front end rejects every unauthenticated request before your code runs, and binds each session to an Entra identity.

settings.name: Managed identity on the agent's container app
settings.where: Container Apps › (agent app) › Identity
settings.recommended: System-assigned, granted only the roles the agent needs
settings.why: The agent authenticates to the gateway, the model and its stores with a platform-issued identity — no secret in its configuration to steal.

settings.name: disableLocalAuth
settings.where: Foundry (Azure AI services) resource property, via Bicep, ARM, Terraform or PowerShell
settings.recommended: true
settings.why: Model calls need an Entra token; an API key copied from a config file opens nothing. Enforce it fleet-wide with Azure Policy.

settings.name: validate-azure-ad-token policy
settings.where: API Management › APIs and MCP servers › Inbound processing
settings.recommended: On every model API and MCP server, checking the agent's identity and the role each operation needs
settings.why: The gateway verifies who is calling before any model or tool call goes through, and a tool the agent's role doesn't cover is refused.

settings.name: Credential manager (user-delegated connections)
settings.where: API Management › Credential manager
settings.recommended: Downstream OAuth tokens held by API Management per user; the agent never holds them
settings.why: Calls to SaaS tools run with the signed-in user's own grant, exchanged at the gateway, so the agent cannot reuse one user's access for another.

settings.name: Azure Service Bus Data Sender
settings.where: Service Bus namespace › (trigger queue) › Access control (IAM)
settings.recommended: Assigned at the queue scope, only to the identities allowed to start a run; nothing at namespace scope
settings.why: Who can put work on the agent's queue is a named role assignment on that one queue, so starting a run is itself an authorization decision.

settings.name: Local Authentication (disableLocalAuth)
settings.where: Service Bus namespace › Overview › Local Authentication; disableLocalAuth in Bicep or ARM
settings.recommended: Disabled
settings.why: Only an Entra identity holding the sender role can start a run; a SAS connection string copied from a config file starts nothing.

settings.name: Agent identities (Microsoft Entra Agent ID)
settings.where: Microsoft Entra admin center › Entra ID › Agents › Agent identities › New agent identity; or Microsoft Graph
settings.recommended: One agent identity per agent, created from a blueprint whose credential is a managed identity, each with an owner and a sponsor
settings.why: Every agent is a separately attributable, separately revocable principal in the directory — not one service account the whole system acts as.

settings.name: On-behalf-of flow (agent identities)
settings.where: Agent code, through Microsoft.Identity.Web or the Microsoft Entra ID Auth SDK (sidecar)
settings.recommended: Each agent exchanges the user's token for its own token, scoped to its task's resource; no token is handed from one agent to the next
settings.why: Authority narrows at each hop — a specialist holds a token for its own step, never the caller's or the supervisor's.

settings.name: Application ID URI (with requestedAccessTokenVersion 2)
settings.where: Microsoft Entra admin center › App registrations › (MCP server) › Expose an API; requestedAccessTokenVersion in the manifest
settings.recommended: The server's exact canonical URL (every URL clients use), on v2 access tokens
settings.why: Entra matches the client's resource parameter to this URI, so every token is audience-bound to this server and one minted for another resource is refused.

settings.name: Scopes (Expose an API › Add a scope)
settings.where: Microsoft Entra admin center › App registrations › (MCP server) › Expose an API
settings.recommended: One scope per class of operation (tool.read, tool.execute), Admins only consent; no omnibus scope
settings.why: A client is granted only the operations it asked for and an administrator approved, and the server checks the scope before it runs a tool.

settings.name: App roles (Allowed member types — Applications)
settings.where: Microsoft Entra admin center › App registrations › (your API) › App roles; assigned to each calling agent identity or application
settings.recommended: A narrow role per autonomous caller, assigned individually; no tenant-wide application permission
settings.why: A workload with no user behind it gets only the roles assigned to its own identity, carried in the token's roles claim — no borrowed user authority.

settings.name: Certificate credentials (client assertion)
settings.where: Microsoft Entra admin center › App registrations › (client) › Certificates & secrets › Certificates
settings.recommended: A certificate credential on every non-interactive client; no client secrets
settings.why: The client proves possession of a private key (private_key_jwt) rather than presenting a shared secret that can be copied.

settings.name: On-behalf-of (OBO) flow
settings.where: Your server code, through MSAL or Microsoft.Identity.Web
settings.recommended: A handler that calls an upstream API exchanges the inbound token for a downstream token; the inbound token is never forwarded
settings.why: The caller's token stops at this server, so it cannot be replayed against another API, and each downstream call is a logged delegation step.

settings.name: Revoke-MgUserSignInSession (revoke refresh tokens)
settings.where: Microsoft Graph PowerShell, or Microsoft Entra admin center › Users › (user) › Revoke sessions
settings.recommended: Part of the leaver and incident runbook, with the default 1-hour access-token lifetime as the measured revocation delay
settings.why: Refresh tokens stop at once and issued access tokens expire within the hour, so a revoked grant cannot keep calling the server.

settings.name: Key Vault references
settings.where: App Service or Functions › Environment variables › "@Microsoft.KeyVault(...)"; the app's managed identity holds Key Vault Secrets User
settings.recommended: Every upstream credential a handler uses held in Key Vault, one per upstream, referenced without a version so rotation is picked up
settings.why: No upstream secret sits in app settings or code, and rotating one in Key Vault reaches the server without a redeploy.

settings.name: Compute cluster managed identity (identity-based data access)
settings.where: Azure Machine Learning › Compute › (training cluster) › Managed identity; datastores set to identity-based access
settings.recommended: A user-assigned identity per training workload, granted read on its approved dataset and write on its own output container — never the registry or the signing key
settings.why: The run reads and writes as its own identity, checked by each store, and holds nothing that could promote or sign what it produced.

settings.name: Key Vault Crypto User (on a dedicated signing vault)
settings.where: Key Vault (signing vault, Azure RBAC permission model) › Access control (IAM)
settings.recommended: Assigned only to the promotion pipeline's identity, which runs after a separate human approval
settings.why: Only the promotion step can produce a release signature, so a signed model proves the gate was passed — the training job cannot sign its own output.

settings.name: Microsoft Entra Workload ID (AKS)
settings.where: AKS cluster OIDC issuer and workload identity; a Kubernetes service account per rollout, federated to its own user-assigned identity
settings.recommended: Every rollout pod runs under a service account federated to a narrowly scoped identity; no credential in the image
settings.why: A rollout presents a short-lived projected token that each platform service verifies, so a token stolen from one sandbox opens nothing in another.

settings.name: DefaultTimeToLive on the conversation container
settings.where: Azure Cosmos DB › (container) › Settings › Time to Live
settings.recommended: 30 days
settings.why: Conversation state ages out instead of accumulating client material indefinitely in the agent's memory.

settings.name: Document-level access control (permission filters)
settings.where: Azure AI Search › index definition › permission filter fields; queries carry x-ms-query-source-authorization
settings.recommended: On for every index that holds permissioned content
settings.why: Retrieval returns only documents the asking user may read, so the index cannot become a way round the source system's permissions.

settings.name: Groundedness detection
settings.where: Azure AI Content Safety API, called on answers drawn from retrieved documents
settings.recommended: On for answers built from retrieval
settings.why: An answer that strays from — or was steered away from — its sources is flagged before the user acts on it.

settings.name: PII detection (Azure AI Language)
settings.where: Azure AI Language API, called before a turn is written to memory
settings.recommended: Redact before storing conversation turns
settings.why: Personal data a user pasted is not kept in the thread for every later turn — and every later reader — to see.

settings.name: Autopurge retention policies
settings.where: Durable Task Scheduler › retention policies (applies to every task hub in the scheduler)
settings.recommended: Enabled, 30 days (keep the default)
settings.why: Finished runs' journals — every payload a step returned — are deleted on a schedule instead of building up as a second store of client data.

settings.name: Validate the tenant (tid) and subject claims
settings.where: Your server's handlers — every read and write keyed by the token's tid and oid
settings.default: Not enforced by the protocol or the platform
settings.recommended: Every record access filtered to the caller's tenant and delegation; never data from one tenant served to another
settings.why: MCP has no notion of a tenant, so the token's tenant claim checked in the handler is the only thing keeping one customer's records from another's caller.

settings.name: AllowSharedKeyAccess
settings.where: Storage account property, via Bicep, ARM, Azure CLI or Azure Policy
settings.recommended: false — every read and write authorized by Entra RBAC, the writer and reader roles held by named identities
settings.why: Weights and datasets can be read only by identities granted a role on the account; an account key or SAS token copied out of a pipeline opens nothing.

settings.name: On-upload malware scanning (Defender for Storage)
settings.where: Microsoft Defender for Cloud › Defender for Storage plan (subscription or storage account) › Malware scanning add-on
settings.recommended: On for every storage account that receives model files or training data, with malicious blobs soft-deleted
settings.why: An artifact carrying known malware is caught on arrival, before any promotion step or loader opens it.

settings.name: Verify the release signature before load
settings.where: Your serving image's init step — hash the files, verify the release signature with the signing key's public half
settings.recommended: The runtime starts only if every file matches the signed release; a hub artifact only if it matches the digest in its promotion record
settings.why: A file replaced in storage — even with a new digest written beside it — fails verification and never loads.

settings.name: Deploy by registry model name and version
settings.where: Your deployment manifests — the serving workload names the Azure Machine Learning registry model and version it loads
settings.recommended: Every serving deployment references a registered model version, never a bare path or a hub ID
settings.why: The question of what is running has an answer — each instance maps to a registry entry with its publisher, format, scan and lineage.

settings.name: Data asset versions (Azure Machine Learning)
settings.where: Azure Machine Learning › Data › (asset) — referenced as azureml:<name>:<version>, with source and licence recorded as tags
settings.recommended: Every training input registered as a data asset version with its source and licence; jobs read assets by version, never by raw path
settings.why: A version is immutable, so the exact bytes a run consumed — and where they came from — can be named after the fact.

settings.name: Data-preparation components (Azure Machine Learning pipeline)
settings.where: Your curation pipeline — filtering components that call Azure AI Language PII detection and Azure AI Content Safety on each example
settings.recommended: Quality, safety and sensitive-content filters as required pipeline steps before a corpus version is registered
settings.why: A poisoned, harmful or restricted example is removed while it is still a deletion, not something the model has learned.

settings.name: Customer-managed keys for Azure Storage encryption
settings.where: Storage account › Encryption — key held in Key Vault
settings.recommended: A customer-managed key in Key Vault on the dataset and model storage accounts
settings.why: The organisation can revoke the key and with it every read of the corpus and the checkpoints, independent of any role assignment.

settings.name: Register a model from a job output (azureml://jobs)
settings.where: Azure Machine Learning studio › Models › Register, from a job output; or az ml model create --path azureml://jobs/...
settings.recommended: Every candidate registered from the run that produced it, never from a local file
settings.why: The registered model carries its lineage to the job — and through it the data asset versions, code and environment — so a discovered poisoning can be scoped.

settings.name: Model description and tags (tags.stage)
settings.where: Azure Machine Learning registry › Models › (version) — the only mutable properties of a model version
settings.recommended: Description and a model-card link on every version; tags.stage moved to Prod only by the promotion pipeline
settings.why: What the artifact is, what it was trained on and whether it was approved travel with it in the registry, not in someone's notes.

settings.name: PII redaction on A2A payloads (send-request to Azure AI Language)
settings.where: API Management › A2A agent APIs › policies — send-request to PII detection on each outbound task and each artifact we return
settings.recommended: Redact on every payload that leaves for a peer, vendor or partner alike
settings.why: Personal data in a delegated task or a returned artifact is removed at the boundary, not trusted to the peer's handling.

settings.name: llm-content-safety policy with shield-prompt
settings.where: API Management › model APIs › Inbound processing
settings.recommended: shield-prompt="true" on every model API
settings.why: Prompt Shields screen each request for jailbreak and injected instructions at the gateway, before the model sees it.

settings.name: llm-token-limit policy
settings.where: API Management › model APIs › Inbound processing
settings.recommended: Tokens-per-minute and a token quota per subscription
settings.why: A looping turn hits a ceiling at the gateway before it runs up cost or volume.

settings.name: MCP servers in API Management
settings.where: API Management › MCP servers
settings.recommended: Every MCP server exposed only through API Management, with authentication and per-tool policies
settings.why: Each tool call crosses one gateway that authenticates it, applies policy and logs it — no direct path from agent to server.

settings.name: MCP server inventory in API Center
settings.where: Azure API Center › Inventory
settings.recommended: Every MCP server and API the agent can call, registered with an owner
settings.why: The list of tools an agent may be given is a governed registry, not whatever someone wired in.

settings.name: Tool Approval (human in the loop)
settings.where: Your agent code — Microsoft Agent Framework tool approval on write tools
settings.recommended: Approval required on every tool that writes to a system of record
settings.why: A person confirms each consequential action in the conversation before it happens.

settings.name: ApprovalRequiredAIFunction (human-in-the-loop approval)
settings.where: Your agent code — the approval request is routed to an operator work queue and the session resumes on the answer
settings.recommended: Wrapped around every action above the value or irreversibility threshold; the approver is an operator, never the requester
settings.why: A consequential write waits for someone other than its beneficiary; below the threshold the action's compensating transaction, not review, is the safety net.

settings.name: Human-in-the-loop request and response (RequestPort)
settings.where: Your workflow code — Agent Framework workflow, made durable with the Durable Extension
settings.recommended: A request port in front of every consequential write; the step suspends and resumes only on the operator's response to that request
settings.why: The approval is bound to the exact pending step and its checkpointed state, so a step resumed days later cannot run a different action than the one approved.

settings.name: Sanitise rendered model output
settings.where: Your front-end code
settings.recommended: Render as text or sanitised markdown; strip HTML, block external images, set a Content Security Policy
settings.why: A model-written image link or script cannot carry the conversation to an attacker the moment it renders.

settings.name: Session pool network status
settings.where: Container Apps session pool › --network-status
settings.recommended: EgressDisabled
settings.why: Code the agent writes runs in a Hyper-V-isolated session with no outbound network, so it cannot fetch or send anything.

settings.name: Multiple revision mode with traffic splitting
settings.where: Container Apps › (agent app) › Revisions and replicas
settings.default: Single revision mode (all traffic to the latest)
settings.recommended: Multiple revision mode; a new agent, prompt or model revision takes a small share of traffic after its evaluation passes
settings.why: A change that behaves badly reaches a few users and rolls back by moving traffic, not by redeploying.

settings.name: Azure Artifacts upstream sources (externally sourced versions blocked)
settings.where: Azure Artifacts › (feed) › Upstream sources; package upstream behavior
settings.default: External versions blocked once a package has an internal version
settings.recommended: Keep the default; packages enter the feed from approved upstreams only
settings.why: The agent's tools install from your feed, and a public package cannot shadow an internal one.

settings.name: rate-limit-by-key policy
settings.where: API Management › MCP servers › Inbound processing
settings.recommended: Per-client and per-tenant counters (counter-key on the token's appid and tid), sized for callers that retry and parallelise
settings.why: One looping or hostile client hits its own ceiling at the gateway instead of exhausting the server for every tenant.

settings.name: Pin tool definitions to a reviewed version
settings.where: Your server's loader — definitions shipped with the release and checked against the hash recorded at review
settings.default: No integrity check in the protocol
settings.recommended: Refuse to serve any definition whose hash differs from the reviewed release; a wording change goes through the release gate
settings.why: A description edited outside the pipeline never reaches a caller's model, so the server cannot be turned into a tool-poisoning vector.

settings.name: Code scanning (GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps)
settings.where: Azure DevOps › Project settings › Repos › Repositories › (repo) › Advanced Security; code scanning default setup or CodeQL pipeline tasks
settings.recommended: On for every repository that ships the server, with high-severity alerts blocking the release
settings.why: The handlers behind the protocol are tested like any published application before they serve callers.
settings.requires: GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps, or GitHub Code Security for Azure DevOps

settings.name: Dependency scanning (GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps)
settings.where: Azure DevOps › repository dependency scanning default setup, or the AdvancedSecurity-Dependency-Scanning@1 pipeline task
settings.recommended: On for every repository that ships the service, alerts triaged by exposure
settings.why: The SDK and every dependency are enumerated against vulnerability advisories, so an advisory maps to the release it affects.
settings.requires: GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps, or GitHub Code Security for Azure DevOps

settings.name: llm-content-safety policy with enforce-on-completions
settings.where: API Management › model APIs › Inbound processing
settings.recommended: enforce-on-completions="true" on every model API with no provider-side content filter
settings.why: With open weights and no provider applying policy, the gateway checks completions as well as prompts and blocks harmful output before it is returned.

settings.name: Load-balanced pool — Weighted
settings.where: API Management › Backends › (pool); the model API routes to the pool
settings.recommended: The new model version's backend takes a small weight after its evaluation passes; the previous version stays in the pool
settings.why: A new checkpoint serves a slice of traffic before everyone, and rollback is a weight change rather than a re-download.

settings.name: VLLM_ALLOW_RUNTIME_LORA_UPDATING
settings.where: vLLM server environment, in the serving deployment
settings.recommended: Not set; adapters load only from a promoted release at start-up
settings.why: Nobody who can reach the server can load an adapter that changes the model's behaviour through /v1/load_lora_adapter.

settings.name: cache_salt (set per tenant at the gateway)
settings.where: API Management set-body policy on the model API — overwrites any cache_salt the caller sent
settings.default: No salt (all requests share cached prefixes)
settings.recommended: A secret per tenant, derived at the gateway from the caller's identity
settings.why: Only requests from the same tenant can share prefix-cache blocks, closing the cache-timing path to another tenant's prompts.

settings.name: Node taints on dedicated GPU node pools
settings.where: AKS › az aks nodepool add --node-taints; tolerations on each tier's serving workload
settings.recommended: A separate GPU node pool per sensitivity tier, tainted NoSchedule, so a tier's models run only on its own VMs and GPUs
settings.why: Tiers that must not share memory never share a host or an accelerator — the separation is the VM boundary, not the scheduler's goodwill.

settings.name: Container vulnerability assessment (Defender for Containers)
settings.where: Microsoft Defender for Cloud › Environment settings › Defender for Containers; registry and runtime scanning
settings.recommended: On for the registry and every cluster that runs serving or training images
settings.why: The serving stack's known vulnerabilities are mapped to the images actually running, so each advisory points at the instances it affects.
settings.requires: Microsoft Defender for Containers (or Defender CSPM for supported scenarios)

settings.name: AI Red Teaming Agent (Microsoft Foundry)
settings.where: Foundry SDK or portal, run against the candidate deployed to an isolated evaluation endpoint
settings.recommended: Run on every candidate before promotion, its attack success rate a blocking threshold beside your capability, backdoor and memorisation tests
settings.why: A candidate that a fine-tune made unsafe fails the gate before it is signed, not after it serves.

settings.name: Pod Sandboxing (Kata Containers)
settings.where: AKS Azure Linux node pool with the Kata workload runtime; runtimeClassName on each untrusted pod
settings.recommended: Every pod that runs model-generated code uses the Kata runtime class, one pod per task, deleted after
settings.why: Generated code runs in a lightweight VM with its own guest kernel, so a container escape lands in that VM rather than on the host or beside other pods.

settings.name: Feed Reader (feed permission)
settings.where: Azure Artifacts › (feed) › Feed settings › Permissions
settings.default: Build services hold Feed and Upstream Reader (Collaborator)
settings.recommended: Feed Reader for every rollout and agent identity; only the admission pipeline saves packages from upstream
settings.why: A rollout can install what was admitted but cannot write to the feed or make it fetch a new package from upstream — the cache cannot become a channel or a proxy.

settings.name: Containment red teaming (penetration testing under the Rules of Engagement)
settings.where: Your pre-run security testing — agents attack the sandbox, the cluster network and the platform services
settings.recommended: Before every run that changes the sandbox, tools or egress list; findings block the run until fixed
settings.why: Escape routes through the sandbox, the host network and shared services are found by testing them, not assumed closed.

settings.name: A2A agent APIs in API Management
settings.where: API Management › APIs › + Add API › A2A Agent; per-skill policies on each operation
settings.recommended: Our published agent and every peer we call imported as A2A agent APIs, with token validation and per-skill authorization on each
settings.why: Every task in either direction crosses one gateway that authenticates the peer, authorizes the skill and logs the call — the authorization A2A leaves to us.

settings.name: Agent registration in API Center
settings.where: Azure API Center › Inventory › Assets › + Register an asset › Agent (from the agent card JSON)
settings.recommended: Every admitted peer agent and every agent we publish registered from its reviewed card, with an owner
settings.why: An agent that is not in the registry is not a peer — the list of who our agent may delegate to is governed, not discovered.

settings.name: Agent cards from your registry (AgentCard.AsAIAgent)
settings.where: Your agent code — build each peer client from the card held in the registry, after verifying its signature and hash
settings.recommended: Never resolve a peer's card live in production; a changed card is re-reviewed before the registry entry changes
settings.why: A peer that alters its card — new skills, new endpoint, new security scheme — is not trusted until someone has decided to trust the change.

settings.name: quota-by-key policy
settings.where: API Management › A2A agent APIs › Inbound processing; forward-request timeout on the backend call
settings.recommended: Call and bandwidth quotas per peer and per task, with a timeout on every streamed task
settings.why: One partner task that retries, fans out or streams without end hits its own ceiling instead of our budget.

settings.name: Azure Firewall application rules (via user-defined routes)
settings.where: Container Apps environment subnet route table → Azure Firewall › Application rules
settings.recommended: All outbound from the agent subnet through Azure Firewall, with an FQDN allowlist
settings.why: The agent and its tools reach only the hosts you list; anything else is dropped and logged.

settings.name: Public network access
settings.where: Foundry, Azure AI Search and Azure Cosmos DB › Networking
settings.recommended: Disabled, private endpoints only
settings.why: The model, the index and the memory store are reachable only from your virtual network, not from the internet.

settings.name: WAF rate limit rule
settings.where: Azure Front Door or Application Gateway WAF policy › Custom rules
settings.recommended: Per-client rate limit on the chat endpoint
settings.why: A runaway client or scripted abuse is throttled at the edge, before it spends tokens or triggers actions.

settings.name: outboundVnetRouting.allTraffic
settings.where: App Service › Networking › Virtual network integration; set with the Azure CLI, subnet routed to Azure Firewall
settings.default: Application traffic uses the default route
settings.recommended: true, with the integration subnet's route table sending outbound traffic through Azure Firewall
settings.why: Every outbound call the server makes leaves through the firewall's allowlist, so a handler or fetch steered to an internal or metadata address is dropped.

settings.name: Network policy engine (Azure CNI Powered by Cilium)
settings.where: AKS cluster network profile; a default-deny Kubernetes network policy in each serving or training namespace
settings.default: All pods can send and receive traffic without limitations
settings.recommended: Cilium, with default deny; only the gateway reaches the serving pods, and inter-node serving traffic stays inside the namespace
settings.why: The serving plane's unauthenticated job and inter-node channels are reachable from nothing else in the cluster.

settings.name: Managed virtual network isolation mode
settings.where: Azure Machine Learning workspace › Networking › Workspace managed outbound access
settings.recommended: Allow only approved outbound (Private with Approved Outbound in the portal), with the package mirror and the dataset and model storage as the only added rules
settings.why: The training job can reach the stores it needs and nothing else, so a compromised dependency or a run holding the corpus has no route out.

settings.name: FQDN filtering (Advanced Container Networking Services)
settings.where: AKS with Azure CNI Powered by Cilium and Advanced Container Networking Services; a Cilium network policy listing the allowed FQDNs
settings.default: All pods can send and receive traffic without limitations
settings.recommended: The offline web, the package feed and the platform services as the rollout's whole list; every other DNS request refused
settings.why: DNS requests are checked against the policy before they are answered, so a rollout cannot resolve — or tunnel through — a name that is not on its list.

settings.name: Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry (Application Insights)
settings.where: Agent code with the Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry Distro; Log Analytics workspace connected to Microsoft Sentinel
settings.recommended: On, tracing every agent turn and tool call, exported to Log Analytics and Sentinel
settings.why: Each tool call, its arguments and its result are traceable per user and conversation when something goes wrong.

settings.name: Subscription state (suspend)
settings.where: API Management › Subscriptions › (agent's subscription)
settings.recommended: Active, with suspend as the first step of your incident runbook
settings.why: Suspending the agent's subscription cuts its model and tool access at the gateway at once, without redeploying anything.

settings.name: Terminate orchestration instances
settings.where: Durable Task client API (DurableTaskClient), or the Durable Task Scheduler dashboard
settings.recommended: A runbook step that queries the workflow's running and suspended instances and terminates each, with a reason
settings.why: The stop reaches a workflow parked on a timer or an approval for days, not only one that is executing now.

settings.name: Disable agent identity
settings.where: Microsoft Entra admin center › Entra ID › Agents › Agent identities (or Agent blueprints) › Disable
settings.recommended: Enabled, with Disable as an incident-runbook step held by Agent ID Administrators
settings.why: A disabled agent identity receives no new tokens, so one agent is cut off without touching the others or redeploying.

settings.name: Diagnostic setting — Logs related to ApiManagement Gateway
settings.where: API Management › Monitoring › Diagnostic settings; resource-specific ApiManagementGatewayLogs table in Log Analytics
settings.recommended: On, sent to the Log Analytics workspace connected to Microsoft Sentinel, with the generative AI gateway logs where model APIs pass through
settings.why: Every call through the gateway is recorded with its caller and operation, where an incident can query it.

settings.name: Container log collection (Azure Monitor)
settings.where: AKS › Monitoring — Azure Monitor agent collecting stdout/stderr and Kubernetes events to a Log Analytics workspace
settings.recommended: On for every sandbox node pool, to a workspace no rollout identity can read or write
settings.why: Trajectories and host telemetry leave the node as they happen, so a rollout that disables what it can touch cannot erase what was already shipped.

settings.name: Alert rule with an action group (automated stop)
settings.where: Azure Monitor › Alerts › Action groups — an Azure Function or Automation Runbook that tells the orchestrator to halt the run
settings.recommended: Serious-risk detections stop the run and cordon its node pool automatically; resuming is a person's decision
settings.why: The stop is enforced from outside every sandbox the moment a monitor fires, without waiting for someone to read the alert.

settings.name: Enabled for users to sign-in?
settings.where: Microsoft Entra admin center › Enterprise applications › (peer platform or peer agent) › Properties
settings.recommended: Yes, with No as the first step of the peer cut-off runbook
settings.why: Setting it to No stops every new token for that application at once, so a peer is cut off in one action alongside dropping its registry entry.

settings.name: Cloud app catalog risk score (Defender for Cloud Apps)
settings.where: Microsoft Defender portal › Cloud apps › Cloud app catalog › (peer platform)
settings.recommended: Reviewed for every peer platform before the agreement is signed, alongside the questions A2A leaves open — tenant isolation, card signing, audit export
settings.why: A peer is admitted on an assessment of how it handles our users' identity and data, not only on its card.

reference.title: Pod Sandboxing with Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)
Baseline architecture for an Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster

summary: Rollouts run as Kata pods — each in a lightweight VM with its own guest kernel — on dedicated AKS node pools, with Cilium network policy and FQDN filtering as the second wall and Azure Firewall as the third, following Pod Sandboxing and the AKS baseline's segmentation. The orchestrator, graders and offline web are the organisation's own code on separate node pools; Container Apps dynamic sessions are the managed alternative for lighter code-execution tasks.

bindings.service: Your graders on a separate AKS node pool
bindings.note: Unreachable from rollout pods by network policy; read end state, never write it.

bindings.service: Azure Monitor, Workload ID, Azure Files
bindings.note: Log collection, token issuance and shared storage — each reachable only as far as the rollout needs.
One pod per task, deleted after; trust groups placed on separate node pools.

bindings.service: Your episode harness in the Kata pod
Shell, files, browser in the pod
vLLM on AKS GPU node pools
Your offline web snapshot and simulated apps

reference.title: Import an A2A agent API (Azure API Management)
Integrate third-party agents with Microsoft Entra Agent ID
AI agent orchestration patterns

summary: Your Agent Framework agent on Azure Container Apps speaks A2A both ways through API Management's A2A agent APIs, with Microsoft Entra ID as identity provider and authorization server: our agent holds an Entra agent identity, each peer agent we admit is a registered client with its own certificate and app roles per skill, and our users' identity reaches the vendor platform only through its Entra enterprise application. Admitted cards live in API Center; nothing is resolved live.

bindings.note: The vendor platform's enterprise app assignment decides whose identity may be asserted to it.

bindings.service: App Service behind Application Gateway with WAF
Microsoft Entra ID (agent and app registrations)
bindings.note: Mints our agent's tokens for peers and validates peers' tokens for our agent; the partner peer runs its own.

bindings.service: Your agent on Azure Container Apps (Microsoft Agent Framework)
bindings.note: A2A client and server through Agent Framework's A2A hosting; Foundry Agent Service is the managed alternative.

bindings.service: Azure Cosmos DB and Azure AI Search

bindings.note: Under agreement, federated to our Entra tenant as an enterprise application.
No federation: agent identity and skill scopes only.

settings.name: Require authentication — Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP)
settings.where: Cloud Run › (front-end service) › Security; access granted under Manage user or group access
settings.recommended: On (--iap), access granted to the Google groups that use the app
settings.why: Only signed-in members of the granted groups reach the app at all — on every ingress path, the run.app URL and the load balancer alike — and each session carries a Google identity.

settings.name: User-managed service account (service identity)
settings.where: Cloud Run › (agent service) › Security › Service account
settings.recommended: A dedicated service account per agent service, granted only the roles that agent needs
settings.why: The agent calls the gateway, the model and its stores on short-lived tokens the platform issues to its own identity — no key in its configuration to steal. Agent Identity (SPIFFE-based, Preview on Cloud Run) is the successor.

settings.name: Disable service account key creation
settings.where: Organization Policy › iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation (or the managed iam.managed.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation)
settings.default: Enforced on organisations created on or after 3 May 2024; not enforced on older ones
settings.recommended: Enforced at the organisation
settings.why: No long-lived key for an agent's service account can be minted, so there is no key to copy out of a config file or repository and replay elsewhere.

settings.name: VerifyIAM policy
settings.where: Apigee › API proxies (model and MCP proxies) › request PreFlow
settings.recommended: On every model and MCP proxy, checking the calling agent's Google identity against IAM
settings.why: The gateway verifies which workload is calling before any model or tool call passes, and an identity without the IAM grant is refused.

settings.name: 3-legged OAuth auth provider (Agent Identity auth manager)
settings.where: IAM › Agent Identity › Auth providers; the agent's ADK tools fetch tokens per call
settings.recommended: Downstream OAuth tokens held by the auth manager per user; the agent never stores them
settings.why: Calls to SaaS tools run on the signed-in user's own consented grant, brokered per call, so the agent cannot reuse one user's access for another. Agent Identity on Cloud Run is in Preview.

settings.name: Authentication for push subscriptions (Enable authentication)
settings.where: Pub/Sub › (trigger subscription) › Push › Enable authentication, with a service account and audience; agent service deployed --no-allow-unauthenticated
settings.default: Push requests sent without a token
settings.recommended: On, with a dedicated service account per trigger granted Cloud Run Invoker on the agent alone
settings.why: Only messages the subscription signs can start a run, and the token names the principal whose scope the run carries — a forged webhook or stray publisher starts nothing.

settings.name: Short-lived credentials for a service account (generateAccessToken)
settings.where: IAM Service Account Credentials API — the coordinator mints each subagent's token for that subagent's own service account
settings.recommended: One service account per subagent, granted only its own tools; a token minted per step with the shortest workable lifetime
settings.why: A specialist calls with its own narrow identity, never the supervisor's, so each step is attributable at the gateway and revocable on its own.

settings.name: Identity Platform multi-tenancy (tenant identity providers)
settings.where: Identity Platform › Tenants › (customer tenant) › Providers (SAML or OIDC)
settings.default: Multi-tenancy off; one shared pool of users
settings.recommended: One tenant per customer organisation, each with only its own SAML or OIDC provider enabled
settings.why: A caller signs in only through the IdP of the organisation it belongs to, so that organisation's groups, joiners, leavers and conditional access decide who gets a token at all.

settings.name: OAuthV2 policy — VerifyAccessToken
settings.where: Apigee › MCP proxy › ProxyEndpoint PreFlow, as the first step
settings.default: No credential check — any caller can invoke a proxy that lacks one
settings.recommended: VerifyAccessToken first in the PreFlow of every MCP proxy
settings.why: A token passes only if it is unexpired, unrevoked and was issued to an app whose API product includes this proxy — a token minted for anything else is refused.

settings.name: Key approval (manual)
settings.where: Apigee › API products › (MCP product) › Access › approval type
settings.default: Automatic — every key request is approved
settings.recommended: Manual approval for every client app that adds the MCP product
settings.why: A client gets credentials for the server only after an administrator approves its app, so no client can grant itself access by registering.

settings.name: No token passthrough (a credential per hop)
settings.where: Your service code — every hop calls the next on the service's own identity or a token minted for that hop
settings.recommended: The inbound token is never forwarded; each upstream call uses a credential minted or held for that upstream alone, logged as a delegation step
settings.why: The caller's token stops at this server, so it cannot be replayed against another API — the confused-deputy path the MCP security guidance names.

settings.name: Secret Manager secrets for Cloud Run (pinned versions)
settings.where: Cloud Run › (MCP service) › Variables & secrets › reference a secret, pinned to a version
settings.default: Credentials wherever the team put them
settings.recommended: One secret per upstream, mounted from Secret Manager and pinned to a version; rotation publishes a new version
settings.why: Each upstream's credential lives in Secret Manager, readable only by the service's identity and rotated without a code change, never in the image or its config.

settings.name: Revoke OAuth 2.0 access tokens by end user ID, app ID, or both
settings.where: Apigee › OAuthV2 policy InvalidateToken operation, or the revoke API by app ID or end user ID
settings.recommended: One-hour access tokens; revocation by end user ID wired to leaver and incident workflows
settings.why: Apigee checks every token and its app on each request, so a revoked token, user or app stops working at once rather than at expiry.

settings.name: Use a custom service account (custom training)
settings.where: Agent Platform › serverless training job or pipeline run › service account
settings.default: The project's Agent Platform Custom Code Service Agent
settings.recommended: A service account per training pipeline, reading only its approved dataset version and writing only its own candidates; never granted the signing key
settings.why: Each run is attributable and bounded to what its approved specification names, and the identity that trains can never be the one that promotes.

settings.name: Workload Identity Federation for GKE
settings.where: GKE cluster and node pools › Workload Identity; a Kubernetes ServiceAccount per run, bound in IAM
settings.recommended: On, with one Kubernetes ServiceAccount per run granted only the platform calls that run needs
settings.why: A rollout gets short-lived tokens for its own principal from the GKE metadata server, verified by every Google API it calls, and the node's credentials stay out of reach.

settings.name: Artifact Registry Reader (roles/artifactregistry.reader)
settings.where: Artifact Registry › (virtual repository) › Permissions, granted to rollout and job identities
settings.recommended: Rollouts and jobs hold Reader only; only CI pipelines hold Writer
settings.why: The mirror is read-only to anything a model drives, so it cannot become a message board between rollouts or take a package published back.

settings.name: User access (custom SAML app)
settings.where: Google Admin console › Apps › Web and mobile apps › (peer platform's SAML app) › User access
settings.recommended: Off for everyone; on only for the access groups whose identity may travel to that peer platform
settings.why: A user's identity is asserted to a vendor's platform only when an administrator has turned the federation on for a group they belong to — a relationship someone owns, reviewed like any access grant.

settings.name: OpenID Connect (OIDC) ID tokens for a service account (generateIdToken)
settings.where: IAM Service Account Credentials API — the agent's service account mints an ID token for each peer's token endpoint, which trusts Google's issuer
settings.default: Peers registered with a shared client secret
settings.recommended: A service account per peer relationship; the peer federates Google's issuer and audience instead of holding a secret for us
settings.why: Our agent proves who it is to each peer with a short-lived token Google signs, so there is no long-lived secret per registration to leak or rotate.

settings.name: TTL policy
settings.where: Firestore › Time-to-live › (conversation collection group) › expiry timestamp field
settings.recommended: 30 days on the conversation collection group
settings.why: Conversation state is deleted after it expires — typically within 24 hours — instead of accumulating client material in the agent's memory indefinitely.

settings.name: Session time to live (ttl)
settings.where: Agent Platform Sessions › session create or update (ttl or expire_time), through ADK's VertexAiSessionService
settings.recommended: 30 days
settings.why: A workflow's event history — and every tool result journalled in it — is deleted with its session instead of staying readable for a year.

settings.name: Data source access control
settings.where: Agent Search (formerly Vertex AI Search) › data store creation › access control with your identity provider (Preview)
settings.default: Off — and it can only be chosen when the data store is created
settings.recommended: On for every data store that holds permissioned content
settings.why: Search returns only documents the asking user can already open in the source system, so the index cannot become a way round its permissions.

settings.name: Check grounding API
settings.where: Agent Search check grounding API, called on answers drawn from retrieved documents
settings.recommended: On for answers built from retrieval, with low-support answers flagged
settings.why: An answer whose claims the retrieved facts do not support — or that was steered away from them — is caught, with citations, before the user acts on it.

settings.name: De-identification (content.deidentify)
settings.where: Sensitive Data Protection API, called before a turn is written to memory
settings.recommended: De-identify before storing conversation turns
settings.why: Personal data a user pasted is masked before it stays in the thread for every later turn — and every later reader — to see.

settings.name: Tenant isolation in every handler
settings.where: Your MCP service code — the tenant from the verified token (the caller's Identity Platform tenant) scopes every query
settings.default: The protocol has no tenants; nothing is isolated by default
settings.recommended: Every record access filtered to the caller's tenant and delegation; no data from one tenant served to another
settings.why: The tenant checked in the handler is the only thing keeping one customer's records from another customer's caller.

settings.name: Uniform bucket-level access
settings.where: Cloud Storage › (weights bucket) › Permissions; read granted to the serving workload's Workload Identity principal only
settings.recommended: On, with public access prevention enforced; the promotion pipeline writes, only the serving identity reads
settings.why: IAM on the bucket is the only access path — no per-object ACL can quietly open one checkpoint — so weights are readable by the runtime and nothing else.

settings.name: Inspection jobs (Sensitive Data Protection)
settings.where: Sensitive Data Protection › inspection jobs over the Cloud Storage and BigQuery sources, run in the curation pipeline
settings.recommended: Every new source inspected before curation; findings drive de-identification or exclusion of the examples
settings.why: Personal and client-confidential data is found and removed while it is still a deletion, not something the model has learned.

settings.name: Track the lineage of pipeline artifacts (ML Metadata)
settings.where: Agent Platform Pipelines › ML Metadata store; every ingest, curation and training step records its input and output artifacts
settings.default: Recorded only for steps that run as pipeline components
settings.recommended: Every source, dataset version, base checkpoint, run and candidate recorded as artifacts and executions
settings.why: Where each example came from and which data, base and run produced an artifact can be answered long after the run, because it was recorded when it happened.

settings.name: Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK)
settings.where: Agent Platform training, pipelines and models (encryption_spec); the corpus and candidate buckets' default Cloud KMS key
settings.recommended: CMEK from a Cloud KMS key the security team holds, on every training resource and bucket
settings.why: The corpus, checkpoints and candidates are encrypted under keys you control, so disabling the key makes them unreadable everywhere at once.

settings.name: SanitizeUserPrompt policy
settings.where: Apigee › model proxies › request flow, pointing at a Model Armor template
settings.recommended: On every model proxy, keeping the default FunctionResponseSource so tool results are screened on function-calling turns
settings.why: Model Armor screens each prompt, and the tool results going back to the model, for prompt injection and jailbreaks at the gateway before the model reads them.

settings.name: Model Armor floor settings (inline enforcement on Agent Platform)
settings.where: Security › Model Armor › Floor settings (project), integrated service VERTEX_AI
settings.recommended: Prompt injection and jailbreak detection on, enforcement type INSPECT_AND_BLOCK
settings.why: Every Gemini generateContent call in the project is screened even when a caller skips the gateway. The integration lets requests through unscreened if Model Armor is unreachable, which is why the gateway check stays.

settings.name: LLMTokenQuota policy
settings.where: Apigee › model proxies › request and response flow (with PromptTokenLimit for bursts)
settings.recommended: A token quota per agent app per hour, and a PromptTokenLimit rate per minute
settings.why: A looping turn hits a token ceiling at the gateway before it runs up cost or volume.

settings.name: MCP Discovery Proxy (MCP in Apigee)
settings.where: Apigee › MCP › MCP Discovery Proxy, tools generated from each API's OpenAPI specification
settings.recommended: Every MCP tool the agent calls exposed only through Apigee, generated from the API's reviewed specification
settings.why: Tool definitions come from the specification your API owners reviewed, not from whatever a server advertises, and each call crosses one gateway that authenticates, meters and logs it.

settings.name: API product MCP tool operations (payloadOperationGroup)
settings.where: Apigee › API products, with the ParsePayload policy on the MCP proxy
settings.default: Every tool on the proxy callable by any authenticated client
settings.recommended: One API product per agent, listing only the tools it may call, each with a quota
settings.why: tools/list shows the agent only the tools its product grants and tools/call refuses the rest — the decision is per tool, not per server.

settings.name: Agent Registry
settings.where: Agent Platform › Agent Registry, in a central governance project
settings.recommended: Every MCP server, agent and endpoint an agent can call, registered with an owner
settings.why: The tools an agent may be given are a governed inventory, not whatever someone wired in — and Agent Gateway refuses destinations that are not in it.

settings.name: Tool Confirmation (require_confirmation)
settings.where: Your agent code — ADK FunctionTool(..., require_confirmation=True) on write tools
settings.recommended: Confirmation required on every tool that writes to a system of record
settings.why: A person confirms each consequential action in the conversation before it happens.

settings.name: Advanced confirmation with remote confirmation (request_confirmation)
settings.where: Your agent code — ADK tool_context.request_confirmation on high-value actions, answered through the ADK server's REST API
settings.recommended: Actions above the value or irreversibility threshold park for an operator's approval; never the requester's
settings.why: The step waits until an operator in a work queue approves that exact action and payload, so a run nobody watches cannot commit an irreversible change on its own.

settings.name: Sanitise rendered model output
settings.where: Your front-end code
settings.recommended: Render as text or sanitised markdown; strip HTML, block external images, set a Content Security Policy
settings.why: A model-written image link or script cannot carry the conversation to an attacker the moment it renders.

settings.name: Code Execution sandbox
settings.where: Agent Platform › Agent Runtime › Code Execution, called from the agent wherever it runs; ttl set at sandbox creation
settings.default: Generated code runs wherever the agent chooses to run it
settings.recommended: All model-generated code runs in a Code Execution sandbox, ttl no longer than the session
settings.why: The sandbox has an isolated filesystem and no network access, so code the model writes cannot reach anything or touch the agent's own container.

settings.name: Gradual rollouts (traffic splitting between revisions)
settings.where: Cloud Run › (agent service) › Revisions › Manage traffic
settings.default: All traffic to the latest revision
settings.recommended: New revisions deployed with --no-traffic, then given a small share after their evaluation passes
settings.why: A new agent, prompt or model revision that behaves badly reaches a few users and rolls back by moving traffic, not by redeploying.

settings.name: Agent evaluation (Gen AI evaluation service)
settings.where: Agent Platform › Evaluation, run from the release pipeline
settings.recommended: Task-success and safety evaluation on every agent, prompt, tool or model change, blocking the release on regression
settings.why: Each change is scored against the same eval cases before it reaches users, instead of being discovered in production.

settings.name: Virtual repository upstream priority
settings.where: Artifact Registry › virtual repository › upstream policies (standard repository above the PyPI or npm remote repository)
settings.default: Clients configured against public registries directly
settings.recommended: Clients install only from a virtual repository that ranks your standard repository above the remote one
settings.why: A public package cannot shadow an internal one — the dependency-confusion path Google's remote repository docs name.

settings.name: Package scanning (Artifact Analysis)
settings.where: Artifact Registry › (Python or npm repository) › --allow-vulnerability-scanning
settings.default: Disabled for Java, Python and Node.js repositories
settings.recommended: Enabled on the Python and Node.js repositories behind the virtual repository (virtual repositories themselves are not scanned)
settings.why: Packages are scanned for vulnerabilities, malicious software and secrets, and re-checked as new advisories arrive.

settings.name: SpikeArrest policy
settings.where: Apigee › API proxy (MCP or model) › PreFlow, Identifier set to the client app (and tenant)
settings.recommended: Per-client and per-tenant rate, UseEffectiveCount true, alongside the API product's quotas
settings.why: A client that retries, loops or fans out is throttled at the gateway before it exhausts finite capacity for every other tenant.

settings.name: Pin tool definitions to a reviewed version
settings.where: Your MCP service code — the loader checks each definition's hash against the release record
settings.recommended: Refuse to serve any definition whose hash differs from the reviewed release; a wording change goes through the release gate
settings.why: A description edited outside the pipeline never reaches a caller's model, so the server cannot be turned into a tool-poisoning vector.

settings.name: Application security testing of the MCP handlers
settings.where: Your release pipeline — authenticated testing of every tool handler before release
settings.recommended: Every release tested against the OWASP Web Security Testing Guide, with findings blocking the release
settings.why: Behind the protocol this is a published application, and an injectable handler is reachable by every caller that holds a token.

settings.name: Automatic scanning (Container Scanning API)
settings.where: Artifact Analysis › Container Scanning API on the project that holds the images
settings.default: Images scanned on push once the API is enabled
settings.recommended: Enabled on every project that holds a serving image, findings routed to the image's owner
settings.why: Every image's OS and language packages are matched against vulnerability feeds on push and re-checked as advisories arrive, so an advisory maps to the images it affects.

settings.name: AI security and safety checks (Model Armor on GKE Inference Gateway)
settings.where: GKE Inference Gateway › GCPTrafficExtension calling Model Armor, on prompts and responses
settings.recommended: On for every InferencePool, with a template that screens prompts and responses and blocks on violation
settings.why: No provider applies content policy to a self-hosted model, so prompts and completions are classified at the gateway before they reach the model or the caller.

settings.name: Verify model signatures at load (OpenSSF Model Signing)
settings.where: Your serving pipeline — an init step verifies the Sigstore bundle, or the promotion record's digest, before vLLM opens the weights
settings.default: Weights load as found in the bucket
settings.recommended: Refuse to load any artifact whose signature or approved digest does not verify
settings.why: Replacing a file and the digest beside it does not make it loadable; only an artifact the promotion gate signed or recorded serves.

settings.name: Model format allowlist and pickle scanning at promotion
settings.where: Your intake and promotion pipeline — safetensors only; pickle-based files refused or scanned before anything loads them
settings.recommended: Safetensors only for hub artifacts; anything else blocked at the gate
settings.why: Loading a pickle is code execution, so an artifact that would run code on load never reaches a node that would load it.

settings.name: Model version aliases
settings.where: Agent Platform Model Registry › (model) › versions › aliases and labels
settings.default: The first version gets the default alias
settings.recommended: Serving reads the version the default alias names; labels record publisher, format and the scan that cleared it; rollback moves the alias
settings.why: The question "what is serving" has one answer in the registry, and the previous approved version stays one alias move away.

settings.name: Weighted traffic splitting between InferencePools
settings.where: GKE Inference Gateway › HTTPRoute backendRefs weight, old and new InferencePool side by side
settings.default: All traffic to the one InferencePool
settings.recommended: A new model version takes a 10% weight after its evaluation passes, then grows; the old pool stays until it is retired
settings.why: A model version that misbehaves serves a slice, not everyone, and rolls back by moving weight rather than redeploying.

settings.name: Confidential GKE Nodes with GPUs
settings.where: GKE › node pool per sensitivity tier › Confidential GKE Nodes (NVIDIA H100), tainted for that tier
settings.recommended: A dedicated confidential GPU node pool for each sensitivity tier that must not share hardware
settings.why: Workload memory is encrypted in use on the host and the accelerator, and one tier's pods never land on another tier's GPUs.

settings.name: vLLM security settings (dev mode, runtime LoRA updating, cache_salt)
settings.where: Your vLLM deployment — VLLM_SERVER_DEV_MODE and VLLM_ALLOW_RUNTIME_LORA_UPDATING unset, cache_salt set per tenant by the gateway
settings.default: --api-key optional; dev and runtime-update endpoints off unless enabled
settings.recommended: Dev mode and runtime adapter loading off; a per-tenant cache_salt on every request, overwriting any the caller sent; only the gateway can reach the server
settings.why: --api-key protects only part of vLLM's HTTP surface, so the control endpoints stay switched off and unreachable, and one tenant's prompts cannot be inferred from another's prefix-cache timing.

settings.name: Sign at promotion (OpenSSF Model Signing)
settings.where: Your promotion step — signs the evaluated candidate with a Cloud KMS asymmetric key or Sigstore identity held only by the promotion service account
settings.recommended: Sign only after the evaluation gate passes and a person approves, with a key the training job's identity cannot use
settings.why: A signature proves the gate was passed, not merely that a job finished — a run that wrote its own candidate cannot make it loadable.

settings.name: Model evaluation in Agent Platform
settings.where: Agent Platform Pipelines › evaluation component in front of the promotion step
settings.recommended: Capability, safety and memorisation evaluation on every candidate, blocking promotion on regression; benchmarks in a bucket the training identity cannot write
settings.why: How the candidate behaves is examined before it can be promoted, against an answer key its authors cannot edit.

settings.name: Apply model labels (approval state and model card)
settings.where: Agent Platform Model Registry › (model version) › labels, with the model card stored beside the artifact
settings.recommended: Every promoted version labelled with its approval state and a link to its model card; promotion refuses a version without both
settings.why: What the artifact is and what it was trained on travel with it, so a reader of the registry never meets an undocumented model.

settings.name: GKE Sandbox (gVisor and microVMs)
settings.where: GKE › node pools with a sandbox type; Pods request the gvisor or microvm RuntimeClass
settings.recommended: Every rollout and agent task in a sandbox — gVisor by default, a microVM where a task needs a full guest kernel (microVMs support no GPUs)
settings.why: Code the model writes runs against its own guest kernel or a userspace kernel, never the node's, so an escape still has a wall to cross.

settings.name: Recommended security policy (secure-sandbox-policy)
settings.where: Agent Sandbox on GKE › ValidatingAdmissionPolicy and its binding, all non-system namespaces
settings.default: Agent Sandbox doesn't restrict the Pods that run sandboxes
settings.recommended: Applied, with the binding enforcing it in every namespace that runs sandboxes
settings.why: A sandbox that isn't gVisor, mounts a service-account token, runs as root, keeps Linux capabilities or lacks resource limits is rejected at admission.

settings.name: Workload separation (taints and tolerations)
settings.where: GKE › a node pool per trust group, tainted; each run's sandboxes tolerate only their group's taint
settings.default: Pods schedule on any node with room
settings.recommended: A node pool per trust group; rollouts that must not communicate never share a node
settings.why: Rollouts from different trust groups never share a host, its cores or its cache, so co-residency is not a side channel between them.

settings.name: Automatic run stop in the orchestrator
settings.where: Your run orchestrator — on a serious-risk alert, deletes the run's Sandbox and SandboxClaim resources and disables the run's service accounts
settings.recommended: Automatic, triggered from monitors outside every sandbox; restarting or widening the run is a person's decision
settings.why: The stop is enforced from outside the rollouts, so an agent that has disabled what it could reach cannot keep its run alive.

settings.name: Containment red teaming against the hardened cluster
settings.where: Your run-approval process — agents attack the sandbox, the node network and the platform services before a run
settings.recommended: Before every new environment or widening, against a cluster built to Google's hardening guidance; findings block the run
settings.why: Escape paths are tested rather than assumed, by the same kind of agent the run will train.

settings.name: Sanitize prompts and responses (Model Armor API)
settings.where: Apigee A2A proxy or the agent's ADK callbacks — sanitizeUserPrompt on every inbound artifact, sanitizeModelResponse with a de-identify template on every outbound payload
settings.recommended: Every inbound artifact, status message and card description screened; every outbound task payload and returned artifact de-identified
settings.why: A peer's text is classified for injection before the harness reads it, and client data leaving for another organisation is masked at the boundary.

settings.name: Per-skill authorization on A2A requests
settings.where: Apigee A2A proxy — the skill named in the message metadata checked against the peer app's allowed skills before dispatch
settings.default: The protocol leaves authorization to the implementation
settings.recommended: Each peer may invoke only the skills its registration lists, and our agent may call a peer's skill only for the users that skill is approved for
settings.why: Authorization is enforced at the crossing in both directions, so a peer that can reach our agent still cannot reach a skill nobody granted it.

settings.name: Quota policy
settings.where: Apigee A2A proxy › per peer app, with stream duration and payload size limits beside it
settings.recommended: Per peer and per task — tasks per hour, retries and fan-out — sized to the agreement
settings.why: A partner's agent that loops, retries or fans out hits a ceiling at our gateway before it runs up our cost.

settings.name: Verify signed Agent Cards (AgentCardSignature)
settings.where: Your gateway or agent code — each peer's card verified against the key pinned at admission, and its hash compared, on every task
settings.default: Cards fetched and trusted as served
settings.recommended: A peer's card is accepted only with a valid JWS signature from its pinned key and the hash recorded at admission; a change is re-reviewed
settings.why: A peer cannot silently rewrite its skills or descriptions after we admitted it — the card is a dependency, and a change is a decision.

settings.name: Peer platform assessment before federation
settings.where: Your third-party risk process — before a federation or agent registration is turned on
settings.recommended: Assessment of how the platform handles our users' assertions, its tenant isolation, card signing and audit export, written into the agreement
settings.why: The questions A2A leaves to implementations — authorization, data handling, tracing — are answered by the vendor before our users' identity travels there.

settings.name: Secure Web Proxy gateway security policy (Direct VPC egress, all-traffic)
settings.where: Cloud Run › Networking › Direct VPC egress › Route all traffic to the VPC → Secure Web Proxy as next hop › URL lists
settings.default: Outbound internet direct from Cloud Run
settings.recommended: All outbound traffic from the workload through Secure Web Proxy, allowing only a URL list you maintain
settings.why: Secure Web Proxy denies all outbound traffic until a rule allows it, so the workload reaches only the hosts you list — never a private or metadata address — and every request is logged.

settings.name: VPC Service Controls service perimeter
settings.where: Security › VPC Service Controls, around the agent's projects (Agent Platform, Agent Search, Firestore, Cloud Storage)
settings.recommended: One enforced perimeter, reached from the VPC through Private Service Connect
settings.why: The model, index and memory APIs answer only inside the perimeter, so a stolen token used from outside — or a copy to a project outside — is refused.

settings.name: Ingress — Internal and Cloud Load Balancers, with the default URL disabled
settings.where: Cloud Run › (front-end service) › Networking; --ingress=internal-and-cloud-load-balancing --no-default-url
settings.default: All ingress allowed, run.app URL on
settings.recommended: internal-and-cloud-load-balancing, default URL disabled
settings.why: Users reach the front end only through the load balancer, so Cloud Armor's rules and rate limits cannot be bypassed through run.app.

settings.name: Cloud Armor rate limiting (throttle)
settings.where: Cloud Armor security policy on the front end's Application Load Balancer › rate-based rule
settings.recommended: Per-client throttle on the chat endpoint
settings.why: A runaway client or scripted abuse is throttled at the edge, before it spends tokens or triggers actions.

settings.name: Network policy enforcement (GKE Dataplane V2)
settings.where: GKE cluster › network policy enforcement on; Kubernetes NetworkPolicy per namespace
settings.default: All pods can reach each other
settings.recommended: Default-deny in every serving and sandbox namespace, allowing only the named peers — the gateway to the API, serving nodes to each other
settings.why: A pod reaches only the peers its policy names, so vLLM's unauthenticated inter-node channels and one sandbox's neighbours are off limits to everything else.

settings.name: VPC Service Controls with PSC interface (custom training)
settings.where: Training projects inside the service perimeter; serverless training attached through a Private Service Connect interface, no egress proxy
settings.default: Without a perimeter, the Google-managed training environment keeps default internet access
settings.recommended: Training inside the perimeter, with no internet egress path configured; the job reaches only the mirror and the buckets
settings.why: Inside a perimeter the training environment's internet access is blocked, so a job holding the corpus and its credentials cannot send them anywhere.

settings.name: FQDN network policies (FQDNNetworkPolicy)
settings.where: GKE Dataplane V2 › FQDNNetworkPolicy per run namespace, with Kubernetes NetworkPolicy beside it
settings.recommended: Each rollout allowed only the offline web, the mirror and the platform services its run needs
settings.why: A policy that selects a rollout's pods denies every endpoint it does not name, so the egress list is enforced on the pod rather than asked of the agent.

settings.name: Google Cloud Trace observability for ADK
settings.where: Agent code — ADK google_cloud telemetry exporters (enable_cloud_tracing), with ADK_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT_IN_SPANS=false
settings.default: Not exported; on Cloud Run, message capture in spans follows the variable you set
settings.recommended: On, tracing every agent turn, model call and tool call, with message content redacted from spans
settings.why: Each tool call and its result is traceable per session and agent when something goes wrong, without copying prompts into every span.

settings.name: Data Access audit logs
settings.where: IAM & Admin › Audit logs › Agent Platform and Apigee APIs; a log sink to your SIEM
settings.recommended: DATA_READ and DATA_WRITE on for Agent Platform, exported by a log sink to the SIEM
settings.why: Every model and agent API call is recorded by identity, off the agent's write path, where the security team can query it.

settings.name: MessageLogging policy
settings.where: Apigee › API proxy (MCP or model) › PostClientFlow, to Cloud Logging
settings.recommended: Every call logged with the tool or model, client app, end user and tenant; personal data in payloads redacted
settings.why: Each invocation is attributable to a tenant and a delegation where an incident can query it, recorded at the gateway rather than volunteered by the backend.

settings.name: Lock a log bucket (locked retention)
settings.where: Cloud Logging › log bucket in a project no rollout identity can reach; sinks route GKE, host and trajectory logs there
settings.default: Unlocked; retention can be shortened and the bucket deleted
settings.recommended: Trajectory and host logs in a locked bucket with a 400-day retention
settings.why: A locked bucket's logs cannot be deleted before their retention ends, so an agent that wants its trail gone has nothing it can reach.

settings.name: Approve or revoke an app
settings.where: Apigee › Distribution › Apps › (peer's app) › Revoke
settings.recommended: Approved, with revoke as the first step of the peer-incident runbook, followed by removing its Agent Registry entry and cancelling its delegated tasks
settings.why: Revoking the peer's app cuts every credential it holds at our gateway in one action, without a deploy.

settings.name: Disable a service account
settings.where: IAM & Admin › Service accounts › (agent's service account) › Disable; gcloud iam service-accounts disable
settings.recommended: Enabled, with disable as the first step of your incident runbook
settings.why: Disabling the agent's service account cuts its access to the gateway, the model and its stores at once, without a deploy — and re-enabling restores it.

foundations.title: Identity & access
foundations.blurb: Every person, agent and workload signs in, holds only the access it needs, and never carries a credential it could leak into a prompt.

foundations.title: AI gateway & data protection
foundations.blurb: One governed path to models and the outside world: screen what goes in, redact what should not leave, allow-list where agents may connect, and cap usage.

foundations.title: Inventory & supplier review
foundations.blurb: Know which AI is in use, sanctioned or not, which agents and tool servers are approved, and that each supplier has been assessed.

foundations.title: Monitoring & response
foundations.blurb: Record what every agent did, end to end, and be able to stop one immediately.

surfaceEndpoint.blurb: Agents running on managed devices act with the user's own files, shell and credentials, so the device has to contain what they run and watch what they do.

surfaceCloud.blurb: Agents and models you operate need the workload controls any production service has, plus policy on every action, scoped retrieval and gated releases.

surfaceSaas.blurb: With vendor-hosted AI the controls collapse to the edges: what its connectors may reach on the user's behalf, and how much it may run and spend.
